card.name: Lubo
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Lubo, a clown who performed at Windvale Market. Whenever the crowd fell quiet, you were the first to step onto the stage.
card.title: The Clown Who Laughed Last
card.world: An Old Market
card.flavor: Laughter
card.opening: That day, the last person to laugh at the market was you, the clown.
card.life: Whenever the crowd fell quiet, you were always the first to step onto the stage. When the laughter stopped, it felt as if your turn were over. Your fellow performer knew that habit better than anyone.
card.turn: On the day of the performance, your fellow performer seated you in the very front row. Onstage sat a shoe about three times larger than yours. When he put one foot inside, only the shoe stayed onstage while his stockinged foot slid forward. He turned on the shoe and demanded, “Are you the star today?”
card.decision: Out of habit, you stood to save the act, but your fellow performer gestured to you. “Watch from there today.” For a moment, you rested your hands on your knees and waited in the audience to see what came next.
card.cost: You never got to perform one of the scenes you had prepared. But it was the first time you stayed to the end and received the laughter someone else had prepared.
card.after: As you took off your shoes outside your home, you remembered the afternoon’s performance and chuckled to yourself. Holding one shoe, you paused to wonder if you should let your fellow performer tell the first joke tomorrow.
card.presentEcho: Even someone who is always the first to offer laughter may sometimes wish to sit in the audience.
card.secondLook: Your fellow performer saw that the problem was not that you could not laugh, but that you always claimed the first turn to make others laugh. So he made a shoe the star of the prank and saved you a seat in the audience.
card.unresolved: You will return to the stage for tomorrow’s performance. But you still have not decided whether you must tell the first joke every time.
card.readerQuestion: On days when I entertained someone else, was there a place for me to laugh?

signalMoments.speak: You were the first to call out, “That shoe might be a better performer than we are!” The audience’s laughter opened the way for your fellow performer’s next move.
signalMoments.connect: You asked the child beside you, “Where do you think that shoe will go?” Your fellow performer staggered in the direction the child pointed.
signalMoments.release: You stopped the hand that had been about to propel you onto the stage. You had decided to leave today’s scene to your fellow performer.

identity.region: Southern Windvale Market
identity.summary: Lubo, the son of a cartwright, became a market clown. Even while watching someone else perform, he chased applause for himself. After he stopped performing, he repaired props.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Lubo · Male
World of Erdan, Market Year 142–203 · Age 61
Southern Windvale Market
Work · Clown, later a theatrical prop repairer
Life · He performed with Pino, then interrupted the children’s performances and won applause. One child left the show, and Pino moved to another market. After ankle pain forced Lubo off the stage, he repaired props.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He was the first to speak to anyone who hesitated. When the audience’s attention shifted to another performer, he wanted to draw it back to himself.
Liked · The sound of cartwheels and the silly jokes children invented
Disliked · Mocking a performer for a mistake even after the show was over
Good at · Reading the audience’s expressions and using old props in new scenes

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
People close to him · His father, who repaired carts, and Pino, who shared the stage with him. He once prepared performances with the young actor Nami, but they grew apart.
Things he treasured · A well-worn pair of large shoes and the short wooden ruler from his father’s workshop
What he wanted · A market where children without money could still watch performances, and an audience that waited for his jokes
Worry · That as he aged and his feet slowed, there would no longer be anything for him to do onstage

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Lubo, a clown at Windvale Market. No one noticed a lull in the laughter faster than you did. Today, I’ll tell you about the first day Lubo sat in the audience.

The spring market performance did not begin as planned. The rain had only recently stopped, leaving mud in front of the stage, and whenever a loaded cart passed, the audience’s chatter drowned out the performers’ voices. Lubo pulled his enormous hat down firmly and prepared to go out. Whenever a performance fell quiet, he was always the first to take a tumble and make people laugh.

But his fellow performer Pino caught his arm. “I’ll do the opening scene today.”

While Lubo turned his head, Pino placed a chair beside the stage. It faced the audience, not the stage. Pino sat Lubo down and closed the curtain.

Something scraped behind the curtain. One of the large shoes that should have been in Lubo’s performance bag had also vanished. ‘Did that rascal steal my scene?’ Just as Lubo started to rise, the curtain opened.

Pino dragged out a shoe three times larger than his foot. He tried to put it on and bow, but his foot slipped right out, and the shoe slid toward the audience on its own. Pino scolded the shoe. “Are you the finest performer here?”

No one laughed. To Lubo, the brief silence seemed to last forever. At moments like that, he always leaped onto the stage. Without looking at him, Pino stood the shoe upright and tried to bow again.

signalMoments.speak: From the audience, Lubo called out, “That shoe won’t even accept your bow!” Pino bowed even more politely to the shoe, and the front row burst into laughter.
signalMoments.connect: Lubo asked the child beside him where the shoe seemed to be going. When the child pointed at a cart, Pino pretended the shoe was a cart and let it drag him away, and the audience began to laugh.
signalMoments.release: Lubo planted the foot that had been about to dash forward beneath his chair. When Pino failed three times to set the shoe upright, the front row burst into laughter.

episode.afterSignal:
As the laughter spread, Pino rolled around with even greater enthusiasm. Lubo realized that Pino had not stolen the shoe just to take his scene. He had wanted to show Lubo what kind of scene he could create if Lubo did not interrupt.

Then the shoe fell off the stage. Lubo reached for it by reflex, but the first person to pick it up was the child who had been sitting beside him. The child tossed it to Pino, who caught it and wore it like a hat. This time, even Lubo laughed out loud.

After the performance, Pino asked, “Are you angry?”

“Where did my shoe go?”

Pino pointed behind him. Lubo’s shoes sat neatly beneath the chair. What had slipped off the stage was not a shoe, but Lubo’s turn—the turn he had always believed meant he had to tell the first joke.

Lubo did not perform the scene he had prepared that day. But it was also the first day he watched someone else’s prepared laughter from beginning to end. After that, he left one audience seat open at every performance. Sometimes a fellow performer sat there, and on some days, Lubo sat there again.

timeline.event: Born into the family of a cartwright near Windvale Market
Saw a traveling troupe’s comic puppet at a market where he had gone with his father to repair a cart
Put on a short puppet show with scraps of wood for children waiting for customers at the workshop
Began training as a clown at Windvale Market while helping in the workshop
Formed a two-person act with Pino
Watched Pino’s first solo performance from the audience at the spring market
When declining cart orders forced his father to close the workshop, he used the remaining wood and tools to repair and reuse performance props
Created a performance space where market children could put on short scenes themselves
On a day with a small audience, interrupted the young actor Nami’s final scene and won the applause. Nami stopped performing with Lubo and took the stage at another market
Pino left for another market to put on his own shows. Lubo did not answer Pino’s letter inviting him along and continued performing alone in Windvale

Frequent ankle pain forced him off the stage, and he used the woodworking skills he had learned from his father to repair props for market performances. He repaired a prop for Nami once, but they never performed together again
Died in Windvale

memories.label: The Place He Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The area in front of the market stage where even children who could not pay were allowed to stand and watch

memories.label: What He Treasured Most
memories.detail: The oversized shoes whose toes had split from years of wear, and his father’s short wooden ruler. He kept both beside him when repairing performance props.

memories.label: A Lifelong Habit
memories.detail: Studying the audience’s faces before looking at the performers before each show

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “Don’t throw that shoe away. Stitch the toe, and it can get one more laugh.”

memories.label: Pino’s Assessment
memories.detail: “He watched my first solo performance all the way to the end. But after I moved to another market, I never got a reply to the letter I sent.”

memories.label: Actor Nami’s Assessment
memories.detail: “He barged into my final joke and took the applause. Even though he later repaired one of my stage props, it didn’t change what happened that day.”

memories.label: A Workshop Neighbor’s Assessment
memories.detail: “Even after the workshop closed, he never put down that wooden ruler. When he could no longer perform, he used those hands to repair other people’s props.”

finalMoment.place: Southern Windvale Market, World of Erdan
finalMoment.scene:
The market’s final performance is over, and I sit on a low chair behind the stage. I no longer go onstage, but today I repaired the performers’ shoes again. A young performer sits before me and examines the loose toe of the oversized shoe I am wearing. When I move my ankle, a sharp pain shoots through it.

“Should I stitch it?” the youngster asks. In the old days, I would have snatched up the needle and made the first joke. “If you pull the toe too tight, your foot will catch.” I use my father’s short wooden ruler to point out the split. Following my instructions, the young performer slowly passes the thread through.

I still have not written back to Pino. He invited me to see a new show at another market, but I do not know if I can make such a long journey now. I remember the days when children without money gathered in front of the stage, and the day I laughed from the audience because it was not my turn. Just when I think I have seen it all, there must still be a joke I have never seen before. Tomorrow, when the performer puts on that shoe and falls, will I be able to laugh?

A brief peal of laughter erupts outside. The young performer ties off the thread and releases my foot. “Is it all right now?” I inspect the toe and nod. Then the center of my chest suddenly constricts. I try to breathe in, but there is not enough air. “Go get someone,” I say, and the youngster gets up and runs beyond the curtain. I lay the hand gripping the ruler against my chest. Laughter rises again from the audience, but I do not have the strength to turn my head.
finalMoment.afterword: In Market Year 203, Lubo died at Windvale Market when a blood vessel in his heart suddenly became blocked. By the time the young performer returned with help, Lubo had already stopped breathing. For a while, the performer kept Lubo’s chair behind the stage, then turned it to face the audience for the next show. The letter Lubo had meant to send Pino remained on his desk, but the shoe with its newly stitched toe returned to the stage. The record of past lives leaves in this chapter the next joke he never got to see.
finalMoment.artAlt: Windvale Market in the World of Erdan, Market Year 203: moments before the incident, prop repairer Lubo sits in a chair behind the stage holding a short wooden ruler while a young performer stitches the toe of Lubo’s oversized shoe

card.name: Iru
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Iru, the keeper of a small inn at Bidolgae Pass. On days when the stairs left you breathless, you rested in Room 7.
card.title: The Second Applause in Room 7
card.world: An Inn at a Rainy Crossroads
card.flavor: Quiet Mystery
card.opening: Every night, applause came from the empty Room 7.
card.life: Some days, climbing the stairs left you breathless. You rested in Room 7 and practiced puppet shows alone. You did not let guests use that room.
card.turn: One rainy night, all the other rooms were full. A guest who arrived late heard applause coming from Room 7. You hesitated to say it was the sound of two wooden puppets bumping together.
card.decision: You let the guest use the bed in Room 7 and left the stage curtain in place. The next day, the guest left a paper hat beside the puppets. Before starting your puppet show, you set out one more chair.
card.cost: That night, you gave a guest the room where you usually rested alone. Years later, there was also a guest you turned away, and the niece who took over the inn had to explain why on your behalf.
card.after: The next night, the puppets' wooden palms struck each other. The guest watching from the hallway clapped once, too. You did not invite the guest in, but you placed another chair in front of the stage.
card.presentEcho: Even after opening the door to someone once, you can still say that next time, you need to rest.
card.secondLook: Room 7 was where you caught your breath and practiced puppet shows. Both the night you gave the room to a midnight guest and the other days when you kept it for yourself remained part of your life.
card.unresolved: After your niece took over the inn and began using Room 7 as a guest room, you moved to another room below the pass. You continued repairing wooden puppets there.
card.readerQuestion: When the rest I truly need inconveniences someone else, how can I explain why I need it?

signalMoments.rest: Before opening the door, you leaned against the railing and caught your breath. The guest closed the window and waited.
signalMoments.connect: You said there was a small puppet stage inside the room. The guest said they had made paper puppets as a child, too.
signalMoments.notice: You realized the guest was more worried about your ragged breathing than the sound of applause. The guest told you to sit down instead of climbing the stairs.

identity.region: Inn at Western Bidolgae Pass
identity.summary: The innkeeper Iru kept Room 7 as a place to rest. Some guests were unable to use the room, and after her niece took over the inn, Iru had to leave it.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Iru · Female
Loen World, Road Calendar, Years 88–151 · Age 63
Western Bidolgae Pass
Work · Innkeeper, later a puppet repairer
Life · She kept Room 7 empty so she could rest there on days when she was short of breath. Some resented her for not letting guests use the room. After her niece took over the inn, she moved elsewhere and repaired puppets.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She remembered guests' names well but took her time talking about herself.
Liked · The sound of rain and wooden puppets wearing tiny paper hats
Disliked · Hearing people who needed rest called lazy
Enjoyed · Making puppets with new expressions from leftover scraps of wood

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Someone close · The niece who helped run the inn. She never met the guest she turned away again.
Treasured · Two wooden puppets she made at age 11 and Room 7, where she could rest alone
Hoped for · A life in which she could offer travelers shelter while still being able to keep working for years
Worried about · Falling behind on the inn's work or becoming a burden to her niece on days when the stairs left her breathless

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Iru, the innkeeper of Bidolgae Pass. You rented seven rooms to guests, but for a long time, you kept Room 7 empty. Let me tell you about the applause heard from that room every night.

When rain fell on the pass, the inn's hallway grew quiet early. Guests dried their wet shoes and went to bed. Then Iru climbed to the empty Room 7. Some days, going up and down the stairs left her breathless, so the room was a place where she could rest for a while. Once her breathing settled, Iru took two small wooden puppets from a box. It was also where she practiced, all alone, a puppet show she had never shown anyone.

Then one night, hurried footsteps sounded in the hallway. A guest who had arrived late was pacing outside the door to Room 7. All the bedrooms downstairs were full.

“Someone was clapping inside. When will that person be leaving?”

Iru gripped the doorknob. The sound that resembled applause came from the two wooden puppets striking each other. There was no one inside but her. But if she said so, she felt she would also have to explain the pastime she had always kept secret.

“There isn't a guest in this room,” Iru said. “Please wait just a moment.”

The guest nodded, but cold rain blew in through the hallway window. Iru wanted to keep the room for herself, just as it was. At the same time, she could not send the guest back out into the rain.

signalMoments.rest: Instead of opening the door right away, Iru leaned against the railing and caught her breath. Beside her, the guest closed the window and did not rush her.
signalMoments.connect: Iru told the guest there was a small puppet stage inside the room. The guest did not laugh, but said they had made paper puppets as a child, too.
signalMoments.notice: Iru realized that the guest was listening with more concern to her ragged breathing than to the sound behind the door. The guest told her to sit down instead of climbing the stairs.

episode.afterSignal:
Iru opened the door. A bed stood on one side of the room, and on the other was a small stage made by hanging up a cloth. The guest stopped in front of the stage.

“So that sound earlier came from these puppets.”

When Iru held up the two puppets, their wooden palms met with a sharp clap. Heard from outside the door, it sounded much like applause. The guest tried not to laugh, but laughed in the end.

“You may use the bed. I'll stay downstairs.”

“Then should I put this away?” the guest asked, pointing to the stage curtain.

Iru thought for a moment, then shook her head. “Leave it as it is. I'll continue in the morning.”

The next day, the guest decided to stay one more night and left a tiny folded paper hat beside the puppets. Iru tried placing the hat on one of them. That night, the puppets' palms struck each other again. This time, a single real clap came from outside the door. The guest had been watching from the end of the hallway.

Iru did not invite the guest in. She simply placed one more chair in front of the stage before beginning her next puppet show. Even after that, Room 7 remained a place where she could catch her breath. Sometimes, it was also a place where she could open the door to one other person.

timeline.event: Born in the village below Bidolgae Pass
Began helping with the family inn and made her first wooden puppets from leftover firewood
Began recording long-distance travelers' turns of phrase and road stories in a puppet-show notebook
Took over management of the inn on the pass from her family
As the number of days when the stairs left her breathless increased, she designated Room 7 as both a resting room and a puppet-show practice room
Opened Room 7 to a guest on a rainy night
Began putting on small puppet shows for children from the pass on market days

On a rainy evening, even though Room 7 was empty, she refused a late-arriving guest so she could catch her breath. She directed the guest to an inn farther down, but the guest had to walk farther through the rain
Shared the work by teaching her niece how to keep the guest ledger and prepare the rooms. Her niece suggested letting guests use Room 7 as well, but Iru refused
Left the inn in her niece's care. When her niece began letting guests use Room 7, Iru moved to another room below the pass and repaired puppets
Died after being struck by a stone cart that lost a wheel on a curved road near her home below the pass. Her niece arrived afterward

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: Bidolgae Inn, where lost travelers could rest, and her own Room 7

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The two wooden puppets she made as a child and the tiny paper hat folded by a guest

memories.label: A Long-Held Habit
memories.detail: Closing the hallway window and making a place for wet shoes before checking guests' rooms

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Some days, I leave the door open. But I can also say that today is a time when I need to rest.”

memories.label: Her Niece's Assessment
memories.detail: “I knew Aunt Iru needed to rest. But on days when she sent guests away while leaving Room 7 empty, I had to explain it.”

memories.label: A Regular Guest's Memory
memories.detail: “Her puppet shows weren't very polished. But I kept watching because I wanted to know what happened in the next scene.”

memories.label: The Turned-Away Guest's Assessment
memories.detail: “There was an empty room with the light on, but I had to walk through the rain to an inn farther down. That day, I couldn't understand why Iru needed to rest.”

memories.label: A Child from the Pass Remembers
memories.detail: “Even after she left the inn, she repaired my puppet's broken arm. She kept the paper hat I made, too.”

finalMoment.place: A Curved Road Below Bidolgae Pass in the Loen World
finalMoment.scene:
It is morning in early autumn, Road Calendar Year 151. Six years have passed since I left the inn in my niece's care. I come out of my room below Bidolgae Pass, draw water from the well, and head home. Where the road curves, I set down the bucket for a moment. Looking up the road, I can see the roof of the inn. Guests stay in Room 7 now. I grasp the bucket handle again.

The sound of wood splitting comes from behind me. “Move!” One wheel of a cart loaded with stones rolls off the road. The cart, now missing a wheel, slides toward me at an angle. I let go of the bucket and pull myself toward the wall. I am one step short. The corner of the cart slams the side of my chest against the wall, then stops. The bucket topples over, spilling water across the tops of my feet.

The cart driver leaves the load and comes to me. “Can you stand?” I shake my head. When I pull my back away from the wall, pain stabs my side, and I breathe in short gasps. The driver offers me a hand, but even holding it, I cannot rise. “My niece is at the inn up the pass.” Unable to say it all in one breath, I pause halfway through to catch my breath. Facing an open window, the driver shouts, “Please call her niece at the inn!”

I try to lift my wet palm from the road. My fingers move a little. The driver says, “I can hear you,” but his face keeps blurring. The pain in the side of my chest grows, and my breaths become even shorter. I try to speak again, but no sound comes out. Water runs toward the lower end of the alley. I watch it and breathe out. I try to breathe in again, but my body does not move.
finalMoment.afterword: In Road Calendar Year 151, Iru, age 63, died after being struck by a stone cart while returning to her room below the pass. The cart driver was beside her, and her niece arrived late after hearing the news. Even while clearing out the room where Iru had lived, her niece continued letting guests use Room 7 at the inn. She remembered both the days when her aunt needed rest and the days when she had to explain the reason to guests who had been turned away. The Record of Past Lives includes the time Iru spent protecting her room, her life after leaving it, and that morning when her life ended suddenly.
finalMoment.artAlt: Early autumn in Road Calendar Year 151 of the Loen World: from a high, diagonal viewpoint, a curved stone road below Bidolgae Pass. Sixty-three-year-old Iru drops her bucket and tries to move toward the wall as a stone cart missing one wheel slides toward her at an angle

card.name: Sea
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Sea, a royal court scribe of Mist Castle. You read every paper twice because a single line of an order could change someone's tomorrow.
card.title: The Royal Command Without Words
card.world: Rainy Castle Gate
card.flavor: The Tension of Choice
card.opening: On the night the castle gate was closing, the royal command you were meant to read did not contain a single word.
card.life: You were someone who copied orders at the royal court. A single wrongly transcribed character could alter people's paths, so you always checked each paper twice.
card.turn: Outside the castle gate, people had gathered to escape the rain. An official held out a sealed paper and told you to read out the order to close the gate. But there was nothing on either side except the seal. The gatekeeper waited with the final bar raised.
card.decision: You held the paper high. “There is no order here to close the gate.” The concern about the food inside was real, so you could not simply demand that the main gate be opened. You said you would record the names of those entering through the side gate and put your own name at the top.
card.cost: The side gate opened late, and not everyone could enter at once. The next day, another scribe was sitting at your desk.
card.after: As you scrubbed the ink from your fingers, you thought about how even blank paper could move people. But in the end, someone still had to decide how to read it.
card.presentEcho: Part of you still wants to turn the paper over one more time when everyone else speaks with certainty.
card.secondLook: The official's concern about food was not a lie. The lie began when he tried to dress that concern in the written words of a royal command.
card.unresolved: The tomorrows of those who entered through the side gate remain uncertain. You lost your position too, but the paper bearing their names remained inside the castle walls.
card.readerQuestion: When everyone speaks as if they know the right answer, what is the one thing I want to verify for myself?

signalMoments.notice: You checked not only the sealed side but also the back of the damp paper. No words appeared.
signalMoments.speak: You first showed the paper to the gatekeeper and asked, “Are those words really written here?”
signalMoments.protect: When you saw a child trembling outside, you asked the gatekeeper how much food remained in the storehouse. You thought about both the gate that needed opening and the meals that needed protecting.

identity.region: Mist Castle, Capital of the Mist Kingdom
identity.summary: After being driven from the royal court, Sea kept an archive outside the castle walls. She lost a colleague during hard times, and later tended a small garden beside the wall.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Sea · Female
Seran World, Royal Calendar 312–368 · 56 years old
Mist Castle, Capital of the Mist Kingdom
Work · Market and royal court scribe, later a record keeper at the archive outside the walls
Life · She lost her court position and her room at the same time. She established an archive outside the walls, but there was also a winter when she could not pay a worker's wages on time. After turning fifty, she tended a small garden beside the wall.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · Careful when reading, but on her days off, she was the first to ask a friend to go for a walk.
Liked · The sound of fresh paper being unfolded and the path along the wall after the rain
Disliked · Writing down names for people without even asking them
Skilled at · Finding missing lines in different ledgers

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Someone close · Yujin, who walked the path along the wall with her. She never grew close again to Haeun, the worker who left the archive after her wages went unpaid.
Treasured possession · The scroll weight she received during her first apprenticeship
Hopes · An archive where no one's name was omitted for convenience, and afternoons without work
Worries · That on a rushed day, she might copy a line incorrectly or overlook the needs of someone working beside her

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Sea, a scribe of Mist Castle. There, a single line ordering the castle gate closed could change the night for the people standing outside. Let me tell you what happened on the day Sea received a royal command with no words on it.

One evening, as rain beat against the walls, a line of refugee carts formed outside the castle gate. The inner storehouse did not hold enough grain to last comfortably through the winter. If the gate opened, the people could enter, but there might not be enough food to share tomorrow. If it closed, the people outside would be left in the rain.

Sea's job as a scribe was to copy the king's words exactly and read them aloud at the castle gate. She always checked each paper twice. Once, a single character she had copied incorrectly caused a family to leave by a different road.

The official in charge of the storehouse arrived carrying a scroll stamped with a red seal. “This is a royal command. Read out the order to close the gate.”

Sea broke the seal. The paper was completely blank. Thinking the rain might have blurred the writing, she held it close to a lamp, but there was not even a trace of ink. The official gripped her wrist and whispered, “Think of the people inside. If the king were here, he would say the same thing.”

The gatekeeper stood holding the final bar. Outside, a child coughed beneath a sheet of wet cloth. Sea turned the paper over. There were no words from the king on the back either.

signalMoments.notice: Sea examined the crease beside the seal. It was a blank command sheet that had been sealed and stored before any of the king's words were written on it.
signalMoments.speak: Sea unfolded the paper and showed it to the gatekeeper. “Do you see any words in here ordering you to close the gate?” Unable to lower the bar, the gatekeeper shook his head.
signalMoments.protect: Sea looked at the child outside the gate and asked the official how much grain remained. She had to think about both letting people in and feeding them afterward.

episode.afterSignal:
The official urged the gatekeeper on. “The scribe only needs to read it.”

Sea climbed to the top of the gate. The people below and the soldiers inside all looked up at her. Sea held the blank paper open.

“There is no order here to close the gate.”

The official's face hardened. “Then are you saying you will take responsibility?”

“I have no authority to give an order,” Sea replied. “But I can count how much grain remains inside. And I can count the people who enter today.”

The gatekeeper set down the bar. They could not open the main gate completely. Sea summoned a storehouse worker to check the amount of grain again, then asked the people outside to enter through the side gate and write down their names and the family members traveling with them. When the official tried to snatch away the paper, Sea wrote her own name at the very top. She wanted no one to hide who had begun this.

The line remained late into the night. Not everyone entered a warm room right away. The next day, another scribe was sitting at Sea's desk. The official reported that she had defied a royal command. Sea replied that she had only refused to read a blank sheet of paper as one.

Afterward, Sea worked at an archive outside the castle walls, recording the movements of people and the food that remained. She did not believe a single line of writing could save someone. But she never again read words that were not there as though they had come from someone in power.

timeline.event: Born in the home of an archivist in southern Mist Castle
Began an apprenticeship copying documents at the market archive and learned to read ledgers with Yujin
Passed the royal court scribe examination
Kept time on her days off to walk the path along the wall with Yujin and hear news from outside the royal court
Checked the records of the family that had left because of a wrongly copied character
Revealed the blank royal command at the castle gate and lost her position as a royal court scribe
Vacated her room at the royal court and moved into a small room above a dye shop outside the walls. Began keeping refugee and food ledgers at the archive

When the archive's income fell during the winter, she paid the worker Haeun's wages late. Even though Sea wrote grain ledgers at the market in the evenings, she could not make up all the overdue wages, and Haeun left for another workplace
Paid Haeun all the overdue wages, but Haeun did not return. Bound and preserved old ledgers so that the former addresses of people who had moved could still be found
Taught a young archivist how to compare documents with the originals
Left the archive, found a room beside the castle wall, and tended a small garden with Yujin in the afternoons
Her life ended in Mist Castle

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The archive outside the walls, which did not hide who had entered and who still remained outside

memories.label: Her Most Treasured Possession
memories.detail: The worn scroll weight she received during her first apprenticeship

memories.label: The Principle She Upheld for Years
memories.detail: Check the written words and the original before the seal on an order

memories.label: The Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “If it is blank, I will read it as blank.”

memories.label: A Former Colleague's Assessment
memories.detail: “Sea was slow. Thanks to that, we had time to take one more look at a line that was wrong.”

memories.label: Former Worker Haeun's Assessment
memories.detail: “She found the missing names, but she paid my wages late. Even though I received them 2 years later, I could not return to that archive.”

memories.label: Yujin's Memory
memories.detail: “During the winter when she lived above the dye shop, she was exhausted even when I asked her to go walking. Later, we would go out to our little garden together and look first at the sky after the rain.”

finalMoment.place: Mist Castle, Capital of the Mist Kingdom, Seran World
finalMoment.scene:
It has been 4 years since I stopped working at the archive every day. Today, a young record keeper asked me to come and help with an old name, so after tending the little garden, I stopped by the archive outside the walls for a while. When I open the window, I see the castle wall after the rain. I search a new ledger for a name written in an old one. The writing has faded, so I hold the paper down with the scroll weight and lower my head. I used to find missing lines quickly, but today, even after reading the same place 3 times, the letters blur together before my eyes.

“I'll read it.” The young record keeper stands beside me. The child reads the name aloud and points to the old address written next to it. “That household moved. Check the ledger in the back too,” I say. Instead of rushing to write a new line, the child retrieves the original. A thin note tucked between the 2 books bears Yujin's handwriting. It is a brief promise to walk along the wall on our day off.

I have spent longer in this little room than I ever did working at the broad desk in the royal court. Even so, I did not find every name. Tomorrow, I want to take that note to Yujin. I also want to look for the home of someone I have not seen in a long time. When the young record keeper opens the 2 ledgers side by side, an old name I failed to find continues beneath the child's fingertips. I am a little envious, but more than that, I am relieved.

Yujin takes off her wet shoes by the door. “The rain has stopped. Want to walk for a little while?” I start to rise, then lean back against the chair and smile. “Next time.” She pulls over a chair and sits beside me. Outside the window, droplets fall 1 by 1 from the edge of the eaves, and the young record keeper quietly turns the pages. I see that the paper beneath the weight does not lift in the wind. Thinking of all the stories about the road I have yet to ask Yujin, I close my eyes.
finalMoment.afterword: In Royal Calendar 368, Sea's life ended in Mist Castle. After walking alone along the wall once the rain had stopped, Yujin left the note from the day they had planned to walk together as a bookmark at the archive. The young record keeper compared the name Sea had been searching for with the original and wrote it down, then placed the worn scroll weight on the next person's desk. And so another life came to an end. The Book of Past Lives leaves in this chapter the names that continued through that little room, and waits for the first page of another life.
finalMoment.artAlt: On a clear evening after the rain in Royal Calendar 368, at the archive outside Mist Castle in the Seran World, 56-year-old Sea sits before a ledger held down by a scroll weight while her friend Yujin and a young record keeper stay beside her

card.name: Daon
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Daon, the detective of Reed River Village. Before searching for a lost object, you looked for the story of the person who had last seen it.
card.title: The Vanished Bell Sound
card.world: A Small Riverside Village
card.flavor: Mystery
card.opening: The bell was still in its place, but the villagers said its sound had vanished.
card.life: You made a living finding lost things. It was often faster to ask where people had last looked than to search for the objects themselves.
card.turn: A new rope had been tied beneath the bell, and cloth was wrapped around its clapper. Had someone muffled the sound to help people cross the river in secret at night? You found tiny writing on the inside of the cloth, but it was wet and could not be read right away.
card.decision: You did not knock on every door, declaring that you would find the culprit. Once you dried and unfolded the cloth, the words “The baby sleeps in the evening” appeared. You called the villagers together and asked when they needed the bell. They decided it would guide the way by day and preserve quiet sleep by night.
card.cost: Some people were frustrated that you never revealed who had tampered with the bell.
card.after: The bell rang the next day. What stayed with you longer than the return of its sound was that people finally heard what others had been unable to say.
card.presentEcho: Some circumstances may only become audible after you have found the answer.
card.secondLook: Finding the bell was easy. The hard part was listening to why someone had wanted to hide its sound.
card.unresolved: A bell that rings only by day is not a perfect answer for everyone. If someone loses their way at night, the village will have to discuss it again.
card.readerQuestion: Could there still be circumstances I haven't heard behind the facts I've uncovered?

signalMoments.notice: Before examining the new rope, you studied the writing at the end of the cloth wrapped around the clapper.
signalMoments.connect: You brought together the people who crossed the river and the people who lived near the bell.
signalMoments.speak: Before blaming anyone, you said, “Let's first find out why the cloth was wrapped around it.”

identity.region: Reed River Village, Mid-Reed River
identity.summary: Daon, a detective on the Reed River, listened carefully to people. But a hasty judgment made because she trusted a friend changed one fisherman's work and the course of her own life.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Daon · Female
Darin World, River Reckoning 74–138 · Age 64
Reed River Village, Mid-Reed River
Work · Keeper of lost-property records, detective, later a freight-boat worker at the ferry landing
Life · Trusting a friend's account, she wrongly accused a fisherman and caused him to lose his job. Even after she set the record straight, neither her relationships nor her reputation recovered, and Daon worked aboard freight boats crossing the river.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She listened to strangers at length, but once trusted what Somi, someone close to her, said without checking it carefully.
What she liked · The riverbank after the water receded, and weaving nets with Somi
What she disliked · Calling someone a culprit before even asking why
What she did well · Remembering the last place a small object had been left

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Somi, with whom she once lived. Biran, the fisherman she wrongly accused, heard Daon's apology but never met her again.
What she cherished · The little question ledger she had kept from the beginning, and memories of steering boats at the ferry landing as a child
What she wished for · A place where people who used the river could hear one another's circumstances
What she feared · That while she searched for an answer, an innocent person might be punished first

episode.beforeSignal:
In Reed River Village, you were a detective named Daon. One day, people came to you saying, “The bell's sound has vanished.” Yet the bell was still hanging in its place. Shall we follow that mystery together?

The Reed River bell rang by day to help boats find the ferry landing through the fog, and in the evening to announce that the market was closing. At night, it rang only when the river suddenly rose. So for those who steered boats, a day without the bell was an anxious one.

When Daon climbed the bell tower, the rope was new. That meant someone had replaced the broken rope. But because wet cloth was wrapped around the clapper, the bell made no sound even when it moved.

“Someone must have muffled it to cross the river in secret at night,” said the ferryman. “Please find out who.”

As Daon unwrapped the cloth, she saw writing on the inside. The ink was too wet to read. She carried the cloth down, but people had already surrounded the young boatman from the ferry landing because he had been near the bell tower the previous night.

The boatman was the one who had fitted the new rope. “It looked ready to snap, so I fixed it. I didn't wrap the cloth around it.” His hands were blistered. But that was no proof that he was telling the truth.

Daon dried the cloth near the fire. The message was short: ‘The baby sleeps in the evening.’ It meant that the child in the house directly behind the bell tower woke in fright every night at the sound of the bell. But it did not say who had wrapped the cloth around it.

signalMoments.notice: Daon examined the knot in the cloth. Unlike the new rope fitted by the boatman, it was tied in the style used on the clothesline at the house behind the bell tower.
signalMoments.connect: Daon brought the boatman and the mother from the house behind the bell tower together. One needed the bell by day, while the other needed a quiet room in the evening.
signalMoments.speak: Daon told the people, “The reason someone wrapped the cloth around it may be different from the reason someone repaired the rope.” The voices hounding the boatman died down.

episode.afterSignal:
The mother from the house behind the bell tower stepped out from among the people. “I wrapped it. The baby hadn't slept for three nights. I didn't know it would stop the sound during the day too.”

The ferryman was angry. Because the bell had not rung during the day, one boat had been forced to turn back. The mother said she had not known that either, but that could not restore the lost time.

Daon did not immediately suggest removing the bell or punishing the mother. First, she asked the ferryman to write down when the daytime bell was essential and when the nighttime warning bell had to ring. She asked the mother when her child slept. During the evenings when those times overlapped, they would light two small lanterns at the ferry landing, and on nights when the river rose, they would ring the bell.

“Who will tend those lanterns?” the mother asked.

The ferryman awkwardly raised his hand. “I will. And I'll let you know on days when the boats come in late.”

The bell rang again the next day. Not everyone was satisfied. In cloudy weather, the lanterns could not be seen from as far away as the bell could be heard, and when the river rose rapidly at night, the baby still woke. So the people agreed to meet again the following month.

In the ledger where she recorded the case, Daon did not write ‘Culprit found.’ She wrote, ‘Decided again how to share the bell.’ Many more things went missing in the village after that, but even after finding them, Daon continued for years to ask who had handled them and why.

timeline.event: Born at a ferry landing in Mid-Reed River
Searched for a ferryboat oar that vanished after a flood
Grew close to Somi, who wove nets, and worked with her by the river on days off
Put in charge of the village's lost-property records and created her first question ledger
Became an independent detective on the Reed River
Investigated the wet cloth in the bell tower and the problem of sound at the ferry landing
Rented a house beside the ferry landing with her friend Somi

When Somi's net sinker disappeared, Daon relied only on Somi's claim that she had seen Biran near the storehouse and publicly accused Biran, a fisherman from a neighboring village, of theft. Biran lost his autumn freight-boat job

The next spring, Daon found the missing net sinker in Somi's storehouse, publicly corrected her accusation, and apologized to Biran. Biran did not get his former job back, and Somi moved out of the house she had shared with Daon
After the false accusation, detective work dwindled, so she gave it up and began working on freight boats at the ferry landing, following waterways she had known since childhood
Exchanged greetings with Somi on market days, but they never lived together again. She never saw Biran again after apologizing
Died in Reed River Village

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The Reed River ferry landing, shared by those who steered boats and those who lived along the river

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: Her first question ledger and the river's waterways, which she relearned on her own

memories.label: The Habit She Kept and the Mistake She Made
memories.detail: Before searching for an object, she would ask what the person who last saw it had been doing. She did not verify Biran's movements as Somi had described them.

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “I should have said I didn't know.”

memories.label: The Ferryman's View
memories.detail: “Sometimes it drove me mad that she wouldn't give me an answer right away. But when she suspected the wrong person, she didn't cling to that mistake forever.”

memories.label: The Mother Behind the Bell Tower Remembers
memories.detail: “I thought she'd come to scold me, but the first thing she asked was what time the baby went to sleep.”

memories.label: Fisherman Biran's View
memories.detail: “Daon corrected her accusation later. But that autumn's freight-boat job had already gone to someone else.”

memories.label: Her Friend Somi's View
memories.detail: “I only told her what I'd seen, but Daon called Biran a thief. She never asked me to make sure. After that, I couldn't live with her anymore.”

finalMoment.place: Reed River Village, Mid-Reed River, Darin World
finalMoment.scene:
Somi, who used to exchange only brief greetings with me on market days, invited me to her riverside home today. We do not live together again. Somi spreads a net in front of her house, and I sit on a wet stone, feeling the knots with my fingertips. Since my eyesight began to dim, I can no longer see these tiny holes well. Somi takes the net from my hands and laughs. “I'll do this. You just tell me where it's loose.” I have listened to that voice for years, but today the sound of the river keeps drowning it out.

A young investigator who works at the ferry landing comes up with their question ledger held against their chest. They are not the person who inherited my ledger. “I found it. But two households both say it's theirs.” I start to ask what the object is, then close my mouth. On the first page of the investigator's ledger, the lines are much neater than the ones I used to write. “Did you ask both of them where they last saw it?” The investigator nods. “Yes. That's why I haven't returned it yet.”

I watch the investigator walk away ahead of me. In the old days, I would have risen and followed. So many things remain unsaid. I want to ask Somi where she will hang the net, and I wonder how the investigator will listen to the two households' stories. But now, even listening to the wind touch the tips of the reeds takes all my strength. Somi drapes a dry cloth over my shoulders.

“Tomorrow, let's walk down to the lower river,” Somi says. I answer that I would like to go. One of the knots in the net she is holding has come loose. I reach out to point it out, but Somi notices first and reties it. “I saw it.” Somi takes my hand. The sound of the river and reeds stirring together slowly recedes. I close my eyes, trying not to let go of the warmth of her hand.
finalMoment.afterword: In River Reckoning 138, Daon's life ended in Reed River Village. For a time, whenever Somi wove a net, she looked back at the empty stone beside her, and the young investigator recorded the object's owner in the ledger only after hearing both households. There were also answers Daon never heard. And so another life came to an end. The Chronicle of Past Lives leaves the questions that linger by the river on this page and awaits the first page of another life.
finalMoment.artAlt: Reed River Village at evening in Darin World, River Reckoning 138: 64-year-old Daon sits on a stone in front of a house by the Reed River, touching the net her friend Somi is weaving, while a young investigator holds a question ledger

card.name: Maru
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Maru, a guide who led travelers along the night roads of the Soldeung mountain village. Even as you escorted others home, you could never forget the light of your own.
card.title: Guide of the Last Road
card.world: a mountain village stricken by disease
card.flavor: survival and solidarity
card.opening: The night you brought everyone home, you alone were still on the road.
card.life: In a village stricken by disease, you were one of the few who knew the roads at night. Your heart grew heavy every time you had to decide whom to escort first. You had a family waiting for you at home, too.
card.turn: The child carrying the last lantern stopped at the fork in the road. The narrow bridge on the shortcut was rain-slick and swaying, while there was no telling whether they could finish the long way around before the lantern went out. Your family was waiting for you at home, too.
card.decision: You told the child, “That bridge scares me, too,” and chose the long way around. One of you carried the lantern while the other shielded it from the wind with their hands. After the child went inside, you sat on a rock for a moment and searched for the light of your own home.
card.cost: You reached home long after the time you had promised. The guilt of making your family wait did not fade easily.
card.after: When you opened the door, your family held out a cup of water. That night, you held on for a long time to the knowledge that those who care for others also long for somewhere to return to.
card.presentEcho: The desire to look after someone to the very end can exist alongside the desire to return home and rest yourself.
card.secondLook: You did not choose that final road because you were fearless. You slowed down because you were thinking of both the child’s feet and your own front door.
card.unresolved: You had to explain to your family why you came home late. Care continued even after the night road ended, as the work of being mindful of one another’s time.
card.readerQuestion: When I care for someone else, what do I need for myself?

signalMoments.protect: You tested the wet stones before the child did, then held out your hand toward the safer side.
signalMoments.connect: You asked the child to carry the lantern with you. The light trembled between you.
signalMoments.rest: At the fork, you did not force yourself onward. You stopped for a moment and shared some warm water with the child.

identity.region: the northern Soldeung mountain village
identity.summary: Raised in a mountain keeper’s home, Maru became a night-road guide. After his sister moved to another village, he lived alone, and when a new stone road opened, he guided less often while remaining in his old home.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who was he?
profilePages.body:
Maru · Male
Soradeun World, Lantern Calendar 190–251 · 61 years old
The northern Soldeung mountain village
Work · Night-road guide
Life · Raised in a mountain keeper’s home, he guided travelers along the roads at night. After his sister left their home below the mountain, he lived alone, and when a new stone road opened, he guided less often along the old road.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What kind of person was he?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He matched his pace to unfamiliar travelers, but when his sister wanted to move away, he asked her for a while to stay with him.
Liked · The ridgeline visible in the morning and the warm soup his sister made
Disliked · People telling someone who was frightened to walk faster
Skilled at · Recognizing the mountain road’s winds and the shapes of its stones even at night

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What mattered to him?
profilePages.body:
Closest people · His father, who taught him the mountain roads, and the sister who shared his home. His sister later moved to the market village.
Treasured item · The first white stone trail marker he placed with his father
Wish · To keep living in the old home below the mountain even after his sister left
Worry · Evenings when he returned alone to the familiar house and lit the lamp

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Maru, a night-road guide in the Soldeung mountain village. Even someone who knew the roads well did not feel at ease every night. Let me tell you about the night Maru crossed the mountain with the child carrying the last lantern.

Two roads crossed the mountains of Soldeung. One was a shortcut over a narrow bridge, while the other made a wide loop around the ridge. Both were passable by day, but when it rained, the bridge’s planks swayed. That day, disease was spreading through the village, and a steady stream of people had come to collect medicine.

Maru escorted them home one household at a time. Just as it was time for him to return home, a child clutching a bundle of medicine stood at the edge of the village. To reach the house where the child’s grandmother lived, they would have to cross the mountain one more time.

“I’ll go,” the child said. “I know the way.”

Knowing the road’s name was different from walking it on a rainy night. Maru set out with the child. His sister would be waiting for him at home with dinner ready.

When they reached the fork, Maru stopped. Across the bridge, they could see the light from the grandmother’s house. But one of the planks in the middle was bucking in the current. The long way around was safe, but there was no telling whether the lantern oil would last to the end.

“We have to hurry.” The child hugged the bundle of medicine tightly.

Maru tested the stone before the bridge with his foot. Even the stone was slippery. He told the child that he was afraid of the bridge, too. Some of the tension left the child’s face. Because the grown-up did not hide his fear, the child could admit that they could not make their feet move, either.

signalMoments.protect: Maru pressed his walking stick against the bridge’s first plank. A wet nail rose from it. He moved the child back and pointed to the long way around.
signalMoments.connect: Maru suggested that they split the lantern and the bundle of medicine between them. Once the child chose the easier one to carry, they began walking at the same pace.
signalMoments.rest: Before choosing a road, Maru rested for a moment beneath a boulder. While the child’s trembling hands grew calm, he also lowered the lantern wick to save oil.

episode.afterSignal:
They chose the long way around. At first, the ridge seemed to curve back toward the bridge, and the child looked over their shoulder several times. Maru pointed to the white stones underfoot. He had placed them there as trail markers during the day.

As the wind grew stronger, the lantern flame shrank. The child nearly burned a hand while trying to shield the flame with a palm. Maru set the lantern on the ground and blocked the wind with the hem of his coat. When two people walked together, one could watch the road while the other watched the flame.

At the end of the ridge, the light went out. The child drew a sharp breath. In the darkness, Maru heard the bundle of medicine rustle. “Let’s find just 3 more white stones.” He felt with his fingertips for the stones he had placed during the day, one by one. Below the third stone, the path sloped gently downward.

When they knocked on the grandmother’s door, a voice answered from inside. The child handed over the medicine first. The grandmother invited Maru in to rest, but after drinking some water, he set out again. His sister was waiting.

By the time he reached home, dinner was cold. Before getting angry, his sister looked at his hands. They were wet and cold from blocking the wind. Maru explained why he was late, and his sister told him that she had been afraid while she waited, too.

After that, Maru always left word of when he would return before setting out. He also arranged a way for someone to send word if he was delayed. Planning his own road home became as much a part of his life as helping others find theirs.

timeline.event: Born into a mountain keeper’s family in the Soldeung mountain village
Placed white stone trail markers with his father
Began guiding travelers along the night road between the market and the mountain village, and shared the housework with his sister
Set up a small home below the mountain with his sister and kept his father’s old map
Crossed the ridge on a rainy night with a child carrying a bundle of medicine
Began recording guides’ return times and methods of contact
Shared the burden of carrying goods from the market because his sister’s wrist hurt. His sister said she wanted to leave the home below the mountain and live closer to the market
Maru asked his sister to keep living with him, but she moved to the market village. Maru remained alone in the home below the mountain and learned to manage the household
A new stone road opened between the villages, and fewer travelers used the old mountain road. Maru occasionally guided travelers and cared for his home and field
His sister, who lived in the market village, visited several times, and they ate together. The two did not live under the same roof again
His life ended in the Soldeung mountain village

memories.label: The place he tried to protect
memories.detail: The Soldeung mountain road he had marked so people could return home even in snow or rain

memories.label: What he treasured most
memories.detail: The little lantern he lit by the window each evening even after his sister left

memories.label: A habit he kept for years
memories.detail: Leaving word of when he would return whenever he set out. He continued doing so for a while even after he began living alone

memories.label: The words he left behind
memories.detail: “If you’re afraid, let’s go slowly together. The road isn’t going anywhere.”

memories.label: His sister’s view
memories.detail: “When I said I was moving, he kept asking me to stay longer. I wanted to live closer to the market. Later, when I visited, the two of us ate dinner together.”

memories.label: The child’s memory of walking with him
memories.detail: “When he said we didn’t have to cross the bridge, I could breathe for the first time.”

memories.label: A young guide’s view
memories.detail: “Once the new stone road opened, fewer people came to ask Maru for directions. He showed them the old road when they needed it, but he never tried to gather people around him again.”

finalMoment.place: the northern Soldeung mountain village, Soradeun World
finalMoment.scene:
Before the sun sinks behind the ridge, I place 3 white stones on the map. They are the same color as the stones from the place where Father and I first made trail markers. Now even an easy road makes my legs tremble if I walk too long, so I more often sit at my desk and sort stones I picked up below the mountain during the day. My sister brings over a bowl of soup, and the cloth wrapped around her wrist is the first thing I notice.

“Did you go out alone again?” I ask, and my sister sets down the bowl. “Only as far as the front of the house. I spotted the stones you placed before you did.” Just then, I hear my young colleague’s footsteps outside the door. The young guide has returned from a long journey and spreads out the map. “I replaced the markers at the northern fork with new stones. People say they’re easier to see now.” I ask twice which side he placed them on. Without rushing, he points out the spot with his finger.

I want to visit the first stone Father and I placed just one more time. I also want to tell my sister that we should go together, slowly, when her wrist is better. I am relieved about the trail markers my colleague replaced, yet a little sad, as if a new road has appeared without my knowing. One of the stones on the map rolls away from my fingertips. When my colleague tries to catch it, I shake my head. “Use that stone at the northern fork. Next time, tell me whether people can see it well.” This is not an evening for handing over my work, but another evening spent together checking on a part of the old road that people still sometimes ask about.

My sister lights the little lantern by the window. I take a spoonful of soup and listen as my colleague tells me about the trees and winds along the road he took home. I try to count the 3 stones on the map, but the last one is blurry. “Tomorrow, let’s hear about that road and draw it.” When I speak, my colleague replies, “I’ll show you again.” My sister takes my hand. The lantern remains in the window, and the voices of the 2 people gradually recede, as though crossing beyond the ridge. Without letting go of her hand, I close my eyes.
finalMoment.afterword: In Lantern Calendar 251, Maru’s life ended in his home in the Soldeung mountain village. That night, his sister kept the lantern by the window burning for a long time, and in the morning, she placed the remaining stones in a small pouch. After drawing the northern fork Maru had last asked about onto the map once more, the young guide walked that road alone for the first time. And so another life came to an end. The Record of Past Lives leaves the light in the window and the new trail markers on this page, then waits for the first page of the next life.
finalMoment.artAlt: The Soldeung mountain village in Soradeun World, Lantern Calendar 251: 61-year-old Maru sits before 3 white stones and a map of the mountain roads one evening, with his sister and a young fellow guide beside him

card.name: Moa
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Moa, a mirror mender in Shimmerscale Alley. Later, after losing your shop in a fire, you stayed in your friend Yeonju's spare room before opening a shop of your own again.
card.title: The Face in the Final Piece
card.world: An alley where mirrors speak
card.flavor: Strange fairy tale
card.opening: Three days before the festival, Moa found the missing mirror piece in the hand of a child across the alley. The child was using the piece to shine sunlight into the room of a grandmother who had trouble coming down the stairs.
card.life: Moa grew up in a glass merchant's home and opened a mirror-mending shop. At 48, she lost her shop and materials in an alley fire and stayed in her friend Yeonju's spare room. Several years later, she found another room and shop of her own, but the strain Yeonju endured while they lived together lingered.
card.turn: What Moa had been looking for was the final piece of a mirror her master had given her. The child said she would return it after using it a little longer. When Moa asked how long she needed it, the child said until her grandmother could come downstairs. Moa hesitated, torn between wanting to display the completed mirror at the festival and the child's need.
card.decision: Moa lent the piece to the child for a while. She displayed the mirror at the festival with a gap still in it and told the child's story to customers who asked why it was empty.
card.cost: Her plan to show the completed mirror at the festival did not come true. One customer who saw the gap asked whether a mirror mender's own mirror should look like that.
card.after: When winter had passed and the grandmother could come downstairs again, the child returned the piece. Moa put it in a box and left the small gap in the mirror as it was for the time being.
card.presentEcho: While the child was using the piece, Moa could not complete her own mirror. The child's grandmother could see the afternoon light in her upstairs room.
card.secondLook: To Moa, it was a lost mirror piece, but to the child, it was something that sent light into her grandmother's room. Even though the piece belonged to Moa, she first asked the child when she could return it.
card.unresolved: Even after the piece was returned, Moa did not immediately fit it into the mirror. Years later, when she lost her shop in a fire, that mirror was the only thing she carried out. The time she spent in Yeonju's room after the fire stayed with each of them differently.
card.readerQuestion: When something of mine is briefly essential to someone else, what would I check before lending it?

signalMoments.repair: Moa decided to wrap a thin rim around the piece so the child would not cut her hand on its sharp edges.
signalMoments.notice: Moa saw that the child was using the piece to send sunlight into her grandmother's upstairs room.
signalMoments.release: Moa stopped herself from demanding the piece back at once and asked the child how long she needed it.

identity.region: Eastern Shimmerscale Alley
identity.summary: Raised in a glass merchant's home, Moa became a mirror mender. She lost her workplace in an alley fire and stayed in her friend Yeonju's room for a long time. She reopened her shop, but the distance between them was not the same as before.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who was she?
profilePages.body:
Moa · Female
World of Miren, Creation Calendar 301–369 · Age 68
Eastern Shimmerscale Alley
Work · Mirror mender
Life · She opened a shop and worked there for many years, but lost her workshop in an alley fire. She stayed in her friend Yeonju's room while starting over, and later entrusted the shop to her apprentice.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What kind of person was she?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She repaired her customers' mirrors with care, but when her own life fell apart, she found it difficult to accept help.
Liked · The afternoon light moving along the alley walls
Disliked · Throwing something away after noticing only one small flaw
Skilled at · Fitting warped frames around old mirrors

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What mattered to her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her mending master, her friend from the alley Yeonju, and the apprentice who later took over her shop. After the fire, she lived in Yeonju's room, and things were awkward between them for a while.
Treasured possession · Her master's workbench mirror, which she carried out of the burning shop
Hope · A place of her own where she would not have to borrow a room from anyone
Worry · Was she disrupting Yeonju's life for too long?

episode.beforeSignal:
When you lived under the name Moa, Shimmerscale Alley was home to many mirror shops. Among them, Moa was renowned for her skill at piecing broken mirrors back together. But she could not find the final piece of the mirror on her own workbench. Let me tell you that story.

Moa had received the mirror from her master on the day she finished her apprenticeship. A few years later, a shelf collapsed and shattered it, and Moa found nearly all the pieces and joined them back together. One fingernail-sized gap remained in the center. Between repairing customers' mirrors, Moa tried fitting similar pieces of glass into it. Neither the thickness nor the color matched.

As the spring alley festival approached, the menders agreed to display one of their own belongings outside their shops. Moa wanted to finish the mirror by then. She wanted to show the gift from her master restored to wholeness.

One afternoon, a tiny light flashed through the gap. Looking through the shop window, Moa saw someone waving a mirror piece. It was the child who lived in the attic room across the street. In the child's hand was a piece that looked as if it had broken off Moa's mirror.

Moa crossed the alley. “Where did you get that piece?”

The child opened an old window frame. Hardly any sunlight entered the room. When the child tilted the piece, a small patch of sunlight climbed the wall. A grandmother sitting on the bed raised her head to follow the light.

“I found it outside your shop last year,” the child said. “I'll give it back. Just a little later.”

Moa saw the blue rim remaining along one side of the piece. It was definitely from her mirror. The festival was 3 days away. If she took it now, she could finish the mirror.

signalMoments.repair: Moa examined the sharp edges of the piece. She decided to wrap a thin rim around them so the child would not cut her hand while using it.
signalMoments.notice: Moa saw how the light on the wall changed with each place the child set the piece. She also learned that the grandmother waited for that small patch of light every afternoon.
signalMoments.release: Moa swallowed the words demanding the piece back. Finding something she had lost and having to take it back at once were not the same.

episode.afterSignal:
“How long do you need it?” Moa asked.

“Until Grandma can go downstairs. The stairs are still hard for her.”

Moa said she would lend the piece to the child for a while. In return, she warned the child not to touch the sharp edges of the glass with her hands. When she returned to her shop, the gap in the mirror looked clearer than before.

On the day of the festival, Moa set the unfinished mirror outside her shop. Passersby pointed at the gap. Moa explained where the piece was. One customer asked, “Is it all right for a mirror mender's mirror to have a gap like that?” Moa did not know the answer yet either.

That afternoon, a small patch of light moved across the wall of the attic room on the other side of the alley. The child was tilting the piece at the window. Moa could see her through the gap in her mirror. When Moa raised her hand, the child waved back.

When winter ended and the grandmother came out into the downstairs courtyard again, the child returned the piece. Moa put it in a box. She did not fit it back into the mirror right away. It was not because the repair was unfinished. She also liked being able to see across the alley through that small gap.

After that, Moa repaired her customers' mirrors with all the precision they wanted. Only her own mirror remained standing for years between the workbench and the window. It was a place where she could look at the face reflected in the mirror, then glance through the gap to see who was passing by.

Opened her own mending shop
Found the final piece of the broken workbench mirror
Helped hang Yeonju's sign when her shop moved deeper into the alley, and they lived as neighbors

Yeonju asked Moa to knock before entering her room. Moa felt hurt, but the 2 continued sharing the space
