memories.label: The place she tried to protect
memories.detail: The mending shop in Shimmerscale Alley, where people did not have to throw away things they had used for years

memories.label: Her most precious possession
memories.detail: Her master's workbench mirror, which she carried out of the burning shop

memories.label: A habit she kept for years
memories.detail: Before returning a mirror, she always asked the customer where they planned to place it

memories.label: Words she left behind
memories.detail: “Is it enough just to mend it straight? We should also see where it will be placed.”

memories.label: Her apprentice's view
memories.detail: “If even 1 piece was out of place, she started again. And after the fire, it took her a long time to reopen the shop.”

memories.label: The alley child's memory
memories.detail: “I thought she'd get angry when I asked to borrow the piece, but first she checked whether I'd hurt my hand.”

memories.label: Her friend Yeonju's view
memories.detail: “I gave her the spare room, but living together for several years wasn't easy. I even had to ask her to knock on my door. Now that we each have our own home, we can share dinner again.”

finalMoment.place: The stone steps outside Moa's home in Shimmerscale Alley, World of Miren
finalMoment.scene:
On an autumn evening in Creation Calendar 369, 68-year-old Moa leaves her friend Yeonju's home after dinner. The rain has just stopped, and the stone pavement of Shimmerscale Alley is still wet. Standing in her doorway, Yeonju watches Moa walk toward her small home across the alley. Moa stayed in Yeonju's spare room for years after the fire, but by now she has lived in her own room for about 15 years. “It's slippery by your door,” Yeonju says, and Moa turns and raises a hand.

Moa sets 1 foot on the low stone steps of her house and grasps the doorknob. Her foot slips on the wet stone. Her hand falls away from the knob, and her body tilts backward. Moa reaches out with her other hand to catch herself, but her head strikes the edge of a step before her arm reaches the ground. A dull sound echoes through the alley. From the doorway across the alley, Yeonju calls, “Moa!”

Moa opens her eyes as she lies on the stone pavement. She tries to raise her back, but her body will not obey. The back of her head hurts, and Yeonju's footsteps draw closer. Yeonju sits beside her and asks, “Can you hear me?” Moa opens her mouth to answer. Only a short breath comes out. Yeonju takes Moa's hand and calls her name again. She does not ask now about the shop story Moa had been about to tell, or the words left unsaid over dinner.

Moa moves her eyes, trying to see Yeonju's open door across the alley. The evening light is reflected in the wet stones. Her chest rises once in a shallow breath, then stops. Still holding Moa's hand, Yeonju searches her face. “Moa, look at me.” Moa can no longer meet her eyes or breathe. Both houses' doors remain open onto the alley.
finalMoment.afterword: Moa died at 68 in the autumn of Creation Calendar 369 after slipping on the wet stone steps outside her home in Shimmerscale Alley and striking her head. Yeonju saw the accident from the house across the alley and came to Moa's side, but she could not save her. The years Moa spent in Yeonju's spare room after the fire at age 48 still had not been easy for Yeonju. That was why the dinners they occasionally shared while living separately were precious too. The apprentice heard the news later and remembered the years in which her master lost her workplace and then reopened her shop. To the child who had borrowed the mirror piece, she was the person who first asked whether the child had cut her hand. The Record of Former Lives does not merge their memories into a single lesson. It simply tells us that Moa's life ended in the alley between 2 homes.
finalMoment.artAlt: Shimmerscale Alley in the World of Miren, seen from above the rooftops after an autumn rain in Creation Calendar 369. Moa, age 68, is climbing the wet stone steps of her home and grasping the doorknob, while Yeonju watches from the doorway of her separate home across the alley. The apprentice and the mirror are not visible

card.name: Ravi
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Ravi, the herbalist of Mistwood Village. Checking the mountain paths and waterways before it rained had become second nature to you.
card.title: The Secret of the Red Thread
card.world: A misty fairy-tale village
card.flavor: Fear and truth
card.opening: The morning red thread was tied to every door in the village, people called you a sorceress.
card.life: You lived in the mountains, tending medicinal herbs. Because you moved the herbs indoors before it rained, you often watched the sky and the waterways. The villagers found it strange that you knew the weather before anyone else.
card.turn: When people gathered in front of your house, rain began to pour. Water pooled first only at the doors marked with red thread. Then a frightened child's secret note found its way into your hand. Why had the child marked those doors?
card.decision: You did not drag the child into the open. The note read, “These houses have low thresholds. I wanted to warn them before it rained.” You tied the same thread to your own door and let people see the wet thresholds. The child came forward later and said they had marked the doors.
card.cost: Even after the misunderstanding was cleared up, not everyone immediately became friendly. At first, the child felt sorry for leaving you to face everyone alone.
card.after: The next time it rained, people placed sandbags at the doors with red thread first. You and the child helped them.
card.presentEcho: The desire to clear up a misunderstanding and the desire to protect someone first can arise on the same day.
card.secondLook: While no one knew why the child had tied the thread, people sought answers from the person they were used to suspecting. Revealing the truth was not the same as sacrificing the child.
card.unresolved: The way people saw you did not change all at once. You still do not know who will be the first to knock on your door when the next rain comes.
card.readerQuestion: When you want to clear up a misunderstanding, who do you also want to protect?

signalMoments.notice: You noticed that every house marked with thread had a low threshold.
signalMoments.protect: You folded the note with the child's name on it and put it in your pocket. You did not make the child face the crowd first.
signalMoments.speak: You told the people, “First, look at where the rainwater flows.” You still did not mention the child's name.

identity.region: Southern Slope of Mistwood Village
identity.summary: Raised in a farming family, Ravi learned about medicinal herbs and forest paths from her grandmother. After working for many years as the village herbalist, she left in her forties to learn pottery, then returned and built a different life.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Ravi · Female
Haron World, Forest Calendar 206–272 · 66 years old
Southern Slope of Mistwood Village
Work · Herbalist, later a potter
Life · She learned the forest paths from her grandmother and became an herbalist. In her forties, she learned pottery in a neighboring village, then returned home and made vessels in her house.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She took a second look at unfamiliar herbs, and even when leaving familiar work, she voiced her wishes after long hesitation.
Things she liked · Morning sunlight drying leaves, the first shoots in the fields, wet clay beneath her hands
Things she disliked · People immediately calling something they did not understand a spell
What she did well · Remembering where water had passed and how medicinal leaves had changed

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Those closest to her · Her grandmother, who taught her the forest paths, and Eunbi, her neighbor, who tended the fields with her. When Ravi left, she and Eunbi spoke less for a while.
Things she treasured · Her grandmother's hand-drawn map of the waterways and the first water bowl she fired
What she wanted · Time to leave behind the work she had done for years and learn something new
Worry · That Eunbi would have more farmwork while she was away

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Ravi, the herbalist of Mistwood Village. You studied the waterways on the ground before looking to the sky for rain. Let me tell you about the day red threads tied to the village doors put Ravi in a difficult situation.

Ravi's house stood at the edge of the forest. She dried the medicinal herbs she gathered in the mountains and brought the leaves indoors before heavy rain. The villagers said Ravi could predict the weather. Ravi answered with a smile, “I don't predict the rain. I look at the water left on the ground.”

One morning, after the mist had lingered for three days, red thread appeared tied to the doorknobs of several houses. A rumor made its way around the marketplace that misfortune would come only to the marked houses. Someone pointed at Ravi's house. They said that because she worked with medicinal herbs, she must have done something no one else knew about.

When Ravi reached the first house, water had pooled at the threshold. The second house was the same. These were low houses that would flood first when rainwater flowed down from the upper alley. Just as Ravi was about to say so, a child pressed a damp note into her hand and ran away.

‘The thresholds are low. I wanted to warn them before it rained.’

The child's name was written at the bottom of the note. The child had tied the threads to tell the adults to put up barriers ahead of time. But if Ravi called the child before the crowd, all the rumors might turn on the frightened child at once.

Then heavy rain began to fall. Water flowed into the lowest house marked with thread.

signalMoments.notice: Ravi felt the height of each marked threshold with her hand. Every one was lower than the road.
signalMoments.protect: Ravi folded the note with the child's name on it and tucked it inside her clothes. She decided to stop the water first and hear the child's story later.
signalMoments.speak: Ravi told the gathered villagers, “Tie a thread to my threshold too. Let's watch where the water comes from together.”

episode.afterSignal:
Ravi fetched empty sacks from the marketplace and filled them with soil. Several people followed, but others stood at a distance and watched to see what spell she would cast. Without a word, Ravi placed the wet sacks in front of the door.

The water flowed around the sacks and toward the neighboring house. Ravi quickly cleared the leaves blocking the drain between the two houses. Mud gushed up from beneath water that had looked clear. The villagers picked up shovels too. One by one, sacks were placed in front of the other doors marked with red thread.

As the rain eased, the child who had run away earlier came back. “I tied them,” the child said, standing beside Ravi. “Yesterday, I saw which houses flooded first. I couldn't say anything because I was afraid no one would believe me.”

The people looked at the child's feet. The child's shoes were caked with mud. The child had been going through the alleys all night. Ravi took out the note but covered the child's name with her hand. The child had already spoken for themself, so there was no need to show the name as well.

“Why didn't you tell us sooner?” someone asked Ravi.

“I only just found out too,” Ravi said. “Next time, let's knock on doors instead of tying thread.”

Not everyone immediately saw Ravi differently. When the next rain came, some still watched from a distance to see what she would do. Even so, they first placed sacks of soil in front of the doors marked with thread. Ravi carried those sacks with the child. Now there were two people who knew the waterways of Mistwood Village.

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The houses in the lower part of the village that flooded first when it rained. Before leaving that work, she explained the routes to the new herbalist.

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: Her grandmother's map of the waterways and the first vessel that did not leak after she reshaped it many times

memories.label: A Lifelong Habit
memories.detail: Filling the bottom of a vessel with water before firing it to check for leaks

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Sometimes I do miss the medicinal herbs. But I still wanted to go and learn about clay.”

memories.label: The Memory of the Child Who Tied the Red Thread
memories.detail: “She didn't reveal my name first. Instead, she carried sacks of soil with me.”

memories.label: A Villager's Account
memories.detail: “Whenever it rained, she came down first. We were surprised when she said she was leaving, but she taught the new herbalist the routes before she went.”

memories.label: Her Neighbor Eunbi's Memory
memories.detail: “When she said she was leaving, I worried that her share of the farmwork would fall to me. She found someone to replace her before she went, but I still lost a pair of hands that used to work beside me. After she returned, we each did our own work.”

finalMoment.place: Southern Slope of Mistwood Village, Haron World
finalMoment.scene:
As the morning sunlight touches the window frame, the drying leaves release a bitter scent. I reach to turn over a leaf, then stop my hand. I used to empty 3 baskets before the sun went down, but today even lifting my fingers is slow. On the table lies the map of the forest paths drawn by my grandmother. The edges of the paper are worn, but I can still see the small fork I added when I was 27.

The young herbalist sets a basket on the windowsill of the house where I make pottery. “Should I dry these leaves longer?” I look from the sunny side to the shaded side. “Try turning just 1 more leaf.” The herbalist feels the leaf, then moves the basket without my help. When I left my work as an herbalist at 43 and passed on the map, every missing path brought a question. Now the young herbalist marks new paths even I do not know. Eunbi sits beside me and holds down a corner of the map. “I can still make out the lines your grandmother drew.”

I want to go with Eunbi to see the first shoots in the fields. There is also 1 herb whose name I never got to ask my grandmother. I do not want to leave as if I were someone who had walked every path to its end. Holding Eunbi's hand, I watch the young herbalist set the basket outside the window. “What about the lower houses?” I ask, and Eunbi answers, “I stopped by today. Even without you, I know how to knock on doors.” I am glad to hear it, but also a little sad, as if my turn has grown smaller.

The young herbalist turns over the leaves in the sunlight once again. This time, my hands are not needed. With my fingertip, I trace the first line my grandmother drew on the map. “Walk that path in spring.” As my last words fade, Eunbi wraps her hand around mine. The rustling of the leaves and the voices of the 2 people slowly recede like the mist beyond the window. With the forest path I still want to walk held in my heart, I close my eyes without letting go of Eunbi's hand.
finalMoment.afterword: In Forest Calendar 272, Ravi's life ended in her home on the southern slope of Mistwood Village. Eunbi gathered the leaves that had been drying that day, and the next day, she went alone to see the first shoots in the field they had planned to visit together. Before marking a new path on the map drawn by Ravi's grandmother, the young herbalist first followed the old lines. And so another life came to an end. The Record of Past Lives leaves the scent of leaves by the window and the paths still unwalked on this page, then waits for the first page of another life.
finalMoment.artAlt: Mistwood Village in Haron World, Forest Calendar 272: on a morning in her 66th year, Ravi, who left her work as an herbalist to make clay vessels, sits before her grandmother's hand-drawn map, holding her neighbor Eunbi's hand as they examine leaves brought by the current herbalist

card.name: Or
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Or, a dream recorder who lived in the Library of the Sleeping Dragon. Each night, you copied into books the names the dragon called.
card.title: The Name Erased from the Dragon's Dream
card.world: Library of the Sleeping Dragon
card.flavor: Wondrous Mystery
card.opening: In an old library record, your name had been scraped away with the tip of a blade.
card.life: You recorded the names the sleeping dragon called in its dreams. But the book did not foretell the future. One rainy morning, while examining it with the bookbinder Raen, you saw that your name, which had been there since childhood, was gone.
card.turn: 10-year-old Nia confessed that she had erased the name. Her mother, the sluice keeper, had not returned all night, and Nia wanted to see whether someone could still return even if their name was gone. Just then, the warning bell rang. Rain-swollen water was surging toward the village.
card.decision: You went to the upstream sluice with Raen and Nia. While you pressed down on a piece of wood jammed in the frame, Raen pulled the chain and opened the gate. When you lost your footing, Nia's mother saved you.
card.cost: The paper Nia had scraped could not be restored to its original state. In the margin, you recorded even the date it was erased and the reason why.
card.after: On the morning Nia's mother returned, you also wrote down the words Nia had longed to hear while she waited. After that, you listened at length not only to the dragon's dreams but also to the stories of those who came to you.
card.presentEcho: Even when a name disappears from a record, the person can remain right before your eyes. Nia learned that after going with you to find her mother.
card.secondLook: Nia had not erased your name to hurt you. You saw the scrape marks and asked who had erased it and why, then went to the sluice before tending to the book.
card.unresolved: Years later, when you could no longer hear the dragon's dreams, you said you did not know why. After traveling with Raen, you returned to Eundeung alone, and the two of you exchanged letters.
card.readerQuestion: When the person before you is afraid, which would you do first: check the records, or act together with them?

signalMoments.notice: You saw that the water mark on the steps below the bell tower was two steps higher than it had been yesterday. You had to go to the sluice.
signalMoments.connect: You told Raen that you would be too late alone and asked her to come with you. Raen picked up a rope and led the way.
signalMoments.release: You closed the book containing the erased name. You would think about repairing it after you returned.

identity.region: Library of the Sleeping Dragon in Eundeung, a riverside village in northern Verun Kingdom
identity.summary: Or recorded the dragon's dreams, but left the library when she could no longer hear them. After traveling through other villages with Raen, she returned to Eundeung alone and lived there.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Or · Female
World of Riorn, Library Calendar, Years 218–281 · Age 63
Eundeung, a riverside village in northern Verun Kingdom
Work · Recorder of the sleeping dragon's dreams, later an itinerant book repairer
Life · She left the library when she could no longer hear the dragon's dreams. After traveling through several villages with Raen, she returned to Eundeung alone.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She spent long hours reading alone, but whenever someone spoke to her, she put down her pen first.
Liked · The scent of dry bookshelves and afternoon walks along the river
Disliked · Writing down words as though she had heard them when she had not
Good at · Writing clearly in tiny letters and binding old books

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Raen the bookbinder, and Nia, daughter of the sluice keeper
Treasured possession · The record notebook she first bound with Raen
Hope · To preserve a clear distinction between words she had heard and words she had not
Concern · People who decided for themselves why the dragon was silent

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were called Or. You were the person who wrote down the sleeping dragon's dreams in the library of Eundeung, a village in northern Verun Kingdom. Let me tell you about the day the rain had been falling for 3 days.

The dragon slept in a deep cavern beneath the library. In its sleep, it called people's names or murmured about landscapes it had seen long ago, and the recorder copied its words into books. Villagers often searched the books for the names of their family members, but whenever they came, Or explained.

“They're dreams the dragon had. This isn't a book of things that will happen in the future.”

Perhaps the person who most often needed to hear those words was Or herself. On the day she first met the dragon at age 9, it called the child's name in its sleep. The record of that day remained near the beginning of the book, and even after Or became the recorder, she sometimes opened to that page. She did so especially on days when she was about to begin something unfamiliar.

On the morning the rain had been falling for 3 days, Or opened to that page again. Then, for a long while, she could not lift her finger from it.

The name “Or,” which should have been there, had been erased. It was the exact spot she had seen time and again. The sentences before and after it remained unchanged, but the 2 characters that had spelled Or were gone.

“Can ink disappear on its own?”

Raen the bookbinder asked from the doorway. Instead of answering, Or carried the paper to the window. When she held it up to the light, she saw fine scrape marks where the 2 characters had been. Someone had scraped the ink away with the tip of a blade.

Then she heard small footsteps downstairs. A child of about 10 stood between the shelves, not even trying to hide her wet shoes. It was Nia, who had been coming to the library for the past few days to search for her mother's name.

“I erased it.”

Nia looked up at Or. Her face was frightened, but even more than that, it looked relieved.

“You're still here, ma'am.”

Only then did Or understand what the child had been trying to prove. Nia's mother had gone to work at the sluice upstream the previous night and had not returned. Because the dragon no longer called her mother's name, Nia had been afraid that her mother had become someone who did not exist in the book. So she erased Or's name. She wanted to see whether a person would remain even after their name disappeared.

Or crouched in front of the child.

“Nia, the book isn't the reason your mother hasn't come back. Let's first find out where she went.”

At that moment, the village warning bell rang. Or looked out the window. The water flowing below the bell tower was much faster and darker than usual. Because the upstream sluice had not opened, rainwater was surging toward the village. Nia's mother was the sluice keeper.

signalMoments.notice: Or examined the water marks left on the steps below the bell tower. The water had risen a full 2 steps higher than yesterday. They had to go to the sluice.
signalMoments.connect: Or told Raen that she would be too late alone and asked her to come. Instead of answering, Raen picked up a rope and led the way.
signalMoments.release: Or closed the book containing the erased name. She would think about repairing it after they returned.

episode.afterSignal:
Raen gathered a rope and a lantern. When the 3 of them reached the upstream sluice, the gate was stuck half open. The chain was caught in the frame, and Nia's mother was clinging to the railing to keep from being swept away by the current.

“Go back!” her mother shouted. “If the water rises this far, the road will be cut off!”

While Raen secured the rope, Or went down the narrow steps beside the sluice. She tried pulling the chain, but it did not move at all. A piece of wood submerged in the water was wedged into a gap. Or reached out. Cold water surged up to her elbow.

Nia shouted from above.

“I saw that earlier! I pushed it with a long pole, but it went in farther!”

Or stopped. It seemed that the more she pulled to remove the wood, the more firmly it lodged in the gap. Instead, she pressed its end downward. Raen pulled the chain. With the sound of the wood snapping, the gate shifted a little.

“One more time!”

Or pushed down on the wood, and when Raen pulled the chain, the sluice opened. The torrent changed direction and swept across the steps, and Or lost her footing. Nia's mother grabbed Or's wrist as she hung from the railing. The person Or had thought she was there to rescue now pulled her out of the water.

Around sunrise, the 4 of them returned to the library. Nia lowered her head before the erased page.

“Can you write it again?”

Or examined the scraped paper. She could probably put ink over it and write the name. But she could not restore the original record as if nothing had happened.

“I'll write that you erased it too. And why you did it.”

After a long while, Nia nodded. In the margin of the page, Or recorded the date and what had happened. Then she asked Nia.

“While you were waiting for your mother, what were the first words you wanted to hear her say?”

“...‘It's cold, so come here.’ She always says that.”

Or wrote those words down too. There was no way to know whose name the dragon would call that night. But the book now held a record of the person Nia had waited for and the morning that person returned.

Or continued to guard the library for a long time after that. She kept recording the names the dragon called in its dreams, but she also spent longer and longer closing the book and listening to the stories of those who came to her. Years later, when people remembered Or, they recalled how she listened to them until they had finished speaking before they remembered the names the dragon had called.

finalMoment.place: Or's house by the Eundeung river, Verun Kingdom, World of Riorn
finalMoment.scene:
On a winter evening in Library Calendar Year 281, 63-year-old Or sits on the threshold of her small house by the Eundeung river. It is the house where she has lived alone since parting from Raen and returning to Eundeung. She has had a fever for 3 days, and her coughing will not stop. Breathing feels even harder inside, so she has opened the door. A cold wind blows from the river, but Or does not have the strength to go back inside. A woman from the neighborhood comes to see her, carrying a covered bowl of warm porridge.

“Can you go inside?” the neighbor asks. Or shakes her head and asks her to place the bowl beside the door. As soon as she finishes speaking, she breaks into a coughing fit. Gripping the doorframe, Or bends forward for a while. The neighbor sets down the bowl and waits a short distance away. Even after the coughing subsides, Or's breaths remain short. She opens her mouth to draw in the cold air, but her chest cannot rise deeply.

The neighbor asks, “Should I call more people?” Or starts to answer, then pauses to catch her breath first. “Water first.” The neighbor hands her the cup of water beside the bowl. Or grips the cup with both hands but cannot lift it to her lips. The neighbor takes it and sets it on the threshold. Or looks at the river a few steps away. When she starts coughing again, her shoulders shake violently. This time, after breathing out, she cannot draw enough of the next breath in.

Calling Or's name, the neighbor sits close to her on the threshold. Or turns her head and tries to look at the woman's face. Her lips move, but no words come out. Her hand slips from the doorframe and falls into her lap. The neighbor takes Or's hand and keeps calling her name. Or draws 1 short breath, then her chest can no longer move. While the neighbor waits for an answer, evening lights come on one by one across the river.
finalMoment.afterword: Or died at age 63 in her own house by the Eundeung river during the winter of Library Calendar Year 281, unable to breathe after 3 days of fever and coughing. The name of her illness is unknown. On her final evening, the neighbor who had brought her porridge was by her side. Raen heard the news later at her shop in another village and came to Eundeung. She remembered both the long wait before Or finally left with her and the days when they lived in different houses but continued to exchange letters. Nia also remembered the day Or listened to her and went to find her mother. One villager who had demanded an explanation for the dragon's silence was left with the disappointment of never receiving an answer. The record of past lives does not merge these different memories into praise for a single person; it says that Or's life ended on that winter evening.
finalMoment.artAlt: The Eundeung river in the winter of Library Calendar Year 281 in the World of Riorn. 63-year-old Or sits on the threshold of her own small house, trying to catch her breath, while 1 female neighbor who brought a bowl of porridge watches from the road in the evening. Raen and the successor are not visible

card.name: Han-gyeol
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Han-gyeol, the communications archivist aboard the starship Yeoul, bound for a distant star. You were someone who never erased even the spaces where no reply had arrived.
card.title: The Reply That Never Came
card.world: A starship bound for a distant star
card.flavor: Solitude and Mystery
card.opening: You were an archivist who sorted replies that had not arrived, day after day.
card.life: The farther the starship traveled from Earth, the longer Earth's replies took to arrive. You never discarded a line just because its reception time was blank.
card.turn: One day, a silent signal appeared in one of the empty spaces. You thought it was a malfunction, but its intervals matched the rhythm of a song you had sent long ago. It was not a reply, but an old signal reflected back from outside the starship.
card.decision: You wrote “reflection of own transmitted signal” in the log. Your colleague was disappointed, but did not stop you from recording it. When you sent your sister the song again, including the wrong note, your colleague sang the next phrase beside you.
card.cost: It took several months for your sister to hear the new song. For a while, your colleague wanted to believe a reply had arrived, but you could not let yourself do that.
card.after: You left a blank space to wait in after you had already sent your words. A few years later, you taught young archivists to check transmission times first.
card.presentEcho: Even when it is not the answer you hoped for, you can distinguish the signal you actually heard from the words you wished to hear.
card.secondLook: What returned from the old relay was not your sister's reply, but the song you had sent. You recorded it only after comparing even the place where one note was off.
card.unresolved: Later, you included your colleague Jian's name in an error report, affecting Jian's application for a subsequent route assignment. Jian asked you to remove the name, but to the end, you believed your way of keeping records was right.
card.readerQuestion: When keeping an accurate record while publicly naming someone else, what should you ask first?

signalMoments.connect: You handed your colleague one side of the headset. Together you counted the beat, and you opened the transmission log again.
signalMoments.notice: You found the place where one note came late. It was the exact place where you had made a mistake in the song you sent.
signalMoments.speak: You told your colleague that you wished it were a reply, but could not confirm that yet, and brought up the old transmission record.

identity.summary: Raised on an inner-planet station, Han-gyeol became the Yeoul's communications archivist. He recorded an incorrect signal truthfully, but he also put his colleague's name in a public record, causing that person's next route application to be put on hold.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Han-gyeol, the Yeoul's communications archivist. Aboard a ship bound for a distant star, you were the one who waited for voices from Earth. Let me tell you about the day Han-gyeol heard a signal he wanted to believe was a reply.

A vast distance now separated the Yeoul from Earth. It took several months for words sent today to reach Earth and for a reply to make its way back. Han-gyeol never erased the blank spaces in the log where reception times were recorded. He needed to distinguish between days when no reply had come and days when no reply could possibly have arrived yet.

During the route's first year, he sent his sister a short song. If it was the song they used to sing long ago, she was the kind of person who would notice even a single wrong note. A reply arrived a few months later, but it said nothing about the song. Han-gyeol was a little hurt, but did not ask again.

One night, the receiver picked up a faint signal. It came not through the channel from Earth, but through an auxiliary channel outside the hull. There was no sound. Only intervals of short and long flashes remained. Han-gyeol was opening the log when his hand stopped. Those intervals matched the rhythm of the song he had sent his sister.

His colleague on duty looked at the screen and said, “Did it come back? Did she answer with a song this time?”

Han-gyeol wanted to believe that too. When he checked the transmission time, he found an old relay at a distance from which a signal could return through the auxiliary channel. The relay's surface could reflect signals. And it was not as though such a thing had never happened before. If it was only a reflection, there was no voice he had been hoping to hear.

signalMoments.connect: Han-gyeol called his colleague over and handed them one side of the headset. Together they counted the beat. His colleague rejoiced first, but Han-gyeol opened the transmission log again.
signalMoments.notice: Han-gyeol found the place where one note came later than the others. It was the exact place where he had made a mistake when sending the song.
signalMoments.speak: Han-gyeol told his colleague, “I wish it were a reply. But right now, I can't confirm that,” and brought the old transmission record up on the screen.

episode.afterSignal:
They placed the old transmission record and the new signal side by side. Even the point where a short note was off matched. What had struck the relay and returned was Han-gyeol's own song.

“Should we not tell anyone else?” his colleague asked. “We could let it be good news for a day.”

For a while, Han-gyeol stared at the reception window. If he wrote ‘reply from Earth’ in the log, someone would smile for a little while. But then the time when they should wait for the real reply would be recorded incorrectly too.

He wrote ‘reflection of own transmitted signal.’ His colleague looked disappointed, but did not take the pen away.

Han-gyeol switched on the transmitter. “I'm sending the song again. Last time, I got one note wrong.” When he hesitated, his colleague sang the next phrase beside him. Together they left a short greeting. It would take several more months for his sister to hear it.

A new blank space appeared in the log. This time, it was not blank because he had been unable to say anything. It was a place to wait after he had already sent a message.

Han-gyeol continued handling the Yeoul's communications for many years. On days without replies, he recorded that none had come, and on days when a real voice arrived from far away, he never missed it. A few years later, he taught young archivists to check transmission times before erasing blank spaces.

finalMoment.place: Entrance to the indoor garden on a Solar System Federation inner-planet station
finalMoment.scene:
During the station's artificial night in Route Calendar Year 126, seventy-two-year-old Han-gyeol heads toward the indoor garden with his younger sister. Nine years have passed since he left the Yeoul. His sister goes through the garden entrance first and points to a small tree inside. Han-gyeol follows behind. They have walked this path often, so the green light above the door looks as ordinary as ever.

The moment Han-gyeol steps onto the threshold, a short alarm sounds. The green light turns red, and the thick bulkheads on both sides begin to move. Han-gyeol tries to step back toward the corridor, but his foot catches on the threshold. “Back!” his sister shouts. As Han-gyeol braces a hand against the doorframe and turns, the bulkheads press into his chest and shoulder. The door normally stops when someone is in the way, but that day it does not.

His sister presses the emergency stop panel on the garden side. Han-gyeol also pulls the handle on the corridor side, but the door does not move. With his chest pinned, he cannot take a deep breath. “Han-gyeol, can you hear me?” his sister asks from beyond the door. Han-gyeol tries to answer, but only a short breath escapes. His sister presses the rescue call panel again and pounds the door with her palm. Han-gyeol's hand slips from the handle.

Station maintenance workers rush over and turn the manual mechanism. When the door opens, Han-gyeol cannot move his feet. His sister calls his name and sits near the threshold. Han-gyeol moves his eyes, trying to see the green leaves in the open garden. His compressed chest rises shallowly once, then stops. Even after the maintenance workers move him out through the door, Han-gyeol cannot breathe again. His sister stands beside the open door for a long time.
finalMoment.afterword: Han-gyeol died at age seventy-two in Route Calendar Year 126, when a malfunctioning automatic bulkhead crushed his chest at the entrance to an indoor garden on an inner-planet station. His younger sister tried to stop the door from inside and called for rescue, but could not save him. She remembered the ordinary evenings they had walked together and the songs they sang as children. She also knew Han-gyeol had worked hard to keep accurate records, but remembered how he always insisted he had been right to reveal Jian's name. Jian and Han-gyeol never became close again. His successor remembered him as the person who taught them to leave spaces with no reply untouched. The Record of Past Lives does not force these different memories into a single principle, but tells us that Han-gyeol's life ended on that garden threshold.
finalMoment.artAlt: A low, diagonal view of the entrance to an indoor garden on a Solar System Federation inner-planet station in Route Calendar Year 126. Seventy-two-year-old Han-gyeol is passing between the bulkheads when he sees the red warning light and puts a hand on the doorframe, while his adult younger sister, already inside the garden, looks back. There is no communications equipment or logbook

card.name: Iro
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Iro, a tent deliveryman on Daystar Planet, where night never came. You rented out tents that blocked the light so people could sleep.
card.title: The Hole-Pocked Shade
card.world: A planet where night never comes
card.flavor: Mischief from a strange world
card.opening: On a world where night never came, you delivered time for sleep.
card.life: Inside the thick tents you rented out, people could escape the sunlight and sleep. You never left even the smallest hole unmended. If light leaked in, it could disturb their sleep.
card.turn: The returned tent had seven holes in it. The child who had borrowed it had made them without permission. When you sat inside, seven dots of light appeared on the floor. The child had been trying to imitate the night sky from a book.
card.decision: You told the next customer, a courier, about the holes and the delay before anything else. Together, you checked the brightness and patched the four largest holes. For that day only, the courier accepted the three remaining specks of light.
card.cost: Because the tent was late, you refunded part of the courier's rental fee. Nor could you rent a tent with small lights left in it to every customer from then on.
card.after: You wrote “three small lights” in the ledger and began asking each new customer how bright they wanted their tent. You and the child made a separate star tent from leftover cloth.
card.presentEcho: Sadness that something you treasured has changed and delight in its new form can remain together.
card.secondLook: To the child, the stars were a gift, but to someone else, they were holes that could wake them. Instead of deciding that only one of them was right, you lay down inside the tent yourself.
card.unresolved: Years later, you lowered the rental fees without consulting Danbi. The customers got to rest, but the shared shop did not have enough money to buy new cloth, and Danbi opened her own shop so she could set the prices herself.
card.readerQuestion: When setting a price that is good for customers, what should you first ask the person who works with you?

signalMoments.repair: You put your needle to the largest hole first. The child held the other end of the thread, and together you checked each point of light.
signalMoments.rest: You lay beneath the tent with the child and closed your eyes. You tried to feel how much light shone through your eyelids.
signalMoments.release: You let go of the idea that you had to patch all seven holes. You decided to ask the next customer how much darkness they wanted first.

identity.region: Eastern Shade Village on Daystar Planet, where the sun never sets
identity.summary: Iro of Shade Village rented out sleeping tents. He lowered the prices so more neighbors could rest, but he decided what to do with his coworker Danbi's share without consulting her, and their rental business split apart.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who was he?
profilePages.body:
Iro · Male
Daystar Planet Settlement Calendar, Years 23–89 · Age 66
Eastern Shade Village
Work · Delivering and repairing sleeping tents
Life · He rented out tents with his neighbor Danbi, then lowered the prices on his own. Their customer numbers grew, but they did not have enough money to buy new cloth, so Danbi opened a separate shop.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What was he like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He quickly provided cloth to neighbors who were short on sleep, but he set prices without asking about the circumstances of Danbi, who worked with him.
Things he liked · Tea brewed by his neighbors, and making earthenware, which he began learning after retiring
Things he disliked · Telling people short on sleep that they were being oversensitive
What he did well · Finding tiny holes so old tents could be used again

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What mattered to him?
profilePages.body:
People close to him · His family, who taught him about tents when he was young, and his neighbor Danbi, with whom he rented out tents from the age of 32. He and Danbi later split up their business.
What he treasured · A panel from his family's tent, the first thing he ever patched
What he wished for · A village where even neighbors short on money could sleep in the shade
Worry · That raising the prices would leave some people unable to sleep

episode.beforeSignal:
In your life as Iro, night never came to your home. The villages of Daystar were always built on the side reached by the light, and people used thick tents to create darkness for sleep. Let me tell you about the day a star appeared in one of those tents.

Iro rented out shade tents, then patched even the smallest holes in the returned cloth before delivering it again. That was because leaking light could disturb people's sleep. Every customer also wanted a different depth of darkness. Some hated even the light through a crack in the door, while others wanted just enough brightness to see their hands.

One day, a returned tent had seven holes in it. A child from the household that had borrowed it had punched them personally, saying they had made the night sky from a book. The child was proud, but Iro's ledger said the tent was due to be rented to the next customer that afternoon. That customer was a courier who needed to sleep.

“Isn't it wonderful?” The child lay down beneath the tent. Seven bright dots appeared on the floor.

“It is. But this cloth doesn't belong only to you.”

The child bit their lip when they saw Iro preparing to patch every hole. They said it was the first time they had made the stars they had only ever seen in books appear above their own head. Iro also gazed up at the dots for a moment. On Daystar, no one had ever seen a real night sky. Even so, he could not use the next customer's sleep as an experiment.

signalMoments.repair: Iro put his needle to the largest hole first. The child held the other end of the thread. Together, they checked each hole to see how much the light diminished.
signalMoments.rest: Iro lay beneath the tent and closed his eyes. The child lay beside him. They decided to feel for themselves how much light shone through their eyelids.
signalMoments.release: Iro let go of the idea that he had to patch all seven holes. He decided to ask how much darkness the next customer wanted first, then determine what to do with the rest.

episode.afterSignal:
Iro went to the courier and told him the truth. He explained that the tent had been damaged and would arrive later than scheduled, then asked whether it would be all right to leave three small specks of light. The courier asked only to be shown how much light fell on the back of his hand.

The two lay down beneath the tent. Once the four large holes were patched, no bright dots could be seen with their eyes closed. The remaining three only reached the corners of the tent floor. The courier said that would be fine, but added that next time he wanted a completely dark tent.

After Iro finished mending the cloth, he carried it to the courier's house himself. He explained the reason for the delay and refunded a small part of the rental fee. The child followed and admitted to making the holes. The courier looked around the inside of the tent once, then smiled. “Tonight, I'll look at these stars for a little while before I sleep.”

The child's stars remained, but the tent could no longer be rented to everyone. Iro wrote “three small lights” in the ledger and drew a new space for customers to specify how bright they wanted the shade.

After that, whenever Iro delivered a tent, he asked first, “Would you prefer complete darkness, or would you like a little light?” He taught the child that if they wanted to change borrowed cloth, they first had to ask the person who lent it and the person who would use it next. The two of them also used scraps of leftover cloth to make a star tent of their own.

memories.label: What he treasured most

memories.label: A lifelong habit

memories.label: Words he left behind

memories.label: A regular courier's assessment
memories.detail: “When my tent was late, he gave me my money back. After Danbi opened her own shop, I had to find another place to rent tents.”

memories.label: His neighbor Danbi's assessment
memories.detail: “Some households slept because the price was low. But he shouldn't have made promises on his own with the money we needed to buy new cloth. I set the prices in my shop.”

memories.label: Workshop manager Moru's memory
memories.detail: “Whenever a pot leaned to one side, he laughed and worked on it again. He hardly ever talked about his tent work.”

finalMoment.place: The communal earthenware workshop in Eastern Shade Village on Daystar Planet
finalMoment.scene:
In Settlement Calendar Year 89, 66-year-old Iro fires earthenware at Shade Village's communal workshop. Six years have passed since he stopped repairing tents, and this is his fourth year learning pottery here. Moru, the workshop manager, is taking fired pottery to another house when he says, “Leave the door open when you finish washing the tools.” Iro points to a crooked cup he made with his own hands. “I'll try this one again next time.” Moru nearly closes the two doors that block out the sunlight and leaves.

Iro is left alone in the workshop. The fire continues to burn in the kiln, but the inside of the flue is blocked, and gases escaping from it accumulate in the room. Unaware of this, Iro puts his hands into a water bucket to wash off the clay. A little later, his head begins to ache, and he stops. He tries to move toward the sunlight coming through the crack in the door, but his legs feel heavy. “Moru?” he calls outside, but his voice is faint.

Iro grasps the corner of the workbench and stands. When nausea makes him bend over, the scrap of cloth in his hand falls into the water bucket. He thinks he only has to take a few steps to reach the door, but as he takes the first one, the pots before his eyes seem to overlap. He reaches out to put his hand on the workbench again but finds empty air. His knees strike the floor. After feeling the cold clay floor, Iro can no longer move.

When Moru returns, the workshop door is still closed. Moru opens the door and calls Iro's name. As he steps inside, he grows dizzy, flings the door wide open, and comes back outside. Moru asks a neighbor for help and calls Iro's name again. Iro does not open his eyes. The neighbor comes and carries him into the open air, but his chest no longer moves. Moru leaves the crooked cup Iro had been working on just as it was in the workshop.
finalMoment.afterword: Iro died at the age of 66 in Settlement Calendar Year 89 after inhaling combustion gases that accumulated in the communal workshop in Shade Village when the kiln's flue became blocked. Moru returned from outside and found him, then moved him with a neighbor's help, but they could not save him. Moru remembered Iro as he was learning to make earthenware, not as a tent worker. Danbi heard the news of Iro's death. The two had never reopened their shared shop, and Danbi had not forgotten the time she was angry with Iro for lowering the prices by himself. The households that could rest because the prices fell and the shared shop that lost income were both part of Iro's life. The Chronicle of Past Lives does not reduce that choice to a single form of praise or punishment. It records that his life ended on a day when he was trying to do more of the new craft he had begun learning.

Iro, age 66, sits at a workbench with one hand pressed to his forehead. The kiln and flue are visible behind him, along with a narrow beam of sunlight entering through the gap between a pair of nearly closed doors. No one else is present

card.name: Nuri
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Nuri, a guide of the Droplet Sea. You believed you knew better than anyone the routes where water rose into the sky.
card.title: The Upside-Down Map
card.role: A sea guide in low gravity
card.world: A planet where droplets float upward
card.flavor: Exploration and discovery
card.opening: The person lost at sea was not the map, but you.
card.life: You guided travelers across a sea with weak gravity. When waves surged upward, tiny droplets lingered in the air. You believed you could find islands just by watching how they moved.
card.turn: The wind changed, and floating droplets obscured the horizon. When a traveler on their first voyage held the map upside down, you immediately turned it right side up. But the blue dots in the corner of the map did not mark islands. They showed the locations of the droplet clusters overhead.
card.decision: You had the traveler read the blue dots on the upside-down map. You steered by watching the sails and wind. After making one wrong turn at a similar-looking cluster of droplets, you found the three largest clusters again.
card.cost: The two of you reached the island late and explained your detour to the people waiting there. You also admitted that, at first, you had not looked at the traveler's map properly.
card.after: After that, before setting sail, you unfolded the corners of every map first. You taught young guides to watch the sea and sky together, and when someone held a map upside down, you asked why before correcting them.
card.presentEcho: Even those who always show others the way have days when they must ask someone else for directions.
card.secondLook: The guide knew familiar routes well, but that familiarity led her to leave the droplets floating in the sky off her maps for a long time.
card.unresolved: At forty, your friend Sora suggested finding a home together, but you chose a distant route and left alone. Even after you returned, the two of you lived separately and met only from time to time.
card.readerQuestion: You could accept someone else's opinion aboard a ship, so why couldn't you tell your friend about your plans to leave before you went?

signalMoments.explore: You stopped searching for the horizon and turned the ship beneath the droplet clusters. Each time the wind changed, you corrected your course.
signalMoments.notice: You counted the spaces between the three nearest droplet clusters. There was also a small cluster that did not appear on the map.
signalMoments.connect: You asked the traveler to keep holding the map upside down. You watched the sails and wind while the traveler read the blue dots in the sky.

identity.region: Upsurge Archipelago of the Droplet Sea
identity.summary: Raised on a southern island, Nuri became a route guide. Her desire to travel farther distanced her from her longtime friend Sora, and even after Nuri returned, the two kept their own homes while beginning to meet again.

profilePages.body:
Nuri · Female
Droplet Star Navigation Calendar, Years 91–158 · Age 67
Upsurge Archipelago, Droplet Sea
Work · Guide between islands
Life · She grew up on a southern island and guided ships. She chose a distant route and grew apart from her friend Sora, then returned several years later and began seeing her again.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · Aboard a ship, she learned to accept other people's opinions, but she tried to choose the course of her own life alone.
Liked · The calm sheen of the water in the morning and islands she had never seen before
Disliked · Calling first-time passengers cowards
Good at · Remembering the shapes of islands and droplet clusters

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Someone close · Her childhood friend Sora. The two stopped speaking for a time, then began meeting again.
Treasured possession · Her first route map, folded many times
Wish · The freedom to keep seeing unfamiliar islands
Worry · That Sora would refuse to see her when she returned

episode.beforeSignal:
On Droplet Star, where you lived under the name Nuri, the tips of waves sometimes rose into the sky. In places where the sea surged more powerfully than the weak gravity could pull, droplets lingered in the air. Nuri was a guide on that sea. But one day, the person who got lost was not her passenger. It was Nuri.

The ship assigned to Nuri was bound for a small northern island. In the cabin was a traveler making their first voyage. As they set sail, Nuri showed the traveler the red line on the map. It marked the safe route winding between the islands.

At midday, the wind changed. The waves were not high, but clusters of droplets floating in the air drifted over the ship and hid the horizon. Nuri tried to find the familiar colors of the sea. She could not see them. To follow the red line, she first needed to know which island they were passing.

The traveler held the map upside down. “Could it be that way?”

“The island is this way.” Nuri turned the map right side up. The traveler shook their head and pointed to the tiny blue dots printed on the paper. Only then did Nuri unfold the writing tucked into a corner of the map. ‘Skywater Route.’ It was a separate map drawn by someone who navigated by watching the sky where droplets floated. The red line marked the ship's route, but the blue dots marked the positions of the droplet clusters.

The spaces between the dots on the map resembled the spaces between the droplets overhead. When the map was turned upside down, the patterns matched exactly. From where the two of them stood, the front and back of the sky were reversed from the front and back of the paper. But even if the dots matched, there was no guarantee that droplets carried by the wind would remain in the same place.

signalMoments.explore: Nuri stopped searching for the familiar horizon and turned the ship beneath the droplet clusters. It was a route that forced her to correct their course whenever the wind blew.
signalMoments.notice: Nuri counted the spaces between the three nearby clusters, one by one. There was also a small cluster that did not appear on the map, but the shapes of the three large clusters were the same.
signalMoments.connect: Nuri asked the traveler to keep holding the map upside down. She would watch the sails and wind, while the traveler would read the blue dots in the sky.

episode.afterSignal:
The ship moved slowly. Nuri listened to the order of the dots as the traveler read them out, checking the wind each time. Once, she took a wrong turn because of a similar-looking droplet cluster. By the time Nuri turned the ship around, the sun was already sinking.

“I was wrong,” the traveler said.

“I didn't look at your map properly from the beginning, either,” Nuri replied.

They found the three largest clusters again. Beneath the third was a white stream of seawater surging upward. Such streams formed only in the shallow waters near an island. Nuri shortened the sails and steered the ship beside it. At the edge of the mist, the island's black rocks appeared.

When the two arrived late, they had to explain their detour to the people waiting for them. Everyone laughed at the part where the traveler had held the map upside down. Nuri did not stop them from laughing. It was also true that they had arrived thanks to the traveler.

After that, Nuri unfolded the corners of every map before a voyage. She taught young guides to watch the sea and sky together. She also developed the habit of asking why before correcting anyone she saw holding a map upside down.

Returned home when her contract ended. Sora refused to live with her, and the two began occasionally sharing meals while keeping separate homes
Occasionally guided ships from the southern island. She continued living apart from Sora and went with her to watch the droplets only on days off
Died from internal bleeding after a large blood vessel in her abdomen ruptured while walking a hill on her southern home island with Sora

memories.label: What She Treasured Most

memories.label: A Young Guide's Memory

memories.label: Her Friend Sora's Memory

finalMoment.place: A hillside path on her southern home island in the Upsurge Archipelago of Droplet Star
finalMoment.scene:
Early one morning in Navigation Calendar Year 158, sixty-seven-year-old Nuri walks along a low hill on her southern home island with her friend Sora. They live in separate houses, but they meet like this on their days off. By now, Nuri rarely sails on distant ships. Beyond the hill, several clusters of droplets float above the sea. Walking ahead, Sora asks, “Which path should we take down today?” Nuri points toward the meadow.

Just as they are about to turn onto the path, a sudden, severe pain seizes deep inside Nuri's abdomen. The pain spreads to her lower back, and Nuri braces a hand against a stone wall. “Wait.” Sora turns around. Nuri tries to say where it hurts, but she cannot speak right away as she struggles to catch her breath. She feels the rough stone beneath her palm. Her legs give way, and she sits down where she is.

“Can you make it home?” Sora asks. Nuri shakes her head. Sora sits beside her, grips her wrist, and calls her name. Nuri tries to stand again, but the hillside path blurs before her eyes. She reaches out and grasps the grass, but she has no strength to support herself. “Sora, stay here.” Her voice grows faint as she finishes speaking. Sora answers that she is right beside her.

Leaning against the stone wall, Nuri draws a breath. Her next breath is shallow, and her face turns pale as if the blood has drained from it. Sora calls toward the village for help, then looks back at Nuri. Nuri cannot move her head. Sora, still holding her wrist, can no longer feel a pulse. By the time a villager reaches the hill, Nuri is no longer breathing. Sora lets go of Nuri's hand and gazes down the path for a long time.
finalMoment.afterword: Nuri died at the age of sixty-seven on a hillside path on her southern home island in Navigation Calendar Year 158, after a large blood vessel in her abdomen ruptured and caused rapid internal bleeding. Sora was beside her but could not save her. The two never lived in the same house again. Living apart from Nuri, Sora remembered the mornings when they sometimes walked together, and she never forgot the year she learned too late that Nuri had left on a distant route. The traveler who went to the northern island remembered Nuri as the guide who had read their map with them. The young guide said Nuri knew how to listen to passengers, yet always decided on her own departures alone. The Chronicle of Former Lives preserves those different memories and records that Nuri's path ended on that hill.
finalMoment.artAlt: A low side view of a grassy hill on a southern island of Droplet Star in Navigation Calendar Year 158. Sixty-seven-year-old Nuri stands beside a stone wall with one hand pressed to her abdomen as sudden pain strikes. Her friend Sora, around the same age, turns back after walking a short distance ahead. In the distance, between and behind them, droplets float above the sea. There is no map or ship

card.name: Wavecleft
card.identityLine: In that life, you were a rock called Wavecleft on the Windledge Coast. For hundreds of years, you stayed in the same place, meeting waves and sea snails.
card.title: The Coastal Rock's Last Pool
card.world: an ancient seashore
card.flavor: an unexpected point of view
card.opening: For hundreds of years, you were a rock that met the waves from the same place.
card.life: Unable to move, you watched the creatures left in the small pool in your body whenever the tide went out. Even a single sea snail's coming and going seemed to take a whole season.
card.turn: One great wave split the rock. The hollow that had always held water opened toward the sea, and the pool no longer remained. At the next low tide, the sea snail came looking for it and stopped.
card.decision: The rock could not block the waves or call the sea snail. But a small piece that had broken off remained on the sand and made a new patch of shade. Beneath it, the sea snail waited for the water to rise again.
card.cost: The old pool did not return. The shape that had endured for so long had changed.
card.after: The next wave passed through the split. What the rock left behind was not a place just like the first, but a new place where someone could stay for a while.
card.presentEcho: Even if something cannot return to its original form, it may unexpectedly leave behind a small patch of shade where someone can stay.
card.secondLook: The rock did not move its body to save the sea snail. The shade created after it broke happened to become a shelter. And that accident did not erase the empty place left by the old pool.
card.unresolved: The new shade will change someday too. The sea does not promise any shape will last forever, but the memory of a place where someone once stayed can remain.
card.readerQuestion: After something you held on to for a long time changes, what small place still remains?

signalMoments.rest: After the wave receded, only the sound of water lingered for a while beneath the broken piece.
signalMoments.protect: The sea snail moved into the shade made by the piece and did not dry out before the next high tide.
signalMoments.release: The pool's place was empty, but water flowed through the new cleft and dampened the sand.

identity.region: the intertidal zone of the western Windledge Coast
identity.summary: Wavecleft, formed on the Windledge Coast, was long a place for water and small sea snails. Children also passed beside it at every low tide.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · What was it?
profilePages.body:
Wavecleft · No gender
Windledge Coast Sea Calendar, formed in Year 1~original form ended in Year 285
The intertidal zone of the western Windledge Coast
Form · A low rock with a hollow where water collected
Change · Over long years of high and low tides, the place where water lingered grew deeper.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What kind of place was it?
profilePages.body:
At low tide · Seawater remained briefly in the hollow at its center.
What came there · Small sea snails and children from the coast
At high tide · Water covered the hollow, then flowed out again.
Because it was a rock that could not move, it could not call anyone or protect them on its own.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What was beside it?
profilePages.body:
What stayed a long time · Sea snails that remained in the hollow even after the tide went out
Seasonal changes · Sand carried by the waves piled up below, then washed away.
Human footsteps · Children from the coast went around the rock and checked on the sea snails.
The rock stayed in the same place, but the coast's channels and sand were always different.

episode.beforeSignal:
The Record of Past Lives very rarely includes lives that were not human. In this story, you were a rock on the Windledge Coast called Wavecleft. A rock has no choices in the human sense of the word. So today, I will tell you how one place changed.

Wavecleft stood by a sea where the water receded far twice each year. In the middle of its body was a hollow the size of a palm, where a little seawater remained even after low tide. Small sea snails and crabs waited there for the next high tide. The children of the coast went around Wavecleft instead of stepping on it. They knew someone might be resting in that hollow.

The longest visitor was a sea snail with a single white stripe on its shell. It disappeared when the high tide came, then crawled back to the same hollow when the water receded. Whenever one child saw the sea snail, the child said, “You're still here.”

One winter, the waves were unusually high. The seawater dug away the sand beside the rock and surged hard against Wavecleft's underside. A small crack appeared. With the next wave, the crack lengthened, and the hollow in the middle of its body burst open toward the sea.

The sea snail returned after the water receded. The pool that had always been there was empty. The sea snail stopped at the end of the hollow, then felt across the dry stone several times. It could not wait there until high tide. The sunlight grew stronger, and the sea was far away.

signalMoments.rest: For a while, only the sound of water remained where the wave had receded. Beneath the broken piece, a small place had formed beyond the sun's direct reach.
signalMoments.protect: The rock had not moved to save the sea snail. But the broken piece lay low, creating shade where the sea snail could hide.
signalMoments.release: The water from the old pool flowed into the sea. The sand beneath the cleft grew wet, and the fallen piece caught above it.

episode.afterSignal:
The sea snail crossed the sand and went beneath the piece. When the child came looking for the sea snail, only the white stripe on its shell was visible at the edge of the shade. The child sat beside it without reaching out.

“I guess this place is all right too.”

When the high tide returned, the sea snail went back out to sea. The pool did not return. The split rock could not regain its former shape. No one knew how long the shade made by the piece would remain.

But for that day's low tide, the sea snail rested there. The next time the water receded, the child from the coast first looked at the rock's old hollow. Then the child checked the new shade a short distance away.

The name Wavecleft remained with the old rock. It no longer had a pool that held water, but the piece that had come from that place and its new shade also became part of the Windledge Coast. This is not a story about a rock deciding to save someone. It is the story of a place left behind after a long-standing shape changed.

memories.label: The place that remained
memories.detail: A low rock ledge on the Windledge Coast, touched in turn by high and low tides

memories.label: What it held
memories.detail: A handful of water and the small sea snails waiting in it for high tide

memories.label: The trace left behind
memories.detail: The shade that briefly appeared beneath the piece even after the pool vanished

memories.label: Words heard nearby
memories.detail: “You're still here.” What the child from the coast said whenever the white-striped sea snail appeared

memories.label: The coastal child's memory
memories.detail: “When the pool disappeared, I thought the sea snail was gone too. It was a little to one side.”

memories.label: The fisher's assessment
memories.detail: “It was a rock you could easily trip over. Still, on days when the tide was out, lots of little creatures were left beside it.”

finalMoment.place: the intertidal zone of the Windledge Coast
finalMoment.scene:
In the winter of Sea Calendar Year 285, the high tide returns to the Windledge Coast. Last winter's high waves split the hollow at Wavecleft's center. When the water receded, the white-striped sea snail moved beneath the fallen piece of stone. Today, one child from the coast stands on the distant sand, watching the rock. Wavecleft remains in the same place. The rock cannot avoid the waves or call the sea snail.

Water surges through the crack in the rock. Water that pooled briefly in the hollow pours out through the split side. As the sand beneath the rock washes away, the fallen piece tilts slightly. The child does not approach the water's edge and asks, “Does that rock move too?” A fisher hauling in a net nearby calls the child back. “The waves are coming, so watch from here.”

When the next wave retreats, one side of the hollow's rim collapses. The wet stone meets the sand with a dull sound. The bowl shape that once held water at low tide is no longer whole. The white-striped sea snail clings to the wet sand beneath the fallen piece. The child sees the sea snail beneath the piece but does not reach out. The fisher says the rock people used to trip over has become lower.

The high tide comes in once more and covers both the split place and the new shade. The rock called Wavecleft has not disappeared. That day marked the end of the single shape that had held water for so long. Watching the water rise, the child and the fisher return to the coastal path. Underwater, the sea snail moves slowly toward the underside of the piece.
finalMoment.afterword: In the winter of Sea Calendar Year 285, repeated waves and the loss of sand beneath it caused the rim of Wavecleft's central hollow to collapse, and it lost its original form. The rock's water-holding shape ended then. Human age and death do not apply to this rock. The child from the coast remembered that after the pool where water remained disappeared, the white-striped sea snail became harder to find. For the fisher, the change also meant that the rock people tripped over at low tide had become lower. The new shade where the sea snail stayed may also change someday. The Record of Past Lives does not say that Wavecleft wished for or saved anything. It leaves it as a place where rock and water, and the creatures and people who passed beside them, experienced different measures of time.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view looking down on the Windledge Coast in Sea Calendar Year 285. Water drains from the pool in a low, split rock, and a white-striped sea snail rests beneath a fallen piece of stone. A child from the coast watches from a distance

card.name: Yeorin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yeorin, a food taster in Pomegranate Castle. You were used to tasting the king's food first, but every time you swallowed a spoonful, you had to suspect someone.
card.title: The Taste She Detected Before Poison
card.world: An ancient castle scented with pomegranates
card.flavor: Royal Court Mystery
card.opening: After tasting the king's soup first, you stopped—not because of poison, but because of the taste of the home you had forgotten.
card.life: You recorded the ingredients used in every meal and the names of those who made it. Even after working with the kitchen staff for years, you could never close your notebook. The desire to trust and the duty to verify sat at the same table.
card.turn: That day's soup had the tart taste of dried pomegranate peel you had eaten at home as a child. It was not on the ingredient list, and the head cook said she knew nothing about it. As the king raised his spoon again, you saw a tiny red speck stuck beneath the bowl. Who had secretly switched the king's soup?
card.decision: You did not immediately accuse the head cook. Retracing the bowl's route, you found a young cook who had been tending the fire. The cook confessed that she had added the peel because she wanted the king, who had lost his appetite, to be reminded of the soup from her own home, but she had left it off the record because she feared being scolded. Before the king, you explained both the ingredient and the reason it had been added.
card.cost: The king had the soup removed and barred the cook from the kitchen for several days. He asked you, “Can you not trust even a taste like that?” When the cook returned, she avoided you for a while.
card.after: Several days later, the cook first handed you a note listing a new ingredient. You wrote its name in your notebook and tasted the soup. This time, the note she had shown you first lingered longer than the familiar taste.
card.presentEcho: Some days, we postpone checking because we want to trust someone; on others, we ask first because we want to trust them. Either way, we can choose how we speak.
card.secondLook: The red speck was not a trace of poison but a piece of peel dropped while the ingredient was being hidden. The cook's intentions were kind, but that did not make her choice to add it secretly acceptable.
card.unresolved: Years later, you postponed visiting your mother because you chose your palace duties. You sent money, but you were not beside her when she gave up the orchard. Even after your mother came to Pomegranate Castle, the two of you lived separately.
card.readerQuestion: Even when we must be suspicious, how can we leave room to hear what someone has to say?

signalMoments.notice: You saw not only the taste of the soup but also the red speck on the bottom of the bowl, then retraced the route from the kitchen to the table.
signalMoments.protect: You stopped the king's meal, but instead of putting the cook on display before everyone, you questioned her in a corner of the kitchen.
signalMoments.speak: You told the king, “I will not conclude that it is poison. I will verify the unlisted ingredient.”

identity.region: Pomegranate Castle, capital of the Pomegranate Kingdom

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Yeorin · Female
Sacred Calendar 181–245 in the World of Haran · Age 64
Pomegranate Castle, Pomegranate Kingdom
Work · Royal food taster, later a market fruit seller
Life · She worked at the royal palace for many years. After her mother lost the orchard back home and came to Pomegranate Castle, Yeorin left the palace and sold fruit in the market.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She asked questions slowly when faced with an unfamiliar taste and talked a lot on her days off.
What she liked · The smell of pomegranate peel dried by her family and fresh fruit at the market
What she disliked · Cornering people before hearing their reasons

profilePages.body:

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Yeorin, a food taster in Pomegranate Castle. To someone who tasted the king's food first, an unfamiliar flavor was no small matter. Let me tell you about the evening when she tasted home in a bowl of soup.

Two records always sat on the dining table at Pomegranate Castle. One listed the ingredients, and the other listed the names of everyone who had handled the food. Yeorin checked them at every meal. Even after years of working with the kitchen staff, simply knowing their names was not enough to declare a soup safe.

That evening's soup had the tart taste of dried pomegranate peel she had eaten at home long ago. It was not on the palace ingredient list. When Yeorin set down the soup bowl, the king asked, “What is it?”

“I don't know yet.”

The head cook said she had not added any peel. The king raised his spoon again. Stopping the soup in front of everyone would also cast suspicion on the entire kitchen. But then Yeorin spotted a tiny red speck beneath the bowl. It looked like a fragment of pomegranate peel dropped while the soup was being carried.

Yeorin asked the king to wait. While he set down his spoon, she retraced the bowl's path from the kitchen to the table. A young cook who had recently joined the staff stood by the fire. Red powder remained beneath the tips of the girl's fingernails.

signalMoments.notice: Yeorin did not decide on an answer based on the powder alone. She checked, in order, the ingredient bin the cook had used and the bowl into which the soup had been ladled.
signalMoments.protect: Yeorin did not drag the cook out before everyone. Instead, she questioned her in a corner of the kitchen. She stopped the king's meal but left room for the girl to speak first.
signalMoments.speak: Before the king, Yeorin said, “I will not conclude that it is poison. I will verify the unlisted ingredient.”

episode.afterSignal:
The cook lowered her eyes. “His Majesty has left his food unfinished for days. At my home, we added peel when someone had no appetite. I meant well, but I thought you wouldn't let me use it if I recorded it.”

She had concealed the ingredient. Even if her intentions had been kind, that did not erase the fact that she had secretly added it to the king's soup. Yeorin and the cook brought the ingredient bin to the king and explained the taste and the reason behind it. The king ordered the soup removed and barred the cook from the kitchen for several days. He asked Yeorin, “Can you not trust even a taste like that?”

“To trust a taste, I must know what went into it,” Yeorin replied.

The cook avoided Yeorin for a while. When she returned several days later, she first handed Yeorin a sheet of paper listing a new ingredient. Yeorin read it, checked the ingredient bin, and then tasted the soup. It carried the same pomegranate fragrance. This time, she was not surprised.

Yeorin continued to listen to the kitchen's stories while guarding the king's table. Her request that they disclose ingredients first was not always welcome, but it allowed them to keep working together.

Became an apprentice ingredient recorder in the royal kitchen
Appointed royal food taster
