Unable to secure a long leave, she chose her palace duties and sent money. She postponed the visit her mother had requested
Her mother sold the orchard and came to Pomegranate Castle. Her mother refused to live in the same house as Yeorin
Left the palace and began selling fruit in the market. Her mother also came to the same market, but the two continued to live separately
Continued tending her market stall. She accepted fruit her mother offered her, but that did not undo the time she had postponed the visit
Shared an empty stall with a market colleague while each set her own prices and chose her own storage space

Died after a stone came loose from the rim of the well in the communal courtyard behind the Pomegranate Castle market, causing her to fall into the water. Her mother, who lived separately, heard the news the next day

memories.label: Where She Worked for Years
memories.detail: The royal kitchen, where she first checked whose food it was and then recorded the ingredients

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The worn ingredient notebook brought from her childhood home

memories.label: The Habit She Kept for Years
memories.detail: Whenever she encountered a new taste, checking the ingredient list before the names of the people involved

memories.label: The Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Even if your intentions are good, please record what you added.”

memories.label: The Cook's Assessment
memories.detail: “She made me step away that day, but she didn't accuse me of adding poison in front of everyone. After I returned, we kept working together.”

memories.label: Her Mother's Memory
memories.detail: “I received the money. But when I asked you to be beside me as I cleared out the trees alone, your answer came late.”

memories.label: A Market Colleague's Assessment
memories.detail: “At first, I thought she'd charge high prices because she'd come from the royal palace. But she chose her words more carefully when her mother came by than when speaking to customers.”

finalMoment.place: The communal courtyard behind the market in Pomegranate Castle, in the World of Haran
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-autumn evening in the Sacred Calendar year 245, at age 64, I draw water for my home from the communal courtyard behind the market in Pomegranate Castle. I have just returned after closing the stall with my market colleague. Mother lives in another house within the same castle. I saw her at the market again today, but we did not come home together. At the door across the courtyard, a neighbor gathers in her laundry and asks, “Is the bucket heavy again?” “It's all right today.”

I brace one hand on the well's stone rim and pull the rope attached to the bucket full of water. Beneath my palm, one of the stones shifts inward. As I try to lean back, the stone comes loose and my body tips into the well. My fingernails scrape against the rough stones. The ground vanishes beneath my feet, and water splashes above my shoulders. I spit out the cold water and look up. The courtyard sky appears as a circle overhead.

“Yeorin!” my neighbor shouts from above the well. I feel along the wall, searching for a foothold. The wet stones are slippery. My neighbor lowers the bucket rope again. “Grab this!” As the end of the rope comes close to my hand, I reach for it. I catch it once, but my water-soaked hand slips. My neighbor's voice echoes down the well as she calls for someone else.

I lift my arm to grab the rope again. My arm rises above the water, then sinks. “Here...” Before I can finish, water enters my mouth. Above me, my neighbor calls my name. I press my palm against the wall and look up once more. The rippling water makes my neighbor's face appear to sway. My hand slips from the stone, and the circle of light in the sky recedes.
finalMoment.afterword: Yeorin fell when the stone rim of the communal well behind the market in Pomegranate Castle collapsed in the Sacred Calendar year 245. Unable to escape the water, she died at age 64. No one learned why the stone had come loose. A neighbor lowered a rope but could not pull Yeorin out. When her mother heard the news the next day, she remembered the years they had lived separately despite going to the same market. She remembered both the money her daughter had given her and the late reply when she was clearing out the orchard. The colleague who had shared an empty stall with Yeorin remembered how she had set the prices of her own goods. This record of a past life tells of the day Yeorin tried not to corner someone at the palace, the days she was late for her family, the life she rebuilt outside the palace, and how that life ended.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high-angle evening view over the well in the communal courtyard behind the Pomegranate Castle market in late autumn of the Sacred Calendar year 245. As 64-year-old Yeorin pulls the rope of a bucket filled with water, one of the stones in the rim beneath her bracing hand begins to fall inward. A neighbor at the house across the courtyard gathers in laundry, and no royal food or tasting tools are present

card.name: Haeru
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Haeru, a cloud painter in Skybridge Village. Your job was to draw rain paths on the undersides of clouds so water would reach the dry fields.
card.title: The Shade of the Smiling Cloud
card.world: A village in the sky where paths are drawn on the undersides of clouds
card.flavor: Wonder and a Small Commotion
card.opening: The cloud on which you painted a smiling face really did smile, but no rain fell on the fields.
card.life: In this village, the patterns on clouds were paths for raindrops to follow. Every day, you looked at where the fields lay and drew long lines. After drawing the same patterns over and over, you wanted to show everyone something different, at least on the day of the festival.
card.turn: When the huge smiling mouth you painted passed across the sky during the festival, the children laughed along with it. But as the corners of the mouth stretched apart, the rain path split too. The cloud passed over the fields, leaving only shade, and the two streams of water fell on rocky ground where no one had planted anything.
card.decision: You did not make an excuse and say, “It will rain soon.” You raised the festival ladder again and, together with an elder who knew the fields, drew a single connecting line on the underside of the cloud. The children were disappointed that the bottom of the smiling face had grown longer, but the first raindrop fell from the end of that line.
card.cost: The festival procession came to a halt while you repainted the cloud. The water that had poured onto the rocky ground could not be brought back, and you also helped carry water to the dry fields.
card.after: That evening, one child drew a smiling cloud on a sheet of damp paper. This time, it had a long chin beneath its mouth leading toward the fields. You laughed when you saw the strange face.
card.presentEcho: A choice that makes someone happy may still fall short somewhere else. Perhaps you can correct it without erasing the joy it brought.
card.secondLook: The cloud had not been teasing the farmers on purpose. You had simply forgotten for a moment that changing the picture changed the rain path too.
card.unresolved: You kept painting clouds for many years afterward, but when the village required prior approval for every line, you quit working as a cloud painter. You gained the freedom to sell paintings on paper in the market, while the farmers and the new cloud painter had to fill the gap for a time.
card.readerQuestion: When do you want to ask how something you chose because you liked it might look to someone else?

signalMoments.repair: Without erasing the smiling mouth, you drew a new line between its two split ends, connecting them to a path toward the fields.
signalMoments.notice: Behind the children's laughter, you saw the faces of those watching the fields grow tense, and you checked the water paths beneath the cloud.
signalMoments.connect: You asked the elder who knew the fields best to call out directions from below the ladder.

identity.region: The dry fields of eastern Skybridge Village in the Skybridge Alliance
identity.summary: Haeru was a cloud painter who sent rain to the fields. When every line in his paintings had to be approved, he quit his job and began painting on paper.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Haeru · Male
Cloudsky World, Bridge Calendar 107–171 · Age 64
Eastern village of the Skybridge Alliance
Work · Cloud painter, later a seller of paper paintings
Life · He painted rain paths on the clouds above the bridge, but quit in protest against the village's new approval rules. Afterward, he sold landscapes painted on paper at the market.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He could listen to others and revise his paintings, but he could not stand being told to seek permission every time he touched brush to surface.
Liked · Clouds drawn by children and the smell of fields after rain
Disliked · Praise for beautiful paintings from people who never looked below
Skill · Changing the pressure of his brush to match the wind

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
People close to him · The neighbors who tended the fields and his first teacher, the child who ran after the cloud during the festival, and the neighbor he played stone games with behind the market
Treasured possession · The old brush his teacher gave him
Wish · Time to paint without having to consider whether a picture was useful
Worry · That the new cloud painter might be overwhelmed with too much work after he left

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Haeru, a cloud painter in Skybridge Village. Here, raindrops gathered and fell along the lines painted on the undersides of clouds. Let me tell you the story of how Haeru painted a smiling face on the day of the festival and ended up running all over the village.

A cloud painter climbed a ladder at the end of a high bridge and reached out with his brush. When he painted a long line on a cloud's underside, droplets gathered along it and fell onto the fields. If the line broke or split, the rain flowed somewhere else. Haeru had done this work for a long time. Sometimes he grew tired of painting nothing but straight lines toward the fields every day.

On the day of the festival, the children pointed at the sky. “Please paint us a smiling cloud today!”

Haeru curved the end of the line leading to the fields into a huge smiling mouth. From far away, the cloud looked as if it were smiling. The children ran after it. But as the corners of the mouth stretched out on both sides, the raindrops split too. Only shade passed over the dry fields, while the water fell on the empty rocky ground to either side.

One farmer picked up a handful of soil that had not gotten wet. “The fields are still dry.”

Haeru could not say that rain would come soon. He had no way of knowing whether the same cloud would pass by again. The festival procession stopped beneath the bridge. If the ladder went up again, the smiling face would change too.

signalMoments.repair: Haeru did not erase the entire smiling mouth. He looked for a place to add a long line between its two split ends, leading toward the fields.
signalMoments.notice: Behind the children's laughter, Haeru saw the faces of those watching the fields grow tense. He also checked the water paths flowing beneath the cloud.
signalMoments.connect: Haeru asked an elder who had tended the fields for many years to call out directions from below the ladder. From high above, the far edge of the fields looked tiny.

episode.afterSignal:
Haeru climbed the ladder again. The wind blew, shifting the edge of the cloud. The elder shouted from below. “A little to the left! Now aim for the edge of the fields!” Haeru painted a single long line down from beneath the mouth. The smiling face now had a strangely long chin.

One child shouted, “It's ugly now!” Haeru almost laughed too, but he did not stop painting. The first raindrop fell at the edge of the fields. Then the dry furrows began to darken.

The procession started moving again, but late. They could not bring back the water that had poured onto the rocky ground, and they still had to carry by hand the water the fields lacked. Haeru put his work apron back on over his festival clothes and picked up a water bucket.

That evening, a child brought him a cloud drawn on a damp sheet of paper. Beneath the smiling mouth was a long chin stretching toward the fields. When Haeru laughed, the child asked, “You'll paint it like this next time too, right?”

“Next time, I'll look at the fields first.”

Haeru continued to paint festival clouds after that. But before making the first brushstroke, he checked the location of the fields together with the others. The village children began playing a game in which they figured out where the rain from each smiling face would fall.

timeline.event: Born to a farming family east of Skybridge
Observed cloud water paths from beneath his first ladder
Began his apprenticeship as a cloud painter
Appointed cloud painter responsible for the dry fields
Received his first teacher's worn brush when the teacher retired and kept it for many years
Corrected the smiling festival cloud's rain path
Walked the fields with farmers and marked water paths that could not be seen from the bridge in his paintings
Established the custom of planning cloud paintings together with farmers
The village established a rule requiring prior approval not only for rain paths, but for every line in a cloud painting
Refused to follow the rule and quit working as a cloud painter. Until a new cloud painter arrived, the farmers were busy readjusting the rain paths
Opened a small market stall and began selling paper landscapes that did not make it rain
Heard that the new cloud painter was short-handed, but did not return to the bridge
The child who had run after the cloud during the festival returned as an adult and bought one paper painting
Spent his evenings playing stone games with a neighbor from a house behind the market

In the late summer of Bridge Calendar 171, while playing a stone game with his neighbor in his room behind the market, he died after sudden chest pain and difficulty breathing. The exact illness is unknown

memories.label: The Place He Left
memories.detail: His post as a cloud painter atop the long ladder. Though he knew which fields needed rain, he refused to seek approval for every line

memories.label: His Most Precious Possession
memories.detail: The worn handle of the cloud brush given to him by his first teacher

memories.label: A Lifelong Habit
memories.detail: Even when painting on paper, he went outside first and spent a long time observing the sky and fields

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “I know which fields need rain. But not every one of my paintings has to make it rain.”

memories.label: The Farmer's View
memories.detail: “On the day of the festival, he ran all the way to our fields. But when the new rule was established, he chose his paintings over us.”

memories.label: The Festival Child's Memory
memories.detail: “As a child, I ran after the smiling cloud. As an adult, I bought one of Haeru's small paintings at the market.”

memories.label: The New Cloud Painter's View
memories.detail: “During the first year after Haeru left, I had to learn the fields' rain paths all over again. He did not come back to teach me.”

memories.label: The Market Neighbor's Memory
memories.detail: “On evenings when he wasn't selling paintings, he came to my room to play stone games. On the days he lost, he was never the first to laugh.”

finalMoment.place: Haeru's room behind the market in Skybridge Village, Cloudsky World
finalMoment.scene:
One evening in the late summer of Bridge Calendar 171, sixty-four-year-old Haeru is playing a stone game with his neighbor in his room behind the market. Every evening, the two of them place stones one by one on the board. Haeru sold several paintings during the day, but for now he has put the paper away. His neighbor sets down a stone and says, “Looks like I'm going to win today.” Without smiling, Haeru chooses his own stone.

Just as Haeru is about to place it, the center of his chest suddenly tightens. The stone slips between his fingers and falls to the floor. He grips the place that hurts and tries to inhale, but cannot draw a deep breath. His left arm grows heavy, and cold sweat beads on his forehead. His neighbor rises from across the board. “Haeru, are you in pain?” Haeru says, “My chest...” and sits down, leaning against the doorframe.

His neighbor pushes the game board aside, opens the door, and calls to someone across the road. Returning to Haeru, he says, “I'm here. I'm watching over you.” Haeru tries to nod, but his neck will not move. One of the stones on the floor rolls to the threshold and stops. Haeru watches it, then looks up at his neighbor's face. His breaths grow too short for him to continue speaking.

Haeru braces a hand against the floor and tries to sit up straighter. His palm slips, and his body strikes the doorframe again. His neighbor calls his name. Haeru's chest moves shallowly, but the next breath does not come. His neighbor looks back and forth between Haeru's face and chest, then calls once more toward the open door. When footsteps sound outside, Haeru does not answer.
finalMoment.afterword: Haeru died at sixty-four in the late summer of Bridge Calendar 171, after sudden chest pain and difficulty breathing in his room behind the market in Skybridge Village. The exact illness is unknown. The neighbor who played stone games with him every evening stayed by his side and called for help, but Haeru did not breathe again. The farmer remembered both the day of the festival, when Haeru carried buckets of water all the way to the dry fields, and the gap he left behind when he later quit his village post. The new cloud painter was left with the memory of that first year, when Haeru did not return to teach him the work. The festival child, now grown, kept the paper painting purchased at the market. The Record of Past Lives does not combine those memories into a single tribute. It tells us that Haeru's life, including the evenings he spent away from work, came to an end that day.
finalMoment.artAlt: An evening view from a high diagonal angle of a room behind the market in Skybridge Village in the late summer of Bridge Calendar 171. Sixty-four-year-old Haeru is playing a stone game with his neighbor when he grips his chest and drops a single white stone from his hand. There are no paintings, brushes, or cloud-working tools, and no one is supporting him or running to call for help

card.name: Do-gyeom
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Do-gyeom, who played the king for one day at the Stoneglow Castle festival. The crown was borrowed, but the words people offered you were real.
card.title: The One-Day King's Long-Standing Promise
card.world: A castle where a crown is borrowed for one day
card.flavor: Reversal of status
card.opening: When you became king for a day, a child asked you to keep a promise even the real king had failed to keep.
card.life: On the day of the festival, you sat in a high chair and listened to playful petitions. You were used to the small laughs, but when a child held out a drawing of an old bridge, the wooden scepter in your hand suddenly felt heavy.
card.turn: The child asked you to repair the collapsed south bridge so they could visit their grandmother across the river. You almost said, “I will fix it.” Then a carpenter told you that the actual bridge repairs had not begun for months because there was not enough money. At sunset, you would have to return both the crown and its authority.
card.decision: You removed the crown in front of the child and said, “I can't fix everything.” Instead, you asked what could be done today with the festival's empty cart and the carpenter's hands. People cleared away the rotten planks at the end of the bridge and put up signs along a safe route around the river. The repairs were not finished that day.
card.cost: You could not give the child a bridge to cross right away, and some people grumbled that you were ruining the festival. Instead of delivering a grand kingly line, you had to return the next day to check the signs again.
card.after: The next day, the child recognized you without the crown. You walked the route around the river with the child and the carpenter. The bridge was not repaired that day either.
card.presentEcho: Even when I cannot make grand promises, I can still leave behind a small promise I am truly able to keep.
card.secondLook: The child did not need someone who looked like a king. They needed one person who would return to the collapsed bridge tomorrow.
card.unresolved: Later, when you took charge of the festival, you raised the market stall fees to increase the acting troupe's pay. Small shops could not attend the festival, and you rejected their petition to lower the fees. In the end, you were voted out of your position as manager.
card.readerQuestion: When faced with a big promise that is hard to keep, what small promise can I keep today?

signalMoments.speak: You removed the crown and said, “I do not have the power to repair this entire bridge today.”
signalMoments.connect: You introduced the carpenter to the child, then asked the carpenter to help you find someone who would lend you the festival's empty cart.
signalMoments.protect: Before promising repairs, you blocked the entrance to the old bridge and marked a safe route around the river first.

identity.region: Riverside Village south of Stoneglow Castle
identity.summary: Do-gyeom played a king at the festival before taking charge of the actual festival operations. He raised the market stall fees to fund a grander stage, then stepped down as manager after opposition from the merchants who lost their places.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Do-gyeom · Male
World of Doren, Sacred Calendar 162–227 · Age 65
Riverside Village south of Stoneglow Castle
Work · Actor playing the king's stand-in, later festival manager
Life · After making a name for himself as an actor, he managed the festival. He raised the market stall fees to expand the stage, then stepped down as manager amid opposition from the merchants.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · Onstage, he honestly admitted that he had no authority, but once he took charge of the actual festival, he did not easily bend on his own plans.
Liked · Hearing an audience laugh for the first time while wearing a new mask
Disliked · Empty promises that vanished as soon as a performance ended
Good at · Turning an audience member's brief remark into an improvised line

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
People close to him · His fellow troupe members and the Riverside Village carpenter who repaired masks
Treasured possession · The wooden mask he first made at age 12
Hope · A grand festival that would leave a lasting mark even in a small riverside village
Worry · Fear that if he lost his position as manager, he might not be able to return to being an ordinary actor

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Do-gyeom, an actor at Stoneglow Castle. Each year, you wore a crown for one day and listened to people's playful wishes. Let me tell you about the day a child held out a drawing of a bridge without smiling.

At the Stoneglow Castle festival, an actor wore a wooden crown. He had no authority to issue a real king's commands. Everyone knew that, yet for one day they made silly requests of the actor seated in the high chair. “Please make it rain only during the day this year.” “Please appoint our goat as a minister.” Do-gyeom answered with playful confidence.

One child waited for their turn. The child neither smiled nor looked at the crown. They held out a drawing of a bridge, its edges worn from being folded so many times.

“Please fix the south bridge. Then I can visit my grandmother across the river.”

The middle of the bridge had collapsed in the last rain, and it had been closed for months. In front of the audience, Do-gyeom almost said, “I will fix it for you.” A line like that would make the festival more exciting. But at sunset, he would have to return the crown, and the bridge would still have a hole in it.

He called over the carpenter standing below the stage. The carpenter said he had been unable to begin the work because there was not enough money to buy new planks and rope. The route around the river had no signs either, which made it confusing for a child to walk alone. The laughter at the festival grew quieter.

signalMoments.speak: Do-gyeom removed the crown and said, “I do not have the power to repair this entire bridge today.” The people who had been ready to applaud looked at one another.
signalMoments.connect: Do-gyeom introduced the carpenter to the child, then asked the carpenter to help him find someone who would lend them the empty cart used for the festival.
signalMoments.protect: Before saying anything about repairing the bridge, Do-gyeom said they should block the collapsed entrance. They needed signs to keep the child from taking that path again.

episode.afterSignal:
A cart beside the stage was made available at once. People removed the rotten planks and put up a sign in front of the collapsed bridge warning others to keep away. As the carpenter walked the route around the river, he tied stones and cloth at every fork. The child, who had hoped to see a finished bridge, gazed across the river for a long time.

“So I can't go today?”

“Not by yourself,” Do-gyeom said. “Will you walk the route around the river with me tomorrow afternoon?”

The festival's grand parade set off late. Some people grumbled that they had been made to work on a day meant for fun. Do-gyeom also missed his chance to deliver a grand kingly line. But at least he could make sure the child did not head toward the collapsed bridge that night.

The next day, the child came backstage. Do-gyeom was packing things away without his crown. “What you said yesterday—the man said it, not the king, right?” the child asked.

“That's right. Which is why I can still go today.”

The two walked the route around the river with the carpenter. The road to visit the grandmother was long, but at every fork, the child found the newly tied cloth.

Do-gyeom continued playing the king at the festival afterward. People still made silly wishes. He would accept them with a smile, but whenever someone made a request that called for real help, he took off the crown for a moment. He had developed the habit of saying only what he could keep.

Made his first wooden mask for a festival parade
Joined the Stoneglow Castle acting troupe
Gave his first performance as the one-day king's stand-in
Wrote a new script using the silly wishes invented by his fellow troupe members and the guests
Met the child carrying a drawing of the south bridge
Took charge of the festival and promised to build a grander stage
Raised the market stall fees to cover stage costs and the acting troupe's pay. Several small shops could not attend the festival
Rejected the merchants' petition to lower the stall fees. The acting troupe received more pay, but its relationship with the merchants grew distant
Stepped down as manager after opposition from the merchants and a vote by the festival organizers
Traveled to festivals in other villages as an actor, but no longer had a say over festival finances

memories.label: The First Thing He Made
memories.detail: The wooden mask he carved at age 12 for the Riverside Village parade

memories.label: What He Held On To
memories.detail: The wooden crown he wore as the king's stand-in. Even after stepping down as manager, he could not bring himself to throw it away immediately

memories.label: A Long-Kept Habit
memories.detail: Removing his crown and listening whenever a real request was made during a performance. After taking charge of the festival, he often forgot that habit

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “I thought everyone would come back if I built a grander stage.”

memories.label: The Carpenter's Assessment
memories.detail: “He really did walk the route around the river with the child. And later, Do-gyeom was also the one who raised the fee for my little stall.”

memories.label: A Festival Actor's Memory
memories.detail: “The year the stall fees went up, our pay increased. I was glad, but some merchants couldn't attend.”

memories.label: A Market Merchant's Assessment
memories.detail: “Our shop couldn't attend the festival that year. Even after Do-gyeom was voted out, we never got back the value of the goods we couldn't sell.”

finalMoment.place: The reed-lined path beside the communal wash place in Riverside Village south of Stoneglow Castle, in the World of Doren
finalMoment.scene:
One early autumn morning in Sacred Calendar 227, 65-year-old Do-gyeom rinses his clothes at Riverside Village's communal wash place. It has been 3 years since he returned to the village. Unlike the days when he traveled to other villages as an actor, he has no bags to pack for a departure today. Across from the wash place, a neighbor draws water. Do-gyeom puts his wet clothes in a basket and climbs the narrow path beside the reeds.

The reeds shake all at once. When Do-gyeom turns, a large wild boar bursts from the thicket. He drops the basket and steps aside, but the path is narrow. The boar's tusk tears through his left thigh as it passes. Do-gyeom falls to his knees on the dirt path. The boar does not come back, disappearing beyond the reeds.

Do-gyeom presses a hand to the gash in his thigh. Blood seeps between his fingers and spreads across his trousers. The neighbor from the wash place approaches, calling, “Mr. Do-gyeom!” The neighbor removes his outer garment, folds it, and presses it firmly against the wound. Do-gyeom tries to remain seated, but the path before his eyes begins to blur. “Keep pressing.” the neighbor says. Instead of answering, Do-gyeom only moves his head.

The neighbor presses the cloth down with both hands. Do-gyeom watches the morning light shining through the reeds. The sound of water flowing close to his ears grows distant. He tries to brace himself with the hand on the ground, but his fingers will not curl. The neighbor calls his name twice. Do-gyeom opens his mouth but cannot speak. One short breath escapes him, and then he stops moving.
finalMoment.afterword: Do-gyeom died at age 65 in early autumn of Sacred Calendar 227, after a wild boar injured his thigh on the reed-lined path beside the communal wash place in Riverside Village south of Stoneglow Castle and the bleeding would not stop. No one knew why the boar had come there. The neighbor at the wash place pressed on the wound but could not save Do-gyeom. The carpenter remembered both the day Do-gyeom walked the route around the river with the child and the later day he raised the fee for the carpenter's own stall. One member of the acting troupe recalled the year when the higher pay had improved their living conditions. The merchant who lost a place at the festival said the value of the goods they could not sell was never returned. Before his death, Do-gyeom did not apologize to that merchant. The Record of Past Lives preserves the words of people who experienced the same festival in different ways, and says that Do-gyeom's life ended on that path that morning.
finalMoment.artAlt: Viewed from a high diagonal angle, the reed-lined path beside Riverside Village's communal wash place in early autumn of Sacred Calendar 227. 65-year-old Do-gyeom stops with a basket of wet clothes in his hands and looks at a wild boar bursting from the reeds. Only 1 neighbor is visible in the distance at the wash place, with no crown, stage, or bridge

card.name: Miru
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Miru, a race judge in Snowhill Village. Because you had to inspect the course before the racers, you sometimes had to forget whose friend you were.
card.title: Footprints Before the Start
card.world: Hills where people race over snow every winter
card.flavor: The tension of a race
card.opening: Before the race had even begun, footprints appeared beyond the finish line.
card.life: The race rules were simple. Step onto the marked snow course only after the starting signal. Even when your friend raced, you tried to read the measurements the same way you did for every other competitor.
card.turn: That morning, you found the shape of your friend's boot heel in the snow beyond the finish line. People whispered that your friend had learned the course in advance. Snow that had already been trodden was firmer than the rest, so running over it would give an advantage to someone who knew the course. But the footprints did not head toward the finish line. They turned beneath a frozen wooden bridge. You also heard that a small whimpering sound had come from beneath the bridge during the night.
card.decision: You paused the race and questioned your friend. Your friend said she had stepped onto the marked course while rescuing a puppy trapped beneath the bridge at night. You understood the reason, but you could not let the race go ahead on a course bearing those tracks. In front of everyone, you chose a new course and delayed the starting time.
card.cost: While the new course was being prepared, racers from distant villages had to wait longer in the cold. Your friend was hurt at being suspected, and you could not easily forget the look on her face.
card.after: After the race ended on the new course, you went to find your friend. “I didn't see what was under the bridge last night. I should have asked you first, but I listened to the rumors instead.” Your friend did not smile right away.
card.presentEcho: The wish to uphold the rules and the wish to hear the circumstances of someone close to you can be on the same side.
card.secondLook: The footprints were not evidence of a false start, but traces of a rescue. That did not mean the tracks left behind would have no effect on the race.
card.unresolved: The following year, someone was assigned separately to inspect the course at night. Even so, you and your friend gradually grew apart, and after the age of 41, you no longer went sledding together.
card.readerQuestion: Even after understanding the circumstances, how can everyone start again fairly?

signalMoments.notice: You looked beyond the heel print at the finish line and checked the direction in which the footprints turned beneath the frozen bridge.
signalMoments.speak: You did not hide your friend's name or leave the matter to rumor. You explained why you had stopped the race and why a new course had to be chosen.
signalMoments.protect: You asked the villagers to open their homes so the racers would not have to stand in the cold for too long while they waited.

identity.region: Northern Snowhill Village
identity.summary: Miru, who grew up in a sled maker's household, became a snow-course judge. She stayed in racing work for many years, but grew distant from her friend and spent the cold seasons away from her hometown.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Miru · Female
World of Heron, Snow Reckoning, Years 93–156 · Age 63
Northern Snowhill Village
Work · Race-course marker, judge
Life · She tried to uphold the same rules for everyone, but could no longer spend time with her old friend as she once had. After it became difficult for her to stand in the cold for long periods, she stayed in the south every winter.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · At work, she checked numbers several times, but she laughed easily with her friend.
Liked · Freshly carved sleds and the quiet after the snow stopped
Disliked · People who claimed they knew someone's reasons just by looking at their footprints
Skilled at · Measuring the depth of snow courses and the spacing between markers

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · The friend with whom she repaired sleds as a child, racers from distant villages
What she treasured · A small sled she repaired with her friend
What she hoped for · A winter race that racers from distant villages could attend without worry
Worry · That even if she made the right ruling, she might never spend time with her friend again

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Miru, a race judge in Snowhill Village. Even on days when her friend raced, she tried to measure the depth of every footprint by the same standard. Let me tell you about the day footprints appeared beyond the finish line before the race had even begun.

In the Snowhill race, racers could step onto the marked snow course only after the starting signal. If someone passed over the course first, the snow became packed and firm. Anyone who knew the course could then sink less deeply and run a little faster. That was why the judge inspected the snow before anyone else did.

That day, Miru saw a familiar heel print beyond the finish line. It matched the boots worn by her closest friend. People whispered that her friend had secretly practiced there during the night. At first, Miru thought so too.

But the footprints did not lead toward the starting line. They turned beneath a frozen wooden bridge. Under the bridge, a small bundle of fur was trembling. It was a puppy that had been trapped there. If someone had climbed down to that spot the previous night, they would have left the same heel prints.

Her friend ran over and gathered the puppy into her arms. “It was here last night. I stepped onto the course while getting it out.”

Miru believed her friend. Even so, they could not use the packed course for the race as it was. Some of the racers already waiting for the starting signal had come from distant villages.

signalMoments.notice: Miru showed everyone that the heel prints did not lead toward the finish line, but turned back from beneath the bridge.
signalMoments.speak: Miru did not make excuses on her friend's behalf. She told everyone why she had paused the race and why they had to choose a new course.
signalMoments.protect: Miru did not leave the racers standing at the cold starting line. She had them warm themselves in nearby homes. Waiting was also a burden of the competition.

episode.afterSignal:
People protested the proposal to make a new course. Leveling the snow and moving the markers would take a long time. Her friend bit her lip too. “If you believe me, why are you erasing my footprints?”

“I believe why you went there,” Miru said. “But if you race here, your feet will sink less than everyone else's.”

Her friend did not answer. Miru and the others made a new starting line on the neighboring slope. The race began late. Her friend entrusted the puppy to someone else and started the race. She did not win.

After the race, Miru went to find her friend. “I didn't see what was under the bridge last night. I should have asked you first, but I listened to the rumors instead.”

Her friend did not smile right away. But when the puppy bit Miru's bootlace and tugged on it, she smiled a little. For a while, the two of them looked at the footprints remaining beyond the finish line.

Starting with the following year's race, Miru assigned someone separately to inspect the course at night on the eve of the race. It meant racers would not have to hide situations that called for a rescue. Even so, the hurt between the friends did not vanish all at once that day.

timeline.event: Born into a sled maker's household in Snowhill Village
Entered her first winter race
Became a race-course marker
Appointed as a judge for the Snowhill race
Repaired an old sled with her childhood friend and rode it along a short trail
Investigated footprints left during the rescue of a puppy beneath the bridge
Introduced a system for nighttime safety inspections of the course on the eve of a race
Stopped riding the short sledding trail with her friend. The two greeted each other when they met, but otherwise kept apart
Changed the spacing between course markers after listening to a racer from a distant village. Her friend felt hurt, saying Miru listened to a stranger but had been slow to listen to her
Continued keeping judges' records, but no longer took out or rode the small sled she had repaired with her friend
When it became difficult to stand in the cold for long periods, she retired from judging and used her saved wages to pay for a room in a warm southern village every winter
Returned to Snowhill in spring, but did not interfere in race rulings
In late spring of Snow Reckoning Year 156, died in her home in Snowhill Village after growing weak from poisoning on the 4th day after eating wild mushrooms from the market

memories.label: What She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: A race in which racers from far away could start on the same snow course. Because of this work, she lost days off with her friend

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The small sled she repaired with her friend in childhood

memories.label: A Lifelong Habit
memories.detail: Measuring the footprints of people she knew exactly as she measured those of strangers

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “I believe you. But let's make the course again.”

memories.label: Her Friend's View
memories.detail: “It was infuriating that she always said the correct thing. I got an apology too, but I didn't want to go sledding with her like we used to.”

memories.label: A Racer from a Distant Village Remembers
memories.detail: “Waiting was cold, but she told us why the race was delayed, so I was able to race again.”

memories.label: A Junior Judge's View
memories.detail: “After she started going south for the winter, she didn't interfere in our rulings. That made things easier for me, but on some days there was no one I could ask.”

finalMoment.place: Miru's home in Northern Snowhill Village, World of Heron
finalMoment.scene:
One morning in late spring of Snow Reckoning Year 156, 63-year-old Miru sits in her room in Snowhill Village. She has returned after spending the winter in the south. Ever since the night she ate wild mushrooms bought at the market 4 days ago, her stomach has hurt and she has vomited. She seemed a little better the next day, but afterward her strength faded again. A woman from the neighboring house enters carrying a bowl of water. “You look worse than yesterday.”

Miru says, “I have to pay for my room in the south.” The woman sets the bowl on a low table. “You're in Snowhill now. You came back in spring, remember?” Looking at her travel bundle in a corner of the room, Miru tries to stand. There is no strength in her knees, and she sits down again. Her stomach twists inside, and Miru grips the edge of the table and closes her eyes for a while.

The woman opens the window for her. Outside, meltwater drips from the edge of the roof beneath the eaves. Even after opening her eyes, Miru stares at her familiar room for a long time. “This... is my house, isn't it?” The woman says it is and moves the bowl of water closer to Miru's hand. Miru moves her head slightly, as if she heard, but does not take the bowl.

Miru reaches toward the bowl, then lowers her hand onto the table. Her eyes, fixed on the open window, close briefly. When the woman calls her name, she opens them again but cannot focus. Her breaths continue softly, then the pauses between them grow longer. The woman takes Miru's wrist and calls her once more. Miru does not open her eyes again, and her chest no longer moves.
finalMoment.afterword: Miru died at age 63 in her home in Snowhill Village in late spring of Snow Reckoning Year 156, on the 4th day after eating poisonous wild mushrooms. The type of mushroom and the exact changes within her body are unknown. The neighbor who brought her water was beside her at the end. Even after hearing the news, her old friend said they had never returned to the days when they went sledding as they once had. She remembered both the day Miru apologized and the year Miru had been slow to listen to her. To the racer from a distant village, Miru was the person who explained why the race had been delayed. The junior judge said that after Miru stepped down, they could stand by their own rulings, but there were also days when no one was there to ask. The Record of Past Lives closes this account with both the fairness Miru tried to uphold and the distance she left between herself and someone close to her, as well as the later years of her life when she spent every winter elsewhere.
finalMoment.artAlt: A diagonal view through the open window into a small room in Snowhill Village in late spring of Snow Reckoning Year 156. 63-year-old Miru tries to sit upright in a chair, but weakness makes her brace herself against the edge of a table as a neighbor sets down a bowl of water. There are no race markers, sled, puppy, supporting arms, or third-person running composition

card.name: Narin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Narin, a tailor in Dalsil Alley. When someone’s shadow tore, you stitched it together with needle and thread, but you always hid your own shadow beneath the worktable.
card.title: The Shadow That Shrunk a Handspan at a Time
card.world: An alley where shadows are sewn like cloth
card.flavor: Strange Fairy Tale
card.opening: Your customers’ shadows grew longer, while yours alone became a handspan shorter every night.
card.life: In Dalsil Alley, people said that when a shadow wore thin, it felt like stepping on a cold floor. So your customers would not have to wait, you would cut off a little from the end of your own shadow and use it as a patch. No one noticed, and you told yourself it was fine.
card.turn: One winter evening, a customer ordered a huge shadow large enough to cover their entire body. You picked up your scissors, but the shadow at your feet was shorter than the legs of your chair. The customer saw the black scraps beneath the worktable and asked, “Were all of these yours?”
card.decision: You said you could not complete the entire large order that day. The customer’s shadow was torn only in the middle, and its ends were sturdy. Instead of cutting your own shadow again, you stitched the torn section. The customer agreed to discuss the rest another day.
card.cost: You lost the payment for the large order, and you still felt sorry for sending the customer away. Your shortened shadow did not return all at once, either.
card.after: As you closed the shop, you gathered the scraps from beneath the worktable one by one. The next morning, your shadow on the floor was still small, but this time the scissors were not pointed toward it.
card.presentEcho: No matter how much you want to help, perhaps kindness does not require you to give away your share as well.
card.secondLook: The customer had never asked for clothes made from your shadow. In your wish to finish quickly, you had decided on that price all by yourself.
card.unresolved: The shortened shadow did not return anytime soon. Years later, even while teaching your apprentice the craft, you did not let the apprentice help make decisions about the shop, and the apprentice left to open a shop of their own.
card.readerQuestion: What would you like to ask the other person before you give something up first?

signalMoments.repair: Instead of cutting another new piece, you brought the torn edges of the customer’s shadow together. The sturdy parts could still be joined and used.
signalMoments.release: You set the scissors down on the worktable. For a moment, you also let go of the need to finish a magnificent garment that day.
signalMoments.speak: You said, “I can’t cut any more from my shadow right now.” Only then did the customer look down at the floor.

identity.region: Tailors’ Street in Dalsil Alley, Dalsil City
identity.summary: Narin was a tailor who cut pieces from her own shadow for her customers. Even after she became unable to endure the cold for long, she would not let go of her shop, driving a wedge between herself and her apprentice.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Narin · Female
Dalsil World, Silryeok Era, Years 121–187 · Age 66
Tailors’ Street, Dalsil City
Work · Shadow Tailor
Life · As the price of cutting and using her own shadow, she lost the ability to endure the cold for long. Even so, she would not let go of decision-making in her shop, so her apprentice left, and Narin eventually sold the shop.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She gave customers even what belonged to her, but rarely trusted anyone else with decisions about the shop.
Liked · Her master’s spool of black thread and the busy sounds in the shop before winter
Disliked · Orders to remake everything without even looking at what was torn
Skilled at · Finding with her fingertips where a seam would split

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Those close to her · Her first master, neighboring tailors, and the apprentice who worked with her for a time
What she treasured · The old scissors from her independent shop
What she wanted · To run her own shop herself for as long as her body allowed
Worry · That if she took on less work, her fellow tailors and customers would stop seeking her out

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Narin, a shadow tailor in Dalsil Alley. People there said that when a shadow wore thin, it felt like walking barefoot on a cold floor. Let me tell you the story of the winter when Narin’s shadow became unusually short.

A tailor would loop black thread through the torn edges of a shadow and stitch them together. If the seam was too wide, it would split open again when the customer walked. So her customers would not have to wait, Narin would cut a little from the end of her own shadow and use it as a patch. “It will grow back anyway,” she would say, but the shadow at Narin’s feet grew a handspan shorter every night.

One winter evening, a large order arrived. The customer wanted a long, thick shadow that would cover their entire body. They promised to pay generously if Narin finished it before daybreak. Narin brought out new thread. But when she spread out the customer’s shadow, she saw that it was torn only in the middle. Its ends were still sturdy.

“Does the whole thing need to be remade?” Narin asked.

“I’d like it to be warmer,” the customer replied.

Out of habit, Narin’s scissors pointed toward the shadow at her own feet. Beneath the worktable was a pile of black pieces she had secretly cut away. The customer saw the scraps and bent down. “Were all of those yours?”

Narin stopped her scissors. Her shadow was shorter than the legs of her chair. The customer had believed they had come to buy a new shadow. They had never imagined that Narin would cut up her own to make it.

signalMoments.repair: Narin brought the two torn edges of the customer’s shadow together. Without cutting any more from her own shadow, she could join the sturdy parts and keep using them.
signalMoments.release: Narin withdrew her promise to make a new shadow overnight. That day, she could do no more than mend the tear.
signalMoments.speak: Narin said, “I can’t cut any more from my shadow right now.” Only then did the customer look back and forth between Narin’s feet and the space beneath the worktable.

episode.afterSignal:
The customer was disappointed for a moment. “But I have to go out into the cold.”

Narin spread out the customer’s shadow again. She stitched the torn section with thick thread, then walked several steps with the customer to make sure it would not split when they moved. It was not a completely new shadow, but it softened the feeling of the cold floor. The customer agreed to discuss the rest another day.

Narin did not receive the payment for the large order. After closing the shop, she gathered the scraps from beneath the worktable. She set aside the pieces that could be reattached and recorded the ones already worn out in her ledger as having been used for customers. Her own shadow did not return at once.

The next day, a new customer opened the door. Narin first spread that person’s shadow across the floor. “Which part is bothering you?” The customer pointed to a single tiny hole. Narin took out only as much thread as she needed.

Narin continued mending other people’s shadows after that. She made large garments too. But first she asked what the customer wanted and what they truly needed. And if an order required her to cut away even the shadow at her own feet, she said she could not do it.

timeline.event: Born in Sewing Alley, Dalsil City
Began apprenticing as a shadow tailor
Set up her first independent worktable
Received her master’s spool of black thread and expanded her business into a shop that also took small repair jobs
Began cutting and using her own shadow for customers’ orders
Revealed that she did not have enough of her own shadow to complete a large winter order
Started a materials exchange gathering for tailors
Her shadow did not return to its former length, making it difficult for her to walk outside on winter evenings
Taught repairs to the young apprentice in her shop but did not let the apprentice set material prices or choose which customers to accept
Refused when the apprentice asked to run the shop together. With the wages they had saved, the apprentice rented a small worktable in another alley and struck out independently
Sold the shop to a neighboring tailor after becoming unable to manage the work during the cold season
Lived in a small room in Dalsil Alley and hardly went out in winter. She had no contact with the apprentice who had opened a shop in another alley
In the depths of winter in Silryeok Year 187, died after breathing in fumes from a charcoal fire in her closed room in Dalsil Alley

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: Her independent shop in Dalsil Alley, which bore not only her customers’ names but her own

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The worn scissors from her first independent shop and the spool of black thread her master gave her

memories.label: A Lifelong Habit
memories.detail: Feeling the torn spot by hand before cutting new cloth

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Before you tell me whether I can give you more, please tell me what is bothering you.”

memories.label: The Winter Customer’s View
memories.detail: “At first, I was angry that she refused even though I was paying her. Only later did I understand what she had been about to cut up and use.”

memories.label: The Apprentice’s Memory
memories.detail: “I learned how to make repairs. But when it came to setting prices, she always listened to me last. I used the wages I’d saved to rent a worktable in another alley.”

memories.label: The Neighboring Tailor’s View
memories.detail: “In the depths of winter, the cold affected her so badly she couldn’t go outside. But until she sold the shop, she still tried to make every decision about the customers’ work herself.” The next day, the tailor brought the water they had promised and found Narin’s room silent when she called.

finalMoment.place: Narin’s small room in Dalsil Alley, Dalsil World
finalMoment.scene:
On a midwinter evening in Silryeok Year 187, sixty-six-year-old Narin is alone in her small room in Dalsil Alley. The neighboring tailor who bought her shop eight years earlier comes to return a bowl borrowed that afternoon. “I’ll bring warm water tomorrow.” Narin takes the bowl from inside the doorway and answers, “Please leave it outside the door.” The neighbor returns to their shop. The apprentice who opened a shop in another alley does not visit that day.

Narin adds more charcoal to the small brazier on its stone stand. Because of the short shadow at her feet, she has difficulty standing on the cold floor for long. When wind slips in through a gap in the window, Narin closes it and soaks beans in water for her evening meal. After a while, her head begins to throb. Narin sets the bowl down and tries sitting, but her stomach churns. There is no burning smell in the room.

As the night deepens, Narin rises to open the window a little. When she stands, the floor seems to tilt, and she puts a hand against the wall. Although the window latch is right in front of her, her fingers keep missing it. “The window…” Narin says, but only the sound of footsteps passes through the alley. She tries to pull the latch again, but the strength drains from her hand. Narin follows the wall down and sits beneath the window.

Narin thinks she should go to the door. But for a moment, she cannot tell which way the door is. She tries to raise her knees, but her legs will not move. The charcoal in the room is still glowing red, and the window remains closed. Narin tries once more to stand, then closes her eyes. Soon afterward, she reaches a state in which she can no longer answer even when her name is called. No one is beside her when her breathing stops that night.
finalMoment.afterword: Narin died at sixty-six in the depths of winter in Silryeok Year 187, after breathing in fumes produced by burning charcoal in her closed room in Dalsil Alley. The neighboring tailor who had bought her shop brought the promised water the next day. When Narin did not answer, the tailor entered the room. The neighbor remembered both the Narin who had tried to set every price herself until she sold the shop and the Narin who had struggled to leave her room during her final winter. The apprentice came after hearing the news but did not say that the two of them had ever worked together again. The apprentice carried both the repair techniques Narin had taught them and the years of being shut out of decisions. The Record of Past Lives does not bind the shrinking of Narin’s shadow and the way she blocked another person’s choices to protect her shop into a single lesson. It simply records the end of this life.
finalMoment.artAlt: On a winter night in Silryeok Year 187 in Dalsil World, the view looks down from high above the alley and diagonally through the window of a small room. Narin, age 66, is dizzy, bracing herself against the wall as she tries to open the latch of the closed window. A small charcoal brazier stands behind her, and Narin is alone.

card.name: Aram
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Aram, the weighkeeper of Blue Spring Underwater Market. Even amid the currents, you tried to measure each person's fair share.
card.title: The Scale with Nothing on It
card.world: A market open beneath clear water
card.flavor: Underwater commotion
card.opening: When one side of an empty scale suddenly sank, the people in the market began searching for an invisible thief.
card.life: At Blue Spring Market, shells and glass beads were placed on underwater scales to set their value. Every morning, you cleaned even beneath the pans and calibrated the weights. Sometimes keeping people from quarreling was harder than reading the scale's markings.
card.turn: One day, the pan with nothing on it kept sinking. One customer suspected the person beside them and pointed at their pocket, and the accused customer grew angry and tried to leave the market. Then the cord running beneath the empty pan trembled slightly. You asked both of them to wait just a little longer.
card.decision: You did not search the customer or dismiss the scale as broken. When you lifted the little basket hanging beneath the pan, shrimp scattered out in a rush. The current had tugged at the basket where the shrimp had gathered. You showed both customers and moved the scale somewhere the current was weaker. The two customers did not make up right away.
card.cost: Trading stopped while the scale was moved. Some people left for another market, saying they could not trust its markings. You also had to admit that you had missed the basket during your morning inspection.
card.after: The next day, the basket was empty. After calibrating the scale, you looked underneath it first. When one customer laughed and asked, “Is there a thief today too?” the two of you checked the basket together.
card.presentEcho: Settling on an answer quickly may put your mind at ease, but it can keep you from seeing what lies beneath the markings.
card.secondLook: The empty pan truly was empty. The weight came not from something hidden by a customer, but from the basket beneath the scale and the current.
card.unresolved: Later, you weighed transactions for your family's shop first, causing other merchants to lose customers. You refused to change the order despite their protests and stepped down as the public weighkeeper.
card.readerQuestion: Before blaming someone, what might be waiting beneath the scale for you to lift and examine?

signalMoments.notice: Instead of looking only at the empty pan, you followed the trembling cord downward and reached beneath it to find a small basket.
signalMoments.protect: You stopped anyone from searching the angry customer's pockets and asked everyone to wait while you weighed things again.
signalMoments.connect: You asked the two quarreling customers to lift opposite sides of the scale together. Only then did the basket come into view.

identity.region: Blue Spring Underwater Market
identity.summary: Raised in a shell shop, Aram became the public weighkeeper. She once protected a customer who had been falsely accused, but later lost the market's trust by giving her family priority in line.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Aram · Female
Blue Spring World, Water Reckoning Years 66–131 · Age 65
Blue Spring Underwater Market
Work · Scale repair apprentice, public weighkeeper, shell shop worker
Life · She learned to use scales in her family's shop. After taking charge of the public scale, she protected a customer who had been falsely accused. But she later gave her family's shop priority in the transaction line and stepped down as weighkeeper.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She admitted when a scale was at fault, but bent the rules when she felt her family might suffer a loss.
Liked · The small shell weight from her family's shop and the clear morning waterways
Disliked · Hearing someone called a cheat without any proof
Good at · Repairing the knots and pans of unsteady scales

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her family at the shell shop and the merchants who used the public scale
What she treasured · The shell weight used by her family
What she wanted · To protect her family's business while remaining a trustworthy weighkeeper in the market
What worried her · If she put her family last, the shop might lose customers; if she put them first, other merchants might suffer

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Aram, the weighkeeper of Blue Spring Underwater Market. Even beneath clear water, you were the one who measured weights and set values. Let me tell you how noisy the market became on the day an empty pan sank by itself.

The people of Blue Spring sold shells and glass beads in underwater passages where they could breathe. Because of the current, the scales were tied firmly to the walls, and a small basket hung beneath each pan to catch anything that fell. Every morning, Aram cleaned the pans and weights. She was supposed to empty the basket too, but that day goods came pouring in, and she rushed.

The first transaction ended without incident. Just as the second customer was about to place some beads on the scale, the empty pan suddenly sank. Another customer pointed at the pocket of the person beside them, accusing them of hiding beads. The accused customer declared that they would leave the market.

Aram pressed down on the empty pan. When she took her hand away, it tilted again. One side was too heavy for the motion to be caused by the current alone. A thin cord trembled beneath the pan. It was the cord holding the basket. Someone might have hidden something in the basket, or Aram might have overlooked something.

signalMoments.notice: Before checking the scale's markings, Aram looked in the direction the basket cord was trembling. The cord was being pulled toward the side waterway.
signalMoments.protect: Aram stopped people from searching the customer's pockets. They agreed that no one would be called a thief until they had looked beneath the scale.
signalMoments.connect: Aram asked the two quarreling customers to lift opposite sides of the scale for a moment. As the pans rose, the small basket underneath came into view.

episode.afterSignal:
When Aram lifted the basket, tiny shrimp scattered in a rush. While the basket sat unemptied that morning, the current had swept the shrimp into it. The cord pulling on the basket had made the empty pan sink.

“Then what about that person's pocket?” one customer asked.

Aram shook her head. “There's no reason to look.”

The customer who had pointed at the pocket turned red. The two did not make up right away. Aram stopped trading and moved the scale toward a wall where the current was weaker. While she recalibrated it, several customers left for another market.

The next morning, Aram looked in the basket first. It was completely empty. The customer who had been suspected the day before returned and asked with a laugh, “No thief today?”

“Not under the scale,” Aram said. “I don't know about anywhere else.”

The two of them checked the basket together and placed new beads on the scale. Aram tended the scale for many years, watching the waterways beneath it as carefully as its markings. Admitting that the scale was wrong was embarrassing, but it had to come before falsely accusing someone.

memories.detail: Her family's shell shop and the public scale used by everyone. When the interests of the two clashed, she put her family first.

memories.label: What she treasured most
memories.detail: The small shell weight she first used in her family's shop

memories.label: A lifelong habit
memories.detail: Whenever a scale's markings wavered, checking beneath the pan before checking anyone's pockets

memories.label: Words she left behind
memories.detail: “Repairing a scale and keeping the line fair were two different things.”

memories.label: A customer's opinion
memories.detail: “I was upset that trading stopped, but she didn't search my pockets.”

memories.label: Another merchant's opinion
memories.detail: “While she weighed her family's shells first, customers wouldn't wait for our goods, and they went unsold.”

memories.label: Her family's memory
memories.detail: “When business was hard, she took our side. She had to give up her market job because of it.”

finalMoment.place: An underwater stone path from the Blue Spring World seaweed garden back to the village
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-summer afternoon in Water Reckoning Year 131, sixty-five-year-old Aram visits the seaweed garden on the market's day off. Another family member is watching the family shop. Aram spends a long while in the garden watching leaves sway in the current. As she passes beneath an old stone arch on her way home, fine stone dust falls from a crack overhead. Aram stops and looks up at the ceiling.

A powerful current suddenly surges in from the side channel. Seaweed clinging to the wall flattens in one direction, and Aram's blue scarf slips loose from her shoulder. A crack in the stone arch spreads, and a heavy stone slab tilts downward. Aram looks back to see if anyone is following her. The path is empty. Bracing one hand against the wall, Aram takes one step back in the opposite direction.

The slab comes down first. Aram ducks her head, but the stone's edge strikes her head and shoulder. Her body is driven to the floor, and her legs become trapped beneath the slab. She can breathe even underwater, but the pressure makes it hard to expand her chest. Aram tries to push the slab away with both hands. The stone does not move. Rough sand clings to her palms. Her loosened scarf drifts before her eyes.

Aram sees the light beyond the path and reaches out again. Her fingertips slip from the slab's edge. “Here...” Her voice is faint. Her head spins until she can barely tell the wall from the floor. The hands pushing against the stone one last time fall still. Aram loses consciousness there and dies soon afterward. No one is beside her.
finalMoment.afterword: Aram died at sixty-five in the late summer of Water Reckoning Year 131, when a ceiling slab collapsed along an old underwater stone path as she returned alone from the seaweed garden. When she had not returned by evening, her family followed the path in search of her and found Aram beneath the collapsed arch. They were grateful that Aram had weighed their transactions first when the shop was struggling, but they also remembered the day she lost her position as weighkeeper because of it. Another merchant spoke both of the time Aram stopped people from searching a customer's pockets and of the time she pushed that merchant's business to the back of the line. The record of her past life preserves those two judgments side by side. Aram's life held the time she spent repairing the market's scales, the time she spent looking after her family's business, and afternoons resting in the seaweed garden on her days off. That life ended on the stone path home.
finalMoment.artAlt: Viewed from a low angle near the floor of a Blue Spring underwater stone path in Water Reckoning Year 131. Sixty-five-year-old Aram is alone, one hand braced against the wall as she tries to step back, while a large slab falls from the cracked ceiling and her blue scarf whips in the current. No one is there to support her or run for help.

card.name: Gaon
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Gaon, a fireworks artisan from Seoritgol Festival Village. You were skilled at making sky flowers, but your shoulders always flinched first at the initial boom.
card.title: The Artisan Who Feared the First Boom
card.world: A valley where a winter festival is held
card.flavor: Laughter and small acts of courage
card.opening: While everyone waited for the biggest firework, you, who had made it, covered your ears first.
card.life: You knew better than anyone which colors would show up well in the night sky. But you never got used to the first boom. When your assistant saw you cover your ears, she began making small lanterns that could be lit quietly whenever she had time.
card.turn: On the day of the festival, the rain arrived earlier than forecast. The equipment was too wet to launch the large fireworks, and the people staring at the sky began to murmur. That was when your assistant brought out the lanterns she had kept covered with cloth. Just as she silently tried to light one, a goat behind the stage sneezed loudly. It was such a funny first sound after all that waiting that everyone lowered their heads and laughed.
card.decision: You did not pretend that the large fireworks would soon go up. After saying they could not be launched that day, you introduced the lanterns as your assistant's work. Together, you placed a small light into each person's hands. There were no sky flowers, but lights moved all across the square.
card.cost: The people who had expected large fireworks were disappointed. The most spectacular sight at that year's festival was not your work, but your assistant's. You chose to make that fact clear.
card.after: After the festival, you dried the wet equipment. The canceled fireworks had still cost money in materials, and you still owed several people an apology. Sodam folded a lantern and handed it to you.
card.presentEcho: Even something you are good at can have a frightening moment. Finding another way together may not be the same as running away.
card.secondLook: You clung to the large fireworks not because you liked the noise, but because you did not want to disappoint the people waiting. Your assistant's lanterns showed you another path that did not require abandoning that feeling.
card.unresolved: Later, as the lantern procession grew longer, you borrowed paper and money from your family's workshop to win visitors back with large fireworks. There were fewer orders than expected, so you could not repay everything, and Sodam opened a lantern workshop of her own.
card.readerQuestion: Who could you share one frightening part of something you love with?

signalMoments.protect: You did not rush to use the wet equipment. You first told the waiting crowd that the plan had changed.
signalMoments.connect: You said to Sodam, “Let's hand out the lanterns together.” The two of you began passing the lights around from the far side of the square.
signalMoments.speak: Pointing at the goat, you said, “I didn't make the first sound this year.” When the laughter died down, you also explained why the large fireworks had been canceled.

identity.region: Seoritgol Festival Village in the northern Seoritgol Valley
identity.summary: Raised in a paper workshop, Gaon became a fireworks artisan. Even after the festival changed, she insisted on large fireworks, leaving her workshop and Sodam to bear the costs.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Gaon, a fireworks artisan from Seoritgol. Though you were skilled at making enormous sky flowers, your shoulders always flinched first at the initial boom. Let me tell you about the day the rain arrived before the festival.

People gathered in the festival square to watch the night sky. Gaon checked the lids of the firework canisters, then checked them again. Beside her, her assistant Sodam arranged small lanterns wrapped in cloth. Knowing that Gaon feared the first boom, Sodam had made them whenever she had time.

Just before sunset, rain poured down. The outsides of the firework canisters were wet, and the ignition fuses had grown damp. Gaon immediately closed the lids. If she launched the large fireworks with this equipment, there was no telling when they would ignite or which way they would shoot. But everyone in the square was staring up at the sky.

“Can't you launch just one?” a child asked.

Gaon opened her mouth, then closed it. Some people had come from distant valleys to see that year's fireworks. Meanwhile, Sodam pulled away the cloth and brought out the small lanterns. As she tried to light the first one, a goat behind the stage sneezed thunderously. Everyone looked up, thinking it was the first firecracker, then saw the goat and laughed. Amid that laughter, a single small lantern came to life.

signalMoments.protect: After checking the wet ignition fuse again, Gaon told the crowd that the large fireworks could not be launched. Speaking directly to the people who had waited came first.
signalMoments.connect: Gaon said to Sodam, “Let's hand out the lanterns together.” The two of them began passing the lights around from the far side of the square.
signalMoments.speak: Pointing at the goat, Gaon said, “I didn't make the first sound this year.” When the laughter died down, she also explained why the large fireworks had been canceled.

episode.afterSignal:
The people who had expected fireworks were disappointed. Some took their lanterns and went home early. Still, those who remained in the square each accepted one of Sodam's lanterns. The light did not soar into the sky, but passed from one person's hands to another's.

“Today, you're the artisan,” Gaon said to Sodam.

Sodam laughed, then asked, “What about the large fireworks next time?”

“We can launch them once they dry. We'll put out your lanterns then, too.”

After the festival, Gaon dried all the wet equipment again. The canceled fireworks had still cost money in materials, and she still owed several people an apology. Sodam folded a lantern and handed it to Gaon. The small light made no sound.

Gaon continued making sky flowers after that. Her habit of flinching at the first boom did not easily disappear. But by placing her apprentice's quiet lights alongside them at the festival, she could create a night that she, too, wanted to watch to the end.

Gaon stopped making large fireworks but did not join Sodam's lantern workshop
On afternoons without work, she began visiting a small hot spring below the valley and soaking her hands in the warm water
