memories.detail: “Even when she didn't talk about work, she would soak her hands in the water and sit there for a long time. She came and went alone on her last day, too.”

finalMoment.place: The stone path leading back to the village from the hot spring below the valley in Seoritgol World
finalMoment.scene:
On an early-spring afternoon in Festival Calendar Year 121, 64-year-old Gaon leaves the small hot spring below the valley. She has just finished soaking her hands until they grew warm. The hot spring keeper says, “The path is muddy. Take it slowly.” Gaon nods and climbs the stone path toward the village alone. After giving up large fireworks, she often came here to rest for a while on days when she had no work.

Water drips from the steep snowy slope above the stone path. The day has grown warmer at midday, leaving the snow wet. As Gaon passes below the slope, she hears a sharp crack. The instant she looks up, clumps of snow and wet earth rush down together. Gaon tries to run toward a large boulder off the path, but the heavy snow strikes her legs first. Her body is shoved sideways, and the walking stick she used to steady herself on the path slips from her hand.

Beneath the snow, Gaon bends her arms and tries to make a pocket in front of her face. The wet snow presses down on her shoulders and chest, keeping her elbows from moving. There is a small empty space before her mouth, but powdery snow enters each time she breathes in. Gaon tries reaching one hand upward. Her fingertips touch nothing but cold, packed snow. Even the sound of water on the path now seems very far away.

Gaon forces her arms once more. Her chest is pinned, and she cannot draw a full breath. She tries to think whether she can make it back to the hot spring, but her vision darkens. Several shallow breaths follow, then stop. On the stone path below the snowy slope, only the walking stick Gaon dropped is visible. No one is beside her when she dies beneath the snow.
finalMoment.afterword: Gaon died at 64 in the early spring of Festival Calendar Year 121, buried in a wet avalanche while returning alone from the hot spring below the valley. When Gaon had not returned by nightfall, her family asked at the hot spring. The hot spring keeper and the villagers searched the path and found the fallen walking stick and Gaon. The hot spring keeper remembered the afternoons when Gaon sat with her hands in the warm water without talking about work. Her family remembered both the money for the paper they never recovered and the days Gaon repaired paper in the workshop. Sodam remembered both the mentor who proudly showed off her lanterns and the mentor who later saw them as competition. After Sodam became independent, the two never worked in the same workshop again. The record of past lives does not describe this accident as punishment for an old debt. Gaon's life held both the years when she made fireworks and the afternoons she spent resting at the hot spring after she stopped, and that life ended on a stone path she was walking alone.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high-angle diagonal view of a stone path in Seoritgol Valley in the early spring of Festival Calendar Year 121. While returning alone from the hot spring, 64-year-old Gaon sees wet snow collapsing down the steep snowy slope and turns her body. No one is supporting her or running to seek help

card.name: Seohu
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Seohu, the gatekeeper of Glass Forest. You stood watch for years before a transparent house, but never once examined the path that led around the back.
card.title: Gatekeeper of the Doorless House
card.world: A forest where a transparent house stood among the trees
card.flavor: A role-reversing mystery
card.opening: A lost child was the first to discover that the house you had guarded for years had no door.
card.life: You stood in front of the house and asked visitors their names. When you first took the job, you were told, “Guard the front,” and you believed it was your duty never to leave that spot. A seam in the glass looked like a door, but it had never opened.
card.turn: A child asking for directions walked around the house, then waved from inside. The house had walls only at the front and on both sides; the side facing the forest was wide open. People coming for the storehouse were already entering and leaving that way. What you had been guarding was not the way in, but the name given to one path.
card.decision: You did not scold the child. You left the front and walked around to the back of the house. With a storehouse worker, you put up markers along the path from front to back, and told visitors that you had given people the wrong directions before. One person grew angry, remembering the day they had been forced to take a long detour.
card.cost: You could not meet again with everyone you had turned away over the years. The post you had guarded for so long also stood empty, and you had to relearn the unfamiliar forest paths behind the house. You had to let go of the belief that you alone knew everyone who came and went.
card.after: When the child returned the next day, you were standing by the open path behind the house. The child asked, “Aren’t you a gatekeeper today?” and you replied, “I’m telling people which way to go.”
card.presentEcho: Even when something you have done for years feels like your entire identity, you can carry the same intention into a different place.
card.secondLook: People had not been sneaking into the house. The open path had always been there while you guarded only the front.
card.unresolved: You continued working at the storehouse for some time, but at 51, you chose a home by the river with Yeoul and left the storehouse. While you learned the new craft of basketmaking, the storehouse workers had to cover the vacancy you left behind.
card.readerQuestion: Where in my life can I make a change without abandoning the desire to protect what matters?

signalMoments.notice: You saw footprints showing that the child had not passed through the glass wall, but had gone around by the open forest path behind the house.
signalMoments.explore: You left the front post where you had always stood and walked around the house. The back path was wider than you had imagined.
signalMoments.connect: You asked a storehouse worker which path they used to bring in the goods. The worker pointed to the back path they had always used.

identity.region: Transparent House Forest Path, Eastern Glass Forest
identity.summary: Raised in a woodworking village, Seohu took charge of the communal storehouse. He continued working there for some time after discovering the back path, and later chose a life making baskets with Yeoul by the river.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Seohu · Male
Glass Forest World, Forest Calendar, Years 104–169 · Age 65
Transparent House Forest Path, Eastern Glass Forest
Work · Supply carrier, communal storehouse guide, basketmaker
Life · Raised in a woodworking village, he took charge of the transparent-house storehouse. He continued working at the storehouse after discovering the back path, but at 51, he moved to the riverside with his partner Yeoul and made baskets.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He tried to stay faithfully at one post for years, but when choosing a home with Yeoul, he let go of the work he knew.
Liked · The smell of wood in the woodworking village and forest paths in the early morning
Disliked · Turning visitors away without even asking their destination
Skilled at · Carrying bundles of medicinal herbs and seeds without damaging them

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
People close to him · Yeoul, who made baskets by the river; his family in the woodworking village; and his former storehouse coworkers
Treasured possession · A forest-path ledger repaired and reused many times
Hope · To learn a new craft with his own hands in the home he shared with Yeoul
Worry · That if he left the storehouse, nothing would remain of him but the routes he had spent years learning

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Seohu, the gatekeeper of Glass Forest. You stood at the front of a transparent house, asking visitors their names and giving directions. But the house you guarded had no front door. This is the story of the day a child discovered that truth.

When Seohu first took the job, the manager told him, “Guard the front.” The glass house was a communal storehouse where medicinal herbs and seeds were dried. A seam in the front glass looked like a door, but Seohu had never once opened it. On days when the door seemed locked, he sent people away. He believed it was his job to know who entered the storehouse.

On a day of thick fog, a lost child arrived. The child said they needed to deliver a bundle of medicinal herbs to their mother inside. Seohu asked the child's name and examined the seam in the glass. It had no lock and no handle.

“You can't go in today.”

The child said they would walk around the house. Seohu hesitated, saying he could not leave the post he guarded, and the child vanished into the fog. A moment later, the child waved from inside the house. Seohu was startled. A storehouse worker was standing behind the child.

signalMoments.notice: Seohu realized that the child had not passed through the glass, but had followed the footprints they had left in the wet soil beside the house and gone around.
signalMoments.explore: Seohu left the front post he had guarded for years and walked around the house. There had never been a glass wall at the back, and the forest path continued straight inside.
signalMoments.connect: Seohu asked the worker inside which path they used to bring in the goods. The worker pointed to the back path they had always used.

episode.afterSignal:
The back of the house was wide open. The storehouse had been built that way to let the wind pass through. The front was a marker showing visitors where to find it, while the path for bringing in goods was behind it. The front post Seohu had guarded was not useless, but from that one spot, he had believed he knew the entire house.

“What about the people who came before?” the child asked. “You told them they couldn't go in.”

Seohu could not answer right away. Some of the people he had sent away had probably returned. Others probably had not been able to.

With a storehouse worker, he put up markers along the path from front to back. They also marked the stretches where people might trip over roots after dark. Then he told visitors to the storehouse that he had given people the wrong directions before. A few laughed in disbelief, and one person grew angry, bringing up the day they had been forced to take a long detour.

When the child returned the next day, Seohu was standing by the open path behind the house.

“Aren't you a gatekeeper today?”

“I'm telling people which way to go.”

Seohu continued working at the storehouse after that. He still asked visitors their names, but first he asked where they were trying to go. Now that he had left the post he had guarded for years, there were many new forest paths he needed to learn.

memories.label: What He Treasured Most
memories.detail: The first clumsy basket handle Yeoul taught him to make

memories.label: A Habit He Kept for Years

finalMoment.place: Seohu and Yeoul's home by the river in eastern Glass Forest
finalMoment.scene:
At dawn in early autumn of Forest Calendar Year 169, 65-year-old Seohu wakes in his riverside home in eastern Glass Forest. He has had a fever for 3 days, and his cough has not stopped. Yeoul has listened to him coughing all night from the adjoining room. Seohu rises from the low bed and opens the window. Fog lies low over the river. He breathes in the cold air, but it does not feel as if it reaches the inside of his chest.

“Would you like some water?” Yeoul picks up a bowl in the room. Seohu nods and places one hand on the windowsill. He takes a sip of water, but a cough makes him set the bowl down. Yeoul wipes his forehead with a damp cloth. “Stay in bed today.” Seohu tries to answer, then pauses to catch his breath. He looks again at the river beyond the window. It is the waterway they have watched every morning since finding this home.

Seohu turns to go back to bed. It is only a few steps away, but he has to stop for breath twice. Yeoul pulls a chair over from beside the door. Seohu sits and hunches his shoulders. His coughing continues, and every time he inhales, a rough sound rises from his throat. “Yeoul, the window...” he says. Yeoul points to the open window. Seohu cannot say anything more to explain whether he wants it closed or left open.

Yeoul sets down the bowl and calls Seohu's name. Seohu tries to raise a hand toward the windowsill, but his arm stops halfway. He can hear the riverside birds, but Yeoul's next words are faint. His breaths grow shorter and shorter. Seohu leans back against the chair and closes his eyes. When Yeoul calls his name again, he does not answer. A short while later, the sound of his breathing also stops.
finalMoment.afterword: Seohu died at 65 in early autumn of Forest Calendar Year 169, at his riverside home in eastern Glass Forest, after 3 days of fever and coughing left him struggling to breathe. No record remains of exactly what illness he had. Yeoul, who was beside him, remembered how Seohu kept looking toward the river through the open window until the end. His former storehouse coworkers benefited from the path ledger Seohu left behind, but they also spoke of the time when they had to handle more visitors until someone new was found. A visitor he had once wrongly turned away said that even after receiving an apology, the long detour they had walked that day remained. The Record of Past Lives includes the days Seohu spent with Yeoul by the river after leaving the storehouse. Even on the dawn when he died, the window they had opened together faced the river.
finalMoment.artAlt: At dawn in early autumn of Forest Calendar Year 169, the open window of a house by the river in eastern Glass Forest is seen at an angle. Seohu, age 65, sits with one hand braced on the windowsill, gazing at the river as fever and coughing leave him struggling to breathe. Yeoul watches from deeper inside the room, holding a bowl of water, with space between them.

card.name: On
card.identityLine: In that life, you were On, the calendar keeper of Four Seasons Village. Whenever anyone asked about the seasons, you answered before the great calendar—but that day, the calendar deceived you first.
card.title: The Missing Page of Autumn
card.world: a village that turns the pages of a great calendar with each season
card.flavor: light horror and discovery
card.opening: When a page of autumn vanished from the calendar, the village began preparing for winter while the weather was still hot.
card.life: In this village, people turned the pages of the great calendar to decide when to sow seeds and when to gather firewood. You checked the dates so often that the corners of the paper wore down. Sometimes, it seemed that people trusted the calendar more than they trusted you.
card.turn: When you opened the page after summer that morning, you found a picture of a snow-covered winter. People shut their storehouses and hurried to pick unripe fruit. You were afraid that autumn had truly disappeared. But the trees outside the window still held green fruit, and a scrap of brown paper remained where a page had been torn from the calendar's metal rings.
card.decision: You hesitated, afraid you might be wrong alone, but you rang the bell and gathered the villagers. “I may be wrong. Even so, please look at the trees with me.” Together, you examined the trees, the wind, and the fruit that remained. You decided to continue preparing for winter but delay picking the fruit for a few days.
card.cost: The unripe fruit already picked could not be put back, and because you rang the bell, the village's work stopped for a while. Not everyone believed what you said.
card.after: That night, a child brought back the missing autumn page. The child had borrowed it to press fallen leaves into bookmarks, then had been too afraid to say so. Before putting the page back, you hung it beneath a tree. People looked at the calendar and the real leaves together.
card.presentEcho: When the record in my hands seems strange, it may take courage to speak about what I have seen for myself.
card.secondLook: Autumn had not vanished by magic. The people who lived by the dates had simply lost sight of the season outside their windows for a while.
card.unresolved: Later, because you did not transfer the farmers' observations onto the calendar, you had to share the key to the calendar room. You also lost some fruit in your older sister's orchard by insisting on a harvest date.
card.readerQuestion: When everyone is looking at the same piece of paper, what scene have I checked for myself?

signalMoments.notice: Before the calendar's winter picture, you noticed the scrap of brown paper left on the metal rings and the green fruit outside the window.
signalMoments.speak: Without hiding your uncertainty, you said, “I may be wrong, but please look at the trees with me.”
signalMoments.explore: You left the calendar room and walked through the fields and storehouses. The air in those other places did not match the paper.

identity.region: Central Four Seasons Village
identity.summary: On grew up in a papermaking household and became the village calendar keeper. After clashing with people over the seasons, she left the calendar room and lived with her older sister, helping tend a small orchard.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
On · Female
Four Seasons World, Calendar Era 206–271 · Age 65
Central Four Seasons Village
Work · Calendar repair apprentice, calendar keeper, orchard worker
Life · She grew up in a papermaking household and took charge of the village calendar. After the autumn page went missing, she disputed control of the calendar room with the farmers. At fifty, she left the job and went to live with her older sister in a small orchard.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She corrected inaccurate records, but when others questioned her judgment, it took her a long time to listen to them.
Liked · The smell of new paper and the slow changes of ripening fruit
Disliked · People changing dates on the calendar without going through her
Skilled at · Mending the torn corners of the calendar

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her older sister, who made paper; the children of the calendar room; and the farmers with whom she disagreed
What she treasured · The first fruit she tended with her older sister in the orchard
What she hoped for · For her records to help the village
Worry · That people would no longer believe her

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were On, the calendar keeper of Four Seasons Village. The villagers turned the pages of the great calendar to decide when to sow seeds and when to gather firewood. Let me tell you the story of the morning when a page of autumn went missing.

Every day, On smoothed the calendar's corners by hand and checked the date. That morning, when she turned the last page of summer, she found a picture of a snow-covered winter. A page bearing autumn's picture and dates had vanished.

The village erupted into confusion. Some people believed that the calendar's pictures summoned the seasons. The storehouse keeper closed the doors, and the farmers began picking fruit that had not yet ripened. On searched behind the calendar. The missing page was not there.

“Has the whole of autumn disappeared?” a child asked.

For a moment, On was afraid too. Every year, the village turned the great calendar on the same day. But the fruit on the trees outside the window was still green. The wind was not cold either. A scrap of torn brown paper clung to one of the calendar's metal rings. It was proof that a sheet of paper had disappeared, not a season.

People carrying unripe fruit they had already picked were entering the marketplace. If On was wrong, she would have stopped everyone's work for nothing. But if she said nothing, even more fruit would fall.

signalMoments.notice: On showed them both the brown paper left on the metal ring and the green fruit outside the window. Torn edges marked the empty place in the calendar.
signalMoments.speak: On rang the village bell and said, “I may be wrong. Even so, please look at the trees with me.”
signalMoments.explore: On left the calendar room and walked through the fields and storehouses. Unlike the paper's winter picture, the soil was warm and the fruit was still firm.

episode.afterSignal:
The people gathered beneath the trees. There was no need to stop all preparations for winter, but they decided to delay picking more fruit. The storehouse keeper opened the doors again. The unripe fruit already picked could not be put back.

When night fell, a child came carrying the autumn page, dried and stuck together, against their chest. The child had removed it from the calendar to try pressing fallen leaves like bookmarks, then had been too frightened to admit it. On had the child sit down first. “If you wanted to borrow it, you should have said so. It's a calendar we all use.”

The child admitted the mistake too. On did not put the page back at once. After smoothing and drying the wet part, she hung it beside a tree the next morning. People looked at the picture of autumn and the real leaves together.

For several days, the people who had picked the unripe fruit searched for ways to dry and eat it. On helped with the work. She believed she also bore responsibility for ringing the bell and stopping the village's work.

On continued turning the calendar's pages afterward. But before turning a page, she formed a habit of looking out the window once and asking anyone who came to consult the calendar what the fields looked like now.

memories.detail: At first, the calendar room; later, the small orchard where she lived with her older sister

memories.label: What She Treasured Most

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Let's leave that tree a few more days. You decide for your own trees, Sister.”

memories.label: The Farmer Who Picked the Fruit

memories.label: The Child's Memory

memories.label: Her Older Sister's Memory

finalMoment.place: The courtyard of a small teahouse in the spring marketplace of a central village in the Four Seasons World
finalMoment.scene:
On a spring afternoon in Calendar Era 271, sixty-five-year-old On is sitting with her older sister at a small teahouse in the Four Seasons Village marketplace. It is their day off from orchard work. When her sister asks for another cup of tea, On rises to pay. Beside the teahouse courtyard, a laden mule is tied to a post. On passes behind the mule on her way to the teahouse keeper.

A metal kettle slips from the teahouse keeper's hands and strikes the stone floor with a loud clang. Startled, the mule twists and raises its hind leg. On hears the sound and turns, but there is no time to dodge. The mule's hoof strikes her side, and On is thrown backward, hitting her head on the stone floor. Her older sister's teacup trembles on the table.

On tries to raise herself. Her side hurts, and the metallic ringing seems to continue in her ears. She braces one hand against the floor, but there is no strength in her arm. Her older sister comes closer and asks, “On, can you hear me?” On turns her eyes toward her sister. “The kettle...” On says. Her sister checks that the mule is tied to the post, then sits beside On.

On looks up at a tree in bloom. The petals and the edge of the roof appear doubled and overlap. She tries to steady her breathing, but no more words come. Her older sister calls her name again. On moves her fingers slightly toward her sister's hand. Soon her eyes close, and her arm stops moving. On loses consciousness in the teahouse courtyard and dies.
finalMoment.afterword: In the spring of Calendar Era 271, On died at sixty-five after a startled pack mule kicked her in the side and she struck her head on the stone floor of a marketplace teahouse where she had gone to rest with her older sister. Her sister, who was beside her, remembered On's final afternoon, when she had risen first and offered to pay for the tea. The two of them had tended the orchard together, but they did not pretend the year when On lost fruit they could have sold by insisting on a harvest date had never happened. One farmer remembered both the day On's bell stopped them from picking more unripe fruit and the later day when his observation marks were left off the calendar. In the Record of Past Lives, the On who made both choices and the On who went out for tea with her older sister remain the same person. That spring afternoon at the teahouse was the end of On's life.
finalMoment.artAlt: Viewed from above the roof of a teahouse in the spring marketplace of Four Seasons Village in Calendar Era 271. Sixty-five-year-old On turns to evade the hind legs of a pack mule startled by the sound of a metal kettle hitting the ground, while her older sister sits at a tea table a few steps away. The moment is just before impact; it is not a scene of someone supporting her or calling for a third party

card.name: Vian
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Vian, an actor in the Black Curtain Troupe. You always played the hated villain and often heard boos before applause.
card.title: The Night the Villain Sat in the Audience
card.world: A traveling theater where the story changes every night
card.flavor: A reversal of roles onstage
card.opening: The curtain rose, but you, the villain, were sitting in the front row instead of standing onstage.
card.life: You were skilled at performing a villain's booming laugh and heavy strides. When the curtain fell, the audience greeted the actors, but playfully pretended to throw stones at you. Even though you knew it was a joke, you remembered those gestures for a long time.
card.turn: That day, the same line came around again. “I will block everyone's path!” You did not go onstage. You sat in the audience. The actor playing the hero waited for you, then started to open the door onstage and stopped. A child in the audience asked, “Why is that door blocked?”
card.decision: From the audience, you said, “I want to know who is behind that door too.” The director lowered the curtain, and the troupe wrote a scene together in which the person blocking the door had a reason to protect their home. You returned to the stage as the villain, but this time, you first showed who was behind the door.
card.cost: By the time the performance began again, some of the audience had already left. The troupe members were angry about the sudden interruption. You also had to apologize for not speaking up sooner about what you wanted to change.
card.after: When the performance resumed, the remaining audience quietly watched the new scene. When the curtain fell, the child who had asked the question said, “Will that person guard the door tomorrow too?” It was a kind of question you had never heard before.
card.presentEcho: When a role you often play starts to look like all you are, you may want to write different words into that role.
card.secondLook: You played a villain onstage, but you were not the same person as that character. Even so, the pretend stone-throwing after the curtain fell did not feel harmless.
card.unresolved: Years later, to protect her own role and pay, you reduced Nami's appearances. Even after Nami left for another troupe, the two of you never stood on the same stage again.
card.readerQuestion: What words have I not yet written into the role I always play?

signalMoments.speak: From the audience, you said, “I want to know who is behind that door too.” The director looked at you from beside the curtain.
signalMoments.release: You let go of the villain's opening line you had always delivered so well. A brief silence became space for a new scene.
signalMoments.connect: You asked another actor to help you imagine who might be behind the door. The actor playing the hero was the first to think of a child.

identity.region: The Black Curtain Troupe, traveling between the northern and southern markets
identity.summary: Raised in a tent-theater family at the southern market, Vian became a traveling actor. She tried to give depth to the villains she played, but years later, she reduced a young actor's roles to protect her own parts and income.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Vian · Female
Berien Traveling Calendar, Years 33–99 · Age 66
The Black Curtain Troupe of the northern and southern markets
Work · Prop hand, actor
Life · Raised in a tent-theater family at the southern market, she became a traveling actor. She once stopped a performance to demand changes, but she also reduced a colleague's appearances to protect her own role. After leaving the troupe, she lived with her younger sister at the southern market.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She protested when roles were written without depth, yet clung to her own share of the applause and pay.
Liked · Mornings when a new tent went up and listening to colleagues read scripts aloud
Disliked · Words that treated an actor and their role as if they were the same person
Skilled at · Speaking loudly enough to be heard even by the farthest members of the audience

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Nami, a colleague who created performances with her; the director who revised scripts with her for years; and her younger sister, who lived at the southern market
Treasured · The old scripts she left behind even after leaving the troupe
Hoped for · A stage where the audience remembered her name
Worried about · A new actor taking her place

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Vian, an actor in the Black Curtain Troupe. Night after night, you played the villain who blocked the path and laughed loudly onstage. Let me tell you what happened one night after the villain did not appear onstage.

The troupe's popular play always included the same line. “I will block everyone's path!” When Vian shouted those words, the hero would rush in and push her aside, and the audience would cheer. Even after the curtain fell, children playfully pretended to throw stones at Vian. Vian smiled at them, but those gestures stayed with her for a long time.

That day backstage, Vian asked the director, “Why does this character block the path?” The director adjusted her makeup and replied, “So the hero has someone to fight.”

When the curtain rose, Vian was sitting in the front row of the audience. The actor playing the hero waited for her in front of the door. When Vian's line did not come, the actor started to open the door and stopped, then tried again and stopped. The audience murmured.

“Why is that door blocked?” a child asked.

Vian wished the director could hear the question too. But she also knew she was ruining the performance.

signalMoments.speak: From the audience, Vian said, “I want to know who is behind that door too.” The director looked at her from beside the curtain.
signalMoments.release: Vian knew the familiar opening line by heart, but did not say it. As the brief silence stretched on, the audience looked at the door onstage again.
signalMoments.connect: Vian asked the actor playing the hero beside her who might be behind the door. The actor said that although it was not in the script, perhaps a young sibling was there.

episode.afterSignal:
The director lowered the curtain. The angry troupe members asked why Vian had not spoken up earlier. Vian could not answer them. If she had raised the issue beforehand, they might not have needed to stop the performance.

Backstage, the troupe quickly wrote a short new scene. Behind the door were children who had lost their home, and Vian's character had blocked the path because she was afraid they would be driven away. That did not make it right for her to have shoved the hero. But now the hero could ask why before fighting.

By the time the performance began again, some of the audience had already gone home. Those who remained quietly watched the new scene. When the curtain fell, the child who had asked the earlier question raised a hand again. “Will that person guard the door tomorrow too?”

Vian could not smile for a while because it was a kind of question she had never heard before. The director kept the scene in the next day's performance. Vian apologized to the troupe for stopping the show and promised that if there was a line she wanted to change, she would speak up before rehearsal.

Vian continued playing villains after that. She did not pretend that every character was a good person. But whenever she received a villain's opening line, she first asked what that person was trying to protect.

finalMoment.place: An alley outside a soup shop at the southern market in the world of Berien
finalMoment.scene:
On an early winter evening in Traveling Calendar Year 99, sixty-six-year-old Vian picks up 2 bowls of hot soup from a soup shop at the southern market. 1 bowl is for her younger sister, who is waiting at home. Vian has often walked through this alley since leaving the troupe. As she is about to step out of the shop, 2 people in the alley begin shouting at each other over money. Vian stops on the threshold, waiting for them to pass.

When 1 person draws a short knife, the other shoves his shoulder. The person holding the knife spins toward Vian. Clutching the soup bowls, Vian steps back, but her foot catches on the narrow threshold. The knife tip strikes Vian's side. The 2 people freeze in shock. 1 bowl falls from Vian's hands, and hot soup spreads across the stone pavement.

Vian sets the remaining bowl on a shelf inside the shop. When she presses a hand to her side, blood stains her fingers. “Sit down,” the soup shop owner says, pushing a low stool toward her. Vian sits and presses the hem of her coat against the wound. “My sister lives behind the big well,” Vian says after catching her breath once. The shop owner nods, saying he knows.

The quarrel in the alley is over, but Vian cannot stand. The pain in her side grows, and her fingertips turn cold. She presses the cloth the shop owner gives her more firmly against the wound. The faces of the people outside the door grow dim. Vian lifts her head, trying to look at the bowl of soup on the shelf, but the strength leaves her neck. The soup shop owner calls her name. Vian cannot answer. Her breathing grows shallower and shallower, then stops.
finalMoment.afterword: Vian died at age sixty-six in the early winter of Traveling Calendar Year 99, after being stabbed in the side by the knife of strangers quarreling at the southern market. The fight had nothing to do with Vian's old troupe or Nami. The soup shop owner remembered how Vian used her final moments to explain where her younger sister lived. Her younger sister was told that 1 bowl of soup had been left on the shop's shelf. The director remembered both the day Vian stopped the performance to demand changes and the day she asked for Nami's lines to be cut. Nami said that the 2 of them never stood on the same stage again. The record of past lives preserves both the day Vian asked about a villain's reasons and the day she reduced Nami's appearances. That life ended in the market alley where she had lived with her sister.
finalMoment.artAlt: A low-angle view inside a soup shop at the southern market in the world of Berien in the early winter of Traveling Calendar Year 99. 66-year-old Vian, holding 2 bowls of soup, including her sister's portion, turns on the threshold just as the knife held by 1 of 2 strangers quarreling in the alley swings toward her. This is before the collision, with no falling, support, or third-party summoning composition

card.name: Roa
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Roa, a windmill keeper who lived on the parched fields of Arha. You gathered the daytime wind to light the lamps of many homes, but you did not have enough money to repair the broken windmill.
card.title: The Night Wind She Did Not Sell
card.world: Wind Calendar Year 214, the frontier of the Stonespring Union on the Kallen Plateau in western Arha. Parched fields where daytime wind was stored to light lamps at night
card.flavor: Survival and choice
card.opening: The day one household offered to buy all the night wind, the lights in the other homes went out one by one.
card.life: On these fields of the Stonespring Union, several households gathered the daytime wind in great bags using a windmill they had built together. At night, releasing that wind little by little turned small wheels and lit their lamps. If one household used too much, the lamps in the others grew dim. You were saving money for repairs so you could replace the old axle.
card.turn: A wealthy visitor from the southern market road offered enough money to replace the axle in exchange for all of the next month's night wind. After hesitating, you agreed to send one night's share to that household as a test. In the distance, the lights in the small homes went out one after another. You had to consider both the money to repair the windmill and the lights that people needed that night.
card.decision: You stopped the deal and divided the wind among the households again. You left the visitor the share he needed as well. The next day, you laid the axle that needed repair in the middle of the fields and showed everyone how it could be fixed and how much it would cost. Some helped with their own hands instead of giving money.
card.cost: By giving up a large sum of money, you delayed the windmill repairs by a month. The visitor closed his purse and asked who else would pay for the damage, and asking for help was not easy for you either.
card.after: On the night the repairs were finished, you counted the lamps beneath the windmill. No one household's windows shone especially brightly, but small lights stretched far into the distance. The lamp in your own home was one of them.
card.presentEcho: There may be a way to repair things together, somewhere between the desire to protect what I truly need and the desire to consider other people's nights as well.
card.secondLook: Simply refusing the deal did not repair the windmill. Only after you showed everyone the broken axle and the shortage of money for the first time could they discuss the share each of them would contribute.
card.unresolved: Years later, when the wind grew scarce, you argued that the central village's lamps should be lit first. When one family from an outlying home left, they asked for their equipment payment back, but you opposed the refund because the windmill needed repair funds.
card.readerQuestion: Who can I show the problem I have been carrying alone?

signalMoments.protect: When you saw the first window go dark, you turned back the valve on the wind bag. The lights in the small homes came back one by one.
signalMoments.connect: You asked each household how much wind they absolutely needed at night. You could leave the wealthy visitor's household the share it needed too.
signalMoments.repair: You took the broken axle from the workbench where it had been covered with cloth. You decided to show everyone the break exactly as it was.

setting.region: the parched fields of the Kallen Plateau

identity.region: The parched fields of the Kallen Plateau, Stonespring Union
identity.summary: Raised on a plateau farm, Roa became the keeper of a communal windmill. She stopped an exclusive deal for the night wind, but years later, when the wind grew scarce, she argued that the nearest homes should be lit first.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who was she?
profilePages.body:
Roa · Female
World of Arha, Wind Calendar Years 168–234 · Age 66
Kallen Plateau, Stonespring Union
Work · Windmill repair apprentice, communal windmill keeper
Life · Raised on a plateau farm, she took charge of the communal windmill. She once rejected a wealthy visitor's proposal for exclusive access. Years later, when the wind grew scarce, she argued for a distribution plan that lit the central village first, leading to a long dispute with an outlying household.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What kind of person was she?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She disclosed breakdowns and costs, but would not change her own judgment about who should receive scarce wind.
Liked · Watching the lamps across the fields come on one by one each evening
Disliked · Leaving broken parts covered up without a word
Good at · Finding leaks in cloth bags and worn axles

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What mattered to her?
profilePages.body:
Those close to her · Her first mentor and the neighbors in the central village, as well as the family from an outlying home who left because of the distribution policy
Treasured possession · A scrap of wind-bag cloth she had stitched with her mentor
Hope · To keep the windmill running so people could continue living on the plateau
Worry · That if the wind were divided little by little among everyone, no home's lamp would stay lit for long

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Roa, who guarded a windmill on Arha's Kallen Plateau. The people there gathered the daytime wind in great cloth bags, then used it at night to turn small wheels and light their lamps. Let me tell you what happened the day someone offered to buy every last bit of that night wind.

The windmill on the parched fields had been built by several households together. The wind was strong during the day and weak at night, so before sunset Roa checked the bags and the distribution valves. The old axle creaked every time. Buying a new one at the southern market would cost a great deal of money.

A wealthy visitor from the market road held out a purse. “Send all of next month's night wind to my house. This is enough to replace the axle, isn't it?”

Roa could not bring herself to refuse and proposed trying it for just one day. When night fell, 10 lamps blazed brightly in the visitor's house. In the small homes at the edge of the fields, the lamps went out one by one. The amount stored in the wind bags had not increased. Sending it to one side meant reducing the other side's share.

The visitor said, “This is only a test, so it's fine.” But as Roa passed the darkened windows, she saw people trying to turn their lamp wheels by hand. If she did not repair the windmill, everyone might be left in darkness the following month. But could she buy tomorrow with the money from selling tonight's light?

signalMoments.protect: Roa turned back the distribution valve. In the distance, the lamps in the darkened homes came back on one by one.
signalMoments.connect: Roa asked each household how much wind they absolutely needed at night. She could leave the visitor's household the share it needed too.
signalMoments.repair: Roa took the broken axle from the workbench where it had been covered with cloth. She decided to show everyone the break exactly as it was.

episode.afterSignal:
Roa told the visitor that she was stopping the deal. The visitor closed his purse. “If it breaks, there may be no one else who can pay as much as I can.”

“That may be true. But this windmill belongs to everyone.”

The next day, Roa placed the broken axle and the money she had saved side by side beneath the windmill. She also wrote down how much was still needed. Asking for help was not easy. It meant admitting that she could not repair the windmill she had managed alone all this time.

Each household could contribute in a different way. Some gave a little money, while others offered to pull a cart all the way to the market. The visitor returned as well and asked her to set the amount of wind he could use when needed. Roa showed him the same standards she used for the other households.

The repairs were delayed by a month. On the night the axle was replaced, no one home shone especially brightly, but small lights stretched all the way to the edge of the fields. Roa's home was one of them.

Roa guarded the windmill for many years. After that, it became a rule to bring breakdowns and costs out beneath the windmill instead of hiding them alone. The night wind did not belong to one person.

finalMoment.place: the stone road leading back to the village from her first mentor's home on the Kallen Plateau in the world of Arha
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-summer afternoon in Wind Calendar Year 234, 66-year-old Roa leaves after eating lunch at the home of her first mentor, who lives on the Kallen Plateau. They still disagree about how the windmill's wind should be distributed, but that day they ate barley porridge together. Her mentor says the sun is fierce and fills her water bottle. Roa walks alone along the parched stone road leading to the village. The houses are visible in the distance, and there is almost no shade along the road.

After walking for a long time, Roa realizes that her water bottle is nearly empty even though she is thirsty. Sweat runs from her forehead and stings her eyes. Her legs grow heavy, and her head begins to throb. She sees the shade of a low rock by the road and heads toward it. “I just need to rest for a moment,” Roa says aloud. But she finds it hard to count how many steps remain before she reaches the rock.

Roa reaches the shade and braces one hand against the stone. She raises the remaining water to her lips, but her hand shakes and she spills some of it. She lifts her head to look at the village, then for a moment cannot tell which road will take her back. She presses her palm to the hot stone, pulls it away, and tries loosening her outer garment. The houses before her blur. Roa tries to move deeper into the shade, but her knees buckle.

Sitting on the ground, Roa searches for cool stone to lean her back against. Her breathing is rapid, and her lips are dry. She puts one hand against the rock and tries to stand again, but there is no strength in her arm. “The village...” Her words trail off. Roa tilts to one side and closes her eyes. She loses consciousness in the midday heat, and her breathing stops there. No one is with her.
finalMoment.afterword: Roa died at 66 in the late summer of Wind Calendar Year 234, overcome by severe heat on the Kallen Plateau while returning from her first mentor's home. When she did not return by evening, her mentor and neighbors followed the road in search of her and found Roa in the shade of a rock. Her mentor remembered both the lunch they had shared and the fact that she had never agreed with Roa's decision to turn off the night lamps of the outlying homes first. A neighbor in the central village spoke of the lamps Roa had kept lit for them. The family that left for the south said they had never received their equipment payment back. The Record of Past Lives does not combine those gains and losses into a single judgment. On the plateau where Roa was born and worked for many years, her life ended on the day she ate with her mentor and set out for home.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view from within the shade of a rock toward the dazzling fields of the Kallen Plateau in the late summer of Wind Calendar Year 234. 66-year-old Roa steps into the shade alone, bracing one hand against the rock and holding an almost empty water bottle. She is dizzy from the severe heat but has not yet collapsed, and there is no windmill, supporting arm, or third-party rescue composition.

card.name: Haemin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Haemin, a porter for a wagon troupe traveling through Gravel Ford in Ivran. You carried more than anyone while setting up the stage, but there was one empty chest you always wished you could put down.
card.title: The Heaviest Empty Chest
card.world: Itinerant Year 73, Gravel Ford in the Luhen Valley of southern Ivran. A wagon troupe traveling between the Riverlight League and the Duchy of Stonewood
card.flavor: A strange incident and its lingering echoes
card.opening: One empty chest was heavier than any prop in the theater.
card.life: In a troupe traveling between the Riverlight League and the Duchy of Stonewood, you loaded chairs and curtains at every ford. On the wagon was an old chest made from afterimage wood that had once lain submerged in the river. Though empty, it was heavy, and the troupe members always made you load it onto the wagon alone. Whenever the lid was opened, each person saw a different scene.
card.turn: Before the performance at the Gravel Ford market, you opened the chest and saw a former colleague you had left without saying goodbye. The actor beside you saw a first performance they had missed, while the lamplighter saw a single extinguished lamp. Once you realized that everyone saw a different scene, no one could explain in a single sentence why the chest was so heavy.
card.decision: You did not press anyone to reveal what they had seen. “Let's leave it here for now. Only those who want to look should open it.” You placed the chest beside the stage and decided it did not have to be used in that day's performance.
card.cost: The market performance, allowed only briefly after the inspection, began a little late. Another person had to be called in to raise the curtain, and you had to explain why you had delayed your own work.
card.after: After the performance, you wrote your former colleague's name on the first line of a letter you had put off for a long time. When you left for the next village, the chest was still heavy, but the actor beside you took hold of one of the handles with you.
card.presentEcho: Even a burden someone else seems to carry easily may contain a scene I know nothing about. And there may be a place where I can set down my own burden with someone else for a while.
card.secondLook: The chest did not mend people's hearts. It merely revealed that each person saw a different scene and left it up to them to decide what to do afterward.
card.unresolved: Years later, even when a young porter offered to help, you took hold of the handle alone first. And when your childhood friend Sejun asked you to come home, you postponed it once again because of the touring work.
card.readerQuestion: What would you like to set down with someone for a while, even if it does not look heavy?

signalMoments.notice: You saw that the faces of those who looked into the chest were all different. You could not assign the same story to everyone.
signalMoments.rest: Instead of lifting the chest again to prove its weight, you set it on the floor beside the stage. You sat down for a moment before the performance.
signalMoments.connect: Instead of asking the actor beside you what they had seen, you asked if they could help carry one of the handles.

What he liked · An empty stage before a performance and long afternoons beside the river back home
What he disliked · Claims that invisible weight must be a lie

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
People close to him · An actor in the wagon troupe and his childhood friend Sejun

What he wanted · To spend an evening with someone without setting a date to leave
Worry · That he might lose someone by putting off his words again

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Haemin, a porter for a wagon troupe that traveled across Gravel Ford. You could easily carry the stage chairs and curtains, yet one empty chest always made you pause to catch your breath. Let me tell you about a day connected to that chest.

The chest was made from afterimage wood that had lain submerged in the river long ago. It looked empty, but it was truly heavy. When someone opened the lid, they saw a scene of something they had never managed to finish. To everyone else, it looked like nothing but an empty chest. The troupe carried this strange object as a stage prop, but Haemin always loaded it onto the wagon alone.

At Gravel Ford, there was little time to use the market after the inspection ended. Haemin unloaded the curtains and chairs, then finally took hold of the chest's handles. His arms trembled. “If it's empty, why is this taking so long?” the troupe leader asked.

Haemin opened the lid. Inside, he saw a former colleague he had left long ago without saying goodbye. The colleague stood with their back turned beside the river, exactly as they had that day. Haemin let go.

The actor beside him peered into the chest. “It's my first performance.” The actor laughed, then fell silent. The lamplighter said they had seen a single extinguished lamp. Though they all looked into the same chest, no one saw the same scene.

signalMoments.notice: Haemin saw that the faces of those who looked into the chest were all different. He could not assign the same story to everyone.
signalMoments.rest: Haemin did not lift it again to prove its weight. He set the chest beside the stage and sat down for a moment to rest his arms.
signalMoments.connect: Instead of pressing the actor to say what they had seen, Haemin asked if they could help carry one of the handles.

episode.afterSignal:
“Do we have to use it in today's performance?” the troupe leader asked.

Haemin shook his head. “Let's leave it here for now. Only those who want to look should open it.”

The performance began a little late. Another person had to be called in to raise the curtain, and Haemin had to explain why he had delayed his own work. Nor was the chest an object that could mend people's hearts. The actor could not perform that first show again, and Haemin could not deliver his unsaid farewell to his former colleague then and there.

After the performance, Haemin took out a blank sheet of paper. He wrote his former colleague's name on the first line. He did not know whether the letter would arrive. Even so, he had done one thing differently from the day he had left without saying goodbye.

When they set out for the next village, the chest was still heavy. As Haemin took hold of one handle, the same actor lifted the other. Together they walked to the wagon without looking inside the chest again.

Haemin traveled with the troupe for a long time. Accounts differ on how long they continued to carry the chest. But one thought stayed with him for years: before someone helps carry a burden, you should not have to prove the story behind it.

finalMoment.place: The river by his home village in the Luhen Valley, World of Ivran
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-summer afternoon in Itinerant Year 108, 67-year-old Haemin walks beside the river in his home village with Sejun. Sejun is a friend he has known since childhood. Since Haemin left the touring troupe, the two have walked this path almost every day. Rain has fallen high in the distant mountains, but sunlight shines in the village. Seeing branches drifting downstream, Haemin says the river is higher than usual.

“Let's go no farther today.” Sejun stops in the meadow farther inland. A few steps ahead, Haemin looks at the river. Soil trickles down from beneath the embankment where he stands. Haemin tries to step back. A long crack splits the ground beneath his feet, and the earth tilts as one toward the river. “Sejun, get back!” Haemin shouts. Sejun retreats farther inland.

Haemin twists around to grab the grass roots, but the ground beneath his feet collapses. His shoulder and back strike the soil before he falls into the river. Cold, muddy water covers his face. Haemin thrashes his arms and lifts his head above the surface. Sejun calls his name from the top of the embankment. Haemin tries to swim toward the bank, but drifting branches block his way, and the current pushes him toward the middle of the river.

The moment Haemin breaks the surface, he shouts to Sejun again, “Get back!” He tries to breathe, swallows water, and coughs. Even when his fingertips briefly touch stones on the riverbed, he cannot find his footing. His head sinks beneath the surface once more. He sees only muddy water and wavering light. Haemin reaches out, but the current spins his body around. Unable to hold his breath any longer, he inhales water. His arms stop moving, and Haemin drifts down past the bend. He can no longer hear Sejun calling.
finalMoment.afterword: In late summer of Itinerant Year 108, Haemin died at 67 after a collapsed embankment and suddenly rising water swept him away beside the Luhen Valley river where he and Sejun always walked. Sejun called to Haemin from the safety of the meadow but could not reach him through the current. After the water subsided, the villagers found Haemin downstream from the bend. Sejun remembered both the Haemin who had long postponed his request to visit and the Haemin who walked with him after returning. A young porter from the old troupe spoke of the days when Haemin refused help, leaving more work to fall on him. The actor remembered the day Haemin did not pry into their story and carried one handle of the chest with them. No one ever learned whether the letter to his former colleague arrived. The Record of Former Lives preserves these differing memories and Haemin's final years beside the river. His life ended on the path the two friends had often walked.
finalMoment.artAlt: Late summer of Itinerant Year 108 in the Luhen Valley, looking up from near the surface of the swollen river at the crumbling embankment. 67-year-old Haemin is turning toward solid ground atop the cracked earth, while his friend Sejun stands farther back in the safety of the meadow. The scene is the moment before the fall, with no afterimage-wood chest, supporting figure, or third party calling for help

card.name: Mira
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Mira, a seed keeper who guarded seeds in Ring Sector 4 of Lamo Orbit. With hands shaped by more than 70 years of life, you could judge the weight of a tiny packet.
card.title: The Three Minutes When Gravity Returned
card.world: Route Year 406, the Nema System of Seraz. A food supply station of the Orbital Habitat Union, floating in Lamo Orbit
card.flavor: Space and Choice
card.opening: During the three minutes when gravity returned to the station, only one of two packets of seeds could touch the soil.
card.life: The rotating ring in Ring Sector 4 could press down on just one soil tray in the germination room for only three minutes each cycle. You kept two kinds of seeds side by side: seeds from the memorial tree whose legacy stretched back to the year the first route opened, and fast-growing leafy vegetable seeds that could be eaten. The next supply ship would not arrive for another 40 days.
card.turn: When the ring broke down and only one bay in the germination room could be activated, the residents gathered and called for the long-awaited memorial tree to be planted. You counted the leafy vegetables left in the food storage room again. There were not enough even for the children to share. You knew that if you mixed both packets in one bay, neither would grow properly.
card.decision: You resealed the packet of memorial tree seeds. You retied the soil tray's securing strap and placed the leafy vegetable seeds inside. In front of the residents, you told them everything: how much food remained, that the next supply run was 40 days away, and that the tree seeds could not sprout during this cycle. No one applauded during the three minutes the ring turned.
card.cost: While the station gained leaves to eat, the tree for an old anniversary had to wait again. There was no guarantee of another chance to germinate it, and you were left to bear the disappointment of the residents who had looked forward to it.
card.after: Ten days later, small leaves appeared on the table. You did not put away the empty tree pot. You left it on the shelf named for the first route. When a child asked why it was empty, you told the story of the seeds that could not be planted that day.
card.presentEcho: Choosing what is needed today may not require us to erase the feelings we have carried since yesterday.
card.secondLook: The people waiting for the memorial tree were not vain. The tree represented the first promise made together by those who had left their homes and come here. That was why you kept a place for that promise even after choosing food.
card.unresolved: No one could ever be certain when the tree seeds would get their next turn. Years later, your daughter Nael asked you to live with her, but you stayed in Ring Sector 4, and the two of you exchanged letters from time to time.
card.readerQuestion: After choosing what is needed right now, is there a promise you still want to remember?

signalMoments.protect: Before placing the tiny leafy vegetable seeds in the germination room, you retied the soil tray's securing strap. It was a careful gesture meant to keep those three minutes from going to waste.
signalMoments.speak: You did not hide the food shortage or the uncertainty of the seeds' next opportunity from the residents who had been waiting for the tree.

identity.region: Ring Sector 4, Lamo Orbit, Orbital Habitat Union
identity.summary: Mira grew up on Lamo Ring and became a seed keeper. Even at seventy-five, she made the planting decision needed to secure food, and later she continued living on the station after refusing her daughter's offer to live together.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Mira · Female
Seraz Route Years 331–413 · Age 82
Ring Sector 4, Lamo Ring, Orbital Habitat Union
Work · Food storage worker, seed keeper
Life · She grew up in Ring Sector 4 and became a seed keeper. At seventy-five, she had to plant leafy vegetables for people to eat. In old age, she refused an offer to live with her daughter in another residential sector and remained on the familiar ring.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · When food was scarce, she counted the actual supplies herself, and even at the request of someone close to her, she did not easily leave the place where she had built her life.
Liked · The first leaves in the germination room and warm meals at the communal table
Disliked · Trusting calculation sheets without looking at empty shelves
Skilled at · Sorting tiny seed packets in zero gravity without spilling them

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her daughter Nael, who lived in another residential sector, and her neighbors at the communal table
What she treasured · The packet of tree seeds marked with the date of the first route
What she wanted · The day a child would see the tree, and evenings spent on her familiar ring
What she feared · Having to leave decisions about food and her own life entirely to others

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Mira, a seed keeper in Lamo Orbit. Here, gravity returned to the germination room only for the three minutes when the rotating ring passed through its proper position. Let me tell you what had to be planted in those brief three minutes.

During the three minutes when gravity returned to the station, only one of two packets of seeds could touch the soil.

The rotating ring in Ring Sector 4 could press down on just one soil tray in the germination room for only three minutes each cycle. Mira kept two kinds of seeds side by side: seeds from the memorial tree whose legacy stretched back to the year the first route opened, and fast-growing leafy vegetable seeds that could be eaten. The next supply ship would not arrive for another 40 days.

Mira took the two seed packets to the food storage room. The calculation sheet said there were enough vegetables, but the actual shelves were about half empty. Someone had even made a small pot for a child who was waiting for the tree. “It can grow this year, right?” Mira could not readily answer.

When the ring broke down and only one bay in the germination room could be activated, the residents gathered and called for the long-awaited memorial tree to be planted. Mira counted the leafy vegetables left in the food storage room again. There were not enough even for the children to share. Mira knew that if she mixed both packets in one bay, neither would grow properly.

signalMoments.notice: Before consulting the supply schedule, Mira counted the leafy vegetables actually in the storage room. She discovered that the amount on hand differed from the estimate written on paper.
signalMoments.protect: Before placing the tiny leafy vegetable seeds in the germination room, Mira retied the soil tray's securing strap. It was a careful gesture meant to keep those three minutes from going to waste.
signalMoments.speak: Mira did not hide the food shortage or the uncertainty of the seeds' next opportunity from the residents who had been waiting for the tree.

episode.afterSignal:
Mira resealed the packet of memorial tree seeds. She retied the soil tray's securing strap and placed the leafy vegetable seeds inside. In front of the residents, she told them everything: how much food remained, that the next supply run was 40 days away, and that the tree seeds could not sprout during this cycle. No one applauded during the three minutes the ring turned.

While the station gained leaves to eat, the tree for an old anniversary had to wait again. There was no guarantee of another chance to germinate it, and Mira was left to bear the disappointment of the residents who had looked forward to it.

Ten days later, small leaves appeared on the table. Mira did not put away the empty tree pot. She left it on the shelf named for the first route. When a child asked why it was empty, Mira told the story of the seeds that could not be planted that day.

After that, before scheduling the germination room each time, Mira checked both the food storage room and the memorial shelf. Some people looked at the empty pot and felt disappointed, but others ate the leaves that appeared on the table ten days later. No one could ever be certain when the tree seeds would get their next turn.

memories.label: A Communal Table Neighbor's Memory

finalMoment.place: The connecting line between Ring Sector 4 and the inner residential sector of the Seraz Lamo orbital station
finalMoment.scene:
On an early-winter evening in Route Year 413, eighty-two-year-old Mira leaves her room in Ring Sector 4. Today she is going to have dinner in the inner residential sector where her daughter Nael lives. When Nael asked her to live together, Mira stayed in Ring Sector 4. They continued to exchange letters afterward, but dinners face-to-face were rare. Mira tells a neighbor that she will see them at the communal table tomorrow, then boards the small passenger car that travels between sectors alone.

The passenger car moves along the station's outer rail. Beyond the window, Lamo's striped clouds are visible. Mira holds the handrail and rests a small packet of cookies for Nael on her lap. As the inner residential sector draws near, a brief metallic sound comes from the floor. A rail joint ahead of the passenger car splits open, and the warning lights turn on. Mira lets go of the cookie packet and grips the handrail with both hands.

The passenger car tilts and slides toward the wall. “Stop,” Mira says, but the car leaves its support and strikes the station wall. The impact slams Mira's body hard against the support beside the seat. The cookie packet falls to the floor. The car's outer shell remains sealed, so no air escapes. But pain in Mira's chest keeps her from taking a deep breath. Blood also runs from her forehead, wetting the corner of one eye.

Mira presses the call button. A response tone sounds in the distance, but she struggles to speak. “Inner sector… Nael…” Mira barely manages to say. The planet's patterns beyond the window seem to turn slowly. Mira tries not to let go of the handrail, but her fingers loosen. Her breaths grow shorter, and even the warning lights before her blur. Mira tries once more to call Nael's name, but no sound comes out. Before the rescue crew opens the car door, Mira stops breathing.
finalMoment.afterword: Mira died at eighty-two in the early winter of Route Year 413, after a rail joint broke in the passenger car between station sectors and sent it crashing into a wall while she was on her way to have dinner with her daughter Nael. The records do not say exactly which injury proved fatal. Nael remembered both her mother's refusal to live with her and the fact that, on that day, her mother had been coming to her sector to keep their dinner plans. Mira's table neighbors in Ring Sector 4 spoke of the many dinners they shared with her, but they did not claim those meals replaced the time she could not spend living with her daughter. The residents who had waited for the memorial tree remembered both the leafy vegetables they ate ten days later and the pot that remained empty for so long. The past-life record preserves both the years Mira spent protecting her room and her place at the table, and that evening when she made one of her rare journeys to see her daughter. Her life ended before she reached Nael.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high exterior view looks down on the Lamo orbital station in Route Year 413. Inside a small transparent passenger car, 82-year-old Mira is holding the handrail as she travels to meet her daughter, while a rail joint ahead has split open and the car tilts toward the wall. It is the instant before impact, with no germination room or seeds, no one supporting her, and no third party making a call.

card.name: Adel
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Adel, a stone-board player from the Free City of Redos. People came to the arena to see how long you would think before placing your final stone.
card.title: The Final You Were Paid to Lose
card.world: Revelation Era 218, Redos in Envar. An indoor stone-board arena where money from the Kingdom of Sor and the artisans' guild gathered
card.flavor: Competition and secrets
card.opening: The night before the final, you were paid for the first time not to win.
card.life: In Redos in Revelation Era 218, the first player to connect three paths with colored stones won. For years, you saved the small prizes you earned, hoping to repair an old game board. A sponsor from the Kingdom of Sor said he wanted to give his 20-year-old daughter confidence and asked you to lose if she missed the third path. The money in the envelope was more than the winner's prize.
card.turn: Halfway through the final, your opponent left an opening so good that anyone could see it. You could win by placing just one stone. But your opponent did not smile, even at the applause. Pointing to the path she had left open, she said quietly, “If you leave it alone, this won't be a real match either.” She already knew that her past victories had been bought.
card.decision: You placed the envelope on the stone board and returned the contract to the sponsor. Then you set your stone on the open path. When the referee declared your victory, protests erupted from the stands before cheers did. You did not leave until your opponent raised her head.
card.cost: The sponsor canceled the contract, and the artisans' guild postponed your next appearance because of the uproar. You still did not have enough money to repair the game board. Nor could you easily say whether your opponent's first honest defeat was something to celebrate.
card.after: A few days later, a small colored stone lay outside the arena door. Instead of words, three paths had been lightly carved into its back. You did not assume it was an application for a new match, but set it beside the game board you still had not repaired.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes, in the name of helping someone, we want to decide even the outcome for them. Leaving them room to face an imperfect result on their own may be the harder kind of support.
card.secondLook: The sponsor was not lying about wanting his daughter to gain confidence. But helping her win and not taking the match away from her were different things. His daughter understood that difference before anyone else.
card.unresolved: Later, you repaired the game board with your friend Iren, but entered a tournament in a distant city before repaying all the money you had borrowed. Even after you returned and explained your repayment plan, the time Iren had spent waiting remained.
card.readerQuestion: Was there ever a time when, rather than giving someone the answer, you wanted to let them choose for themselves?

signalMoments.notice: Before you saw the path your opponent had left open, you noticed that she was not smiling. Only then did you wonder why such an easy winning move had appeared.
signalMoments.speak: You returned the contract envelope to the sponsor and said, “The people placing the stones should decide this match.”
signalMoments.release: You let go of a contract payment larger than the winner's prize. You chose to accept the outcome on the stone board, not the outcome desired by the person who had decided to buy it.

identity.region: Free City of Redos
identity.summary: Adel, who grew up in the Redos market, became a stone-board player. She rejected a contract that paid her to lose, but years later, she left for a distant tournament before repaying the debt for repairs to her game board, growing distant from her friend.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Adel · Female
Envar, Revelation Era 164–229 · Age 65
Free City of Redos
Work · Stone-board player
Life · She grew up playing on stone boards in the market and traveled to many arenas. Even after rejecting a contract that paid her to lose, her hunger to compete did not fade. She left for a distant tournament before fully repaying the friend who had lent her the repair costs.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She refused to let money change the outcome of a match, but when a chance to win presented itself, she put off even promises to those closest to her.
Liked · The feel of worn colored stones and small matches in the market
Disliked · People who announced the outcome before a match
Skilled at · Reading the next move along the three paths

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her friend Iren, who lent her the money to repair the board, and the opponent who faced her honestly in the final
Treasured possession · The old colored stone she first learned with

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Adel, a stone-board player from Redos. There, the first person to connect three paths with colored stones won. Let me tell you about the envelope you received the day before the final, holding more money than the winner's prize.

The night before the final, Adel was paid for the first time not to win.

In Redos in Revelation Era 218, the first player to connect three paths with colored stones won. For years, Adel saved the small prizes she earned, hoping to repair an old game board. A sponsor from the Kingdom of Sor said he wanted to give his 20-year-old daughter confidence and asked Adel to lose if she missed the third path. The money in the envelope was more than the winner's prize.

Adel ran her hand over a cracked corner of the old game board. With the contract payment, she could have it repaired at once. Her opponent's father said, “If she wins once, she'll pick up the stones again.” But he never asked his daughter what she wanted.

Halfway through the final, Adel's opponent left an opening so good that anyone could see it. Adel could win by placing just one stone. But her opponent did not smile, even at the applause. Pointing to the path she had left open, she said quietly, “If you leave it alone, this won't be a real match either.” She already knew that her past victories had been bought.

signalMoments.notice: Before Adel saw the path her opponent had left open, she noticed that the young woman was not smiling. Only then did she wonder why such an easy winning move had appeared.
signalMoments.speak: Adel returned the contract envelope to the sponsor and said, “The people placing the stones should decide this match.”
signalMoments.release: Adel let go of a contract payment larger than the winner's prize. She chose to accept the outcome on the stone board, not the outcome desired by the person who had decided to buy it.

episode.afterSignal:
Adel placed the envelope on the stone board and returned the contract to the sponsor. Then she set her stone on the open path. When the referee declared her victory, protests erupted from the stands before cheers did. Adel did not leave until her opponent raised her head.

The sponsor canceled the contract, and the artisans' guild postponed Adel's next appearance because of the uproar. She still did not have enough money to repair the game board. Nor could Adel easily say whether her opponent's first honest defeat was something to celebrate.

A few days later, a small colored stone lay outside the arena door. Instead of words, three paths had been lightly carved into its back. Adel did not assume it was an application for a new match, but set it beside the game board she still had not repaired.

After that, Adel continued traveling from one small arena to another, placing her stones. Repairing the game board took even longer. But whenever someone left an easy path to victory open, Adel first studied the face of the person who had made that move.
