finalMoment.place: The small room Adel rented and its courtyard in the Free City of Redos, in the world of Envar
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-autumn night in Revelation Era 229, 65-year-old Adel is alone in the room she rents near the Redos market. During the day, she had tea with a neighbor. Beginning that evening, her stomach twists, and she suffers several bouts of watery diarrhea and vomiting. She thinks lying down will make it better, but her legs weaken as she goes back and forth to the toilet. Through the open door, Adel sees the water jar in the courtyard.

Before dawn, Adel drags a low stool beside the jar. Her mouth is parched, and her fingers tremble. She scoops up some water and drinks a sip, but her stomach soon turns again. Adel sets the cup on the rim of the jar and catches her breath. Sweat covers her back despite the cold air. She tries to stand and return to her room, but her feet will not obey, and she sits on the stool again.

The courtyard door opens, and her friend Iren enters. Long ago, they repaired the game board together, but Adel never fully repaid the repair money she borrowed. Iren came after hearing from a neighbor that Adel had been sick all night. “When did this start?” Adel says, “Last night.” Iren fills the cup with fresh water, but Adel reaches for it and stops. “I need to get someone.” Iren looks back toward the door.

Adel tries to lift her head and look at Iren. For a moment, Iren's face seems to move far away, then close again. “Stay seated.” Adel hears Iren's words but has no strength to answer. She takes her hand from the jar and leans against the wall beside the stool. Iren calls her name. Adel opens her eyes once and moves her lips, but no words come out. Her body can no longer endure the severe dehydration. A moment later, Adel stops breathing.
finalMoment.afterword: Adel died at age 65 in late autumn of Revelation Era 229, in her rented room in Redos, from dehydration after a sudden bout of severe diarrhea and vomiting. The pathogen that caused it was never recorded. Her friend Iren witnessed Adel's final dawn in the courtyard. Iren remembered both how they had repaired the game board together and how Adel had left for a distant tournament before repaying all the money she had borrowed. The opponent who had honestly lost to Adel that day on the stone board remembered the days when they played again, but she did not forgive the waiting on Iren's behalf. The record of Adel's past life preserves both the fact that she was a player who rejected a contract paying her to lose and the fact that she delayed repaying her friend for the sake of her own chance to compete. That life ended in the courtyard in the early dawn.
finalMoment.artAlt: Viewed at an angle from above the roof, a small courtyard in Redos at dawn in late autumn of Revelation Era 229. Weakened by severe intestinal symptoms, 65-year-old Adel sits on a stool beside a water jar, holding a cup in a trembling hand. There are no game pieces and no one beside her to support her; this is the moment before Iren arrives.

card.name: Danu
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Danu, an errand runner for the bakery in Solmaru Valley. You memorized the different shapes of the door handles on every house up the hill, so you could find your way even when it snowed.
card.title: The Stone That Came Instead of Bread
card.world: Late spring in Hearth Year 132, in Solmaru Valley of the Bidam Confederation in northern Ornel. The southern flour wagon was late, and snow fell again that day
card.flavor: A mistake and a small commotion
card.opening: One snowy morning in late spring, you delivered a warm stone to a house waiting for bread.
card.life: In Solmaru in Hearth Year 132, there was only one road connecting the community bakery below to the houses above. The flour wagon from the south was delayed, so the bakery sent out bread baked from the remaining dough and clay stones warmed by the heat of the oven, keeping them separate. You loaded two baskets while recalling the door handles of the homes that were to receive bread and those that were to receive stones. The packages were the same size, but the bread was tied with striped cord and the stones with smooth cord.
card.turn: When the child at the first house opened the package, out came a round stone wrapped in cloth. You realized you had loaded the baskets the wrong way around. The child touched the stone and smiled. Their fingertips were cold because the oven had gone out during the night. But the morning bread the child had been waiting for still had not arrived. Down below, the household waiting for a stone had set aside the bread they had received by mistake without opening it.
card.decision: You started to say, “But at least the stone helped,” then stopped. You asked the child if you could borrow the stone for a little while, went back down to the bakery, and reported that you had loaded the baskets incorrectly. You first redirected bread that had not yet been delivered to fill the bread orders, and promised each household that you would collect the cooled stones again that evening. You personally carried newly heated stones to the homes that had been waiting for them.
card.cost: While you climbed the road twice, the bread arrived late. You were left out of the next market-day delivery and missed seeing the first spring flowers with your younger sibling as you had planned. The bakery owner separately recorded the amount to be refunded from the price paid by those who received their bread late. Just because the child had been warm for a little while did not mean the late bread had arrived on time.
card.after: That evening, the child held out the cooled stone. To tell the stones and bread apart, you tied different knots on the basket handles. The next day, your younger sibling left a small spring flower in front of the bakery door. You slipped the flower into your pocket and reread the delivery list that was still unfinished.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes a mistake unexpectedly helps someone. Even so, there is still work to finish by returning to the person who did not receive what they were waiting for.
card.secondLook: It was true that the child had held the stone and smiled. The hunger of the neighbor who received bread late was real too. You did not erase either truth, but walked the wrong road again to make things right.
card.unresolved: Years later, when your younger sibling said they wanted to open their own shop, you worried first about the vacancy at the bakery and opposed the idea. Your sibling opened a separate shop, and when you reduced deliveries to distant homes to pay a new worker's wages, several customers also left.
card.readerQuestion: When a mistake changed the course of events, have you ever recognized both the unexpectedly good result and the work that still needed to be fixed?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Danu, who worked alongside his younger sibling in Solmaru Valley. The two of you later ran shops of your own. First, let us go to the day you were 24.

One snowy morning in late spring, Danu delivered a warm stone to a house waiting for bread.

In Solmaru in Hearth Year 132, there was only one road connecting the community bakery below to the houses above. The flour wagon from the south was delayed, so the bakery sent out bread baked from the remaining dough and clay stones warmed by the heat of the oven, keeping them separate. Danu loaded two baskets while recalling the door handles of the homes that were to receive bread and those that were to receive stones. The packages were the same size, but the bread was tied with striped cord and the stones with smooth cord.

Danu recognized the door handle of the first house up the hill. It was the right house. But snow had piled on the handles of both baskets, making the cords hard to see. He was about to check the cords again when he heard a child calling from inside and knocked on the door first.

When the child at the first house opened the package, out came a round stone wrapped in cloth. Danu realized he had loaded the baskets the wrong way around. The child touched the stone and smiled. Their fingertips were cold because the oven had gone out during the night. But the morning bread the child had been waiting for still had not arrived. Down below, the household waiting for a stone had set aside the bread they had received by mistake without opening it.

signalMoments.notice: Danu saw the smooth cord on the first package and noticed that it was different from the striped cord used for bread. Only then did he realize that he had loaded the baskets the wrong way around.
signalMoments.repair: Danu retraced his path through the snow and corrected the orders, then tied different knots on the two basket handles so he would not confuse them on the next delivery.
signalMoments.connect: Danu asked the child if he could borrow the stone for a little while, then personally visited the house that received its bread late, explained what had happened, and promised to collect the stone that evening.

episode.afterSignal:
Danu started to say, “But at least the stone helped,” then stopped. He asked the child if he could borrow the stone for a little while, went back down to the bakery, and reported that he had loaded the baskets incorrectly. He first redirected bread that had not yet been delivered to fill the bread orders, and promised each household that he would collect the cooled stones again that evening. He personally carried newly heated stones to the homes that had been waiting for them.

While he climbed the road twice, the bread arrived late. Danu was left out of the next market-day delivery and missed seeing the first spring flowers with his younger sibling as they had planned. The bakery owner separately recorded the amount to be refunded from the price paid by those who received their bread late. Just because the child had been warm for a little while did not mean the late bread had arrived on time.

That evening, the child held out the cooled stone. To tell the stones and bread apart, Danu tied different knots on the basket handles. The next day, his younger sibling left a small spring flower in front of the bakery door. Danu slipped the flower into his pocket and reread the delivery list that was still unfinished.

After that, Danu tied a different knot on every delivery basket. Even after many years had passed and he took charge of the bakery, he remembered the money refunded for the late bread that day. But when his younger sibling said they wanted to open their own shop, he worried about the vacancy at the bakery before thinking about the life his sibling wanted.

finalMoment.place: A grassy hill and low rock shelter above Solmaru Valley in the world of Ornel
finalMoment.scene:
On a late summer afternoon in Hearth Year 174, 66-year-old Danu walks across a grassy hill above Solmaru with his younger sibling. The two travel this far only on days when both of their shops are closed. His sibling sells dried flowers and herbs at the market, while Danu still tends the oven at the community bakery. They sit beside a rock and drink the water they brought. When his sibling says, “Let's not talk about the shops today,” Danu nods.

Thunder sounds beyond the distant valley. The sunlight dims, and the grass bends in one direction. The two walk toward a low rock shelter along the path down to the village. His sibling reaches the shelter first and looks back from beneath the rock. Danu is a few paces behind, crossing an exposed part of the hill. “Hurry.” His sibling calls out. Danu quickens his steps but places his feet carefully among the stones beginning to grow wet.

A white light strikes the ground just ahead. Danu feels his body jerk violently at the same instant a tremendous sound rings in his ears. He tries to turn his head toward the rock shelter, but his legs give way. As he tries to brace a hand against the ground, his arm stops moving too. Danu collapses onto the grass. His sibling, who had been before his eyes, quickly disappears from view.

Beneath the rock, his sibling calls Danu's name. There is no answer. His sibling runs over and kneels beside him. Danu's eyes are closed, and his chest does not move. His sibling calls his name again and takes his hand, but Danu does not open his eyes. Immediately after lightning struck nearby, Danu's breathing and heart stopped.
finalMoment.afterword: Danu died at 66 in the late summer of Hearth Year 174, immediately after lightning struck the ground nearby on the grassy hill above Solmaru, where he had gone to rest with his younger sibling. His sibling remembered the days when they still occasionally rested together even after each had taken charge of a separate shop. They also remembered that at first, Danu had not listened to the end when they said they were leaving the bakery. The new worker remembered that Danu reduced deliveries to distant homes to protect the worker's wages. Several customers who left continued going to another bakery. The Record of Past Lives notes both that Danu made amends for a delivery mistake and that he tried to prevent his sibling from making their own choice. His life ended on the hill from which the two had meant to return without talking about work.
finalMoment.artAlt: A distant view from inside the rock shelter of the grassy hill above Solmaru in the late summer of Hearth Year 174. Lightning strikes the ground near 66-year-old Danu as he stands on the hill, while his younger sibling looks back at him from beneath the rock. There is no bread, oven-warmed stone, or snowy road, and the composition does not depict a collapse, someone offering support, or a third party calling for help

card.name: Theo
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Theo, an apprentice apology courier who crossed back and forth between the two sides of Lamer Canal, carrying other people's words. You always watched the sun, determined not to miss even the last letter before the bridge was raised.
card.title: Two Apologies Sent to Each Other
card.world: Bridge Year 156, Lamer Canal in Omber. A folding bridge where goods from the Fern Waterway Alliance and the Red Grand Duchy meet
card.flavor: A small mystery under time pressure
card.opening: When the sun sets, the bridge is raised. But two people on opposite banks came looking for you, each asking you to deliver an apology to the other.
card.life: In Lamer, people sometimes sealed words they found hard to say aloud in wax and entrusted them to couriers. You were an apprentice courier who looked only at the address and name and never changed the words inside. Not long before, the iron wedge holding the central bridge's axle had split. The repairer on the west side had closed the bridge early, bringing trade to a halt, and the repairer on the east side suspected him of hiding a part. Without explaining themselves to each other, they each took one half of the split iron wedge and worked on opposite banks.

Both said, “Please don't wait for an answer.” You carried the first letter, entrusted to you on the west side, across to the east. When the recipient opened the envelope, one half of the split iron wedge rolled out from beneath the words, “I'm sorry I closed it without saying anything.” He took the other half from his own bag. He had taken it to check the bridge's safety too, but he had never said so.

You delivered both the second apology, which had not yet reached the west side, and the new reply. As they measured the length of a new wedge, you held one end of the ruler. One person asked the other, “Where should we start measuring?” No one could tell whether the apologies had been accepted yet.
card.presentEcho: There may be someone who apologizes first and someone who is not ready to hear those words yet. The moment feelings reach another person may not be the same as the time it takes to repair what was broken.
card.secondLook: Both people asked you not to wait for an answer, but perhaps they were afraid of what might come back to them. The wedge inside one letter was proof of the apology, but it also carried the weight of the work still left to do.
card.unresolved: Years later, after taking charge of the delivery office, you sent a merchant's letter first to protect your income. Hira received a job letter too late and lost the work, and she refused the free delivery you later offered.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever needed more time even after hearing someone say they were sorry?

Theo · Male
Omber, Bridge Years 137–206 · Age 69
Lamer Canal, Fern Waterway Alliance
Work · Canal letter courier, delivery office operator, ferryboatman
Life · He grew up on the east bank, carried letters, and took charge of the delivery office. Once, to honor a contract with a merchant, he delayed another neighbor's letter. After leaving the delivery office, he operated a small boat.

Disliked · Opening envelopes to guess at other people's words

episode.beforeSignal:
The Record of Former Lives first takes us to Theo at nineteen, after he had grown up along Lamer Canal. Years later, he would run a delivery office and operate a small boat, but at this time, he was still an apprentice.

When the sun sets, the bridge is raised. But two people on opposite banks came looking for Theo, each asking him to deliver an apology to the other.

In Lamer, people sometimes sealed words they found hard to say aloud in wax and entrusted them to couriers. Theo was an apprentice courier who looked only at the address and name and never changed the words inside. Not long before, the iron wedge holding the central bridge's axle had split. The repairer on the west side had closed the bridge early, bringing trade to a halt, and the repairer on the east side suspected him of hiding a part. Without explaining themselves to each other, they each took one half of the split iron wedge and worked on opposite banks.

Theo read the addresses on the two envelopes in turn. The two repairers were fixing the same bridge, but they were on opposite sides. The bridge axle's iron wedge had split, and trade had stopped. Theo did not think that simply delivering the letters would bring their feelings back around. Still, he wanted to make sure each recipient had time to see their own name and open the envelope.

That day, the two repairers separately left letters at the delivery office beside the bridge, each naming the other as the recipient. Both said, “Please don't wait for an answer.” Theo carried the first letter, entrusted to him on the west side, across to the east. When the recipient opened the envelope, one half of the split iron wedge rolled out from beneath the words, “I'm sorry I closed it without saying anything.” He took the other half from his own bag. He had taken it to check the bridge's safety too, but he had never said so.

signalMoments.notice: Theo first realized from the addresses that the two envelopes were headed to opposite sides of the same bridge. One was unusually heavy for a letter, but he did not break the seal.
signalMoments.connect: Even though Theo had been asked not to wait for a reply, he accepted only an answer written by the repairer himself and delivered it. He left room for the two people to continue in their own words.
signalMoments.repair: The next day, while the length of the new wedge was being measured, Theo held one end of the ruler. He could not make peace for them, but he could lend a hand in repairing the bridge.

episode.afterSignal:
Theo did not take it upon himself to add new words to the letter, such as, “The other person has a piece of the wedge too.” He received a short reply written by the east-side repairer himself, and after the bridge was raised, he used the money he had earned that day to hire a small boat. He delivered both the second apology, which had not yet reached the west side, and the new reply. The two did not see each other face-to-face that day, but each separately promised to inspect the bridge axle together the next morning.

The late-delivery fee for the second letter was deducted from Theo's first day's wages, and Theo also paid the fare for the small boat. The bridge remained closed that night. The losses from halted trade and the words they had thrown at each other did not vanish because of two letters.

The next morning, the two halves of the split iron wedge were fitted together on a workbench beneath the bridge. They could not be put back into place. As they measured the length of a new wedge, Theo held one end of the ruler. One person asked the other, “Where should we start measuring?” No one could tell whether the apologies had been accepted yet.

Theo later took charge of the canal's delivery office. He long remembered how he had not spoken the two repairers' apologies for them. But when the delivery office's income fell, he sometimes sent first the letters of merchants who paid more. Even after a neighbor lost a job because of that, he kept the contract for one more season.

finalMoment.place: The stone gate at the autumn market on the east bank of Lamer Canal in the world of Omber
finalMoment.scene:
On an autumn evening in Bridge Year 206, sixty-nine-year-old Theo visits the market on the east bank of Lamer Canal. It is his day off, and he is not operating his boat. He meets a former passenger of his by a fruit stall, and they agree to meet again outside the stone gate when the market closes. Looking at the lanterns hanging over the alleys, Theo slowly makes his way toward the gate.

The bell rings to announce that the market has ended. People emerging from two alleys head together toward the only stone gate. A stall's canopy beside the gate and its stacked baskets make the passage even narrower. Theo stops close to one of the gateposts. The people ahead are not moving, but those behind cannot see that and keep walking forward. “Stop for a moment!” Theo shouts, but his voice is lost beneath the ringing bell and the market noise.

The gaps between the people disappear, and Theo's chest is pressed against the cold stone post. He tries to turn sideways, but even his shoulders cannot move. He lifts one arm to make space in front of his chest, but his elbow is trapped. He tries to draw a breath, but his chest cannot expand. A few steps behind him, the former passenger sees Theo and calls his name. The passenger is also trapped among the others and cannot come closer.

Theo tries to move the palm pressed against the post, but there is no strength in his fingertips. He tries to breathe in once more, but only a brief sound escapes his throat. The yellow lantern light blurs. Theo closes his eyes, and the strength leaves his body. When the people on the outside step back and the way opens, Theo is slumped against the base of the post. The former passenger calls his name again. Theo does not answer, and he is not breathing.
finalMoment.afterword: Theo died at sixty-nine in the autumn of Bridge Year 206, after his chest was crushed when people surged all at once into the narrow stone gate at the market on the east bank of Lamer Canal. The former passenger who had visited the market with him remembered how Theo lingered over the lanterns on his day off longer than he ever did on days when he operated the boat. The two repairers spoke of how nineteen-year-old Theo had not added new words to their sealed letters of apology. Whether the two forgave each other cannot be known from that. Hira remembered refusing Theo's offer of free delivery after her job letter arrived late. That offer did not restore the work she had lost. The Record of Former Lives preserves both the Theo who never changed other people's words yet sent first the letters of merchants who paid more, and the Theo who visited the market on his final evening. His life ended at the stone gate as he was returning home from the market.
finalMoment.artAlt: Lamer Canal's east-bank market seen from a high rooftop viewpoint on an autumn evening in Bridge Year 206. Among the people crowding toward a single stone gate after the market closes, 69-year-old Theo braces one hand against the gatepost and tries to turn sideways. There is no boat or letter, and the composition does not show anyone collapsing, being helped, or calling for a third party

episode.beforeSignal:
This time, the Record of Past Lives will tell you an imagined account of a day in the life of a real person. You were John T. Daniels, a coastal lifesaving crewman at Kill Devil Hills. On December 17, 1903, you stood before a camera you had never touched before. The story follows known facts, but the unrecorded thoughts and dialogue are imagined.

The day he was asked to photograph a flying machine, John T. Daniels had never used a camera before.

December 17, 1903, Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, United States. A signal made by waving a cloth appeared near the lifesaving station. The Wright brothers were going to launch their airplane from the sand again that day. John T. Daniels, the other lifesaving crewmen, and local residents helped move the aircraft onto a wooden rail laid across level ground. The wind was strong, and the weather was cold.

The sea wind drove the sand low across the ground. When Orville Wright pointed to the camera he had positioned in advance, Daniels took the rubber bulb connected to its shutter. He had never learned photography. But from his work at the lifesaving station, he was used to recognizing the moment when waiting had to end. He looked back and forth between the rail and the tip of the wing.

Orville called John T. Daniels over to the camera he had set up in advance. In his hand was a small rubber bulb that operated the shutter. Before him stood a machine with two tiers of wings, and beside it was Wilbur, ready to run while holding the wing. With no way to check what would appear in the photograph, John T. Daniels waited amid the sound of the wind for the moment the machine left the rail.

signalMoments.notice: John T. Daniels followed the machine with two tiers of wings with his eyes as it left the wooden rail. He pressed the shutter at the very moment he had been waiting for in front of the camera.
signalMoments.explore: John T. Daniels was given the task of operating the shutter with the rubber bulb of a camera he had never touched before. Even with an unfamiliar tool, he performed the one action needed that day.
signalMoments.connect: John T. Daniels, the lifesaving crewmen, and local residents moved the aircraft onto the rail in the sand together. Beside the brothers' experiment, different hands helped with the same preparations.

episode.afterSignal:
Orville climbed onto the machine, and Wilbur ran beside it. The moment the aircraft left the end of the rail, John T. Daniels squeezed the rubber bulb. The flight ended after twelve seconds. John T. Daniels could not tell whether the picture had been taken, but he had seen the machine fly over the sand with his own eyes. The brothers and the others moved the aircraft back and launched it three more times that day.

After the fourth flight, a gust flipped the aircraft over. John T. Daniels tried to hold it down but became tangled between the wings, leaving him scraped and bruised. The aircraft was too badly damaged to fly again. Nor could the photograph John T. Daniels had taken be viewed there.

Only after the brothers returned to Dayton and developed the photograph did anyone know that brief moment of takeoff had been preserved. No record says what John T. Daniels thought of first when he returned to the station that day. From here, we imagine a scene in which he thinks of the wind and the sand left on his hands.

Daniels continued working along the coast and at sea for many years after that day. He lived with his family and settled in Manteo later in life. The world remembers him for the photograph of the first flight, but his entire life was not contained in those twelve seconds.

finalMoment.scene:
In January 1948, John T. Daniels's life is nearing its end. In 1903, he pressed the shutter of the camera the Wright brothers had set up. But far more of his life afterward unfolded beyond the frame of that photograph. He finished his work with the coastal lifesaving service, worked with machinery at a shipyard, and operated a ferry for a time. In the 1940s, he lived in Manteo.

The National Register of Historic Places documentation records that he suffered from pneumonia. It also says he contracted pneumonia at a 45th-anniversary celebration of the first flight, but that anniversary number does not align with the year of the first flight and his date of death. The exact event and day when he was infected cannot be established. Records show that he had a wife, Amanda, and six children, and that his daughter's family and grandchildren lived in the same house for a time. But the documents do not say who was beside him during his final days with pneumonia, what room he was in, or what words were spoken.

On January 31, 1948, Daniels died of pneumonia. The record gives the date and the illness but not the exact place where he drew his final breath. If we added the sound of a door opening or someone holding his hand here, it would appear to be fact. The Record of Past Lives does not claim to have seen an unknown scene. It stops where confirmation ends.

After his death, Amanda filed his will as its executor. It stated that the house and land were to be divided equally among their six children. The document names the next owners of the house and land where even their daughter's family had once stayed. Daniels's end cannot be explained by a single twelve-second photograph. Though no image of his final room survives, the long years of family and work remain in the record.
finalMoment.afterword: John T. Daniels died of pneumonia on January 31, 1948, at the age of 74. The place where he died, the people beside him, and his last words have not been confirmed. After his death, Amanda executed his will, and the house and land were left in equal shares to their six children. How every member of the family received this is not recorded. The Record of Past Lives does not invent dialogue of grief where none can be confirmed. It presents plainly the coastal lifesaving service, the labor of the shipyard and ferry, the years spent with his family in Manteo, and the end of a life whose date and illness are known.
finalMoment.artAlt: An interpretive exterior illustration evoking John T. Daniels's home in Manteo, North Carolina, in the 1940s. It shows only an empty porch viewed from outside, a large tree, and winter light, without recreating the actual room where he died, the people present, or any conversation.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Kim Hae-won, who ran a pawnshop in Jongno, Gyeongseong, during the Japanese colonial period. Hae-won and the people of this alley were created for this story. Let me tell you about a spring day when a customer returned one day late to reclaim a pair of scissors.

Just before closing, a customer came to reclaim a pair of old sewing scissors. She had brought the correct amount of money, but she was one day late.

Jongno, Gyeongseong-bu, in the spring of 1930, when Korea was under Japanese colonial rule. Pots, winter coats, watches, and scissors sat on the shop shelves with paper tags attached. Unlike the fine streets south of Cheonggyecheon, the alleys to the north were home to customers who temporarily pawned their belongings and used the borrowed money to make it through to their next job. Kim Hae-won, too, had to make the numbers in the ledger add up if she wanted to keep the shop open.

Hae-won could not bring herself to remove the paper tag tied to the scissors. Seorim had to cut fabric the next morning so she could earn money. Without the scissors, it would be hard for her to repay her next debt as well. But the shop could not simply close its ledger every time this happened. Hae-won pointed out the date to Seorim. “The deadline was yesterday.” Seorim nodded. “I know. That's why I've been gathering the money since dawn.”

Seorim, who worked as a seamstress, counted out the principal and the interest accrued so far. Kim Hae-won placed the pawn ticket beside the ledger. There was a difference of one day. According to the terms written on the ticket, she had to calculate the additional interest for the late day, but Seorim did not have that money. She needed the scissors today to cut the clothes she had been hired to make tomorrow.

signalMoments.notice: Kim Hae-won placed Seorim's pawn ticket beside the ledger and confirmed for herself that the dates were off by only one day. She also heard that Seorim absolutely needed the scissors for the next day's work.
signalMoments.speak: Kim Hae-won did not hide from Seorim that interest was still due for the late day. Then she clearly told her that this time, she would take that money out of her own share.
signalMoments.repair: Kim Hae-won did not erase the unpaid interest from the ledger, but covered it from her own income. She decided to write the dates more clearly on the pawn tickets and read them aloud again to the next customer.

episode.afterSignal:
Kim Hae-won did not hide the fact that interest was still due for the late day. Instead, she deducted that amount from her own income and entered it in the ledger. As she returned the scissors to Seorim, she told her to be sure to check the date next time.

That day's ledger showed the reduced income. Kim Hae-won had to delay setting aside money to take in the shop's next item. Her younger sibling, who worked with her, said she could not do the same for every customer. Kim Hae-won could not deny it.

The next day, Seorim passed by carrying a piece of cloth she had cut with the scissors. The other items still had repayment dates attached to them. Kim Hae-won read the tickets again, but she did not write down yesterday's choice as the answer for everyone.

Hae-won continued opening the shop and taking in people's belongings afterward. She did not reduce every charge. On the day she returned the scissors, her younger sibling went home late after recounting the remaining items. Hae-won recorded the amount she had yielded to the customer in the ledger, but for a while, she did not record the time her younger sibling had put in.

memories.label: A Customer's View · Fictional

memories.label: Her Younger Sibling's View · Fictional

finalMoment.place: A rented room where she lives alone near Jongno
finalMoment.scene:
In the winter of 1952, I have been coughing for 3 days alone in the room I rent near Jongno. In the morning, I lift the pot to boil water, but lose my grip on the handle. I sit down on the floor and catch my breath. The lower part of my chest hurts whenever I inhale. Outside the door, my regular customer Seorim calls, “Ms. Hae-won.” I try to answer, but a cough comes out first.

Seorim opens the door and sets down a bowl of water. “Should I let your younger sibling know?” I nod. The last time my sibling and I ate together was 1 month ago. Even that day, we did not finish calculating the wages I still owed. I try to tell Seorim where my sibling works, but the whole address will not come out at once. I give her the name of the alley in broken phrases, and Seorim repeats it after me. I ask again whether I told her correctly.

In the afternoon, a neighbor brought by Seorim goes out to find someone who can examine me. I try to get up and put on my outer coat. I stop with 1 arm inside a sleeve. My breath is too short. “Take it slowly.” I hear Seorim's voice and look at the open door. I think I will try to leave the room when the neighbor returns. After I swallow 1 sip of water, Seorim asks me something, but no sound comes out. My chest rises once. I open my mouth to draw in the next breath, but my body does not follow.
finalMoment.afterword: Hae-won died in 1952 in a rented room near Jongno after a severe lung infection. Seorim brought her water and stayed beside her, while Hae-won's younger sibling heard the news and arrived late that day. Her sibling remembered that even after their older sister began recording their working hours in the ledger, she had never managed to pay all the wages owed from before. Seorim remembered both the day Hae-won returned the scissors and the other days when she strictly collected what was due. The share owed to Hae-won's younger sibling, never fully settled, is not erased from Hae-won's record in the Book of Past Lives.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view through the window of a rented room in Jongno in the winter of 1952. Hae-won, age 68, sits catching her breath while her regular customer Seorim sets down a bowl of water.

card.identityLine: In that life, you were Nora O'Rourke, a seamstress who mended clothes for third-class passengers aboard RMS Titanic as it sailed across the North Atlantic. You learned to sew in Belfast and boarded a ship bound for America. You tried to return other people's belongings to the right owners, but you also had a habit of being slow to believe people when they were in a hurry.

identity.summary: You learned to sew in Belfast and boarded a ship bound for America. You tried to return other people's belongings to the right owners, but you also had a habit of being slow to believe people when they were in a hurry.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Nora O'Rourke · Female
1880–1912 · Age 32
RMS Titanic, sailing across the North Atlantic
Work · Seamstress who mended clothes for third-class passengers
Life · You learned to sew in Belfast and boarded a ship bound for America. You tried to return other people's belongings to the right owners, but you also had a habit of being slow to believe people when they were in a hurry.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She did not easily believe anything she had not verified. As a result, things were rarely lost, but while she asked twice about urgent requests, she kept people waiting.
What she liked · The worn-in feel of old clothes rather than new fabric
What she disliked · Moving luggage without name tags
What she did well · Finding seams and buttons by touch, even in the dark

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
What she treasured · The small scissors her mother gave her and her passage ticket
People close to her · Her younger sister Mary, and Annie and her mother Catherine, whom she met aboard the ship
The life she wanted · A life working with her sister at an alterations shop in New York
Her worry · Losing her money and tools before she even reached America
The cost she paid · By insisting on confirming the owner of the lost coat, she delayed Catherine's trip up to the deck. Too late, Nora admitted that her judgment was not always the safest guide.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Nora O'Rourke, a seamstress traveling in third class aboard Titanic in 1912. You crossed the ocean to open an alterations shop with your younger sister in New York.

A small coat was found in the corridor beside the dining room. Only loose threads remained inside near the buttons where the name tag had fallen off. Catherine said it belonged to her daughter, Annie, but Nora asked again what color the lining was.

Even after the ship struck an iceberg, there was little commotion at first. When a crewman told them to put on life jackets and go up, Catherine said they should take the child first and forget the coat.

signalMoments.notice: In the coat pocket, Nora found one of the blue buttons Annie collected. She realized that no further confirmation was needed.
signalMoments.repair: Instead of sewing the fallen name tag back on, Nora fastened the front of the coat with a large safety pin. Keeping out the cold came first.
signalMoments.connect: Nora handed the coat to Catherine and took Annie's hand. The three of them followed the stairs and signs to the upper deck together.

episode.afterSignal:
Nora put the coat on Annie and climbed the stairs with Catherine. Only when she saw water spreading through the lower corridor did she realize that the collision had not been a minor accident.

On deck, crewmen were putting women and children into lifeboats. Nora sent Catherine and Annie into the line, then waited for her own turn.

Catherine reached out for Nora to board with them, but a crewman moved the child farther inside first. Nora checked that Annie's coat was buttoned and stepped back.

Catherine and Annie boarded the lifeboat, while Nora remained on the ship. Both the minutes lost while she verified the coat's owner and her choice to go up to the deck with them became part of that night's record.

timeline.event: Born in Belfast, Ireland. Her personal life is fictional
Learned sewing from her mother and began altering clothes
Ran a small alterations stand while helping pay her younger sister Mary's hospital bills
Boarded Titanic in third class to travel to New York
Returned the coat to Annie after searching for its owner and went up to the deck with the mother and daughter
Died in the North Atlantic when Titanic sank. The characters and dialogue are fictional

memories.label: What she did for years
memories.detail: Made worn sleeves and fallen buttons usable again

memories.label: What she liked
memories.detail: The moment an owner immediately recognized a garment she had finished mending

memories.label: Words she left behind
memories.detail: “Forget the coat. Take the child's hand first.”

memories.label: Catherine's assessment
memories.detail: “Nora was slow to believe us, but once she did, she climbed the stairs with us.”

memories.label: Mary's memory
memories.detail: “My sister was precise. Sometimes she made people wait while she searched for the exact answer.”

memories.label: History and fiction
memories.detail: The collision and sinking on April 14–15, 1912, are historical facts, while the private lives of Nora and the people around her are fictional.

finalMoment.place: The stern deck of RMS Titanic in the North Atlantic
finalMoment.scene:
In the early hours of April 15, 1912, Titanic's stern deck tilted to one side. Nora fastened the wet coat of Bride, a fellow third-class passenger, then gripped the railing. The lifeboats were already far away. The sound of steel plates twisting rose from below the ship.

“Don't let go.” Nora seized Bride's wrist. The two moved toward the higher side, where fewer people had gathered, but the deck's slope grew steeper. When the icy seawater covered her shoes, Nora drew a short breath.

As the ship sank into the water, their hands came apart. Nora tried to grab a floating piece of wood, but her fingers had stiffened. In the darkness, she called Bride's name once. The cold water drained the strength from her arms and legs, and soon she could no longer keep her head above water.
finalMoment.afterword: Nora died of hypothermia and drowning when Titanic sank. Bride's fate is not recorded in this fictional account. Her sister in Belfast kept the letter that was never returned and the clothes Nora had mended for many years. The private lives of Nora and those around her, set against the real sinking, are fictional.
finalMoment.artAlt: The tilted stern deck of Titanic at dawn in 1912, with Nora the seamstress gripping the railing above the cold North Atlantic

card.name: Rao
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Rao, who watched over the water-level marks of Seven-Gate Free City. With hands more than sixty years old, you wiped clean the three lines on the stone wall every day.
card.title: The Blue Line the Fish Swallowed
card.world: Early summer of Tally Year 94, in Seven-Gate Free City of the Oran Estuary Federation in western Maren. A marketplace where the river flows down from the upstream Swell Autonomous Territory and empties into the eastern sea
card.flavor: Marketplace commotion and a small act of courage
card.opening: A huge fish painted on the marketplace wall had swallowed the blue line that said to move the goods when the water rose.
card.life: There were three blue lines on the stone wall of the Seven-Gate marketplace. The lower line marked the usual water level, the middle line showed when to move the marketplace goods to the high steps, and the upper line told people when to climb the steps. You cleaned the lines every morning. Even when artists painted a fish on the wall before this year's festival, you had asked the marketplace committee to make sure the three lines remained visible.
card.turn: On the morning of the festival, you saw that the fish's blue fin covered the middle line. The fresh paint was exactly the same blue as the marker. Just then, a dispatch boat from the upstream Swell Autonomous Territory waved a cloth warning of high water. The marketplace people put up their awnings, saying the water they could see was still low. You ran to the wall and pointed to where the middle line should have been, between the lower and upper lines.
card.decision: You first explained the situation to the artist, then scraped away one side of the fin with a small scraper. The hidden middle line appeared again. The water had not yet reached it, but you told the marketplace about the dispatch boat's signal and how much time remained. Some merchants folded their awnings and lost customers, and you helped carry the artist's paints, which would be ruined if they got wet, up to the high steps.
card.cost: That afternoon, the water came close to the middle line and then receded. The goods that had been moved stayed dry, but business at the festival ended early. The artist had to repaint the damaged fin, and the merchants confronted you, saying they had closed too soon. You agreed to pay part of the cost of the replacement paint from your own wages, but that money could not bring back the customers lost that day.
card.after: The next morning, the artist continued the fish's fin beside the blue line instead of over it. You smiled when you saw the new painting, then wiped away the water stains left on the lower line. One merchant said they should leave the area in front of the markers clear at the next festival.
card.presentEcho: Even when the thing you feared does not become a disaster, the time spent acting early and the losses remain real. What would you say first afterward?
card.secondLook: The person who painted the picture had not meant to ruin the festival either. The similar color hid an important line, and Rao had to face both the task of repairing the wall and the time the marketplace had lost.
card.unresolved: Rao worked with the artist to choose a place for the picture at the next festival so it would not cover the markers. But he could not undo the way he had tried to force his nephew Kion into water-level work. Unable to repair his relationship with Kion, Rao lived alone in his house on the hill.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever been glad you prepared ahead of time, even though nothing serious ended up happening?

signalMoments.protect: Before the water reached them, you moved the merchants' goods and the artist's paints up to the high steps. Even the goods that stayed dry were still there because someone had lifted them first.
signalMoments.speak: You told everyone both the warning sent by the dispatch boat and which line the river was still below. You did not hide the fact that nothing had flooded yet.

setting.region: Seven-Gate Free City, downstream from the Swell Autonomous Territory

identity.region: Seven-Gate Free City, Oran Estuary Federation
identity.summary: Rao grew up beside the river in Seven-Gate and watched over the marketplace's water-level markers. He cared for his sister's son for many years, but they grew distant after Rao tried to force him into the same work. In old age, he left the waterfront and lived in a small house on a high hill.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Rao · Male · Tally Years 31–111 · Age 80
The world of Maren · Seven-Gate Free City, Oran Estuary Federation
Work · Keeper of the riverside marketplace's water-level markers
Life · He learned the waterways downstream and watched the marketplace markers. While his sister was away on a long voyage, he looked after his nephew Kion. After Kion grew up and left to follow his own path, Rao saved money to find a home where he could live alone.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · He readily recognized dangerous watermarks but was slow to notice the different hopes of those close to him.
Preferences · He enjoyed riverside walks, which he had learned to love from his father, and the pictures children drew on walls.
Daily life · During the day, he watched the marketplace markers, and in the evening, he prepared meals for his nephew Kion. After Kion left, he cooked for himself.
World · Maren's federation and Tally Calendar are fictional elements created for this work.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Those close to him · His sister Sora, who went on long voyages; his nephew Kion, who lived with him for a time; and the marketplace's artist and merchants
Hopes · To send the marketplace people to high ground in time and live in a small house under his own name
Worries · Being left alone after Kion's departure and having no one listen to the next warning
Later years · Unable to repair his relationship with Kion, he moved to a small house on the hill.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Rao, keeper of the water-level markers at the Seven-Gate marketplace. After learning the waterways from your father, you watched over the lines on the stone wall. One festival morning, a newly painted fish led you into an argument with the merchants.

A huge fish painted on the marketplace wall had swallowed the blue line that said to move the goods when the water rose.

There were three blue lines on the stone wall of the Seven-Gate marketplace. The lower line marked the usual water level, the middle line showed when to move the marketplace goods to the high steps, and the upper line told people when to climb the steps. Rao cleaned the lines every morning. Even when artists painted a fish on the wall before this year's festival, he had asked the marketplace committee to make sure the three lines remained visible.

Rao liked seeing children looking at the new painting in front of the wall. Then he saw that the fish's blue fin covered the middle marker. That line showed when the marketplace goods had to be moved to high ground. A dispatch boat from upstream waved a warning cloth, but the merchants refused to take down their awnings, saying the water before their eyes was still low.

On the morning of the festival, he saw that the fish's blue fin covered the middle line. The fresh paint was exactly the same blue as the marker. Just then, a dispatch boat from the upstream Swell Autonomous Territory waved a cloth warning of high water. The marketplace people put up their awnings, saying the water they could see was still low. Rao ran to the wall and pointed to where the middle line should have been, between the lower and upper lines.

signalMoments.notice: Rao noticed that the blue of the fish's fin overlapped the blue of the old marker. With his fingertips, he confirmed that the line had not vanished but had been covered.
signalMoments.protect: Before the water reached them, Rao moved the merchants' goods and the artist's paints up to the high steps. Even the goods that stayed dry were still there because someone had lifted them first.
signalMoments.speak: Rao told everyone both the warning sent by the dispatch boat and which line the river was still below. He did not hide the fact that nothing had flooded yet.

episode.afterSignal:
Rao first explained the situation to the artist, then scraped away one side of the fin with a small scraper. The hidden middle line appeared again. The water had not yet reached it, but Rao told the marketplace about the dispatch boat's signal and how much time remained. Some merchants folded their awnings and lost customers, and Rao helped carry the artist's paints, which would be ruined if they got wet, up to the high steps.

That afternoon, the water came close to the middle line and then receded. The goods that had been moved stayed dry, but business at the festival ended early. The artist had to repaint the damaged fin, and the merchants confronted Rao, saying they had closed too soon. Rao agreed to pay part of the cost of the replacement paint from his own wages, but that money could not bring back the customers lost that day.

The next morning, the artist continued the fish's fin beside the blue line instead of over it. Rao smiled when he saw the new painting, then wiped away the water stains left on the lower line. One merchant said they should leave the area in front of the markers clear at the next festival.

After that, Rao continued wiping away the water stains every morning. Before the next festival, he and the artist chose the fish's position together. Rao never forgot that even on a day when the water did not rise high, the marketplace had still lost time.

timeline.event: Born downstream in Seven-Gate Free City
Walks by the river with his father and observes watermarks
Appointed keeper of the marketplace markers
Hears different accounts of the water's timing from dispatch boat crews and marketplace merchants and records them in a ledger
His sister Sora leaves on a long voyage and entrusts Rao with her 12-year-old son, Kion. Rao spends the money he had saved for a house on a room where the 2 of them can live.
At age 20, Kion leaves for another landing to learn boat repair. Rao tries to stop him by urging him to take up marker work, and the 2 lose contact for a time.
Sora returns and tells him that Kion has settled at another landing. Rao abandons his request that she tell Kion to come back.
Restores a warning line hidden by the festival's fish painting
Establishes warning procedures between the dispatch boats and the marketplace
Uses his savings to obtain a small house on a high hill and leaves his rented room by the river.
Retires from tending the marketplace markers and hands his ledger to the new keeper. He still does not see Kion.
Dies of a sudden intracranial hemorrhage while drinking tea at a teahouse on a hill in Seven-Gate. His sister Sora arrives later, and he never sees Kion again.

memories.label: A Merchant's View
memories.detail: “We closed early because of Rao. Still, next time I'll look at the lines first.”

memories.label: His Sister Sora's Memory
memories.detail: “While I was voyaging, he fed Kion and gave him a place to sleep. But when Kion left, Rao tried to keep him by his side.”

memories.label: His Nephew Kion's Memory
memories.detail: “I know Uncle took care of me. That didn't mean he could choose my work for me.”

finalMoment.place: A teahouse on a high hill in Seven-Gate Free City, in the world of Maren
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-autumn morning in Tally Year 111, I stop at a teahouse on a high hill in Seven-Gate. It has been 5 years since I left my marketplace work. I had planned to come down from my house, drink some warm tea, and then visit my sister Sora. As the teahouse owner sets down my cup, he says, “You're alone again today.” I smile and lift the cup. Just then, a sudden, severe pain erupts on one side of my head, and the cup slips from my hand.

The cup shatters on the floor. I try to raise the arm that dropped it, but my elbow will not move from the edge of the table. The teahouse owner comes around from across the table and asks, “Rao, can you hear me?” I try to say that I can, but only my lips move. I grip the chair with my other hand and try to stand, only to sit down again. The owner's voice calling for someone else seems to come from far away.

With the hand that can still move, I catch hold of the owner's sleeve. I want to tell him to inform Sora. I manage to say, “So...” before my tongue stops obeying me. The owner peers closely at my face, then replies, “I'll let Sora know too.” I try to nod, but I have no strength in my neck. The spilled tea on the floor flows toward the door.

The pain in my head grows worse. I try tapping the table with the hand that can still move, but my fingertips soon go still. The owner calls my name again. I stare at the shards of the cup, then try to shift my gaze toward him. My vision narrows, and I can no longer understand his voice. I open my mouth to answer once more, but no sound comes out.
finalMoment.afterword: Rao died at age 80 from a sudden intracranial hemorrhage at a teahouse on a hill in Seven-Gate in the late autumn of Tally Year 111. The teahouse owner was beside him, and his sister Sora arrived later. Sora remembered both the days her brother had spent his own money to feed Kion and give him a place to sleep and the day he had stood in Kion's way when Kion chose different work. Kion, who lived at another landing, heard the news but never saw Rao again. The marketplace merchants also remembered the day they lost customers because of Rao's early warning. The chronicle of his past life closes Rao's story by recording together his work of sending people to high ground, his joy in obtaining a home where he could live alone, and the way he had blocked the path of someone close to him.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high-angle side view of a hilltop teahouse in Seven-Gate on a late-autumn morning in Tally Year 111 in the world of Maren. Rao, age 80, sits at a table just after dropping his cup, gripping the chair with one hand, while the owner stands at a distance watching him. There is no smoke or fire

card.name: Rina
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Rina, the night watchwoman who guarded the old observatory on the western hill of the Free City of Orsi. Even when you stood alone at night, you tried to look unruffled.
card.title: The Night the Ghost Knocked Three Times
card.role: Night watchwoman at the old observatory
card.world: Late autumn, Astral Year 83, in the Free City of Orsi, Belnu. The old observatory overlooking the road descending from the Numar Mountain Alliance to the plains
card.flavor: An eerie commotion and a little courage
card.opening: At the supposedly haunted observatory, you made the first two knocks. But that night, a third knock answered.
card.life: After the new observatory opened, the old star charts were stored in the old building on the western hill. When people began slipping in to steal the brass pulleys, you struck an empty drainpipe twice with a wooden spoon to start a ghost rumor. Whenever you heard frightened footsteps fleeing, it felt as though you could guard the building all by yourself. It was a prank you never told the head of security about.
card.turn: On a night after the rain stopped, you struck the drainpipe twice as usual. From the locked chart room at the end of the corridor came an answer: knock, knock, knock. You dropped the spoon. The drainpipe was on the left wall, but the sound had clearly come from behind the door on the right. The wet edge of a sheet of paper protruded beneath the door. You remembered the chart keeper saying during the day that rain was leaking through the roof.
card.decision: You shouted to the neighbors outside the corridor, “I made the first two sounds. The person knocking three times is inside.” Three people came running with lamps. You pressed your ear to the door and confirmed the chart keeper's voice. The rain-swollen door would not open until all of you lifted it by its hinges. The star charts inside were wet, but the keeper walked out safely.
card.cost: The doorframe and lock had to be replaced. The head of security acknowledged that you had helped with the rescue, but separately questioned you about frightening the neighbors with the ghost rumor. You paid part of the repair costs from your wages and were not allowed to take the night shift alone for a while. The leak in the roof had not been fixed yet, either.
card.after: A few days later, you hung the wooden spoon beside the new door. When the keeper saw it and laughed, you left the spoon where it was. You promised that from then on, whenever you heard a strange sound, you would check the end of the corridor together before inventing an explanation by yourself.
card.presentEcho: The sound you made to hide your fear nearly drowned out the sound of someone who truly needed help. When you stop pretending to be unruffled, you may also see the people who can help you open the door.
card.secondLook: The third knock was not a ghost's prank but a distress signal from the rain-soaked chart room. That did not erase the prank behind the first two knocks. Rina had to tell the neighbors she had frightened the truth herself.
card.unresolved: After that night, Rina shared the night watch with her neighbors. But when she sold her house to fund her travels, she did so knowing that Derin grew vegetables in its yard. Even after she returned, Derin's garden never came back.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever delayed asking for help because you were pretending to be fine?

signalMoments.notice: You realized that the two knocks from the drainpipe and the three from the chart room door came from different directions. You also saw the wet paper beneath the door.
signalMoments.speak: In front of the neighbors, you first admitted that the two ghostly knocks had been your prank. You also made it clear that someone was trapped inside.
signalMoments.connect: Instead of trying to force the door open alone, you called three people carrying lamps. Together, you lifted the door by its hinges and opened a way for the keeper to escape.

setting.region: Orsi's western hill on the southern border of the Numar Mountain Alliance

identity.region: Western hill of the Free City of Orsi
identity.summary: Rina grew up in Orsi and guarded the old observatory. Later, wanting to see faraway cities, she sold the house she had inherited, and the neighbor who grew vegetables in its yard lost the place she depended on. When Rina returned from her travels, she could not undo that loss.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Rina · Female · Astral Years 49~115 · Age 66
World of Belnu · Western hill of the Free City of Orsi
Work · Star chart archive assistant, night watchwoman at the old observatory
Life · She guarded the old observatory, then took time away from work to travel through the southern cities. She sold her inherited house to fund the trip and rented a room after returning.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · There were times when she endured things alone to hide her fear, and her desire to leave sometimes narrowed her view of other people's lives.
Tastes · She liked walking the routes marked on maps and writing down the words she heard in unfamiliar markets.
Daily life · When she was young, she guarded the observatory at night. After her travels, she lived in a rented room and helped with archive work during the day.
World · Belnu's Astral Calendar and the Orsi observatory are fictional settings created for this story.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered
profilePages.body:
People close to her · The chart keeper and her neighbor Derin, who used her yard
Dream · To walk the routes others had drawn and, after returning, write her own days for herself
Worry · That if she never left Orsi, she would live forever without knowing what lay beyond the map
Later years · She returned after her travels, but Derin's vegetable garden was never restored.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Rina, the keeper of Orsi's old observatory. You wanted people to say you could handle the watch alone, so you invented a rumor to drive thieves away. One night after the rain stopped, that rumor frightened you before it frightened anyone else.

At the supposedly haunted observatory, Rina made the first two knocks. But that night, a third knock answered.

After the new observatory opened, the old star charts were stored in the old building on the western hill. When people began slipping in to steal the brass pulleys, Rina struck an empty drainpipe twice with a wooden spoon to start a ghost rumor. Whenever she heard frightened footsteps fleeing, it felt as though she could guard the building all by herself. It was a prank she never told the head of security about.

Every night, Rina knocked twice on the drainpipe to spread the rumor that there was a ghost. But the third sound she heard tonight came from the chart room on the right. It came from a different direction than the drainpipe on the left. A wet sheet of star chart paper protruded beneath the door. Rina gripped her lamp. She had to find out whether someone was inside.

On a night after the rain stopped, Rina struck the drainpipe twice as usual. From the locked chart room at the end of the corridor came an answer: knock, knock, knock. Rina dropped the spoon. The drainpipe was on the left wall, but the sound had clearly come from behind the door on the right. The wet edge of a sheet of paper protruded beneath the door. She remembered the chart keeper saying during the day that rain was leaking through the roof.

signalMoments.notice: Rina realized that the two knocks from the drainpipe and the three from the chart room door came from different directions. She also saw the wet paper beneath the door.
signalMoments.speak: In front of the neighbors, Rina first admitted that the two ghostly knocks had been her prank. She also made it clear that someone was trapped inside.
signalMoments.connect: Instead of trying to force the door open alone, Rina called three people carrying lamps. Together, they lifted the door by its hinges and opened a way for the keeper to escape.

episode.afterSignal:
Rina shouted to the neighbors outside the corridor, “I made the first two sounds. The person knocking three times is inside.” Three people came running with lamps. Rina pressed her ear to the door and confirmed the chart keeper's voice. The rain-swollen door would not open until they all lifted it by its hinges. The star charts inside were wet, but the keeper walked out safely.

The doorframe and lock had to be replaced. The head of security acknowledged that Rina had helped with the rescue, but separately questioned her about frightening the neighbors with the ghost rumor. Rina paid part of the repair costs from her wages and was not allowed to take the night shift alone for a while. The leak in the roof had not been fixed yet, either.

A few days later, Rina hung the wooden spoon beside the new door. When the keeper saw it and laughed, Rina left the spoon where it was. They promised that from then on, whenever they heard a strange sound, they would check the end of the corridor together before inventing an explanation alone.

Even after rescuing the keeper, Rina was not allowed to take the night watch alone for a while. The neighbors remembered her call for help and her frightening prank as separate things. But that night did not define the whole of Rina's remaining life.

Returned to Orsi, rented a room, and helped with chart archive work during the day. She no longer ate evening meals with Derin as she once had.

Died after slipping on the wet stone steps of Orsi's western hill and striking her head.

finalMoment.place: The stone steps on the western hill of the Free City of Orsi in the world of Belnu
finalMoment.scene:
It is midday in late spring, Astral Year 115. Rina, 66, is walking down the newly repaired stone steps on Orsi's western hill. The morning shower has ended, and the market awnings are being spread again. It has been a long time since Rina returned from her travels, but she still sometimes walks the altered alleys, writing down the words of the market people. Today, she has tucked a small notebook inside her clothes and is on her way to the bakery at the bottom of the steps.

Halfway down, her right foot lands on the wet edge of a loose stone. The stone tilts, and her sole slips. Trying not to drop the notebook, Rina flings out an arm to brace herself against the wall. “Huh?” Her fingertips brush the wet wall, but her body is already pitching downward. Her knee hits the steps first, and then the side of her head strikes the edge of the next stone hard.

Rina comes to a stop several steps below. The sky and roofs seem to tilt to one side. She plants her palm to push herself up, but there is no strength in her arm. The baker, who was watching from the shop doorway, asks, “Can you hear me?” Rina opens her mouth to say she can. Only a short breath comes out instead. The notebook that slipped from inside her clothes lies within reach.

The baker climbs the steps and asks her name. Rina tries to move her tongue to say it, but the word will not come. The voices of the market drift farther away. The stone steps before her blur. Rina reaches toward the notebook, but her hand stops before her fingertips touch its cover. The baker asks her name again. Rina's short, faint breaths cease.
finalMoment.afterword: Rina stepped on a wet, unstable stone stair on Orsi's western hill in late spring of Astral Year 115 and fell. She died at 66 after striking her head. The baker came to her side, but Rina could not even say her own name. The chart keeper remembered how Rina had hidden the difficulties of guarding the observatory alone before eventually sharing the work with others. Derin still remembered losing her vegetable garden the day Rina sold the house to fund her travels. Neither the time Rina spent in the southern cities nor the days she walked Orsi's changed streets after returning erased Derin's loss. The record of past lives sets down all these memories together. On the day she went out to see the new roads, Rina's life ended before she returned home.
finalMoment.artAlt: Midday in late spring, Astral Year 115, in the world of Belnu: the wet stone steps of Orsi's western hill, seen at an angle from a window across the way. Rina, 66, slips after stepping on a loose stone and reaches toward the wall, while the baker from the shop below turns to look from the doorway. No one is supporting her or running to call for help

card.name: Mojin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Mojin, the stall-lottery host at Toram Free Market. You loved seeing people laugh, but you were also responsible for the numbered tokens behind that laughter.
card.title: The Cat Who Chose the Sunlight
card.world: Early winter, River Calendar year 161, at Toram Free Market in the Yeosan River League of western Hamin. A riverside market where boats from the Duchy of Solken cross southward
card.flavor: A cheerful market commotion
card.opening: On market day, when the cat chose the first stall, Godo walked toward the far-left basket as always. But Mojin did not ring the bell.
card.life: Whenever a new market opened in Toram, the merchants’ name tags were tied to five cloth baskets of the same size. The merchant whose basket Godo, the old gray cat in Mojin’s care, approached first won the first riverside spot, greeting customers as they stepped off the boats. The other four spots were drawn with wooden numbered tokens. Mojin made sure the baskets were all the same height and set Godo down before the starting line. Whenever the spectacle began, the market filled with laughter.
card.turn: On an early winter morning when the boats from the north arrived, Godo sat down at the starting line. One of the waiting merchants laughed and said, “It’ll be the far left again this year, won’t it?” Mojin remembered that the last two results had also been on the left. When Godo stood and stretched a paw that way, Mojin picked up the cat before he could touch the basket. Low sunlight slipping through a gap in the awning warmed only the basket on the left. The basket beside it was cold. When Godo was set down again, he curled up on the warm cloth without even looking at the name tag.
card.decision: When the bell fell silent, Mojin set the two baskets before the crowd. “Godo can’t read names. He was looking for the warm basket.” The merchant whose name tag hung on the left shouted, “If you knew that, why did you wait until now to stop it?” Mojin could not rush to invent an answer. Nor could he say that every past result had been wrong. But he could not let the first spot be decided this way today. A committee member brought the box of wooden numbered tokens used for the remaining spots. Mojin clearly read out the names of all five merchants as he placed five identical tokens inside. The committee member and one merchant counted them again. When the first token from the box was opened, the first riverside spot went to Dohee’s small fruit stall, whose basket had waited at the very end.
card.cost: The market opened late. The committee deducted part of the promised payment for hosting the lottery show and said it would also review past stall assignments. Mojin felt hurt. The merchant whose name tag had hung on the far left did not nod in agreement easily, either. For a while, some people called him the man who had deceived a cat, while others called him the man who had let a cat rest.
card.after: After the baskets were cleared away that afternoon, Godo fell asleep on the lid of the token box. Mojin spread a cloth beside Godo and counted the applications for the next market again. He never made Godo the star of the event after that, but he kept a warm spot for him in a corner of the market.
card.presentEcho: Even a method that has brought joy can be reexamined if it decides what someone receives. Only after Mojin lost the applause did he begin counting the tokens with others.
card.secondLook: Godo had never chosen a merchant’s name. Even so, the event Mojin created drew people to the market. The problem was that he confused that enjoyment with the fairness of the first stall assignment.
card.unresolved: Mojin stopped asking Godo to choose the first spot and counted the tokens together with the merchants. Even so, Uran’s complaint that he had lost customers in an earlier lottery was never resolved. After Godo died, Mojin continued living in Toram, spending his days off visiting other markets.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever reexamined, together with someone else, a method you trusted simply because it was familiar?

signalMoments.speak: You asked the committee member to lower the bell for a moment. When you had the five merchants touch the two baskets, one of them said, “They really are different.” Only then did you explain what Godo had chosen.
signalMoments.release: You drew back the hand that was about to place Godo on the starting line again. Even if it meant losing the scene people loved, you decided not to keep moving the old cat around to get an answer. After asking the committee member to lower the bell for a moment, you set Godo on the cloth beside your coat.
