identity.region: Toram Free Market, Yeosan River League
identity.summary: Mojin oversaw the stall lottery at Toram Market. Even after the death of his cat Godo, he remained at the market and enjoyed spending his days off crossing the river to visit other markets before returning. The complaints surrounding earlier lotteries were never fully resolved.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Mojin · Male · River Calendar years 118~190 · Age 72
World of Hamin · Toram Free Market, Yeosan River League
Work · Market guide, market stall-lottery host
Life · He learned to count sacks from his aunt and took charge of the market lottery. He lived with an old cat named Godo, and after Godo died, he spent his days off visiting markets at other ferry crossings. He never left Toram to live elsewhere.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He had a gift for making people laugh, but because he did not want to lose their attention, he was slow to correct an unfair lottery.
Tastes · He liked the warm cloth where Godo rested and unfamiliar objects from other markets.
Daily life · On market days, he checked the merchants’ names and stall locations. On his days off, he took a boat across the river to visit other markets.
World · Hamin’s River Calendar and Toram Market are fictional settings created for this story.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
Those close to him · The aunt who taught him to count sacks, the fruit seller Dohee, the merchant Uran who protested the lottery, and Godo the cat
Wish · To keep living in Toram, where people gathered, while occasionally seeing other markets too
Worry · That because he could not calculate every loss caused by past lotteries, people would remember him as someone who also avoided responsibility
Later years · After working at the market, he took short trips to ferry markets across the river.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Mojin, the stall-lottery host at Toram Free Market. Everyone coveted the first stall by the river because it greeted customers as soon as they stepped off the boats. Let me tell you about the early winter morning when an old cat named Godo was to choose that spot.

On market day, when the cat chose the first stall, Godo walked toward the far-left basket as always. But Mojin did not ring the bell.

Whenever a new market opened in Toram, the merchants’ name tags were tied to five cloth baskets of the same size. The merchant whose basket Godo, the old gray cat in Mojin’s care, approached first won the first riverside spot, greeting customers as they stepped off the boats. The other four spots were drawn with wooden numbered tokens. Mojin made sure the baskets were all the same height and set Godo down before the starting line. Whenever the spectacle began, the market filled with laughter.

Dohee, the fruit seller whose name tag hung at the very end, asked, “Do you think Godo will even make it as far as my basket?” Mojin laughed as he scratched Godo’s back. “Even I don’t know which path Godo will take.” At that, even more people crowded forward. Mojin had cared for Godo for eleven years, but today his attention was drawn more to the crowd’s expectations than to the cat.

On an early winter morning when the boats from the north arrived, Godo sat down at the starting line. One of the waiting merchants laughed and said, “It’ll be the far left again this year, won’t it?” Mojin remembered that the last two results had also been on the left. When Godo stood and stretched a paw that way, Mojin picked up the cat before he could touch the basket. Low sunlight slipping through a gap in the awning warmed only the basket on the left. The basket beside it was cold. When Godo was set down again, he curled up on the warm cloth without even looking at the name tag.

signalMoments.notice: Mojin touched the far-left basket and the basket immediately beside it in turn with the back of his hand. Only one was warm. After confirming that Godo had followed the sunlight rather than the name tag, he asked the committee member to lower the bell for a moment.
signalMoments.speak: Mojin asked the committee member to lower the bell for a moment. When he had the five merchants touch the two baskets, one of them said, “They really are different.” Only then did Mojin explain what Godo had chosen.
signalMoments.release: Mojin drew back the hand that was about to place Godo on the starting line again. Even if it meant losing the scene people loved, he decided not to keep moving the old cat around to get an answer. After asking the committee member to lower the bell for a moment, he set Godo on the cloth beside his coat.

episode.afterSignal:
When the bell fell silent, Mojin set the two baskets before the crowd. “Godo can’t read names. He was looking for the warm basket.” The merchant whose name tag hung on the left shouted, “If you knew that, why did you wait until now to stop it?” Mojin could not rush to invent an answer. Nor could he say that every past result had been wrong. But he could not let the first spot be decided this way today. A committee member brought the box of wooden numbered tokens used for the remaining spots. Mojin clearly read out the names of all five merchants as he placed five identical tokens inside. The committee member and one merchant counted them again. When the first token from the box was opened, the first riverside spot went to Dohee’s small fruit stall, whose basket had waited at the very end.

The market opened late. The committee deducted part of the promised payment for hosting the lottery show and said it would also review past stall assignments. Mojin felt hurt. The merchant whose name tag had hung on the far left did not nod in agreement easily, either. For a while, some people called him the man who had deceived a cat, while others called him the man who had let a cat rest.

After the baskets were cleared away that afternoon, Godo fell asleep on the lid of the token box. Mojin spread a cloth beside Godo and counted the applications for the next market again. He never made Godo the star of the event after that, but he kept a warm spot for him in a corner of the market.

Mojin continued working at Toram Market afterward. The first spot was decided by counting the tokens with the merchants, without asking Godo. Some merchants welcomed the new drawing that day, but no one got back the customers they had lost on earlier market days.

timeline.event: Born in a house beside the riverside market at Toram Free Market
Begins counting sacks unloaded from boats while following his aunt, a porter
Guides customers and organizes the row of stalls at the market entrance
Takes charge of hosting the market committee’s stall lottery
Begins caring for Godo, a gray stray cat
Helps his aunt organize cargo on days other than market days and walks along the river with Godo
Discovers the cat’s choice of sunlight and changes the method used to draw the first stall

The merchant Uran says he lost customers because he failed to win the first spot in an earlier lottery. The committee cannot verify losses from past market days and provides no compensation. Mojin also says he has no money to repay the loss himself.
The old cat Godo dies. On his days off, Mojin begins taking boats across the river to visit other markets.
Introduces a sealed token box checked jointly by a committee member and a merchant
Teaches his successor, Onjae, to count applications and tokens together
Even after reducing his market work, he visits Dohee’s fruit stall and takes short trips to other ferry crossings.
After returning from another market, his torso is crushed between a drifting boat and a stone pillar at the Toram ferry landing, ending his life

memories.detail: Toram’s bustling market and the river ferry where he passed on his way home

memories.label: What He Treasured Most
memories.detail: A piece of cloth where Godo used to rest and small objects brought back from other markets

memories.label: The Merchant Dohee’s Assessment
memories.detail: “He must have hated losing his show. Still, that day he changed what he said in front of us.”

memories.label: The Merchant Uran’s Assessment
memories.detail: “Who will give back the customers I lost at the last market? Just because there are new numbered tokens doesn’t mean what happened that day never happened.”

memories.label: His Successor Onjae’s Memory
memories.detail: “He was meticulous on market days. On his days off, he talked much longer about the things he had seen at other markets.”

finalMoment.place: The river ferry landing at Toram Free Market in the world of Hamin
finalMoment.scene:
One late autumn morning in River Calendar year 190, I returned to Toram after visiting a market across the river. I carried the blue cloth I had bought, wrapped into a small bundle. After stepping off the boat, I was passing the edge of the stone landing when the boatman tied the boat to a post with a rope. As the river surged, the side of the boat drifted little by little toward the landing.

I saw frayed strands sticking out from the rope beside the post. “That rope is worn.” The boatman looked up and shouted for me to step back. The rear side of the boat struck the stone with a thud. I tried to step backward, but my side was caught between the boat and a pillar on the landing. Even when I tried to expand my chest, my body would not move.

From inside the boat, the boatman pushed the vessel away with a long pole. When the side moved back a little, I sank to my knees on the stone ground. The bundle was still looped over my arm. At the boatman’s instruction, the passengers moved to the opposite side. I tried to stand, but the place crushed between the boat and the stone hurt deep inside. “Just a moment,” I said, and the boatman sat beside me.

Each time I drew a breath, my side hurt more. I tried to move away from the pillar. My palm slipped on the wet stone. The boatman asked where it hurt. I pointed to my side, but no more words came. Listening to the morning river lap against the stone, I closed my eyes.
finalMoment.afterword: Mojin died at the age of seventy-two in late autumn of River Calendar year 190, after his torso was crushed between a boat and a stone pillar at the landing where he had returned to Toram from visiting another market. It was never determined what had been injured inside his body. The boatman remembered moving the passengers to the far side of the boat and pushing the hull away with a pole. A few days later, among the things Mojin had left behind, Dohee saw the worn cloth where Godo used to rest. His successor, Onjae, remembered the days when they counted the tokens together as he inspected the token box. Uran admitted that the new lottery method was good, but said it still had not repaid the value of the customers he had lost long ago. The Record of Past Lives preserves together Mojin’s wish to see the market people laugh, the lottery he corrected too late, the days he lived with Godo, and the time he spent crossing the river on his days off. His final journey ended at the Toram ferry landing.
finalMoment.artAlt: The moment before the accident at Toram ferry in late autumn of River Calendar year 190, viewed from a high diagonal angle. Mojin, age 72, holds a blue bundle and examines a worn mooring rope beside a post on the landing. The side of the boat is drifting toward the landing, and the passengers remain aboard. The composition shows no one supporting him or running to call for help.

card.name: Darin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Darin, a dance-shoe maker in Biel Harbor. Your hands were quick, but you tried to inspect every shoe by yourself.
card.title: Twenty-Four Left Shoes
card.world: Early autumn, Marching Calendar year 204, Biel Harbor in the eastern Miro Merchants’ League, Midden. An autumn parade running from the warehouses to Clocktower Square
card.flavor: A race-against-time workshop commotion
card.opening: Two hours before the twelve dancers were due to leave, all twelve pairs—all twenty-four shoes—in your workshop were left shoes.
card.life: Biel Harbor’s autumn parade featured a dance with high kicks. The dance shoes were made with symmetrical soft soles, while diagonal instep straps and padding sewn inside the ankle distinguished left from right. You hung up a single left-shoe sample for your apprentice, Robin, and said, “Make twelve pairs.” That evening, other repair orders piled up, so you never opened the box to check.
card.turn: The next morning, when Raon, the lead dancer, tried on the first pair, the strap and padding on the right shoe twisted to the outside and scraped the ankle. All twenty-four shoes in the box were the same. Outside the window, the parade’s first drum sounded. It was Robin’s mistake, but only the single left-shoe sample you had given him hung on the wall.
card.decision: You removed the strap and padding from one shoe and sewed them back onto the opposite side. The symmetrical sole could stay as it was. Once Raon ran in it and said it fit, you called Soman, the craftsperson across the street, and two apprentices. Everyone divided up the shoes and sewed, and Robin took six of them. You delivered the last pair before the parade turned toward the square. You tightened a loose strap with a lace taken from your own shoe.
card.cost: The dance went on, but the other repairs you had promised to do that day were delayed. You explained what had happened to the waiting customer and charged less. You also paid Soman for the thread and shared work. You could not put all the blame on Robin.
card.after: After the parade, you and Robin hung a new right-shoe sample on the wall. Whenever Soman teased, “How many feet this year?” you counted the shoes first and answered, “Two each.”
card.presentEcho: Even with quick hands, some things cannot be checked alone. With the festival drums sounding, Darin shared the work and admitted her own part in the mistake.
card.secondLook: The twenty-four left shoes were not caused by Robin’s stitching alone. Darin had left only a left-shoe sample, said, “Make them like this,” and failed to inspect the box.
card.unresolved: Darin charged less for the delayed repair order. Later, she and Soman started a joint workday for young apprentices, and Darin herself joined an evening dance group. She kept her workshop open but accepted fewer festival-shoe orders.
card.readerQuestion: Have I ever tried to finish quickly and missed a chance to check something together with someone else?

signalMoments.notice: You first confirmed that all twenty-four shoes were stitched on the same side. As Robin looked back and forth between the sample he had seen and the box, you also understood how the same mistake had continued.
signalMoments.connect: You had Robin clear an empty workbench and divide the thread into several bundles. First, you made room to borrow other people’s hands.
signalMoments.repair: You untied one shoe’s knot and examined the needle holes. There was no time to make new shoes, but the strap could be reattached through the existing holes.

setting.region: The Free City of Biel Harbor, east of the Kingdom of Doran

identity.region: The Free City of Biel Harbor, Miro Merchants’ League
identity.summary: Darin grew up in a harbor repair shop and opened a dance-shoe workshop. For a long time, she only made dance shoes for others, but in her fifties, she began attending an evening dance group herself. She reduced her workload but never closed the workshop.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Darin · Female · Marching Calendar years 165–233 · Age 68
World of Midden · The Free City of Biel Harbor, Miro Merchants’ League
Work · Leather repairer, dance-shoe maker, workshop owner
Life · After learning the craft in her mother’s repair shop, she opened a workshop at the harbor. When she was young, she only made shoes for dancers. Starting in her fifties, she attended an evening dance group herself.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · Pride in her quick hands sometimes made her put off checking her work, but when learning unfamiliar dance steps, she did not rush.
Tastes · She liked soft leather and the slow dances held in the square at night.
Daily life · By day, she repaired festival shoes and workers’ worn-out footwear. Once a week, she attended a dance group.
World · Midden and the Marching Calendar are fictional settings created for this story.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Those closest to her · Her mother, Seon; her apprentice, Robin; her neighboring craftsperson, Soman; and the members of her evening dance group
Wish · To find time beyond making other people’s shoes to dance on her own feet
Worries · That she might fail to finish workshop orders on time or misstep at the dance group
Later years · She reduced her orders, kept the workshop open, and continued attending the evening dance group.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Darin, a shoemaker in Biel Harbor. You were entrusted with making shoes for twelve people who would dance in the autumn parade. Let me tell you about the day, two hours before they were due to leave, when all twelve pairs—all twenty-four shoes—in the workshop turned out to be left shoes.

The parade from the harbor warehouses to Clocktower Square featured a dance with high kicks. The shoes were made of soft leather. The soles were the same shape on both sides, but a strap running diagonally across the instep and padding inside the ankle distinguished the left shoe from the right. Darin hung up a single left-shoe sample for her apprentice, Robin, and said, “Make twelve pairs. I’ll check them this evening.”

That evening, repair orders from customers who had come ashore piled up, and Darin merely pressed down the lid of the box. The next morning, when Raon, the dancers’ leader, came to collect the shoes, Robin proudly took out the first pair. When Raon tried them on, the strap on the right shoe crossed over the outside of the ankle.

“Can you wear it the other way around?” Robin asked. Balancing on one foot, Raon shook their head. The padding on the outside scraped the ankle while dancing. Darin unfolded the second shoe, then the third. They were all the same. All twenty-four were left shoes. From outside came the boom, boom of the parade’s first drum being tested.

Robin’s face went white. Darin opened her mouth, then looked at the sample hanging on the wall. There was only one left shoe. She was also the one who had said, “Make them like this.” It was true that Robin had attached the straps incorrectly, but Darin had not looked inside the box the night before.

signalMoments.notice: Darin confirmed that the ankle padding on all twenty-four shoes had been stitched to the same side. She realized the shoes did not need to be thrown away; only the positions of the straps had to be changed.
signalMoments.connect: Darin had Robin clear space on the workbench and divide the thread into several bundles. They had not removed a stitch yet, but she first made room to borrow other people’s hands.
signalMoments.repair: Darin untied the final knot securing one shoe’s instep strap. The holes the needle had passed through could be used again. With no time to make new shoes, that meant there was a way to repair them.

episode.afterSignal:
Darin removed the instep strap from one shoe. There was nothing wrong with the sole. She reattached the strap and ankle padding on the opposite side, and Raon ran a few steps in it. It fit. But Darin and Robin’s two pairs of hands were not enough to repair the remaining eleven shoes. Raon ran off to tell the dancers to wait in front of the warehouses for now.

Darin raced to the workshop across the street and called for Soman, a neighboring sewing craftsperson. Ordinarily, she would have disliked anyone else touching the shoes in her workshop, but this time she held out an awl and thread first. “I’ll remove the straps on this side. You attach them to the other side.” Soman brought both apprentices along. Robin tried to take hold of all eleven remaining shoes alone, but accepted only the six Darin handed over.

Each time the bell rang, another completed right shoe was placed beside a left one. Nine pairs, then ten. As they cut the thread on the eleventh shoe, the parade passed in front of the workshop. Darin tucked the final pair against her chest and ran. At the corner where the parade turned toward the square, Raon took the shoes and put them on. On the third step, a strap came loose. Darin pulled the lace from her own shoe and tied it once more around Raon’s ankle. Raon stamped a foot to test it, then ran into the parade. Carrying her own loosened shoe in one hand, Darin followed on foot.

The dance did not stop. But repairs promised to another customer that morning were delayed. Darin found the customer, explained the wait, and charged less. She told Robin, “You made a mistake,” and also said, “I didn’t check.” That evening, the two of them hung a new right-shoe sample beside the left one. Soman charged for a bundle of thread, and Darin laughed as she entered it in the ledger.

Darin continued making Biel’s dance shoes afterward. Even on days without festivals, she had her apprentices try on both the left and right shoes. Whenever Soman teasingly asked, “How many feet this year?” Darin counted the shoes before answering, “Two each.”

Starts a joint workday for young apprentices with Soman
Reduces festival-shoe orders but keeps the workshop open. Attends an evening dance group once a week.
At an evening dance group in Biel Harbor, she suddenly grows dizzy and has difficulty breathing, then dies after sitting down on a chair. The exact cause is unknown.

finalMoment.place: The evening dance group’s hall in the Free City of Biel Harbor, World of Midden
finalMoment.scene:
On a late-autumn evening in Marching Calendar year 233, sixty-eight-year-old Darin is at a dance-group hall in Biel Harbor. By day, she opens her workshop; by night, she dances on her own feet. Through the window, she can see the lights of ships at anchor. When a slow song begins, Darin matches steps with the woman opposite her. Just as they complete one turn and prepare to change places, dizziness strikes, as though the floor is sliding far away.

Darin cannot take the next step. “I need to rest for a moment.” The woman opposite nods. Darin walks to a long bench by the wall on her own and sits down. She grips the end of the bench tightly. The drums and footsteps continue, but she struggles to hold her body upright. The woman opposite stops dancing and looks back. Darin tries to raise a hand to show that she is all right, but rests it on her knee again.

She tries to take a long breath, but only a short sound comes from her throat. Darin tugs her collar loose. Looking at the empty space beside her, she says, “Some water…” The woman takes a few steps closer and offers her a cup of water. Darin tries to take it, but her fingers do not close in time. The cup remains in the woman’s hand. Only then do the dancers’ footsteps around them stop.

Darin raises her head to look at the woman’s face. Her lips move, but no other words come out. One hand is still gripping the end of the bench. The ceiling lamps look blurred. As she tries to breathe once more, the strength leaves her hand. The woman calls her name, but Darin cannot answer. Darin’s breathing stops, and only the sound of someone setting down the cup of water remains in the hall.
finalMoment.afterword: Darin died at age sixty-eight in late autumn of Marching Calendar year 233, after suddenly becoming dizzy and having difficulty breathing at an evening dance group in Biel Harbor. The exact cause was never determined. The woman who had been dancing opposite her remembered that Darin first said she needed to rest and walked to the chair on her own feet. Robin, once her apprentice, remembered the day Darin did not place all the blame on Robin for the badly made shoes. Soman, the neighboring craftsperson, remembered how Darin spent years making other people’s dance shoes before belatedly learning to dance herself. There was also the other customer’s order that had been delayed on that long-ago parade day, and the reduced price Darin charged. The record of her past life preserves both the Darin who hurried in the workshop and the Darin who learned to step slowly in the square. Before the dance group’s next song began, Darin’s life ended.
finalMoment.artAlt: Viewed from the ceiling beams above the dance-group hall in Biel Harbor on a late-autumn evening in Marching Calendar year 233 in the World of Midden. 68-year-old Darin sits alone on a long bench by the wall, catching her breath, while her dance partner opposite her turns to look from a few steps away. It is the moment when the surrounding dance stops; the composition does not show a collapse, physical support, or a call for rescue.

card.name: Serin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Serin, a roof keeper in Levon Autonomous City. You were someone who once watched only the high rooftops and missed the water bowls below.
card.title: The House the First Rain Passed By
card.world: Late spring, Rainroad Year 172, in Levon Autonomous City at the southern edge of the Terran Highland Federation in Luan. A communal roof that divides the first rain after a long dry season between two cisterns
card.flavor: Responsibility and solidarity in a downpour
card.opening: The first rain came, but not a single drop fell into the water bowls below.
card.life: On Levon's communal roof, rainwater flowed past a divider board into two cisterns, upper and lower. You repaired the worn upper channel and tied the board toward it for testing. You meant to return it to the center, but after going to inspect another leak, you came back, tied a seal cord to the knot, and climbed down.
card.turn: Before dawn, rain suddenly poured down. Water overflowed from the upper cistern and soaked the cloth stalls, while the neighbors below stood holding empty bowls. The red seal cord on the roof was still holding the board toward the upper side.
card.decision: If you waited for permission from the management office, the first rain might stop. You first told your coworker Boram that you had failed to turn the board back. As Boram steadied the ladder, you fastened a safety rope, climbed up, and cut the seal. Together, you pulled out the wooden wedge and tugged the hook, turning the board back to the center.
card.cost: Water flowed below as well, but stains remained on several sheets of cloth above. The management office held you responsible for breaking the seal and delaying the inspection, and docked your inspection allowance for one season.
card.after: After that, you never checked the divider board alone. When Boram asked about the upper side before it rained, you first listened for the sound of water in both cisterns below.
card.presentEcho: Something you believe you finished alone may remain unfinished in someone else's day. Only after admitting her mistake did Serin see both waterways again.
card.secondLook: The rain did not miss the lower side because of the weather. Serin failed to return the divider board after the test, and Boram saw the knot but did not ask about it.
card.unresolved: The docked allowance and stained cloth could not be restored. Serin lived with Boram, splitting the rent, but Boram did more of the evening meal preparation. Though they learned to check things together on the roof, they never divided the housework equally.
card.readerQuestion: Could there still be empty bowls below the things I think I have finished?

signalMoments.notice: You listened in turn to the upper channel overflowing and the lower channel falling silent. You realized the problem was not the amount of rain, but the direction of the board.
signalMoments.speak: You shouted down, “No water is reaching the lower cistern!” The neighbors holding empty bowls and Boram all looked up together.
signalMoments.connect: Instead of moving the ladder alone, you called Boram. That way, one person could watch the board above while the other watched the waterway below and the ladder.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Serin · Female · Rainroad Years 120–193 · Age 73
World of Luan · Levon Autonomous City, Terran Highland Federation
Work · Roof repairer, communal rainwater roof keeper
Life · She learned about water channels in the lower district and repaired communal roofs. After her inspection allowance was docked for one season, she lived with her coworker Boram and split the rent. Even after she cut back on work atop high roofs, she never left Levon.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She admitted her own mistakes, but for a long time failed to notice how much more work Boram did at home.
Preferences · She liked the dry sound of roof channels before rain and warm soup in the evening.
Daily life · By day, she inspected waterways. While living with Boram, she split the rent and firewood equally, but Boram usually prepared the evening meal.
World · Luan's Rainroad Calendar and communal roof system are fictional creations.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her father, who carved her first hook; Boram, her coworker and housemate; and the neighbors above and below
Hopes · To send water to both cisterns and live without worrying about paying rent alone
Worries · That if her daily wages fell, she might have to live alone again
Later years · She continued living with Boram, but they did not measure out equal shares of the housework.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Serin, a roof keeper in Levon Autonomous City. In that city, the first rain after the long dry season was collected on communal roofs and divided between upper and lower cisterns. Let me tell you about the day the first rain came but the water bowls below remained dry.

Levon's houses clung in tiers to the highland slope. Beneath the uppermost communal roof was a wooden board that divided the rainwater. Pushing the board left sent water into the upper channel, while pushing it right sent water into the lower channel. When it was centered, the two channels shared the water. During the dry season, Serin repaired the worn upper channel and tied the board to the left to test it. She was supposed to turn it back to the center once the repairs were complete, but she rushed away when word came of a leak on the next roof. By the time she returned, darkness had fallen. Serin tied the management office's red seal cord over the knot and climbed down from the roof. She meant to check it in the morning.

The rain came before morning. When Serin opened the window, water was overflowing from the upper cistern and soaking the covers of the cloth stalls. But below, she heard water bowls scraping against the ground. Children from the lower district stood in front of the communal cistern holding empty bowls. Serin looked up at the roof through the rain. The red seal cord fluttered above the board held to the left.

signalMoments.notice: Serin listened in turn to the water on both sides of the roof. It gushed through the upper channel, while not a single drop fell from the lower one. She realized the problem was not the amount of rain, but the direction of the board.
signalMoments.speak: Serin leaned out beneath the window and called first, “Is anyone at the lower cistern? No water is coming down!” Boram looked up along with the neighbors holding empty bowls.
signalMoments.connect: Instead of moving the ladder alone, Serin called Boram. One person needed to watch the board while the other watched the ladder and the waterway below.

episode.afterSignal:
The seal could be removed only with permission from the management office. The first rain might stop while Serin was away getting permission. Below, her coworker Boram brought over the ladder. “Who tied the board last?” Serin bit her lip, then said, “I did. I tested it and left it that way.” Boram did not immediately set a foot on the ladder. “Then climb up and untie it with your own hands. I'll hold the ladder from below.”

The rainwater weighed heavily on the board. Serin tied her safety rope to a sturdy roof beam and hooked her tool into the ring on the board. It did not move on the first pull. Boram reached up and pointed to the wooden test wedge jammed beside the board. Serin pulled out the wedge and cut the seal cord. When they pulled the hook together, the board swung back to the center. One stream still flowed upward, while the other followed the lower channel down the slope.

When the first sound of water came from the lower cistern, there was no cheering above. The owner of the upper cloth stall was busy spreading out the wet goods, and an employee from the management office picked up the severed seal cord. Serin could have said only, “The rain came suddenly.” Instead, she said she had not turned the board back after testing the upper channel and had put off checking it until morning. As Boram set down the ladder, she added, “I saw that knot yesterday, but I didn't ask whether the upper-channel test was finished.” Neither of them erased the other's words.

Enough water collected in the lower cistern for everyone to share the first rain. The wet cloth from above dried, but several stained sheets could not be sold for full price. The management office docked Serin's inspection allowance for one season and put it toward the cleanup costs. For someone who counted every drop of water through the dry season, it was not a small sum. Serin stared at the knot in the seal cord for a long time, then changed the next inspection sheet so that two people had to record the divider board's position together.

Serin kept climbing onto roofs after that. Before it rained, Boram would ask from below, “How is it up there?” Before touching the board, Serin would first look at the bowls below. Even after she grew old and handed the work over to a junior, the sound of the first rain would make her glance out the window. She was not checking whether the roof was wet. She wanted to hear water in both cisterns.

timeline.event: Born into a roof-repairing family in lower Levon
After her first dry season, cleared mud from the rainwater channels with her father
Became an apprentice repairer on the communal roof connecting two residential districts
Became a roof keeper responsible for inspecting the divider board and cisterns
Replaced the worn upper channel with new wood alongside Boram
Publicly admitted her failure to reset the divider board during the first rain and divided the waterway again
Began living with Boram to reduce rent costs after her allowance was docked. They split the rent and firewood equally.
Established an inspection sheet requiring representatives from the upper and lower districts to verify the board's position together
Boram said she prepared dinner almost entirely by herself. Serin took responsibility for market days, but Boram still did more of the meal preparation.
Handed high-roof work over to a junior and taught her how to tie a safety rope. She continued living in the same house as Boram.
After suffering from a fever for three days, died at the table in the Levon home she shared with Boram. The illness is unknown.

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The first wooden hook her father carved for her and the two rice bowls they shared at home

memories.label: An Old Habit
memories.detail: After a repair, tugging each knot one more time—and later, listening for the lower cistern before climbing down

memories.label: The Flaw She Admitted
memories.detail: Believing it was enough to check alone and missing the fact that someone below was waiting

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “I'll go to the market today. We can make dinner together, right?”

memories.label: Coworker Boram's Assessment
memories.detail: “On the roof, she didn't hide her mistakes. At home, she thought that splitting the rent meant she was also doing half the evening work.”

memories.label: The Upper Cloth Stall Owner's Memory
memories.detail: “We lost the full price of several sheets of wet cloth. When the next rain came, Serin checked our channel too.”

memories.label: The Lower Neighbor's Assessment
memories.detail: “We thanked her when we saw the rainwater come down. But we also heard why it hadn't come the day before.”

finalMoment.place: The house Serin and Boram shared in Levon, in the world of Luan
finalMoment.scene:
One late-autumn evening in Rainroad Year 193, 73-year-old Serin sits at the table in the small Levon home she shares with Boram. She has had a fever for three days and could not even go to the market today. Boram bought vegetables instead, and a pile of untrimmed leaves lies beside their bowls. Though Serin grips her spoon, she cannot lift the warm soup. When she strains her wrist, the tip of the spoon strikes the bowl.

Boram turns from stirring the soup at the hearth. “Do you want to go to your room?” Serin shakes her head. “I'll stay here. You already went to the market today.” Boram brings a fresh bowl, ladles a little soup into it, and places it on the table. Throughout their life together, they split the rent and firewood evenly, but Boram prepared dinner more often. Saying she will trim the vegetables, Serin picks up a stalk. The leaves slip from her hand and fall onto the table.

“Just leave it.” Boram puts out the hearth fire and sits in the empty chair across from her. Serin picks up the spoon again. She can smell the soup, but her throat is so dry that she cannot swallow even a sip. She sets down the spoon and asks Boram for water. Boram hands her a cup. Serin brings it to her lips, then coughs. Water from the cup runs over the back of her hand. “It's cold,” Serin says.

Boram finds a cloth and wipes her wet hand. Serin takes the cloth and tries to wipe it herself, then lowers her hand to her lap. “Serin, can you hear me?” Boram asks. Serin turns her head but cannot keep her eyes open for long. The pauses between her breaths grow longer, and the steam fades from the bowl. Serin opens her mouth and tries to call Boram. The name does not come. Her last breath escapes softly, and Serin's hand grows still in her lap.
finalMoment.afterword: Serin died at age 73 in her Levon home one late-autumn evening in Rainroad Year 193, after suffering from a fever for three days, with Boram seated beside her. No name for the illness survives. Boram remembered both the day on the roof when Serin did not hide her mistake and the many years when Serin left more of the evening meal preparation to her. The owner of the upper cloth stall remembered failing to sell several sheets of wet cloth for full price. The neighbors below spoke both of Serin setting the waterway right and of why the water had not come before that. The record of her past life preserves both the day Serin admitted her mistake on the roof and the days when Boram prepared dinner more often at home. Serin's life ended at a table set with two bowls.
finalMoment.artAlt: A low view from the threshold of a small Levon kitchen, not a communal roof, on a late-autumn evening in Rainroad Year 193 in the world of Luan. Feverish 73-year-old Serin sits at the table with one hand resting beside her soup bowl, while her housemate Boram turns from the hearth to look at her. There is no collapse, physical assistance, or call to a third party.

card.name: Doyun
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Doyun, a portrait painter in Lumi Free City. Before painting someone's face, you listened to the people who remembered it.
card.title: One Person Remembered by Three
card.world: Early winter, Gallery Calendar 286, Lumi Free City in the northwest of the Seha City Alliance in Ovel. A small portrait studio in a city without photography
card.flavor: Family memories and portraits
card.opening: Three siblings commissioned a portrait of their late mother. But each of them remembered a different face.
card.life: In Lumi, where there was no photography, the face of someone who had never been painted could be recreated only through the memories of those left behind. Doyun had never met Mira, a fabric dyer. The eldest, Jin, remembered a young Mira with a blue headscarf and round cheeks. The second child, Sol, remembered a middle-aged Mira with a red headscarf and a slender face. The youngest, Ian, remembered her later years, when she wore no headscarf. The wooden frame for the memorial hall had already been fitted.
card.turn: No one recognized their mother in Doyun's first portrait, which blended all three memories. Only two days remained until the memorial, and the more he reworked the face through the night, the thicker the paint became. In Mira's dye workshop, he saw the blue and red headscarves hanging side by side. The three accounts were not wrong. They described Mira at different points in her life.
card.decision: Rather than pretending to know a face he did not know, Doyun proposed preserving the three periods in three panels within a single painting. Across the bottom, he continued the motion they all remembered: Mira's hands spreading out cloth. Jin hesitated, saying this was not the single face they had agreed on, but Sol and Ian placed their respective pieces of cloth beside the painting and looked at it together.
card.cost: He had to discard the first layers of paint and the night's work. Doyun did not charge for the draft and also paid to alter the wooden frame for the three panels. Even after the portrait was finished, Jin did not say it looked exactly like their mother.
card.after: On the day of the memorial, the three siblings stood before different panels. Jin asked who had shown him Mira's hand movements, and Doyun replied that the siblings themselves had demonstrated them in the workshop. After that, whenever he received a commission, he first asked which period of whose life they wanted to preserve.
card.presentEcho: People can remember someone differently and still miss the same person. Instead of pretending to know a face he did not, Doyun created a place where three people's stories could stand together.
card.secondLook: None of the three siblings had described the wrong face. The blue headscarf, the red headscarf, and the uncovered head belonged to different periods of Mira's life.
card.unresolved: Doyun could never know Mira's true face, and Jin never said the portrait looked exactly like her. Doyun himself also left the care of his father to his younger brother, Geonu, for a long time. They divided the expenses, but the nights Geonu spent alone and the distance between the brothers remained.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever listened to the end when someone remembered the same person differently from you?

signalMoments.notice: You rewrote Jin's account of the blue headscarf and Sol's account of the red headscarf in chronological order. Rather than two colors belonging to one face, they might have belonged to different periods.
signalMoments.connect: You asked the three siblings to show you the workshop where Mira had worked. Before they argued over their memories again, you wanted them to stand in the same place.
signalMoments.speak: You covered the draft and told the three of them, “I never saw your mother. Right now, I've mixed your three accounts together and pretended they were one face.”

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Doyun · Male · Gallery Calendar 222–301 · Age 79
World of Ovel · Lumi Free City, Seha City Alliance
Work · Sign shop assistant, portrait painter, studio owner
Life · He learned about color in his father's sign shop and opened a studio in Lumi. As the studio grew, he left the care of his father to his younger brother, Geonu. He later paid his share of the caregiving expenses, but the brothers never became as close as before. After handing the studio over to his apprentice Hari, he painted small portraits.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · Quick and attentive with commissions, but prone to putting off answers when his family asked for help.
Preferences · He liked sketching people's hand movements before their faces, and he liked small sheets of paper.
Daily life · He met clients at the studio and studied signs in the old town on his days off. He could never stay long at Geonu's house.
World · Ovel's Gallery Calendar and Lumi's galleries are fictional creations.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
People close to him · His father, a sign craftsman; his younger brother Geonu; his apprentice Hari; and Mira's three children.
Hopes · To finish each commissioned painting on time and repay his debt to his family.
Worries · That money could never fully make up for the time Geonu had shouldered alone while Doyun was absorbed in his work.
Later years · Even after handing over the studio, he painted small portraits. He and Geonu met only briefly on holidays.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Doyun, a portrait painter in Lumi. In the early winter of Gallery Calendar 286, Doyun was asked to paint the face of someone he had never met. Let me tell you about the day her three surviving children each remembered a different face.

There was no photography in Lumi. To preserve the face of someone who had gone far away or passed from the world, a painting had to have been made while that person was still alive. Mira had no such painting. She had spent her whole life dyeing cloth and never had time to sit for a painter. Before her memorial, Mira's three children commissioned a portrait of their mother from Doyun. The wooden frame for the memorial hall had already been fitted.

Doyun seated the three of them before a blank canvas. Jin, the eldest, said, “She wore a blue headscarf. Her cheeks were rather plump.” Sol, the second child, immediately shook their head. “The mother I knew wore a red headscarf. And her cheeks weren't that round.” Ian, the youngest, looked from one to the other and said, “I never saw her wearing a headscarf. She combed her hair back.”

Each of them added details about the eyes and mouth they remembered. Doyun took notes, selected the eyes and nose they said looked most like her, and drew a draft. When Jin saw it, they frowned. “That's my mother's headscarf, but the face looks like someone else.” Sol also spoke. “The mouth looks like hers, but she never wore that expression.” Ian said nothing and picked up the empty wooden frame. Two days remained until the memorial.

That night, Doyun reworked the face in the draft again and again. If he changed the eyes, it drifted further from Jin's memory. If he changed the mouth, he felt Sol would find it unfamiliar. By dawn, the brushstrokes had grown thick before the pigments could even dry. Doyun covered the painting.

signalMoments.notice: Doyun reread his notes in chronological order. Jin, who had mentioned a blue headscarf, and Sol, who had mentioned a red one, might have been talking about their mother at different times in her life.
signalMoments.connect: Doyun asked the three siblings to show him the workshop where Mira had worked. Before they argued over each other's accounts again, he wanted them to stand in the same place.
signalMoments.speak: Doyun spoke to the three siblings first. “I never met your mother. Right now, I've mixed your three accounts together and pretended they were one face.”

episode.afterSignal:
Doyun went to Mira's dye workshop. A faded blue headscarf and a red one, long kept folded and frayed at the edges, hung side by side on the wall. Ian said, “When I helped her work, she used to take off her headscarf and tie her hair back because it kept slipping.” Doyun realized that their accounts were not wrong but pointed to Mira in different years. Yet that alone was not enough to paint her face accurately. After all, he had never met her.

Years of pressure from hands had worn the corner of the worktable smooth. Jin gripped the folds of a blue cloth and spread it out. Sol held down one edge with a thumb. Ian shook out the folded end, then aligned it neatly. All three performed the same motion in slightly different ways. “Mother taught us to do it like this,” Ian said, and Jin smiled for the first time. “Even if I forget the color of her headscarf, I'll never forget those hands.”

Doyun proposed dividing the single portrait into three panels. He would place the young Mira, the middle-aged Mira, and the old Mira in one picture, then continue the movement of hands spreading cloth beneath all three panels. “I can't promise the faces will be exactly right,” Doyun said. “Because I never saw her. But I can preserve the times each of you saw without erasing any one of them.”

Jin stared at the canvas for a long time. “I asked for one person's face.” Doyun nodded. He would have to repaint it, and the wood inside the frame would need to be altered to fit the three panels. Doyun said he would not charge for the discarded draft and would pay to alter the frame himself. Jin still hesitated, but Ian placed the blue headscarf beside the first panel. Sol hung the red headscarf beside the second.

On the day of the memorial, the three siblings stood side by side before the painting, but each person's gaze rested somewhere different. Jin looked at the first panel for a long time, and Sol pointed to the red headscarf. Ian traced the hand in the last panel with a finger. In the end, Jin did not say, “It looks exactly like Mother.” Instead, before leaving the hall, Jin asked Doyun, “Where did you see those hands?” “The three of you showed me in the workshop.” Jin looked at the painting again and, this time, slowly examined the other two panels as well.

Doyun continued painting portraits in Lumi after that. Whenever he received a commission, he first asked whose life they wanted to preserve, and from what period. There were still days when he could not capture a face accurately. On those days, Doyun began by admitting what he could not claim to know.

memories.label: The youngest, Ian's memory

memories.label: His apprentice Hari's assessment

finalMoment.place: A street in front of a fruit stall in the old town of Lumi Free City, world of Ovel
finalMoment.scene:
In the daytime in early autumn, Gallery Calendar 301, seventy-nine-year-old Doyun bought fruit to take home from a stall in Lumi's old town. Even after handing his studio over to Hari, he walked this street on his days off. Holding the bag in one hand, Doyun walks along the narrow stone road. When the wind lifts the stall's awning high, the fruit seller grabs a corner. From the wall above comes the sound of wood splitting.

Doyun looks up. A heavy wooden sign on the shop across the street has slipped free of one hook and is tilting toward the road. Doyun raises a hand to shield his face and tries to step away from the wall. “Look out!” the fruit seller shouts. Before Doyun can take his next step, the corner of the sign strikes his head and shoulder. The bag slips from his hand, and the fruit rolls across the street.

Doyun collapses onto the stone road. A brief sound rings in his ears, and the fruit seller's voice seems distant. He presses a palm against the ground, but his arm cannot support his body. One yellow fruit rolling before his eyes comes to a stop. The seller approaches and asks, “Can you hear me?” Doyun tries to answer that he can, but no sound leaves his mouth.

Doyun turns his eyes toward the seller's face. He can see only a blurred outline. The hand he had stretched out to pick up the fruit lies on the stone. The seller asks his name again. Doyun cannot gather enough breath to speak it. He tries to close his eyes once and open them again, but his eyelids do not rise. Before the seller finishes the last question, Doyun stops breathing.
finalMoment.afterword: Doyun died at seventy-nine in the early autumn of Gallery Calendar 301 after a falling shop sign struck his head in Lumi's old town. The fruit seller saw Doyun raise a hand as he tried to avoid it, but there was no time to pull him out of the street. His apprentice Hari remembered a teacher who listened to his clients before he painted. His younger brother Geonu separately remembered the nights he had spent alone caring for their father and the belated division of the expenses. The two brothers never closed the distance between them. The Record of Past Lives preserves both Doyun, who refused to carelessly merge other people's memories into a single face, and Doyun, who could never repay the time his own family had lost with money alone. His life ended in daylight as he was returning home with fruit.
finalMoment.artAlt: A ground-level view looking up at a street in Lumi's old town during the daytime in early autumn, Gallery Calendar 301, in the world of Ovel. 79-year-old Doyun, carrying a bag of fruit, notices a heavy wooden sign falling from above after its hook comes loose and raises a hand. The fruit seller watches in alarm from the collapsed stall; no composition suggesting assistance or a rescue request

card.name: Woojin
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Woojin, a parade-float maker in Tevan Autonomous City. You were a craftsman happiest when people marveled at your decorations.
card.title: The Paper Whale That Raced Down the Hill
card.world: Late summer, Procession Calendar year 123, in Tevan Autonomous City, southwest of Braon's Dor Plains Federation. The summer festival route ran downhill from the assembly yard on the hill to the market square.
card.flavor: A fast-paced festival mishap and a choice
card.opening: One hour before the festival, the paper whale you had made rolled downhill with no one aboard.
card.life: Tevan's parade floats were four-wheeled wooden carts with ropes tied to the front for people to pull. No one could ride inside Woojin's enormous turquoise paper whale. At the assembly yard on the hill, wedges had to be placed against both sets of wheels and the front rope tied to a stake, but his apprentice Hani merely stood one wedge beside a wheel. Busy fixing the whale's eye, Woojin only signed the checklist without personally inspecting the wedges or the worn knot.
card.turn: When a strong wind pushed the tail, the knot in the front rope came undone and the cart began to move. By the time Hani returned with the wedge, the wheel had already left its place. Woojin saw Miso's pottery stall on the market road below and the empty straw yard beside it. After clearing the space in front of the stall and stopping Hani from trying to block the cart with her body, he ran toward the fork alongside the moving towrope.
card.decision: Though he knew the whale's tail would catch on the low wooden fence, Woojin and his fellow carter Dabok pulled the rope to the right, steering the float toward the empty straw yard. Once the front wheels crossed a flat stone, the whale came to a stop in the straw pile, and the wooden frame of the tail he had spent 3 days making broke.
card.cost: Miso's pottery did not break, but she had to send customers away and set up her stall again. With its damaged tail, the whale was disqualified from the festival judging, and Woojin paid for the new wood and paper. He recorded both Hani's missing wedge and the knot he himself had failed to inspect.
card.after: When he was barred from entering a large parade float the following year, Woojin repaired market carts alongside Hani. Woojin checked the wheels and knots together with her, and when he eventually built large parade floats again, he put Hani in charge of choosing the colors of the decorations. Even in old age, when he taught others to make small floats, he kept a torn fragment of the whale's tail hanging on the workshop wall.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes you have to sacrifice the part you treasure most. Woojin put the market road before a prize, and afterward he also took care to inspect the wheels hidden from view.
card.secondLook: The wind was not the only reason the parade float rolled away. The wedge stood beside the wheel, and Woojin's signature was no substitute for an actual inspection.
card.unresolved: The customers Miso lost and the cost of the new tail remained even after the festival ended. Woojin could not build a large parade float the following year and repaired market carts instead. He eventually entered the festival again, but whenever his float approached, Miso cleared her stall first.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever focused so much on the most noticeable part that you had to go back and look beneath it?

identity.summary: Woojin loved the applause parade floats earned, so he built a great whale. After the accident, he could not build a large parade float for 1 year, but he never gave up his desire to enter the festival again.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Woojin · Male · Procession Calendar years 80–153 · Age 73
The world of Braon · Tevan Autonomous City, Dor Plains Federation
Work · Cart repairman, festival parade-float maker
Life · Born into a family of carpenters, he learned to make wheels and opened a workshop in Tevan. After the paper whale accident, he was barred from making large parade floats for 1 year and repaired market carts instead. He later entered the festival again, and after turning the workshop over to Hani at age 62, he traveled to village festivals as a spectator.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Kind of Person He Was
profilePages.body:
Personality · After the accident, he no longer left inspections entirely to others, but he also held on for a long time to his desire to win applause with a spectacular float.
Tastes · He loved the sight of paper tails swaying and the sound of new wheels rolling quietly.
Daily life · For 1 year, he repaired market carts and endured the frustration of being unable to prepare for the festival. After handing over the workshop, he shared seats with festival spectators who had come from far away.
World · Braon's Procession Calendar and Tevan Autonomous City are fictional settings.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Those close to him · His maternal uncle, who taught him about wheels; his apprentice Hani; the carter Dabok; and the merchant Miso.
Desire · To build another large parade float and earn people's applause.
Worry · That if he failed to inspect the next float's wheels properly, he might frighten the people in the market again.
Later years · After turning the workshop over to Hani, he watched festivals in several villages as a spectator. Miso remained wary of his floats.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Woojin, a parade-float maker in Tevan Autonomous City. Let me tell you about the day his paper whale went down the hill with no one aboard, 1 hour before the summer festival began.

Tevan's parade floats were not powered by horses or engines. Long ropes were tied to the front of four-wheeled wooden carts, and people pulled them slowly. The paper body of the turquoise whale Woojin had made was as large as a single-room house. It was too light to carry anyone, but its raised tail swayed like a living thing whenever it caught the wind. When Woojin heard that the most beautiful float would be chosen in the festival judging, he spent 3 days perfecting that tail.

The assembly yard stood at the very top of the hill. Before testing a cart, wooden wedges had to be pushed against the wheels on both sides and the pulling rope tied to the stake in front. His apprentice Hani stood one wedge beside a wheel. She thought she had put it in place. Woojin only straightened the whale's crooked eye and signed the checklist. He did not inspect the other wedge or the knot in the old rope.

The wind pushed the whale's tail. The worn knot around the front stake slowly came undone, and the cart moved a handspan. By the time Hani picked up the wedge, the wheel had already left its place. “Master Woojin!” Hani cried as the paper whale raced downhill. No one was aboard the whale, but Miso's pottery stall stretched along the market road below.

For the first few steps, Woojin watched only the tail. He was afraid the tail he had spent 3 days making would strike the stone wall. Then he saw Miso ushering customers away from between her boxes of jars. Running down the road, Woojin shouted, “Clear the space in front of the stall!” The customers retreated into a side alley. As the whale's broad body came downhill, 1 child began to cry after first laughing. Woojin sent the child into the alley, then grabbed Hani's arm as she tried to stop the cart with her body. “Don't stand in front of it.”

signalMoments.notice: Woojin looked back and forth between the towrope being dragged ahead of the cart and the flat stone at the fork. Before the stone, there might still be a chance to use the rope to change its direction.
signalMoments.connect: Knowing he could not pull that weight alone, Woojin looked at Dabok, the carter running beside him. Dabok matched his pace as he waited for a signal.
signalMoments.release: Woojin tore his eyes away from the whale's tail he had spent 3 days making and looked at the low wooden fence around the straw yard. He decided to send it that way even if the tail tore.

episode.afterSignal:
Halfway down the market road was a fork where the ground leveled out. To the left was the pottery stall; to the right, an empty yard where straw was stacked. A low wooden fence stood at the entrance to the empty yard. Woojin knew the whale's tail would catch on it and tear. The towrope being dragged out in front was reaching the fork ahead of the cart. Woojin shouted to Dabok, the carter running beside him. “Grab the rope and pull right! We'll send the whale toward the straw.”

Dabok grabbed the end of the rope, and Woojin took hold farther up. Without stepping in front of the cart, the 2 men stood beside the fork and pulled the rope to the right. At first, only the whale's head swayed. When Woojin pulled again, the front wheels crossed the flat stone and turned toward the empty yard. The instant the cart buried itself in the straw pile, the wooden frame of the tail snagged on the fence and snapped with a crack. Turquoise paper fluttered like snow. Someone started to applaud, then stopped.

Miso spent a long time counting her jars to see whether any had broken. Not 1 had, but she was furious that she had lost customers while setting up her stall again. Woojin apologized and helped clean up. The festival judge said a tailless whale could not join the parade. Only then did Woojin look at the fallen decorations. He won no prize that day, and the cost of the wood and paper for a new tail was his to bear.

Hani returned carrying the missing wedge. “I didn't put it in.” Woojin pointed to his name on the checklist. “The truth is, I looked without seeing.” He wrote both failures on the paper: ‘One wedge not inserted; knot in front rope not inspected.’ That evening, Woojin and Hani cleared away the broken tail and left only the whale's rounded head in a corner of the yard. Children stood in front of it and drew whales on paper. Even without a tail, they knew it was a whale.

Woojin continued making Tevan's parade floats after that. But he could not start again immediately. The festival judge informed him that no large float of his would be accepted the following year. Woojin spent that year repairing market carts with Hani. Once he was permitted to make floats again, he put Hani in charge of choosing the colors of the decorations, and they inspected the wheels and knots together. Even so, he still wanted to display a large float before a crowd. After he grew old and turned the workshop over to Hani, he traveled to festivals in other villages.

timeline.event: Born into a family of carpenters below the hill in Tevan Autonomous City
Began shaping cart wheels for his maternal uncle, a carpenter
Apprenticed in repairing market carts
Built Tevan's first small paper parade float
Opened a summer-festival parade-float workshop
Took Hani on as an apprentice and taught her to make decorations
The paper whale parade float rolled downhill and stopped in the straw yard; lost eligibility to build a large parade float the following year
Unable to enter the festival, kept the workshop going by repairing market carts
Resumed building large parade floats and established a rule requiring 2 people to inspect the wheels and ropes
Turned the workshop over to Hani and began attending festivals in neighboring villages as a spectator
In late summer, while returning from a festival in another village, fell on wet hill steps, fractured his pelvis, and died from internal bleeding

memories.label: The Place He Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The assembly yard on the hill and the market road below. A place where stall owners could continue their work while parade floats passed

memories.label: What He Treasured Most
memories.detail: The first wooden wheel carved by his maternal uncle and the festival admission ticket he kept even in the year after the accident

memories.label: An Old Habit
memories.detail: Looking at a completed float's face from afar first, and later spending a long time crouched beside its wheels

memories.label: The Flaw He Admitted
memories.detail: He was so busy inspecting the whale's tail that he failed to check the wedges and knot. Even afterward, he had no intention of giving up applause.

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “Next time, I'll look at the wheels before the whale's eyes.”

memories.label: Apprentice Hani's Assessment
memories.detail: “I was the one who forgot the wedge. Master signed his own name on the checklist too. During the year he couldn't enter the festival, he repaired market carts with me.”

memories.label: Pottery Merchant Miso's Assessment
memories.detail: “Just because no jars broke doesn't mean I wasn't angry. Even when Woojin started building large floats again, I cleared my stall first.”

memories.label: Memory of a Later Festival
memories.detail: “He applauded other people's parade floats, but Woojin kept his head lowered until the wheels had passed before looking up at the tail.”

memories.label: Carter Dabok's Memory
memories.detail: “If I'd pulled alone, the cart wouldn't have turned. Woojin first decided which way we were going to send it.”

finalMoment.place: Hill steps leading back to Tevan Autonomous City in the world of Braon
finalMoment.scene:
It is a late-summer afternoon in Procession Calendar year 153. At 73, Woojin is returning home after visiting a festival in a village beside Tevan. Even after turning the workshop over to Hani 11 years ago, he continued traveling to other villages to watch their processions. Today he applauded for a long time after seeing someone else's float take a corner smoothly. He folds the paper ticket he received as a spectator and slips it into his pocket. The rain stopped in the afternoon, but the hill steps are still wet.

Woojin descends the stone steps toward Tevan 1 at a time. The step below looks level, so he takes a long stride. The sole of his shoe slips on the wet stone. “Huh?” Woojin reaches for the wall beside him, but his hand cannot reach it. His lower back strikes the edge of a step, and his body tumbles down several more. A sharp pain rises from his pelvis.

A spectator who had been following comes down and says, “Don't move.” Instead of answering, Woojin props himself up on his elbows and tries to rise. The moment he moves his legs, the pain makes him collapse again. The spectator places a folded coat behind his back. “Tell Hani...” Woojin begins, then stops. There is no longer any workshop work for him to ask Hani to handle. Still, he wants someone to tell her that he was on his way back.

After calling to people on the road below for help, the spectator remains by Woojin's side. Woojin waits at the foot of the steps until the sun goes down. Blood continues to pool inside around the fractured pelvis. Though no blood is visible outside, Woojin grows steadily colder and dizzier. When the spectator asks his name, Woojin answers, “Woojin.” A while later, even when he hears the question again, he cannot form an answer. The spectator touches his shoulder. Woojin looks once more at the steps before him, then breathes his last.
finalMoment.afterword: In late summer of Procession Calendar year 153, Woojin fell on the steps while returning to Tevan after visiting a festival in another village and fractured his pelvis. The internal bleeding did not stop, and he died that evening at age 73. The spectator following him stayed at his side and heard Woojin's name, but could not save him. Hani was not there, and even after receiving the news, she continued making floats under her own name. She also remembered how Woojin had repaired market carts alongside her for 1 year after the accident. When pottery merchant Miso heard of Woojin's death, she still remembered the road down which his whale float had come. The record of his past life closes the story of Woojin's life by preserving both the day his love of applause made him neglect an inspection and the days he spent traveling to watch other people's festivals after leaving his workshop.
finalMoment.artAlt: Late summer, Procession Calendar year 153, in the world of Braon: a horizontal scene from a high, diagonal viewpoint looks down on wet stone steps leading back to Tevan. The 73-year-old Woojin is on the verge of losing his balance after misstepping on the stairs, while the spectator following far behind stands at the top. There are no falling rocks, no one supporting him, and no one running to call for help

card.name: Nari
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Nari, a kite maker in Bar Free City. Before fixing a kite that would not fly straight, you first watched where the wind was going.
card.title: The Kite That Went Right
card.world: Early spring, Kite Year 207, Bar Free City south of the Hajin Mountain Alliance in Asen. Wind Hill, where a target hung between the stone pillars on the right
card.flavor: Sibling rivalry and a reversal in the wind
card.opening: On the entry form for the contest you had agreed to enter together, your older brother wrote only his own name. You climbed the hill alone, carrying a kite with one short tail.
card.life: Bar's spring contest was not won by the highest kite, but by the first person to touch an orange cloth target suspended between the tops of two stone pillars with the tip of their kite. The target stood to the right of the starting point, while the morning wind blew straight ahead. Nari repeatedly tested small kites and found that a short tail made them curve right when they caught a crosswind. Her older brother Dogyeom, who had wanted them to compete together, feared that the crooked kite would cost them the victory, so he put only his own name on the entry form.
card.turn: Nari did not fix the asymmetrical tail and entered on her own. Her kite wobbled in the first wind, making the crowd laugh, while Dogyeom's straight-flying kite rose ahead of it. When the second bell rang to announce the time remaining, a crosswind rose from the valley, and Dogyeom's kite passed to the left of the target.
card.decision: Though Nari knew the kite might drift too far away to bring back, she let out the string one finger joint at a time. The short right tail lifted, and the kite tilted that way. When she stopped the string at the last moment, its yellow nose brushed the orange cloth first.
card.cost: Nari won, but Dogyeom did not congratulate her right away. For a while, even at the workbench behind the same cloth shop, neither touched the other's kite, and they tested their kites on different hills. Nari opened her own workshop without the team name they had shared.
card.after: Nari opened an independent workshop in Bar, making both straight-flying and curving kites to suit the wind. Many years later, she and Dogyeom taught with different kites on the same hill, but the tails of their kites still did not match.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes what makes others excel looks different from the shape of my own kite. Nari tested for herself when and where her kite would go, and trusted the results.
card.secondLook: The crooked tail was not a mistake that needed to be fixed in a hurry. It wobbled in the morning, but when it met a crosswind from the right, it created a path to the target.
card.unresolved: Even after her victory, Nari and her older brother Dogyeom did not touch each other's kites. Later, they taught kite-making separately on the same hill, but they did not meet often. Nari handed her workshop over to Miru and recorded the winds of many hills alone.
card.readerQuestion: Has something others told you to fix ever created the direction you needed?

signalMoments.connect: You saw your mother in front of the cloth shop holding up a piece of scrap fabric. When its end streamed to the right, you remembered the wind on the day of your test.
