identity.summary: Nari tested different winds from her older brother and opened an independent workshop. After handing the workshop over to Miru, she walked mountain paths alone and recorded the winds of many hills.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Nari · Female · Kite Years 188~263 · Age 75
World of Asen · Bar Free City, Hajin Mountain Alliance
Work · Cloth shop assistant, kite maker, workshop owner
Life · She made kites from scrap fabric at her mother's cloth shop. She opened an independent workshop, using methods different from those of her older brother Dogyeom. After handing the workshop over to Miru at age 63, she walked mountain paths alone each year and recorded the winds of many hills.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She had to test things with her own eyes before she believed them, and there were days when she left alone even if someone asked her to stay with them.
Preferences · She liked collecting the different crosswinds of each hill and the colors of scrap fabric.
Life · She made kites in the workshop, and in her later years, she used the money she had saved to walk mountain paths and fill notebooks.
World · Asen, the Kite Calendar, and Bar Free City are fictional settings.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her mother, who opened the cloth shop; her older brother Dogyeom, with whom she made kites; and Miru, who took over the workshop.
Wind · Not imitating other people's kites, but recording the winds of hills she had walked herself.
Worry · She worried that if she spoke about her methods at the same workbench as Dogyeom, they would grow apart.
Later years · She handed the workshop over to Miru and walked mountain paths alone. After returning, she lived in a small room in Bar and rarely saw Dogyeom.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Nari, a kite maker in Bar Free City. In the spring when she was nineteen, Nari found herself standing alone in a contest she had planned to enter as a team with her older brother. Let me tell you how the crooked kite everyone laughed at flew.

Bar's spring contest was not about who could fly a kite the highest. The contestants launched their kites from the same hill. Between the tops of two stone pillars in front of the hill hung a piece of orange cloth no bigger than a handkerchief. The first person to touch it with the tip of their kite won. The cloth was to the right of the starting point, but the morning wind always came straight at them. People flew their kites high, then tugged the strings to turn them right.

Nari and her older brother Dogyeom, who was four years older, made kites side by side behind their mother's cloth shop. The two tails of Dogyeom's kite were the same length, so it rose straight. The right tail of Nari's kite was one handspan shorter. A few days earlier, while testing a small kite on the hill, Nari had seen its body tilt toward the shorter side when a crosswind blew. She attached the same tail to a larger kite. Dogyeom lined up the tails on the workbench and said, “It'll wobble in the first wind like this.” Nari knew that too. The kite had fallen twice in the first wind. But when the wind shifted in the afternoon, it had gone right all three times.

They had agreed to compete together. On the contest entry form, solo competitors wrote one name, while teams wrote two. That morning, Nari saw the form Dogyeom had brought back and stopped what she was doing. Only Dogyeom's name was in the box. “I thought we'd lose the contest if we entered with our kite.” Dogyeom folded the paper. “Your kite still needs more testing.” Nari did not snatch away the paper that left out her name. Instead, she took out the crooked kite stored beneath the workbench.

Before the registration bell rang, Nari entered her name alone. Though it was still morning, the grass on the hill briefly bent to the right again and again. Nari did not fix the kite's short tail. She only turned the string reel in her hand three times to test it. Dogyeom came over and said, “At least make the tails match.” Nari answered, “That cloth is on the right.” Dogyeom looked at the cloth, then returned to his own platform.

When the first bell rang, Dogyeom's kite shot straight up. Nari's kite wobbled once near the ground. Laughter came from behind her. Nari did not rush to let out the string, but drew it in little by little. When the kite stood upright again, its paper wings trembled. Dogyeom's kite was already high overhead. Nari looked down at the red mark the string had left across her palm. The cloth was still far away.

The second bell was not a signal that the wind had changed direction. It told the contestants how much time remained. After it rang, Nari saw the long grass beside the rocks bend all at once. Wind rising from the valley pushed against the sides of the kites. Dogyeom's straight-flying kite held its height well, but passed to the left of the cloth. He pulled hard on the string. The kite tilted for a moment, then straightened again.

signalMoments.notice: Nari looked again at the tips of the grass beside the rocks. They were falling in the same direction as on the afternoon when she had tested the small kite.
signalMoments.connect: Nari saw her mother standing in front of the cloth shop. The end of the scrap fabric her mother held streamed to the right as well. She remembered the wind on the day of her test.
signalMoments.release: Nari opened one finger from the hand gripping the string reel. She eased up a little on the force that had tried to hold the kite straight, giving it room to move with the crosswind.

episode.afterSignal:
Nari nearly dropped the string reel. If she let out more string now, the kite might drift so far that it would be difficult to bring back. But this was the crosswind she had been waiting for from the start. She let out the string one finger joint at a time. The short right tail lifted first, and the kite's nose turned right. “It's going that way!” someone shouted. Nari let out the string once more, then stopped it just in front of the cloth. The kite's yellow nose brushed the orange fabric. The cloth fluttered.

The judge called Nari's name. Before looking at the kite that had won, Nari looked at Dogyeom. He was slowly lowering his own kite. “That crosswind was a perfect match,” he said. Winding the string around her reel, Nari answered, “Yes. That's why I waited for it.” Dogyeom did not congratulate her. Nari did not explain any further. Their mother kept the cloth shop open until they returned and cleared two separate spaces for their dusty kites.

Nari received a small silver string reel as her prize that day. When she returned to the workbench she shared with Dogyeom, she hesitated for a long time over where to hang her kite. At last, she hammered a nail into one side of the cloth shop. The next day, Dogyeom did not touch Nari's kite, and Nari did not fix his tails. Though they worked in the same place, they went to different hills to test their kites for a while.

Later, Nari opened a small kite workshop in Bar. She made straight-flying kites for those who wanted them, and when a kite needed to turn sideways, she told people to look at the wind first. It was many years before she and Dogyeom flew kites together again. Even then, the tails of their two kites were not the same length.

timeline.event: Born into a cloth-dyeing family in Bar Free City
Made her first kite tail from her mother's scrap fabric
Began making contest kites at the same workbench as her older brother Dogyeom
Started a small notebook to record Bar Hill's winds by time of day
First touched the spring contest's orange cloth target with a short-tailed kite
Opened an independent kite workshop beside her mother's cloth shop
Completed a maker's notebook comparing wind and tail length on different hills
Taught separate kite classes with Dogyeom on the same hill again
Handed the workshop over to her apprentice Miru and began walking mountain paths alone to record the winds on different hills
Cut back on journeys to distant hills, returned to a small room in Bar, and organized her wind notebooks
Encountered a sudden blizzard on a road near Bar's Wind Hill and died of hypothermia

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: Bar's Wind Hill. A place where anyone could test a kite made with their own hands

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The tail of her first kite, made from her mother's scrap fabric, and the wind notebooks she added to on every hill she walked alone

memories.label: An Old Habit
memories.detail: Checking which way the tips of the grass swayed before letting out the string

memories.label: The Flaw She Admitted
memories.detail: When she thought her way was right, she would stop explaining and leave to test it alone first

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “The tails don't have to match. Let's just look at where they need to go.”

memories.label: Her Older Brother Dogyeom's View
memories.detail: “She was lucky that day too. But I didn't know Nari had been waiting for that wind. Later, she went alone to hills even I had never visited.”

memories.label: Her Mother's Memory
memories.detail: “They both made kites from my fabric, but their hands wound the string very differently.”

memories.label: Her Apprentice Miru's View
memories.detail: “After she handed over the workshop, I handled the orders and rent alone. Nari would send a wind notebook now and then, then leave for the mountain paths again.”

finalMoment.place: A winter road near Wind Hill in Bar Free City, in the world of Asen
finalMoment.scene:
It is a winter morning in Kite Year 263. Seventy-five-year-old Nari locks the door of her small room in Bar and steps outside. She has cut back on journeys to distant hills since she was sixty-nine, but she still walks the roads near her home alone. A neighbor who lives across from her looks at the sky and asks, “Are you going out again today? It looks like snow.” Nari tightens her scarf and answers, “I'll only go as far as the entrance to the hill.”

Nari starts up the road to Wind Hill. At first the snow falls lightly, and she can still see the grass between the stones. Just as she passes the rocky shelter and is about to turn back, the wind grows stronger. Snow strikes her face, and she cannot keep her eyes open for long. Nari turns to look for the village rooftops, but through the white snow, both forks of the road look the same. She takes a few steps down the path she thinks she came from.

Her toe catches on dry grass. This is not the stone path she walked earlier. Nari stops and looks for the nearby rocky shelter. She sees the shadow of a rock a few steps ahead. “Just that far.” Her voice is lost in the wind. She tries to retie her scarf with her fingers, but cannot manage the knot. Even when she rubs her hands together, the feeling does not return. She tries to walk again, but her knees buckle, and she sits beside the rock.

Snow piles on her knees, and she cannot see the rooftops of Bar. Nari knows she must stand, but whenever she puts strength into her legs, her body shakes. The trembling gradually weakens. She leans her back against the rock and slips her hands inside her sleeves. It sounds as if someone is calling in the distance, so she opens her mouth and says, “I'm here,” but the sound is very faint. Even when she tries to open her eyes, her eyelids are heavy. Unable to hold on to the thought of standing again, Nari loses consciousness and dies there.
finalMoment.afterword: Nari died of hypothermia at age seventy-five in the winter of Kite Year 263, after encountering a blizzard on a hill road not far from her home in Bar. The short walk she mentioned to her neighbor that day became her final outing. When Nari did not return, the neighbor searched the road the next day and found her beside a rock. Miru remembered handling the orders and rent alone after taking over the workshop. Her older brother Dogyeom recalled the long years when they tested kites on different hills, but did not say that they had grown close again at the end. The record of this past life closes the story of Nari by recounting not only the crosswind she waited for, but also the years she spent choosing paths alone and the times those choices left work for others.

card.name: Minrok
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Minrok, an illusionist from Seon Free City. You dazzled audiences, then became someone who also credited by name the hands that worked behind the stage.
card.title: The Name Behind the Wall
card.world: Late autumn, Makryeok Year 114, in Seon Free City, west of the Radan League of Traveling Cities in Noir. A small wooden theater lit by lanterns
card.flavor: Stage illusions and hidden contributions
card.opening: An advertisement for the theater across the street showed your red ribbon and the wall. But it named your former colleague as the one who had made that wall alone.
card.life: At the center of Seon Theater's movable wooden wall was a narrow door concealed in the grain. The carpenter Bohyeon carved the hinges and latch, while Minrok redirected the audience's gaze with a drum, lanterns, and a red ribbon. Minrok truly passed through the wall by way of that door. The two performed together for many years before parting ways, and Bohyeon claimed in an advertisement for his new troupe that he had created the wall passage alone. Minrok, too, had called it “my wall” in earlier performances without mentioning Bohyeon's name.
card.turn: When Minrok confronted Bohyeon, Bohyeon held up an old hinge and said Minrok had erased his craftsmanship too. The theater owner said the advertisement could not be changed unless they showed the audience proof onstage. Tickets for the evening performance had already been sold, and if they revealed the door, tickets for the wall passage might stop selling the next day.
card.decision: Minrok performed the wall passage once as usual, then stopped the drum. He brought a lantern close to the wall's grain, opened the hidden door, and publicly explained that Bohyeon had made the hinges while he had guided the audience's eyes with the red ribbon. He admitted that he, too, had previously spoken as if he had made the wall alone.
card.cost: Some members of the audience laughed, but others demanded refunds. Ticket sales for the wall passage fell the next day, so the theater owner cut Minrok's performance fee. Even after Bohyeon removed the word “alone” from his advertisement, he and Minrok did not reconcile right away.
card.after: Minrok searched for a new illusion and listed the names of both the maker and the director in the performance program. When he grew older, before putting an apprentice's device onstage, he first asked whose hands had made it.
card.presentEcho: Hands unseen may stand behind the moments everyone sees. Minrok was slow to break his habit of claiming the stage's name for himself alone.
card.secondLook: The wall passage was not magic. It was an illusion created by a real narrow door in the wall and a red ribbon that drew the audience's eyes.
card.unresolved: Minrok and Bohyeon never stood on the same stage again. After the wall's secret was revealed, ticket sales fell, and Minrok closed his troupe, scattering his colleagues. He performed with other troupes and later opened a small class.
card.readerQuestion: Is there someone I should credit by name, even for something I said I accomplished alone?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Minrok, an illusionist from Seon Free City. When two people made a wall together, could either one claim to have made it alone? Let me tell you about a late-autumn evening when Minrok had to find the answer before an audience.

Seon Theater had a wooden wall mounted on wheels. At every performance, Minrok set it at center stage and walked around its front and back to show that no one was hiding behind it. Then he dangled a red ribbon from his fingertips. As a lantern illuminated the ribbon and a small drum sounded, Minrok appeared on the other side as if he had passed through the wall. The audience could not come close enough to touch it, but in that moment, everyone doubted their own eyes.

It took two people to make that wall. Night after night, Minrok changed his gestures to test when the audience would look at the ribbon. His fellow performer, a carpenter named Bohyeon, hid the door's seam among the patterns of the wood and carved hinges that allowed the small door to open silently. The door was not part of a passage that went around the back of the wall. It was right in the middle of the wall. Minrok opened the door and truly passed through the wall. All he did was draw the audience's eyes toward the ribbon.

The two worked in the same troupe for many years before parting ways. Bohyeon rented a large theater across the street and opened his own troupe. One morning, Minrok saw an illustrated advertisement outside the new theater. It showed a red ribbon and a wooden wall. Beneath them were the words, “The wall passage Bohyeon made alone.” Minrok could not take his hand away from the advertisement. After all, he was the one who had dangled the red ribbon from his fingertips.

He went straight to Bohyeon. “You can't put your name on my direction too.” Bohyeon showed him an old hinge lying on his workbench. “You called it ‘my wall’ at every performance. You never once said who carved this.” Minrok opened his mouth, then closed it. It was true that he had never spoken Bohyeon's name before the audience. But the advertisement claiming that only one of them had made the wall was not true either.

The owner of Seon Theater shook his head and said he could not turn away people who had bought tickets because of the advertisement. “Arguing about it won't tell the audience anything. Can you show them onstage who did what?” Minrok looked at the remaining tickets for that evening's performance. If he revealed the secret, perhaps no one would pay to see the illusion from the next day onward. But if he performed while keeping the wall hidden, he would continue avoiding, before the audience, the very truth he had confronted Bohyeon about.

signalMoments.notice: Minrok looked again at the words “Minrok's Wall” printed in the performance program. He realized that Bohyeon's advertisement was not the only thing that was wrong.
signalMoments.connect: Minrok asked the drummer to stop playing during the final scene and shine a lantern on the wall's wood grain. He could not show the audience the seam of the door clearly on his own.
signalMoments.speak: Minrok told the theater owner he would open the door after the evening performance. The theater owner frowned, saying some customers would demand refunds.

episode.afterSignal:
The first part of the evening performance began as usual. The theater owner showed the audience the empty space behind the stage, and Minrok slowly turned the wall to display its front and back. One audience member shouted, “Show us the side too!” Minrok rolled the wall's wheels and turned it sideways. Its thick edge appeared briefly in the lantern light. Bohyeon stood in the last row. Even after seeing him, Minrok took out the ribbon.

The drum sounded. The end of the red ribbon spun beneath the lantern. Minrok placed a hand on the wall and stepped forward, and one side of the stage went quiet. At the next drumbeat, Minrok walked out from the other side. Familiar applause followed. Someone in the front row rose from their seat, eager to see again what had just happened.

Minrok did not bow. Instead, he raised a hand to signal the drummer to stop. “I'll show you one more time. This time, don't look at the ribbon.” He brought the lantern close to the patterns on the wall. With a finger, he pressed a line of finely painted wood grain. With a small click, a narrow door opened. Minrok walked into the open gap and came out again. The person who had applauded earlier was the first to laugh. From elsewhere came shouts demanding refunds.

Minrok pointed to the hinges inside the door. “Bohyeon is the one who carved these so the door would open silently. While the drum sounded and the lanterns shone, I led your eyes to that red ribbon. All this time, I called it only my wall.” Bohyeon came forward from the last row. He pushed the door once and said, “The latch still fits well.” Minrok asked, “Can you change the advertisement that says you made this performance alone?” Bohyeon did not answer at once. The open door remained between them.

The next day, only a few tickets for Seon Theater's wall passage were sold. The theater owner counted the empty seats and reduced Minrok's fee for his next performance. The word “alone” was removed from Bohyeon's advertisement, but the two men did not join the same troupe again. Minrok left the wall standing backstage and began searching for a new illusion. A young apprentice asked if they could touch the hinges. Minrok gazed for a moment at the wood bearing the marks of Bohyeon's hands, then opened the door.

Minrok continued to perform in Seon afterward. On the program for his next wall, he included the maker's name alongside his own. But with the decline in ticket revenue, he could not keep his troupe running for long. Even after closing the troupe and being hired by other touring shows, he liked it when audiences called his name loudly. Years later, whenever he taught young performers how to focus an audience's gaze, he began by asking, “Whose hands made that device?”

finalMoment.place: A small rented room in Seon Free City, in the world of Noir
finalMoment.scene:
On a winter morning in Makryeok Year 153, seventy-six-year-old Minrok eats bread alone in his rented room in Seon. A neighbor is sweeping snow outside the door. Minrok takes a sip of warm water, then picks up the remaining bread. At that moment, a pain begins as though something is pressing down on the center of his chest. He puts down the bread and straightens his back. He thinks it will pass if he rests for a moment.

The pain does not go away. His left arm begins to hurt, and cold sweat forms at the back of his neck. Minrok slowly rises from his chair and walks toward the door. With each step, his breath grows shorter. His hand slips from the doorknob. On his second try, he opens the door and calls toward the courtyard. “Please come here for a moment. I can't breathe.”

The neighbor puts down the broom and comes to the threshold. “Sit down. I'll call someone.” Minrok tries to nod but grips the doorframe instead. He returns to the room and sits in the chair, but he cannot draw a deep breath. The neighbor pushes a glass of water toward him. Minrok looks at it but cannot reach out his hand. “My chest...” No more words follow.

The neighbor calls his name. Minrok turns his face toward the sound. Winter light coming through the window touches the edge of the table. The light blurs, and the neighbor's voice grows distant. As Minrok's body slumps in the chair, the neighbor comes to his side. Minrok does not open his eyes again. His breathing stops as well.
finalMoment.afterword: Minrok died at age seventy-six of a myocardial infarction in his rented room in Seon during the winter of Makryeok Year 153. His next-door neighbor remembered the morning when Minrok opened the door himself to ask for help. A performer who had studied under Minrok in his youth recalled how he would ask for the name of the person who made a stage device. For the colleague who had played the drum in his old troupe, there also remained the memory of having to seek work in another city after the troupe closed. There is no record that Minrok and Bohyeon ever stood onstage with the same troupe again. The record of this past life preserves both the Minrok who belatedly revealed another person's contribution and the Minrok who still wanted to hear his own name. His life ended on a winter morning with no performance.
finalMoment.artAlt: On a winter morning in Makryeok Year 153 in the world of Noir, a small rented room in Seon Free City is seen from the courtyard through an open door. Seventy-six-year-old Minrok sits at a table with bread on it, clutching his chest. There are no performance props or other people, and the composition does not depict a collapse, someone supporting him, or a third party summoning help.

card.name: Ajeong
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Ajeong, an interpreter who knew the languages of both Durim Free Port and Moren. You went from merely translating one side's words to creating agreements that both sides could verify together.
card.title: Two Last Ferries
card.world: Late spring, River-Crossing Year 91, at Durim Free Port of the Isol River Union in Seraun and Moren Ferry Landing of the Har Mountain Realm. A ferry crossing with two different bell towers and a shared lantern in the middle of the river
card.flavor: Different Words and Different Times of Promise
card.opening: Because of an agreement signed identically by both riverbanks, only the travelers from one side missed the last ferry.
card.life: Durim considered the day over when the bell rang for the second time around sunset, while Moren believed the day ended only when the second night-watch bell rang about an hour later. The contract for the shared ferry crossing stated identically in both languages, “The last ferry will depart before the second bell rings.” Ajeong told Jangwon that the two bells rang at different times, but the head of the ferry office ordered her to use the same wording.
card.turn: After Durim's second bell, Moren merchants and children arrived to board the last ferry. Moren's second night-watch bell had not yet rung. Jangwon tied up the ferry and demanded an expensive special-ferry fare, then pointed to Ajeong, who had translated the contract, and said she had deceived the travelers.
card.decision: Ajeong opened the records she had kept for months of when the two bells rang and read them before the ferrymen from both sides. She even revealed that she had known about the difference but followed orders and left the wording ambiguous. She had both ferrymen confirm that the lantern at the midriver landing was still lit, then persuaded them to launch the remaining Durim ferry at the regular fare.
card.cost: The travelers crossed the river, but some of the merchants' vegetables spoiled while they waited. Jangwon fired Ajeong and refused to pay her overdue wages. For a while, people on both sides found it hard to trust her translations.
card.after: Ajeong later became an independent interpreter and created agreements in which both parties pointed to the same object and confirmed it in both languages. The two ferry landings established the lowering of the lantern in the middle of the river as their shared deadline for the last ferry.
card.presentEcho: Hearing the same words does not mean everyone imagines the same time. Ajeong long remembered the time she had assumed the other side knew about a difference she herself understood.
card.secondLook: The contract's two sentences were exactly the same. But Durim's evening bell and Moren's night-watch bell were not the same second bell.
card.unresolved: The vegetables that spoiled that day and Ajeong's unpaid wages were never recovered. After she established her independent interpreting office, Bern and his daughter Rumi became her family, but she lost them both in a great flood when she was seventy. Ajeong lived alone in a room high on Market Hill and continued teaching a few lessons.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever used the same words as someone else but imagined a different scene?

signalMoments.speak: Ajeong told the people in front of the office first, “I knew about this difference, and I still signed the same sentence.” She gave Jangwon no chance to stop her.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Ajeong · Female · River-Crossing Years 45–123 · Age 78
World of Seraun · Durim Free Port of the Isol River Union and Moren Ferry Landing
Work · Market order-form interpreter, ferry-office interpreter, owner of an independent interpreting office
Life · She learned both languages while crossing the river with her ferryman mother. After signing an ambiguous ferry contract, she lost her office job and overdue wages. She began again at a borrowed table and eventually opened a small interpreting office. She lived with the carpenter Bern and his daughter Rumi, but lost them both in a great flood at age 70. She moved to a room on Market Hill, lived alone, and continued teaching only a few lessons.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · There was a day when she knew the contract's wording was flawed but could not stand up to her employer. After losing her job, she confirmed both the object and time her client pointed to.
Preferences · She enjoyed recording how the bells sounded differently on the two sides of the river, as well as unfamiliar words.
Daily life · For a time, she translated order forms at a borrowed market table. Even later, she kept traveling between the two riverbanks.
World · Seraun, the River-Crossing Calendar, and the systems of the two ferry landings are fictional settings.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her ferryman mother Haejin, the carpenter Bern and his daughter Rumi who lived with her, Ruo of Moren, and a young interpreter.
Hopes · For people on both sides to make agreements while pointing to the same time and object, and for Rumi to choose the work she loved.
Worry · That a new contract alone could not restore a customer's trust once lost.
Later years · She left her mother's oar in the shared storehouse. After losing Bern and Rumi in the flood, she lived alone in a high room on Market Hill and reduced her lessons. Ruo and her student visited occasionally.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Ajeong, an interpreter in Durim Free Port. You could even understand the language of Moren across the river. Let me tell you about a late-spring evening when two villages that had signed the same sentence waited for different last ferries.

A narrow but swift river flowed between Durim and Moren. One wooden ferry from Durim and one from Moren took turns carrying passengers. A lantern hung at the shared landing in the middle of the river. Its light could be seen from either bank, but the ferries stopped according to the bells. Durim rang its evening bell twice around sunset, while Moren rang its bell twice about an hour later to begin the night watch. When the wind was calm, people could hear the bells from the opposite bank.

Ajeong had learned both languages from the age of ten, crossing the river with her mother, who was a ferryman. Whenever a traveler said “soon,” her mother would ask which bell they meant it should happen before. Even after becoming a merchant, Ajeong never forgot that habit. When she translated market order forms, she wrote down the date and quantity, as well as the item the other person had pointed to.

That spring, the two ferry landings set the last ferry's departure time in a single contract. The sentence presented by Jangwon, the head of the office, said, “The last ferry will depart before the second bell rings.” The sentence on the Moren side meant the same thing. Before signing, Ajeong pointed to the two towers. “Durim will think of the evening bell, and Moren will think of the night-watch bell. They're an hour apart.” Jangwon lowered his voice and said that the later the ferry ran, the easier it was to charge for a special crossing. “Let both sides believe it means their own bell. We'll follow Durim's bell.” Ajeong could not put down her brush. She was an interpreter he had employed, and her overdue wages were still being withheld by the office. In the end, she wrote her name beneath both sentences.

Even so, Ajeong began recording the time Durim's bell rang on the left side of her notebook and Moren's on the right. After ten days, then twenty, the difference between them remained almost the same. She showed the notebook to Jangwon again, but he said, “There haven't been any complaints yet, have there?” and shut it. Ajeong, too, said nothing in front of the ferry travelers.

One evening in late spring, two merchants from Moren and a young daughter returned from Durim's market carrying crates of vegetables. When Durim's evening bell rang for the second time, the Durim ferryman tied the ferry's rope. A merchant pointed to Moren's tower. “Our bell hasn't rung yet.” The child pushed a crate taller than she was toward the ferry. The moisture that had gathered on the tips of the vegetable leaves during the day was drying.

Jangwon appeared holding the contract. “The last ferry is over. If you want to cross, you must pay three times the fare for a special ferry.” When the merchant protested in Moren's language, Jangwon called for Ajeong in front of everyone. “This is the person who translated the words for both sides. If that's what you heard, ask Ajeong.” Ajeong heard the final echo from Durim's tower fade away. Moren's tower across the river was still silent. Her own name beneath the contract looked unusually dark.

signalMoments.notice: Ajeong compared the interval between the bells she heard from the two riverbanks with the records in her notebook. Moren's second bell had not yet rung.
signalMoments.speak: Ajeong told the people in front of the office first, “I knew about this difference, and I still signed the same sentence.” She gave Jangwon no chance to stop her.
signalMoments.connect: Ajeong called the ferrymen from both sides beneath the lantern at the midriver landing. They needed a time that three people could see together, not one person's interpretation.

episode.afterSignal:
Ajeong opened her notebook. In the left column, Durim's bell had rung today as soon as the sun slipped behind the mountain. In the right column, the line for Moren's bell was still blank. “The contract doesn't say which of the two bells it means.” She spoke in both languages so the merchants and ferrymen could all hear. “I knew that, and I still signed my name. Master Jangwon also said that we would follow Durim's bell when I asked him.” Jangwon tried to snatch the notebook, but when he saw both ferrymen watching him, he withdrew his hand.

The Durim ferryman pointed to the rope he had already tied. “Even if the contract is flawed, I can't launch the ferry again by myself.” The Moren ferryman had come as far as the midriver landing in an empty boat. Ajeong led everyone beneath the lantern. Its light could be seen from both riverbanks, and that day it was still hanging high. “For today, please accept that the regular ferry is still available until this lantern is lowered. Starting next time, the two villages can write a new closing time together.” When Ajeong held out her hand first, the Moren ferryman took it. The Durim ferryman looked at Jangwon once, then untied the rope. Jangwon could no longer stop the two of them together.

The child and the crates boarded the Durim ferry. Ajeong helped lift the bottom of the last crate. Crushed leaves poked through the gaps in the damp wood. As the ferry passed the midriver landing, Moren's second night-watch bell rang. The child raised her head at the sound, and the merchant placed the regular fare directly into the Durim ferryman's hand.

Even after they crossed, the vegetables at the bottom of the crates had already spoiled. That loss could not be recovered. The next day, Jangwon dismissed Ajeong from the office and refused to pay her overdue wages. The Moren merchant thanked Ajeong but did not entrust her with a new order form. After all, it was also true that she had signed her name to the ambiguous sentence.

That summer, the two ferry landings replaced the bells with the moment the lantern in the middle of the river was lowered as the deadline for the last ferry. When Ajeong read the new sentence, this time both ferrymen raised and lowered the lantern themselves. Ajeong later became an independent interpreter. Whenever she wrote down an object and date, she asked the client to point to them with her, and even when she felt certain of a word, she asked once more.

Ajeong kept crossing the river for many years. Whenever a young interpreter asked, “Why do you keep checking when the words are the same?” she would sometimes show them the two columns in her notebook. It was not the revised contract that put the travelers aboard that evening, but the choice of the two ferrymen. And Ajeong remembered the days when she had waited too long to speak before winning that choice.
