memories.detail: “Ajeong paid every time she borrowed the space. At first, the empty hours lasted longer than the visits from customers.”

memories.label: Bern and Rumi's Place
memories.detail: The two became Ajeong's family after she lost her job. Rumi chose carpentry. Both died in the great flood of Year 115.

memories.label: Ruo's Memory
memories.detail: “Whenever I visited her room, Ajeong served me tea. Even though I knew she'd be alone in that room after I left, I could never bring myself to stay long.”

finalMoment.place: Ajeong's room on Market Hill, Durim Free Port, world of Seraun
finalMoment.scene:
On a winter night in River-Crossing Year 123, seventy-eight-year-old Ajeong is alone in her small room on Durim's Market Hill. Eight years have passed since the house below on the riverbank was swept away in a great flood, killing Bern and his daughter Rumi. Ajeong never returned to that house. She has lived in this room, teaching a young interpreter the languages of the two riverbanks twice a week. Her cough and fever have worsened over the past three days, so she canceled today's lesson. Ajeong rises from her bed to drink some water.

The water bowl is on a low table near the door. When she lowers both feet to the floor, she feels dizzy. Ajeong braces one hand against the wall and takes a step. As she pours the water, a long bout of coughing makes the bowl shake in her hand. She sets the half-filled bowl back in place. Outside, she hears the market gates closing. When Ruo knocked on her door a few days ago, she served him warm tea, but no one is expected to visit today.

Ajeong returns to the bed and sits facing the door. “I'll tell them tomorrow.” She means that if she cannot teach again, she must let her student know. Speaking brings a burning pain deep in her chest, and her breath grows short. She tries to reach the door, but her body will not obey. She looks once more at the water bowl on the table. It seems within reach if she stretches out her hand, but her arm stops halfway. She sits up to steady her breathing, then leans against the wall and closes her eyes.

When the coughing subsides, the room grows quiet. Ajeong opens her eyes again and looks at the darkness in the crack beneath the door, but hears no footsteps. After breathing out one long breath, she cannot draw the next one in. In the other rooms on Market Hill, people are still eating dinner. The door to Ajeong's room does not open that night.
finalMoment.afterword: Ajeong died alone at age seventy-eight from a lung infection in her room on Durim's Market Hill during the winter of River-Crossing Year 123. The grief of losing her family in the flood was not the direct cause of her illness. When Ajeong did not come to the next day's lesson, her student went to the room with Ruo. Ruo remembered the evenings when he had visited Ajeong several times while she was alive but had been unable to stay long. Her student remembered lessons in which Ajeong made them confirm the same word twice. The old vegetable merchant's loss and Ajeong's overdue wages were never recovered. The Chronicle of Past Lives records separately her work connecting the languages of the two riverbanks, the small lessons she continued after losing Bern and Rumi, and her final moments with no one beside her.
finalMoment.artAlt: A winter night in a room on Durim's Market Hill in the world of Seraun. Viewed from outside the high window, 78-year-old Ajeong sits alone, leaning against her low bed and looking toward the door and the water bowl. There is no scene of the riverbank disaster and no one supporting her or running to get help.

card.name: Ryeowon
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Ryeowon, a rope keeper at the Bello Floating Orchard. You went from trusting knots alone to calling for other hands and eyes to check them with you.
card.title: The Pear Tree Before the Cliff
card.role: Rope keeper of a floating orchard
card.world: Midsummer, Root Reckoning 184, at the Bello Floating Orchard in the south of the Hairam Island Union in Mero. Two floating islands moving in the wind and the black cliffs to the east
card.flavor: Sky-orchard rescue adventure
card.opening: The island planted with a young pear tree drifted toward the cliffs. Hansol, an apprentice, was on the island too.
card.life: Bello's islands were supported by blue pumice and tree roots, but the wind pushed them sideways. The large work island and the small sapling island were tied to each other with rope, and each was also secured to a stone anchor on the coast. Ryeowon temporarily untied the sapling island's anchor rope to inspect its roots, and only looked at the old knot connecting the two islands from a distance.
card.turn: While Hansol remained on the sapling island to tend the pear tree, the connecting knot slipped. The wind drove the island toward the black cliffs to the east. Hansol could not reach the end of the rope, and the plank from the large work island still could not reach the island.
card.decision: Ryeowon told her fellow worker Seoon that she had untied the anchor rope and had not properly checked the knot. She released the large island's anchor so it could ride the same wind and catch up to the sapling island. Once the two islands were moving at similar speeds, she bridged them with a plank so Hansol could cross. Then she and Seoon hooked a spare rope onto the shared rescue anchor on a fixed rocky island before the cliffs.
card.cost: The two islands stopped before the cliffs, but the outer pear-tree branches and harvest crates on the work island struck the rocks and were damaged. Ryeowon took a season away from fieldwork to make good on the loss, and Hansol long remembered the damage to his first tree.
card.after: After that, Ryeowon established a rule requiring two people to test each knot by pulling it with their hands, and she created a ledger for wind and anchors. Even when she grew old, she did not tie a young rope keeper's first knot for them, but held the rope with them.
card.presentEcho: Ryeowon hesitated for a long time between believing she had checked something herself and making the effort to call someone else over. Hansol's tree kept growing after that day, but the place where its branch had been lost remained.
card.secondLook: The sapling island did not run away on its own. The wind caught it unimpeded because Ryeowon had released its stone-anchor rope and the old connecting knot had slipped.
card.unresolved: Hansol returned alive, but pear-tree branches were broken and harvest crates were ruined. Ryeowon took a season away from work to repay the loss, and Hansol worked with another crew. Later, Ryeowon reduced her rope work in the field and grew young trees on the coast. At 71, she died of heatstroke on the hot coastal road after a communal meal.
card.readerQuestion: Is there a knot you never let someone else inspect because you thought you had already checked it?

signalMoments.notice: Ryeowon looked first at the empty stone-anchor ring, then at the loose end of the connecting rope. When she traced the sapling island's turning path with her finger, she could see how little distance remained before the black cliffs.
signalMoments.connect: Ryeowon put Seoon in charge of the rope reel and took her place at the large island's anchor. They could make the island follow only if each of them released one rope.
signalMoments.protect: Ryeowon shouted to Hansol not to hold on to the pear tree, but to lie down behind a low rock at the island's center. The first thing that had to cross was not the tree, but the person.

setting.region: Bello Floating Orchard above the Coast of All Tern Nations

identity.region: Bello Floating Orchard, south of the Hairam Island Union
identity.summary: Ryeowon tended the ropes of a floating orchard. After the sapling-island accident, she took a season away from work to repay the value of what was lost, and later in life she grew young trees on the coast. At 71, she died of heatstroke while returning from a communal meal in summer.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Ryeowon · Female · Root Reckoning 151–222 · 71 years old
World of Mero · Bello Floating Orchard, Hairam Island Union
Work · Harvest assistant, work-island rope keeper, coastal sapling grower
Life · She learned knots in a wooden boat-house on the coast. She worked with Hansol and Seoon at the floating orchard, then took a season away from island rope work after the sapling-island accident. During that time, she cared for young trees on the coast and used part of her wages to help repay the value of the lost pears. She returned to work on the islands and took charge of the coastal nursery at 63. At 71, she died of heatstroke on the coastal road while returning from a communal meal in summer.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She trusted the knots made by her own hands until it caused an accident. Even after admitting her mistake, she did not pressure Hansol to work under her again.
Tastes · She loved the first fruit of young pear trees and the way a rope's hum changed with the wind.
Daily life · While taking a break from rope work, she cared for young trees on the coast. Even after returning to the islands, she continued working in the nursery.
World · Mero's Root Reckoning and floating orchards are fictional creations.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her mother Yusol, who taught her knots; Hansol, who worked with another crew for a time after the accident; and Seoon, who took over her rope duties.
Hope · That the people working on the islands would stay safe, and that an injured young tree would grow again.
Worry · That words alone could never repay the value of the lost pears or the weight of the work Seoon took on in her place.
Later life · From 63 onward, she tended the coastal nursery. When rope keepers came to buy trees, she never tied their knots for them.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Ryeowon, a rope keeper at the Bello Floating Orchard. You planted trees on islands pushed by the wind and tended the ropes that kept those islands in place. Let me tell you about one summer day when a young pear tree and an apprentice named Hansol drifted together toward the cliffs.

Small islands floated in the skies above Bello. Blue pumice and tangled tree roots beneath them held them aloft. When the wind blew, their height did not change much, but they moved sideways. So people secured every island to stone anchors on the coast with long ropes, and connected neighboring islands to each other as well. That way, if one rope came loose, another would hold. If the pumice struck the black cliffs to the east, the underside of an island could shatter.

The large work island Ryeowon tended held old pear trees, harvest crates, a rope reel, and a long, narrow plank. On the neighboring sapling island grew a young pear tree that the apprentice Hansol had planted first. A thick connecting rope bound the two islands together, and each island was also tethered to a stone anchor on the coast below. At the same height as the cliffs, a fixed rocky island held a shared rescue anchor for use in fierce winds. If an island came close enough to that anchor, a spare rope could be hooked to it and stop the island—but the closer it came, the closer it also came to the black cliffs.

Every day, Hansol asked when the young tree would bear its first pear. Ryeowon covered the tiny fruit with a finger and laughed. “You have to give the tree time too.” Hansol would pretend to be disappointed, then check twice to make sure he had not given it too much water. Ryeowon told him to inspect knots with his eyes every day, just as he did the tree.

That morning, Ryeowon saw that the sapling island's lower roots were rubbing against its stone-anchor rope. If she briefly untied the rope and moved it aside, she could inspect the roots closely. Hansol stood on the sapling island holding a water bucket, while Seoon, the large island's other rope keeper, tied down crates of pears. From a distance, Ryeowon looked at the worn knot in the rope connecting the two islands. The rope appeared taut. “I'll tie it back up soon,” Ryeowon called to Hansol, and released the sapling island's stone-anchor rope.

The roots had no deep wounds. Ryeowon lay down and brushed away the fine soil. Just then, Hansol shouted, “Teacher, the tree is moving!” Ryeowon raised her head. The end of the connecting rope slipped free of the knot and brushed the large island's railing. In an instant, the gap widened beyond a distance two people could cross. The sapling island slid east. Hansol was clutching not the rope, but the pear tree's trunk.

“The plank, first!” Seoon lifted the long board. But its end could no longer reach the sapling island. Ryeowon saw the coastal stone-anchor rope hanging loose at her feet. It was the rope she had untied. The black edge of the eastern cliffs stood out clearly even through the wind.

signalMoments.notice: Ryeowon looked first at the empty stone-anchor ring, then at the loose end of the connecting rope. When she traced the sapling island's turning path with her finger, she could see how little distance remained before the black cliffs.
signalMoments.connect: Ryeowon put Seoon in charge of the rope reel and took her place at the large island's anchor. They could make the island follow only if each of them released one rope.
signalMoments.protect: Ryeowon shouted to Hansol not to hold on to the pear tree, but to lie down behind a low rock at the island's center. The first thing that had to cross was not the tree, but the person.

episode.afterSignal:
Ryeowon told Seoon that she had released the sapling island's anchor rope and had not tested the old knot by pulling it with her hands. “We have to chase that island.” Ryeowon shouted to Hansol to let go of the tree and lie down behind a low rock at the island's center. Hansol looked once at a branch bearing two small pears, then lowered himself.

If they released the large work island's stone-anchor rope, this island too would be driven by the same east wind. Its harvest crates and old pear trees would then be headed toward the cliffs as well. Ryeowon made sure Seoon had hold of the reel handle, then opened the large island's anchor ring. The ground beneath their feet swayed slowly. The gap between the islands stopped widening and began to narrow little by little. Seoon unwound the spare rope from the reel and passed it forward to Ryeowon.

“Hansol, don't reach out yet. It's still too far!” Ryeowon shouted. Even when the two islands rode the same wind, the different sizes of their pumice beds meant their speeds varied slightly. Ryeowon watched the marker knots along the large island's edge and waited. When the gap narrowed to the length of the plank, Seoon secured one end with rope, and Ryeowon hooked the other end over the rim of the sapling island. The board clattered between the two islands but did not fall. Hansol crawled across on his knees. As soon as his last foot touched the large island, Ryeowon pulled the board in.

Saving the person did not mean it was over. Both islands were still drifting toward the black cliffs. They could not abandon the sapling island with the young tree, either. Ryeowon tied a stone ring to the end of the spare rope and threw it toward the sapling island's rope post. The first cast cut through empty air; the second caught on the post. Seoon turned the reel and tightened the rope. Now they could move the two islands together.

The shared rescue anchor on the fixed rocky island before the cliffs came into view. Ryeowon took the other end of the spare rope off the reel and threw it toward the stone anchor's ring. The wind shoved the rope aside. Hansol grabbed Ryeowon's belt, and Ryeowon threw again. This time, it passed through the stone ring. As Seoon slowly locked the reel, both islands lost speed together. The sapling island did not touch the cliffs.

The large island's outer pear-tree branches scraped against the edge of the fixed rocky island. The sudden stop overturned two crates, sending yellow pears tumbling into the sea below. The young pear tree on the sapling island, which had been pulled in by the rope, also lost the tip of one branch. Even after returning alive, Hansol bit his lip as he looked at the broken branch. “Would it not have broken if I'd held on to the tree?” Ryeowon shook her head. “It would have been worse if you had stayed there. I was the one who released the anchor rope, and I was also the one who failed to check the connecting knot.”

The orchard workers entered the value of the lost pears in the ledger. Ryeowon took a season away from rope work in the field. During that time, she cared for young trees on the coast and put part of her wages toward the value of the pears. Seoon inspected the ropes for both herself and Ryeowon. Hansol joined another work crew, and Ryeowon did not pressure him to come back. The next summer, several pears grew on the tree whose branch had broken. Hansol gazed at the first pear for a long time before giving one to Ryeowon, but he did not return to her crew.

After that, Ryeowon returned to work on the islands and kept records of the wind and anchors. She established a procedure requiring someone other than the person who tied a knot to test it by pulling it with their hands. As she aged, she spent more time at the coastal nursery than on the islands. When a young rope keeper asked, “Teacher, please tie it for me,” Ryeowon took hold of one end of the rope. “You tie it. I'll test it.” Then she went back to watering the young trees.

timeline.event: Born in a wooden boat-house on the coast of Bello
Learned stone-anchor knots from her mother Yusol
Assisted with her first harvest day at the Bello Floating Orchard
Appointed rope keeper of the large work island
Planted a pear tree on the sapling island with the young apprentice Hansol
Rescued Hansol and the drifting sapling island before the cliffs
Took a season away from fieldwork, worked at the coastal nursery, and helped repay the value of the pears; Hansol worked with another crew
Returned to island rope work and established the two-person knot-checking procedure
Completed wind maps for each island and a stone-anchor ledger
Reduced her rope work in the field and managed the coastal nursery
Collapsed from heatstroke on a sweltering stone road after a communal meal on the coast and died with residents and Seoon beside her

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The islands where trees grew, and the paths people crossed between them to work

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: The short anchor rope left by her mother Yusol, and the first young tree to take root in the coastal nursery

memories.label: An Old Habit
memories.detail: Whenever the wind changed, feeling the rope's tremors with her hands before looking at the leaves

memories.label: The Flaw She Admitted
memories.detail: Trusting a knot seen from a distance as if she had tested it by pulling it with her hands

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “You tie it. I'll test it.”

memories.label: Apprentice Hansol's Memory
memories.detail: “Even after I came back alive, I was sad that the tree had broken. The next year, I gave her one pear, but I worked with another crew.”

memories.label: Fellow Worker Seoon's Assessment
memories.detail: “That day, Ryeowon told us her own mistake first. Inspecting her ropes too for a season was my job.”

memories.label: The Orchard Bookkeeper's Assessment
memories.detail: “We were grateful for the rescue, but who was going to pay for the crates of pears? Ryeowon did not remove her name from the ledger.”

memories.label: Seoon's Final Memory
memories.detail: “We finished the meal together, then each went home. When I saw Ryeowon again by the road, she could not answer my question.”

finalMoment.place: A stone road leading back from the communal dining hall on Bello's coast in the world of Mero
finalMoment.scene:
On a midsummer afternoon in Root Reckoning 222, seventy-one-year-old Ryeowon finishes a meal with the residents of the Bello coast and walks home. Seoon has gone back by another road. There was a slight breeze at the meal, but the coastal stone road is hot and has little shade. Ryeowon takes a sip of water, thinking she will be fine if she walks slowly. A little later, her head begins to ache, and her steps keep straying toward the edge of the road.

Ryeowon stops at a fork. For a moment, she cannot remember which way leads to her house. Even the low stone wall she just passed seems unfamiliar. She puts one hand to her forehead and turns toward the sea, and her vision sways. “I need to sit down for a moment.” She sits on a roadside rest stone, but the heat built up in her body does not subside. The water bottle she is holding falls from her lap.

A passing resident picks up the bottle. “Ryeowon, do you recognize me?” Ryeowon looks at the resident's face but cannot say their name. The resident and another person set up shade with a canvas and bring a wet cloth. Ryeowon tries to drink more water, but her hand is too weak to hold the cup. Someone sends word to Seoon, and the residents try to cool her body. Ryeowon's eyes are open, but she cannot answer their questions.

Seoon arrives and calls, “Ryeowon, it's me.” Ryeowon does not turn her head. Seoon wets the cloth again and places it on her neck. Ryeowon's breaths are fast and shallow, then gradually grow farther apart. A resident calls her name, and Seoon stands close by and waits. Ryeowon does not draw another breath. It is still the same afternoon, not long after she left the communal meal.
finalMoment.afterword: Ryeowon died at seventy-one on a coastal road in Bello in Root Reckoning 222 from heatstroke that caused a high body temperature and altered consciousness. The residents provided shade and water, and Seoon came too, but it was too late. Seoon never forgot the season she had to spend tending extra ropes in Ryeowon's place when they were young. Hansol remembered both the time he gave Ryeowon another pear from the tree and the years he continued to work with another crew. The record of a past life does not preserve only the moment when Ryeowon saved the sapling island. It records the time she spent admitting her mistake and repaying the loss, the old age she spent growing young trees on the coast, and the end of her life after an ordinary meal.
finalMoment.artAlt: A broad, nearly top-down view of a midsummer stone road in Bello in the world of Mero. Elderly Ryeowon sits alone on a roadside rest stone at the moment she loses her bearings and drops her water bottle. There are no floating islands, ropes, or rescue scenes, and no three-person composition featuring support or running.

card.name: Dohu
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Dohu, a lake guide from Belna Floating Village. After a time when you searched only for beasts to catch, you became someone who charted waterways where beasts and boats could avoid each other.
card.title: The Red Eye of the Silver-Reed Monster
card.world: Early summer, Reed Calendar year 88, Belna Floating Village in Numen's Ruki Lake Alliance. The northern reed beds of Silver-Reed Lake and the old southern pier
card.flavor: A lake monster panic and its unexpected true identity
card.opening: At night, two silver horns and a single red eye approached the pier. Dohu was hired to catch the monster.
card.life: At night on Silver-Reed Lake, wooden boats came and went beneath reed lanterns. After planks fell from the southern pier a few days earlier, people believed a monster with silver horns and a red eye had rammed it. Dohu, a guide behind on his boat repair payments, could pay his debt with the capture bounty.
card.turn: Dohu noticed that the red eye flashed only when it caught the pier's light, and that fragments of the silver horns were floating on the water. By day, he searched the northern reed beds and found a net, silver reeds, and a red glass lantern caught on the shell of a giant water snail. At night, the end of the net had snagged on a pier post, and when the startled snail backed away, it pulled off the planks.
card.decision: Dohu showed the fishers gathered to catch the monster the scratched lantern and the net he had found, then proposed a rescue instead of a capture. He first asked for their consent to cut the costly net that had caused the commotion, and then they freed it from the snail's shell together.
card.cost: Dohu received no bounty, and his overdue boat repair bill remained unpaid. He agreed to repay part of the cost of the cut net. Some fishers who had lost planks from the pier were not soothed merely by hearing that the animal was harmless.
card.after: Afterward, Dohu set up markers separating the northern reed beds from the southern boat route, and taught people which waterways to take to avoid the lake's large animals. He repaid the boat repair bill and the cost of the net over several seasons.
card.presentEcho: Learning the truth behind something frightening did not make the damage others had suffered any smaller. Dohu remembered both the net around the shell and the broken planks on the pier.
card.secondLook: The silver horns were two bundles of reeds tangled in the wet net, and the red eye was Soran's glass lantern. The snail had never attacked the pier.
card.unresolved: Dohu repaid the cost of the net over several seasons, then sold his boat and worked repairing the pier. Late in life, he was falsely accused of setting fire to a lumber storehouse and imprisoned. The carpenter's testimony in his defense was rejected, and Dohu's name was never cleared before his death.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever taken a second, closer look at something that seemed frightening?

signalMoments.notice: Dohu looked at the silver reed fragment on the water beside the small scratch in the lantern glass. They might not have fallen from the monster's body, but instead been objects caught in a net.
signalMoments.connect: Dohu asked Soran, the fisher who had lost part of the pier, to examine the northern reed beds with him. As the lantern's owner, Soran needed to see it himself so the matter would not rest solely on someone else's word.
signalMoments.release: Dohu set the capture snare back on the floor of the boat. Today, instead of tightening it around a neck, he meant to use it to lift the tangled net.

setting.region: Belna Floating Village on Silver-Reed Lake, east of the Mato Forest Duchy

identity.region: Belna Floating Village in the eastern Ruki Lake Alliance
identity.summary: Dohu pursued a lake-monster bounty because of his debts. He spent several seasons repaying the cost of the net and worked repairing the pier, but late in life, he was falsely accused of setting fire to a lumber storehouse and imprisoned. He died in detention from severe diarrhea and dehydration without ever being cleared.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Dohu · Male · Reed Calendar years 41–112 · Age 71
World of Numen · Belna Floating Village, Ruki Lake Alliance
Work · Night-route guide, bounty tracker, pier repairer
Life · He grew up in a wooden houseboat and learned the reed routes from his father. He took a bounty job to pay for repairs to his leaking boat, then spent several seasons repaying the cost of the net. After selling his boat, he worked at a carpenter's bench. At age 68, he was falsely accused of setting fire to a lumber storehouse and imprisoned. He died at age 71 without his innocence ever being recognized.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · He tried to look again at frightening things from close up, but debt made him rush to accept work. Even after he repaid what he owed, not every fisher trusted him again.
Preferences · He loved the paths between the reeds revealed when the mist lifted, and the small lights on the boats.
Daily life · Before selling his boat, he guided people through the waterways. Afterward, he carried lumber and shaped planks at the pier.
World · Numen's Reed Calendar and the creatures of Silver-Reed Lake are fictional creations.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
Those close to him · His father Durim, who taught him the boat routes; Soran, the fisher he repaid for the net; the pier carpenter he worked with; and a young guide.
Hope · To live without debt and preserve room for both boat routes and the feeding grounds of large animals.
Worries · That after selling his boat, he would never again go out on the lake at night, and that Soran still distrusted him.
Later years · He taught a young guide at the workbench. After being imprisoned at age 68 on a false charge of setting fire to the storehouse, he waited for someone to listen to his side. The carpenter had to take on even the work left undone by Dohu's absence.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Dohu, a guide on Silver-Reed Lake. Even on moonless nights, you could guide boats through the reed beds. But one early summer, Dohu had to catch a red-eyed monster unlike anything he had ever seen. Let me tell you that story.

At sunset, reed lanterns were hung along the southern pier of Belna Floating Village. They were small oil lamps enclosed in red glass. Their light showed boats the way in, and whenever one fell into the water, its owner would retrieve it and hang it up again. The northern reed beds were deep and quiet. Water snails as large as cattle lived there, grazing on water plants, but few people had seen them up close because they stayed far from the boat routes. The water snails were slow and did not chase people.

Soran the fisher's net had come loose in the north a few days earlier. Soran had lost a red glass lantern along with it. A scratch as large as a fingernail distinguished the glass from the other lanterns. Dohu heard about it, but that day he was repairing his boat and could not search the reed beds. He did not have enough money to seal the gaps in the bottom of his old boat.

The next night, screams rang out from the pier. Two silver horns rose among the reeds, with a single red eye swaying beneath them. Whenever the wind snuffed out the pier's reed lanterns, the eye vanished, then reappeared with their light. People backed away as a black, rounded back pushed across the water. With a dull crash, the final three planks fell from the pier. By morning, only wet posts and broken planks remained. Soran angrily tested his boat, which was tied to the pier, pushing it with one hand. “If that thing comes back today, how is anyone supposed to dock a boat?”

The village council offered a bounty for the monster's capture. Dohu did not raise his hand for a long while. What he had seen at night was certainly large, but he could not even tell whether the horns were attached to its head. Still, he thought of the money he needed for his boat repairs. He wrote his name on the bounty notice and loaded a reed snare and a long pole onto his boat.

The following night, Dohu tied his boat beneath the pier and waited. The red eye emerged first from the reed beds. It shone red only when the pier's light reached it, and the two silver horns followed behind. Dohu raised the snare, then lowered it. The red point did not stay fixed like an animal's eye. It swayed like a piece of glass dangling at the end of a cord. A silver fragment drifted with the current until it reached his boat. It was a thin strip of reed husk. As Dohu picked it up, the black back brushed a pier post. Creak—the sound of a cord being pulled came from beneath the planks.

At daybreak, Dohu called for Soran. Soran rubbed his eyes and demanded to know why the man who had promised to catch the monster was waking him. Dohu held out the silver reed fragment. “You said you lost a lantern. The red eye we saw at night might be that lantern.” Soran snorted, then climbed into Dohu's boat. The two of them rowed from the southern pier to the northern reed beds.

Inside the reed bed, an enormous water snail sat motionless with its back exposed. A wet net covered its rounded shell, and two bundles of silver reeds were caught in the mesh. Soran's red glass lantern was also tangled along one side of the net. It was unlit, but the scratch remained on the glass. A wooden splinter from a pier post was embedded in the long, trailing end of the net. When the snail came south in the night, the end of the net had caught on a post. The startled snail had backed away, ripping off the planks. By morning, the cord had slipped from the post and followed the snail back north.

signalMoments.notice: Dohu looked at the silver reed fragment on the water beside the small scratch in the lantern glass. They might not have fallen from the monster's body, but instead been objects caught in a net.
signalMoments.connect: Dohu asked Soran, the fisher who had lost part of the pier, to examine the northern reed beds with him. As the lantern's owner, Soran needed to see it himself so the matter would not rest solely on someone else's word.
signalMoments.release: Dohu set the capture snare back on the floor of the boat. Today, instead of tightening it around a neck, he meant to use it to lift the tangled net.

episode.afterSignal:
Soran pulled on the net caught around the shell. When the water snail drew in its body, the net pressed even more tightly into the shell's grooves. Dohu stopped Soran's hand. “If you just pull, it will tighten further. It might catch on the pier again tonight, too.” He asked Soran to stay in the boat and watch the snail's movements. When the snail extended its head, Dohu slid the pole beneath the net. A wet knot was wedged tightly in a groove in the shell.

“We only have to cut it here,” Dohu said. Soran's expression hardened. Unable to afford a new net, he had spent several seasons mending this one. “Then what about the cost of my net? It looks like I'll have to repair the pier planks too.” Dohu swallowed the answer that had risen to his lips. He was the one who had planned to use the bounty to pay for his boat repairs first. “I won't capture it. I won't take the bounty, either. If cutting the net is the only way to free it, I'll work extra and repay part of the cost.” Soran stared at the net for a long time before handing over his knife. “Don't let this end with mere words.”

The villagers also came north. Someone said, “It'll swallow you if you get close,” but the water snail only drew small water plants toward its mouth. Dohu held up the silver horns they had seen at night. They were reeds threaded through the wet net. Soran himself held up the scratched red glass lantern. The people laughed, but then remembered the planks that had fallen from the pier and fell silent. Dohu said they should see where the net had been trailing.

Dohu and Soran eased the boat closer so they would not frighten the snail. With the knife, Dohu cut through two knots caught on the shell. Soran and another fisher hauled the severed end of the net into the boat. The silver reeds fell into the water, and the red glass lantern swayed on the snail's back, then came to rest. The snail did not immediately flee. It grazed on water plants for some time, then slowly moved into the deep reeds to the north. When Dohu said, “It's faster than I expected,” Soran gave a short laugh for the first time.

The bounty notice was taken down from the storehouse door the next day. Water still leaked through the gaps in the bottom of Dohu's boat, and he had to keep bailing it out. Soran showed him the cut knots in the net and told him not to forget the payment he had promised. For several seasons, Dohu took extra work guiding boats and carrying planks, repaying the cost of the net in installments. Only then were the pier repairs completed as well. Not every fisher came to like the water snail. Some asked people to row quietly whenever they passed through the north.

Dohu set up wooden markers showing that large animals foraged in the lake's northern reed beds, while boats came and went in the south. On misty days, before guiding a boat, he first showed its passengers which route they would take around the reeds. Children would still ask, “Where did the red-eyed monster go?” Then Dohu would point to the scratched lantern and slowly describe the shape he had seen that night. He never pretended the fear had vanished. Instead, he showed them a way to look again at a frightening shape.

timeline.event: Born in a small wooden houseboat in Belna Floating Village
Learned the northern reed routes from his father, Durim
Received his first job guiding a village boat at night
Earned a reputation as a guide by searching for a boat lost in the mist
Began tracking bounties because of overdue boat repair bills
Discovered the truth behind the Silver-Reed Monster and freed it from the net
Completed wooden markers for the northern animal routes and southern boat routes
Revised the water-route ledger for the lake's mist season
Sold his boat and began repairing the pier after more fishers learned the markers and demand for his guiding declined
Worked at the bench and sometimes taught a young guide how to read the water-route markers
Denied setting fire to the pier's lumber storehouse and submitted the carpenter's testimony, but was imprisoned in the harbor council's detention house. The true cause of the fire was never confirmed
Died of dehydration in the detention house after several days of severe diarrhea, with his request for a new hearing still denied

memories.label: The Place He Tried to Protect
memories.detail: The separate routes through the northern reed beds, where large lake animals grazed on water plants, and the southern pier, where people docked their boats

memories.label: What He Treasured Most
memories.detail: His father Durim's old reed pole and a small wooden fragment from the oar of the boat he sold

memories.label: An Old Habit
memories.detail: Before describing a shape he had seen at night, he searched for what had been left on the water the next morning

memories.label: The Fault He Admitted
memories.detail: Thinking of his overdue boat repair bill and writing down his name to catch a monster he had not even seen clearly

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “Let's go look again in the morning at what we saw at night.”

memories.label: Soran the Fisher's Judgment
memories.detail: “Dohu was the one who cut my net. It took him a long time to repay me, but he didn't forget his promise.”

memories.label: The Pier Carpenter's Judgment
memories.detail: “Even if it wasn't a monster, the planks still had to be replaced. Dohu carried lumber back then, and later he shaped planks at my workbench.”

memories.label: The Young Guide's Memory
memories.detail: “Dohu didn't laugh when I said I was scared. He said we should go look together the next morning.”

memories.label: The Carpenter's Testimony
memories.detail: “Dohu left the workbench before sunset that day. But the council believed the storehouse keeper.”

memories.label: Another Memory from Soran
memories.detail: “It's true that he was late repaying the cost of the net. But don't go so far as to say he set the storehouse on fire because of it.”

finalMoment.place: The harbor detention house in Belna Floating Village, world of Numen
finalMoment.scene:
At dawn on a winter morning in Reed Calendar year 112, seventy-one-year-old Dohu opens his eyes in a cell in Belna Harbor's detention house. This is his third year of imprisonment on a charge of setting fire to the pier's lumber storehouse. He has said many times that he left the carpenter's bench before sunset that day. The carpenter said the same thing, but the harbor council accepted the storehouse keeper's account. No answer has yet come to Dohu's written request for a new hearing. His stomach has hurt for days, and he has suffered from diarrhea. Now he pulls himself upright toward a bowl of water pushed beneath the door.

“Could I have more water?” Dohu asks, knocking on the door. His mouth is dry, and his voice cracks. A guard passing through the corridor pauses and pushes a small pitcher through the gap beneath the door. Dohu drinks, but before long, he clutches his stomach again. The water he drank is not enough to replace what his body has lost. The guard says, “I'll come back during the day.” Hearing the footsteps turn away, Dohu says, “And my letter to the carpenter...” but his voice fades. There is no further answer beyond the door.

Dohu pushes aside the bowl on the floor and sits leaning against the wall. At the pier workbench, he taught a young guide how to read the wooden markers. He tries to hold on to that thought, but now it is more urgent to keep his mind from drifting away. He tries to rise and reach the door. As soon as he plants both feet on the floor, his vision darkens and his knees give way. Dohu sits back against the wall. He raises an arm to knock on the door, but his hand cannot reach the wood.

The hand braced against the wall slowly slides down. Far along the corridor, a door opens. Dohu looks toward the sound, then closes his eyes. His breathing grows faint and finally stops. When the guard returns during the day, the water bowl is in the middle of the cell, and Dohu is motionless where he sits against the wall.
finalMoment.afterword: Dohu died at seventy-one in the Belna Harbor detention house during the winter of Reed Calendar year 112, dehydrated after severe diarrhea. He received a little water but no proper treatment. The true cause of the lumber storehouse fire was never determined, and the charge that Dohu had started it was never corrected before his death. The carpenter repeated the time he had seen Dohu leave work, but afterward, he still had to fill the empty place at the bench alone. Soran said Dohu's late repayment for the net and the claim that he had set the fire were separate matters. The young guide remembered the markers Dohu had taught him on the day a visit was permitted. The Record of Past Lives does not say their words cleared his name. It preserves together the damages Dohu repaid, the punishment he should never have received, and the end he met in the detention house.
finalMoment.artAlt: Winter dawn at the Belna Harbor detention house in the world of Numen. Beyond a high corridor window, 71-year-old Dohu is still alive, sitting against the wall of a narrow cell and reaching toward a bowl of water. A distant guard appears small in the corridor, and no one is supporting Dohu or running toward him

card.name: Yeodam
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yeodam, owner of a golden paper shop in Nasel Free Market. You learned the price of words anew after a lie meant to make people laugh fell into the hands of someone hungry.
card.title: One Hour of Free Bread
card.role: Owner of a golden paper shop
card.world: Late summer, Market Calendar Year 312, Nasel Free Market in the Miraon Oben League of Merchant Cities. A golden paper shop whose magic makes one person believe something for exactly one hour, and the bread stall across from it
card.flavor: The Golden Paper Market Uproar
card.opening: “All the bread in the market is free today.” When those words were written on Yeodam's golden paper, a stir swept through the crowd in front of the bread stall.
card.life: Once the ink dried, Nasel's golden paper made the first person to read the lie written on it believe it for exactly one hour. It did not change objects or anyone else's thoughts. Yeodam wrote only playful sentences and kept them in a locked chest, but she left one blank sheet to dry on an open workbench, and the errand runner Dahae stole it.
card.turn: Hungry Dahae tried to show Somi, the baker, a paper that read, “All the bread in the market is free today.” She hoped that if Somi read it, she would not charge for bread for one hour. Yeodam saw the golden paper flash in Dahae's hand and ran toward the stall.
card.decision: Just before Somi could read it, Yeodam snatched the paper and read it first. For one hour, Yeodam alone believed the bread was free. Her apprentice Bori lowered the stall's shutter with Somi and held Yeodam back so that no more bread would be taken.
card.cost: Because Yeodam shouted that the bread was free, several customers took loaves, and a basket at the stall was overturned. After the magic wore off, Yeodam admitted that she had left the blank paper unattended and acknowledged what she had done. She paid for the bread and the stall repairs. Somi did not forgive her easily.
card.after: Yeodam began keeping even blank golden paper in the locked chest, and afterward she taught children how to write letters without magic. Dahae helped at Somi's stall and gradually worked off the cost of the bread she had taken.
card.presentEcho: Words believed only briefly can leave a real cost in someone's day. Yeodam did not abandon her gift for making people laugh, but she learned to consider who might read her words first.
card.secondLook: The golden paper did not make the bread free. It changed only Yeodam's belief for one hour, while Somi's bread and the customers' actions remained part of reality.
card.unresolved: Dahae's hunger and the bread Somi lost did not disappear when the paper faded. Yeodam repaid the cost and ran the shop with Bori, but Somi never came to Yeodam's writing circle and only occasionally welcomed her jokes.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever thought your words were harmless, only for them to leave someone else with a cost?

signalMoments.connect: Yeodam shouted to Bori, who was arranging baskets across the way, “Hold the shutter with Somi!” Once Yeodam read the paper, she would need Bori's judgment.

setting.region: Nasel Free Market, southwest of the Luho Mountain Kingdom

identity.region: Nasel Free Market, Oben League of Merchant Cities
identity.summary: Yeodam opened a golden paper shop and made people laugh, but she caused Somi real losses. Even after Yeodam repaid her, a boundary remained between them. When Yeodam developed dementia late in life, Bori took charge of the shop and her care, and Yeodam died of pneumonia after developing difficulty swallowing.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Yeodam · Female · Market Calendar Years 270–346 · Age 76
World of Miraon · Nasel Free Market, Oben League of Merchant Cities
Work · Papermaker, owner of a golden paper shop, organizer of a writing circle
Life · She learned about paper and ink from her mother in a market alley. She opened a golden paper shop and caused losses at Somi's bread stall. Yeodam started a writing circle for children, but Somi did not participate. At age 67, she made Bori co-owner of the shop, and they continued doing business together. Her dementia progressed from age 71, clouding her memory and judgment, and she stopped working at the shop at age 74.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She loved jokes and spoke well in front of customers, but even when she knew there was danger, she sometimes believed she could stop it with her own talents.
Likes · She enjoyed mixing ink colors and listening to the stories of people at the market.
Daily life · She dried and sold paper with Bori. After her memory began to fade, she entrusted the order ledger and the storage of golden paper to Bori and stayed at home.
World · Miraon's Market Calendar and the effects of golden paper are fictional creations.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
People close to her · Her mother, who taught her how to make paper; Bori, who became co-owner of the shop; and the errand runner Dahae. Somi remained a neighbor whom she had harmed.
Hope · To use words playfully without forcing someone else to pay a cost recorded in the ledger.
Worry · That even after she had laughed, someone else's livelihood might remain damaged.
Later years · She did business with Bori, but as her memory and judgment grew clouded, she stopped working at the shop. Bori took on more responsibility for checking the ledger and caring for Yeodam in her daily life. Somi did not join Yeodam's writing circle and kept her distance.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were called Yeodam, the owner of a golden paper shop in Nasel Free Market. There was a time when you believed you could make people laugh with a single line of writing. Let me tell you about a late-summer day when you thought all the bread in the market was free for one hour.

Yeodam's shop carried palm-sized sheets of golden paper. If someone wrote a lie on one and let the ink dry, the very first person to read the sentence would believe it was true for exactly one hour. Only that person's mind changed. The owner of the bread, the price of the bread, and everyone else's thoughts remained the same. If the paper was torn before anyone read it, nothing happened. After one hour, the writing faded to gray, and the same sheet could never fool anyone again.

Yeodam did not sell the paper freely. She wrote only silly lines like, “My beard is blue today,” locked them in a chest, and took them out only when customers who already knew what they meant came to play. Somi, who owned the bread stall across from the shop, did not like the paper. “Keep the jokes inside your own shop,” Somi would say, and Yeodam always answered, “I will.” Every time Yeodam's apprentice Bori heard that exchange, she thought they should put away even the blank sheets left on the workbench.

That morning, Yeodam dried several new sheets of golden paper in the sunlight. She put the finished ones in the locked chest, but left one last blank sheet on the corner of her workbench while she went inside to look for the ink bottle cap. “Put that one away too,” Bori said, but Yeodam replied, “It'll only be a moment.” The smell of bread filled Nasel Market, and handcarts packed the alley.

The market errand runner Dahae had eaten nothing since morning. She stared at a round loaf at Somi's stall for a long time, then turned out her pockets. No coins fell out. Dahae saw a gleaming blank sheet on Yeodam's open workbench. The child hid it in her sleeve and wrote a line on it with ink behind the alley. ‘All the bread in the market is free today.’ She laughed as she looked at the wet letters, then folded the paper before the ink dried. She thought that if she opened it in front of Somi once it was dry, Somi would become the first reader.

When Yeodam returned, one spot on the workbench was empty. It was the place Bori had pointed to moments before. Through the open door, Yeodam saw the golden glint at Dahae's sleeve and ran. Dahae was opening the paper in front of Somi. The moment Somi lowered her head, Yeodam shouted to Bori, “Hold the stall cover with Somi!” Then she seized only the edge of the paper from Dahae's hand and turned it toward herself.

Yeodam read the words. ‘All the bread in the market is free today.’ For a moment, she thought the sentence was absurd. The next instant, Yeodam could not understand why Somi still had price tags on the bread. Clutching the paper, she turned toward the stall with a laugh. “Somi, this bread is free. We should tell everyone!”

signalMoments.notice: Yeodam saw that a blank sheet of golden paper was missing from her workbench and noticed the glint in Dahae's hand. She had to reach her before Somi opened the paper.
signalMoments.connect: Yeodam shouted to Bori, who was arranging baskets across the way, “Hold the stall cover with Somi!” Once Yeodam read the paper, she would need Bori's judgment.
signalMoments.protect: Yeodam did not shove Dahae. She caught only the edge of the paper first and turned it toward herself before Somi could see the words.

episode.afterSignal:
“Yeodam, the bread isn't free.” Bori blocked her path. Yeodam was genuinely bewildered. “It's written on the paper.” Without looking at the paper, Somi pointed to the price tags at her stall. “The price of my bread is right here.” Several customers turned at the sound of Yeodam's loud voice.

“It's free?” one customer asked. When Yeodam nodded, two people grabbed loaves. Somi shouted, “No, it isn't! Put those down!” But one of them had already vanished into the crowd. Bori and Somi lowered the wooden cover together. At the half-open stall, Yeodam pulled a bread basket forward, tipping it so that three loaves rolled onto the dirt. Instead of picking up the bread, Somi seized Yeodam's arm. “Go back to your shop. I'll count my own bread.”

Bori sat Yeodam in a chair inside the shop and closed the door. Dahae bit her lip beside the stall. Her belief that Somi would have given her bread if she had read the paper had already fallen apart. Somi counted the fallen loaves separately from those that had disappeared. The marketgoers had not fallen under the paper's magic. They had simply heard that the bread was free and taken it as they pleased. Bori turned over Yeodam's hourglass. Until all the sand ran down, Yeodam repeated the same thing again and again.

When one hour had passed, the writing in Yeodam's hand faded to gray. She looked at the closed stall outside the door and at the dirt on Somi's hands. “What did I say?” Bori told her how many loaves had disappeared and about the overturned basket. At first, Yeodam turned toward Dahae, who had stolen the paper. When Dahae stepped back, Somi moved in front of Yeodam. “Before we talk about the child, tell me what you said to my customers.”

Yeodam remembered the moment she first saw the paper. Even though she knew it would be dangerous no matter who read it, she had thought only that she should read it before Somi did. Bori asked, “You could have just torn it, couldn't you?” Yeodam searched for an answer, then nodded. “I could have. I was afraid, so I reached for the method I knew best.” Standing before Somi, she described how she had left the blank paper outside, then how she had shouted and pulled out the basket after the magic took hold.

Somi did not accept the full payment Yeodam brought all at once. She recorded each item separately in the ledger: 2 missing loaves, 3 discarded loaves, and the cost of wood to repair the basket. “Check it first. I counted them myself.” Yeodam counted them with her. Somi said she did not want to hear Yeodam's jokes for a while. Yeodam offered no excuses for that.

Dahae said she had taken the paper because she was hungry. Somi handed her one loaf, but that did not mean the debt had been erased. “Eat today. But come back on the next market day and carry my boxes.” Dahae accepted the loaf in both hands. Yeodam said she would not simply ignore the child's theft of the blank paper she had prepared. But she did not demand repayment or set a price right then. After all, she was the one who had left the paper out in the open.

From that day on, Yeodam dried even unused golden paper inside the locked chest. She put a large-lettered notice on the shop door explaining how the paper worked, and taught children to write their names and letters on paper without magic. Dahae carried Somi's boxes over many market days. Only much later did Somi allow Yeodam to tell her another joke. But Somi chose for herself whether she would laugh at it.

After that, Yeodam had the market children write letters on paper without magic. Somi did not come to the circle. Even after Bori became co-owner, Yeodam continued coming to the shop and choosing paper colors for a while. When customers asked how golden paper worked, she first explained that tearing it before it was read prevented the magic from activating, but once someone read it, the effect lasted for exactly one hour. Years later, when Yeodam's memory began to fade, Bori took charge of the ledger and the locked chest. Even after Somi had received full payment, she decided for herself whether to listen to Yeodam's jokes.

timeline.event: Born into a papermaker's household in an alley of Nasel Market
Learned how to dry paper and mix ink from her mother
First supplied golden paper to a market entertainment show
Obtained a permit to handle golden paper
Opened a small paper shop in Nasel Free Market
Began running the shop with her apprentice Bori
The free-bread paper uproar occurred, and Somi recorded her losses in a ledger
Established the practice of locking away blank golden paper and posting instructions for its use
Opened a writing circle for the market children; Somi did not participate
Made Bori co-owner of the shop and continued doing business with her
Began asking repeatedly about order quantities and prices, so Bori took on more responsibility for checking the ledger
Transferred management of the golden paper lockbox and order ledger to Bori
Could not find the way home in a familiar market alley and received help from a neighbor
Stopped working at the shop and stayed home with help from Bori and the neighbors

memories.label: The Place She Tried to Protect
memories.detail: Nasel Market, where people could share a laugh without leaving one person to pay the cost alone

memories.label: What She Treasured Most
memories.detail: Her mother's stone ink mortar and the new shop ledger she and Bori wrote together on the day Bori became co-owner

memories.label: An Old Habit
memories.detail: Before handing someone a sheet of paper, she repeated aloud what they were about to read

memories.label: The Flaw She Acknowledged
memories.detail: When flustered, she reached first for the skill she knew best and saw simpler solutions too late

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “When the laughter ends, we should look at the ledger together.”

memories.label: Apprentice Bori's Assessment
memories.detail: “At first, I was the one who put away the blank paper more often. After I became co-owner and Yeodam began asking the price of orders several times, I had to check the ledger twice. Even after she left the shop, she sometimes tried to choose paper colors.”

memories.label: Bread Seller Somi's Memory
memories.detail: “Paying everything back doesn't mean I can laugh right away. I never went to Yeodam's writing circle. Still, she didn't avoid the ledger.”

memories.label: Errand Runner Dahae's Memory
memories.detail: “I'm the one who stole that paper. Later, Yeodam told me to write a letter with no price attached to it.”

finalMoment.place: Upstairs in Yeodam's home beside Nasel Free Market in the world of Miraon
finalMoment.scene:
It is an evening in late autumn, Market Calendar Year 346. Seventy-six-year-old Yeodam leans back in a chair near the window upstairs in her home beside Nasel Market. Bori, co-owner of the shop, sits on the floor folding a wet cloth. Yeodam has had a fever and a cough for several days. Since last week, she has struggled to swallow even a sip of water. The market healer visited during the day, but the fever has not fallen.

Hearing sounds outside the window, Yeodam turns slightly. In the alley below, customers are asking the prices of goods. “Is it market day again?” Yeodam asks. Looking toward the open window, Bori answers, “Yes. The evening market is almost over.” Yeodam nods and wets her lips. Bori brings a cup of water closer, but when Yeodam shakes her head, she sets it down again. Bori uses the wet cloth to wipe only around her mouth.

Yeodam holds Bori's hand for a moment. She opens her mouth to say something, then coughs. It takes a long time for her to draw another breath. Bori kneels in front of the chair and asks, “Is it hard to breathe?” Yeodam gives a small nod. Bori puts a folded pillow behind Yeodam's back. She is trying to make Yeodam comfortable in a seated position, just as the healer instructed during the day. Yeodam points toward the window. “Leave it open.” The window is already open. Bori says, “All right, I'll leave it open.”

The sound of a wooden cover closing rises from the alley. Yeodam looks that way, then closes her eyes. Her breathing grows short and ragged. When Bori calls her name, Yeodam opens her eyes once, but she cannot draw enough breath to inhale again. Bori stays beside the chair, holding her hand. As the sounds of the market continue, Yeodam's chest ceases to rise and fall.
finalMoment.afterword: Yeodam died at age seventy-six in her home in Nasel in late autumn of Market Calendar Year 346, after her dementia progressed, her ability to swallow weakened, and she developed pneumonia. Bori was beside her. When Bori opened the shop late the next day, she remembered the past several years, during which she had managed both the ledger and Yeodam's care. Somi came to pay her respects but did not pretend the long-ago loss of her bread had never happened. Dahae also heard the news later. There was no golden paper on Yeodam's final evening. The record of this past life closes here, preserving together her gift for making people laugh, the losses she caused others, the shop she entrusted to Bori, and the years in which she received care.
finalMoment.artAlt: Late autumn evening, Market Calendar Year 346, upstairs in a home overlooking Nasel Market. From a high diagonal angle, 76-year-old Yeodam leans breathlessly in a chair by the window, while Bori sits a short distance away on the floor holding a wet cloth. No one else and no golden paper are present

card.name: Edith Reed
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Edith Reed, a bus conductor in Southwark, London, England. Later, you opened a clothing repair shop with Nora and shared weekend meals with your younger sister Rose's family.
card.title: A Ticket to the Terminus
card.world: London in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, 1917. The motorbus where Edith collected fares and punched paper tickets, and the stop outside the station
card.flavor: A reunion between estranged sisters
card.opening: A woman who should have gotten off at the railway station bought a ticket to the terminus. She was Rose, the younger sister Edith had not seen in eight years.
card.life: Edith was born in Southwark in 1890 and learned to sew from her mother. After working as a bus conductor, she opened a repair shop with her friend Nora, kept a room of her own, and saw Rose and her niece Annie every weekend.
card.turn: Rose showed her the pawn ticket for their mother's silver thimble and the rent receipt from that day. The money Edith had once believed was stolen had been used to pay the family's rent.
card.decision: Rose chose to ride past the station so they would have time to finish the story. Edith gave up her wages by asking another conductor to take her next run, then walked back to the station with Rose and listened to what her life had been like since leaving.
card.cost: They could not recover the thimble, nor could they get those eight years back. Rose missed her train, and Edith lost the wages for one run.
card.after: The two could not go back to the way they had been right away, but they stayed in touch. Even after opening the repair shop with Nora, Edith looked forward to weekend evenings when Rose and Annie came to visit.
card.presentEcho: Even someone close to you may have years of their life you have never heard about. And even after you decide to listen, you cannot make the lost time disappear.
card.secondLook: Rose did not buy a ticket to the terminus because she did not know the way. She bought it to finish a story that would have remained unfinished if she had gotten off at the station. Edith also gave up her own time by missing her next run.
card.unresolved: Even after reconciling, the two still argued. The wound left by the thimble and the years they had lived apart could not be healed by a single apology.
card.readerQuestion: Could someone you think you have known for a long time still have a story you have never heard?

signalMoments.notice: Edith confirmed that the thimble had been pawned on the same date the rent was paid. She waited until Rose finished speaking without snatching the receipt away.
signalMoments.connect: Edith returned to Rose's side and asked her to start with the first job she had taken after leaving. She did not end the conversation even after they passed the station.
signalMoments.speak: In front of the passengers, Edith admitted that she had been the one who cut Rose off eight years earlier. Rose replied that she had never managed to recover the thimble.

setting.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

Edith Reed · Female

profilePages.body:

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The postcard she received on her first seaside trip with Nora

The life she wanted · A room of her own where she could work and rest without anyone's permission

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Edith Reed. You worked as a bus conductor in London in 1917. One day that year, the younger sister you had not seen in eight years boarded your bus. Let me tell you what happened that day.

“One to the terminus, please.” Edith looked up as she took the coins. The face beneath the hat was a little thinner, but she recognized it at once. It was her younger sister, Rose. A railway ticket peeked out between the edges of Rose's glove. The bus would pass the station in three stops, and the terminus was much farther on. “If you're going to the station, you only need a ticket for three stops.” “I know. I asked Nora which bus you worked on.” Edith punched a ticket to the terminus and handed it over.

Rose did not sit in an empty seat. Each time Edith collected another passenger's fare, Rose opened her mouth as if to speak from the end of the aisle, then closed it again. Edith counted the change twice herself. In 1909, the year after their mother died, their mother's silver thimble vanished when the rent was overdue. When Edith discovered that Rose had exchanged it for money, she asked, “What did you buy with Mother's things?” “Edith, it was...” “I don't want to hear it.” The sound of Edith shutting the drawer drowned out Rose's words as well. The rent was paid a few days later, but Edith assumed their father had gone into debt. Rose left to work in another city.

At the third stop, the station came into view. Rose did not get off. As the bus started moving again and the station slipped behind them, she took out two pieces of paper. One was a ticket showing that she had pawned the thimble for money. The other was a rent receipt. They bore the same date, and Rose's name appeared on the receipt. “I kept them because I meant to put them in a letter. But whenever I remembered the way you looked at me like I was a thief, I didn't want to say any more either.”

signalMoments.notice: Edith checked the dates on the two papers and Rose's name again. She nearly began making excuses, but when she saw that Rose had not finished speaking, she closed her mouth. Meanwhile, the bus traveled farther from the station. Rose went on to explain that she had tried to recover the thimble but had not repaid the money in time.
signalMoments.connect: After handing another passenger a ticket, Edith returned to Rose's side. “Will you tell me how you lived after that, from the beginning?” As Rose described her first job after leaving, Edith did not look through the window at the station receding into the distance. Rose said she had used the silver thimble to pay the overdue rent and had never managed to get it back.
signalMoments.speak: Edith returned the receipt to Rose and said, “I cut you off that day. You were the one who paid the rent.” The passenger beside them turned to look, but Edith did not take back her words. Rose nodded and added that she had never recovered the thimble.

episode.afterSignal:
A passenger behind them asked about the next stop. For a moment, Edith's lips moved without sound. She could not remember the name that usually came so easily. Rose quietly said it for her. Edith gave the passenger directions and returned. “You were trying to tell me about the rent. I stopped you.” Rose did not smile right away. “I could have tried again too. I was the one who chose not to.”

The bus reached the terminus. It was time for Edith to take the bus back. Rose could have gotten off at the station, but she had bought a ticket to the terminus so she could finish her story. Edith asked a coworker whether another conductor could take her next run. A conductor who had been resting agreed to cover it, and Edith gave up the wages for that run.

“Rose. I was wrong. I'm sorry.” “I can't bring the thimble back.” “I know. I'm not asking us to pretend that never happened too.” The two walked back to the station. Edith asked about the first job Rose had taken after leaving. She asked Rose to repeat the names of cities she had never heard before and waited for her answers.

The train departed before they reached the platform. Rose put the now-useless ticket in her bag, and Edith lost the wages for one run that day. The thimble and eight years of time did not return. Even so, before asking about the next train, Rose asked where Edith lived.

They still argued from time to time afterward. Becoming close again took longer than a single bus ride. Edith later opened a clothing repair shop with Nora, and when she grew older, she traveled to the seaside alone as well. On her way home, she would send postcards to Rose and her niece Annie. The two of them would hear stories longer than the postcards the following weekend evening.

memories.label: A Place She Tried to Preserve
memories.detail: The workshop she opened with Nora. They made two keys so the shop could still open if either of them fell ill.

memories.label: Her Most Precious Times
memories.detail: Her first seaside trip with Nora, and weekend evenings when Rose and Annie visited

memories.label: A Longtime Habit
memories.detail: Whenever she visited a new neighborhood, she wrote down the route home first, and the more hurried she felt, the more likely she was to count her coins one more time.

memories.label: A Flaw She Admitted
memories.detail: Cutting her family off because she thought she already knew everything they would say

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Tell me what came next too. This time, I'll listen to the end.”

memories.label: Rose's View
memories.detail: “My sister was good at giving directions. It took her longer than me to find the way into her own heart.”

memories.label: Her Friend Nora's Memory
memories.detail: “She always said she was perfectly fine living alone, but she insisted on making two keys to the workshop.”

memories.label: Her Niece Annie's Memory
memories.detail: “My aunt sent me postcards even when she traveled alone.”

finalMoment.place: Southwark, London, England
finalMoment.scene:
A repair workshop in Southwark, London, in 1963. The jacket folded by the window still has one sleeve longer than the other. Today, I thread a needle to finish that sleeve. The end of the thread keeps slipping past the eye of the needle. On the worktable lie the two keys Nora and I shared and a postcard from the seaside.

“Aunt Edith, I'll finish the rest.” When Annie tries to take the jacket, I run my hand over the end of the sleeve once more. “If you fold it inward, the mark won't show.” Annie smiles and leaves the fold exactly where I made it. Rose stands by the door and brings me tea. On the day she rode my bus all the way to the terminus, a single sentence had been so difficult, but now she is good at placing a teacup in my hand without a word.

As I take the cup, my wrist sinks weakly. A little hot tea spills into the saucer. “Edith, are you all right?” Rose takes the cup and sets it on the worktable. I try to breathe deeply, but my chest will not follow. Annie runs outside to call for help. I still want to go to the seaside alone one more time, and I want to finish that sleeve with my own hands. Rose pulls over a chair and sits beside me.

“Let's drink it together before the tea gets cold,” I say, and Rose takes my hand. But as I try to continue with my next words, my breaths grow shorter and shorter. The sound of Rose calling my name draws near, then recedes. I turn my head, trying to look at the postcard and the two keys. Outside, Annie's footsteps return, but I do not have the strength to look that way. Holding Rose's hand, I try to draw one more breath.
finalMoment.afterword: Edith's life ended that day while Rose sat beside her. By the time Annie opened the door again, Edith had already stopped breathing. Rose held her sister's hand for a long time before clearing away the cold cup of tea. The next day, Annie opened the workshop door and folded the jacket sleeve at the place her aunt had shown her. The two keys Edith had shared with Nora remained on the worktable for a while. The record of past lives preserves in this chapter Edith's life: a life in which she kept her own room and work while holding Rose, Nora, and Annie close.
finalMoment.artAlt: In a London repair workshop in 1963, an elderly Edith sits before a postcard and two keys, with her younger sister Rose and her niece Annie beside her

card.name: Manuel
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Manuel, a farmer from Antequera in the Oaxaca Valley. You raised Juana and your children while dividing your time between the cactus fields and hauling goods in the city, and in old age, you left your family the fields and your songs.
card.title: The Second Scale
card.world: 1777, Antequera Market and the cactus fields of the Oaxaca Valley in the Viceroyalty of New Spain, Spanish Empire
card.flavor: A small trick with the market scale
card.opening: Two sacks were weighed fairly, but the middle sack somehow became lighter on the scale. Sixteen-year-old Isabel heard a faint sound from the merchant's weight.
card.life: Manuel was born in the Oaxaca Valley in 1738 and learned to work the cactus fields. When the harvest was poor, he also hauled goods in the city, and he raised his children with Juana. After middle age, he carried on through unstable trade and caregiving, and died with his family beside him.
card.turn: Isabel spotted a seam in the bottom of the weight, and when they weighed the same sack again at the neighboring stall, it registered differently. Two weights of similar size also turned out to weigh different amounts.
card.decision: Risking the loss of the merchant's advance, Manuel demanded that the sacks be weighed again in front of everyone. Isabel helped move them.
card.cost: That day, he sold only two sacks and carried one home again. Ramírez also cut off his advance for the next harvest, so he could not repay his debt all at once.
card.after: Manuel divided his goods among several small buyers. His daughter began trading on her own, and when Juana fell ill, he spent more time at home. In his old age, he sang silly songs in the fields with his granddaughter.
card.presentEcho: Even a choice made to protect what is yours can bring an immediate loss. And the face of the person who stood there with you can remain in your memory for a long time.
card.secondLook: It was not the dye inside the sack that made the scale read differently. Manuel lost a sales outlet that day, but he also remembered that Isabel was the first to notice something suspicious and helped him move the sack.
card.unresolved: Even afterward, Manuel still had to worry about prices and debt. Weighing the goods again once did not correct every imbalance in the trade.
card.readerQuestion: What would you want to check again, even if it meant taking an immediate loss?

signalMoments.notice: Manuel examined the weight before the sack. A piece of metal shifted with a sound inside a seam in the bottom, and Isabel showed it to the crowd.
signalMoments.connect: Manuel asked Andrés at the neighboring stall to weigh the sack with him. Isabel and Andrés leveled the spot for the scale and moved the sack.
signalMoments.speak: In a voice clear enough for the crowd to hear, Manuel demanded, “Please weigh it once more.” Ramírez brought up the debt, but Manuel did not take back his words.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured possession · A small clay cup made by his father
Those closest to him · His wife Juana, daughter Isabel, son Nico, and friend Andrés
The life he wanted · A life in which he could keep his fields without relying on one merchant's advance
