episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Manuel. This was when what is now Oaxaca, Mexico, belonged to the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Manuel raised tiny cochineal insects that lived on cacti. When dried and crushed, the insects became a red dye used to color cloth. One day, when he was thirty-nine, a market scale unsettled his household's livelihood for the entire year. Let me tell you that story.

Manuel entered the Antequera market and set down three sacks. His sixteen-year-old daughter, Isabel, felt the knots tied around them. “Father, one has come loose.” “Tie it again for me. Since this morning, my hands have only been good at making music.” Manuel hummed a tune. In truth, he had no reason to laugh. He needed to sell the dye to repay the money he had borrowed from the merchant during the previous harvest.

The merchant Ramírez weighed the first sack and wrote down the price. There was no problem with the third, either. But when he weighed the second sack, the pan tipped with a jerk. “This one is light. If you want me to take all three sacks, you'll have to lower the price.” Manuel inspected the opening of the sack. There was no sign that it had leaked or gotten wet. Isabel picked up the weight Ramírez had just set down. A faint click sounded in her palm.

“Father, look underneath.” A narrow seam ran across the bottom of the weight. Ramírez quickly reached out his hand. “Enough games. Just sell your goods. Other customers are waiting.” Manuel thought of the money he owed. If he caused trouble here, Ramírez might refuse to pay him in advance next year. But Isabel would not let go of the weight.

signalMoments.notice: Manuel examined the weight before the sack. When he pressed a fingernail into the seam at the bottom, a heavy piece of metal shifted inside. “Let's weigh this weight again as well.” Isabel held it at eye level and showed the seam to the crowd.
signalMoments.connect: Manuel beckoned to Andrés, who was weighing grain nearby. “Will you put this sack on your scale, too?” Isabel checked the knot again and helped move the sack. Before looking at his friend's face, Andrés carefully leveled the ground where the scale stood.
signalMoments.speak: Manuel spoke clearly enough for the waiting crowd to hear. “If my sack is light, it will be the same on another scale. Please weigh it once more.” When Ramírez tried to bring up the debt, Isabel picked up the sack and walked to the neighboring stall first.

episode.afterSignal:
They placed the same sack on Andrés's scale. This time, it weighed no less than the first sack. Andrés also weighed his own weight, which was marked with the same value, against Ramírez's. Only Ramírez's side tipped downward. Someone spotted the new seam beneath the weight in Isabel's hand, and the crowd began to murmur.

Ramírez's face hardened. “Are you saying you mean to do business in someone else's stall?” “I won't sell here today.” Manuel retied the opening of the sack. He did not feel as though he had won some great victory. Ramírez had said, “Then I suppose there will be no advance for you next harvest, either.”

Manuel and Isabel shouldered the sacks and made another circuit of the market. Two small buyers each purchased one sack, but they had to carry the last one home. Manuel could not repay all the money he owed that day, either. Isabel asked, “Father, would it have been easier if we'd just lowered the price a little and sold them?” Manuel shrugged the shoulder on his empty-handed side. “The walk would have been easier. The next scale would have been even heavier.”

When they reached home, Juana saw the remaining sack and their reddened hands. Before Manuel could begin a long explanation, Isabel imitated the click that had come from the weight. Juana was the first to laugh. That night, the three of them counted on their fingers as they worked out how to repay the debt in installments. Their laughter did not erase the debt, but no one was left out of the reckoning.

After that, Manuel still saw days when prices were good and days when they were bad. His daughter grew up and began trading on her own, and when Juana fell ill, he spent more days at home than at the market. The red dye was not the only thing he left behind after his long life. His family kept the clumsy songs his granddaughter used to imitate, and the time they spent checking the weight together before opening a sack.

memories.label: The place he tried to protect for years
memories.detail: The small cactus field he cultivated with Juana. They faced both good years and bad years there.

memories.label: His most precious possession
memories.detail: A small clay cup made by his father. When guests came, he first filled it with water and offered it to them.

memories.label: A habit that brought him joy
memories.detail: Making up songs with silly lyrics, especially on days when nothing went right

memories.label: A worry he carried for years
memories.detail: Whether he could keep the fields through the next season if one merchant cut off his advance

memories.detail: “You can't lift a sack alone. Sometimes people are like that, too.”

memories.label: Juana's opinion
memories.detail: “His songs were always wrong. But he never skipped his turn at the housework.”

memories.label: His daughter Isabel's memory
memories.detail: “Father hesitated in front of the scale that day. So I remember that I stood there with him.”

memories.label: His son Nico's memory
memories.detail: “My sister and Father talked about the market for years, but with me, he argued about why you mustn't touch pottery before it dries.”

memories.label: His granddaughter's memory
memories.detail: “Grandfather changed the words at the end of his song every time. Whenever I laughed, he made up new ones.”

finalMoment.place: Near Antequera in the Oaxaca Valley, Viceroyalty of New Spain
finalMoment.scene:
My home in the Oaxaca Valley, 1806. Unable to go out to the fields for several days, I sit in a chair by the door to watch the evening sunlight. I cup the small clay cup my father made in both hands. Even after taking a sip of water, I find it hard to set the cup down. The shadows of the cacti at the edge of the field stretch long. Juana has been gone for four years, yet at this hour, I still feel as though she will offer me water one more time.

Isabel returns from the market and sits beside me. She now sells her own goods under her own name, and before telling me about prices, she tells me what the road was like today. “Father, shall I hold the cup for you?” I shake my head. My hands keep trembling whenever I put the cup down. Instead, I ask my daughter what song her daughter has been singing. “The one where you changed the lyrics every time.”

I hear a child's voice outside. My eight-year-old granddaughter adds the name of a flower that was never in the lyrics I made up. Tomorrow, I want to show the child the new shoots in the field. I want to see one more piece of pottery Nico made, too. “What comes next?” Isabel asks. “You listen. This song is new to me, too.” The long sentence leaves me short of breath, and I fall silent for a while. Isabel does not urge me to sing. She simply sits beside me.

My granddaughter pokes her face through the doorway and sings the changed lyrics again. I try to sing along, but no sound comes out. When the clay cup tilts in my hand, Isabel supports it. She calls my name. Instead of answering, I press one finger against the back of her hand. I force my chest to draw breath, but the next one is shallower. The child's song stops for a moment. With my head turned toward the two of them, I wait to breathe again.
finalMoment.afterword: That evening in 1806, Manuel stopped breathing. Isabel held her daughter and remained beside her father for a while longer. When Nico arrived late, she told him that their father had pressed her hand one last time. They washed the clay cup and placed it on a shelf, and the next time his granddaughter went to the fields, she changed the end of the song again. The record of past lives says that Manuel's life—spent protecting his fields while worrying about advances and singing lyrics he changed with his family—ended that day.

card.name: Bakari
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Bakari of the Kabala Ferry Landing. You rose from porter to boatman, and after injuring your leg, you repaired boats and shared a waterside household with your sister's son, Sari.
card.title: The Sacks Left on the Sandbar
card.world: 1548, south of Timbuktu in the Songhai Empire, at the Kabala Ferry Landing on the Niger River
card.flavor: Boats and passengers in the river wind
card.opening: Wood scraped beneath the boat. When Bakari lowered his pole, the embankment they needed to return to was farther away than he had thought.
card.life: Bakari was born in Kabala in 1517. He began working as a porter while helping his sister Awa with their household, then pooled his share with Isa to buy a boat and traveled the river. After injuring his leg, he took on more boat repair work and taught his nephew Sari the trade. He died in 1576.
card.turn: Driven by the wind, the boat ran aground on a sandbar, and water seeped through a gap between the planks on one side. Unless they unloaded some cargo, they could not carry the passengers back into deep water.
card.decision: Instead of unloading someone else's sacks of salt, Bakari set his own sacks of grain, which he had planned to sell, down in the shallows and asked Isa and the passengers to help lighten the boat.
card.cost: The passengers reached the embankment, but the soaked grain fetched less than its full price. Bakari also refunded part of the fares because of the delay, so he could not pay for the boat repairs right away.
card.after: Bakari continued working the ferry with Isa. After injuring his leg and cutting back on long journeys, he repaired boats and carried on his waterside life with his nephew Sari.
card.presentEcho: One choice did not make the losses disappear. The people who helped Bakari push the boat that day also remain in that memory.
card.secondLook: Bakari knew the river well, but faced with the wind and the sandbar, he had to unload his own grain first. Nor did the passengers simply stand by and wait to be rescued.
card.unresolved: The soaked grain and refunded fares did not come back that day, and he had to calculate his share of the next boatload all over again.
card.readerQuestion: Have you ever felt torn between wanting to protect your share and wanting to help someone else cross first?

signalMoments.notice: Bakari lowered his pole and measured the depth near the sandbar again. The bow was stuck in the shallows, but the stern was in deep water. He told everyone not to crowd to one side and to move the cargo first.
signalMoments.connect: Bakari handed the pole to Isa and reached out to the passengers. As they lowered the grain sacks one by one into the shallows, Hassan held his salt sacks in place so they would not roll.
signalMoments.protect: Bakari saw the water seeping through the bottom of the boat and untied his own grain sacks. “These are mine. Let's unload them first.” He sent the passengers toward the dry planks and pushed the boat with Isa.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Bakari. It was a time when Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, belonged to the Songhai Empire. Bakari began as a porter at the Kabala Ferry Landing south of the city and became a boatman. Here is the story of the day, at age thirty-one, when his boat stopped in the middle of the river.

The boat carried sacks of salt, sacks of grain, and five passengers. Isa, holding the pole at the stern, laughed and said, “This time, you choose the route.” Bakari pointed to an embankment in the distance. A first-time passenger had asked, “Will it take long to get there?” “We'll arrive in the time it takes to sing one song,” Bakari replied, turning the boat.

Then the river wind blew from the side. The boat did not even have a sail, but an empty sack billowed and the boat began drifting sideways little by little. Isa thrust out his pole. Thud. The boat stopped. When Bakari lowered his pole, its wooden tip struck sand almost at once. The bow had run aground on a shallow sandbar.

“Let's push backward.” Isa leaned into the pole. The boat did not move. As the cargo and passengers crowded to the same side, a thin layer of water rose through a gap in the bottom planks. One passenger pointed at the salt sacks. “Why don't we unload those?” Hassan, the owner of the sacks, stepped in front of them. “Why should my goods be thrown overboard first?” Bakari thought Hassan had a point. His own grain sacks were on the boat, too.

The water was not ankle-deep, but there was enough to wet the floor. Isa slipped on the soaked planks. Bakari told everyone to stay still for a moment, then used his pole to check the depth on both sides of the boat. The water beside the bow was shallow, while the water behind the boat was deep. If they made the boat a little lighter and turned it, they could break free. The question was what to unload.

signalMoments.notice: Bakari touched the wet mark on the pole with his finger. “Only this side is shallow. It's deep at the stern.” He had the passengers change places so they would not crowd to one side, then said he would unload his own grain sacks into the shallows first.
signalMoments.connect: Bakari handed Isa the pole at the bow. “I'll unload my sacks, so hold the stern steady.” Hassan and the passengers also joined hands to keep the sacks from rolling. No one person could free the boat alone.
signalMoments.protect: Untying his grain sacks, Bakari said, “I won't touch someone else's salt. We'll unload mine first.” After moving the passengers to the planks the water had not reached, he prepared to push the boat with Isa.

episode.afterSignal:
As Bakari hauled up one sack, a few grains rolled across the wet bottom planks. Isa laid a plank at an angle toward the shallows. Together, they lowered Bakari's three sacks over the end of the plank and onto the sand. Water seeped into the sacks, making them so heavy that the skin peeled from Bakari's palms. While protecting his salt, Hassan used his body to keep the sacks from rolling into the middle of the boat.

“Back now!” Isa shouted. Bakari pushed against the sand with his pole, while the passengers shifted their feet inside the boat to distribute the weight. At first there was no sound. On the second push, a long scraping noise came from beneath the boat, and the bow turned slightly. On the third, the tip of the pole suddenly plunged into deep water. Isa almost fell in after it, but Hassan grabbed his arm.

When the boat reached the embankment, the first-time passenger said he had not managed to sing even one line of a song. Bakari could not laugh. He still had to retrieve the grain sacks left in the shallows. He waded in with several others and recovered them, but they were soaked to the edges. Because the journey had been delayed, he refunded part of the fares he had collected.

At the ferry landing, the grain buyer opened the sacks and lowered his offer. No matter how Bakari argued, wet grain was not the same as dry grain. The money was not enough to repair the split planks right away. Beside him, Isa said, “I'll put in my share, too.” Only after a long pause did Bakari reply, “Without your pole, we'd still be out there.”

Bakari continued traveling the river after that. Once he injured his leg, he spent more days repairing boats at the ferry landing than making long river journeys. After his sister Awa died, he lived with Sari's family and fetched water for the household. He did not give up the chore even after Sari's child was born. On days when his leg hurt, he sometimes grew angry when Sari offered to do it instead. At those times, if the child brought him a cup of water, Bakari accepted it and sat resting for a while.

memories.label: His Colleague Isa's Memory

finalMoment.place: Kabala Ferry Landing, Songhai Empire
finalMoment.scene:
A house in Kabala in 1576. My fever has not broken for three days, and I lie on a mat in the shade of the courtyard. One water jar is empty. I would usually have filled it, but today I cannot get up. Sari's twelve-year-old child grasps the jar's handle. “I'll go fetch water.” I open my mouth to object, but a cough comes, and I lie back down.

Sari hands the child a small jar. “I'll carry the big one.” When they go out the door, I hear their footsteps on the dry ground. When my sister Awa was alive, she fetched the water first. After she died, I insisted on doing it myself. Every time Sari offered to take over, I grew angry, afraid there would no longer be a place for me. Today, though I see the empty jar, I do not have the strength to say those words.

The child returns and holds out a cup of water. When my hand trembles and I nearly drop it, Sari supports the cup. I do not push him away, and I drink a little. The child sings a song heard at the market, changing the last words into something silly. “Who taught you that?” I ask, and the child laughs. “You did, Uncle. I made up the ending.” Tomorrow, I want to hear those last words once more. I want to tell Sari that it is all right for him to take over the water fetching, but my mouth is dry, and my words come out short.

The sun sinks below the courtyard wall. Each time I try to breathe in again, my chest feels heavy. Sari props folded cloth behind my back. “I'm here, Uncle.” I take Sari's arm and pull him toward me. I hear the child's song close by and the sound of Sari setting the cup on the ground. The strength leaves my fingertips. I try to move my chest, but no breath comes in.
finalMoment.afterword: That evening, Bakari died in the courtyard with Sari and the child beside him. No one knew the name of his illness. The next day, Sari still remembered the words he had spoken in anger to his uncle, and the child kept the water jar full. The pouch Awa had mended remained in the house, but it was not in Bakari's hand that day. This record of a past life tells us that the life ending here belonged not only to the man who steered a boat, but also to an uncle who struggled to accept help and to Bakari, who listened to a child's song.
finalMoment.artAlt: A fictional house courtyard in Kabala in the Songhai Empire in 1576, where 59-year-old Bakari lies feverish on a mat at evening while his nephew Sari and a twelve-year-old child sit beside him with a water jar

card.name: Shen Lan
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Shen Lan, a fan painter in Lin'an. You ran a shop with your younger brother and reunited with your friend Mei, but often postponed your plans with her. After her hand began to hurt, she took fewer painting commissions and taught her 12-year-old niece how to choose colors.
card.title: The Two Switched Fans
card.world: A small family fan shop near West Lake in Lin'an, capital of the Southern Song, in 1248
card.flavor: Where two very different gifts ended up
card.opening: A fan painted with empty stone steps arrived at a birthday party, while a fan with lively, leaping fish arrived at a home sharing quiet memories.
card.life: Shen Lan was born in Lin'an in 1213 and opened a small fan shop with her family. She and her friend Mei were separated and later reunited, but Shen Lan kept postponing their plans because of work at the shop, and they grew apart. After pain in her hand forced her to take fewer painting commissions, her younger brother Shen Zhao handled more of the wrapping and deliveries, while her niece Xiao Hua learned first about colors and then about wrapping.
card.turn: The name slips on two orders tied with the same blue cord were switched. When Shen Zhao told her how Grandmother Zhang had reacted, Shen Lan compared the order ledger with the sequence in which she had wrapped the fans.
card.decision: Shen Lan admitted that she had wrapped them and visited both homes herself. She did not take the fan from the child's hands, refunded the elderly woman, and then painted a new West Lake fan.
card.cost: Shen Lan paid for the new materials and the refund, and after staying up all night to repaint the fan, she could not open the shop the next morning. She would never know what orders might have come in. The elderly woman did not forget that Shen Lan had missed the promised day.
card.after: Shen Lan changed the wrapping procedure with her younger brother Shen Zhao. She also walked with Mei after her friend returned, but she often postponed their plans, and they grew apart. After pain in her hand forced her to take fewer painting commissions, Shen Zhao handled more of the wrapping and deliveries, and Xiao Hua learned about colors at 12.
card.presentEcho: A mistake made in haste can touch someone else's day. Setting it right costs time and money, and sometimes you must wait until the other person's anger has passed.
card.secondLook: The two fans had only their cords in common; their paintings were different. The deliveries were reversed the moment Shen Lan put off checking them, and after the child came to like the unexpected painting, a simple exchange was no longer possible.
card.unresolved: The elderly woman received the belated West Lake painting, but the family gathering she had lost that day could not be restored. Shen Lan also never knew what orders might have come in the following morning.
card.readerQuestion: If my small mistake affected someone else's important day, what would I set right first?

signalMoments.notice: Shen Lan traced the two addresses in the order ledger with her finger. The house holding the birthday party was on the way to Grandmother Zhang's home. Shen Lan decided to check the West Lake fan at the party first, then visit Grandmother Zhang.
signalMoments.repair: Shen Lan took out a new blank fan she had set aside. “I'll have to repaint this using my own materials.” She gathered her brushes and set out first for the two homes that had received the wrong gifts.
signalMoments.connect: Shen Lan first asked Shen Zhao, who had returned from making the deliveries, what he had seen at the two homes. “Who opened the fans?” After Shen Zhao described each home in turn, Shen Lan asked him to go with her.

identity.region: Lin'an, capital of the Southern Song, and West Lake

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:

People closest to her · Her younger brother Shen Zhao, her niece Xiao Hua, and her old friend Mei
The life she wanted · To keep the shop going without losing the time to see her friend

episode.beforeSignal:
In a former life, you were called Shen Lan. It was a time when present-day Hangzhou in China was known as Lin'an, the capital of the Southern Song. Shen Lan sold round fans painted with small landscapes. When she was 35, the cords wrapped around two fans caused far more trouble than the paintings themselves. Let me tell you that story.

Shen Lan placed 2 round fans side by side on her worktable. On 1, she painted West Lake's stone steps and a willow tree. She deliberately left the steps empty. Grandmother Zhang, who had ordered it, wanted to remember the times she and her late younger sister had rested there together. On the other fan, Shen Lan painted 2 fish brushing each other's tails underwater. It was a birthday gift for an 8-year-old child.

Her younger brother Shen Zhao peered through the shop door. “Should I deliver both of them today?” “Yes. Just don't mix up the name slips.” With her own hands, Shen Lan wrapped the fans in 2 lengths of matching blue cord. The next customer called to her from outside the door, and Shen Lan hurriedly tucked in the 2 remaining slips. Shen Zhao picked up the wrapped fans in order and left.

Around sunset, Shen Zhao returned. “Grandmother Zhang asked why you painted fish.” Shen Lan set down the brush in her hand. Grandmother Zhang had requested empty stone steps, not fish. Shen Lan opened the order ledger she kept at the shop. The addresses and paintings were recorded correctly. Shen Lan herself had reversed the name slips while wrapping the fans.

“Shen Zhao, did they open the fans at both homes?” Shen Zhao nodded. “The child's family had already started the party, and Grandmother Zhang's family had gathered at her home.” Shen Lan stared at the remaining blue cord. Shen Zhao had only delivered the fans to the addresses written on them.

signalMoments.notice: Shen Lan traced the addresses of the 2 homes in the order ledger with her finger. The house holding the birthday party was on the way to Grandmother Zhang's home. Shen Lan decided to check the West Lake fan at the party first, then visit Grandmother Zhang.
signalMoments.repair: Shen Lan took out 1 blank fan she had prepared in advance. She planned to visit both homes first and admit her mistake, then return and paint a new West Lake scene using her own materials. She gathered her brushes and the blank fan and set out with Shen Zhao.
signalMoments.connect: Shen Lan asked Shen Zhao in turn who had received the fan at each home. Shen Zhao replied that the child had unwrapped the gift personally and Grandmother Zhang had opened hers in front of her family. Shen Lan said, “You didn't make the delivery mistake. Please come with me.”

episode.afterSignal:
They arrived at the child's home first. Before Shen Lan could even begin to apologize, the child held the West Lake fan high. “The steps here are empty. Can I sit there?” The child's mother was surprised that it was not the fish painting, but when she saw how much the child liked the fan, she said they would keep it. Shen Lan let go of the thought that taking the painting back would solve everything more quickly. “I sent the wrong fan. If you change your mind, I'll paint you a new picture.”

Grandmother Zhang's home was quiet. The 2 fish meant for a celebration gleamed in her hands as though they were leaping. “What does this have to do with my sister?” the elderly woman asked. Shen Lan did not look back at Shen Zhao. “I put the slips in backward. The painting you meant to view with your family that day will arrive late.” Shen Lan returned the payment and promised to repaint the empty steps by the following morning. Grandmother Zhang accepted the money, but merely set down the fish fan without answering.

That night, Shen Lan took out a blank fan she had set aside for another customer. Shen Zhao held the new frame while Shen Lan painted a quiet lake and a small flight of stone steps. Whenever the brush tip began to hurry, Shen Lan stopped her hand. This time, she had to leave the steps empty. At daybreak, while Shen Zhao briefly closed his eyes to rest, Shen Lan carried the fan back to Grandmother Zhang's home.

Grandmother Zhang studied the new painting for a long time. “The steps are empty.” “Yes. Just as you requested.” The elderly woman nodded, but she did not smile. The day before, when her family had gathered together, had already passed. Shen Lan also missed whatever orders might have come in that morning because she could not open the shop. When Shen Zhao returned and said, “Let's stop using blue cord,” Shen Lan smiled briefly. “If we only change the cord, I'll just rush again.” From then on, they agreed to check each painting and name together before wrapping the fans.

Afterward, Shen Lan once again walked along West Lake with her friend Mei, who had returned from a distant region. But whenever orders flooded the shop, Shen Lan postponed the days they had planned to walk. Mei increasingly found herself waiting for Shen Lan and then returning home alone. After pain developed in her fingers, Shen Lan took fewer painting commissions, but her younger brother Shen Zhao had to handle more of the wrapping and deliveries. When her niece Xiao Hua turned 12, Shen Lan chose colors with her, and 2 years later, she also taught her how to wrap fans. She occasionally had tea with Mei on days they had set in advance.

memories.label: The Place She Kept for Years
memories.detail: The small fan shop she opened with Shen Zhao. Even after closing for the day, she arranged the brushes on her worktable.

memories.label: Her Most Treasured Possession
memories.detail: The short paintbrush her aunt had placed in her hand when she was a child

memories.label: The Person She Waited For
memories.detail: Her friend Mei, who sent her letters even after moving far away. After they reunited, Shen Lan postponed their plans so many times that Mei stopped waiting.

memories.label: Her Changing Body

memories.detail: “Before you finish painting, ask who will hold it.”

memories.label: Shen Zhao's Assessment
memories.detail: “Even after my sister took fewer painting commissions, the wrapping and deliveries remained. She was slow to acknowledge that I had taken on more of that work.”

memories.label: Her Friend Mei's Memory
memories.detail: “After I came back, she said we should walk together, but she always postponed our plans when work came up at the shop. Later, we only had tea on days arranged in advance.”

memories.label: Her Niece Xiao Hua's Memory
memories.detail: “I learned about colors when I was 12. My aunt didn't immediately correct the colors I chose. She first asked why I had chosen them.”

finalMoment.place: A wet dirt path and the water's edge beside the West Lake ferry landing in Lin'an, Southern Song
finalMoment.scene:
One morning in late spring of 1271, I walked along West Lake in Lin'an with my old friend Mei. It had rained the day before, and the dirt path beside the ferry landing was wet. Mei pointed toward a teahouse ahead. “We only have to make it that far.” I took a step toward a willow at the lakeshore. Beneath my feet came the sound of wet earth collapsing.

I reached for the tree's roots. The soil fell away with my feet, and my body slid toward the water. “Mei!” I cried, and my friend turned around. My hand brushed the roots but failed to grasp them. The cold water rose to my waist, and the next moment, my feet could no longer touch the bottom.

Mei lay facedown on a section of the dirt path that had not collapsed and reached out her hand. I stretched out my arm, but without anywhere to plant my feet, my body drifted a little farther away. Gathering up the hems of my wet clothes, I turned toward the tree. When I surfaced once, I heard Mei calling my name. Instead of answering, I closed my mouth and reached out my hand again.

This time, even the earth my fingertips touched fell into the water. I tried to lift my face above the surface, but no strength remained in my arms. Mei's voice grew distant. Water entered my mouth, and I tried to cough. After that, only the sound of the water was close.
finalMoment.afterword: That day, 58-year-old Shen Lan died after the dirt path beside the West Lake ferry landing collapsed and she fell into the water. Unable to descend to the water's edge for fear that more earth would collapse, Mei called for help. By the time people at the ferry landing approached by boat, Shen Lan had already stopped breathing. When Mei brought the news, Shen Lan's younger brother Shen Zhao and 17-year-old niece Xiao Hua came. Mei remembered both the days when she had waited for Shen Lan and gone home first, and the morning they had walked together that day. The Record of Former Lives closes this chapter on Shen Lan's life, which held both days when she postponed her plans and days when they walked together.
finalMoment.artAlt: A wet dirt path beside a ferry landing at West Lake in Lin'an, Southern Song, in late spring of 1271. Just before the ground beneath 58-year-old Shen Lan's feet collapses, Shen Lan reaches for a willow while her startled friend Mei stands a few steps behind, stretching out a hand. The 2 women, the lake, and the crumbling bank are viewed from an oblique middle distance.

card.name: Salvatore Bella
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Salvatore Bella, the owner of a puppet theater in Palermo. You ran the theater with Maria, but when audiences dwindled, you insisted on continuing the performances, increasing Maria's sewing work. Belatedly, you began repairing puppets as well and entrusted the stage to your daughter Lucia. Your son Nino chose other work.
card.title: The Knight Who Could Not Raise His Sword
card.world: A small family theater staging knightly puppet shows in Palermo, Kingdom of Italy, in 1887
card.flavor: The broken rod and the next scene
card.opening: Just as the duel was about to begin, the sword arm of the knight puppet went limp. Cries of “Fight!” erupted from the benches.
card.life: Salvatore was born in Palermo in 1853 and learned puppetry from his father. He built a small theater with his spouse, Maria, and raised Lucia and Nino. When audiences dwindled, he insisted on continuing the performances, so Maria covered their living expenses by sewing for other households. Belatedly, Salvatore reduced the number of performances and began repairing puppets as well. In his later years, he sat in the audience and watched Lucia stage her own shows.
card.turn: During a performance, the control rod for the knight puppet's arm broke. If they continued with the planned sword fight, the puppet's arm and even its armor could be damaged.
card.decision: Salvatore paused the performance and announced the malfunction. When Lucia said, “He still has his shield,” Salvatore gave the knight lines about buying time by protecting the people with his shield.
card.cost: Some audience members who had been waiting for the duel took refunds and left. Salvatore canceled the next day's performance and spent money repairing the arm and rod.
card.after: Salvatore worked with Pietro again. While he insisted on continuing the performances even as audiences dwindled, Maria took on more sewing work outside the home. He eventually began repairing puppets as well, but her burden did not disappear at once. After Maria died, Lucia took charge of her own shows, while Nino chose work outside the theater.
card.presentEcho: Even when the scene everyone was waiting for disappears, you can find another path on the spot. But you must also pay the price owed to those who did not like that path.
card.secondLook: Even after Lucia thought of the shield, the broken arm could not be fixed that day. Salvatore saw that hiding the malfunction could ruin the larger puppet too, so he lowered the curtain first.
card.unresolved: No one knows whether the audience members who left returned for the next performance. Lucia also had no idea that what she said that day would one day lead to a stage of her own.
card.readerQuestion: If I could no longer show the scene everyone had been waiting for, what would I say first?

signalMoments.notice: Before shaking the puppet's arm again, Salvatore examined the broken end of the rod backstage. The wood had split. He gestured to Pietro to hold the opposing puppet still for a moment.
signalMoments.speak: Salvatore lowered the small curtain and stood before the audience. “The knight's arm is broken. We cannot show you the sword fight as planned.” He let them choose whether to keep watching or receive a refund.
signalMoments.repair: Salvatore removed the broken rod and braced with cloth the place that would tear if he shook the arm any more. He decided to finish with a different scene today, cancel the next day's performance, and make a new rod.

identity.region: Palermo, Sicily, Kingdom of Italy

He insisted on keeping the same number of performances even as audiences dwindled, burdening Maria with sewing work outside the home. Belatedly, he began repairing puppets as well and handed decisions about the stage to his daughter Lucia, but his son Nino chose a different life.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were known as Salvatore Bella. You ran a small puppet theater with your family in Palermo, in what is now Sicily, Italy, in 1887. Today, I will tell you about a performance one evening when he was thirty-four. It is the story of how a knight who could not raise his sword finished the show.

The worn benches were packed with spectators. The children in the front row elbowed one another, eager to see the duel they had been waiting for since the day before. Salvatore's friend Pietro held the black-armored puppet, while Salvatore moved the silver knight. Behind the curtain, his seven-year-old daughter Lucia watched only the tips of her father's shoes. Maria took the last audience member's ticket and closed the door.

The black knight blocked the castle gate. Pietro spoke in a deep voice. “Hand over the sword. Otherwise, the people inside the gate cannot leave.” Salvatore raised the sword arm of the knight puppet. The entire audience leaned forward at once.

Snap. The wooden rod in his hand suddenly grew shorter. The end hidden below the stage had broken in two. The knight's arm dangled and swung beside its armor. When Salvatore pulled it again, threads sprang loose from the thin cloth. Any more force would tear not only the arm but the armor as well. A child in the front row shouted, “Why isn't he fighting?”

Pietro held the black knight still. Salvatore set down the rod and closed the small curtain. “Just a moment. The knight puppet's arm is broken.” Someone in the back shouted, “I paid to see the duel!” Salvatore heard that too. After all, he was the one who had promised this fight from the beginning.

signalMoments.notice: Salvatore carried the broken end closer to the light backstage. The wood had split lengthwise, and even if he joined the pieces, it did not seem likely to withstand that night's sword fight. He told Pietro to hold the black knight still.
signalMoments.speak: Salvatore clearly told the audience, “We cannot show you the sword fight today.” He continued, “You may stay and watch a different scene through to the end, or leave now and receive a refund.” He asked Maria to bring the money pouch.
signalMoments.repair: Salvatore removed the broken rod and bound the knight's arm with cloth so the armor would not tear any further. He told Maria they would cancel the next day's performance and set aside wood for carving a new rod.

episode.afterSignal:
Behind the curtain, Lucia tugged at her father's sleeve. “He can't raise his sword, but he still has his shield.” Salvatore looked at the puppet's other hand. The shield was still attached. “Then he can make it as far as that castle gate.” Pietro shifted the black knight's position slightly as well.

The curtain rose again. Salvatore slowly placed the silver knight in front of the castle gate. “My sword will not obey me. But while I stand here, the people inside can escape.” As the black knight approached with a laugh, the knight blocked the way with his shield. Pietro made sounds of the enemy circling to the right and leaping to the left. Moving only the one good hand, Salvatore showed the knight being driven back one step at a time.

“He could just fight!” An adult at the back stood up. Behind the curtain, Lucia silently counted on her fingers. Three, two, one. At that moment, Salvatore pulled the painting of the castle gate to the side. Lucia pushed forward two small human puppets that had been placed behind the gate. The children in the front row were the first to point at them. While the black knight turned to look, the silver knight raised his shield and cleared the way. Pietro said in a low voice, “You have won today. But bring your sword next time.”

Not everyone in the audience applauded. One child grumbled that the knight had not drawn his sword, and three adults collected refunds from Maria and left. Salvatore watched them go. The money he would take home that day was reduced by the amount he refunded. When Maria said, “We will have to cancel tomorrow's performance,” he nodded. He could not break the puppet again and break another promise too.

The next day, Salvatore posted a notice on the theater door saying they were closed and carved a new rod. Beside Maria, Lucia held up the torn piece of armor cloth. “Should we tell the story again, like yesterday?” the child asked. Salvatore smiled. “Yesterday, you were the one who told it first.” He raised the repaired arm only once. The sword moved now, but he did not know whether the audience members who had left the day before would return.

Salvatore continued running the theater with Maria after that. Years later, when audiences dwindled, he could not bring himself to reduce the number of performances, so Maria had to take on sewing for other households. Only later did he begin repairing puppets as well. Lucia grew up and staged her own shows, while Nino chose work outside the theater. In his later years, Salvatore watched his daughter's performances from the audience. The broken rod was only one evening in his long life, but he remembered for a long time how he had listened to Lucia that day.

finalMoment.place: Salvatore's home in Palermo
finalMoment.scene:
In late spring 1925, I eat lunch alone at my home in Palermo. Lucia has gone to work, and Nino is at his own workplace too. The moment I set down my spoon, a sharp pain strikes the center of my abdomen. I brace myself against the table and wait for a moment. When I try to straighten my back, my entire abdomen hurts. Drinking water does not help. I cannot pick up the spoon that has fallen beneath the table.

I slowly make my way to the doorway and call for a neighbor. “Please tell Lucia.” After watching the neighbor turn away, I sit in a chair. I wonder if taking short breaths will ease the pain in my abdomen, but it does not. When Lucia arrives and tries to help me up, I raise a hand to stop her. “Nino needs to know too.” I finish speaking and bite my lip. Lucia brings water and returns to my side.

The next day, my fever rises. Even turning over in bed is difficult. Nino stands near the door, and Lucia replaces the bowl of water. I look from one to the other, then say, “Please open the door.” When Nino opens it, I hear the sounds outside. I try to take a deep breath, but my abdomen tightens and the pain reaches my chest. Lucia calls my name. I try to turn my head, then stop. My next breath does not come.
finalMoment.afterword: Salvatore died in Palermo in 1925 after a perforation in an abdominal organ caused severe inflammation to spread through the peritoneum. He first felt the pain at the table in his home, and died the next day in a room with Lucia and Nino present. Lucia remembered the years when her father had entrusted the performances to her. Nino remembered how his father had avoided the subject for a long time after Nino chose other work. Nor could a final word erase the burden of the sewing work Maria had borne in his place while she was alive. The record of this past life says that both the dinners the family shared and the price Maria paid were present at Salvatore's end.
finalMoment.artAlt: Front-facing view from across the dining table in a Palermo home in 1925. Salvatore, age 72, sits bracing himself against the table as sudden abdominal pain strikes.

card.name: Clara Ward
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Clara Ward of San Francisco. After the earthquake, you started your business again in a rented storefront, but as you kept the shop open late, your daughter Lucy had more housework to do. After your husband died, you lived near your friend Ellen.
card.title: The Black Thread in the Red Shawl
card.world: San Francisco, United States, 1906, in the temporary shelters at Fort Mason and the Presidio after the earthquake and fires
card.flavor: Among rows of look-alike tents
card.opening: “I saw the old woman in the red shawl.” At those words, Clara left the tent, but there was more than one red shawl.
card.life: Clara was born in San Francisco in 1870 and grew up helping in her mother's store. She built a home with Daniel and raised Lucy and Samuel. When she rented a small storefront and resumed business after the earthquake, Lucy often took care of her younger brother's dinner. Years later, Lucy left for another city, and Samuel learned to bake. Clara cared for Daniel through his illness until he died, then lived near her friend Ellen until 1949, when she was struck and killed by a truck in the street.
card.turn: Unable to learn what had become of Daniel and Ruth after they were separated by the earthquake and fires, Clara heard that an elderly woman in a red shawl had been seen at the Presidio. One corner of Ruth's shawl had black stitching Clara had sewn herself.
card.decision: Clara left the children with Ellen, then walked to the Presidio. The first red shawl belonged to someone else, but she kept asking the people in the tents and narrowed her search by finding someone who remembered the black stitching.
card.cost: Even after Clara found Daniel and Ruth, the injured Daniel could not return that day. Clara made her way back to Fort Mason after the sun had dipped low, while the children and Ellen waited until late evening. The home and store they had lost did not return either.
card.after: The following year, Clara rented a small storefront and resumed business. While she kept the shop open late, Lucy often took care of Samuel's dinner at home. Years later, Lucy left for another city, and Clara looked back belatedly on the work she had left to her daughter. After Daniel died, she lived near her friend Ellen.
card.presentEcho: In desperate moments, a small clue can sometimes open a path. While you check the facts and take action, however, you may also leave someone waiting.
card.secondLook: A red shawl alone was not enough to tell whether the woman was Ruth. Only when the black-stitched corner was combined with what another person in the tents had said did the path become clear.
card.unresolved: Clara found her family again, but their old home and store were gone. Even in the place she opened the following year, she could not live exactly the same life as before.
card.readerQuestion: If I found a clue that might lead me to my family but was not certain, what would I check?

signalMoments.notice: Clara asked the man who brought the news whether he had seen black thread in one corner of the red shawl. The man shook his head. Even after hearing that he could not be sure, Clara decided to go to the Presidio and check for herself.
signalMoments.connect: Clara reminded Ellen which tent Lucy and Samuel would stay in and when she planned to return. “If I'm late, wait for me here.” Ellen called the children to her side and made sure they had water and something to eat.
signalMoments.explore: Clara wrote the names of the two shelters on the back page of her small ledger and set out on the road to the Presidio. If she did not find them in one tent, she planned to ask again at the next. The children remained with Ellen.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Clara Ward. In April 1906, after a great earthquake struck San Francisco in the United States, fires burned for days. Clara was thirty-six and had come to a temporary shelter with her two children. Let me tell you about the day Clara walked in search of her family.

The tents at Fort Mason were not quiet even in the morning. Every time people passed on their way to collect water, dirt rose from the ground. Clara rested a hand on eleven-year-old Lucy's shoulder and gave seven-year-old Samuel a piece of bread. Two days earlier, when people scattered near their home, Clara had lost sight of her husband Daniel and Daniel's aunt Ruth. Clara had led the children away from the flames first, and she still did not know where the other two were.

“I saw an old woman in a red shawl over by the Presidio,” said a man returning with water. Ruth owned a red shawl. Clara had mended one corner with black thread, so she thought she could recognize it even from a distance. But the man had not seen that corner. Lucy asked, “Mom, are we going too?” Clara pictured the paths between the tents, all of them alike. She could not wander through them aimlessly with both children.

Just then, her friend Ellen, who was staying in the same row of tents, sat down beside the children. “I'll stay here with them. You remember where to come back, don't you?” On the back page of her worn ledger, Clara wrote the two names Fort Mason and the Presidio. Though the store was gone, the ledger had remained in her bag. Clara told Lucy, “I'll try to be back before sunset. If I'm late, stay with Aunt Ellen.” That was as far as she could make any promise.

signalMoments.notice: Clara called the man who had brought the news back and asked whether he had seen black stitching on the shawl. “I didn't see that.” The answer offered less than she had hoped. Clara let go of her certainty and wrote “red shawl, black thread unknown” in the ledger before setting out for the Presidio.
signalMoments.connect: Clara checked again which tent Ellen and the two children would sit by. “If I'm late, stay here.” Ellen gave Lucy and Samuel water and promised to remain with them until Clara returned. Only then did Clara begin walking toward the Presidio.
signalMoments.explore: Clara wrote the names of the two shelters on the back page of her ledger and began asking for directions. Instead of trusting one person's memory, she planned to ask at every tent in the Presidio herself. She left the two children with Ellen and set out alone.

episode.afterSignal:
When Clara reached the Presidio, she looked down at her dirt-covered shoes. In the distance, another row of identical tents stretched on. A red shawl hung on a bench beside the water station. Clara ran to it, but its corners were clean. There was no black thread. The old woman who returned to the bench was not Ruth either. “Are you looking for someone?” the woman asked.

Clara showed her the name written on the back page of the ledger. “Ruth Ward. Her shawl is mended with black thread. She may be with a man named Daniel.” The old woman said she did not know them. Clara moved on to the next tent. Twice, then three times, she repeated the same words. At one place there was no answer; at another, someone knew a different Ruth. Neither the name nor the red shawl was enough of a clue.

A woman carrying a tub of water stopped when she heard Clara. “Black thread? Stitched like a big X at the end of the shawl?” Clara looked up. She had mended it exactly that way, using black thread from her mother's store. The woman pointed behind the tents. “She was with a man who hurt his foot. I heard they moved him over there because he had trouble walking.” For the first time, Clara could follow the black stitching rather than the color red.

Ruth emerged from behind a tent carrying a small bowl of water. The black X was visible in one corner of her shawl. When Clara called her name, the water rippled in the bowl. Daniel was sitting inside the tent. He said he had injured his ankle while keeping hold of Ruth amid the crowd and could not walk a long distance. “The children?” he asked first. “They're with Ellen. They're both all right.” Only after saying that did Clara examine Daniel's foot.

Clara realized that neither of them could leave right away. She had to leave them at the Presidio that day and return on her own. “Tell the children we're here,” Ruth said, showing her the corner of the shawl. Clara wrote down which row the tent stood in and set out again. When she reached Fort Mason, Samuel was dozing on Ellen's lap, and Lucy was watching from outside the tent. “Did you find them?” “Yes. Let's go see them together tomorrow.” Only then did Lucy sit down.

Finding her family again did not bring back the home and store they had lost. The following year, Clara rented a small storefront and reopened for business. For the first few years, she closed the shop late, and her daughter Lucy often prepared dinner at home for young Samuel. When Lucy grew up and left for another city, Clara thought about the work she had left to her daughter all those years. Later, when Daniel became ill, she shortened her shop hours, and after her husband died, she lived near her friend Ellen. The day she found her family and the life that followed belonged to different times.

finalMoment.place: A street near Ellen's home in San Francisco, United States
finalMoment.scene:
One afternoon in late spring of 1949, seventy-nine-year-old Clara returns from grocery shopping with her friend Ellen. They live in different homes in the same neighborhood. Ellen lifts a small paper bag and says, “Come over for tea tomorrow.” Clara replies, “I'll come in the morning.” At the corner, Ellen walks toward her house on the left, while Clara heads for her own home across the street.

Clara stands by the road and lets a passing car go by. She can see her front door across the street. The bag in her hand is not heavy, and home seems only a few steps away. As she starts to cross, a small delivery truck turns the corner to her right. Hearing a short blast of the horn and the sound of wheels braking, Clara turns her head. The truck is already close.

The impact knocks the bag from her hand. Clara lies in the road, trying to draw a breath. Her legs and torso hurt, and she cannot turn onto her side. The driver stops the truck and gets out. “We need help!” he shouts to the people nearby. Clara opens her eyes and searches among them for the back of Ellen, whom she has just left. She tries to speak, but her breath is too shallow for much sound to come out.

Hearing the vehicle, Ellen turns back. “Clara, I'm here.” Clara moves her eyes toward the voice. She can see Ellen's face, but there is no time to choose what to say. The bag she was holding lies a short distance away in the road. Clara tries to draw another breath, then stops. Ellen calls her name once more, but Clara cannot answer.
finalMoment.afterword: Clara died at the age of seventy-nine after being struck and gravely injured by a delivery truck on a San Francisco street in 1949. Ellen had been walking with her and returned when she heard the sound just after they parted, but she did not see the moment of impact. Lucy, who lived in another city, remembered both how she had often been responsible for Samuel's dinner during the year her mother reopened the shop and how her mother had belatedly recognized that effort. Samuel remembered what his mother had said when she accepted his decision to become a baker. The driver's later whereabouts were not recorded. This chronicle of a past life preserves together at the end of this life the day Clara walked among the tents in search of her family in 1906, the decades of shopkeeping, family, and friendship that followed, and the final journey that ended without warning.
finalMoment.artAlt: An afternoon view of a small San Francisco intersection in 1949, seen from a tall building across the street. Clara begins crossing with a paper bag in her hand as a small delivery truck turns the corner. Only the street and their paths just before the collision are visible; there is no three-person composition showing an injury, someone offering support, or someone running to call for help.

card.name: Elena Rojas
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Elena Rojas of Buenos Aires. You earned your own income by keeping ledgers, and after an accident at 52 left you unable to move your legs, you continued writing letters while being cared for by your family.
card.title: The First Beat in the Palm
card.world: Buenos Aires, Argentina, 1941, a tango gathering at a neighborhood club
card.flavor: A Song Two People Began Again
card.opening: The moment Rafael missed the first note, the hem of Elena's skirt caught beneath his shoe. They stopped in the middle of the dance floor.
card.life: Elena was born in Buenos Aires in 1892. She worked as a telephone operator, then left that job after marrying Rafael. Even while raising Inés and Daniel, she wanted an income of her own, so she kept the books for neighborhood shops. After a delivery truck accident in 1944, she could no longer move either leg, and Rafael and their children helped her move around the house and manage daily life. After her husband died, she moved to Rosario to live near her daughter. Her daughter cut back on her morning work to care for her, and Elena felt both grateful and sorry for the time she gave up. She also continued exchanging letters with her friend Rosa.
card.turn: At the neighborhood club, Rafael missed the beginning of the music and stepped on the hem of Elena's skirt. When someone laughed, he said they should go home because he did not want others to see that his hearing had weakened.
card.decision: Elena asked Rafael what kind of signal he needed. They sat out one song and agreed on a starting signal—a light press of the palm. After Rafael said he wanted to, they returned to the dance floor.
card.cost: The two songs Elena had been waiting for passed, and Rafael had to tell others that he could not hear well. Even when they danced again, their steps crossed once more.
card.after: Rafael's hearing did not return to the way it had been after that night. Elena was paid for her ledger work. After the accident in 1944, she could no longer move her legs, but even while receiving help from her family, she continued writing ledgers and letters by hand. After her husband died, she moved to Rosario to be near her daughter Inés, and felt grateful and sorry about the wages Inés lost by working less. She exchanged letters about music with her friend Rosa.
card.presentEcho: Even when two people hear the same song, the moment when each begins may be different. Sometimes, before taking each other's hands again, they need to ask about each other's pace.
card.secondLook: It was not that Rafael disliked dancing. After missing the first note, he was afraid of making a mistake in front of others. Elena, too, pulled him by the hand before asking how he wanted to do it.
card.unresolved: There is no way to know how other people saw that dance. Nor did that one song change his later hearing loss or their eventual parting through death.
card.readerQuestion: If someone could no longer do something we used to do together the way they once had, what would I ask first?

signalMoments.notice: Elena saw that Rafael's gaze was fixed not on the other dancers but on the musicians' hands. He waited to hear the first note and missed the start. Elena pointed to an empty seat near the stage.
signalMoments.speak: Elena asked, “Where did you lose it?” Rafael answered, “The sound at the very beginning. I can tell once everyone else starts moving.” Elena asked if she could signal the start with her palm.
signalMoments.rest: Elena said, “Let's sit out just one song,” and sat with Rafael in an empty chair. Over the table, they practiced starting with one press of the palm and slowing down with two presses.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Elena Rojas. In 1941, you lived with your family in Buenos Aires, Argentina, while keeping the books for neighborhood shops. Let me tell you about an evening when you went dancing with Rafael at a neighborhood club. It was the day a couple married for years came to look at each other as if meeting for the first time.

Elena folded the two admission tickets and laid them on her palm. By the door, Rafael was already touching his shirt collar for the third time. When they were young, the two of them had danced easily even in a crowd. But for the past few years, Rafael had often missed voices calling from a distance. At home, he could read Elena's words by watching her face, but he did not know whether he could do that in front of an orchestra.

Their friend Rosa had saved two empty chairs. “You're late today. The first song is starting.” Elena hurriedly took off her coat. Rafael still had not offered his hand. Elena took his arm and led him onto the dance floor. The violin drew out a long note, and the bandoneon player leaned forward.

Everyone around them moved at once. Rafael alone stepped half a beat late. The hem of Elena's skirt caught beneath his shoe. There was a small tearing sound, and the two stopped where they stood. The woman in the couple beside them swallowed a startled laugh. Elena pulled her skirt free, but Rafael let go of her hand. “Let's go. There's no need to make ourselves look any more ridiculous here.”

Elena started to say, “It was one mistake,” then stopped. She was the one who had pulled him in before the first note even sounded. “Did I rush you?” Rafael looked toward the stage. “I couldn't catch the sound at the start. I only knew after everyone else's feet were moving.” People waiting for the next song passed between them.

signalMoments.notice: Elena saw Rafael turn his head, trying not to miss the orchestra's hand signals. “Let's sit near the stage. I'll signal you with my hand when it starts.” He nodded, and they went to the empty chairs.
signalMoments.speak: Elena asked Rafael, “Is it only the beginning you can't hear, or the middle too?” “The beginning is the hardest. After that, I can watch your feet.” Elena asked if she could take his hand, and they agreed that she would press his palm at the start.
signalMoments.rest: Elena said, “Let's sit and listen to the next song.” Sitting in the chairs beside Rosa, they practiced over the table: one press of the palm meant start, and two meant walk slowly. Rafael turned his hand over himself and asked to try it again.

episode.afterSignal:
Rosa placed glasses of water in front of them. “What about your skirt?” “Only the edge tore a little.” Elena lifted one ankle to show her. Only then did Rafael's mouth relax. As the first song and the next one passed, they sat in the empty chairs and lightly pressed each other's palms. One press meant start; two meant a little slower. When Elena asked, “Shall we go back?” Rafael stood first.

Before the third song began, Rafael spoke to Rosa in a low voice. “Lately, I can't hear the first sound very well.” Rosa looked at him for a moment, then said, “Then I'll stay here and guard your seats.” Elena did not pull Rafael along. She waited for his hand to rise first.

When the bandleader raised his bow, Elena pressed Rafael's palm once. Keeping his eyes on her, Rafael took the first step. They did not make any quick moves. They walked a short distance between the other couples. When the bandoneon grew louder, Elena pressed his hand once more, but Rafael misread the direction, and his shoulder bumped into someone else. He said, “I'm sorry,” and paused.

This time, Elena did not laugh. “Do you want to keep going?” Rafael did not let go of her hand. “Yes. Just a little more slowly.” They moved to the edge of the dance floor and began walking again. The edge of her skirt was still slightly torn, and someone must have seen it. When the song ended, there was no great applause and no special miracle. Rosa drummed her palm on a chair and gestured for the two of them to sit down.

On the way home, Rafael asked, “Will you press my hand next time too?” Elena put the two remaining ticket stubs in her coat pocket. “If I start walking too fast, you stop me.” Rafael pressed the back of Elena's hand once. Until they reached home, he still could not hear the sounds coming from across the street very well. Whenever that happened, Elena spoke from where he could see her face.

After that, the number of sounds Rafael could no longer hear increased. Elena continued keeping the books for neighborhood shops and cherished the days when she was paid for her own work. In 1944, on her way home, she was struck by a delivery truck and could no longer move either leg. Rafael helped her move between the bed and chair, and Inés and Daniel each made time to help as well. Elena continued writing ledgers and letters to Rosa by hand. After Rafael died, she moved to Rosario to be near her daughter Inés. Inés cut back on her morning work to help Elena, and although Elena was grateful, she worried about the wages her daughter had lost. Rosa remained in Buenos Aires, and the two exchanged letters about music. The one song they danced together in 1941 does not explain the later accident or the care her family provided.

memories.label: Work After the Accident
memories.detail: Although she could not use either leg after 1944, she wrote ledgers by hand and sent letters to her friend. She needed help from family and neighbors to move around the house.

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “If I answer too quickly, ask again whether you've finished speaking.”

memories.label: Rafael's View
memories.detail: “She was firm when balancing numbers, but when it came to the children's worries, she took her time choosing an answer.”

memories.label: Rosa's Memory
memories.detail: “After she went to Rosario, we could only talk about music in letters. I liked it better when we sat face-to-face and listened.”

memories.label: Inés's Memory
memories.detail: “When Mother said she was sorry, I did sometimes think of the morning wages I had given up. But I decided for myself how to divide my time between caring for her and my work.”

memories.label: Daniel's View
memories.detail: “Whenever Mother thanked me, I remembered the days I couldn't go. On days when I had work to do at home, I had to ask a neighbor to help.”

finalMoment.place: Elena's room near Inés's home, Rosario, Argentina
finalMoment.scene:
It is a winter evening in Rosario in 1971. Seventy-nine-year-old Elena sits in a wheeled chair in her own room near her daughter Inés's home. She has been unable to move either leg since a delivery truck struck her in the street at 52, and now she has had a fever from pneumonia for several days. Her daughter Inés comes after finishing her evening work and heats water. Elena has spread the letter she was writing to her friend Rosa across the table and reads the final line. Her hand can move, but her cough makes it hard to hold the pen for long.

“You can keep writing tomorrow.” Inés places the cup close to Elena's hand. Elena picks it up, moistens her throat, and points to where it should be set down again. “How many hours did you miss at the shop today?” Before answering, Inés wrings out a wet cloth. “Two hours. I decided that.” Elena thanks her. Then, thinking of the money her daughter would have earned during that time, she adds, “I'm sorry.” Inés says, “It's not that the money doesn't matter,” and pulls the bowl of water closer to where Elena is sitting.

Her son Daniel stops by after finishing dinner at his own home and sits by the door. He spreads a blanket on his mother's bed, but Elena asks him to fold the letter first. “Send it to Rosa. Tell her I haven't written the last line yet.” As Daniel folds the paper, Elena coughs hard. Even when she tries to steady her breathing, her chest quickly tightens again. Inés and Daniel help move her from the chair to the bed. Elena tells them where to place their hands so she will be comfortable, and even after lying down, she checks that the folded letter is on the table.

As the night deepens, her fever rises and her breathing quickens. Looking at Inés's face, Elena says, “Thank you for coming again today.” She tries to say something more, but a cough comes first. Daniel opens the window a little, and Inés sits beside her. Holding her daughter's hand, Elena tries to draw one deep breath, but cannot fill her lungs completely. Inés calls her name. Elena turns her head toward her, closes her eyes, and cannot breathe again.
finalMoment.afterword: Elena died of pneumonia at 79 in her room in Rosario in 1971. Although she had been unable to use either leg since the 1944 accident, the accident itself was not the direct cause of her death that day. Inés remembered both her mother's gratitude and her apologies. She also remembered the work she had reduced to provide care, and the time she had chosen to give of her own will. Daniel sent the unfinished letter to Rosa, and Rosa missed the days when she and Elena had sat face-to-face listening to music. Rafael had died first, but the night in 1941 when they found a beat he could hear together also remained with the family. The record of this past life closes by preserving together the cost of the care Elena received, the work she chose for herself within that care, and the years she spent feeling both grateful and sorry toward her family.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high-angle view from one side of a small room in Rosario in the winter of 1971, showing 79-year-old Elena seated in a chair beside a table holding an unfinished handwritten letter. Her daughter Inés is placing a glass of water within reach, and Elena cannot move either leg. There is no dance scene, no one collapsing or being supported, and no one running to seek help

card.name: Mabel Connor
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Mabel Connor of Melbourne. You shared a mending room with your friend Annie, but after putting off a conversation about dividing the income, you began working separately. You continued doing alterations after your husband died, then entrusted the shop to your daughter when your eyesight worsened.
card.title: The Unpicked Hem
card.world: A small tailoring room in Melbourne, in the British colony of Victoria, 1897
card.flavor: Clothes a friend can ride in
card.opening: “Try riding.” Annie mounted the bicycle in the skirt Mabel had made. On the third push of the pedal, the hem was sucked toward the back wheel.
card.life: Mabel was born in Melbourne in 1871 and learned the tailoring trade. She married Thomas and altered clothes at home while raising their two children. She shared a mending room with her friend Annie, but after putting off a conversation about dividing the income, Annie got a separate worktable. The two sometimes had tea, but they never went into business together again. Mabel kept working after her husband died, then entrusted the shop to her daughter Mary when her eyesight worsened.
card.turn: Her friend Annie asked her to make a cycling skirt for a club ride. Pressed for rent, Mabel skipped testing the hem, and when Annie mounted her bicycle, the fabric nearly caught in the wheel.
card.decision: Mabel admitted her mistake and unpicked the hem with Annie to refit the skirt. She returned part of the agreed price and made sure the fabric stayed clear of the wheel before Annie rode again.
card.cost: Annie missed the club's departure and bruised her arm. Because of the money Mabel returned, she came up short on the rent and had to ask Thomas and the landlord for a few more days.
card.after: For a while, Annie did not ask Mabel to make her any new clothes. Later, the two shared a mending room, but when Mabel put off discussing how to divide the money, they ended up with separate worktables. Their friendship continued through infrequent teas. After Mabel's eyesight worsened, she entrusted the shop to her daughter.
card.presentEcho: Even when someone you cherish asks for a favor, rushing can make you miss things. And even if you get a chance to try again, the time and money lost the first time do not return.
card.secondLook: Mabel skipped the test because she was worried about the rent, but that reason did not erase Annie's bruise. Annie was still angry when she put the clothes back on and tested them again.
card.unresolved: There was no way to know whether the landlord would wait three days. Nor was Mabel's friendship with Annie restored all at once that day.
card.readerQuestion: If something you want to finish quickly seems dangerous to someone, what would you check first?

signalMoments.notice: Mabel saw the fabric hanging close to the wheel and stopped the bicycle. She and Annie slowly turned the wheel to find which side of the hem was touching it.
signalMoments.speak: Mabel said, “I didn't check whether it would catch in the wheel. It's my fault.” She asked Annie whether there was time to remake it right away and said she would return the money Annie had paid.
signalMoments.repair: Mabel removed the pins and folded up the long hem again. While Annie mounted the bicycle herself and pedaled, Mabel stood a step away and watched to see whether the fabric touched the wheel.

She raised two children and, after her husband died, entrusted the shop to her daughter when her eyesight worsened.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Mabel Connor. In 1897, you earned money altering clothes in Melbourne, in the British colony of Victoria. Let me tell you about one afternoon in that life—the day a friend nearly could not wear the clothes you had made for her.

Mabel hung the finished dark teal skirt over a chair. Her friend Annie planned to wear it to a cycling club ride. Ordinary skirts got in the way when pedaling. This time, Mabel had made ties that could lift the sides. When Annie pulled on the fabric, the hem rose to just below her knees. “This should do, shouldn't it?” Mabel asked.

Before she heard an answer, Thomas coughed from the doorway. Taking off his hat, he held out a small slip of paper. It was a note saying the rent collector would come tomorrow. Since Thomas's warehouse work had dried up, the money Mabel earned from alterations had become the household's main source of income. She needed Annie's payment to cover the shortfall. Mabel swallowed the suggestion that they test the skirt beside the bicycle first.

Annie put on the skirt and mounted the bicycle waiting outside. “Last time, it took ages to get my old skirt out of the chain.” Mabel pretended to pick up a piece of thread that had fallen from the chair. Annie turned the pedals once, then twice. On the third turn, the hem dragged backward. The spokes made a sound as they tugged at the fabric.

“Stop!” Mabel cried. Annie put a foot down, then collapsed onto one knee. The bicycle toppled sideways, and a blue bruise began to rise on Annie's elbow. Mabel pulled the fabric free of the wheel. The tie was secure, but the hem on the other side was too long. Annie held out her hand. “Did you even try riding in it?” Mabel could not answer.

signalMoments.notice: Mabel checked Annie's elbow first. The skin was not broken, but the bruise was spreading quickly. Together, they set the bicycle upright and slowly turned the wheel. The inner hem sagged below the tie and touched the spokes. Mabel marked the spot with chalk.
signalMoments.speak: Mabel spread the skirt over her knees. “I didn't test it on a bicycle. It's my fault.” Annie asked, “Why?” Mabel started to mention the rent, then stopped. “Even if I needed the money, I shouldn't have let you fall.” Annie rubbed her elbow without a word.
signalMoments.repair: Mabel ran outside and set the bicycle upright. Instead of tugging at the fabric caught in the wheel, she marked its position with pins, then unpicked the thread little by little. As Annie sat clutching her elbow, Mabel said, “Before I fix it, I need to know if you're all right.”

episode.afterSignal:
Annie sat by the window with a wet cloth pressed to her bruised elbow. “I'll be late for the club today.” Mabel apologized. Annie said, “Instead of saying that, show me why only this side ended up longer.” Mabel spread out the skirt and showed her how pulling only one tie made the fabric on the opposite side sag. Annie picked up that part of the fabric. “Then each side needs to be hitched up separately.”

Mabel unpicked the seam. Annie looked at the clock, then heard the wheels of other bicycles passing outside. The group they had planned to join had already left. Thomas came to the door to bring up the rent, but Mabel said, “We'll talk tonight.” He picked up the fallen bicycle and leaned it against the wall.

An hour later, they retied the straps on both sides of the skirt. Mabel said, “This time, you don't have to go far.” Annie chose the bicycle herself. She pedaled slowly and returned from the end of the road. Mabel was so focused on the wheel that she did not see Annie's face. “It isn't catching this time,” Annie said, then added, “But my arm hurts.”

Mabel deducted part of the agreed price and returned it to Annie. At first, Annie refused to take it. “What about your rent?” “I'll find another way. You fell today.” Annie took the coins and slipped them into a small pouch. Even as she left with the repaired skirt, she did not say she would order her next dress from Mabel.

That night, Mabel and Thomas wrote the landlord a note asking him to wait just three more days. Mabel slept fitfully until they received an answer. Annie did not visit again until the following week. This time, instead of an order for new clothes, she brought tea for them to share. A faint bruise still marked her elbow. They did not avoid talking about the skirt, but neither did they end the conversation with laughter.

Mabel continued altering clothes and raising her children. For a while, she and Annie shared a mending room, but Mabel put off discussing how they would divide the money, and they ended up with separate worktables. They still had tea together sometimes, but they never ran the same shop again. Mabel continued working after her husband died, and when her eyesight worsened, she entrusted the shop to her daughter Mary. Her friendship with Annie was not decided by one repair or one apology.

memories.detail: The small mending room where she supported her family and repaired the neighborhood's clothes

memories.detail: In months when orders were scarce, she calculated the rent and the children's food costs first.
