memories.detail: “Tell me if it doesn't fit. I can unpick it and sew it again.”

memories.label: Annie's Assessment
memories.detail: “Mabel always finished a repair. But she kept putting off the question of how we'd divide the money, so I found a worktable of my own.”

memories.label: Hugh's Memory
memories.detail: “Even on days when she was busy with work, she sewed a new pocket inside my old coat.”

memories.label: Mary's Assessment
memories.detail: “Even after Mum handed the shop over to me, she still liked to feel the fabrics. But I made sure I was the one who held the needle.”

finalMoment.place: Mabel's home in Melbourne
finalMoment.scene:
On a morning in Melbourne in 1943, I serve tea to Annie, my oldest friend, who has come to my home. My daughter Mary has gone to the mending room. I point to the window box, trying to tell Annie that a new leaf has appeared. But the word leaf will not come out of my mouth. Annie asks, “What leaf?” The strength drains from the right hand holding my teacup, and the cup strikes the table.

I try to say that I am all right, but my voice tangles. Annie rises from across the table. “Mabel, look at me.” When I try to turn my head, my body leans to one side. Annie catches the chair. I brace my left hand against the edge of the table. Annie opens the door and calls for a neighbor. I know what I was trying to say, but I cannot force the word past my lips.

Mary returns and calls my name. I am lying in bed, unable to lift my right hand. Annie says, “I'll sit here with you.” Even now, I want to ask about the share of the money from long ago. I cannot form those words either. When Mary takes my hand, I turn my eyes toward my daughter. The intervals between my breaths keep slipping out of rhythm. Mary calls my name again. I move my lips to answer, but no breath comes.
finalMoment.afterword: Mabel died at her Melbourne home in 1943 after a sudden stroke took away her speech and the strength in her right hand. Annie was beside her from the beginning, and Mary arrived later. Mary remembered how her mother continued to inspect customers' clothes even after entrusting the mending room to her. Annie never forgot the day they ended up with separate worktables because they failed to discuss in time how to divide the money. The record of Mabel's past life leaves us with this: do not turn the end of that friendship into a story in which every loose thread was neatly tied up.
finalMoment.artAlt: High-angle view of a tea table in a Melbourne home in 1943. The teacup of 72-year-old Mabel, who has lost her speech and the strength in her right hand, is tilting as her friend Annie watches.

card.name: Govind Patil
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Govind Patil of Bombay. You came from the countryside and delivered lunchboxes before opening a tea shop with your wife. You objected when your son chose different work, and after your wife died, you lived near your daughter.
card.title: Two Spoons
card.world: The railway stations and lunchbox delivery routes of Bombay, British India, in 1912
card.flavor: The Place Where Lunch Was Awaited
card.opening: For three days, Hari's lunchbox had disappeared near the station instead of reaching his office. On the fourth morning, Hari's wife stopped Govind. “Please put it directly into his hands today.”
card.life: Govind was born in 1882 in a village near Pune and moved to Bombay as a young man. He supported Savita and their two children by delivering lunchboxes, and when his knees began to hurt, the couple opened a tea shop. He objected when their son Dev chose different work, but Dev did not return. After Savita died, Govind lived near their daughter Nila.
card.turn: Hari had lost his job but could not tell Rekha, so he collected his lunchbox near the station. On the day Rekha, who had seen him there the previous day, asked Govind to hand it to him directly, Hari was not in his usual place.
card.decision: Govind wondered whether to deliver his remaining lunchboxes first, but instead went looking for Hari at the tea shops around the station. When he found him, he placed the lunchbox in his hands, and when Rekha arrived, Govind did not hide where he had delivered it.
card.cost: Govind's next delivery was late, so he lost part of that day's pay. Hari's unemployment was not resolved then and there, and Govind could not have the couple's conversation for them.
card.after: When Govind's knees weakened, he opened a tea shop with Savita. When their son Dev chose different work, Govind visited his new workplace, but did not withdraw his disapproval. The two saw each other less often than before. After Savita died, Govind moved closer to their daughter Nila.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes what matters most about a lunchbox is not which desk it reaches, but whether it reaches the hands of the person waiting for it.
card.secondLook: Hari hid his unemployment and collected his lunchbox near the station. Govind did not know why, and did not ask further about the location of his new workplace. Rekha had already realized the truth and came because she wanted to hear it directly from her husband.
card.unresolved: Govind never heard what Hari said when he went home. Nor did a job appear that day.
card.readerQuestion: If I discover someone's hidden circumstances while doing the work entrusted to me, how much should I reveal?

signalMoments.notice: Govind saw the empty water glass Hari always left near the station. When the tea shop owner said, “He went into the shade over there today,” Govind carried the lunchbox in that direction.
signalMoments.speak: Govind asked the tea shop owner, “Have you seen Mr. Hari? I have to put this directly into his hands today.” The owner pointed toward the shade behind the station as he rinsed a glass.
signalMoments.explore: Govind walked a full circuit from the station entrance, where Hari usually stood, to the back of the tea shop. He stopped when he saw Hari's familiar shoes beneath a tree.

identity.region: Bombay, Bombay Presidency, British India
identity.summary: He came from the countryside to Bombay and delivered lunchboxes. When his knees began to hurt, he opened a tea shop with his wife. He objected when his son chose different work, and the distance between them remained even after he visited his son's new workplace. After his wife died, he lived near his daughter.

Govind Patil · Male

profilePages.body:

Liked · Empty streets in the early morning, stories his daughter Nila read to him
Disliked · Lunchboxes with loosely fastened lids

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured possession · The shoulder strap Savita had mended for him
People closest to him · His wife Savita, daughter Nila, son Dev, and colleague Sadashiv

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were known as Govind Patil. In Bombay, British India, in 1912, you carried lunches prepared in people's homes to their workplaces. Let me tell you a story from the middle of the day in that life. It happened on the day one lunchbox held two spoons.

Govind pressed a finger against the lid of the metal lunchbox. Click—it was firmly shut. Rekha held on even as she passed it to him at the door. “Please make sure you put it directly into Hari's hands today.” “I always do,” Govind replied, but Rekha shook her head. “Don't leave it with the guard at his office.”

Hari had not been outside his office for three days. Around lunchtime, he would stop Govind in front of a tea shop near Victoria Terminus. “My workplace changed.” That was what he said, but he never once named the new workplace. Whenever Govind came to collect the empty lunchbox, Hari was always there. Govind was paid to put food into the designated person's hands, so he asked no further questions.

His colleague Sadashiv hoisted the other lunchboxes onto his shoulder and urged him on. “I'll take that alley. Just finish Mr. Hari's delivery and come back.” Govind carried the final two lunchboxes to the station. In front of the tea shop where Hari always stood, there was only an empty glass. Hari's face was nowhere among the people waiting for lunch.

Govind looked at the station clock. The lunchbox he had collected from the next house also had to be delivered before the food went cold. He could leave Hari's at the shop and go. But his hand brushed the little cloth knot Rekha had tied over the lid. He heard again the voice that had asked him to deliver it directly.

signalMoments.notice: Govind saw that the water glass Hari used was still on the shop's table. The tea shop owner followed his gaze, then pointed toward a tree behind the station. Govind tightened the straps on the remaining lunchboxes and walked into the shade.
signalMoments.speak: Govind asked the tea shop owner, “Have you seen Mr. Hari? I have to put this directly into his hands today.” The owner set down a wet glass and pointed toward the shade behind the station. Govind thanked him and headed that way.
signalMoments.explore: Govind turned back from the station entrance and walked as far as the rear of the tea shop. In the shade of a tree, a familiar pair of shoes caught his eye. The person who looked up was Hari. Govind raised the hand holding the lunchbox.

episode.afterSignal:
Hari was sitting on a stone ledge beneath the tree. As he reached for the lunchbox, Govind asked, “Why weren't you over there today?” Hari shifted aside to make room. “I left the company four days ago. At home, they still think I go out every morning.” Govind did not sit. Hari looked at the lunchbox lid and laughed. “I don't have any money now, but I'm still spending it on delivery fees.”

When they opened the lunchbox, two small spoons lay wrapped in cloth beside the rice and side dishes. Hari lifted one. “Why are there two?” Then Rekha's voice came from behind them. “I brought mine too.” She approached, catching her breath. Only then did Govind understand why Rekha had stopped him that morning.

Hari hurriedly closed the lunchbox lid. “How long have you known?” “I saw you here yesterday.” Rekha glanced at Govind. “Did you put it into his hands?” “Yes. Here, not at the office.” That was all Govind said. He did not know why Hari had left or what work he would do next.

Rekha sat on the stone ledge and took out one of the spoons. Hari opened the lid again, but did not scoop up any rice. “I was going to tell you.” “Then tell me while we eat.” Rekha's voice was calm, but her hand was tense. The silence between them was not a comfortable one. Govind did not wait any longer. He hoisted the next lunchbox onto his shoulder and stepped out into the narrow road.

The final customer received his lunchbox after lunchtime because Govind arrived late. Govind lost part of that day's wages. Sadashiv grumbled, “You should've just given me both earlier.” Govind replied, “I didn't even know where he was then.” After he returned home, Savita asked, “Did you eat?” and he remembered that he had skipped his own lunch. He never learned how the conversation at the station ended.

Govind continued delivering lunchboxes for many years afterward. When his knees could no longer endure as they once had, he and Savita opened a small tea shop. When their son Dev chose different work, Govind objected. He even visited Dev's new workplace, but Dev did not return to the shop, and the two saw each other less often than before. After Savita died, Govind moved closer to his daughter Nila. Govind did not find Hari a new job, nor could he make every choice in his own family turn out as he wished.

memories.label: Well-Traveled Roads
memories.detail: He used the wayfinding skills he had learned at the country market on his delivery routes in Bombay.

memories.label: Treasured Possession
memories.detail: A shoulder strap Savita had mended many times. He did not throw it away even after he stopped carrying heavy lunchboxes.

memories.label: Precious Time
memories.detail: Evenings when his daughter Nila read aloud the writing she had newly learned

memories.label: Change of Work
memories.detail: After knee pain forced him to cut back on long routes, he brewed and sold tea with Savita.

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “Press the lid again first. Once you're on the road, it's hard to go back and fix it.”

memories.label: Savita's View
memories.detail: “He didn't say much at home, but he remembered what the children wanted to eat.”

memories.label: Sadashiv's Memory
memories.detail: “He remembered the roads better than I did. But he never admitted he was hungry, right to the end.”

memories.label: Nila's View
memories.detail: “Father never tried to choose my work for me. But he always asked which road I was taking when I left.”

memories.label: Dev's Memory
memories.detail: “He got angry when I said I wouldn't take over the shop. He did come to my new workplace, but he never said it was all right for me to keep doing that work.”

finalMoment.place: A railway station platform in Bombay
finalMoment.scene:
On a Bombay afternoon in 1959, I sit at the end of a long bench in the station, waiting for Nila's train. Three years have passed since I moved closer to my daughter after Savita died. Watching the stairs where people will come down, I stretch out my left leg. My calf has felt heavy for several days, but I could still manage the walk here. Just as I try to stand at the sound of the train arriving, I cannot breathe.

I sit back down. When I breathe in deeply, a sharp pain stabs one side of my chest. I say, “Wait...” to the person beside me, but the rest will not come. The passengers turn toward the train. I raise a hand to look for Nila, then lower my arm. No matter how quickly I breathe, there is not enough air. The bench's cold wood touches my palm.

Nila sees me from the stairs and stops. “Father?” Nila comes toward me. I recognize her face and move my lips. I try to tell her to send word to Dev as well, but no sound comes out. Nila calls to the people around us for help. My daughter's hand touches the back of mine. My chest jerks once and my vision narrows. Nila calls me again, but I have no breath left to answer.
finalMoment.afterword: Govind died at a Bombay station in 1959 after a blood clot blocked the vessels in his lungs and suddenly left him unable to breathe. Nila reached the bench where her father had been waiting, but she could not take him home. Dev came later and remembered how his father had grown angry when he said he would not take over the shop. He also remembered that his father had come all the way to his new workplace. Nila and Dev did not explain those two things in the same way. The shop Govind built with Savita, his last three years near Nila, and the distance that remained between him and Dev all stood, still different from one another, at the end of Govind's life. The Book of Past Lives erases none of them for the sake of another.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high viewpoint from across a Bombay station in 1959. 77-year-old Govind sits at the end of a long bench, suddenly unable to breathe, while passengers stand near distant stairs.

card.name: Yun Dallye
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yun Dallye of Mapo Ferry. After losing your husband at a young age, you raised your niece and took over your mother's tavern. In old age, you passed the tavern on to a young neighbor.
card.title: The Warmest Spot She Kept Open
card.world: A small tavern beside Mapo Ferry during the reign of King Sunjo of Joseon in 1832
card.flavor: A Guest After Four Years
card.opening: “Do you have a bowl of soup and a warm room?” The guest carrying a child on her back raised her head. It was Dallye's niece Yeonhui, whom Dallye had told never to return four years earlier.
card.life: Dallye was born near Mapo in 1787. She married Yi Taek but lost him at a young age, then returned to her mother's tavern and raised her younger sister's daughter, Yeonhui. She kept the tavern even after Yeonhui left home. Later, she taught the work to a young neighbor named Manbok and handed the tavern over to him in her old age.
card.turn: Yeonhui, who had left after an argument four years earlier, arrived like a guest with her young daughter. Dallye had already promised the warmest room to another traveler.
card.decision: After checking that the tavern across the road had a vacant room, Dallye returned the money to the traveler she had promised first and guided him there. She gave the room to Yeonhui and was the first to bring up the words “never come back,” which she had once said.
card.cost: She lost that night's room fee, and Dallye had to voice the regret she had long kept hidden. Yeonhui left with her daughter the next day, and the two did not immediately go back to living as they had before.
card.after: Yeonhui's family began visiting Mapo occasionally again in 1837. Even after that, the two exchanged words that hurt each other. Dallye taught the work to a young neighbor named Manbok, and after her legs began to hurt, she handed the tavern over to him.
card.presentEcho: Opening the door to someone returning after a long absence and understanding everything that happened in the meantime come at different speeds.
card.secondLook: Even after Yeonhui left, Dallye said she had been right. Yeonhui also found it hard to explain why she had left without sending any word. She returned with her child not just because she needed a place to stay, but because she wanted to see Dallye.
card.unresolved: One night's soup and lodging could not fill the emptiness of four years. Even afterward, the two could still wound each other with their words.
card.readerQuestion: When someone I have been distant from for a long time comes to see me, what will I say first?

signalMoments.notice: Dallye saw the small scar on the back of Yeonhui's hand from when she had burned it on a cauldron as a child, the hand now supporting her child. She stopped asking about the room fee as if Yeonhui were a stranger and first checked whether the child was cold.
signalMoments.speak: Dallye asked, “Yeonhui, is this your child?” Yeonhui replied that she had told the child about Grandmother Dallye in Mapo. Dallye remembered what she herself had said four years earlier.
signalMoments.protect: Dallye saw the child's wet shoes and gestured toward the warm inner part of the kitchen. “Sit her down. Let's feed her some soup first.” When Yeonhui again said she would pay for the room, Dallye said they could talk about that later.

Yun Dallye · Female

Mapo Ferry outside the walls of Hanseong Prefecture, Joseon, 1832

profilePages.body:
Personality · Quick to attend to guests, but struggled to wait for those close to her to think differently.
Liked · The sound of boats arriving in the evening, mixing rice into hot soup and eating it
Disliked · Guests who ran off without paying

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The ladle her mother had used for years
People close to her · Her niece Yeonhui, the young neighbor Manbok, and regular customers from the riverside
Life she hoped for · For the tavern's fire to keep burning long after her body slowed down
Worry · That she might never hear how Yeonhui was living far away

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Yun Dallye. In 1832, you ran a small tavern at Mapo Ferry outside the walls of Hanseong Prefecture in Joseon. Let me tell you about an evening in that long life when you welcomed a guest. You knew her name, yet could not bring yourself to say it right away.

When Dallye lifted the lid of the soup cauldron, steam rose into her face. From the river came the clatter of wood against wood as a boat unloaded its final cargo. Dallye tested the warmest spot on the room's heated floor with the back of her hand. It was warm. She had promised Merchant Yi, who had stopped by during the day, that she would give him the room when he returned that evening. Dallye placed the coin he had paid beside the ladle, apart from the rest.

A woman with a child on her back stopped at the threshold. “Do you have a bowl of soup and a warm room?” Familiar eyes showed beneath her face, darkened by the fading light. It was Yeonhui. Four years earlier, at sixteen, Yeonhui had left for a relative's house, saying she planned to marry and live elsewhere. Dallye had said, “If you're going, never come back.” Yeonhui had done as she was told and had not returned, and Dallye had heard news only from the relatives with whom Yeonhui had first stayed.

When Dallye set down the ladle, Yeonhui lowered her head. “I came as a guest. I'll pay too.” The child buried her face in Yeonhui's shoulder. Dallye wanted to ask, “Whose child is she?” but the first words out of her mouth were, “I've already given the room to another guest.” Yeonhui nodded. “Then we'll just have some soup and go.”

At that moment, Yi approached from the river carrying an empty wooden pack frame. He stopped briefly when he saw the two women at the door. “Is my room warmed?” Instead of answering, Dallye lowered the fire beneath the soup cauldron a little. There was only one warmest room. The child squirmed and whined to be let down.

signalMoments.notice: Dallye looked at Yeonhui's hand wrapped around the child's foot. The small scar from burning it on a cauldron as a child was still there on the back of her hand. Dallye closed the mouth that had been about to ask for the room fee and said, “The child's feet are cold.”
signalMoments.speak: Dallye asked, “Yeonhui, is this your child?” Adjusting the child on her back, Yeonhui replied, “Yes. I've told her about Grandmother Dallye in Mapo.” At those words, Dallye remembered the sound of her own voice four years earlier.
signalMoments.protect: Dallye saw the child's wet shoes touching the kitchen threshold and gestured inside. “Sit her down. Let's feed her some soup first.” When Yeonhui said again, “I'll pay for the room,” Dallye replied, “We'll talk about that later.”

episode.afterSignal:
Yi took a spoonful of soup and asked about the room again. With Yeonhui standing beside her, Dallye did not offer a long explanation. “Please wait a moment.” She ran to the tavern across the road and checked whether it had a vacant room. One dry spot remained. She returned and gave Yi back the money she had received during the day. “I changed my promise. They have a room over there. I've already asked them to open it for you when you arrive.” Yi counted the money, then nodded. He did not leave behind any kind words.

Dallye pointed Yeonhui toward the warm room. “Go in with the child.” When Yeonhui held out the room fee, Dallye said, “I'll take payment for the soup. You don't owe anything for the room tonight.” Yeonhui did not put the money back inside her skirt. She set it on the edge of the table and put the child down. Neither told the other to sit first.

The child fell asleep before the soup went cold. Yeonhui slowly set down her spoon. “I'm raising this child with my husband near Yangcheon. I hadn't planned to come here, but she's old enough to say people's names now. I wanted to teach her your name too.” Dallye put down the cloth she had been using to wipe the ladle. “Back then, I told you never to come back.” Yeonhui raised her head. “I heard those words. I still don't know why you had to go that far.”

Dallye said, “I was afraid I'd be left alone if you went away.” She added that this still gave her no right to hold Yeonhui back. Yeonhui did not immediately say it was all right. “I could have sent word at least once too.” After that, the two stared only at their soup bowls for another long while. When the child turned in her sleep, Yeonhui pulled the edge of the blanket over her.

The next day, Yeonhui set out with her daughter on her back around the time the first boat departed. Dallye pressed the packed rice she had prepared into Yeonhui's hand. “When will you come again?” Without smiling, Yeonhui replied, “I'll come if I can.” Dallye did not use those words to set a date. She watched Yeonhui's retreating back and the empty place by the river for a long time. The money Yeonhui had left for the room still lay on the table, but Dallye did not take it that day.

Yeonhui's family began visiting Mapo occasionally again in 1837. Dallye welcomed guests and taught Manbok how to tend the cauldron, and after her legs began to hurt, she handed the tavern over to him. At their next meeting, she and Yeonhui again exchanged words that hurt. Even so, they did not forget each other's names.

memories.detail: The ladle her mother had used. She carved the handle down several times to make it smooth again.

memories.label: Place She Protected
memories.detail: The cauldron fire in the small tavern where riverside boats and guests came and went

memories.label: Favorite Sound
memories.detail: The sound of wood striking wood when the evening boats came in

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Before you ask if they want more soup, look at their rice bowl.”

memories.label: Yeonhui's Assessment
memories.detail: “Aunt Dallye raised me, but she tried to decide my path too. When she grew old, sometimes she asked me first.”

memories.label: Manbok's Memory
memories.detail: “On days when the soup was too salty, she told me not to hide it, but to add more water.”

memories.label: Regular Customer Yi's Assessment
memories.detail: “There was a time she changed her promise. Still, she put the money back in my hand herself.”

finalMoment.place: Dallye's small house near Mapo
finalMoment.scene:
In early winter of 1857, I live alone in a small house near Mapo. I have handed the tavern over to Manbok. My lower abdomen has hurt for several days, and it burns when I urinate. Today I mean to go out to draw water, but when I push aside the bedding, my entire body shakes. I walk as far as the threshold, then sit down again inside the room. In the yard, Manbok calls my name.

Manbok sets down a water jar and comes inside. “I'll find a physician.” I ask whether Yeonhui is supposed to come today. Manbok says this is not the day she promised. A little later, I ask the same question again. “I'll send someone to Yeonhui.” I hear Manbok's words and nod. Looking at the unfamiliar wall beyond the yard, I am briefly confused about whether this is my house. Manbok touches my hand. My fingertips are cold.

Night falls. I lift a cup to swallow a sip of water, but my hand trembles. Manbok takes it and slowly holds it out to me. “When Yeonhui comes…” I say. While I search for the next words, Manbok replies that he has already sent someone. I watch the evening light entering through the open door. When Manbok calls my name, I try to open my eyes. It takes a long time to breathe in. The next time I hear my name, I no longer have the strength to move my lips.
finalMoment.afterword: Dallye died in 1857 at her house near Mapo after a urinary tract infection spread throughout her body. Manbok brought her water and remained beside her, while Yeonhui arrived later. Yeonhui remembered both the years her aunt had spent raising her and the years when she had tried to decide Yeonhui's path. Manbok recalled how Dallye had taught him not to hide it when he made the soup too salty. Dallye's final words remained unfinished. The record of her past life does not fill that silence with words of reconciliation.
finalMoment.artAlt: The view from the yard of a house near Mapo in 1857, looking toward an open door. Dallye, age 70, sits inside the room, while Manbok stands some distance away holding a water jar.

card.name: Livia Secunda
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Livia Secunda of Ostia. You washed and mended cloth while raising two children, and you continued doing repairs even after arguing with a coworker over how to divide their wages.
card.title: The Missing Blue Tunic
card.world: The Roman Empire's port city of Ostia in AD 147
card.flavor: The Secret of the Bakery Basket
card.opening: “We have to find it before sunset.” A customer's blue tunic had vanished without a trace. Livia picked up a single grain of flour directly beneath the line where the garment had hung.
card.life: Livia was born in Ostia and learned sewing from her mother. She worked at a cloth-washing shop while raising two children with Titus. She put off discussing wages even as the number of customers assigned to her coworker Aula grew, and when Aula began taking customers of her own, they divided and recorded their work. After her wrists began to hurt, Livia focused on mending, and after her husband died, she lived near her daughter.
card.turn: The blue tunic that had to be returned to a customer vanished from the shop. Livia had almost no time left to find it without taking work away from her coworker too.
card.decision: Livia left the remaining orders with her coworker and went to search the bakery across the street herself. She found that a tunic the apprentice had hastily set down had become mixed in with the bakery's cloth basket, and she cleaned it again.
card.cost: She returned the tunic on time, but stayed late to remove the flour, and she shared that day's wages with the coworker who finished the other orders in her place. She was also late for the dinner she had promised to attend at home.
card.after: Later, she put off discussing fair wages for Aula's extra labor, and when Aula began taking customers of her own, they divided and recorded the work assigned to each of them. After her wrists weakened, Livia focused on mending, and after her husband died, she stayed near her daughter.
card.presentEcho: When a day unexpectedly goes awry, sometimes the first thing that comes to mind is not the lost object, but the place where I will arrive late.
card.secondLook: The apprentice did not hide the tunic. He took it down from the drying rack and placed it on another pile of cloth, which became mixed up with the bakery basket. Livia did not check that basket at first either.
card.unresolved: Even after receiving the tunic, the customer did not praise it for looking like new. Her coworker's extra labor and the time her family spent waiting at home could not be erased.
card.readerQuestion: If something entrusted to me is missing as the promised time draws near, where would I search first?

signalMoments.notice: Livia saw flour beneath the place where the tunic had hung, along with the broad handle mark left by the bakery's cloth basket. Before deciding someone had stolen it, she chose to look at the shop across the street.
signalMoments.speak: When Livia asked Felix, “Where did you put the blue tunic last?” he answered that he had taken it down from the drying rack swaying in the wind and placed it on the basket by the door. Just then, someone from the bakery took that basket away.
signalMoments.explore: While searching through the laundry baskets again, Livia saw two wet marks left side by side outside the door. She followed the path taken by a missing empty basket toward the bakery.

identity.region: Ostia, Roman Empire

She argued with a coworker over how to divide their wages and spent many years helping her son Quintus, who had difficulty walking from birth, with his daily life. profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Livia Secunda · Female
AD 112–178 · 66 years old
Ostia, a port city of the Roman Empire
Work · Washing cloth and mending clothes
Life · She learned sewing from her mother. She worked while raising two children with Titus and argued with her coworker Aula over how to divide their wages. For many years, she helped her son Quintus, who had difficulty walking from birth. After her husband died, she moved with her son to live near her daughter Marcia. In her later years, the illness in her breast grew worse.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She tried to finish customers' work quickly, but delayed decisions when it came to determining her coworker's share.
Liked · The smell of cloth dried in the sun and neat patterns along the edges
Disliked · Calling someone a thief without even seeing what mistake they had made
Good at · Layering new thread over worn places so clothes could be worn longer

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The short needle her mother left her
Those closest to her · Her husband Titus, her daughter Marcia, her son Quintus, and her coworkers
The life she wanted · A home where there would still be work she could do with her own hands even when her wrists slowed, and where Quintus could speak his own mind
Worry · Who would help Quintus go out and bring him water and meals when she was ill
Later years · Marcia shared the work, but Livia never stopped making sure Quintus had the water and cloth he needed before he fell asleep.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Livia Secunda. In AD 147, you washed and mended cloth in Ostia, a port city of the Roman Empire. Let me tell you about one of the busiest afternoons of that life: the day a blue tunic disappeared from the laundry.

“Here, the ends of the sleeves are sewn with two rows of stitches. It must not be mixed up with another garment.” The customer, who said he was leaving the port, handed over the blue tunic. Livia spread out a sleeve and inspected the stitches. Two lines of blue thread ran where one would normally have been enough. It was an easy mark to remember. “I'll come back for it before sunset.”

That afternoon, the wind rushed through the doorway. The wet garments struck one another on the drying racks as if they were fighting. The apprentice Felix held up a rack that looked ready to topple, while Livia pulled cloth that had been washed underfoot out of a large vat. Someone from the bakery next door appeared at the entrance to collect flour-stained work cloths. Felix called, “Just a moment!” but the sound of water drowned him out.

The customer returned as the sun began to sink. Livia searched for the blue tunic, starting with the highest drying rack. It was not there. She went through the pile of dry cloth three times and even searched around the edges of the vats. The customer folded his arms. “It's part of the baggage I'm taking aboard the ship. Where is it?” Livia said, “I'll find it. Please wait just a little.” But she could not see so much as a scrap of cloth in the same color.

A few specks of white powder lay on the floor. Livia rubbed them between her fingertips. Unlike the white clay used in the shop, it was fine flour. But the fact that someone from the bakery had visited did not necessarily mean they had taken the blue tunic too. Felix was stacking empty baskets and could not even meet her eyes. The customer asked again, “Have you found it?”

signalMoments.notice: Livia saw a round mark from the bottom of a basket beside the powder. It was where the bakery's cloth basket had stood. “I know where to ask,” she told the customer as she looked across the street.
signalMoments.speak: Livia stopped Felix and asked, “Where did you put the blue tunic last?” Felix's face brightened, then went rigid. “I took it down because of the wind and put it on the basket by the door.” Someone from the bakery had already taken that basket.
signalMoments.explore: Livia lifted the empty baskets one by one and examined their bottoms. The trail of wet marks leading outside ended in front of the bakery door. A basket from another shop might have become mixed in with theirs.

episode.afterSignal:
Livia left the remaining two bundles of cloth with her coworker Aula. “Finish these for me. I'll share today's wages with you.” Aula raised an eyebrow. “Didn't you say you were having dinner at home?” Livia nodded and ran to the bakery. It was the evening she had promised Titus and their ten-year-old daughter Marcia that she would return early.

The bakery was filled with the warm smell of bread. The workers pulled a small basket out from between sacks of flour. Only worn work cloths lay on top. “There's nothing else.” The baker turned the basket around to show her. Livia saw a folded piece of blue cloth at the very bottom. Two lines of blue thread ran along the end of the sleeve. The tunic had not vanished. It was simply covered in flour among the bakery cloths.

“Who put this in here?” the baker asked. Felix, who had followed her, stood on the threshold. “I moved it. I thought the drying rack might fall. I didn't know it was the bakery's basket.” Livia checked the end of the sleeve. The thread was intact, but when she shook the tunic, white powder spread through the air like sunlight. “We haven't found a thief. We've found more work.” The baker tried to hold back a laugh, then sneezed.

Livia ran back to the shop. The customer stood at the entrance watching the setting sun. “I found it. But if I give it to you right now, you'll have to take the flour with you.” The customer frowned. “I don't remember ordering bread.” When Livia started to wet the tunic again, he raised a hand. “If you do that, I can't wait for it to dry.” Livia shook out the tunic and brushed the sleeves and collar with a dry brush. She wrapped cloth around the point of a needle to remove the flour from the narrow folds.

When she finished cleaning the last hem, the customer put on the tunic. He dusted off the shoulders and said, “It's a blue tunic, but it smells like bread.” Livia apologized. The customer paid and left, but he did not praise it for looking like new. In the meantime, Aula had finished another customer's cloth as well. As promised, Livia gave her part of her wages. Felix tied a small marker to the basket. He said that starting tomorrow, he would ask who owned a basket before putting cloth on it.

By the time Livia reached home, Titus and Marcia had finished eating. Marcia held out half a piece of cold bread. “This is yours, Mother. Were you working at the bakery?” Livia laughed, then looked at the flour still on her hands. “I was late because I was looking for a bakery tunic.” Her daughter asked what that meant, so this time Livia told the story from beginning to end. Unexpectedly, the cold bread tasted delicious.

After that, Livia continued working at the laundry while raising two children. A few years later, although the number of customers assigned to Aula grew, Livia put off deciding how to divide their wages. Only after Aula began taking customers of her own did Livia start counting the work each of them handled. Her son Quintus, born in 155, could not stand on both legs for long, but he learned language and arithmetic and chose fabric patterns for himself. Livia and Titus arranged a low place for him in the house and helped him when he went out. As Livia's wrists weakened, she mended clothes instead of handling heavy cloth. After Titus died, Livia mainly helped Quintus with meals and outings, while Marcia, who lived separately, regularly shared the work. In 175, as the illness in Livia's breast grew worse, she moved with Quintus to live near Marcia. For many years, Marcia called the day her mother came home late “the day of the tunic that smelled like bread,” but she also remembered the years afterward when the two of them helped each other.

memories.label: Her Most Treasured Possession
memories.detail: The short needle her mother used. Its length was familiar to her fingertips, so she kept it for many years.

memories.label: Her Favorite Time
memories.detail: Evenings when, after finishing work, she could eat cold bread without rushing

memories.label: The Work She Kept Doing
memories.detail: Mending clothes and returning them to customers even after her wrists weakened

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Turn the garment inside out. The places you can't see from the outside wear out first.”

memories.label: Marcia's Memory
memories.detail: “Mother worked quickly, but she always asked first what Quintus wanted to wear and where he wanted to go. After she became ill, there were more days when I brought the water.”

memories.label: Quintus's Choice
memories.detail: “It's true that Mother helped me when I went out. But I chose the patterns and the replies to send to customers.”

memories.label: Aula's Assessment
memories.detail: “Even when the number of customers I handled in her place increased, she put off talking about wages. Only when I said I would take customers of my own did she finally count the work each of us did.”

memories.label: Titus's Memory
memories.detail: “Even on days when work ended late, she came home and listened to the children's stories all the way to the end.”

finalMoment.place: Livia's room near Marcia's house in Ostia, Roman Empire
finalMoment.scene:
It is late at night in Ostia in AD 178. Sixty-six-year-old Livia is with her son Quintus in a small room near her daughter Marcia's house. Quintus is twenty-three. Since birth, he has had difficulty standing on his legs for long, and he works seated at a low place, choosing fabric patterns. Livia has been ill for months since the lump in her breast grew, and for the past few days, even crossing the room has left her short of breath.

From his place, Quintus folds the fabric samples he will show a customer tomorrow. “I want the blue stripes on this side.” Livia moves closer and looks at the side he chose. “All right. You choose.” She places a bowl of water within his reach and sets the cloth he uses at night beside him. It is their usual routine, but today, after setting down the bowl, she braces her hand against the wall for a long time. Quintus asks, “Mother, should I call my sister again?” Livia catches her breath and answers, “She can come in the morning.”

Quintus clears a place for Livia to sit. She sits on the low bed beside her son and rests for a while, then watches him lie down. Quintus checks, “The water is here, right?” When Livia points to the bowl, he reaches out on his own to make sure where it is. “All right. You should rest now too, Mother.” The footsteps in the alley outside grow quiet. Quintus's breathing becomes steady, and he falls asleep.

Livia lies down in her own place. The pain deep inside her breast worsens whenever she moves. She tries to turn to look toward her sleeping son, but she cannot draw a deep breath. She pulls the cloth behind her to adjust her position and takes one more breath. The bowl of water is close to her son's hand, and Marcia lives just beyond this alley. Livia closes her eyes. The next breath does not come. Quintus does not wake.
finalMoment.afterword: Livia died at sixty-six from advanced breast cancer in her room in Ostia in AD 178. Her son Quintus was asleep beside her. In the morning, Quintus first reached for the water his mother had left, and when she did not answer, he called the neighbors and Marcia. After that, Marcia helped Quintus with his outings, but let her brother choose the patterns and the order of his work. Her coworker Aula also remembered how long Livia had put off discussing wages. The record of this past life closes by preserving together the hands with which Livia cared for her son for many years, her effort not to decide his wishes for him, and the time when she received help from her family after she became ill.
finalMoment.artAlt: Seen through the crack of a door is a small room in Ostia in the Roman Empire in AD 178. Ill, 66-year-old Livia lies with her eyes closed on a low bed, while her 23-year-old son Quintus sleeps on a mat beside her with a bowl of water within reach. No other people or props from the blue tunic incident are present.

card.name: Umar Ba
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Umar Ba of Timbuktu. You copied books and raised a family, but often put off the household records, so your wife and daughter took charge of them themselves. In old age, you handed long copying jobs over to an apprentice.
card.title: Four Sheets of Paper
card.world: The book market of Timbuktu in the Songhai Empire, 1554
card.flavor: The night before a friend left
card.opening: “I want you to write down the story of that day.” Idris made the request of Umar the day before leaving for Gao. Umar stopped his pen. He also had to finish a customer’s book by dawn.
card.life: Umar was born in Timbuktu in 1508. He learned his letters beside his father and learned manuscript copying from his uncle. He raised two children with Saliha, but often put off recording the household grain expenses, so Saliha and their daughter Amina made a separate ledger. His daughter chose weaving, and after Umar’s hands began to tremble, he turned long copying jobs over to his apprentices.
card.turn: Before leaving for Gao the next day, Umar’s old friend Idris asked him to write in his own hand the story of the time they had lost their way together. Umar also had to finish a copy promised to a customer that same night.
card.decision: Umar set aside the customer’s copy and wrote four pages about getting lost with his friend in their youth. The next day, he personally told the customer that he had not finished it.
card.cost: The customer reduced part of the payment because Umar had broken his promise. His friend left at dawn, and they did not decide when they would meet again. Umar had no time to revise the four pages he had written.
card.after: Because Umar repeatedly put off recording the household grain expenses, Saliha made a ledger with their daughter instead. After his hands began to tremble, Umar reviewed his apprentices’ writing instead of taking on long copying jobs, and his daughter Amina chose weaving.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes my awkward words, given before someone leaves, remain longer than words polished to perfection.
card.secondLook: What Idris wanted was not a book that would sell well. He wanted Umar to write down, in his own hand, the youth they both remembered. The customer’s decision to reduce the payment also remains a justified grievance.
card.unresolved: No one knows how long his friend kept those four pages in Gao. Nor is there any record of whether Umar’s customer hired him again.
card.readerQuestion: If I had to share words I had put off for a long time today, how would I begin?

signalMoments.notice: Umar saw Idris’s bundled luggage by the door. He had already packed everything for Gao. Umar gave up the excuse that there was still plenty of night left and brought four blank sheets of paper to the front of his desk.
signalMoments.speak: Umar asked, “Which exact moment do you want to hear about?” Idris described the look on Umar’s face when he had insisted they were going the right way at the house where they asked for directions. Umar thought of the first line.
signalMoments.connect: Umar asked Saliha whether she remembered the story of how they had lost their way that year. Saliha laughed and said that when they came home, each had blamed the other. Umar was amused that his friend’s memory differed from his own.

identity.region: Timbuktu, Songhai Empire
identity.summary: He learned to write from a grain ledger, made a living copying manuscripts, and raised a family. He put off the household grain records until Saliha took charge of them herself, and after his hands began to tremble, he watched his children and apprentices follow different paths.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The old grain ledger his father had used
Those closest to him · His wife Saliha, daughter Amina, son Hasan, and friend Idris

Worry · That if his hands trembled more, he would not be able to teach his apprentices properly

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Umar Ba. You lived in Timbuktu in the Songhai Empire in 1554, copying books by hand. Let me tell you about the night in that long life when you wrote four new pages. The hand that had spent a lifetime copying other people’s words could hardly move that day.

“I can finish through this line today.” Umar lifted his hand and caught his breath so the wet letters would not smear across the paper. He had promised to deliver a copy to a customer who bought books at the market by the next morning. Only the last two pages remained. Even the warm grain porridge his wife Saliha had brought was growing cold beside his pen.

His friend Idris knocked on the door. A man who usually began with a joke stood there that day holding his luggage. “I’m leaving at dawn tomorrow to help my brother with his work in Gao.” Umar put down his reed pen. “Already? Last month you said next month.” “Next month is here.”

Idris took out a folded sheet of paper. In clumsy handwriting, it read, ‘The Day Umar Got Lost.’ Umar laughed. “You were the one who got lost.” “Then correct it in your handwriting. I want you to write down the story of that day.” Idris placed the paper at the edge of the table. When they were young, the two had been running a book errand at the market when they went around two similar-looking alleys twice, entered the wrong house, and were even given water to drink.

Umar held up a blank page. With a customer’s text, he knew where to stop and where to begin. But with his friend’s story, he was stuck from the very first line. “This isn’t the kind of thing you put in a book.” Idris shook his head. “I want to take something you wrote. The market is full of well-written books.”

The two sat together until the lamp flame grew weak. Umar said, “I can give it to you tomorrow morning,” and Idris pointed to the luggage by the door. “You’ll have to deliver the customer’s book then. And I’ll be gone.” Umar looked back and forth between the long commissioned copy and the four blank sheets of paper on his desk.

signalMoments.notice: Umar gazed at Idris’s bundled luggage by the door. A pair of shoes comfortable for walking was tied on top. He was fully prepared to leave. Umar pulled four blank sheets of paper toward himself.
signalMoments.speak: Umar asked, “Which exact moment do you want to hear about?” Idris laughed. “The look on your face at the house where we got water, when you insisted to the owner, ‘This is the right way.’” Umar thought of the first line.
signalMoments.connect: Umar asked Saliha, “Do you remember the story of how we got lost that year?” Saliha burst out laughing. “When you came home, each of you blamed the other.” Umar found it amusing that the road his friend remembered differed from the one he remembered.

episode.afterSignal:
Umar closed the customer’s manuscript. The first line took a long time. ‘That day, we passed down the same road twice and insisted we had never seen it before.’ Idris looked at the words and pointed to ‘we’ with his finger. “Both of us got lost? At last, you’re writing the truth.” Umar dipped the tip of his pen again.

On one page, he wrote about the low threshold of the house where they had been given water. On the next, he wrote about how they had pointed in opposite directions even on their way back. He left out the names of alleys he could not remember clearly. Whenever Idris added his own memory, they argued briefly and then laughed. Saliha left the cold porridge beside them without warming it again. The night grew short.

The sentence Umar wrote on the last page was not long. ‘We will be wrong again. Even so, let us ask the way together next time.’ Idris read the line aloud. “What about a road without me?” Umar rolled the pen between his fingers for a moment. “Then you ask first.” Idris stacked the four pages and placed them inside a leather cover. He did not sew them together. The two parted at the door at dawn without deciding when they would meet again.

Soon the customer who had placed the order arrived. Umar showed him the last two pages of the copy he had left unfinished during the night. “I did not finish it by the morning I promised. I can give you the rest this afternoon.” The customer flipped through the empty space, and his expression hardened. “Then I cannot pay you the full amount I promised.” Umar counted the reduced payment. After paying for that day’s paper and ink, little remained. He could not revise the four pages he had given Idris, either.

After the customer left, Saliha asked, “Do you regret it?” Umar held up Idris’s crooked first page, which still lay on the table. It was the draft Idris had thrown away before leaving. “It says here that I was the one who got lost.” Saliha laughed. “That part is true.” Umar laughed too. He finished the customer’s final two pages that afternoon.

Umar continued copying books in Timbuktu afterward. When Saliha asked him to record the household grain expenses, he put it off again and again, saying that he would finish his customers’ copies first. Saliha made a separate ledger with their daughter Amina and never entrusted the records to Umar again. Amina chose weaving. When Umar’s hands began to tremble, he took on fewer long copying jobs and reviewed his apprentices’ writing instead. He never learned how far Idris read through those four pages in Gao.

finalMoment.place: A market road in Timbuktu and Umar’s home
finalMoment.scene:
One morning in Timbuktu at the beginning of the 1581 dry season, I walk along the market road to visit a distant relative’s home. Saliha told me to return before evening. I stop in every patch of shade to catch my breath. Up ahead, a laden camel moves into the crowd. Its handler pulls on the rope, but the camel turns sideways. I take one step toward the wall.

A cargo sack strikes my chest hard. I fall to the ground and try to breathe in, but I cannot. The handler backs the camel away, and a merchant nearby asks my name. “Tell my family.” I barely get the words out. I try to stand, but a stabbing pain inside my chest makes me sink back down. I cannot go to my relative’s home.

Saliha and Hasan take me home. On the second day, one side of my chest hurts more, and I cannot breathe deeply. Amina brings water. I ask my daughter whether she has set aside her weaving to come today. “Just for today.” Amina places the bowl close to me. I swallow one sip. Saliha calls my name. I breathe in to answer, but the injured side of my chest does not move. The last thing I see is Hasan receiving the water bowl by the door.
finalMoment.afterword: Umar died in 1581, two days after colliding with a laden camel on a market road in Timbuktu and injuring his ribs and lung. The handler who witnessed the accident stopped the camel and sent word to his family. Saliha remembered how her husband wrote customers’ words quickly while putting off the household grain records. Amina recalled how, on the day she chose weaving, her father first asked about the length of the thread. The record of Umar’s past life does not choose only the good memories at his end. It also preserves the recordkeeping that Saliha and Amina had to take on.
finalMoment.artAlt: A rooftop view of a market road in Timbuktu in 1581. At the moment before impact, 73-year-old Umar turns toward a wall to avoid a laden camel.

card.name: Ono Genzo
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Ono Genzo of Osaka. You worked puppets while raising two children, and at your wife Yuki's tea shop, you put your fellow performers first until you came to follow the rules Yuki set.
card.title: The Day the Puppet Knelt
card.world: A ningyo joruri stage in Osaka under the Edo shogunate in 1760
card.flavor: The Left Arm That Came Loose on Stage
card.opening: At the moment the merchant puppet was supposed to raise the debt document, its left arm went limp. As the audience stirred, Genzo could not make the puppet retreat even a single step.
card.life: Genzo entered a puppet theater after helping his father repair wooden chests, progressing from the feet to the arms before becoming the lead puppeteer. He raised two children with Yuki, but they quarreled when he brought fellow performers to her tea shop and let them take up the seats. After his wrists weakened, he helped at the shop according to Yuki's rules while teaching younger puppeteers. At 72, he rescued his mother from a fire but died from smoke inhalation.
card.turn: During a performance, the control rod for the left arm came loose, and the document fell to the floor. Genzo was controlling the puppet's head and right arm, while the narrator and musician waited for the next line.
card.decision: Genzo signaled with his eyes to the puppeteer controlling the feet, making the puppet kneel. He used the right hand to pick up the fallen document, while the puppeteer controlling the left arm held the limp arm so it would not snag again.
card.cost: The scene ended, but the loose rod tore the sleeve. Before the next performance, the three puppeteers had to split the repair cost from their wages and rehearse the movements again. Some audience members noticed the moment of hesitation.
card.after: When Yuki opened a tea shop, Genzo brought fellow performers there and let them occupy the customers' seats. They quarreled when Yuki established an ordering rule, but she did not change it. After his wrists began to hurt, Genzo taught younger puppeteers and helped at the shop in the way Yuki had set.
card.presentEcho: When someone you work with falls a beat behind, one person's small gesture can change everyone's next move.
card.secondLook: The kneeling onstage was not a scene Genzo created alone. It came from Ryo on the feet, Saburo on the left arm, the narrator, and the shamisen player each matching the others for a single beat.
card.unresolved: Not everyone in the audience saw that day's movement as clever staging. The torn sleeve and dislodged rod also had to be repaired by real hands after the performance.
card.readerQuestion: When something we are doing together suddenly goes wrong, who will I signal first?

signalMoments.notice: Genzo saw the wooden rod beneath the puppet's left sleeve swinging lower than usual. He gave Saburo a quick glance to tell him not to force the arm up.
signalMoments.connect: Genzo met the eyes of Ryo, the puppeteer crouched low to control the feet. When Ryo gave a small nod, Genzo prepared to shift the puppet's weight forward.
signalMoments.protect: Genzo turned the puppet's body slightly inward to keep the limp left arm from catching on the stage screen. That gave Saburo time to support the arm.

identity.region: Near Dotonbori, Osaka, under the Edo shogunate
identity.summary: He grew up in a wooden-chest repair shop and became the lead puppeteer after progressing from the puppet's feet to its arms. He also disrupted business by bringing his fellow performers to his wife's tea shop. After his wrists weakened, he taught younger puppeteers. At 72, he rescued his mother from a fire but died from smoke inhalation.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Ono Genzo. In 1760, you performed on a ningyo joruri stage in Osaka, then ruled by the Edo shogunate. One person moved the puppet's head and right arm, another its left arm, and a third its feet. Now I will tell you about the evening when the breathing of those three fell out of step for a moment.

Backstage at a small theater near Dotonbori, Genzo dipped the puppet's head once. The right arm moved naturally in his hand. Saburo tested the left arm, while Ryo, the youngest, crouched down and slipped his feet into position. Today's scene showed a merchant presenting a document when he came to repay a debt. Genzo's fourteen-year-old daughter, Haru, had come to watch. She had hurried over after eating the dinner Yuki had prepared.

The narrator told the tale as if singing, and the shamisen supported him between lines. Above the stage screen, the merchant puppet walked out. As Ryo pushed its two feet forward, Genzo straightened the body, and Saburo brought the left hand out from inside its robe. Without speaking, the three counted the same beat. Someone in the front row moved their head along with the puppet.

On the next line, the puppet was supposed to raise the debt document in its left hand. Saburo pulled the rod that moved the hand. A small wooden joint came loose, and the left arm dropped. The document also slipped onto the stage floor. It looked as though the puppet had lost the document. A sound came from the audience that might have been laughter or surprise.

Saburo reached inside to fit the rod back in. But he could not bend the puppet's arm backward in front of everyone. When Genzo froze the scene while holding the head, the narrator's next words were delayed as well. A shamisen string sounded briefly and stopped. Should they halt the performance and repair it? Or make the other hand pick up the fallen document? Genzo did not have long to think.

signalMoments.notice: Genzo saw the end of the wooden rod protruding beneath the sleeve. Pulling it any farther would tear the cloth. He glanced at Saburo to tell him not to force the arm up and held the puppet's body straight.
signalMoments.connect: Genzo turned his eyes toward Ryo, crouched low. Ryo nodded and eased some of the strength in both feet. Receiving that signal, Genzo was able to tilt the puppet forward.
signalMoments.protect: When Genzo saw that the puppet's limp arm was about to catch on the edge of the screen, he turned its torso inward. In that brief opening, Saburo supported the arm to keep it from tearing farther.

episode.afterSignal:
Genzo lowered the puppet's head ever so slightly. Ryo bent both legs and made the puppet kneel. Saburo supported the broken left arm so it would not bend backward. Genzo lowered the right hand, which he controlled, toward the floor. The fingertips touched the document once, then slipped off. This time, clear laughter came from the audience. It looked as though the puppet was searching for the document because he regretted his mistake.

Genzo lowered the hand again. The edge of the document caught in the right hand. Only then did the narrator draw out his next words. The shamisen followed in a low voice. Still kneeling, the puppet held out the document. It was not the scene they had rehearsed. But at least it showed how deeply the merchant in the story wanted to repay his debt.

After finishing the scene and retreating behind the screen, Saburo lifted the puppet's left sleeve. The loose rod had torn the lining a little. “We could have stopped back there,” he said. Genzo nodded. “Then the audience would have waited too.” Ryo still could not straighten the back he had kept bent. “If you ask me to kneel one more time, I can't do it.” Only then did all three laugh together.

The theater manager told them to repair the sleeve and rod before the next performance. The three each contributed a little from that day's wages to buy materials. Sewing up the torn cloth was easy, but matching their breathing again in the same scene the next day took separate practice. Some people said they liked the kneeling scene that day, while others said something about it had seemed strange.

When Genzo returned home, Haru was waiting at the door. “Father, why did that merchant suddenly kneel?” Genzo hesitated, wondering whether to tell her about the stage malfunction. “His left arm wouldn't listen.” Haru let her own arm hang like a puppet's and imitated it. “But he still picked up the document.” Pouring tea, Yuki asked, “None of you three hurt your hands today, did you?” Genzo told her their wages had been reduced and unfolded the torn sleeve to show her. The next morning, instead of going to the theater, he first had to find a place that could repair it.

Genzo continued to perform on Osaka's stages after that. When Yuki opened a tea shop, Genzo often brought his fellow performers and let them sit there for a long time. When other customers turned away because his companions did not buy tea, Yuki made a rule that they had to order at least one cup instead of paying for their seats. Genzo objected in front of everyone, and the two argued about it for some time. Yuki did not change the rule. After his wrists began to hurt, Genzo cut back on long performances and taught young puppeteers. Only then did he also take on the work of carrying teacups according to the way Yuki had set. Their son Shota chose to repair boats, and Yuki's shop remained Yuki's shop to the very end.

finalMoment.place: Shino's house and Yuki's tea shop in Osaka under the Edo shogunate
finalMoment.scene:
One afternoon in early autumn of 1794, seventy-two-year-old Genzo smells smoke in an Osaka alley. Fire has caught on the eaves beside his mother Shino's small house. Shino is ninety-three, and she walks slowly. His younger sister, who usually takes care of her meals and firewood, has gone to the end of the alley to fetch water. Genzo approaches the open door of Shino's house. From inside, his mother calls his name.

Genzo holds a wet cloth from the well over his mouth and goes through the door. Even though it is daytime, the room is dim. Shino is standing with one hand against the wall. “Mother, take my hand.” When Genzo reaches out, Shino takes it. The two walk slowly toward the door. A burning sound comes from the roof, and Genzo coughs. When Shino stops, Genzo puts her arm over his shoulder, and they begin moving again, one step at a time.

Outside the door, his younger sister returns and takes Shino's other hand. Genzo sees his mother breathe in the alley air and stand on her own feet. “Let's go to the shop.” He points to Yuki's tea shop. But after only a few steps, his head begins to spin. He sits on a low stool in front of the shop. Yuki brings water, and Genzo tries to take a sip but sets down the cup because he is coughing.

As the sun sinks, his breaths grow shorter. Yuki sits beside Genzo, and Haru opens the door to let in the breeze. Shino is sitting outside with his younger sister. “What about Mother?” Genzo asks. Yuki replies, “She's outside. She's alive.” Genzo tries to nod but coughs again. He braces a hand on the edge of the stool and tries to draw a deeper breath, but his chest does not move. When Yuki calls his name, Genzo's hand slips from the stool.
finalMoment.afterword: Genzo's breathing worsened because of the smoke he inhaled during a fire in Osaka in 1794, and he died that evening at Yuki's tea shop. Shino made it outside and survived. Shino remembered her son taking her hand at the door, while his younger sister recalled all the time she had spent caring for their mother's meals and firewood before that day. Yuki remembered both the day Genzo tried to give the shop's seats to his fellow performers and the final day when he sat on a stool at her shop. Haru and Shota spoke differently about their father's performances. The record of his past life tells of the times Genzo waited for his fellow performers' breathing onstage, the times he was slow to listen to Yuki at home, and the final day when he led his mother out of a burning house, carrying the story through to the end of his life.
finalMoment.artAlt: A distant side view of the doorway of a small house in an Osaka alley in 1794. Amid the smoke, 72-year-old Genzo walks out through the door holding the hand of his 93-year-old mother, Shino. His mother is standing and walking out on her own feet, while another figure remains far away. There is no three-person composition of supporting someone or running for help

card.name: Amina binti Rashid
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Amina binti Rashid of Kilwa Kisiwani. You ran a bead shop and held on to your own ledgers for years, even after your daughter began trading independently.
card.title: The Twelfth Strand Broke
card.role: Merchant who strung and sold beads
card.world: An Indian Ocean port in the Kilwa Sultanate in 1481
card.flavor: A stone causeway at rising tide
card.opening: The last of twelve strands of beads meant to be loaded onto a ship broke. The merchant wanted to cut the price in half, and the rising tide was reaching the end of the stone causeway.
card.life: Amina was born in Kilwa in 1440 and learned to trade from her mother. She raised two children with Yusuf while running a bead shop. Even after her daughter Samira began trading independently, Amina held on to her own ledgers for years. Only when her eyes began to tire did she ask Samira to keep the records for her mother's shop. Samira's own business remained separate.
card.turn: One of the twelve strands in an order bound for a ship had broken. The merchant said he would pay only half the total price. The ship might leave while they unpacked everything to find the cause.
card.decision: Amina laid out and inspected all twelve strands. She pointed out the mark where the lid had pressed down on the broken strand and offered him the eleven intact strands at their agreed price.
card.cost: The merchant said he needed to load all twelve strands together, so he boarded the ship without buying them. Amina lost that day's sale and her time, and she had to restring the broken strand.
card.after: Samira argued over the cost of missing the ship, and Amina admitted that she had also held firm because she could not bear to lose the full price. Samira later began her own business, but when her mother's eyes began to tire, she cut back on time with her own customers to help keep the records for her mother's shop as well.
card.presentEcho: When a transaction is urgent, you may feel both the need to check everything with your own hands and the fear that the opportunity will slip away while you do.
card.secondLook: There was no proof that the merchant had deliberately broken the strand. No one knew who had set the heavy lid on top, and they could not determine on the spot whether Amina's knot had been weak.
card.unresolved: They still did not know how much the eleven intact strands would sell for later. Samira never fully agreed with her mother's decision that cost them the sale.
card.readerQuestion: When time is short, what will I check for myself, and what will I let go?

Amina binti Rashid · Female
1440–1500 · Age 60
Kilwa Kisiwani, Kilwa Sultanate, 1481
Work · She strung and sold strands of glass and carnelian beads.
Life · She learned to trade at her mother's side and built a workplace of her own. She raised two children with Yusuf and held on to her own ledgers for years, even after her daughter Samira became independent. When her eyes began to tire, she asked Samira to keep the records for her shop.

profilePages.body:

Liked · The sound of footsteps on the stone causeway after low tide
Disliked · Setting a price before the goods had even been counted
Skilled at · Stringing tiny beads and remembering the colors her customers chose

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The old bead basket her mother had used
Those closest to her · Her husband Yusuf, her daughter Samira, and her son Hamid

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Amina binti Rashid. In 1481, you strung and sold beads in Kilwa Kisiwani, an island city in the Kilwa Sultanate. Today, I will tell you about the afternoon when you were to load twelve strands of beads onto a ship before the sea returned over the stone causeway.

“Twelve. We have them all this time, right?” Her daughter Samira peered into the basket. Amina counted the strands with her finger, one by one. Twelve necklaces with alternating red carnelian and blue glass beads. The merchant Bashir was to load them onto a ship and take them to another port. Yusuf remained at home because his injured arm kept him from carrying heavy loads. Amina and nineteen-year-old Samira walked out to the harbor along the low stone causeway.

The ship waited beyond the shallows. The rising tide was slowly creeping over the edge of the causeway. Bashir stood where he was to receive the goods and picked up one strand. Several beads bounced across the ground. The thread of the last strand had broken. “What if all twelve are like this?” he asked, rolling the beads in his palm. “I will pay only half.”

Samira quickly held up another strand. “This one is fine.” Bashir shook his head. “The ship is waiting. I do not have time to inspect them one by one.” Amina opened her mouth, then closed it. If she accepted even half price, they would not have to return empty-handed that evening. But if she let all eleven good strands go for next to nothing, the days they had spent stringing them at home would be wasted.

Amina saw that the thread beneath the broken strand had been flattened. She also noticed the rough edge of the wooden crate lid resting atop the basket. She could not be sure whether they had set the lid there while moving the goods or one of Bashir's porters had done it. At the end of the causeway, a sailor waved. Amina looked from Bashir's face to the rest of the packaging, which appeared undamaged.

signalMoments.notice: Amina showed Bashir the pressed place on the broken thread. “It does not look like a knot coming loose, but I do not know who pressed down on it.” She removed the lid and unpacked the other strands to check whether they had been pressed in the same place.
signalMoments.speak: Amina spoke loudly enough for the sailor on the causeway to hear. “If you cannot wait, you may leave. But do not call eleven strands you have not even examined worth half price.” Then she took them out one by one and arranged them neatly on the stone.
signalMoments.connect: Amina handed half the package to Samira. “Check the six strands on the right. I might miss something.” Mother and daughter each tugged the threads, then confirmed together that eleven strands were intact.

episode.afterSignal:
The eleven strands were unbroken. Amina tugged one of them to demonstrate. The thread of the last, broken strand had been flattened where it had touched the rough edge of the lid. “I am not trying to argue about who put it there. I will deduct the cost of restringing one strand. Please buy the other eleven at the price we agreed on.”

Bashir looked back at the sea. Someone aboard the ship was pulling in a rope. “I need twelve strands. With eleven, I cannot fill the order at the other port.” Bashir put the few loose beads back into Amina's basket. “I cannot wait for the next ship.” When he started toward the ship, Samira tried to call him back. Amina did not grab her daughter's arm.

“We should have taken half price,” Samira said. “Now we have to carry everything home because of one strand.” Amina picked up the remaining beads. Seawater filled the grooves in the causeway, wetting her fingertips. “I know. Part of me held firm because I could not bear to lose the full price.” Samira fell silent for a moment. Amina did not search for another reason that would prove she had been right.

The two divided the baskets between them and returned home. Yusuf opened the lid with one hand and found the broken thread. “This can be restrung.” Samira replied, “But we cannot catch the ship again.” Yusuf's eyes moved from one of them to the other. Amina was the one who could not put the proceeds from the goods on the dinner table. The eleven strands would remain at home until she found another customer.

Amina continued selling beads in Kilwa. Beginning in 1485, Samira met with customers of her own, while Hamid learned ship repair from his father. Even after her daughter's business began, Amina held on to the ledgers for her own shop for years. In 1492, when her eyes began to tire easily, she asked Samira to keep the records for her mother's shop. Samira helped without mixing them with her own business ledgers, and as a result had less time to meet her own customers. Amina remained on the island after Yusuf died. Samira remembered both the ship they had missed and how late her mother had handed the ledgers over to her.

finalMoment.place: Amina's home in Kilwa Kisiwani
finalMoment.scene:
Kilwa Kisiwani, 1500. After meeting a distant relative, I am resting at home. My body began to feel chilled yesterday, and by morning my head aches and my fever is rising. Across the courtyard, my daughter Samira calls, “Mother, I brought water.” I say I will get up, but when I lower my feet, my legs have no strength. Samira brings the water into the room.

Hamid goes out to find someone who can examine me. After I ask several times when my son left, Samira says it was only a little while ago. My daughter has put off her own business to sit here. “What about your customers?” I ask. Samira says, “Someone else will go today.” I mean to say I am sorry, but my mouth is dry, so first I take a sip of water.

Even after the sun goes down, my body shivers, and I pull up the blanket. Samira lays another cloth over me. I recognize my daughter's face, but it is difficult to keep my eyes open for long. Hamid returns and sits by the doorway. I turn my head slightly, trying to look at them one after the other. The pauses between my breaths grow longer. Samira calls, “Mother.” I try to open my eyes to answer, but my eyelids will not rise.
finalMoment.afterword: Amina died at her home in Kilwa Kisiwani in 1500 from a rapidly worsening fever. The pathogen that caused it is unknown. Samira entrusted her business to someone else that day so she could remain by her mother's side. She remembered the days when helping with her mother's ledgers had cost her time with her own customers. Hamid thought back to the time he had spent at home talking about ship repairs with his father, Yusuf. In this family, trade and caregiving never carried the same cost for everyone. The Record of Past Lives also records the time Samira gave up.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view across a courtyard in Kilwa Kisiwani in 1500. Amina, weakened by fever at age 60, sits in the shade of a doorway while her daughter Samira holds water.

card.name: Lucius Faustus
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Lucius Faustus, who lived in Pompeii in Campania, Roman Empire, working as the bookkeeper of a laundry and dyeing workshop. He kept the accounts at a laundry in Pompeii. Trying to reduce losses, he delayed the worker Tiro's wages, and on the day the volcano erupted, he tried to repay that debt.
card.title: Wages Before the Ash Fell
card.role: Bookkeeper of a laundry and dyeing workshop
card.world: AD 79 · Pompeii in Campania, Roman Empire
card.flavor: Delayed wages at a workshop beneath Mount Vesuvius
card.opening: In the summer of AD 79, Lucius recalculated the wages he had withheld as gray dust fell into the courtyard.
card.life: He kept the accounts at a laundry in Pompeii. Trying to reduce losses, he delayed the worker Tiro's wages, and on the day the volcano erupted, he tried to repay that debt. He withheld part of Tiro's wages because of the cost of ruined cloth. Tiro's household had less grain to buy that week.
card.turn: His desire to finish calculating the wages collided with the need to flee at once.
card.decision: Lucius stopped calculating and handed over the wages he had withheld.
card.cost: He withheld part of Tiro's wages because of the cost of ruined cloth. Tiro's household had less grain to buy that week.
card.after: Tiro went to his family, while Lucius and Julia failed to escape the city.
card.presentEcho: Some debts must be repaid before the calculations are perfect.
card.secondLook: The final payment did not erase the earlier delay.
card.unresolved: There is no record of whether Tiro escaped the city.
card.readerQuestion: Ash had begun to fall when you were asked for wages you had delayed. What would you do first?
