episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Lucius, the bookkeeper of a laundry and dyeing workshop in Pompeii.

While rinsing a customer's cloak, the worker Tiro caused the red dye to bleed. Lucius withheld part of Tiro's wages until he could determine the compensation owed.

Several days later, the ground shook again, and a huge cloud rose above Mount Vesuvius. Light pumice began to fall in the streets. Tiro asked for his wages, saying he had to leave the city with his family.

signalMoments.notice: Before looking at the ledger, Lucius noticed the pumice piling up on the courtyard floor and the roof trembling.
signalMoments.speak: “Take the money I withheld, too. I'll balance the ledger later.” Lucius spoke loudly enough for Tiro and Sabina to hear.
signalMoments.release: Lucius abandoned his calculation of compensation for the ruined cloak and handed the purse to Tiro.

episode.afterSignal:
Tiro took the money and ran to find his family. Sabina asked the people in the workshop whether they should head toward the harbor or the city gate.

Lucius headed home to fetch his wife Julia. Pumice had piled up to his ankles, making even the familiar streets slow to cross.

The two tried to leave the city, but the darkened streets and collapsed roofs kept them from reaching the southern gate. They decided to wait out the night in a nearby storeroom.

finalMoment.place: A storeroom near Pompeii's southern gate
finalMoment.scene:
On the morning of the second day of the eruption in AD 79, Lucius and his wife Julia crouched in a storeroom near Pompeii's southern gate. Pumice had piled up on the roof throughout the night. Lucius covered Julia's mouth with a wet cloth and opened the door a crack.

Though it was daytime, it was dark outside. The two tried to step through the doorway, but hot ash and powdered stone surged into the alley. “Get back.” Lucius pushed Julia toward the inner wall. Soon the door shook, and their throats burned with every breath.

Lucius lay flat on the floor and reached for Julia's hand. The air in the room suddenly grew hot, and all sight vanished. He squeezed her hand once more, but soon he could no longer move.
finalMoment.afterword: Lucius and Julia died amid the heat and ash of the pyroclastic flow that engulfed Pompeii. It is unknown whether Tiro, after receiving his wages, escaped the city alive. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79 and the burial of Pompeii are historical facts; the three characters and the workshop incident are fictional.
finalMoment.artAlt: At the doorway of a dark Pompeii storeroom in AD 79, ash surges through the street as Lucius reaches for his wife's hand

card.name: Margaret Hall
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Margaret Hall of Christchurch. You raised your daughter through sewing and opened a dressmaking workshop, then ran it with Annie, though the two of you clashed over order deadlines.
card.title: A Different Ballot
card.world: Christchurch, New Zealand, on the day of the first general election in which women voted in 1893
card.flavor: A day between the workshop and the polling station
card.opening: “If I go, who will finish the walking dress?” Annie had returned from the polling station. One hour remained until the promised noon deadline. Margaret drew out her needle and looked at the line outside the door.
card.life: Margaret was born in Christchurch in 1851 and learned sewing from her mother. After her husband died, she raised her daughter Clara and opened a workshop. Even after she began running it jointly with Annie, Margaret accepted late orders without consulting her, so Annie refused evening work and began taking her own orders separately. After Margaret’s fingers grew painful, she left the workshop in Annie’s care and moved to be near her daughter.
card.turn: On the day of the first general election in which women voted, they had to finish a customer’s walking dress by noon. Annie came back because the voting line was so long, and Margaret could hardly keep the promise alone.
card.decision: Margaret, who had cast her ballot early that morning, sent Annie back to the polling station. She decided to finish the walking dress by herself.
card.cost: In front of the customer, Margaret discovered that an inside button was missing and took the dress back to repair it. Because she delivered it after noon, she was not paid part of her fee.
card.after: Annie returned after casting her ballot. The two had chosen different candidates, but they worked together again the next day. Later, even after they began running the workshop together, Margaret accepted late orders without consulting Annie, so Annie refused evening work and took her own orders separately.
card.presentEcho: Leaving room for someone you work with to feel differently from you is also a difficult choice.
card.secondLook: They did not lose the customer’s money simply because Annie came back late. Margaret was the one who failed to check the button, and Margaret was the one who chose to fix it and deliver the dress late.
card.unresolved: The money the customer withheld was never recovered. The two never decided which candidate had been right.
card.readerQuestion: If someone uses an opportunity I worked hard to create in a way different from mine, can I remain by their side?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Margaret Hall. In November 1893, you ran a small dressmaking workshop in Christchurch. That year, women in New Zealand were able to vote in a general election for the first time. Let me tell you about the hours Margaret spent between her workshop and the polling station that day.

“One button is missing.” Annie knelt beneath the worktable. Four buttons ran down the front of the dark green walking dress. One small button meant to fasten the inside had rolled somewhere across the floor. Margaret looked at the wall clock as she threaded her needle. The customer was due to collect the dress at noon.

Annie had gone to the polling station early that morning but soon returned. She had seen the line stretching down the alley outside. “If I go back now, who will finish the dress?” Annie asked. Margaret stopped with the end of the thread at her lips, where she had been wetting it. If Annie stayed, they could deliver the dress at the promised time. If Margaret worked alone, she could not guarantee it.

“You checked that your name is on the electoral roll, didn’t you?” Margaret asked. “Yes. But the line reaches all the way to that corner.” Two years earlier, the two had signed a petition calling for women to have the vote. Back then, all they had to do was pass along a sheet of paper, but today they had to actually leave the shop unattended. Margaret had already cast her ballot early that morning before opening the shop.

Margaret gripped Annie’s coat sleeve, then released it. In her pocket was a small slip of paper bearing her candidate’s name. She wondered whether to hand the name to Annie as well. Annie asked again, “Will it really be all right if I go?” The line outside the door was still long. Margaret looked back and forth between the button under the chair and the unfinished walking dress.

signalMoments.notice: Margaret picked up the button that had rolled across the floor and set it on the worktable. Outside the window, the voting line still continued around the corner. After calculating whether she could finish the dress alone before Annie returned, she said, “Go. I’ll take care of things here.”
signalMoments.connect: Margaret called to Annie, who had reached the door. “When you get back, just check the inside of the dress once. I’ll finish the rest.” Then she added that if they missed the deadline, she would explain it to the customer herself. Annie nodded and went to the polling station.
signalMoments.release: Margaret started to hand Annie the small slip on which she had written her candidate’s name, then folded it. “Choose your own vote. I’ll take care of the dress.” When Annie disappeared around the corner, Margaret put the slip in her pocket and returned to the worktable.

episode.afterSignal:
Annie fastened her coat and ran down the alley. Margaret remembered the moment inside the polling station when no one else could see her choice. Now Annie, too, would cast a ballot there under her own name. Margaret did not put down her needle until the customer arrived.

The walking dress was heavier than she had expected. Margaret straightened the shoulder line again and pushed a finger through each buttonhole. Four buttons fastened smoothly. Trusting that the fifth would as well, she covered it with the lining. As noon approached, the bell on the door rang.

As soon as the customer draped the walking dress over her arm, she tried fastening every button. Her fingers stopped at the last one. Margaret saw that the small button meant to be sewn inside the dress was still sitting on the worktable. She had found it, but had not sewn it on. The customer asked, “Am I supposed to take it like this?”

“Please wait just a moment.” Margaret took the dress back and opened the lining. She could have handed it over with one button missing. But then the inside would gape whenever the customer took off the dress away from home. The needle pricked Margaret’s finger. As she threaded it again, the wall clock passed noon.

The customer tried on the dress and raised both arms before the mirror. This time, the inside fastened properly too. But the customer said the promised time had passed and deducted a few coins from the remaining fee. Margaret did not count the money again. Only after the customer left did she raise her pricked finger to her lips.

That was when Annie returned. “Did you cast your ballot?” Margaret asked, and Annie nodded. “I didn’t vote for the person you mentioned.” Margaret opened her mouth, then closed it. She was the one who had told Annie to leave the line before, and she was the one who had promised to mind the shop. “Then you chose for yourself.” A brief silence followed those words.

“What about the dress?” Annie asked. Margaret pushed the needle case on the worktable with one finger. “It was late. And I lost a little of the fee.” When Annie apologized, Margaret shook her head. “I’m the one who didn’t check the inside all the way through.” Together they mended another customer’s sleeves until evening. They did not discuss which candidate was right.

Afterward, Margaret continued writing letters to her daughter Clara and working with Annie. In 1905, the two began running the workshop together. But when Margaret accepted late orders from customers, she did not ask Annie first. In 1908, Annie said she would no longer take evening work and began accepting her own orders separately. The two shared the workshop, but set their workloads and hours separately. After Margaret’s fingers became painful, she reduced her share of the work, and later she left the workshop in Annie’s care and moved to be near her daughter in Lyttelton. Annie remembered not only the day they both cast their ballots, but also the day she defended her own evenings.

finalMoment.place: Lyttelton, Dominion of New Zealand within the British Empire
finalMoment.scene:
The evening light slowly cools the waterfront of Lyttelton. Lying by the window in Clara’s house and looking out at the harbor, I rest the needle case my mother used on my lap. The lid is worn, and the fabric has been mended many times. Though it has been six years since I left the workshop in Annie’s care, my fingertips still move as if seeking an empty needle hole. But even curling my fingers sends pain rising through them.

My grandson’s small jacket lies on the table. When I heard earlier today that the end of one sleeve had come loose, I said I would mend it. The ten-year-old smiled and said, “If you do it, Grandma, I can wear it for a long time.” The thread never once passed through the eye of the needle. When Clara picks up the jacket, I say for no reason, “Look at the inside first.” My daughter turns the sleeve inside out and shows me. “I know, Mother. Annie says that first too.”

The letter Annie sent from Christchurch lies open. She writes that the new person she hired finishes the inside of each garment neatly. I am glad, yet imagining that person sitting at my worktable leaves a slight ache in my heart. I ask Clara to read the letter again. My daughter puts down the jacket and pulls her chair closer. She reads one sentence, then pauses. “Mother, are you tired?” I shake my head. I want to hear once more the part about Annie doing her work well in her own way.

The child by the door asks if we can go see the ships tomorrow. I want to go. Before that, I want to secure the end of the sleeve with even one stitch. But Clara’s hand over mine is warm, and I loosen my grip on the needle case a little. “You try it. Don’t forget the inside.” The child nods. As Clara reads the final line of the letter, the sounds of the harbor grow quieter and quieter. My daughter’s hand still covers mine. Thinking of the thread I never managed to put through the needle, I follow the warmth of her hand and close my eyes.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1926, Margaret’s life ended at her daughter’s home in Lyttelton, Dominion of New Zealand. Clara folded away the needle case her mother had held, then turned her son’s loose sleeve inside out to inspect it. When the news reached Annie, she checked the inside of the dress she had finished that day one more time. And so another life ended. The record of past lives leaves the unthreaded strand and the hands that carried on in this chapter, then waits for the first page of another life.

card.name: Yusuf
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yusuf from the outskirts of Isfahan. After an injured ankle forced you to change jobs, you tended a pigeon tower, and when Farhad found work of his own, you hired another laborer as well.
card.title: The Day the Tower Took Flight
card.world: Farmland and a pigeon tower outside Isfahan in the Safavid dynasty, 1616
card.flavor: Why the birds all left at once
card.opening: Inside the pigeon tower, wings thundered. When Yusuf saw his assistant Farhad standing by the door, he suspected him first. Then he found other tracks at the base of the tower.
card.life: Yusuf was born near Isfahan in 1576 and injured his ankle while working in the fields. He tended a pigeon tower and lived with Shima and their daughter, Laleh. When Farhad began choosing his own schedule and taking jobs in neighboring fields, Yusuf hired another laborer as well. In old age, he handed over the repair of the tower's high walls and the work in his small field separately.
card.turn: The day before the manure was to be collected, the birds inside the tower suddenly erupted into a commotion. Hearing that Farhad had been nearby, Yusuf thought he had played a prank, but in a broken gap in the smooth outer wall were marks left by a snake.
card.decision: Yusuf admitted to Farhad that he had judged him too quickly. He opened the work door so the birds could escape the danger inside, then drove the snake out with a long pole.
card.cost: Some of the birds did not return to the tower that day. The promised manure collection was delayed, and Yusuf spent a day replastering the wall with his family. Farhad did not immediately speak to him as he had before, either.
card.after: Some of the birds returned, but empty nests remained. Though Farhad helped repair the wall that day, he did not joke as he had before. Later, he chose his own dates for working at the tower and took separate repair jobs in neighboring fields.
card.presentEcho: When you want to find the cause quickly, you may blame the person who happened to be closest. What you say and do afterward stays in the relationship.
card.secondLook: Farhad said the birds had cried out first and that he had struck the door with the pole because he was trying to look inside. Yusuf suspected him even after hearing that explanation. Only after seeing the snake's trail by the crack outside did he change his mind.
card.unresolved: The birds that did not return and the delayed harvest remained real losses. Even after hearing Yusuf's apology, Farhad could not smile again right away.
card.readerQuestion: If I suspect someone the moment a problem arises, what will I check next, and how will I speak to them?

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were called Yusuf. In 1616, you tended a pigeon tower among the fields outside Isfahan. This tower was not used to send messages. It was a place where birds roosted so their manure could be collected for the fields. Let me tell you about the day a thunderous beating of wings erupted inside it.

Yusuf was checking the irrigation channels in the melon field. Suddenly, the pigeon tower seemed to shake from within. Countless wings were striking the walls all at once. Birds burst from the openings at the top of the tower, while many more wheeled through the cramped space inside. Dragging his injured left foot, Yusuf ran toward the tower.

Farhad stood before the low work door. He held a long wooden pole. Hassan, a farmer from a neighboring field, came running too. “I saw that boy banging on the tower earlier,” Hassan said. Yusuf looked from the pole to the door. “Did you frighten them?” Farhad's eyes widened. “The birds started crying out first. I hit the door with the pole because I was trying to look inside.”

Without answering, Yusuf touched the latch. If he opened the door, even more birds would escape. If the tower lost birds, there would be less manure to collect next time. Hassan was supposed to haul that manure to his field tomorrow. “Let's keep the door shut for now and wait until they calm down,” Hassan said. Inside the tower, the wings beat even more fiercely.

Farhad pointed toward the base of the wall. Around the outside of the pigeon tower was a smoothly plastered band that snakes could not easily climb. Beneath that band was a crack wide enough for a finger, and it ran through to the inside of the wall. In the dry earth before the crack was the long trail of something that had dragged its body across the ground. As Yusuf bent closer, the birds burst up once again from the low nests inside the tower.

“A snake.” The words slipped from Yusuf's mouth. Farhad set the pole on the ground. Yusuf looked at him but could not apologize at once. Hassan took hold of the door. “If you open it, what about the manure I'm supposed to take tomorrow?” Before he had finished speaking, a bird inside struck the work door hard. Yusuf stood between the latch and Farhad.

signalMoments.notice: Yusuf noticed both that the ground beneath the crack in the wall was still damp and that the birds had crowded toward the inner part of the tower. They could not leave the birds trapped while they repaired the crack first. He told Farhad, “I suspected you first. I was wrong,” and put his hand on the work door's latch.
signalMoments.speak: In front of Hassan, Yusuf spoke to Farhad. “I thought it happened because you were banging on the door. I'm sorry. A snake got in.” He showed Farhad where to stand aside when the birds came out, then gripped the work door's latch.
signalMoments.protect: Yusuf put the birds beating their wings inside the tower now before his promise to collect manure tomorrow. He motioned for Farhad to step back. “I got angry at you first. I'm sorry.” He lifted the latch.

episode.afterSignal:
When the door opened, white dust and several birds poured out first. Startled, Hassan stepped back. Farhad braced the door so it would not swing shut again. Yusuf picked up the long pole and bent toward the light shining inside. Between the low nests, he saw the slender tail of a snake.

“Keep the pole in front of you,” Yusuf said, and Farhad took his place on the opposite side. Trying not to disturb the nests, Yusuf pushed his pole low. When the snake moved along the wall, Farhad blocked its path, and the snake slipped out through the open door. It disappeared beyond the furrow where Hassan had retreated. All three men were speechless for a moment.

When Yusuf went to close the door, Farhad said, “We need to seal the gap first.” He was right. Yusuf mixed water and earth and filled the broken section. While he reapplied smooth plaster over it, Hassan stood with an empty manure sack over his shoulder. “So I won't be able to haul it tomorrow morning.” Yusuf shook the mud from his hands. “Give me one more day. I need to inspect the inside.”

When evening came, many of the birds returned and perched in the openings. But several of the places Yusuf always watched were empty. He could not count exactly how many were missing. Hassan was unable to haul the manure the next day, and Yusuf repaired the wall once more with water and earth brought by his daughter Laleh and his wife Shima. He could not claim to know in advance how much of next year's harvest would be lost, but the empty nests were plain to see.

While carrying earth for the repairs, Farhad did not call Yusuf “Uncle.” Nor did he joke as usual. When Yusuf said again, “You came first to warn me, and I got angry before I listened,” Farhad merely held out the trowel. “This part is still rough.” Yusuf took it and smoothed the spot flat.

Yusuf continued tending the field with Shima, and he saw Laleh establish a household on a neighboring farm. Farhad helped with the tower, but he no longer promised that he could come on any day. When Yusuf chose a date first and informed him, Farhad refused, saying he had work in another field. Beginning in 1620, he also took separate repair jobs in neighboring fields. Yusuf had to hire another laborer on the days he needed help. Farhad later acquired a field of his own and left, and when Yusuf's shoulders grew weak, yet another laborer repaired the high walls. Yusuf apologized to Farhad, but he could not keep deciding Farhad's workdays as he pleased.

finalMoment.place: Outside Isfahan, Safavid Iran
finalMoment.scene:
As the sun sinks behind the tower, pigeons settle into each opening. I count to 6, then lose track of the next bird. I used to climb to the very top of the tower to estimate their number, but now even watching from the threshold leaves me catching my breath. On my lap lies the wooden trowel I have used since I first learned to work on the tower. It has been a long time since my shoulder allowed me to grip it and plaster a wall.

Laleh cuts open the first melon of the year and offers it to me. She brought it from her own farm. “Father, this is the sweet side.” When I take a bite, the tip of my tongue feels cool. I want to look at the tower's shaded side once more tomorrow. I cannot stop wondering whether the earth around the high opening I missed today has dried out. “The new laborer checked that side.” Laleh answers before I can even ask. I rub the trowel's handle with my thumb.

Shima props another pillow behind my shoulder. “Why do you always wait until evening to say it hurts?” I have heard those words since I was young, so I try to smile instead of answering. A brief clatter of wings comes from the tower, and my body tries to rise before I can think. Shima gently lays her hand on my arm. Laleh goes out through the door instead and looks up at the tower. “They're all inside, Father.” As she tells me again, I do not ask which opening is empty.

I want another piece of melon, but my lips will not move properly. Tomorrow, I should ask how Farhad is doing on his own field. I wish I could also tell Shima that I will look after her shoulders before the walls. Laleh stands on the threshold, watching until the last bird returns. The trowel remains in my palm, but the sound of wings grows more distant. Following the sound of the birds as my daughter describes it, I close my eyes.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1653, Yusuf's life ended at his home outside Isfahan, with Shima and Laleh beside him. Shima placed the wooden trowel her husband had been unable to let go beside the door. At the next harvest, Laleh cut open the first melon and shared it with the young laborer who repaired the tower. When Farhad heard the news, he came and stood for a long while before the tower's work door. And so another life came to an end. The Record of Past Lives leaves a single trowel and the sound of returning birds on this page, then waits for the first page of another life.

card.name: Marcella
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Marcella of the province of Britannia. You learned to sew and mended clothes for family and neighbors in Vindolanda and Corbridge, raised a daughter, and grew old after living to see your granddaughter.
card.title: The Second Cart
card.world: Vindolanda in Roman Britannia, AD 104
card.flavor: Her daughter's empty place on moving day
card.opening: On the morning they were leaving Vindolanda, only her daughter Neria's bundle was missing from the cart. When Marcella went to find her, Neria said she had moved her belongings into Sabina's room and would stay there.
card.life: Marcella was born near Corbridge and learned to sew from her mother. She married Lucius and gave birth to Neria. Following her husband to his place of work, she lived in Vindolanda and shared mending work with Sabina. In old age, she took on less work in Corbridge and waited for visits from her daughter and granddaughter.
card.turn: On the day the family was to move, Neria said she would stay in Vindolanda and work with Sabina, and had already moved her belongings. Afraid because she did not know where her daughter would sleep or what work she would have, Marcella went to inspect Sabina's room herself.
card.decision: Marcella stopped herself from putting Neria on the cart and instead looked over the room where her daughter would live and the clothes she had taken on. She sent her husband and their belongings ahead, stayed behind for one more day to check on Neria's work, and then followed.
card.cost: The first cart did not wait. Marcella paid the fare for another cart the next day, and Lucius had to unload their belongings alone. She could no longer live with Neria under the same roof every day as before.
card.after: After paying a separate cart fare and arriving in Corbridge the next day, Marcella saw the empty sleeping place Neria had left behind. Neria's next job had not yet been settled, and her parents could not immediately grow used to their daughter's absence.
card.presentEcho: Even someone close to me may have a path different from the one I imagined. Checking the practical realities of that path takes longer than words.
card.secondLook: Neria had not changed her mind suddenly. She had spent months learning the work beside Sabina, but kept putting off the day she would tell her mother because she feared disappointing her. Marcella, busy preparing for the move, had not asked her either.
card.unresolved: Neria's choice to stay in Vindolanda cannot simply be declared right. The days when they lived near each other did not return, and every time they met, the two had to learn about each other's new lives all over again.
card.readerQuestion: When someone I expected to leave with me says they will stay, what will I check first?

signalMoments.notice: Marcella said, “I'll see the room first,” then checked Neria's sleeping place and the clothes she had taken on at Sabina's house. Her daughter's bundle was already there.
signalMoments.connect: Marcella asked Sabina whether her daughter could sleep there and learn the work. After seeing the room and the clothes she had taken on, she told Neria, “So this is how much you prepared without me.”
signalMoments.speak: Marcella was angry, but said she had been afraid because she did not know where her daughter would sleep. She listened without interrupting while Neria explained Sabina's room and the clothes she had taken on.

identity.region: Vindolanda and Corbridge in the Roman Empire's province of Britannia

Marcella · Female
AD 69–142 · Age 73
The Roman Empire's province of Britannia · Vindolanda and Corbridge

What she disliked · Throwing away clothes that could still be worn

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
What she treasured · A small needle case from her mother
Those closest to her · Her husband Lucius, her daughter Neria, and her neighbor Sabina

Worry · How they would carry on the cart-repair work if her husband's wrists grew weak

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Marcella. You lived in Britannia under the Roman Empire, beside the timber fort at Vindolanda, mending other people's worn clothes. Let me tell you about one moving day in that long life—the day her 18-year-old daughter never climbed onto the cart she was meant to take.

Two carts stood on the wet roadside. Lucius had found cart-repair work near the fort at Corbridge. They had to leave before the sun rose high. As Marcella loaded blankets and her needle case, she looked for the third bundle. It held the clothes Neria had kept with her until that morning. Hounded by the demands of moving, Marcella had left the worn lining of her own cloak unmended.

“Neria's things are in the rear cart, aren't they?” Marcella asked. Lucius rummaged through the load. “No. She'll bring them herself.” But their daughter was nowhere in sight either. The driver of the first cart wound the reins around his hand. “If everything's loaded, let's go.” Marcella tucked the needle case inside her clothes and ran down the narrow road.

Wet cloth hung outside the bathhouse beside the fort. Beneath the wall leaking steam, Neria and Sabina were folding dry fabric. The bundle lay at her daughter's feet. When Marcella approached, Neria put down the cloth. “Let's load that first. The cart's waiting.” Neria did not pick up the bundle. “I'm not going.”

Marcella almost laughed. This was no time for jokes. Neria said, “I'm staying here to mend clothes with Sabina. Someone is coming next week to collect a tunic I stitched.” Marcella looked at her daughter's hands. The cloth they had folded together only yesterday was now being called someone else's order. “Do you mean you'll stay a few days and follow us?” “No. I'm going to live here.”

“Where will you sleep, and what will you eat if the work dries up?” Marcella's voice rose. Neria raised hers too. “I tried to tell you every time. You were busy, so….” Marcella cut her off. “Is that my fault?” Instead of answering, Neria tightened the knot on her bundle. Inside were 2 changes of clothes and several old needles. From a distance came the sound of a cart wheel turning once.

Sabina stepped between them. “Would you like to see the room?” Marcella could take her daughter away with her right then. A room Marcella had already chosen was waiting in Corbridge. But if she left her daughter behind, Lucius would have to unload everything alone, and she would have to pay the fare for another cart tomorrow. Above all, she could not make herself leave without seeing whether her daughter truly had a place to live.

signalMoments.notice: Marcella said, “I'll see the room first.” Sabina opened the small space in her house behind the bathhouse. It had enough room for Neria's bundle, and the tunic Neria had agreed to mend was hanging there. Only then did Marcella realize her daughter had already begun moving her life there.
signalMoments.connect: Marcella asked Sabina, “Can my daughter sleep here and learn the work?” Sabina showed her the small room they would share and the 1 garment Neria had taken on. Marcella turned to Neria and said, “So this is how much you prepared without me.”
signalMoments.speak: Marcella suppressed the urge to drag Neria to the cart. “I am angry. But I was afraid because I didn't even know where you would sleep.” Marcella did not interrupt until Neria had finished explaining Sabina's room and the clothes she had taken on.

episode.afterSignal:
There was just enough room for the two of them to lie down with their feet touching. Beside Sabina's blanket, a thin cloth Neria had brought lay spread out. The torn underarm of the tunic hanging near the door was already half stitched. Sabina said, “When this garment is finished, I'll give Neria a share of my pay. I can't promise there will be another job after it.” Marcella found that last statement the most trustworthy.

“When did you decide?” Marcella asked. Neria could not look her mother straight in the eye. “This winter. Sabina and I mended 3 garments together.” For months, her daughter had eaten supper under the same roof without saying this. Marcella, too, had counted only the bundles they would move and had never asked whether Neria wanted to stay. Marcella released the handle of the bundle.

Outside, Lucius waved to them. Marcella stepped onto the road and said, “Take the belongings ahead. Neria says she's staying here. I've seen the place where she'll live with Sabina.” Lucius stood beside the cart, looking toward his daughter for a long while. “Then what about you?” “I'll follow tomorrow.” Lucius said, “I suppose I'll have to unload everything alone.” Marcella apologized. The wheels of the first cart crunched over the gravel and receded into the distance.

Neria came out after her and asked, “Should I take you there tomorrow?” Marcella shook her head. “Finish the garment you took on first.” Neria lifted her mother's cloak to show her. Its worn lining had been joined with her daughter's crooked stitches. “I mended it yesterday. It would be a problem if it came apart on the road.” The two stood at the door and smiled awkwardly. During the rest of the day, Marcella checked once more on the sleeping place and food Sabina had described, and the share Neria would receive. It did not take her worry away.

The next day, Marcella paid a different driver a separate fare. When she arrived in Corbridge, Lucius had unloaded everything alone and raised blisters on his hands. “What about our daughter?” he asked. Marcella said, “She has 1 garment to mend. She doesn't know what comes after that yet.” That night, in the unfamiliar room, each of them looked once at Neria's empty sleeping place.

In time, Neria completed the first regular job she had secured with her own hands beside Sabina, while Marcella continued mending clothes in Corbridge and helping with Lucius's cart work. She outlived her mother, later lost her husband as well, and after spending 1 season with her granddaughter, passed her needle case on to a younger worker. Whenever Marcella went to Vindolanda to see her daughter, she packed lightly. After all, she had a road home. But every time she rode a second cart, she remembered the empty place from that first moving day.

finalMoment.place: The small yard of Marcella's house in Corbridge, in the Roman Empire's province of Britannia
finalMoment.scene:
In the late spring of AD 142, at 73, I came out to sit in the small yard of my house in Corbridge. My belly had hurt for 4 days, and since the day before, I had kept vomiting whatever I ate. My adult granddaughter, visiting from Vindolanda for a few days, sat across from me. “Would you like to go inside?” she asked. “It's less stifling here.” I rested a hand on my swollen belly and searched for a slightly more comfortable position.

The pain eased for a moment, then surged back. When I bent over, my granddaughter came closer. “Should I send word to Mother?” It would take time for a message to reach Vindolanda, where my daughter Neria lived. “Send it. But you stay here today.” My granddaughter gave a passing neighbor a message for Neria and returned.

My granddaughter set down a small stool in the yard and sat. I tried stretching out my legs, but when my belly hurt more, I bent my knees again. As the wind came in, my granddaughter half closed the door. “Leave it open,” I said. She opened the door again. The late-spring sunlight reached even the dark side of the house. Watching that light, I placed my palm against the ground of the yard.

As the afternoon deepened, it became hard to answer my granddaughter right away. “Grandmother.” At the sound of her calling me, I opened my eyes and turned my head. She climbed down from the stool and sat beside me. I tried again to tell her to stay here with me now. My lips moved, but no voice came out. My granddaughter's face blurred.
finalMoment.afterword: In AD 142, Marcella died at age 73 in the yard of her Corbridge home after suffering abdominal pain and vomiting for several days. The exact illness is unknown. The granddaughter beside her remembered that her grandmother had told her to leave the door open. When Neria heard the news, she came from Vindolanda. She also remembered that old moving day when her mother had stayed 1 extra day to inspect her sleeping place, but did not use that 1 incident to explain the long distance between them. The record of this past life closes by recounting the household Marcella built as she moved with Lucius, the daily life she continued after she was left alone, and the time her daughter and granddaughter spent in their own places.
finalMoment.artAlt: The yard of a modest house in Corbridge in AD 142. Seen from a low vantage point inside the open door, 73-year-old Marcella sits with a hand on her belly while her adult granddaughter sits a few paces away, watching her

card.name: Amalia Rojas
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Amalia Rojas of Buenos Aires. You learned confectionery from your parents, ran a stall and a shop, lived for many years beside your sister and nephew, and eventually handed over the business.
card.title: Confections on Ice
card.world: An indoor skating rink in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 1910
card.flavor: Cream pastries gliding across the ice
card.opening: As Amalia carried pastries to the upstairs café at the skating rink, she dropped one plate. Five cream pastries rolled over the railing and raced across the ice.
card.life: Amalia learned dough-making and bookkeeping in her parents' small confectionery workshop, then opened her own stall. She and her friend Inés built up a shop together before going their separate ways, and her widowed sister and nephew later returned to live under the same roof with her. After her wrists grew weak, she handed the shop over to her nephew.
card.turn: A customer was waiting in the upstairs café for twelve pastries. Five fell onto the ice, and skaters were heading toward them. While clearing away the fallen pastries, Amalia had to decide how to serve the remaining seven.
card.decision: Amalia warned everyone about the plate on the ice and cleared away the five fallen pastries with Inés. After showing the customer the remaining seven, she offered to cut six in half and give the birthday guest the one whole pastry as an extra.
card.cost: She could not charge for all twelve. Some customers laughed over their half pieces, but others were unhappy that the pastries came late. When Amalia returned, she showed her father the shortfall and mixed dough again for the pastries they would sell the next day.
card.after: Once they were outside, Amalia and Inés saw the cream on Amalia's skirt and laughed. They later opened a shop together, and even after Inés started her own confectionery, they still visited each other from time to time.
card.presentEcho: Even on a day when you make a mistake, there can still be laughter. But the funny scene and the money lost are entered in the same ledger.
card.secondLook: Amalia was the one who dropped the pastries, but if she had left them on the ice, a skater could have been hurt. Inés's help was welcome, but it did not change the fact that the customers did not receive their full order.
card.unresolved: The customer paid roughly half the original price, and not everyone was satisfied. Amalia and Inés laughed about that day in later years, but the lost payment and the five missing pastries could not be recovered.
card.readerQuestion: If I made a mistake in front of everyone, what would I set right first?

signalMoments.notice: Amalia saw the ice gleaming with cream beside the plate and warned, “It's slippery over there!” While Inés blocked the plate, Amalia gripped the railing and stepped down to the edge of the ice.
signalMoments.speak: Amalia shouted that a plate had fallen and told people not to come that way. She told the café worker that the five pastries could not be served and asked them to tell the customer, then went down the stairs.
signalMoments.connect: Amalia asked Inés, who was on the ice, to block the plate first. While Inés stood in front of it, Amalia held the railing and made her way down to the edge.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Amalia Rojas. You ran a confectionery stall in Buenos Aires in 1910. Let me tell you about the day you delivered pastries to a newly opened indoor skating rink and unexpectedly became part of the spectacle on the ice.

“Twelve, all topped with cream.” Amalia spread out her fingers and counted the order from the upstairs café again. She put seven on a large tray and five on a small metal plate. Organ music echoed through the rink, and below, people circled the ice. Amalia carefully turned toward the railing.

Someone behind her called, “Excuse me!” as they passed. Amalia pulled the tray toward her chest. She saved the large tray, but the small plate struck the railing. The plate and five cream pastries fell below. The sound of the plate skidding across the ice cut through the organ music. One pastry spun around, then overtook the plate.

“Who ordered that dance?” someone upstairs laughed. Amalia's face burned. Looking down, she saw a skater heading toward the plate. If someone fell, that would be far worse than the cost of the pastries. Her friend Inés was also skating below. Amalia handed the seven pastries she still held to a café worker. “These didn't fall. Please hold them for a moment.”

As she ran down the stairs, Amalia calculated. Five out of the twelve could no longer be used. Twelve guests were waiting. If she picked up the ones that looked clean and added fresh cream, perhaps no one would notice. But she did not want to serve guests anything that had touched the floor. First, she had to stop someone from getting hurt on the ice.

signalMoments.notice: Amalia saw a gleaming patch of ice where cream had smeared beside the plate. “It's slippery over there!” she shouted, waving her hand. While Inés stopped the plate with her skate, Amalia gripped the railing and stepped down to the edge of the ice.
signalMoments.speak: Amalia shouted, “A plate fell! Please stay away from there for a moment!” Even when someone laughed, she did not stop speaking. She told the café worker, “The five can't be served. Please tell the customer that too,” and then went down the stairs.
signalMoments.connect: When Amalia spotted Inés below, she waved. “Inés, block the plate first! I'll come down.” Inés glided across the ice and stopped in front of the plate, while Amalia clung to the railing and lowered herself one step at a time to the edge.

episode.afterSignal:
Without skates, Amalia's shoes refused to obey her on the ice. When her right foot slid sideways, her left followed. She barely managed to remain standing by clinging to the railing. Inés wobbled too as she pushed the plate toward her. The two grabbed each other's arms and, without even a moment to laugh, picked up the plate first. A passing skater veered around them.

They gathered up all five pastries and carried them back. One still looked perfectly intact. As Amalia picked it up, she remembered the words of the customer upstairs. “Twelve.” Inés asked, “Can it be saved?” Amalia shook her head. “It touched the ice.” Meltwater clung to the soles of her shoes as she went back upstairs.

Twelve cups were set out at the café table. The person who had ordered counted the seven pastries Amalia placed before them, then asked, “Where are the other five?” “They fell on the ice. These seven stayed upstairs. I can't charge you for twelve.” The customer glanced down at the rink. “But there are twelve of us.” With a small knife borrowed from the café, Amalia cut six pastries in half. “I can give each of the twelve of you half a pastry. May I give the last whole one to the birthday guest as an extra?” Amalia pointed to the one intact pastry.

For a moment, no one spoke. Beside her, Inés pressed her lips tightly together. The customer said, “Then please cut the price almost in half too.” Amalia thought about the amount she would enter in the ledger, then nodded. No one could mistake those pieces for whole pastries. Some customers laughed about the birthday guest getting a whole one alone, while others frowned at the pastries that had arrived late.

Once they were outside, Inés pointed at the hem of Amalia's skirt. A streak of cream marked it. “There's one of your pastries.” Amalia burst out laughing. “I don't think I can sell this one.” But after returning to the stall, she had to show her father the shortfall. He looked from the cream-stained skirt to the ledger and said, “Tomorrow, carry only one plate.” That night, Amalia mixed dough again to make the pastries they would sell the next day.

Amalia later built up a small shop with Inés. Their partnership ended in 1926, when Inés opened her own confectionery in another neighborhood, but the two still visited each other from time to time. Later, Amalia welcomed her widowed sister Paloma and her nephew Tomás into her home. After her wrists grew weak, she spent more time holding the ledger than working dough, and eventually handed the shop over to Tomás. Not every customer from the skating rink became a regular. Still, whenever Inés visited and teased, “How many plates are you carrying today?” Amalia would answer, “One. If there are two, you're carrying one of them.”

finalMoment.place: The living room of the home Amalia shared with her sister Paloma, Buenos Aires, Argentina
finalMoment.scene:
On a winter evening in 1951, seventy-year-old Amalia was listening to the radio with her sister Paloma at their home in Buenos Aires. It had been four years since she handed the shop over to her nephew Tomás. Amalia set the newspaper on the table and turned her head to ask again about something said on the broadcast. At that moment, the fingers of her left hand refused to move as she intended and trembled twice. Amalia looked down at her hand.

“What's wrong?” Paloma asked. “Just a moment,” Amalia said. The trembling traveled up her arm. She tried to grasp the armrest, but her body stiffened. As Paloma stood, Amalia slid sideways and fell to the floor. Paloma pushed the chair away to clear the space. Amalia's arms and legs shook again and again, and she could not answer when Paloma called her name.

“Someone, please come!” Paloma shouted toward the door. When she returned, Amalia's body had grown still for a moment. Paloma sat beside Amalia and looked at her face. “Amalia, can you hear me?” Amalia did not open her eyes. Her breathing was harsh, and Paloma called her name once more. Then her body began to tremble briefly again.

Paloma pushed the chair farther aside and remained beside Amalia. Even after the trembling stopped, Amalia did not open her eyes. Paloma called her name and waited, but her breathing gradually grew fainter. As footsteps approached from beyond the open door, Amalia stopped breathing. The program they had been listening to continued on the radio.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1951, while listening to the radio with her sister Paloma in Buenos Aires, Amalia's body suddenly stiffened and began to shake. She died at the age of seventy without regaining consciousness. The exact cause and diagnosis are unknown. After a neighbor came in, Paloma turned off the radio and sat in her chair for a long while. The next day, Tomás opened the shop ledger and remembered how his aunt never let a blank space pass without question. When Inés, who ran a separate shop, heard the news, she remembered the years when they continued to visit each other long after ending their partnership. There had been a day when customers laughed over half pastries, but Amalia's life was not defined by that day alone. The record of her past life also preserves her final years under the same roof as Paloma and the visits from Inés that continued for so long.
finalMoment.artAlt: A winter evening in 1951, viewed from a high diagonal angle in a modest Buenos Aires living room. 70-year-old Amalia sits in a chair beside the radio, feeling the first tremor in her hand, while her sister Paloma turns to look from a chair a few steps away

card.name: Genji
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Genji, a carpenter in Nihonbashi, Edo. You learned the trade from your father, had a daughter with Mine, rebuilt your workshop, and grew old with your apprentice and grandson by your side.
card.title: The Wall I Tore Down
card.world: The wooden residential districts of Edo in 1846, under the Tokugawa shogunate
card.flavor: The box left behind before the flames
card.opening: When flames appeared on a roof a few houses down the alley, the fire brigade captain ordered Genji to tear down his own workshop. Inside was a small box that had belonged to his late wife, Mine.
card.life: Genji learned carpentry from his father and set up a narrow workshop. He and Mine had a daughter, Yuki, and after Mine died, he and Yuki carried on their household together. After the fire, he established another workshop and taught an apprentice named Taro. In old age, he made wooden toys with his grandson.
card.turn: The fire at a neighbor's house reached the roof of Genji's workshop. The fire brigade captain ordered him to tear down the empty workshop to create a gap between the houses. Genji came out carrying only his father's ink-line box from beside the door, while Mine's box remained farther inside.
card.decision: Genji started to go back in for the box, then stopped when he saw embers at the edge of the roof. He told the firefighters no one was inside, then took hold of a hook and rope and helped tear down his own workshop's roof and walls.
card.cost: He lost some of the workshop's lumber and tools, and all he found of Mine's box beneath the collapsed wall was a piece of its lid. Yuki remembered for a long time that her father had saved the ink-line box first. The neighboring house's eaves did not immediately catch fire, but the damage remained.
card.after: Genji received planks from a fellow carpenter and rented space in another workshop. Two years later, he secured a small place of his own. Yuki handed him nails when he installed the new door, but she did not mention Mine's box.
card.presentEcho: The weight of what is left behind in an emergency can linger differently for each person, even after the crisis has passed.
card.secondLook: The ink-line box Genji carried out had been beside the door, while Mine's box was farther inside. Yuki saw only the box in her father's hand, but the difference of those few steps had taken away his time to choose.
card.unresolved: The demolished workshop was rebuilt, but Mine's box never returned. Even if Yuki eventually began listening to her father again, that did not mean she accepted the loss.
card.readerQuestion: If someone lost something because of a choice I made in haste, how would I listen to their anger?

signalMoments.notice: Genji saw the embers at the edge of the roof and the distance to the shelf inside. Unable to keep his companions waiting any longer, he shouted, “There's no one inside!” and hooked the wall.
signalMoments.protect: Genji saw that the eaves of his workshop and the neighboring house nearly touched. Leaving Mine's box behind, he handed the rope to a companion and said, “Let's pull the roof down first.”
signalMoments.speak: Genji told Yuki, “I couldn't get Mine's box out.” When embers flew again, he told the captain no one was inside and took hold of the rope.

Work · Carpenter and neighborhood firefighter

In old age, he left the work on high places to Taro and made small toys with his grandson.

What he disliked · Hiding a crooked pillar with paper

profilePages.body:
What he treasured · The ink-line box inherited from his father

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Genji. You were a carpenter in Nihonbashi, Edo, and when a fire broke out in the neighborhood, you served with the fire brigade. Over your lifetime, you repaired the doors of many houses. Today, I'll tell you about the day when, among all those buildings, you had to tear down your own workshop with your own hands.

“Fire!” The cry erupted at the end of the alley. Genji was in his workshop, shaving the corner of a new door panel. Orange light shone through the doorway. Genji picked up his father's ink-line box from beside the door and stepped outside. Flames were visible on a roof a few houses away. He pulled on the dark blue coat of the neighborhood fire brigade and took hold of a long hook.

The fire brigade captain and the other firefighters came running into the alley. The eaves of the narrow houses nearly touched. The captain pointed at Genji's workshop. “Is that place empty? Bring down the roof first. We need a gap to keep the fire from reaching the next house.” Genji looked back at the door he had built with his own hands. Inside were dressed lumber and tools. Farther in was a small box that had belonged to Mine, who had died five years earlier.

His daughter Yuki came running from the corner of the alley. “What about Mother's box?” Instead of answering, Genji looked into the workshop. The ink-line box was in his hand. Mine's box was on a shelf at the back. It seemed only two steps away. Yuki looked back and forth between her father's hand and his empty one.

When Genji put one foot on the threshold, an ember fell from the edge of the roof. A firefighter set his hook and waited. “Genji, is anyone inside?” “No.” “Then stand back.” Genji looked once more toward the box. If the roof caught fire, the flames would spread not only through his workshop but to the neighboring house's eaves. The captain had already uncoiled the rope.

signalMoments.notice: Genji saw the embers at the edge of the roof and the distance to the shelf inside. Even if it was only two steps, he could not keep the people ready to pull the rope waiting any longer. “There's no one inside!” he shouted, hooking the wall.
signalMoments.protect: Genji saw how closely the eaves of his workshop and the neighboring house stood together. Leaving Mine's box inside, he handed the rope to a companion and said, “Let's pull the roof down first.”
signalMoments.speak: Looking at Yuki, Genji said, “I couldn't get Mine's box out.” Before Yuki could speak, embers flew from the roof again. He told the captain no one was inside and took hold of the rope.

episode.afterSignal:
One man hooked the roof while the others pulled the rope. Genji planted his feet on the ground and added his strength. At first, the post held. On the second pull, the eaves buckled with the sound of dry wood breaking. Behind him, Yuki drew a sharp breath. Genji could not turn around. They had to pull the rope sideways to keep the burning timber from falling toward the neighboring house.

The workshop's front wall and part of the roof collapsed. The firefighters cleared the remaining timber from the middle of the alley. Smoke escaped through the open space, and they doused the neighboring house's eaves with water. The fire did not immediately spread to the house next door. The sound of flames still came from farther away. No one knew who could ever count all the damage done that day.

When Genji let go of the rope, the skin of his palms had been scraped raw. The ink-line box was smeared with dirt. He searched beneath the shattered wall for Mine's box, but found only a piece of its lid. The small comb and old cloth that had been inside were nowhere to be seen. Yuki approached. “What about Mother's things?” Genji held out the fragment. Yuki did not take it.

“You brought your own thing out.” Yuki pointed at the ink-line box. Genji said, “It was beside the door...” Even if that was true, he knew it was not an answer that could reach Yuki's heart. He picked the fragment up from the ground again and tucked it inside his robe. Yuki said nothing else to her father until that evening. Genji could not invent another excuse either.

The neighboring carpenters gave him a few planks they had left. For a while, Genji worked in a borrowed corner of someone else's workshop, and two years later he secured a smaller place of his own. Yuki handed him nails when he installed the new door, but she did not mention Mine's box. Even on the days they worked together, the two of them did not remember the lost object in the same way.

In later years, Genji turned the roofing work over to his apprentice Taro and made wooden toys with Yuki's son after she established a household in another neighborhood. Even as he aged, he remained strict about the measurements of a door panel. The open stretch of alley from that day eventually filled with houses again, but whenever Genji passed the new wall, he first remembered the shelf at the back where Mine's box had stood. What Yuki remembered was the ink-line box in her father's hand.

finalMoment.place: Genji's home in Tokyo
finalMoment.scene:
It is a late autumn morning in 1871, in my home in Tokyo. My daughter Yuki lives in another neighborhood, and I prepare breakfast alone. My stomach has burned since yesterday, but I wash the rice as usual. When I rise holding the bowl, nausea rolls through me. I open the door halfway and set the bowl down in front of me. I try to breathe the outside air, but my knees give way and I sit on the wooden floor.

After retching, I vomit dark red blood into the bowl. For a while, I can only stare at the color. The cloth I use to wipe my mouth is stained with blood too. “Is anyone there?” A neighbor answers from beyond the wall. He says he heard my voice and asks if he may come in. I try to stand to greet him, but the ground tilts beneath my feet and I sit again. “The door is open.”

The neighbor enters, sees the bowl, and crouches in front of me. “I'll call someone.” I nod. He calls outside for help, then quickly returns to my side. I set the damp cloth on the floor. I remain seated because I think standing will make me dizzier, and my fingertips grow cold. “Yuki isn't due to visit today.” I do not know why I say it. The neighbor replies, “I know. I'll send word to her.”

I vomit blood again. I try to pull the bowl closer, but there is no strength in my arm. The neighbor moves the bowl closer and sits beside me without touching my back. Outside the window, I hear someone calling my name. I open my mouth to answer, but the doorframe before me blurs. I press my cold palm against the wooden floor and try to raise myself. My hand slips, and I cannot draw my next breath all the way in.
finalMoment.afterword: Genji died in 1871 after vomiting blood in his own home in Tokyo. It is unknown where the bleeding began. The neighbor who was with him told Yuki that her father had spoken his daughter's name at the end. Even after coming to the house, Yuki did not take those words as a request for reconciliation. She still remembered the day Mine's box was lost differently, and she also knew of the small toys her father and son had made together. Taro remembered the years when Genji had handed the work on high roofs over to him. The record of this past life does not reduce Genji to a single fire or a single remark. It sets down both the days he lived and the morning when his life suddenly ended.
finalMoment.artAlt: Viewed through the lattice door facing the yard of Genji's Tokyo home in late autumn 1871, 66-year-old Genji sits alone on the wooden floor, looking at a bowl holding a little dark red blood as he wipes his mouth with one hand

card.name: Vimal Shah
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Vimal Shah of Bombay. You learned to paint signs, then played the harmonium in a silent cinema. After films changed, you continued making music with theater troupes, at weddings, and alongside neighborhood children.
card.title: Chase Music on a White Screen
card.role: Harmonium player at a silent cinema
card.world: A silent cinema in Bombay, British India, in 1932
card.flavor: The film stopped, but the music kept running
card.opening: In the middle of a chase scene, the movie screen flashed white. The projector had stopped, but Vimal's harmonium kept racing on.
card.life: Vimal grew up beside his sign-painter father and learned to play the harmonium. He accompanied silent films with Dinesh, but as talkies became more common, he moved among theater performances, wedding music, and sign painting. He stayed close to his sister Leena and his niece Tara, and in old age he taught rhythm to neighborhood children.
card.turn: The film broke, freezing the chase scene. The cinema owner told them to keep playing and hide the malfunction, but the audience watched the blank screen and heard the rapid music, then began to murmur.
card.decision: Vimal stopped the music and announced that the screening had been temporarily interrupted. While the projection booth spliced the film, he and Dinesh invented what the thief on-screen might do next and turned it into a short musical drama.
card.cost: When the screen came back on, the thief's actual next move was different from Vimal's guess, and the audience burst out laughing. Even so, several people who had left early received refunds, and the owner docked part of both musicians' pay for that day because of the lost income.
card.after: Dinesh said that his pay had been cut too, and Vimal should have asked him first. Vimal apologized, and Dinesh did not smile right away. They continued playing together afterward, but within a few years, the cinema's regular accompaniment work ended. Vimal picked up his sign-painting brushes again and also made music for a small theater troupe and at weddings.
card.presentEcho: Trying to hide something that has stopped working can make the scene even stranger. The laughter and the loss that follow the truth remain separately.
card.secondLook: The fake next scene Vimal created held the audience for a while, but it was the projection booth worker who repaired the broken film. Dinesh improvised with him and shared the burden of the docked pay.
card.unresolved: Even though the improvisation made some audience members laugh, the refunded ticket money and docked pay from that day never came back. A few years later, their regular accompaniment work also ended as the cinema screened fewer silent films.
card.readerQuestion: When something happens that we must bear together, when do I speak first to the person beside me?

signalMoments.connect: Vimal told Dinesh that the child in the front row had noticed the thief's shoe, then asked if the two of them should make the thief run once more. When Dinesh nodded, Vimal told the audience that the screening had stopped.
signalMoments.speak: Despite the owner's gesture, Vimal told the audience that the film had broken and asked them to wait while it was repaired in the projection booth. As the murmuring grew louder, he briefly asked Dinesh to play with him.

profilePages.body:
Vimal Shah · Male
1896~1970 · Age 74
Bombay Presidency, British India · Bombay
Work · Silent-film accompaniment, theater and wedding performances, and sign painting
Life · He learned sign painting beside his father and played the harmonium in a cinema. After films changed, he continued moving between other stages and painting work. He shared a household with his sister and niece, and in old age he taught children.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · In large gatherings, he tended to listen, but when he played, he smiled first and changed the rhythm.
Liked · Rounded lettering on signs that could be recognized from far away
Disliked · Playing a wrong note louder instead of correcting it
Skilled at · Changing the music to match the walking speed of the person on-screen

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · A harmonium used so long that one handle had worn smooth
People close to him · His sister Leena, his niece Tara, and the tabla player Dinesh
The life he wanted · To keep a place for both music and painting, even when his work changed
Worry · That no one would remain to play music with him

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Vimal Shah. In 1932, you played the harmonium in a small cinema in Bombay. A harmonium is a wooden instrument played by pumping air by hand and pressing keys. Silent films had music in those days too. Musicians in front of the screen watched the actors' footsteps and expressions and changed the music to match. Today, I'll tell you about the night his music ran ahead of the film.

The thief on-screen dashed beneath a market awning. Vimal pressed the harmonium keys rapidly. Beside him, Dinesh chased the thief's footsteps on the tabla, two small drums played by hand. A child in the front row perched on the edge of the seat. The door in the film seemed about to open.

Snap—a sound came from the projection booth in the back. The screen suddenly turned white, then dark. Vimal played two more measures before stopping his hands. Dinesh's hands also froze above the drums. The thief neither opened the door nor got caught.

“Why isn't he running away?” the child in the front row asked. In the back, someone shouted toward the projection booth. The cinema owner came over to Vimal and pressed his palm downward in a quieting gesture. “Keep playing while they splice the film. Don't say it's broken.” Vimal began the chase music again. But the screen was black, and the rapid music only made the audience more anxious.

Vimal looked back and forth between the owner's face and Dinesh's drums. If he kept playing, the audience would hear nothing but a chase that never ended. If he explained why it had stopped, some people might leave. The child in the front row asked again, “Where did that man's shoe go?” Just before the film broke, one of the thief's shoes had been left beneath the awning.

signalMoments.notice: Vimal realized that his hands were still playing racing music even after the white screen went dark. He took his hands off the keys. “The film has broken. Please wait a moment while they splice it back together.”
signalMoments.connect: Vimal turned to Dinesh. “That child noticed the shoe. Shall the two of us make the thief run once more?” When Dinesh nodded, Vimal told the audience that the screening had stopped.
signalMoments.speak: Despite seeing the owner's gesture, Vimal turned toward the audience. “The film has broken. Please wait while they repair it in the projection booth.” As the murmuring grew louder, he briefly asked Dinesh to play with him.

episode.afterSignal:
In the projection booth, they were splicing the film back together. Vimal asked the front row, “Then will the thief come back to look for his shoe?” The child raised a hand high. “No. He'll just keep running!” Dinesh struck the drum twice with his palm, imitating bare feet. When someone else shouted, “He's coming back!” Vimal added slow footsteps in the harmonium's low notes.

The audience split into two sides, each guessing what the thief would do next. Each time, Vimal and Dinesh changed the tempo. Even the person in the very back who had first shouted, “Give me my ticket money back!” laughed. But several audience members who went out through the door did not return. Vimal did not stretch out the performance to try to hold them there.

They heard the projection booth door open. The thief reappeared on the screen. He neither ran fast as Vimal had played nor slowly searched for his shoe. He ran out from under the awning holding one shoe in his hand, backed away, then tripped over a small cart parked behind him. The child in the front row slapped a knee and laughed. Dinesh took his hands off the drums and looked at Vimal. “The thief we made up was smarter.”

After the curtain came down, the ticket attendant handed the owner several refunded tickets. The owner deducted part of that day's lost income from the two musicians' pay. “I told you to play and not say anything.” Outside, Dinesh stopped Vimal. “You could have asked me first. My pay was cut too.” Vimal apologized. Dinesh nodded but did not smile right away. They still had to play together on other days.

The next day, Vimal played at the same cinema again. A few years later, when it almost stopped showing silent films, his regular work there ended. Vimal carried his harmonium to theater performances and weddings, and once more picked up the sign-painting brushes he had learned to use from his father. Years later, when he taught rhythm to Dinesh and the neighborhood children, someone would sometimes ask, “What if the screen stops?” Instead of answering, Vimal would take his hands off the keys and wait for the children's next sound.

finalMoment.place: A room connected to the rooftop of his sister Leena's home in Bombay
finalMoment.scene:
On a rainy afternoon during the 1970 monsoon, seventy-four-year-old Vimal is visiting his sister Leena's home. His niece Tara goes out onto the rooftop to gather the laundry as it begins to get wet. Vimal follows and picks up a shirt lying just outside the door. Inside the room, Leena prepares a late lunch. Tara hears thunder and says, “Uncle, come inside now. I'll just leave the rest.”

Still holding the unfolded shirt, Vimal turns toward the door. “All right, just this one.” Tara leaves the door open and waits for Vimal to come inside. Rainwater wets the tops of Vimal's feet. He slowly moves one foot, careful not to let his wet shoes slip on the threshold. At that moment, the sky beyond the roof opposite them flashes white.

Lightning strikes the rooftop where Vimal is standing. The tremendous sound makes the dishes inside the room rattle. Vimal drops the shirt and collapses onto the rooftop. Tara freezes on the threshold for an instant, then approaches him. “Uncle?” Vimal does not answer. Tara calls his name again, but he does not open his eyes. She cannot hear him breathing either.

Tara calls Leena from inside the room. Leena comes out and sits beside Vimal. The two speak to Vimal and check his breathing. A neighbor who heard the thunder comes upstairs and calls more people. Vimal never regains consciousness. The wet shirt Vimal dropped remains in Tara's hands. The rain continues to soak the shirt and the rooftop floor.
finalMoment.afterword: Vimal died at seventy-four in Bombay in 1970 after being struck by lightning on the rooftop of his sister Leena's home. Leena and Tara were right beside him, but they could not wake him again. For some time, Tara could not bring herself to fold the shirt from that day. Dinesh had already died four years earlier. While alive, he said he resented what happened in 1932, when Vimal failed to consult him and caused him to lose part of his pay, yet the two continued playing together for many years. Leena remembered the days her brother often came over for meals even while living alone. The record of his past life closes Vimal's story by preserving the years he spent painting, playing music, and living among family and colleagues—years that lasted longer than a single frozen scene in a film.
finalMoment.artAlt: A rainy afternoon in Bombay in 1970, viewed from inside a room in his sister's home through the open rooftop door. Seventy-four-year-old Vimal is about to come inside carrying a wet shirt, while his forty-five-year-old niece Tara watches from within the doorway. Lightning flashes beyond the rooftop

card.name: Sari
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Sari of Semarang. You learned batik from your mother, shared cloth orders with Lati, and made a home with your husband and daughter. After your eyes began to tire, you taught young workers.
card.title: The Hand Frozen in the Photograph
card.role: Worker who drew designs on batik cloth
card.world: 1866, Semarang, Java, Dutch East Indies
card.flavor: If you stay still, the cloth will be ruined
card.opening: The photographer told everyone not to move. But hot wax was about to drip from the tip of Mother's copper pen onto the cloth.
card.life: Sari learned batik from her mother, Warsi, and drew designs on cloth with her neighbor Lati. When her husband Darso fell ill, she took on more work to support the household, and she stayed at the workshop even after her daughter Mina chose different work. In old age, she drew fewer fine lines and taught young workers.
card.turn: While photographing the workshop, the photographer told Warsi to hold still with her tool in hand. When Warsi moved her hand just as the wax was about to drip onto the cloth, the photographer said he would leave her out of the next photograph.
card.decision: Sari said she did not want a photograph without her mother, set down her pen, and asked to take it again. She asked what Warsi wanted and said she would pay for the extra glass plate out of her own fee for posing.
card.cost: Warsi remained in the photograph, but the three women's ordered cloth was late. Even though Lati calculated the time and finished the cloth, the customer reduced the price. Sari also paid for the extra photograph, leaving her with the smallest share that day.
card.after: Sari and Lati later moved to a larger workshop. Her daughter Mina chose market bookkeeping instead of batik. After Sari's eyes began to tire, Lati, who had kept track of orders and schedules, took charge of the workshop, while Sari taught beginners how to use the tools.
card.presentEcho: Some scenes survive only because someone's hands are made to stop. We can also remember the work that continued outside the frame.
card.secondLook: Warsi thought the ordered cloth was more urgent than the photograph, while the photographer thought it wasteful to lose a glass plate and the sunlight. Lati was also paid less because the cloth was late, but she counted the money again and divided it among the three of them.
card.unresolved: Even though Warsi's image remained in the photograph, it did not capture the patterns her fingertips had been making or the price they lost because the cloth was late.
card.readerQuestion: When I try to preserve one scene, will I also notice who is spending their time outside its frame?

signalMoments.notice: Sari pointed to a spot of hardened wax on the cloth and told the photographer that wax would drip if they merely held the pens still. She asked him to let them set down their pens and take the photograph again, offering to pay for the new glass plate out of her own fee for posing.
signalMoments.protect: Sari folded the ordered cloth to move it away from where more wax might drip. She said they could not throw the cloth away and asked the photographer to let the pen cool, then photograph them again with Warsi. She paid for the new glass plate out of her own fee for posing.
signalMoments.speak: When Warsi started toward the shade, Sari told the photographer that the ordered cloth would be ruined if Warsi did not move. She asked him to let them put down their pens and take the photograph again, offering to pay for the extra glass plate out of her own fee for posing.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small copper pen her mother Warsi used
Those closest to her · Her mother Warsi, husband Darso, daughter Mina, and neighbor Lati
The life she wanted · To leave time for dinner with her family even on days when there was work
