episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Sari. In 1866, you drew batik cloth with your mother in Semarang on the island of Java. Making batik means drawing lines in wax on cloth and then dyeing it. The dye does not soak into the places touched by wax, so when the wax is later removed, a pattern appears. Today, I will tell you about an afternoon when three women stopped their hands for a single photograph.

Long lengths of white cloth hung across the veranda. Sari filled a small copper pen with melted wax and continued a line across the cloth. Beside her, Lati folded finished cloth and counted the days until the orders were due. “We have to finish two more by tomorrow morning.” Sari was about to answer when a man carrying a large wooden box entered from the yard.

The man was a photographer. He said he wanted to photograph batik work in Semarang and had already arranged it with the owner of the workshop. He set his camera on a tripod and moved the cloth into the sunlight. Because they would be paid for the time away from their work, Sari and Lati briefly stopped their hands. “I'll finish drawing the edge,” Warsi said, keeping hold of her pen at the side.

The photographer looked at Warsi and shook his head. “Sit just like that. Keep holding the pen, too. You must not move until I tell you.” Warsi glanced at her daughter. The copper pen's narrow spout held hot wax. If she kept it poised over one place too long, the wax could suddenly drip where it was not wanted. Sari nearly said so, but when she saw the ordered cloth spread out before the camera, she closed her mouth.

The photographer ducked his head beneath the black cloth. “Now.” Warsi held her hand still for a while. Soon, a tiny drop swelled at the tip of the pen. Drip. Warsi quickly moved her hand. The wax hardened in an empty corner of the cloth, and the photographer frowned as he removed the glass plate. “Your hand moved. Next time, I'll take the photograph without you.” He pointed Warsi toward the shade beyond the veranda.

signalMoments.notice: Sari touched the spot of hardened wax on the cloth with her fingertip. “This is what happens if we just hold them still.” She asked the photographer to let them put down their pens and take the photograph again. When he said using a new glass plate would cost more, Sari offered to pay for it out of her own fee for posing.
signalMoments.protect: Sari quickly folded the ordered cloth to move it away from wax that might drip from the pen. “We can't throw this cloth away. Please let the pen cool and take the photograph again with my mother.” When the photographer said someone would have to pay for a new glass plate, she gave up her own fee for posing.
signalMoments.speak: Sari did not block Warsi as she started to leave for the shade, but spoke to the photographer. “If Mother doesn't move, this cloth will be ruined. Can't we put down the pens and take the photograph again?” When the photographer asked who would pay for the extra glass plate, Sari said she would cover it with her own fee for posing.

episode.afterSignal:
Warsi answered first. “I don't need to be in the photograph. Let's finish the cloth.” Sari did not hold her mother back. “I don't want a photograph that leaves out the person who drew lines on this cloth today. But if you don't want to, Mother, we won't take it again.” Warsi looked down at the pen and the cloth, then laughed. “Then where should I put this? I can't do it if he tells me to hold it again.”

The photographer grumbled that the sunlight would soon shift. Lati placed the fully cooled pen on a dish beside the cloth. “You can sit over there,” Sari told Warsi. Warsi nodded. This time, no one stopped with a pen poised over the cloth. As the photographer prepared a new glass plate, he muttered, “It's a photograph of people working, but everyone has put down their hands.” When Warsi said, “A moment ago, you told us to stop our working hands,” Lati lowered her head to hide her laughter.

While they took the photograph again, the shadows in front of the house grew long. Only after the photographer left did the three women refill their pens with wax. Sari carefully scraped away the drop that had hardened earlier. Even so, a small, unintended spot remained. Lati unfolded the ordered cloth and calculated the time. “We can finish it by tonight. But it will be hard to dry it by tomorrow morning.” Sari decided not to force the cloth into a fold.

The next day, Sari and Lati delivered the cloth later than they had promised. The customer cared more about the time spent waiting than the wax mark and reduced the price. Lati returned home and placed the remaining money in front of Sari. “There were three of us in the photograph. All three of us finished late. But you're the one who paid for the new plate.” Sari said, “I was the first to ask for it.” Lati counted the day's earnings again and divided the money among the three of them. Sari's share was the smallest.

The photograph arrived a few weeks later. Sari did not find Warsi right away because Warsi was sitting at the edge of the photograph with her hands resting on her knees. She almost never sat like that. “That doesn't look like me. It looks like someone resting,” Warsi said. Mina looked back and forth between her mother and grandmother, then pointed toward the bottom of the photograph. “The lines Grandmother drew are here.” The cloth was spread out in front of her knees. Warsi brought the photograph closer and studied it.

In the years that followed, Sari and Lati still argued and laughed over order dates. The two moved their workshop to a wider veranda. When Mina grew up, she chose market bookkeeping instead of batik, and Sari did not try to pass her work on to her daughter. After Sari's eyes began to tire easily, Lati, who had always kept track of orders and dates, ran the workshop. There, Sari showed young workers how to hold the tools. That photograph did not contain even a full day's work. Still, it preserved the place where Warsi had sat and one piece of cloth the three women had spread out together.

finalMoment.place: Sari's home in Semarang, Dutch East Indies
finalMoment.scene:
On a clear morning in 1896, 61-year-old Sari sits alone inside her home in Semarang. 10 days ago, a piece of bamboo pierced the sole of her foot in the backyard. The wound was small, but for the past few days her jaw has been stiff, making it hard to chew. Her husband Darso has briefly gone out to fetch their daughter Mina. Sari looks at the bowl of water on the floor and tries to drink even a sip.

Sari pulls the bowl closer and opens her mouth. Her jaw will not open as she wants it to. When she forces down some water, her throat constricts, and she sets the bowl down. “Darso.” She tries to call him, but the name comes out garbled. Sari grips a folded, thin quilt. Her body suddenly stiffens from her neck to her back, and both hands pull hard on the fabric.

She hears Darso and Mina's footsteps outside the door. Darso enters the room and says, “I'm here.” Sari tries to turn her head, but her muscles stiffen again. Mina sits in front of her mother. “Did you drink a little water?” Instead of nodding, Sari moves her eyes toward the bowl. When she tries to straighten her back, her body shudders again and again, and it becomes difficult to draw breath.

Darso calls her name. Mina also asks, “Mother, can you hear me?” Sari tries to release the quilt in her hands, but her fingers will not straighten. When the tension briefly eases, she opens her mouth and tries to breathe. But her throat constricts again, and her chest does not move. Darso bends close to Sari's face. They both keep calling to her, but she no longer answers.
finalMoment.afterword: Sari died at age 61 in her home in Semarang in 1896, after a wound to the sole of her foot was followed by stiffness in her jaw and body and difficulty breathing. This course resembles tetanus, but no record confirms Sari's illness. Darso and their daughter Mina were with her at the end. It took Mina a long time to tell her own child that Grandmother had died. Lati saw Sari's empty place at the workshop, but she did not turn the pay they had lost together in 1866 into a fond memory. Darso remembered how Sari used to correct his handwriting while they looked over the ledgers together. The Chronicle of Past Lives closes this life by preserving Sari's family, her workshop, and their differing memories—a story longer than a single photograph.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high, diagonal view from near the ceiling of a room in Sari's Semarang home in 1896. 61-year-old Sari sits upright, gripping a thin quilt in both hands as spasms seize her body and jaw. A bowl of water sits beside her, and no one else is visible

card.name: Matteo Belli
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Matteo Belli of Venice. You took over your father's boat, rowed a gondola, and raised a family. After handing the boat on, you helped Lucia with her market work.
card.title: The Masked Passenger
card.world: The 1722 Carnival in the Republic of Venice
card.flavor: Two passengers, one boat
card.opening: A passenger in a black cloak held out some money. The low voice was unfamiliar, but the red knot on the basket handle was the one Matteo had tied the night before.
card.life: Matteo learned to row a gondola from his father and carried passengers. He and Lucia raised Rosa and Carlo, and he kept rowing long after paying off the debt from repairing the boat. When his wrists grew weak, he handed the boat to a younger gondolier and helped at Lucia's vegetable stall.
card.turn: Matteo had planned to take Lucia out in the boat on the afternoon of Carnival, but he accepted a merchant's cargo booking. Then Lucia appeared as a masked passenger, followed by the merchant with his cargo.
card.decision: Matteo told the merchant he could not take him and asked his fellow gondolier Angelo to carry the cargo. He paid Angelo's share out of his own fare.
card.cost: He earned less that day, and the merchant gave his next two trips to Angelo as well. One afternoon with Lucia did not erase all the promises Matteo had put off over the years.
card.after: Matteo rowed his gondola for many years, but when his wrists began to hurt, he handed the boat to a young gondolier. At Lucia's expanded market stall, he kept the accounts and ran errands with his granddaughter.
card.presentEcho: When promises to spend time together keep getting postponed, someone may end up waiting in line like a customer.
card.secondLook: Lucia closed her vegetable stall early and paid the fare as well. Angelo took the heavy crates instead and accepted the fare Matteo added. Before setting off, he checked the weight of the crates first.
card.unresolved: Even after that boat outing, Matteo did not always keep his promises on busy days. For a while, the merchant sought out other boats.
card.readerQuestion: While I kept saying I was busy, how did the person waiting for me spend the day?

signalMoments.notice: Matteo recognized the masked passenger as Lucia when he saw the red knot he had tied on her basket the night before. After telling Angelo he would add money from his own fare if Angelo carried the merchant's crates instead, Matteo told the merchant that the person he had promised first had arrived.
signalMoments.connect: Matteo hailed Angelo's empty boat and told the merchant that it could take him to Rialto, and that Matteo would pay the extra cost. Then he asked the masked Lucia if he could carry her basket.
signalMoments.speak: Matteo told the merchant that he had pretended to forget a promise he had made to his family first that morning. When he said Angelo could carry the cargo and that he would pay the difference, the merchant pointed to Angelo's boat with a displeased look.

identity.region: Venice, Republic of Venice
identity.summary: He learned to row a gondola from his father and raised his children with Lucia. After handing on the boat, he grew old helping Lucia with her market work.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was He?
profilePages.body:
Matteo Belli · Male
1690~1759 · 69 years old
Republic of Venice · Venice
Work · Gondolier; helped at a market stall in old age
Life · He learned to handle a boat from his father and carried passengers for many years. He and Lucia raised two children and paid off the debt from repairing the boat. After the children chose their own paths, his wrists weakened, so he handed on the boat and helped at Lucia's vegetable stall.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was He Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · Quick to make decisions on the water, but often put promises at home off until later.
Liked · Quiet waterways in the early morning with no passengers
Disliked · Passengers who hid the weight of their luggage before boarding
Good at · Turning the boat in narrow waterways without collisions

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The old wooden oar his father left him
Those closest to him · His wife Lucia, daughter Rosa, son Carlo, and fellow gondolier Angelo
The life he wanted · To honor both his days on the boat and his days with his family
Worry · That his boat might break down or his wrists might weaken and cost him his livelihood

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Matteo Belli. You rowed a gondola in Venice in 1722. During Carnival that year, masked people gathered in Piazza San Marco. It was a day when no one could clearly tell who anyone was. Now I'll tell you about an afternoon when one masked passenger made Matteo count his fare again.

Matteo moored his boat at the stone steps by the water. A merchant was due shortly with two heavy crates. Carnival brought many passengers, and that fare would let Matteo set aside a little money for boat repairs. That morning, Lucia had said, “Let's take the children out in the boat today,” but Matteo had replied, “After I move this one load.” Lucia had heard those words many times before.

A passenger in a black cloak and white mask appeared on the steps. The passenger carried a market basket. “To Rialto. And please come back slowly.” The voice was slightly lowered. Matteo named the fare. When the passenger set down the basket, he saw a red cord tied around its handle. It was the very knot Matteo had tied the night before to hold the split handle together.

Matteo looked again at the masked face. It had to be Lucia. He began to ask, “Why are you here like a passenger...?” but stopped. The merchant was approaching from the other direction, carrying one of the crates. Matteo's promise to give Lucia the afternoon had been left at home, while his promise to move the merchant's cargo had followed him here. The merchant reached out to place the crate inside the boat.

“Aren't you both going to Rialto?” the merchant asked. But with crates that heavy and another passenger aboard, the small boat would be packed tight. Besides, Lucia had asked to take the return trip slowly. In the distance, Matteo saw his fellow gondolier Angelo returning with an empty boat. If Matteo gave up some of his own money, Angelo could take the merchant's cargo. Just then, the masked passenger picked up her basket again. “If your boat isn't available, I'll try somewhere else.”

signalMoments.notice: Matteo looked again at the red knot on the basket. Lucia's hand rested on it. He raised a hand to Angelo. “Will you take the merchant's crates instead? I'll make up your share.” When the merchant asked why he was suddenly changing the arrangement, Matteo said that someone else he had promised had arrived.
signalMoments.connect: Matteo hailed Angelo's empty boat and explained the situation to the merchant. “Angelo will take you to Rialto. I'll pay the extra cost.” Then he held out a hand to the masked passenger. “May I carry that basket?”
signalMoments.speak: Matteo did not falter in front of the merchant. “I had another promise first. I pretended to forget it this morning. Angelo can carry your cargo, and I'll pay the difference.” The merchant pointed to Angelo's boat with a displeased look.

episode.afterSignal:
The merchant pressed his lips together for a moment. “Just don't keep me waiting.” Angelo rowed over. Matteo helped transfer the two crates to his boat, then gave Angelo part of the fare he had been promised. Angelo looked at the masked passenger and the red basket, then at Matteo's face. “So that's how an empty boat finally became available.” There was amusement in his voice, but he checked the weight of the crates first before setting off.

Lucia boarded the boat. Matteo took up the oar. For a while, neither of them mentioned the mask. When the drums from San Marco had faded and only the sound of water remained, Lucia spoke first. “Whenever I ask you at home, it always has to wait until your work is done. I thought if I came as a passenger, maybe I could ride now.” Matteo slowed his strokes. “I knew it was you from the knot. But I still took your money.” Lucia placed the basket between her knees. “I work at the market too. I paid for this boat ride with my own share today.”

Matteo tried to return her coins. Lucia shook her head. “It isn't that I don't want you to take my money. I just wanted you to understand how many times I've waited.” Matteo closed his hand around the money again. Coins were not the only debt he owed. But he did not want to give a long string of excuses while rowing, either. As he turned the boat toward Rialto, he asked, “What do you want to see first?”

“Under the bridge we first crossed with the children.” Lucia removed her mask. Matteo rowed slowly along the waterway. Beneath the bridge, they discovered that they remembered that long-ago day differently. Matteo said Rosa had cried, while Lucia said Matteo had been the one crying. Little Carlo, on his first boat ride, had dropped his hat into the water. When Matteo insisted that was not true, Lucia laughed. This time, while their boat passed beneath the bridge, he stopped rowing and let them linger, listening to the current.

Lucia's sister and the children were waiting on the steps across the water. “Papa, it's our turn!” Rosa cried, trying to leap into the boat first. Matteo took her hand and helped her aboard slowly. Lucia showed him the empty basket and said, “I closed the market early too. So all four of us could ride.” Only then did Matteo realize that Lucia had taken time away from her own work that day as well. Carlo wanted to touch the oar, but Matteo chose instead to seat the little boy on his lap.

That day's earnings were lower than usual. The merchant rode in Angelo's boat two more times afterward. Matteo and Lucia still argued again whenever the days grew busy. Later, pain in Matteo's wrists made him cut back on long trips, and eventually he handed the boat to a younger man. Lucia expanded her vegetable stall at Rialto, and Matteo spent more days there keeping the accounts. One afternoon without masks did not repair every day of their marriage. Still, they always remembered exactly the same place their boat had gone that day.

finalMoment.place: A narrow path beside a waterway near the Rialto market in Venice
finalMoment.scene:
It is an early autumn evening in 1759 near Venice's Rialto market, after the rain. Sixty-nine-year-old Matteo leaves his wife Lucia's vegetable stall first and walks home. Lucia is still closing the stall. Tied at Matteo's waist is a small pouch containing the day's earnings. He no longer rows a boat as he did when he was young, but he continues to help with the market accounts and errands. As he turns onto a narrow path beside a waterway, he hears footsteps following behind him.

A stranger blocks the path and shows him a small knife. “Hand over the money.” Matteo tries to untie the pouch. His weakened wrists keep his fingers from moving quickly. “I'll give it to you, but wait.” The stranger grabs the pouch and pulls. The cord catches around Matteo's hand. As he pulls his hand free, the point of the knife stabs his side. A door closes in the distance, and the stranger drops the pouch and vanishes at the end of the alley.

Matteo braces one hand against the wall and presses the other to his side. Something warm spreads beneath his shirt. He can see the lamps toward the market, but he does not know if he can walk that far. He sees a single coin left on the stone pavement. Rather than bending to pick it up, he leans against the wall and catches his breath. “Is anyone there?” His first call is drowned by the sound of water in the canal.

Matteo calls toward the market once more. At the end of the path, someone who had been closing a door turns around. When the person comes closer, Matteo says, “Lucia is at the market.” He tries to explain more, but his breath grows short. The strength leaves the hand pressed to his side. He looks from the wet stones at his feet to the distant lights, and his knees buckle. He tries to rise again, but his arm cannot push him away from the wall. His breathing stops before he can say another word.
finalMoment.afterword: Matteo died at the age of sixty-nine in 1759 after being stabbed by a robber on a path near Venice's Rialto market. It is not known whether the robber was caught. Lucia came when she heard the news, but a passerby delivered Matteo's final words to her. She remembered both their later years selling vegetables and keeping accounts together, and the days when he had come home late while he was still rowing a boat. His daughter Rosa did not forget her father's absences, while his son Carlo remembered that his father had not forced him to work on boats. A single outing in 1722 did not mend every promise made to the family. The record of this past life ends here, setting down Lucia's work beside Matteo's, along with the family's time as each of them remembered it differently.
finalMoment.artAlt: A low-angle view near the surface of a Venetian waterway in 1759, looking toward a narrow path. Sixty-nine-year-old Matteo stands alone, bracing himself against a wall as he presses a hand to his stabbed side. A dropped coin pouch lies on the wet stone pavement, and the lights of the Rialto market glow in the distance.

card.name: Tochtli
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Tochtli of Xochimilco. You raised a family on a chinampa and divided a field with your younger brother. After his knees began to hurt, he taught his daughter Ama, who lived in a separate home, how to plant seeds.
card.title: Half the Field
card.world: The lake fields of Xochimilco in 1490
card.flavor: Land divided in half, only one place to dock the boat
card.opening: Tochtli measured the field into two exact halves. But his brother's half had no path for carrying the harvest to the boat.
card.life: Tochtli learned to farm the lake fields from his parents. He made a home with Itzel and their two children, and shared the work of the waterways with his younger brother Tlalli and his friend Acalli. After his knees began to hurt, he taught his daughter Ama, who lived in a separate home, how to plant seeds.
card.turn: After their father died, Tlalli wanted to decide for himself what to plant in the long field the brothers had worked together. Tochtli measured the field in half, but his brother's share was cut off from the docking place at the front.
card.decision: Tochtli decided to remove a row of his own corn to make a path, and Tlalli gave up space in front of the boat for turning around. Together, they moved the stakes and made the path themselves.
card.cost: Both men lost some of the corn they had planted, and the harvest was smaller that year. Even after making the path, the brothers still disagreed about which days to work and what to plant in the field.
card.after: Tlalli grew other crops on his share, while Tochtli continued farming along the same canal as he raised his children with Itzel. In old age, he did less work by the water.
card.presentEcho: Even when something is divided equally, one person may need more of a path to be able to use it.
card.secondLook: Tlalli wanted to move his own harvest without asking his brother's permission every time. While the brothers measured the field, Itzel saw to the household meals and the children.
card.unresolved: The narrow path was made, but the next year the brothers still had to clear mud from the waterway together and decide their workdays all over again.
card.readerQuestion: When dividing something once shared, would you have considered the paths and time as well?

Tlalli pointed to the young shoots on his own share in front of the boat.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured · A short wooden planting stick from his father
Those closest to him · His younger brother Tlalli, his partner Itzel, their two children Micho and Ama, and his friend Acalli
The life he wanted · A life in which the harvest fed his family and the children chose their own work
Worry · That the canal would become blocked or that painful knees would keep him from working by the water

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Tochtli. Long ago, in 1490, you farmed a field beside a canal in Xochimilco. The people there piled up soil from the lake to make long fields, then floated boats along narrow waterways to carry their harvests. Today, I'll tell you about the day Tochtli measured a field into two exact halves, only to pull up the stakes again.

Tochtli drove a wooden stick into the mud. He counted his steps from there to the far end, then returned and planted another stick in the middle. It marked the place where the long field the brothers had once tended together was divided into front and back halves. For 2 years after their father died, Tochtli's younger brother Tlalli had planted seeds on the days Tochtli chose and harvested when Tochtli decided. This year, he said he wanted to decide for himself what to plant on his share.

“Half is yours.” Tochtli tapped the center stake. Tlalli walked past it toward the rear. New corn leaves brushed his knees. Tochtli had taken the front section, where the boat was tied. At the water's edge, Itzel held up a water jug and waved it at the two men. They both raised a hand, but Tlalli did not come over for a drink.

After midday, Tlalli lifted a sack of corn. It was not yet a fully ripened harvest. “Let's see how I'll get this out in the fall,” Tlalli said. Trying to reach the boat from the back of his land, he stepped between the rows of Tochtli's corn. Large leaves snagged on the sack, snapping the stalks. Tochtli blocked his way. “That side is my half.” Tlalli lowered the sack. “Then where's the path from my half to the boat?”

Tochtli tried walking along the edge of the field. On one side stretched deep mud and a line of driven stakes; on the other stood corn as tall as his shoulders. There was no way around to the place where the boat was tied. The field had been measured equally, but the line dividing front from back also stopped the feet of the man behind it. Tochtli said, “I'll load your sacks for you at harvest time.” Tlalli answered at once. “Then it isn't really divided. I'll have to wait again until you have time.”

Tochtli gripped his father's short planting stick, then loosened his hand. If he removed one row of corn that had already sprouted, there would be less to feed his family of 4. Tochtli had tended that corn all spring, watching the water. Tlalli also pointed to a small patch in front of the boat. “I'll clear the shoots on my side here too. We need at least this much room to turn around with a sack.” Then Itzel held out an empty sack to the two men. “Carry it and try walking the route. If you decide with words alone, you'll miss something again.”

signalMoments.notice: Tochtli carried an empty sack from the rear stake to the boat. His shoulder caught on the corn stalks, and his foot sank into the mud. He set his stick down across one row on his side. “Let's clear this.” Tlalli pointed by hand to the young shoots on his share in front of the boat.
signalMoments.connect: Tochtli asked Itzel to carry the sack and walk ahead. Wherever Itzel's feet came to a stop, he drove in a stick. Acalli also stepped down from the boat and showed them how much space they needed to load the sack. Tochtli agreed to remove one row of his corn, and Tlalli agreed to make room in front of the boat for turning the sack.
signalMoments.speak: Tochtli told Tlalli, “I thought measuring the same length was enough. I didn't ask how you would move your harvest.” Pointing to the row of corn on his share, he said he would make a path. Tlalli said he would also remove his own shoots in front of the boat to make room for turning the sack.

episode.afterSignal:
Tochtli pulled up the first stalk. Its roots were deeper than he had expected. When the soil rose with it, he laid the stalk back down and packed the edge with mud carried up from the water. Tlalli also removed the still-small shoots from the docking place at the front. Itzel and Acalli piled everything the two men pulled up in one place. A green scent spread over the water.

The path was too narrow for 2 people to walk side by side, but wide enough for 1 person carrying a sack on his back. As a test, Tlalli shouldered the sack and walked from the rear field. Tochtli pulled up his own stake that stood at the front and moved it to the side. The boat rocked a little when Tlalli set the sack down in it. “Now you can get here,” Itzel said.

Tlalli picked up the empty sack again. “I told you about this path from the very beginning.” Tochtli searched for an answer, but only brushed the dirt from his palm. Tlalli was right. It was not that Tochtli had failed to hear him; he had believed that once he measured the field in half, there was no need to listen to anything else. “Yes,” Tochtli finally said. Tlalli did not laugh loudly or embrace him. Instead, he pressed the new stake into the ground once more.

That evening, Micho and Ama came running to the field. The children were surprised to see the cleared row. “Where did the corn go?” Tochtli answered, “We'll eat a little less this year.” Itzel had the children tie up and carry the small stalks. Tlalli returned to his rear field and pointed with his finger to the place he would plant next. Tochtli did not like the spot, but he held his tongue. Tlalli was now the one who decided what happened on that land.

Both brothers had a slightly smaller harvest that year. The following year, they still had to clear mud from the waterway together, and they sometimes argued over their workdays. Even so, Tlalli walked to the boat on his own feet, carrying his sack. Years later, Tochtli's son learned boat work, and his daughter Ama made a home elsewhere. After painful knees made Tochtli cut back on work by the water, he placed the planting stick in Ama's hand at her separate home and showed her how to plant seeds. The empty row where they pulled up the corn that day had long since turned green again, but the narrow path the brothers made together remained.

finalMoment.place: Tochtli's home in Xochimilco under Mexica rule
finalMoment.scene:
During the day in 1510, 58-year-old Tochtli picks up an outer garment inside his Xochimilco home. Itzel, who lives with him, is in the courtyard, and their adult daughter Ama, who lives separately, has come to visit and is talking with Itzel. Tochtli has cut back on work by the water because of his painful knees, but he still walks around the house alone. Just as he is about to step through the doorway, he hears dry wood splitting above his head.

Tochtli looks up. One end of a beam supporting the roof sags, and woven reeds spill through the gap. “Get outside!” Itzel shouts from the courtyard. Tochtli turns toward the door. His painful knee makes his next step a moment too slow. As he raises an arm to cover his head, the beam strikes his chest hard. The packed earth beneath his feet jolts, and he falls sideways.

Tochtli opens his eyes and hears Itzel's voice. He cannot turn his body because the wood lies across his chest. The spot hurts each time he tries to draw a short breath. Ama comes through the doorway and grabs the end of the beam, but the wood does not move. Itzel calls to a neighbor across the courtyard to help lift it. Tochtli says to his daughter, “Watch your hands.” Only then does Ama see that her father's eyes are open.

A neighbor arrives and lifts the end of the beam with Itzel. Ama clears away the reeds that fell beside Tochtli's body. Even after the wood is removed, he cannot get up. Tochtli turns his head slightly, trying to see the sunlight outside the door. He tries to breathe in, but his chest cannot move enough. Itzel calls his name, and Ama also waits for an answer. After Tochtli's gaze grows still, there is no more sound of breathing.
finalMoment.afterword: Tochtli died at age 58 in 1510 after a collapsing roof beam struck his chest in his Xochimilco home. Itzel and his adult daughter Ama were beside him, but they could not save him. No one knows why the accident happened that day. His younger brother Tlalli came when he heard the news. Only the day before, he had argued with his brother about their turns working on the waterway, and he remembered the day his brother had been slow to understand what he needed. Ama used the farming methods her father taught her while making her own decisions about her household. Itzel said that Tochtli did not change his mind at home as quickly as he did in the field. This record of a past life closes the story by noting both the family's time together and the disputes that remained between the division of a field and a sudden end.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view from a steep angle above, just before a light wood-and-reed roof collapses in Xochimilco in 1510. 58-year-old Tochtli stands alone, looking up at the splitting beam with 1 hand raised. Sunlight enters through the open doorway leading to the courtyard

card.name: Mele
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Mele of Apia. You loaded fruit onto a boat to sell at the harbor and lived with your older sister and nephew. After the storm, you sometimes carried fruit on foot, and when wrist pain forced you to cut back on boat work, you taught a young neighbor.
card.title: The Cut Mooring Line
card.world: The Great Storm in Apia, Samoa, in 1889
card.flavor: One Oar and One Nephew
card.opening: In the storm, Peni ran to Mele's boat to retrieve his father's oar. When the next wave came, it seemed the sea would drag away even his arm, tangled in the line.
card.life: Mele learned the fruit-boat trade from her father and spent many years going back and forth to the harbor. She lived with her older sister, Sina, and her nephew, Peni, and after losing her boat in the storm, she and her neighbor Alipa obtained another small boat. Once, she loaded only her own fruit first, causing Alipa to miss his chance to sell. After her wrist began to hurt, she taught others how to choose fruit rather than working on the boat.
card.turn: During the storm that struck Apia Harbor in 1889, Mele's fruit boat bucked on the beach. Peni grabbed the boat's line to retrieve the oar that had belonged to his late father, and a large wave wrapped the line around his wrist.
card.decision: Mele cut the line holding the boat she worked from and pulled Peni out of the water. With Sina, she took Peni to higher ground.
card.cost: The boat broke apart, and Peni's father's oar disappeared. With no boat, Mele spent several years selecting fruit and carrying it on foot to the harbor. Peni was angry that Mele had abandoned the oar, and after that, he did not bring up the storm first.
card.after: Mele selected and carried fruit grown by relatives inland, then obtained another small boat with Alipa. She also once loaded only her own fruit onto their shared boat first, delaying Alipa's sales. Peni grew up and left to find his own work, then returned, and the two lived in separate houses.
card.presentEcho: Peni remembered the day he was rescued and the day his father's oar was lost as the same day. Later, Alipa also remembered the day his fruit was pushed aside on their shared boat.
card.secondLook: To Peni, the oar was something his late father had used. Alongside her younger sister, who had saved her son, Sina worried about how the three of them would make a living after losing the boat, and she carried fruit baskets.
card.unresolved: The oar never returned, and it took several years to buy another boat. For a while, Peni did not bring up the storm first.
card.readerQuestion: If you saved someone but caused them to lose something precious, how would you begin the conversation afterward?

signalMoments.notice: Mele saw that the line had wrapped twice around Peni's wrist and that there was no time to untie the knot. She cut the line on the boat's side with her knife, and when Sina reached out, she pushed Peni up onto the beach.
signalMoments.protect: Mele looked away from the boat and pulled Peni's body toward her first. When the line drew taut, she cut it with her knife, and while the boat spun away, she checked whether Peni could stand.
signalMoments.connect: Mele shouted to Sina that she would cut the line and told her to grab Peni. When Sina caught Peni beneath the arms, Mele cut the line, and together they dragged him up onto the high sandbank.

setting.polity: Pre-partition Samoa, amid civil war and foreign intervention

identity.region: Apia, Upolu Island, pre-partition Samoa
identity.summary: She learned the boat trade from her father and lived with her older sister, Sina, and her nephew, Peni. After the storm, she obtained another boat with Alipa, but by using their shared boat first for herself, she caused Alipa a loss. After Sina died, she lived alone and kept in touch with Peni.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Mele · Female
1857–1913 · Age 56
Near Apia, Upolu Island, Samoa
Work · Loading fruit onto a boat, taking it to the harbor, and selling it
Life · She learned from her father how to handle a narrow boat. She lived with her older sister, Sina, and her nephew, Peni. After losing her boat in the great storm, she and her neighbor Alipa obtained another small boat. Once, trying to sell her own fruit first, she delayed loading Alipa's fruit and caused him a loss. After her sister died, she lived alone. Her nephew asked her to live with him, but she remained in her own home.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She made quick decisions at sea. But even after buying a shared boat, she tried to load her own fruit first.
Liked · Ripe fruit shared with her older sister before setting out for the harbor
Disliked · Customers who took fruit and promised to pay later
Good at · Moving baskets in a rocking little boat without getting them wet

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured possession · A small fruit basket inherited from her father
People close to her · Her older sister Sina, her nephew Peni, and her neighbor Alipa, who gathered fruit with her
Life she wanted · To continue working at the harbor while giving Peni room to choose his own path
Worry · That the boat would be damaged or her wrist would hurt too much to load fruit

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Mele. In 1889, Mele launched a small boat in Apia Harbor, Samoa, and sold fruit. That March, a great storm smashed many boats in the harbor. Let me tell you what happened the day the boat Mele was trying to protect and her sister's son ended up hanging from the same line.

The raindrops had grown heavy by the afternoon. Mele carried every fruit basket inside the house, then returned to the beach. Her boat was still tied to a wooden stake. One old oar remained inside. It had belonged to Peni's father. He had died six years earlier, and 16-year-old Peni had learned to row with that oar in his hands.

“Leave the boat. Let's get to higher ground,” Mele said. Her older sister Sina called to Peni from near the house. But Peni was already running toward the water. “I'll just get the oar!” He grabbed the boat's line while standing in water up to his knees. When Mele followed him, she saw a large ship in the distant harbor being shoved sideways by the wind. The roar of the wind drowned out Sina's shouts.

Peni stretched into the boat, but his hand could not reach the end of the oar. A wave lifted the boat high. Just as Peni tried to release the line, the wet rope wrapped around his wrist. The knot at the stake had loosened, and the boat was being dragged toward the sea. Mele seized Peni's arm. Even the boy's body slid one step forward. If the line slipped free now, the boat would not be the only thing swept away.

Mele drew a small knife from her waistband. She had lost count of how many cords around bundles of fruit she had cut with it. If she cut the boat's line, she would also lose her way of taking fruit to the harbor tomorrow. Sina reached out from higher up the beach. “Peni first!” Peni raised his aching wrist and shook his head. “My father's oar is in there.” The boat surged upward again. Mele's heels came loose from the sand.

Mele looked at the oar once. She knew how angry Peni would be without it. But if the line tightened around his wrist before the water rose again, there might be no one left to be angry. Mele slipped the knife blade beneath the wet line.

signalMoments.notice: Mele confirmed that the line had wrapped twice around Peni's wrist. There was no time to untie the knot by his wrist. Mele set the knife against the line on the boat's side and slashed with all her strength. When Sina reached out, Mele pushed Peni up onto the beach.
signalMoments.protect: Mele looked away from her boat and pulled Peni's body toward her first. When the line drew taut, she cut it with her knife. While the boat spun on the water, Mele checked whether Peni could stand.
signalMoments.connect: Mele shouted toward Sina. “I'll cut the line. You grab Peni!” The instant Sina caught Peni beneath the arms, the knife sliced through the line. Together, the two women dragged Peni up onto the high sandbank.

episode.afterSignal:
The severed end of the line lashed over the water like a snake. The boat spun once, then vanished beyond a wave. Mele did not chase it. With Sina, she took Peni to higher ground above the beach. Peni rubbed the red marks left on his wrist and stared only at the sea. “What about the oar?” Before Mele could answer, the next wave hid the boat.

Still in their wet clothes, the three of them moved to a relative's house farther inland. All night, they heard rain hammering the roof and trees snapping outside. Peni refused the warm water Mele offered him. “Aunt Mele abandoned Father's oar,” Peni said, looking at Sina. Sina lowered her head, exhaustion on her face. Mele swallowed the words, “But you're alive and here.” Those words would not bring the oar back.

The next morning, shattered large ships could be seen in the harbor. Mele's small boat was also found on a distant stretch of sand with its side broken open. The oar was gone. Mele untied and took the basket cords that remained inside the boat. Much later, Peni walked over and examined the broken side. Together they turned over pieces of wood, but they did not find the oar.

For several days, Mele searched for a way to sell fruit without a boat. Alipa introduced her to work selecting fruit grown by relatives inland. Because the job included carrying it on foot to the harbor, the pay was lower than when she transported fruit by boat. Sina and Peni divided the baskets between them too. Peni walked beside Mele, but he did not talk about the storm. Mele did not tell him to forget the oar either.

Three years later, Mele and Alipa obtained another small boat. Before boarding it, Peni brought his new oar. “This time, I'll look after it.” Mele examined the oar, then cleared a place for it inside the boat. In 1894, Mele loaded only her own fruit and left, delaying Alipa's sales. Some of Alipa's fruit spoiled, and Mele later contributed part of its value. Not long afterward, Peni left to learn work somewhere else, and even after he returned, he did not live in Mele's house.

Mele continued living under the same roof as Sina and working at the harbor. When Sina fell ill, she and Peni took turns caring for her. After Sina died, Mele's wrist began to hurt, so she spent fewer days on the water and taught a young neighbor how to choose fruit. Peni asked her to live with him in his house, but Mele stayed in the home she had shared with Sina. Peni sometimes came for dinner, and sometimes he could not. On the days they ate together, Mele cut the fruit ahead of time. Neither of them said much about the loss of his father's oar.

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Money can be earned again. But I can't forget what you lost for you.”

memories.label: Sina's Assessment
memories.detail: “Mele was the one who saved Peni. I was the one who started thinking the very next day about how the three of us would make a living.”

memories.label: Peni's Memory
memories.detail: “I remember the hands that pulled me up. I also saw my father's oar float away. Both are true.”

memories.label: Peni's Evenings
memories.detail: “I asked her to come live at my house, but Aunt Mele said she was comfortable in her own home. Sometimes we ate together, but there were many days when I couldn't go.”

memories.label: Alipa's Words
memories.detail: “We bought the boat together, but there was a day Mele loaded only her own baskets and left. When my fruit spoiled, she paid part of its value, but that customer never came back.”

memories.label: The Young Neighbor's Words
memories.detail: “She took my hand and taught me to press the fruit first. She waited more patiently than she had when she did the work herself.”

finalMoment.place: The threshold of Mele's home near Apia
finalMoment.scene:
On an evening in Apia in 1913, I sit on the threshold of the house where I live alone and wait for my coughing to stop. The coughing has dragged on for months. These days, even walking to the far end of the yard leaves me needing to rest. I have cut back on carrying fruit, but I still set aside days to teach a young neighbor how to choose ripe fruit. Even after he leaves, my breathing does not become steady again.

Alipa comes to return something he left with me, then pauses. “Should I tell Peni?” I nod. I remember delaying Alipa's fruit and causing him to lose money. But I do not have the breath to bring that up now. Alipa sets down water and sends someone for Peni. I take two steps, trying to go inside. There is no strength in my legs, so I sit on the threshold again.

Peni arrives. “Aunt Mele, shall we go inside?” “It's better here.” After those few words, I begin coughing again. He has asked me many times to live with him in his house. Every time, I have said I would stay in this one. Peni stands before me, and together we look out over the open yard. I say his name once, and Peni answers. I open my mouth to draw another breath, but my chest does not move properly. I hear his voice again, but I cannot say anything more.
finalMoment.afterword: Mele died in 1913 at her home in Apia from pulmonary tuberculosis that had persisted for several months. Peni came one last time to the house where his aunt had chosen to live separately. He remembered both surviving the storm of 1889 and losing his father's oar. Alipa also remembered the day the shared boat kept him from selling his fruit. This past-life record closes the story of Mele, whose life held rescue and loss, days spent living together and days spent apart.
finalMoment.artAlt: A distant side view of the front yard of an Apia home in 1913. Mele, age 56 and weakened by pulmonary tuberculosis, sits on the threshold to greet her nephew Peni.

card.name: Beatrice Conti
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Beatrice Conti, a baker in charge of a communal oven in the Republic of Florence. She managed the communal oven and flour ledger in Florence. She drew protests by lending scarce grain first to families she knew, and after the Black Death spread, she organized distributions at the door.
card.title: Flour Beneath the Black Flags
card.role: Baker in charge of a communal oven
card.world: 1348 · Republic of Florence
card.flavor: A communal oven in a city ravaged by the Black Death
card.opening: In Florence in 1348, as more homes flew black flags, Beatrice set each share of flour outside the oven door.
card.life: She managed the communal oven and flour ledger in Florence. She drew protests by lending scarce grain first to families she knew, and after the Black Death spread, she organized distributions at the door. She lent flour to Marco, whom she knew, before serving Angela, delaying Angela's turn by a day. Angela's children ate only thin porridge that day.
card.turn: The custom of helping longtime neighbors first became a problem when everyone's survival depended on the distribution.
card.decision: Beatrice refused requests from people she knew and kept to the order in which they had arrived.
card.cost: She lent flour to Marco, whom she knew, before serving Angela, delaying Angela's turn by a day. Angela's children ate only thin porridge that day.
card.after: The distribution was put right, but Beatrice could not escape the disease either.
card.presentEcho: Closeness can be a reason for consideration, but it cannot take the place of fairness.
card.secondLook: Angela remembered not only the help but also the day she had been pushed back.
card.unresolved: It is not known how long Lucia and Angela kept the oven going.
card.readerQuestion: Bread is scarce in a city where disease is spreading. Whose share would you decide first?

signalMoments.connect: Beatrice had Lucia read out the names and asked Angela to check the remaining shares herself.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Beatrice, the keeper of a communal oven in Florence.

Before the disease spread, when flour ran short, she filled the sack of her longtime neighbor Marco first. Angela, who had come from the outskirts, protested that her turn had been passed over.

By spring, more people were suffering from high fevers and swellings. People were afraid to gather inside the cramped bakehouse, so Beatrice distributed bread outside the door.

signalMoments.notice: Beatrice saw that Angela's mark had been pushed back again and recognized the wrong in the old ledger.
signalMoments.speak: “Today, I will set out the shares in order of arrival. I will not serve a family first just because I know them.”
signalMoments.connect: Beatrice had Lucia read out the names and asked Angela to check the remaining shares herself.

episode.afterSignal:
People stood outside the door, keeping their distance from one another. Beatrice and Lucia put the bread into baskets and set them on the threshold.

Marco asked to be served first as before, but Beatrice did not change the order in the ledger. Marco stormed off angrily.

A few days later, Beatrice developed a fever too. She handed the oven key to Lucia and asked Angela to teach her how to read the ledger.

memories.label: What She Did for Years
memories.detail: Baked dough from many households in the same oven without letting it burn

memories.label: Her Daughter Lucia's View
memories.detail: “Mother put the order right, but by then she had fallen ill, and it was too late.”

memories.label: History and Fiction
memories.detail: The Black Death epidemic in Florence in 1348 is the historical backdrop; the characters and the distribution incident are fictional.

finalMoment.place: The room in Beatrice's bakery on the outskirts of Florence
finalMoment.scene:
In the summer of 1348, Beatrice had been feverish for 3 days in a room behind her bakery on the outskirts of Florence. The swelling in her armpit had grown larger, and every swallow of water made her stomach turn. Her younger brother Angelo set a bowl of water and bread outside the door and called her name.

Beatrice tried to crawl to the door but could not manage even 2 steps. “Angelo, don't come inside.” Her voice cracked. From beyond the door, he asked where she had left the ration list. Beatrice tried to point to the box above the oven, but she could not lift her hand.

By the time the evening bell rang, she was struggling to breathe. Beatrice watched the light coming in beneath the door and listened to her brother's footsteps. At the end, she could no longer answer.
finalMoment.afterword: Beatrice died after developing symptoms of infection in Florence during the Black Death of 1348. Angelo sealed the room with the neighbors and, unable to hold a funeral, entrusted her body to the corpse collectors. The surviving baker's apprentice remembered both the ration list she had corrected and the people who had gone hungry before she corrected it. Her personal life amid the historical epidemic is fictional.
finalMoment.artAlt: A dark room behind a bakery in Florence in 1348, with light beneath the closed door and Beatrice beside the bed

card.name: Farida
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Farida of Cairo. You ran the shop you had learned from your father and sister for many years and raised your niece Salma. You worked with your neighbor Nabila, but later handed the shop over to young Hassan without asking Nabila.
card.title: The Empty Seat in the Front Row
card.world: A neighborhood shop and theater in Cairo, Kingdom of Egypt, 1927
card.flavor: My Voice Heard from the Stage
card.opening: When Farida went to see Salma's first play, she heard her own favorite expression from the stage. Then an actress even spoke private words Farida had said to her ailing sister.
card.life: Farida learned the shop trade from her father, and after her sister died, she raised young Salma. She and Nabila bought stock together, but when she handed operations over to Hassan, she did not ask Nabila. With her daily wages reduced, Nabila found bookkeeping work elsewhere.
card.turn: In the short play Salma had written, an actress copied Farida's way of speaking and private family matters exactly. No one had told Farida that she would appear in the performance.
card.decision: Though Farida felt humiliated, she did not leave in the middle of the performance and watched until the end. Afterward, she praised Salma but also told her clearly that she was angry about the scenes Salma had used without permission.
card.cost: Farida closed the shop early and missed a large evening order, and her conversation with Salma remained unresolved that night. Salma agreed to ask Farida first the next time she wrote about their family.
card.after: Salma left to follow the theater troupe's work, then returned to Cairo with her child. Farida and Nabila stocked the shop together, but in 1954 Farida handed operations over to Hassan without asking Nabila. To make up for her reduced daily wages, Nabila found bookkeeping work at another shop.
card.presentEcho: What Salma did by putting Farida into the performance without asking her first stayed with them for a long time. Years later, Farida likewise failed to ask Nabila before handing over the shop. The two women's losses occurred at different times.
card.secondLook: To Salma, the play was a family story she had carried in her heart for a long time, but to Farida, it was a place where strangers heard words from inside her home. For Nabila, even while the two were arguing, the work of opening the shop the next day remained.
card.unresolved: The missed order did not return, and the family matters already spoken aloud in Salma's play could not be erased.
card.readerQuestion: If someone close to you used your story in a work without permission, what would you want to say first?

signalMoments.notice: When Farida heard the words she had said to her ailing sister spoken onstage, she stepped into the aisle. Unable to leave without seeing the final scene, she sat back down and decided that after the performance, she would tell Salma exactly which words had hurt her.
signalMoments.speak: Farida started to leave, then stopped and told Nabila in a low voice that she had to say both that the play was well written and that she was angry. She sat back down, watched the performance to the end, and spoke directly to Salma.
signalMoments.connect: Farida tapped the back of Nabila's hand and said she wanted to leave but also wanted to see the ending. When Nabila pointed to the seat beside her, Farida sat down again, and after the curtain fell, she suggested that they find Salma together.

When she handed the shop's operations over to Hassan, she did not first ask Nabila, who had worked beside her for many years. Even after retiring, she could not forget her old shop, but she walked through the neighborhood with her neighbor Layla.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small scale her father had used
People close to her · Her niece Salma, her coworker Nabila, Hassan, whom she taught the shop trade, and her neighbor Layla, who walked with her after retirement
The life she wanted · To protect the shop while letting Salma find the path she wanted

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Farida. In Cairo in 1927, Farida ran a small grocery store. One evening, she went to see the first play written by her niece Salma. Let me tell you about the words Farida unexpectedly heard from the stage that day.

Salma placed a paper ticket on the counter. “My story is going onstage tonight.” Farida checked the time printed on the ticket. It was when the shop was busiest. “Will they perform it again?” “Tonight is opening night.” For the past two months, Salma had rushed to the theater after the shop closed. Farida had never seen her rehearsing during that time.

That afternoon, the owner of a nearby teahouse ordered enough dried dates and grain to feed twenty evening customers. The teahouse owner told Farida that he would pay in advance. Farida set the ticket down beside the scale. If she kept the shop open, she could fill the order, and she could ask Salma how she was doing later. There had already been many such “laters.”

Before sunset, Farida told the teahouse owner that she would be closing early that day. He turned away, saying he would go to another shop. Farida locked the door and walked to the theater with Nabila. Nabila asked, “I heard Salma wrote something. Is she going to be onstage too?” Farida only showed her the ticket. Only then did it occur to her that she had not asked Salma herself.

There was an empty seat in the front row. Salma had saved it for her. Farida and Nabila arrived late and sat at the back of the audience. The lights dimmed, and an actress opened the door of the shop onstage. Tapping the scale, she said, “Anyone who asks for an extra handful always pays a handful less!” The audience laughed. Farida crumpled the ticket on her lap. That was something she always said in the shop.

At first, she thought it was merely a similar line. But in the next scene, the actress even spoke words Farida had said to her ailing sister. “If you rest, who's going to open the shop?” After saying that to her sister that day, Farida had sat beside her all night. Onstage, the audience heard only the first sentence. Someone at the back whispered, “Isn't that woman Farida?” Farida rose from her seat. The aisle was right beside her.

signalMoments.notice: When Farida heard the words she had said to her sister, she stepped into the aisle. She could not leave without seeing where the story onstage was going. She sat down again and decided to watch through the final scene, then tell Salma exactly which words had hurt her.
signalMoments.speak: Farida started to leave, then stopped. She decided to say what troubled her directly after the performance and sat down again. “I have to tell her both that it was well written and that I'm angry.” She spoke softly to Nabila beside her and turned her eyes to the stage.
signalMoments.connect: Farida lightly tapped the back of Nabila's hand. “I want to leave, but I want to see the ending.” Without a word, Nabila pointed to the seat beside her. Farida sat down and watched the performance to the end, then suggested that they find Salma together after the curtain fell.

episode.afterSignal:
In the final scene, the shopkeeper did not put out the light. She left a lamp by the door and waited until her sick relative fell asleep. Even after seeing that scene, Farida's anger did not fade. Salma had not portrayed her as entirely bad. But that did not mean she had the right to speak Farida's words to her sister in front of other people. When the curtain fell, the audience laughed and applauded. Farida clapped a few times, then stopped.

When Salma came out through the back door, her face lit up at the sight of Farida. “You came? The front-row seat stayed empty, so I thought you couldn't make it.” Farida opened the hand that had clutched the ticket until it was damp. “I came in late. It was well written.” Just as Salma began to smile, Farida added, “But I didn't want to hear the words I said when your mother was sick spoken in front of other people.”

For a moment, Salma could not answer. “But I wrote the scene where you stayed beside her at night too.” “I know. I saw that scene.” Farida glanced back toward the stage. “But that doesn't erase the earlier words. I wish you'd asked me first.” Salma could not take in all at once both the joy of having people recognize her writing and the reason her aunt's face had hardened. The two stood silently outside the theater doors for some time.

On the way home, Nabila was the first to speak. “What time should we open the shop tomorrow?” Farida remembered the teahouse order she had missed. The stock she had planned to buy with that money would be delayed too. “We should open at the usual time.” Salma walked a little behind them. Farida turned and said, “I want to read your play again. But next time you write about our family, tell me first.” Salma nodded, but said nothing more that night.

The next day, all three opened the shop together. The teahouse owner had already bought his goods elsewhere. For a while, Farida and Salma did not talk about the performance as they moved sacks and wrote down prices. A few weeks later, Salma brought in a new page she had written. “This time, I'll show you first.” Farida closed the ledger. She did not yet know what was written on that page, but she could step away from her place and read it.

Several years later, Salma moved to another neighborhood to follow the theater troupe's work, and even after returning to Cairo with her child, she lived apart from Farida and visited back and forth. Farida and Nabila bought the shop's stock together. In 1954, Farida handed the shop's operations over to Hassan without asking Nabila. When Hassan reorganized the books, Nabila's purchasing work and daily wages decreased. Nabila had to find bookkeeping work at another shop as well. After Farida left the shop in 1960, she walked through the neighborhood with her neighbor Layla in the late afternoons. One day in 1961, when Layla suggested taking another alley, Farida looked back once toward her old shop. Then she walked on beside Layla.

finalMoment.place: A neighborhood alley in Cairo
finalMoment.scene:
Cairo, late afternoon in 1962. I am walking through an alley with my neighbor Layla. It has been two years since I left the shop. Layla is telling me about a family that recently moved in. I try to answer, but my steps slow. Suddenly, it feels as though something is pressing down on the center of my chest. Thinking it might ease if I stand still for a moment, I put a hand against the wall. Layla stops talking.

“Let's go home.” I nod at Layla's words. But I cannot make my feet move. The pressure in my chest spreads to my arm, and sweat beads on my forehead. Layla calls to a nearby house and asks someone to bring help. I sit beside the wall and say, “Tell Salma...” I want to ask whether my niece is having dinner with her child today, but my breathing quickens. I do not have the strength to finish the next words.

“Can you hear me?” I look at Layla's face and blink once. Footsteps sound in the alley, but I cannot turn to see who is coming. The pressure on my chest grows stronger, and my shoulders lift once. Layla calls my name again. I open my mouth to answer, but cannot draw another breath.
finalMoment.afterword: Farida died in a Cairo alley in 1962 when the flow of blood to her heart was blocked. Layla was with her for her final steps, and Salma heard the news afterward. Salma remembered the night her aunt had watched her first play to the end. Nabila repeated that when Farida handed the shop over to Hassan without asking her first, her daily wages had decreased. Her loss was not repaid simply because she attended the funeral. The record of this past life tells both of the years Farida spent raising Salma and of Nabila's loss.
finalMoment.artAlt: A long side view of a Cairo alley in 1962. Seventy-four-year-old Farida braces herself against a wall in sudden chest pain while her neighbor Layla watches beside her.

card.name: Anneke
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Anneke of Haarlem. You ran an inn with Pieter and raised two children. After outliving your husband, you stopped serving cheap suppers, and after handing the business over to Maarten, the two of you bought the building they had rented for so long.
card.title: The Ball Beneath the Sled
card.world: Winter in Haarlem, Dutch Republic, 1652
card.flavor: A contest everyone saw, a distance no one saw
card.opening: When the ball game on the ice ended, everyone proclaimed Jan the winner. Anneke saw another ball beneath a child's sled.
card.life: Anneke helped with her parents' work, then opened a rented inn with Pieter. She raised Lies and Maarten and cared for her father. After her husband's death, she stopped serving cheap suppers to cover expenses, forcing the canal workers to eat elsewhere. Later, she handed the business over to Maarten, and at the independent Lies's home, she silently moved bundles of cloth, leaving her daughter to sort them all over again. In the winter of 1677, she pooled her savings with Maarten's and bought the inn building.
card.turn: In the one-shot ball game on the ice between Jan and the cloth merchant, the merchant's ball was hidden beneath a sled. The crowd cheered after seeing only Jan's ball, but the hidden ball was closer to the stake.
card.decision: Even though Anneke knew Jan, a worker at her inn, had lost, she moved the sled and showed everyone the distance of both balls. She also refused the reward the merchant offered.
card.cost: For a while, Jan thought Anneke had sided with a regular customer, and several spectators spread rumors at the inn. Meanwhile, Pieter had served the guests alone, and Anneke took on extra work the following morning.
card.after: Jan moved to another workplace and later sent his regards. After Pieter's death, Anneke stopped serving cheap suppers to cover the inn's expenses. Workers with little money had to eat elsewhere, and Anneke kept the inn going until she handed it over to Maarten. Years later, at her daughter Lies's home, she silently moved bundles of cloth, forcing Lies to sort them again by customer.
card.presentEcho: Jan resented Anneke despite the accurate ruling. Later, the canal workers remembered the supper table Anneke took away to keep the inn afloat.
card.secondLook: Jan believed Anneke was on his side. The merchant felt wronged when his ball was hidden, while Pieter handled the mounting work at the inn alone as Anneke judged the contest.
card.unresolved: Measuring the distance settled the contest, but Jan's resentment did not vanish at once. Nor could every rumor spread by the spectators be taken back.
card.readerQuestion: When everyone has already proclaimed one side the winner, how would you tell them if you saw a different result?

signalMoments.speak: Amid the cheering, Anneke said that they had not yet seen one of the balls. When the child moved the sled, the merchant's ball appeared, and Anneke repeated the agreed rule and called both men over to the stake.

She handed the business over to Maarten and, after years of saving, bought the inn building in both their names, but her life ended as she made her way home alone that night.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were called Anneke. In the winter of 1652, Anneke welcomed guests at a small inn in Haarlem. When the canals outside the city froze, people took to the ice and struck balls with sticks. Let me tell you about the day when one ball appeared only after the contest was over.

A merchant who had come to buy cloth joked with Jan, a worker at the inn. “Let's say whoever sends it closest to the stake wins.” The two men had the sleds and people move behind the stake and agreed to strike a ball once each from the same place. It was not an official tournament, just a small wager on a winter afternoon. They had been promised that the winner's name would go on the wooden board outside the inn door.

Anneke was laying out supper for her two children when she looked outside. Jan had been helping at the inn for 4 years. He often made mistakes stacking firewood, but when he struck a ball, his shoulders seemed light. The merchant was a longtime regular at the inn. “If they both play well, they can play again tomorrow.” Pieter laughed as he spoke. Anneke closed the ledger by the door and agreed to judge the distance.

The merchant swung his wooden stick first. The ball rolled a long way across the ice and stopped in front of the stake. Anneke fixed its position in her mind. Just then, a child pulled a small sled out from the edge of the snow. The child wanted to give a ride to a younger sibling frightened by the sound of the stick striking the ball. The sled hid the merchant's ball. No one saw it touch the ball.

It was Jan's turn. He did not hit the ball too hard. It spun once in front of the stake and stopped. The sled hid the merchant's ball, leaving only Jan's ball gleaming in sight. Someone shouted, “Jan won!” People rushed toward the inn door to find the wooden board. Jan looked at Anneke with a smile. Seeing his smile, Anneke smiled for a moment too.

When Anneke followed the marks left by the sticks and went closer to the stake, she saw a rounded edge beneath the sled's footboard. It was the merchant's ball. It lay about a handspan from the stake, a little closer than Jan's. If she announced the result before moving the sled, she thought no one would believe her. If she left it where it was, Jan's name would go on the wooden board. Pieter was inside the inn, welcoming another guest.

signalMoments.notice: Anneke asked the child to stop the sled for a moment. When the footboard was moved aside, the merchant's ball appeared. Anneke called Jan and the merchant over together and showed them both balls.
signalMoments.speak: Anneke spoke above the cheering. “We haven't seen one of the balls yet.” When the child moved the sled, the merchant's ball appeared. Anneke repeated the rule they had agreed on and called both men over to the stake.
signalMoments.connect: Anneke asked the child to pull the sled back just a little, then beckoned Jan and the merchant closer. “Whoever won, you both need to see for yourselves.” The three of them stood beside the stake and examined the two balls.

episode.afterSignal:
Anneke fetched a short length of cord used for tying bundles at the inn. She stretched it from the stake to the merchant's ball, then from the stake to Jan's. Jan's length was a little longer. The merchant coughed once and laughed. Jan did not. “The sled moved. It might have pushed the ball too.”

Anneke examined the mark where the sled's runner had passed through the snow beside the ball. The ball's trail continued from the place where the merchant had struck it. “If the child had pushed the ball, the trail would have changed direction here.” Anneke pointed. Jan looked at the trail too. He said nothing more, but slung the stick over his shoulder and returned to the inn ahead of them. Several spectators whispered, “Of course she's pleased her regular won.”

The merchant, his delight in victory restored, tapped the wooden board outside the door. He handed Anneke a small coin. “For judging the distance so well.” Anneke did not take it. “You only asked me to see who won.” The merchant looked embarrassed for a moment. His name went on the wooden board that day. But many people had not seen Anneke refuse the money.

Inside the inn, uncleared cups had piled up. Pieter had carried supper tables by himself while finding room for the guests. When Anneke came in, he said, “The match is over, and now it's our turn here.” The two of them scrubbed the floor and tables until late. Anneke said she would handle the firewood and the guests' tables alone the following morning. While she had judged the contest outside, Pieter had carried the burden of that time as well.

For several days, Jan said only what was necessary. When Anneke tried to explain, he replied, “I saw what the cord measured.” He was not upset because he did not understand the result. He had believed Anneke would be on his side. Anneke did not tell Jan that he would win the next game. Those words could not change the distance between the balls this time.

After that, Anneke continued raising Lies and Maarten while running the rented inn. Even after Jan moved to another workplace, he occasionally sent his regards. When Pieter died, Anneke had to cover the cost of firewood and ingredients alone. In 1662, she stopped serving the cheap suppers she had sold to canal workers. The inn's expenses became easier to manage, but workers with little money had to eat elsewhere. Later, Anneke handed the running of the inn over to her son Maarten. When she visited her daughter Lies's home in 1675, she moved bundles of cloth to make room to sit. Lies had to delay supper while she sorted the cloth again by customer. “Please ask me first next time.” Lies's words hurt Anneke, but from her next visit on, she did not touch the cloth. In the winter of 1677, the landlord said he would sell the inn building. Anneke pooled her savings with Maarten's and bought the building they had rented for so long. They planned to invite Lies over the next day and show her the room they would prepare.
