finalMoment.place: A narrow alley on the way back to the inn, Haarlem, Dutch Republic
finalMoment.scene:
One winter evening in 1677, 63-year-old Anneke completed the purchase of the small inn building in Haarlem. Decades had passed since she and her husband Pieter first began renting it. Her fingertips trembled as she tucked away the document bearing both her name and her son Maarten's. Maarten had gone back to the inn first to prepare a celebratory supper. Anneke said a final goodbye to the landlord and entered the alley alone.

The alley where light spilled from the inn's windows was still some distance away. Anneke decided that tomorrow she would show her daughter Lies the room they would prepare. “You can choose the spot by the window.” She laughed after speaking the words to herself. Now she and Maarten could protect the place they had rented for so long. Unlike the last time, when she had moved Lies's cloth without asking, this time she meant to ask first how her daughter wanted to use the room. That did not erase the winters endured by the canal workers after she had to stop serving cheap suppers.

Water that had melted on the alley's stones during the day had frozen into a thin layer. Anneke steps sideways to avoid a dark doorstep. Her foot slides forward, and her body tilts backward. She reaches out, but cannot touch the wall. The sound of the back of her head striking the corner of a stone echoes through the narrow alley. The document slips from inside her clothes and out past her collar.

Anneke opens her eyes. The light from the inn is faint at the end of the alley. Her head hurts, and she tries to rise, but her elbows cannot support her body. “Maarten.” She thinks she calls his name, but only a small breath escapes her lips. She moves her fingers toward the paper. Her vision blurs until she can no longer make out the letters, and her eyelids fall shut. No one is in the alley to hear the sound. Anneke never rises again.
finalMoment.afterword: Anneke fell in a frozen alley in Haarlem during the winter of 1677 and badly injured her head. She died at 63 from bleeding inside her skull during the night. When his mother did not return, Maarten searched the alleys, but he did not find her that night. The next morning, a passerby found Anneke clutching the document. Lies entered the room her mother had planned to show her, but never heard her say to choose a spot by the window. Maarten was left with the inn they had bought together, while Jan was left with his lingering resentment over a ruling on the ice long ago. The canal workers remembered the years when the cheap suppers never returned. The record of Anneke's past life preserves both the evening she gained the place she had waited for most, and the ending that denied her a tomorrow to live there.
finalMoment.artAlt: A high, diagonal view from above the rooftops looks down on a narrow stone alley in Haarlem in the winter of 1677. 63-year-old Anneke walks alone toward the inn's light with the deed tucked inside her clothes. Thin ice is visible before her feet, and there are no onlookers, no one supporting her, and no one running to summon help.

card.name: Benta
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Benta of Recife. You ran a fruit stall using the trade your mother taught you and shared a home with your younger sister. After caring for your nephew, you passed the stall on to young Lia in old age.
card.title: A Voice for Two
card.role: Fruit seller at São José Market
card.world: Renovation of a market in Recife, Republic of Brazil, in 1906
card.flavor: A hoarse fruit seller and a fish seller who shouted too loudly
card.opening: On the first day after the market renovations forced her to move her stall, Benta lost her voice. The fruit prices that Zeca, the fish seller next to her, called out for her were different from the ones she had written down.
card.life: Benta sold fruit with her mother before setting up a stall of her own. After her mother died, she lived with her younger sister Mariana and cared for her nephew Tomás. She continued trading for many years, then handed her place over to Lia. At age 67, she drowned while rescuing a child who had fallen into a river.
card.turn: To help the hoarse Benta, Zeca called out the prices for both stalls. But he mixed up the two lines on her slate and announced that the mangoes were being sold cheaply, and the customers who crowded in blocked Benta's sign and fruit from view.
card.decision: Benta stopped the customers, rewrote the correct price for each kind of fruit, and showed them herself. Instead of standing by and leaving it to Zeca, she explained the prices to the customers one by one.
card.cost: Zeca took home less income from his fish because he had to make up the difference caused by the wrong price he had called out. Benta sold a crate of bruised fruit cheaply, and while Zeca was helping her, he failed to sell some of his fish.
card.after: Zeca brought Benta the difference caused by the wrong price he had called out, and the next day they opened their stalls side by side again. Even after her nephew became independent, Benta stayed at the market. When her knees began to ache, she taught Lia how to choose fruit and run the stall, then handed it over to her.
card.presentEcho: Zeca brought Benta the difference caused by the wrong price he had called out. Benta also had to sell the bruised mangoes cheaply, while Zeca missed fish customers. The next day, they opened their stalls side by side.
card.secondLook: Zeca rushed because he was afraid Benta would lose customers. The customers trusted the price they had heard, and Benta lost the time she needed to choose the fruit and set its price.
card.unresolved: Even after they apologized to each other, the losses on the fruit and fish that day could not be undone. Zeca's wish to help and Benta's reason for being angry both remained.
card.readerQuestion: If a friend tried to help by naming a price for me and got it wrong, what would I do first in front of the customers?

signalMoments.notice: Benta realized that Zeca had mixed up the two lines and moved the slate in front of the baskets where every customer could see it. She began by recounting the money she had already received.
signalMoments.speak: The hoarse Benta struck an empty tin cup three times with a spoon. When the customers turned, she raised the slate, said these were the prices she had written, and pointed to the lines for mangoes and bananas one at a time.
signalMoments.connect: Benta took Zeca by the sleeve and brought him in front of the slate. While Zeca pointed to the mangoes and bananas in turn before the customers, Benta pulled the sign forward so they could see both lines.

identity.region: Recife (then part of the Republic of Brazil)
identity.summary: A girl who sold fruit with her mother set up a stall of her own. She shared a home with her younger sister, cared for her nephew, and later handed the work over to Lia. At age 67, she pushed a child who had fallen into a river to a boat, then drowned.

profilePages.body:
Benta · Female
1870–1937 · 67 years old
Recife · Republic of Brazil in 1906
Work · Fruit seller at São José Market
Life · She followed her mother to the market, then set up a stall of her own. After her mother died, she lived with her younger sister Mariana and cared for her nephew Tomás. When her knees began to ache, she handed her place over to Lia. In 1937, she drowned while rescuing a child who had fallen into a river.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She remembered blemishes on fruit and customers' faces well. On busy days, her hands sometimes began moving before she had listened to the other person to the end.
Liked · The smell of a mango freshly cut in the morning
Disliked · Piling good fruit on top of bruised fruit at the bottom of a basket to make it look better
Good at · Selling fruit in order of ripeness and estimating how much would remain

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small slate on which she and her mother wrote prices
People close to her · Her younger sister Mariana, her nephew Tomás, the fish seller Zeca, and the young vendor Lia
The life she wanted · To trade for many years while leaving room for someone else to learn
Worry · That if her body began to hurt, she would not be able to keep her stall for long

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Benta. In 1906, you sold fruit at São José Market in Recife. One morning, while the stalls had been moved during renovations, Benta was too hoarse to call out her prices. Let me tell you what happened that day.

She had thought resting her voice overnight would make it better. But when she reached the market, the clang of hammers rang out beyond the iron pillars. Because of the construction, Benta's fruit stall had been moved right next to Zeca the fish seller. The two had known each other for years. If Benta was late, Zeca kept a space open for her baskets, and Benta could often guess how much he had sold that day before his remaining fish spoiled.

On the slate she had used with her mother, Benta wrote two lines in chalk. “Three coins for two mangoes. Two coins for three bananas.” In place of her voice, she propped the sign toward the customers. Holding up a fish, Zeca asked, “Want me to call in customers for you today?” Before Benta could even nod, Zeca's voice thundered across the market. “Fresh fish! Ripe mangoes right next door!”

The first customer approached with a smile. While choosing a fish, Zeca glanced over his shoulder at the slate. He saw the number of mangoes on the upper line and the price of bananas on the lower one. He called out the two lines as if they were one. “Two coins for three mangoes!” Benta waved her hand, but Zeca was wrapping the fish and did not see her. The customer had already put down two coins and picked up three mangoes.

From then on, customers flooded in. “Didn't you say two coins for three mangoes?” someone asked. Benta tried to point to the slate, but the crowd blocked it from view. One customer pulled a basket closer, afraid of losing their turn. A crate of mangoes tilted, and the fruit at the bottom was crushed against the other pieces. Zeca called out again. “They're Benta's! I'm speaking for her!” The shouting that had begun as help drowned out Benta's sign.

Benta looked at the coins the customers had put down and the dented mangoes. She could not suddenly demand more money from people who had bought the fruit believing that was the price. But if she kept selling at that price, she would not recover what she had paid for the fruit she had brought that day. At Zeca's stall, fish he had not yet sold were still lying out. First, Benta had to stop the customers.

signalMoments.notice: Benta pointed to the top and bottom of the slate. Realizing that Zeca had mixed up the two lines, she moved the sign in front of the baskets. As the customers read it one by one, Benta began recounting the coins she had already received.
signalMoments.speak: Benta struck an empty tin cup three times with a spoon. The customers turned. “These are the prices I wrote.” Her hoarse voice was quiet, but Benta raised the slate and pointed to the lines for mangoes and bananas one at a time.
signalMoments.connect: Benta took Zeca by the sleeve and led him in front of the slate. “Look at both lines together.” Zeca pointed to the mangoes and bananas in turn before the customers. Meanwhile, Benta pulled the sign forward so the customers could see both lines.

episode.afterSignal:
The customer at the front, still holding three mangoes, asked, “Then what about the money I already paid?” Zeca set down the fish in his hand. “I called out the wrong price. Those who already took fruit can have it at that price. I'll pay the missing coins.” Benta looked at him. He meant to pay the price for the words he had spoken in her place. Without arguing further, she handed the customer the mangoes.

Benta erased the two lines from the slate and wrote the mango and banana prices again, leaving a wide space between them. She stood the sign in front of the two baskets. She called the customers forward one at a time and counted the fruit and coins together. When Zeca tried to call out for her again, Benta shook her head. Zeca closed his mouth and returned to his fish. Meanwhile, several customers went to other fish stalls.

Much later, a construction worker shouted for them to clear the way. Zeca pushed his basket of fish, and Benta lifted and moved her fruit crates. Their shoulders bumped, but neither spoke for a while. Benta picked out the bruised mangoes and sold them cheaply. Zeca counted the fish he had left. Both had less than the share they had expected that morning.

When the sun rose high and the market entrance grew quiet, Zeca brought her some coins. They made up the difference caused by the wrong price he had called out. Benta placed the coins beside the slate. “You started before I even nodded this morning.” Zeca gave an awkward smile. “I thought you hadn't heard me.” “It wasn't that I didn't hear you. I couldn't speak.” Benta pointed to her throat. This time, Zeca waited until she had finished.

“You'll be in the same place tomorrow, right?” Zeca asked. Instead of answering, Benta wrote the amount of fruit she would sell the next day in a corner of the slate. Beneath it, in small letters, she wrote, “Ask Zeca about the price of Zeca's fish.” Zeca laughed, and Benta laughed too. Laughter could not make the bruised mangoes good again or sell the unsold fish, but the next day, the two opened their stalls side by side.

After that day, Benta continued to share a home with her younger sister Mariana and watched her nephew Tomás grow up. After Tomás left to find work of his own, she taught young Lia the order in which fruit ripened. Even after aching knees made her hand over the stall, she sometimes visited the market. When she ran into Zeca, they exchanged greetings. The fruit price he had paid for and the fish customers he had lost remained separate losses.

finalMoment.place: Unnamed stone steps on a riverbank in Recife, Brazil
finalMoment.scene:
One late-summer afternoon in 1937, sixty-seven-year-old Benta walks beside stone steps on a riverbank in Recife. Five years have passed since her aching knees made her hand her fruit stall over to Lia. Today, she is on her way home to eat dinner with her younger sister Mariana. From below the steps comes a splash. A young child has slipped and fallen into the river. The child tries to grab the steps but cannot reach them.

“You in the boat, come this way!” Benta calls. In a nearby boat, a boatman holding an oar turns his head. Benta grabs a rope tied to the steps and enters the water one step at a time. The water rises above her knees and flows swiftly. Her hand tightens on the taut rope. When the child reaches out one arm, Benta catches it with her other hand.

The boat draws closer, but the child cannot steady their body. Struggling not to let go of the rope, Benta pushes the child toward the boat. From the boat's edge, the boatman grabs the child's clothes and hauls them aboard. The child coughs and draws a breath. “Give me your hand now!” The boatman reaches an arm toward Benta. Benta raises her hand too, but the wet rope slips through her palm.

Her body drifts away from the steps. Benta tries to grasp the side of the boat, but her fingertips cannot reach it. Water covers her face. When she raises her head, she catches a brief glimpse of the child and the boatman in the boat. Benta tries once more to lift her body and take a breath. The current pulls her downstream, and she sinks beneath the water again. The boatman turns the oar and follows, but Benta does not resurface.
finalMoment.afterword: Benta's life ended in 1937 when she drowned in a river in Recife after pushing a child to a boat. The child survived. The boatman remembered the distance that had kept him from reaching Benta's hand. Mariana cleared away the dinner she had set while waiting for her sister. The next day, Lia opened the fruit stall Benta had entrusted to her, and Zeca remembered how, in 1906, he had called out Benta's prices incorrectly and caused them both to suffer losses. Those losses and their long friendship are not erased by one final rescue. The record of this past life tells of the end of this life alongside all the years Benta spent setting her own prices, caring for her nephew, and handing her work over to a young vendor.
finalMoment.artAlt: A wide view of the Recife riverbank in 1937, seen from a high vantage point on the opposite side of the river. Sixty-seven-year-old Benta clings to the rope by the steps and pushes a child through the water toward a small boat while the boatman reaches out to the child. There is no third person supporting them or running to call for help.

card.name: Ilyas
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Ilyas of Beirut. As a child, you carved wooden boats with a friend and looked after your younger sister. You worked at the port, built a family with Farah, endured the hardships of wartime, and died at thirty-three.
card.title: The Bag Tied with a Red Cord
card.world: The port of Beirut in the Ottoman Empire, 1908
card.flavor: A young porter who hid some luggage to keep his sister from leaving
card.opening: On the day his younger sister Miriam was leaving, Ilyas did not carry the bag tied with a red cord onto the ship. He believed she could not go without her luggage.
card.life: After losing his father at an early age, he helped his mother and younger sister while learning to work at the port. He remained close to his friend Nabil and married Farah. After injuring his shoulder, he mended ropes as he lived through the war years.
card.turn: Miriam entrusted him with her bag, saying she was going to Alexandria to work for their aunt, but Ilyas hid it under an empty awning. She said she would leave even without the bag.
card.decision: Ilyas confessed that he had hidden the bag and went to retrieve it himself. He stopped trying to change his sister's choice for her.
card.cost: The supervisor withheld Ilyas's wages for that day because he had failed to move the cargo on time, and reduced his work the following week. Miriam boarded the ship, but she did not forgive him right away.
card.after: Ilyas managed by finding other work with Nabil. It took time before he and his sister began exchanging letters. He later lived with Farah, then died young from an illness.
card.presentEcho: Even if you want to stop someone close to you from leaving, you cannot decide that person's future for them.
card.secondLook: Miriam needed Ilyas's help, but she also tried to protect her right to leave and find work of her own. Afraid of a home without his sister, Ilyas used the luggage entrusted to him against her.
card.unresolved: He could return the bag, but the mistrust created that morning and the wages he lost could not be restored at once.
card.readerQuestion: The ship your sister plans to board will depart soon. If she is looking for the bag you hid, what would you do first right now?

signalMoments.connect: Ilyas told Nabil that he had hidden Miriam's bag beneath the awning and asked him to help find it. Without asking why, Nabil moved the empty crates with Ilyas.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Ilyas. You carried cargo at the port of Beirut in 1908. That year, your younger sister Miriam planned to leave for Alexandria, where their aunt lived. Let me tell you what Ilyas did that day.

The port was noisy even before the ship arrived. Ilyas was moving wooden crates with the other porters when he spotted Miriam in the crowd. His nineteen-year-old sister had tied a red cord around the handle of her bag. “That'll make it easy to recognize once I'm on the ship, won't it?” Miriam asked. Ilyas tightened the cord for her once more.

The bag held a change of clothes and sewing tools. Miriam planned to mend and sell clothes with their aunt in Alexandria. A woman from their neighborhood who had gone there ahead of her was due to take the same ship that day. At home, their mother was worrying that Miriam had not packed enough bread. Ilyas had a different worry. If his sister boarded this ship, he would no longer hear Miriam's laughter in the house he returned to that evening.

“I'll carry your bag.” He spoke to his sister with a familiar look. When Miriam let go of the handle, Ilyas took a few steps toward the loading area. Then he turned toward the awning beside an empty warehouse. He shoved the bag behind some empty wooden crates and covered it with a piece of cloth. The end of the red cord showed for a moment. He tucked it out of sight with his finger.

‘She won't be able to go today without her luggage.’ That was what he thought. Maybe by tomorrow, his sister would change her mind. But when he rejoined the crowd, Miriam immediately asked, “Where's my bag?” Ilyas pretended to look toward the sea. “I'll bring it soon.” Miriam exchanged a glance with the woman from their neighborhood. “I need it before I board.”

One load of cargo was moved toward the ship. The supervisor called to Ilyas and pointed at the next lot, but Ilyas only watched the place where Miriam stood. Miriam bit her lip for a moment, then told the woman from their neighborhood, “I'll go even without my bag. I can borrow needles from my aunt.” The rope Ilyas was holding slipped from his hands. He was the only one who had believed a single bag could keep his sister there.

“Ilyas.” Miriam came over to him. “Where did you really put it?” Behind him, the supervisor called again. He had little time left to answer his sister and find the bag.

signalMoments.notice: Ilyas looked over the luggage being loaded for departure and confirmed that the red cord was nowhere among it. Pointing toward the awning where he had shoved the bag, he said, “It's over there.” Then he ran toward the empty crates.
signalMoments.speak: Ilyas looked Miriam in the eyes. “I hid it. Because I didn't want you to go.” Before Miriam could answer, he told her where he had hidden it behind the awning and ran that way.
signalMoments.connect: Ilyas grabbed Nabil, who was nearby. “I hid Miriam's bag under the awning. Help me find it.” Without asking why, Nabil moved the empty crates with Ilyas.

episode.afterSignal:
The bag was still there beneath the cloth. Gripping the red cord, Ilyas pushed through the crowd. Miriam had stepped out of the line heading toward the ship and was waiting for him. When she took the bag, she ran her fingers over the cord on its handle. “I gave you my luggage because you know your way around here.” Her voice was low. “I didn't give it to you so I could get your permission to leave.”

Ilyas opened his mouth, then closed it. “I'm sorry.” Those were the only words he managed. Miriam pulled the bag close to her side. The woman from their neighborhood beckoned to them. The line was moving forward. Ilyas started to follow, then stopped. This time, he did not put his hand on the bag's handle.

Miriam took two steps, then looked back. “Tell Mother I boarded safely.” “Write to us.” “I will. But I won't forget what happened today.” Without waiting for him to speak again, Miriam followed the woman from their neighborhood toward the ship. On the deck, the red cord fluttered once. Ilyas could not tell whether his sister had raised her hand or the wind had moved the cord.

The supervisor was waiting by the rest of the cargo assigned to him. “Nabil moved those crates while you were gone.” Ilyas told him about the hidden bag and his sister. The supervisor shook his head. “You won't get your share today. I'll give you less cargo next week, too.” This was not because of some established rule. The supervisor was angry with Ilyas for abandoning the work he had promised to do. Ilyas went home empty-handed that day.

That evening, he saw the bread their mother had set aside for Miriam and told her what he had done beneath the awning. His mother did not put the bread away. “You were afraid of her going far away too, weren't you?” Ilyas nodded. “But does hiding her bag make the house any less empty?” He could not answer. The next day, he went out with Nabil to find other work and spent the week earning meager wages.

No letter came from Miriam before the year ended. Ilyas wrote to her twice but could not bring himself to send either letter. The following year, a brief note arrived. It said she was mending clothes with their aunt. Only then did he write back. It took even longer before the two of them could joke comfortably again.

Ilyas later injured his shoulder and did more work mending ropes and nets. He made a home in a small room with Farah. After war came, they lived with constant worries about work and food. He and Miriam exchanged letters across the distance. That morning with the red cord was only one day in his life, but he remained ashamed for a long time that he had taken the luggage from the hands of someone who was leaving.

finalMoment.place: A small house in Beirut
finalMoment.scene:
It is morning in Beirut in 1919. I have been feverish for four days in the small room where I live with Farah. Since last night, my chest has felt tight every time I breathe in. I ask Farah, who is sitting beside the bedding, to open the window a little. I try to get up, saying it is my job, but I cannot even set my feet on the floor.

When Farah opens the window, the rumble of cartwheels and the voices of people drift in from the street. I turn my head and look outside. I remember the days when Nabil and I sat by the water on our days off. I try to say we should go again sometime, but a dry cough comes first. “You don't have to speak,” Farah says, supporting my back.

Farah calls to a neighbor outside the door and asks for help. I try once more to turn toward the window. My breaths grow shorter whenever I move. Farah returns and puts a hand on my shoulder. “Ilyas, can you hear me?” I touch the back of Farah's hand with my fingers.

The rumble of wheels in the street continues. I open my mouth, but no sound comes out. I try to breathe in again, but my chest moves only a little, then stops. The fingers pressing Farah's hand go slack.
finalMoment.afterword: Ilyas died beside Farah in their Beirut home in 1919. No record remains of the illness. When Nabil heard the news, he remembered the waterside where they used to sit on their days off. Miriam later received a letter in Alexandria. Even after she read that her brother had died, that morning when he hid her bag was not erased. Farah was left with the memory of Ilyas's voice as he came home from work. The record of this past life mournfully notes a life that ended at thirty-three, and all the days he never had the chance to enjoy. In your life today, there may be one small meeting that you do not need to put off.
finalMoment.artAlt: A modest room in Beirut in 1919, where 33-year-old Ilyas, weakened by illness, turns toward the sounds outside an open window as his wife Farah supports his shoulder one morning

card.name: Zofia Kowalska
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Zofia Kowalska, a former tram conductor who served as a courier between underground shelters in Warsaw, Poland, under German occupation. After working as a tram conductor in Warsaw, she took charge of communications between shelters during the war. She moved people quickly but quarreled with her younger brother because she withheld information about danger.
card.title: The Back of a Stopped Tram Ticket
card.role: Former tram conductor and underground shelter courier
card.world: 1944 · Warsaw, Poland, under German occupation
card.flavor: A wartime courier who traveled between shelters
card.opening: In Warsaw in 1944, Zofia wrote the safe alleys on the back of an old tram ticket.
card.life: After working as a tram conductor in Warsaw, she took charge of communications between shelters during the war. She moved people quickly but quarreled with her younger brother because she withheld information about danger. She sent Janek on an errand without telling him about the checkpoints, and he was nearly arrested. Afterward, neither of them trusted the other's judgment.
card.turn: The desire to move people quickly clashed with their right to know the danger.
card.decision: Zofia did not hide the danger and offered alternatives along with it.
card.cost: She sent Janek on an errand without telling him about the checkpoints, and he was nearly arrested. Afterward, neither of them trusted the other's judgment.
card.after: The patients were moved, but her long-standing mistrust with Janek could not be resolved with a single sentence.
card.presentEcho: When you hide information in the name of protecting someone, you also take away their ability to choose.
card.secondLook: Zofia's speed saved lives, but it also left her younger brother wounded.
card.unresolved: It is unknown whether Janek kept the tram ticket after the war.
card.readerQuestion: You have heard rumors that the evacuation route is dangerous. What would you tell the people waiting first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Zofia, who had worked as a tram conductor. As the war dragged on, she carried news about water and medical supplies between basement shelters.

The rear door of one shelter was blocked by shelling debris. Maria suggested moving the patients to the building to the north, but there were rumors of snipers along that route.

Zofia feared that if she mentioned the rumors, people would refuse to move. Janek said they should tell everyone about the danger and let each person choose.

signalMoments.notice: Zofia saw that a new passage had opened between the route drawn on the back of the tram ticket and an actual collapsed wall.
signalMoments.speak: “The northern route is dangerous too. But there is a shorter way over this wall.” Zofia explained without hiding anything.
signalMoments.connect: Zofia had Maria and Janek count the patients and stretchers together. The three of them divided up the order of departure.

episode.afterSignal:
Even after hearing about the danger, the people chose the new passage. They decided who would walk in front and who would guard the rear of the stretchers.

Zofia handed Piotr the tram ticket and told him to use it as a marker all the way to the next shelter.

After most of the patients had been moved, Janek told his sister he wished she had spoken to him this way before. Zofia could offer no excuse.

finalMoment.place: An underground shelter in German-occupied Warsaw
finalMoment.scene:
In 1944, in an underground shelter in Warsaw, Zofia was distributing water containers to 2 children and her neighbor Janusz. The sound of artillery fire drew closer above them. When lime dust began falling from the ceiling, Zofia told the people near the exit to move against the inner wall.

After a massive explosion, the stairs and door collapsed. Beneath a small ventilation opening, Zofia and Janusz cleared away stones. Dust clogged her throat, and debris pinned her left leg. “Send the children through the gap first.” She widened the low opening with her hands.

After the children escaped into another room, a second collapse occurred. Zofia was listening to Janusz's answer when she could no longer stop coughing. As the air ran out, her consciousness faded. She stopped breathing before the rescue team arrived.
finalMoment.afterword: Zofia died from crush injuries and suffocation in a shelter destroyed by shelling in Warsaw in 1944. Janusz and the 2 children were rescued through another passage. Her companions remembered both the Zofia who judged dangerous information alone and shared it too late, and the Zofia who clearly announced the order of escape at the end. The characters and the shelter incident are fictional.
finalMoment.artAlt: The collapsed stairs and low escape gap of a Warsaw underground shelter in 1944, with Zofia amid the dust

card.name: Dara
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Dara, from near Angkor. You learned to work the rice fields from your mother, made a home with Chen, and raised a daughter. You also caused conflict by postponing orders for the injured Chen's pottery without consulting him. You continued farming even after your daughter became independent.
card.title: The Two-Loop Reed Knot
card.world: Rice fields and waterways near Angkor in the Khmer Empire, 1190
card.flavor: A waterway changed overnight and a child wrongly accused
card.opening: On the morning Soma's rice field dried up, people suspected the child who had been near the waterway the day before. Dara saw her own reed knot tied to the earthen plug.
card.life: She grew up tending the rice fields with her mother and weaving fish traps with her friend Soma. She lived with Chen and their daughter, Nie. When Chen was injured, she postponed his orders without consulting him, and afterward Chen set the promised dates for his small pottery orders himself. Dara continued farming even after Chen's death.
card.turn: The night before, Dara secretly moved the small earthen plug shared by the two households so more water would flow to her field. The next day, Soma's young rice seedlings had dried up.
card.decision: In front of the child, Dara revealed that she had changed the waterway. She replaced the plug with Soma and offered the young rice seedlings and seed she had saved.
card.cost: Soma's withered seedlings could not be revived, and Dara's own share was reduced. For a while, the wrongly accused child and Soma could not feel at ease around Dara.
card.after: The two households tended the waterway together again, but they did not return to laughter as quickly as before. Dara kept farming through Chen's injury and death and Nie's independence, then moved closer to her daughter.
card.presentEcho: A small plug moved out of fear that my own share will not be enough can change someone else's entire day.
card.secondLook: Dara wanted to protect her family's seedlings. Soma did not know why her field had suddenly dried up, and the child was the first to bear the adults' suspicions.
card.unresolved: They restored the waterway, but they could not undo the dead seedlings or the suspicion the child had heard that day.
card.readerQuestion: Because of an earthen plug I moved during the night, my neighbor's field has dried up, and an innocent child is under suspicion. What would I do first now?

signalMoments.speak: Dara stood beside Kiri. “The child didn't touch it. I moved the plug last night.” She told Soma she had sent more water to her field because she was worried about her family's seedlings.
signalMoments.connect: Dara told Soma and Kiri that she had moved the plug and said they should restore the waterway first. While Soma held the plug, Dara untied the knot and told Nie to bring her own young rice seedlings.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Dara. In 1190, you farmed rice fields around Angkor in the Khmer Empire. During a season when water was scarce, something happened at a small earthen waterway shared by two households. Let me tell you the story of Dara and Soma.

The two households' rice fields lay side by side, separated by a single low embankment. Water from the main canal divided at a small fork. Moving the earthen plug in the middle even slightly changed how much water flowed to either side. Dara and her longtime friend Soma often watched each other's waterways when they planted rice seedlings. The fish trap they had woven together as children still hung on the wall of Dara's house.

That evening, the newly planted seedlings in Dara's field drooped. Her husband Chen was working late firing pottery, and her fourteen-year-old daughter Nie felt the soil with her hand. “They'll last a little while, until morning.” But Dara kept touching the dried tips. If their share of the harvest shrank that year, there would be many things the family would have to go without.

That night, Dara went to the fork alone. A shallow layer of water still covered Soma's field. Dara pushed the earthen plug a palm's width toward Soma's side. More water flowed into her own field. To keep from losing the plug, she tied a single reed in two loops and lodged it in the earth. “I can put it back at dawn.” She meant to finish before Soma ever found out.

But at dawn, Chen asked Dara to warm his aching hand, and Nie went out to the seedbed, so Dara reached the fork late. When she arrived, Soma was holding a handful of dried seedlings. The soil-coated root tips crumbled. “Water was flowing on this side yesterday, too,” Soma said quietly.

Soma's nephew Kiri stood beside her. The day before, Kiri had caught small fish beside the canal. Someone remembered seeing him there and said, “Could the child have touched it?” Kiri shook his head hard. “I only looked at the fish.” Even Soma could not answer right away. Dara looked at the fork. She could see the reed lodged in the earthen plug. One loop, and beneath it another loop she had tied herself.

Nie came to Dara's side and looked at the reed. “That's the knot Mother uses when she weaves fish traps.” Her voice was quiet, but Dara heard it clearly. Kiri was avoiding Soma's eyes. Dara knew who would remain under suspicion if she did not tell them what she had done during the night.

signalMoments.notice: Dara gently lifted the reed's two loops from the earth. “I tied this knot.” She showed Soma where the plug had been displaced and the direction in which more water had flowed toward her own field.
signalMoments.speak: Dara stood beside Kiri. “The child didn't touch it. I moved the plug last night.” She told Soma she had sent more water to her field because she was worried about her family's seedlings.
signalMoments.connect: Dara approached Soma and Kiri. “I moved it. Let's restore this waterway first.” While Soma held the earthen plug, Dara untied the reed knot and told Nie to bring her own young rice seedlings.

episode.afterSignal:
Kiri looked at Dara first. “Then I didn't do it, right?” “No, you didn't.” Dara said the same thing in front of Soma. Soma looked down at the dried seedlings. “If we turn the water back, will these seedlings stand again?” Dara could not answer. Water began flowing into Soma's field again, but the seedlings that had fallen over and dried up did not move.

Dara brought the young seedlings that had not yet grown in her own seedbed, along with her remaining seed. Nie picked up a handful first, but Soma did not take it for a moment. “Your field is short, too.” “I know.” Dara sat down by the fork. “But my field got the extra water that night.” Only then did Soma take the seedlings from Nie's hand and lay them at the edge of her field.

Kiri walked back along the top of the embankment without setting foot in the wet soil. Dara called to him, but he only raised a hand once. Only then did Dara realize that for a young child, the morning's suspicion might linger longer than the earthen plug moved during the night. Chen arrived late and looked at the divided waterway. Rather than take anyone's side, he spent a long time watching to see whether water reached both fields again.

That evening, Dara started to mend the small fish trap hanging in her house, then stopped. When she and Soma had sat by the water tying two loops at a time, they had trusted each other's hands. Now the same knot had exposed what Dara wanted to hide. Nie asked, “Will Aunt Soma come weave fish traps with us again?” Dara answered, “I don't know.” The answer hurt, but it was true.

The next day they divided the water, Soma reached the fork first. Together, the two women watched which field the water reached first. They did not begin with laughter as they had before. Several rows of young seedlings were missing from Soma's field. Dara saw the empty rows, and whenever Kiri came to the canal, she gave him space. In time, Kiri returned to catch fish, but he did not speak to Dara for long.

When Chen injured his back in 1193, Dara told his customers that she would postpone two orders for large pottery without consulting him. Chen said he wanted to decide the dates for his own customers himself. From 1194 onward, Chen set the promised dates for his small pottery orders himself, while Dara recorded how much grain the household would use. Though they lived together, they agreed to manage those matters separately.

In 1198, Nie joined another workshop and left home. In 1203, Dara repaired the canal embankment with Soma's family again, but Soma said they were not as close as they had once been. After Chen died in 1206, Dara tended the rice field alone. In 1211, she moved closer to Nie's family. Even then, she never heard Kiri say he had forgotten the suspicion directed at him that morning.

finalMoment.place: Dara's home near her daughter Nie's house, near Angkor in the Khmer Empire
finalMoment.scene:
One late afternoon in 1214, sixty-year-old Dara sat on the plank floor of her home near Angkor. Her daughter Nie's house was close enough to reach on foot. Dara had been feverish and weak for several days. When Nie opened the door carrying thin porridge, Dara tried to rise and greet her. Her knees would not support her, and she sat back down. “Just stay seated.” Nie set down the bowl.

Dara took the spoon and ate a little porridge. Her hand trembled, so she set down the bowl. “Did you finish your work at home?” Dara asked. “Yes. I'll come again tomorrow morning.” Nie sat beside her for a moment, then returned to her own home. Dara watched the open door until the sound of her daughter's footsteps faded. She could hear people talking outside. Dara moved the remaining porridge closer and leaned against the wall.

As darkness fell, Dara's clothes grew damp with sweat. Her body was hot, but her fingertips were cold. Dara pressed a hand to the plank floor to shift her position. Her arm trembled, and she leaned against the wall again. If she called for a neighbor, someone might hear. “In here…” Dara said toward the door, but her voice was quiet. The footsteps outside did not stop. Dara started to call again, then closed her mouth to catch her breath.

The night deepened. Dara lay on her side and pulled at the hem of her clothes. Wind came through the gap in the open door. Dara breathed in, then out again. Her next breath was short. She tried to push herself up, but her palm slipped on the plank floor. Dara looked toward the door, then closed her eyes. The sound of her breathing ceased. The morning when Nie had promised to return was still far away.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1214, after several days of fever and weakness, Dara died alone at age sixty in her home near Angkor. The exact cause of her illness is unknown. Nie came the next morning carrying a bowl of porridge and found her mother. She remembered how her mother had asked about the work at her home the day before. Nie kept that remark and the memory of her mother letting her join another workshop in 1198 as two distinct memories. Soma later heard the news and recalled the day she and Dara had repaired the embankment together. But that did not erase the withered seedlings or the suspicion her nephew Kiri had endured. The record of this past life closes the story of this life by noting both the times Dara worried about those close to her and took it upon herself to decide their affairs, and the final three years when she lived separately but near her daughter.
finalMoment.artAlt: A late afternoon in 1214, viewed from a high diagonal angle inside a small house near Angkor. Fever-weary Dara, age 60, sits in place while her adult daughter Nie enters through the door a few steps away carrying thin porridge

card.name: Asha
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Asha of Calcutta. You raised two children while continuing the laundry work your mother taught you with Navin. After Tara chose different work, you cut back on new orders because you were short-handed. Even after losing Navin, you worked with Mina.
card.title: The Cut Clothesline
card.world: A neighborhood laundry yard in Calcutta, British India, in 1910
card.flavor: A young goat barging into the middle of the laundry
card.opening: At the laundry yard, where white clothes fluttered in the wind, a young goat suddenly ran off dragging the clothesline. When the line caught around its neck, even the people who had been laughing fell silent.
card.life: She learned laundry work from her mother, made a home with Navin, and raised two children. When Tara chose different work, Asha asked her to come back during a year when they were short-handed. After Tara refused, she stopped accepting some new orders. After losing Navin, she worked with Mina, and when her hands began to hurt, she sorted clothes.
card.turn: The goat ran between the clothes, and the line slipped from its horns toward its neck. If Asha did not cut the line, the goat could be hurt even more, but if she cut it, the clothes due for delivery would fall into the dirt.
card.decision: Asha told Tara to support the goat's body and cut the line. She called to Navin and Mina to separate out the clothes that needed rinsing again.
card.cost: The clothes that had been drying fell into the dirt and had to be washed again. She missed the promised delivery time for one household, and Asha refunded that household's laundry fee.
card.after: Dinu, the goat's owner, brought a new line. Even after hearing why the clothes were late, the customer gave the next order to someone else. Tara later left to find a workplace of her own, and Asha continued working as her family changed.
card.presentEcho: Even after saving the goat, the delivery promise missed that day remained. Asha knew she could not fix everything alone and asked her family and Mina to help rinse the clothes again.
card.secondLook: For Dinu, the injured goat came first, while for the customer, receiving the clothes when they were needed mattered. Asha listened to both sides.
card.unresolved: The goat was safe, but the next order from one household and that day's wages never returned.
card.readerQuestion: A young goat has caught its neck in a clothesline. If you cut the line, clothes due for delivery soon will fall into the dirt. What would you do first?

signalMoments.connect: Asha had Mina hold the end of the line and told Tara to support the goat. When Dinu caught its forelegs, she cut above the knot, and the goat and the clothes fell separately.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Asha. In 1910, you washed and dried customers' clothes in Calcutta, British India. Today, I'll tell you about the day a guest no one had invited ran into her workplace.

When Asha fastened the edge of a white garment to the clothesline, her daughter Tara slid clothespins toward her from the other end. Her husband Navin set aside a place to fold the clothes in delivery order. “This household first, before noon.” Asha pointed to the garment on top. Beside her, Mina shook out a wet cloth and laughed. “The wind is on our side this time.”

The wind really was good. The problem was Dinu's young goat. It had been grazing beside the path next to the laundry yard, but then it chased a fallen leaf and poked its nose between the clothes. When Tara said, “Excuse me, customers have to wait in line,” Mina burst out laughing. Asha raised an eyebrow too. That was when the goat leaped backward.

The clothesline had caught behind its horns. When the goat backed up once more, all the drying clothes were pulled taut at once. Two clothespins flew off, and the white garment at the far end brushed the dirt. “Dinu!” Navin called for the owner. While Dinu came running, the goat twisted forward. The line slipped from its horns toward its neck.

The laughter stopped. Tara reached out to loosen the line, but as the goat thrashed, the knot tightened. Beside Asha was a small pouch where she kept her scissors. Cutting the line would free the goat at once. But customers' clothes that were not yet dry still hung from that line. Among them were the clothes for the household expecting a delivery at noon.

“The clothes will fall,” Tara said. Asha looked once at the white clothes. The time it would take to wash them again flashed through her mind. The goat tilted back its neck and gave a short cry. Asha opened her scissors pouch.

signalMoments.notice: Asha pointed to where the line had slipped from the horns to the neck. “Pulling will only tighten it. Stop the goat first!” Tara supported its body to keep it from being pushed backward, and Asha cut the line just above the knot.
signalMoments.protect: Asha told Tara to hold the goat. The moment Tara gathered the small body into her arms, Asha cut the line beside its neck. The white clothes fell into the dirt, but the line came loose from the goat's neck.
signalMoments.connect: Asha had Mina hold the end of the line and told Tara to support the goat. When Dinu ran over and caught the goat's forelegs, Asha cut above the knot. As the force held by all three was released, the goat and the clothes fell separately.

episode.afterSignal:
The first white garment fell, and the second landed on top of it. Mina stretched out an arm and saved one, but the rest touched the wet dirt. The goat caught its breath in Dinu's arms. Though a faint line mark remained on its neck, it walked well. Dinu bowed his head. “I should have blocked the path.”

Asha counted the dirt-stained clothes. It was no time to laugh. Tara spoke first. “I'll rinse the white ones again.” Mina divided the wet clothes and the already dry clothes into two piles, and Navin rewrote the delivery order. Only after Asha had asked everyone to help did she realize she was still holding the scissors.

As they fetched more water and washed out the dirt, the sunlight shifted. Navin left to deliver some of the clothes first. But the clothes promised to the household at noon did not dry in time. When Asha knocked on that household's door herself, the customer saw an empty basket instead of dry clothes.

“I cut the line to free a goat. The clothes fell, so we're washing them again.” Asha held out the laundry fee in her hand. The customer closed her eyes for a moment, opened them, and took the money. “I'm glad the goat wasn't hurt, but I needed these clothes today.” Asha said that was fair. She promised to bring the clothes the next day, but the customer said she would send her next laundry elsewhere.

When Asha returned, Dinu was waiting with a new line. “I'll pay for it.” Asha accepted the line. The price of the line was not the same as the money from the lost work. Still, after watching Dinu lead his goat away by a wide route, Asha hung the line again. When Tara handed her a new clothespin, Mina stood beneath the line and said, “This time, I'll watch this end.”

That evening, Navin pointed to an empty space in the delivery ledger. Tara said, “If you'd called me from the start, I could have caught a few of the clothes.” Asha replied, “You're right.” A moment later, Tara said, “Someday, I want to try other work too.” Asha stopped with her hand halfway through passing over the next basket. “What kind of work?” she asked. Tara continued doing laundry work at home that year. Even months later, that customer's laundry did not return. The four of them knotted the cut ends and adjusted the length of the new clothesline.

In 1915, Tara started her own work in another neighborhood. Asha washed and sorted clothes with Navin and Mina. When orders piled up in 1917, Asha asked Tara to come back for just a few days, but Tara said she could not leave her own workplace. Asha stopped accepting some new orders. After Navin died in 1928, and after her hands began to hurt in 1933, she left the heavy laundry to Mina. The goat story sometimes brought laughter to the family table, but Asha never forgot the empty basket at noon or what the customer had said that day.

finalMoment.place: The alley between Asha's house and Jitu's house, and Asha's house, Calcutta, British India
finalMoment.scene:
One morning in late summer 1940, sixty-eight-year-old Asha stepped out through the door of her home in Calcutta. Her stomach had hurt for two days, and frequent watery stools had sent her to the backyard latrine several times during the night. She set out into the alley to tell her son Jitu, who lived nearby, but after only a few steps she grew dizzy and stopped. Jitu was coming out to fetch water when he saw his mother. “Mother, why did you come out alone?” Asha replied, “I was going to you.”

Jitu returned to her house with Asha. She sat down on a mat in the room and drank water a little at a time. Her mouth quickly grew dry again. “Has it been like this since yesterday?” Jitu asked. Asha said, “Since the day before yesterday.” After asking a neighbor to call a doctor, Jitu returned to the room. Asha took one more sip of the water he handed her, but her hand trembled as she set down the cup.

By afternoon, Asha had no strength in her legs even when she tried to stand. Jitu opened the window, but Asha remained seated on the mat, opening and closing her eyes. “Tara must be working today too, right?” Asha asked. “Yes. I'll send her word,” Jitu replied. Asha asked no more questions. Her eyes followed the sound of people's footsteps outside.

Jitu felt his mother's hand growing cold. When Asha opened her eyes again, he said his own name. Asha tried to turn her head toward her son but could not lift it all the way. Her breathing quickened, then gradually weakened. Jitu called her name. Asha opened her mouth but could not answer. Her breathing stopped while the sun was still at the window. The doctor arrived afterward.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1940, Asha died at her home in Calcutta with her son Jitu beside her after growing weak from severe diarrhea for two days. The cause of the illness and exact diagnosis are unknown. Jitu looked at the short alley his mother had walked back and forth after moving close to his house. Her daughter Tara arrived the next day and remembered the day in 1917 when her mother asked her to return from her own workplace, and the time they continued exchanging letters after Tara refused. Mina remembered how Asha was slow to say when things were hard, even as they shared the work. The record of this past life tells of the life Asha built with her family and neighbors, the waiting she left a customer with, and the orders she cut back on as she accepted her children's different paths, and brings this life to its end.
finalMoment.artAlt: A morning view from above of a narrow alley in Calcutta in 1940. 68-year-old Asha has stopped alone for a moment, dizzy on her way to alert Jitu's household. No one is supporting her or running toward her

card.name: Sabina
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Sabina of Pompeii. You carried on the food business you had learned from your mother with Petra. After leaving the city, you opened another eatery in Neapolis (present-day Naples), and after losing Petra, you worked with Lycia but argued with her over wages.
card.title: My Name Written on the Wall
card.world: A roadside eatery and election graffiti in Pompeii, Roman Empire, AD 78
card.flavor: An endorsement she never authorized
card.opening: The morning she opened the eatery, Sabina saw her name written in large letters on the outside wall. It was an endorsement of a candidate she had never made.
card.life: She learned the food business from her mother and ran an eatery with her friend Petra. She kept in touch with her younger brother Felix, though they sometimes argued. In AD 79, she left Pompeii and started her business again in Neapolis. After Petra's death, she did not raise Lycia's wages enough when her cooking duties increased.
card.turn: Hoping for an introduction that might lead to hauling work, Felix summoned a sign painter and had him write Sabina's name on the wall without her permission. Customers believed Sabina supported the candidate.
card.decision: Sabina called the sign painter back and had him paint over her name and replace it with an advertisement for food. She told her customers that she had not requested the endorsement.
card.cost: She paid the sign painter's fee again, and some customers who supported the candidate stopped coming. The introduction Felix had hoped for also became uncertain, and the siblings argued for a while.
card.after: Sabina continued running the eatery with Petra, then left Pompeii during the volcanic eruption the following year. She opened another small shop in Neapolis. After Petra died, she carried on the shop with Lycia, but the two argued over wages for Lycia's increased workload.
card.presentEcho: Correcting words that someone else has attributed to you can cost both money and relationships. Sabina tried to choose for herself at least the words that would remain on the wall.
card.secondLook: Felix desperately needed work and wanted to win favor with the candidate's people. While the two argued, Petra handled the customers and the hot dishes. Some customers had come to the eatery because they believed the writing on the wall.
card.unresolved: The writing on the wall was corrected, but the customers who left that day and the introduction Felix had hoped for did not immediately return.
card.readerQuestion: An endorsement of a candidate that I never authorized has appeared on my eatery wall. The customers believe it represents my wishes. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Sabina pointed to the wet white undercoat and said she would find out who had requested the writing. When Felix admitted that he had summoned the sign painter, she took him with her and stood before the wall.
signalMoments.speak: Sabina told the customers at the door that she had not requested the endorsement. She told Felix that she would listen to his worries about finding work, but first they had to correct the words spoken in her name.
signalMoments.repair: Sabina called the sign painter back and asked him to erase her name and write up that day's hot bean dish. The candidate's name remained on the wall, and Sabina paid a second fee.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Sabina. In AD 78, you ran a small eatery with your friend Petra in Pompeii, a city of the Roman Empire. One morning, what Sabina saw outside her door was neither a customer nor a delivery of ingredients. Her own name covered one side of the wall. Let me tell you what happened that day.

Whenever it was time to elect people to city offices, people wrote endorsements of candidates on roadside walls. Sabina could not vote, but she could write on the wall of her busy eatery to say whom she supported. The words now on the wall, however, were not something Sabina had requested. “Sabina endorses Marcus.” The black letters stood neat against the freshly painted white background.

Petra carried bowls into the eatery and stared at the writing for a long moment. “When did you say that?” “I never did,” Sabina replied. They had barely opened when two customers stopped before the writing. One nodded, while the other turned away, saying, “I won't be coming here anymore.” Sabina had lost a customer before the morning's business had even begun.

Sabina examined the wall closely. The edge of the white undercoat was still damp, and beneath the black letters was a tiny dot left when someone had set down a tool. It was the mark the neighborhood sign painter always left behind. He could not have gone far. When Sabina rounded the street corner, she found him washing his brush in front of another house's wall.

“Who asked you to write that?” Sabina asked. At first, he laughed. “Someone from your shop. He said he was your brother.” Sabina returned to the eatery. Felix was setting down a basket of ingredients, but when he saw his sister's face, his hands froze.

“Did you put my name there?” Felix gripped the basket handle. He said he had hoped someone connected to the candidate would introduce him to hauling work. “I thought if it looked like our shop supported him, they might listen to me too.” “It isn't our shop's name. It's mine,” Sabina said. Petra moved the hot dish that sat between them. Outside the door, they again heard a customer reading the new writing aloud.

Felix spoke quietly. “If you erase it, I won't even be able to show my face to them.” Sabina turned toward the wall. If she left it alone, customers would read the words as her own wishes from that day forward. If she erased them, she would be left with the cost of rewriting the sign and Felix's anger. Inside the eatery, the first pot began to boil.

signalMoments.notice: Sabina pointed to the still-wet white undercoat. “This was written at dawn today. I'll find out who asked for it, and then I'll erase it.” When Felix admitted that he had summoned the sign painter, Sabina took him with her and stood before the wall.
signalMoments.speak: Sabina spoke to the customers reading the words outside the door. “I did not request that endorsement.” She also told Felix, “I'll listen to what you hoped to gain. But first, let's correct the words spoken in my name.”
signalMoments.repair: Sabina called the sign painter back. “You can decide what to do with the candidate's name. Erase the part with my name and write this instead.” She pointed to that day's hot bean dish and counted out a second fee.

episode.afterSignal:
The sign painter covered Sabina's name with a fresh coat of white paint. When only the candidate's name remained on the wall, the customers became even more curious. Sabina had him write a short notice about that day's bean dish beneath it. Petra read it from the threshold and laughed. “People will look at the pot before they look at the candidate.” But laughter could not make the money paid to the sign painter disappear.

Felix slammed down the pot lid too hard. “Now I won't even get to meet that man.” “Did he promise to introduce you?” Sabina asked. Felix did not answer. There had been no promise. Sabina understood how her younger brother felt about needing work, but she could not let his feelings speak in her name.

At lunchtime, two regulars who supported Marcus walked straight past the eatery. Another customer asked, “Is the soup still the same?” and Petra served him a bowl. Sabina grasped a hot handle, then released it. The two who had walked past did not return that day. That evening, she saw that a few fewer bowls than usual had been emptied.

That evening, Felix returned carrying an empty basket. Sabina pushed a bowl of soup toward him. They ate side by side, but neither brought up the wall again. At last, Felix spoke. “Tomorrow, I'll look for other hauling work too.” Sabina said, “Ask me if you need help.” Those words did not immediately reconcile them.

As Petra closed the shop, she read the new writing on the wall. That day's food was listed beside the candidate's name in black letters, which looked a little absurd. Sabina washed the small ladle her mother had used. The writing on the wall could always be painted over again. But she could not know whether the customers who had left that morning would come back.

When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79, Sabina left Pompeii with Petra and Felix. In 81, she and Petra opened another small eatery in Neapolis, present-day Naples. Felix found separate hauling work in 85, and the siblings saw less of each other.

After Petra died in 94, Sabina carried on the shop with Lycia. In 99, Sabina's wrist began to hurt, and Lycia had to do more of the cooking, but Sabina granted only part of the wage increase Lycia requested. Lycia decided that she would not take on the additional work of buying ingredients and keeping the accounts. The two continued to see each other at the shop, but they did not agree about the matter.

finalMoment.place: The shared courtyard of Sabina's home in Neapolis, Roman Empire
finalMoment.scene:
One late-summer afternoon in AD 102, I was 58 years old and watering the potted plants in the shared courtyard of my home in Neapolis. It was my day off from the food shop. Across the courtyard, the woman next door shook out a wet cloth by her doorway. Just as I reached for the second bowl, a bee stung my forearm. “I've been stung by a bee.” I rubbed my arm, and the woman looked up.

At first, I thought only my arm stung, but then my lips swelled. My collar suddenly felt as though it were strangling me, so I tugged it loose with my hand. I still could not draw breath. “Please call someone.” The woman next door shouted toward the alley, and someone answered that they would summon a doctor. I sat down beside the potted plants and opened my mouth. A harsh sound came from my throat whenever I tried to breathe in.

The woman knelt before me and asked my name. I tried to say Sabina, but my voice was faint. The bowl fell from my hand and rolled across the ground. “I'm here,” the woman said again. Watching her sleeve, I tried to nod. Her face blurred, and the sounds grew distant.
finalMoment.afterword: In AD 102, Sabina was stung by a bee in the courtyard of her home in Neapolis and rapidly developed difficulty breathing. She died beside the potted plants at the age of 58. The precise medical cause of death and the species of bee are unknown. The woman next door remembered the words Sabina had spoken when she asked for help herself. Her younger brother Felix arrived later and stood outside the door of the house where his sister had lived. Although they had occasionally shared meals even after they began seeing less of each other, they had not planned to meet that day. Lycia, who was at the shop, closed the account book when she heard of Sabina's death. The fact that Lycia had taken on more cooking but received only a small wage increase could not be erased. The record of this past life recounts both the evenings Petra and Sabina created together and the cost Sabina imposed on Lycia because of the money she tried to protect, and thus brings this life to its end.
finalMoment.artAlt: An afternoon view from inside a doorway into a modest shared courtyard in Neapolis in AD 102. Sabina, age 58, stands examining the arm where a bee stung her, and no one else is visible

card.name: Elsa
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Elsa of Stockholm. You learned to write down numbers beside your father and worked for many years as a telephone operator. You lived with Olle and your daughter Karin, and after leaving the telephone exchange, you kept the books for an alterations shop. A record also remained there of the time you assigned responsibility for missing fabric to your coworker Ingrid.
card.title: The Sister Behind the Glass
card.world: The 1922 telephone operators' strike in Stockholm, Kingdom of Sweden
card.flavor: Her sister entered the exchange room on the first day of the strike
card.opening: On the first morning the telephone operators stood outside their workplace, Elsa saw her sister Marta plugging in lines behind the glass.
card.life: She learned to write down measurements and numbers from her father and became a telephone operator. She married Olle and raised Karin. Later, she trained new operators and kept the books for an alterations shop. She assigned the loss of fabric she could not account for to the tailor Ingrid, and Ingrid left the shop after receiving less work.
card.turn: Marta entered the exchange room, saying she would work for only one day on the first day of the strike because she owed rent and needed money to feed her daughter Inga. Elsa could neither condemn her sister in front of their coworkers nor secretly cover for her.
card.decision: Elsa listened to Marta, then went with her to the union office to check the support available to operators with children. When it was still not enough, she lent Marta part of the rent from her own household money. In front of their coworker Anna, she let Marta say herself that she had worked that day.
card.cost: She postponed repairing her daughter Karin's shoes until the following week. Even after Marta returned to the picket line, their coworkers' distrust did not immediately fade, and Elsa also argued with her husband Olle about the money.
card.after: After working for one day, Marta stood beside the other operators again. The strike ended ten days later, but the two sisters did not claim that they had come to understand each other easily. Elsa trained junior operators and later kept the books for an alterations shop. Her choice there not to record what Ingrid said was not erased by the fact that she had helped her sister on the day of the strike.
card.presentEcho: Even when people want to stand on the same side, their circumstances at home are not always the same. Elsa did not cover up her sister's choice, but she listened to what had led her to make it.
card.secondLook: Marta needed money for rent that was due immediately. Her coworkers worried that one person filling an empty seat could weaken the strike. To Olle and Karin, the money Elsa lent was no small amount either.
card.unresolved: Part of the rent was covered, but the bond between the sisters and the trust of their coworkers did not return in a single day.
card.readerQuestion: The operators are standing outside their workplace, but your sister is inside connecting calls. She owes back rent. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Elsa read the date on the rent notice and asked whether one day's wages would be enough to pay it all. When Marta shook her head, Elsa said they should first find out what money she could receive from the union.
signalMoments.speak: Elsa took Marta around the street corner. She said that she had heard why Marta went inside but would not lie for her, and suggested that they ask together about the support she could receive.
signalMoments.connect: Elsa admitted to Marta that all she knew was the slogan. Together, they passed through their coworkers and went upstairs to the union office to ask what money Marta could receive.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Elsa. You worked as a telephone operator in Stockholm, Kingdom of Sweden, in 1922. One day, you saw someone behind the glass who should not have been there. It was your sister Marta, who worked with you. Let me tell you what happened that day.

That morning, Karin placed her shoes beside Elsa's worn pair. The toes had split open, exposing her own toes. “I'll have them fixed this week,” Elsa said, and Karin put the shoes back on. At the table, Olle silently broke the bread in half and pushed the larger piece toward his daughter. Ever since Olle's repair work dried up a few years before, every bit of the household money always had somewhere it needed to go first.

The telephone office had an exchange room where people manually connected multiple lines. An operator had to plug the cords into a long, wall-like switchboard before two people far apart could speak. Elsa had done that work for fifteen years. But the women operators had decided to stop working at seven that morning, demanding better wages, days off, and treatment when they were ill. Elsa rubbed her hands together among her coworkers outside the workplace.

A small light came on at the switchboard beyond the glass. A woman pulled out a cord and plugged it into another jack. Elsa recognized the blue thread tied around her wrist. Elsa herself had tied it around Marta's wrist the previous winter. “Marta?” A coworker beside her also looked up at the window. “Is that your sister in there?” Elsa could not answer.

Marta lived alone with six-year-old Inga. Even after losing her husband, she had never once asked Elsa for money to buy food. So Elsa had gone on without knowing how short of money her sister was. But now Marta truly was connecting calls behind the glass. At the very hour her coworkers had stopped working.

After noon, Marta came out through a side door. Elsa followed her, and her sister spoke first. “I'm only doing it for one day.” “Why didn't you tell me?” Elsa's voice rose. Marta took a folded paper from inside her coat. It was a notice demanding the back rent. “I didn't want to hear them tell me to leave our home in front of Inga,” Marta said.

Elsa started to say that the union paid a little money even during a strike, then closed her mouth. She did not know exactly how much it paid, or whether Marta would receive more because she was raising a child. The blue thread was still tied around her sister's wrist. Two coworkers standing at a distance watched them.

signalMoments.notice: Elsa first read the date on the rent notice. “Can you earn enough here today to pay it all?” Marta shook her head. Elsa said, “Then let's first find out what money you can receive from the union.”
signalMoments.speak: Elsa took Marta around the street corner. “I've heard why you went inside. I won't lie for you. Let's ask together whether there's any money you can receive.” Marta folded the notice and held it in her hand.
signalMoments.connect: Elsa held out her hand to Marta. “All I know is the slogan. Let's go to the union and ask together what you can receive.” The two passed through their coworkers and climbed the narrow stairs to the office.

episode.afterSignal:
A ledger listing the operators' names lay on the desk in the union office. The person in charge pointed out the money they could receive during the strike and explained that people with children received a little more. Marta added up the amount. It was still not enough for the rent. “Then I'll have to go back inside,” her sister said, putting the notice in her pocket.

Elsa thought of the split toes of Karin's shoes. She could not spend the same money both on repairing the shoes and on helping with the rent. “I'll lend you what you're short.” Marta shook her head. “Olle's work still isn't steady.” “That's why I'm lending it to you. We'll decide together when you can pay me back.” Elsa wrote the amount in her notebook. It was not money she could simply promise and then forget.

Their coworker Anna was waiting for them at the bottom of the stairs. “You did work today, didn't you?” Elsa did not answer for Marta. Marta herself said, “I did. Tomorrow I'll stand outside.” Anna looked from one sister to the other for a moment. “We pay rent too.” She turned away. Marta did not follow her. Elsa could not say Anna was wrong either.

At the dinner table that evening, Karin touched the toe of her shoe again. Elsa told her they would have to postpone going to the repair shop until the following week. When Olle asked why, Elsa confessed that she had lent money to her sister. “You could have told me first,” Olle said. Elsa started to argue, then stopped. They were the exact words she had said to Marta that morning. Only the sound of chewing bread remained at the table.

The next day, Marta stood beside her coworkers rather than behind the glass of the exchange room. Anna did not move away, but neither did she speak first. Elsa and Marta stood together in that narrow space. Karin went to school that day too, wearing shoes with split toes. They had been able to cover the immediate rent, but they had not settled every debt between their hearts.

Ten days later, the operators returned to work. Elsa connected telephone lines for many years, and later taught new operators those hand movements. After leaving the telephone exchange, she kept the books for an alterations shop. In 1947, she could not confirm who was responsible for a missing bolt of fabric, but as the owner demanded, she entered it under the tailor Ingrid's name. Elsa continued keeping the books even after Ingrid's orders dwindled and Ingrid left the shop. The day she spent household money for her sister and the day she did not write down Ingrid's statement remained together in one person's life.
