finalMoment.place: A neighborhood market in Stockholm, Sweden
finalMoment.scene:
It is a morning in Stockholm in 1964. I have come alone to the neighborhood market. The vendor puts carrots in a paper bag and tells me the price. I used to guess the price with my daughter Karin, and we would laugh over who got it right. Today, I spread coins across my palm to buy only my share. “There are smaller ones too,” the vendor says, pointing to a bunch of carrots.

As I try to choose the coins, the vendor in front of me suddenly seems far away. The sounds of the market stay the same, but the ground seems to tilt. The bag slips from my hand, and the carrots roll around my feet. I grasp the corner of the vendor's counter. “Just a moment.” As soon as I finish speaking, my breath grows short. The vendor takes my arm and leads me to a small chair behind the stall.

The vendor turns toward the market and calls for help. Even so, the vendor does not leave me. Sitting in the chair, I reach down to pick up one carrot. There is no strength left in my arm, and my hand falls to my knee. The vendor crouches in front of me. “Can you tell me your name?” “Elsa.” After that one word, I close my mouth and struggle to catch my breath.

My eyes move between the vendor's face and the bag at my feet. I want to tell Karin what I bought today. I open my mouth, but no voice comes out. I try to draw another breath, but my chest does not move. The vendor calls my name again. The sounds of the market grow faint. My hand, reaching toward the bag, comes to rest beside the chair.
finalMoment.afterword: Elsa died at a Stockholm market in 1964 while a market vendor remained by her side. The exact cause of her sudden dizziness and change in breathing was never recorded. When Karin arrived afterward, she took home the bag of carrots the vendor had repacked and placed it on the table. Marta remembered the afternoons when she and her sister took turns caring for their grandchildren. The ledger entry that cost Ingrid her work was never corrected. The record of this imagined past life closes Elsa's story by recording both that entry and the carrots on Karin's table.
finalMoment.artAlt: Daytime in 1964, viewed diagonally from above a vegetable stall at a neighborhood market in Stockholm. 76-year-old Elsa sits on a chair beside a bag of carrots, one hand on her chest as she struggles to catch her breath, while a market vendor makes eye contact with her from the front. No one nearby is supporting her or running to call for help

card.name: Nicolás
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Nicolás of Buenos Aires. Using the repair skills you learned from your father and uncle, you worked on pianos. You ran a shop with your business partner, Emma, and lived with your longtime partner, Inés. At first, you tried to stop your nephew Luis from striking out on his own, but in your later years, you passed some of your tools on to him.
card.title: The Night the Pianos Were Switched
card.world: A tango café in Buenos Aires, Argentine Republic, in 1935
card.flavor: The wrong note that rang out before the performance
card.opening: Just before the café's first tango began, the pianist struck a key and asked, “You call this tuned?” Nicolás had definitely spent more than an hour tuning it.
card.life: He learned to work with his hands in his father's workshop and learned piano tuning from his uncle. He opened a repair shop with his business partner, Emma, and had a long relationship with Inés, a dance teacher. When his nephew Luis opened a separate shop, he repeatedly urged him to stay. After his hearing weakened, he focused on repairing keys and training new workers.
card.turn: When the two pianos were temporarily switched so the floor could be repaired, Nicolás looked only at the blue ribbon on the bench and tuned the practice piano. He failed to check that the two pianos had been returned to their original places before the performance, or to look for the repair mark beneath the performance piano's keys.
card.decision: Nicolás admitted his mistake to the café owner and the band. There was no time to retune all the strings, so he helped move the piano he had already tuned into the performance space.
card.cost: The music started late while the customers waited. The café owner deducted part of his tuning fee, and Nicolás also missed the repair appointment he had scheduled at the next house.
card.after: The band finished its performance on the piano they had moved. Afterward, Nicolás made a habit of checking for small repair marks. When Luis struck out on his own, Nicolás tried to persuade him to stay at his shop, but on opening day, he helped move the workbench into Luis's new place.
card.presentEcho: When you do not hide a mistake, sometimes a path to starting over appears. But even along that path, there may still be people kept waiting and appointments missed.
card.secondLook: The performer heard the wrong sound from the first note and became angry. The workers repairing the floor had moved the two pianos and then put them back, while Nicolás had looked only at the blue ribbon on the bench instead of checking the instrument. The café owner had to keep the customers waiting.
card.unresolved: That night's performance ended, but the lost wages and the missed repair appointment never came back.
card.readerQuestion: There is little time left before the performance, and a wrong note comes from the piano you believe you just tuned. There is another similar piano beside it. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Beneath the keys of the stage piano, Nicolás found the triangular repair mark he had attached a few days earlier. The piano he had tuned that afternoon did not have the mark. He realized the instrument he had tuned was in the next room.
signalMoments.speak: Nicolás called over the band and the café owner. He admitted that he had looked only at the blue ribbon on the bench and tuned the other piano, and said there was no time to fix every string on the stage piano.
signalMoments.repair: Nicolás started to place his tuning hammer on the stage piano, then stopped. Even if he fixed one note, the others would remain as they were. Hearing the sound he had tuned coming from the next room, he said they should move the two instruments again.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Nicolás. You were a piano repairman in Buenos Aires, Argentine Republic, in 1935. One night, just as the customers were coming in, the band's first note sounded wrong. Let me tell you the story of the night Nicolás was certain he had tuned that piano.

A small dance café in Barracas kept two upright pianos: one for the stage and another in the next room for rehearsals. Nicolás remembered the small triangular piece of wood he had attached beneath the keys of the performance piano a few days earlier. It marked the spot where he had patched a break. The café owner had tied a blue ribbon to the bench in front of the performance piano. “Please tune that one today.”

On the afternoon of the performance, while his partner Inés taught dancing on the café floor, workers switched the positions of the two pianos. They needed to clear the area so they could repair the floor. Only the bench remained in its original place. Nicolás arrived late and first noticed the bench with the blue ribbon. He did not look for the repair mark beneath the keys. He opened the piano in front of it and turned the metal pins little by little with his tuning hammer. He sat there for more than an hour, until the strings tightened and the sound became clear.

The repair ledger that his business partner Emma brought listed an appointment at the next house. “We have to go straight there when you're done.” As Nicolás packed his tools, he nodded. While he looked at the ledger, the workers finished fixing the floor and returned the two pianos to their original places. Nicolás did not see them do it. Outside the café door, early customers stood laughing in line. Inés finished the last dance step and drank some water.

Then the performer sat at the stage piano and pressed the opening note of the first piece. Tang—a strange sound rang out. He pressed the same key again. “You call this freshly tuned?” The café owner looked at Nicolás. Nicolás began to say, “I'm certain,” but swallowed the words. The sound onstage was different from the one he had just heard.

Inés pointed beneath the stage. “They switched the two pianos this afternoon to fix the floor, then just put them back in their original places.” Too late, Nicolás remembered that the blue ribbon had been tied to the bench, not the piano. In front of the piano in the next room was a bench with no ribbon. There was not enough time before the performance to tune all the many strings of the stage piano. The customers' footsteps were already crossing the threshold.

signalMoments.notice: Nicolás ran his fingers beneath the keys of the stage piano. There was the triangular repair mark he had attached a few days earlier. But the instrument he had spent all afternoon tuning did not have that mark. “The one I tuned is in the next room now.” He realized the two pianos had been switched and then put back.
signalMoments.speak: Nicolás called over the band and the owner. “I looked only at the blue ribbon on the bench and tuned the other piano. There isn't enough time to fix the entire stage piano now.” The performer closed his eyes for a moment, then opened them.
signalMoments.repair: Nicolás started to place his tuning hammer on the stage piano, then stopped. Even if he fixed one note, the other notes would remain as they were. When he heard the sound he had tuned coming from the next room, he said, “We have to move the two pianos again.”

episode.afterSignal:
“Then let's move them,” Nicolás said first. The performer was still angry, and the owner looked toward the customers at the door. Inés called over two members of the band and a worker. After saying again that it was his mistake, Nicolás pulled out a piece of cloth caught beneath one of the next room piano's wheels. When the four of them pushed, the instrument caught once on the doorframe.

“Wait. If we push it like that, we'll break the door.” Nicolás lifted the front slightly and changed its angle. His sleeve snagged on the rough wood and tore. One of the customers waiting behind them said, “Even the piano is learning to dance.” Someone laughed, but the café owner did not. The first song could not begin while the two instruments onstage changed places.

The piano now standing onstage had no triangular repair mark beneath its keys. It was the instrument Nicolás had spent all afternoon tuning. The performer played a short melody. The harsh note from moments earlier was gone. “It's right this time.” Only then did he raise a hand to the band. People came out onto the floor when the tango began late.

The owner counted out the tuning fee, then slid a few coins back toward himself. “You kept the customers waiting.” Nicolás did not protest. It was already time for the next repair house in Emma's ledger to close. He slipped a note through the crack in that house's door saying he was late, then folded his torn sleeve to hide it.

Inés untied the blue ribbon from the bench and handed it to Nicolás. “Next time, look at the piano instead of the bench.” Nicolás laughed. The owner did not take the ribbon back. Nicolás felt beneath the keys once more for the small piece of wood. The people who danced that night quickly forgot how late the music had started, but Nicolás could not erase the money he had lost or the appointment he had missed from the ledger.

After that, Nicolás ran the repair shop with Emma for many years, lived with Inés, and taught the work to his nephew Luis. In his later years, when his hearing weakened, he examined where the keys moved instead of tuning notes. The night the pianos were switched was one mistake among the countless instruments he repaired over his lifetime. What I have told you is the story of the day Nicolás did not hide his mistake and switched the instrument onstage.

timeline.event: Born in Barracas, Buenos Aires
Begins spending time in his father's furniture repair workshop

finalMoment.place: Nicolás and Inés's home in Buenos Aires, Argentina
finalMoment.scene:
It is an evening in Buenos Aires in 1970. I am having a late meal at home with my partner, Inés. Inés tells me about a neighbor she met during the day, and I listen while chewing a piece of bread. We have lived together for a long time, but whenever Inés talks about the people she saw that day, a name I have never heard before comes up. “Would you like to meet that person tomorrow?” Inés asks.

As I try to answer, the bread catches in my throat. I cough, but the piece does not move. I put a hand to my throat and stand up. Inés sees my expression and stops talking. “Nicolás?” I try to say I am fine, but no sound comes out. When I try to breathe in, only my chest heaves.

Inés comes to my side, bends me forward, and strikes my back. The piece of bread does not come out. I grip the edge of the table and try to remain standing. Inés shouts toward the front door for a neighbor, then speaks to me again. “Nicolás, look at me.” I want to lift my head, but I cannot draw a breath.

Inés strikes my back again. One by one, my fingers slip from the edge of the table, and my knees touch the floor. Inés bends beside me, calling my name. Both plates remain untouched on the table. When a neighbor's reply comes through the open door, I can no longer raise my head. Inés watches my chest, but it does not move.
finalMoment.afterword: That day, Nicolás died at the age of 72 after bread became lodged in his throat at his home in Buenos Aires. Inés tried to help him at his side, but she could not remove the piece of bread. For a while, Inés told no one the story about the neighbor whom Nicolás had been unable to answer. When his nephew Luis came after hearing the news of his death, he remembered both the day his uncle had tried to stop him from striking out on his own and the day he had helped move the workbench into the new shop. This chronicle of a past life records Nicolás's repair work, his difficult conversations with Luis, and the dinners he shared with Inés, and now tells of this life's end.
finalMoment.artAlt: An evening in 1970 at the dining table in their Buenos Aires home, where 72-year-old Nicolás struggles after bread becomes lodged in his throat and his longtime partner, Inés, rises from across the table and reaches toward him

card.name: Okbun
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Okbun from the coast of Jeongui-hyeon on Jeju. You learned diving from your mother and worked in the sea for many years, made a home with Mansik, and raised Yeonhwa and Deoksu. In old age, you repaired diving tools and taught young jamnyeo divers.
card.title: The Bitchang Left in the Sea
card.world: A seaside village on Jeju in Jeongui-hyeon, Joseon, in 1862
card.flavor: Between the abalone and her mother's tool
card.opening: Okbun's fingertips caught on a large abalone. The iron bitchang she had inherited from her mother was also wedged in a crack in the rock. She had very little time left to hold her breath.
card.life: She learned to work in the sea from her mother, Geumrye. She made a home with Mansik and raised Yeonhwa and Deoksu, and often went diving with Bokrye. As she grew older, she worked in shallow water and repaired tewak floats and mangsari net bags.
card.turn: The bitchang she was using to pry off a large abalone became wedged in a crack in the rock. The current shifted and she was running out of breath, but the tool had belonged to her late mother, and she had used it for many years.
card.decision: Okbun left the bitchang where it was and rose to the surface. She signaled to the approaching Bokrye not to dive any deeper, and the two returned to shore together.
card.cost: She lost her mother's bitchang and the abalone she would have harvested that day. Until she could buy a new bitchang, she borrowed Bokrye's worn spare and saved money for one from her own share of the earnings.
card.after: Okbun went back to diving, but as she aged, she spent less time in deep water. She gradually devoted more time to repairing tools and nets and teaching young jamnyeo how to read the currents.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes you have to let go of something you have treasured for years. The pain of losing it does not diminish all the other years you shared with it.
card.secondLook: Bokrye wanted to dive down and help Okbun, but she knew that both of them could be caught in the same current. Seeing her mother's empty hands, Yeonhwa felt relieved, yet she also worried about the cost of a tool for the next day's work.
card.unresolved: Okbun returned alive, but her mother's bitchang remained in the sea, and the cost of buying a new tool weighed on the household for some time.
card.readerQuestion: A precious iron tool is wedged in a crack in an underwater rock. It will take more time to retrieve, and you are running out of breath. Nearby, you see a companion coming to help. What will you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Okbun looked up and saw the gourd tewak drifting sideways quickly. To retrieve the bitchang, she would have to dive down again against the strong current. She let go of the handle and kicked toward the surface.
signalMoments.protect: When Bokrye dived toward her, Okbun opened her empty palm to signal that she should not come closer. After Bokrye turned back toward the surface, Okbun released the bitchang and pushed off the rock to rise.
signalMoments.release: Okbun started to twist the bitchang harder, then opened her fingers. The iron handle remained in the crack, and Okbun pushed off the rock and rose empty-handed.

identity.region: Jeongui-hyeon, Jeju (Joseon)
identity.summary: She learned diving from her mother and worked in the sea for many years. She made a home with Mansik and raised their children, and in old age she repaired diving tools and taught young jamnyeo divers.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Yang Okbun · Female
1813–1887 · Age 74
Southeastern Jeju Island · Jeongui-hyeon, Joseon
Work · Jamnyeo diver, diving-tool repairer
Life · She learned to work in the sea from her mother, Geumrye. She made a home with her husband, Mansik, and raised their daughter, Yeonhwa, and son, Deoksu. After reducing her deep-water diving as she aged, she repaired gourd tewak floats and net bags and taught young jamnyeo how to read the sea.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · She was the first to smile in front of others, but when the current changed, she would watch in silence for a long while.
Liked · Tapping a well-dried tewak in the sunlight and listening to its clear sound
Disliked · People borrowing someone else's tools without asking and leaving them where they were
Good at · Reading the direction of the current and repairing worn spots on gourds and nets

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The bitchang she received from her mother, and Bokrye, the friend who worked beside her for many years
Those closest to her · Mansik, Yeonhwa, Deoksu, Bokrye
The life she wanted · A life where she earned her own food and could still find work to do on the shore when she grew old
Worry · Whether she would become a burden on her family when the day came to work less

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Okbun. You were a diver on the coast of Jeju Island in Joseon in 1862. Let me tell you about the day you left the iron bitchang inherited from your mother in the sea and came back to the surface.

Before sunrise, Okbun set her gourd tewak afloat on the seawater. A net bag for holding her catch hung beneath it. Okbun and Bokrye planned to work only until they had enough to empty that bag, then return home. Yeonhwa had laid out a place in front of the house to dry the seaweed her mother would bring back.

“The water behind that rock is fast today.” Bokrye pointed to a distant rock. Okbun also saw the seaweed stems moving on the surface. Still, there might be abalone clinging to the shallow side in front of the rock. Saying she would only take a quick look, she gripped the bitchang that her mother, Geumrye, had once used. A bitchang was an iron tool for prying abalone from rocks. After Geumrye died, Okbun had replaced and gripped its handle many times as she continued using it.

Below the water, it was quieter than she had expected. Beneath the rock, Okbun found an abalone the size of her palm. When she carefully slid in the tip of the bitchang, one side of the abalone lifted. At that moment, the bitchang caught fast in a crack in the rock. Okbun twisted her wrist and pulled once. The tool did not move.

Above her, the tewak drifted away from the rock. It meant the current had changed. Still holding both the abalone and the bitchang, Okbun pulled once more. Her chest tightened. While she struggled to let go, Bokrye waved from the surface and angled her body down into the water. Okbun did not want Bokrye to dive deeper because of her. But she did not want to leave the bitchang behind either. It was the tool Geumrye's hands had worn smooth from use.

signalMoments.notice: Okbun looked up. The gourd tewak was drifting sideways faster than a moment before. To retrieve the bitchang, she would have to dive down again against the current. Okbun took her hand off the handle and kicked toward the surface.
signalMoments.protect: Bokrye dived toward Okbun. Okbun opened her empty palm to signal that she should not come closer. After making sure Bokrye had turned back toward the surface, Okbun released the bitchang and pushed off the rock to rise.
signalMoments.release: Okbun nearly twisted the bitchang harder to pry off the abalone. Then she opened her fingers. The iron handle remained in the crack in the rock. Okbun pushed off the rock and rose empty-handed.

episode.afterSignal:
When Okbun's face broke the surface, her breath burst out in a long gasp. Bokrye grabbed the gourd tewak first. “Your hands?” “They're here.” Okbun held up both hands. Bokrye looked relieved, then saw that Okbun's hands were empty and asked no more questions.

When they reached the shore, Okbun sat on a wet rock. Bokrye offered to dive back in, but Okbun shook her head. The water was already surging hard around the back of the rock. The abalone and the bitchang would still be down there, but she did not want Bokrye to put her hand into the same crack.

Yeonhwa came out to collect the seaweed for drying and saw the empty net bag. “Was there not much today?” Okbun told her daughter the whole story of the rock and the bitchang from the beginning. Yeonhwa fell silent for a moment, then said, “It belonged to Grandmother.” Okbun answered, “Yes.” Together, they folded up the straw mat they had spread out that day.

On the next diving day, Okbun borrowed the worn spare bitchang Bokrye kept for use. In the meantime, she set aside a little from her own share at a time to pay for a new iron tool. Even when she passed beneath the deep rock again, she did not dive down to search for her mother's bitchang. Whenever Okbun lingered too long on the surface, Bokrye brought her tewak alongside Okbun's first.

Much later, Okbun told Yeonhwa, “I hated losing the abalone that day, and I hated losing the bitchang even more.” When Yeonhwa asked, “Even now?” Okbun smiled briefly. “Even now. But that day, I came back to you, even if it was empty-handed.” Instead of answering, Yeonhwa held the loose knot in the net her mother was repairing.

After that, Okbun worked in shallow water with Bokrye for several more years. After Mansik died, she spent more time repairing tewak floats and mangsari net bags, and she taught young jamnyeo how to read the currents near the shore. What I have told you is the story of one brief breath in Okbun's long life—the moment when she had to leave her mother's tool behind and rise out of the sea.

finalMoment.place: Okbun's house in a coastal village in Jeongui-hyeon, Jeju, Joseon
finalMoment.scene:
It is 1887, in my home in Jeongui-hyeon, Jeju. I have had a fever for three days and could not even go out into the yard today. My daughter Yeonhwa has gone to sell dried seaweed. My son Deoksu visited this morning, and now my old friend Bokrye sits beside me. When Bokrye lifts a cup of water, I try to sit up. I brace my hands on the blanket, but my elbows keep slipping.

“I'll hold you.” Bokrye supports my back. Yeonhwa helped me drink water yesterday too. I hate that today I must even lean on Bokrye, so I reach out, but the hand holding the cup trembles. I swallow one sip of water and give the cup back. When Bokrye tries to wipe the water from the back of my hand, I say, “That's enough,” and take the cloth. Even holding the cloth is difficult, and I soon lower it onto my lap.

I hear someone's footsteps passing outside. “Will Yeonhwa be done at the market?” I ask. Bokrye answers, “Deoksu went to fetch her.” When Yeonhwa was young, she chose to dry and sell seaweed instead of doing the diving I did. When she comes back, I want to hear about the market today. “Wake me when she comes.” Bokrye nods. I close my eyes, open them, and look toward the door again.

The fever has left my throat dry. Bokrye lifts the cup again, but now, even when I part my lips, I do not have the strength to swallow. The pauses between my breaths grow longer. Bokrye sets down the cup and calls my name. “Okbun, I'm here.” Trying to answer, I take Bokrye's hand. My fingers curl once. I wait for footsteps outside the door and try to draw another breath, but my chest does not move. My hand loosens from Bokrye's.
finalMoment.afterword: That day, Okbun died in her own home with Bokrye beside her. The cause of her fever and the exact illness are not known. Yeonhwa returned with Deoksu but was unable to tell her mother about that day's market. Yeonhwa asked Bokrye why she had not summoned them sooner, and Bokrye remembered those words for a long time. Deoksu thought of both the tasks his mother had insisted on doing alone and the days when he had helped her. This chapter of the past-life record closes the story of Okbun's life—not only her years as a diver, but also how she accepted Yeonhwa's different work, remained Bokrye's friend for many years, and held that friend's hand at the end.
finalMoment.artAlt: Inside a modest home in Jeongui-hyeon, Jeju, Joseon, in 1887, 74-year-old Okbun lies weakened after three days of fever, holding the hand of her old friend Bokrye as Bokrye sets down a cup of water in the daytime

card.name: Hasan
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Hasan of Cairo. You spent your life working as a bookbinder, a craft you learned as an apprentice, and you and your wife Maryam each earned money to raise your daughter Nura. There was also a day when you put your own order first and caused Maryam to miss a cloth delivery. In old age, when your hands hurt, you taught a young bookbinder and lived near your daughter.
card.title: Two Blank Covers
card.world: Cairo in the Mamluk Sultanate, 1352
card.flavor: Who owns a mother's record of her recipes?
card.opening: Two sisters entered Hasan's workshop clutching a bundle of their mother's recipe notes. They wanted different covers, but there was only one bundle of papers.
card.life: He grew up watching his carpenter father work and learned the trade from a master bookbinder. He and his wife Maryam raised Nura on both their incomes. Because he was busy with his own order, he failed to write Maryam's promised cloth delivery in the ledger, causing her to lose a customer. Maryam took back the ledger, and later, when Hasan's hands began to hurt, he taught an apprentice.
card.turn: The older daughter had kept the original safe for years, while the younger had cooked with their mother and filled in the blank spaces. Each said the record bore the marks of her own hands and asked him to bind it as her book.
card.decision: Hasan did not choose either side. He had them look at the original together in the workshop and borrowed paper and writing tools from his cousin Zayd so they could each copy the parts they needed themselves.
card.cost: Hasan missed the promised completion time for two earlier book orders because he made two blank covers for the sisters and gave them space to work. One customer withdrew an order, and Hasan lost part of that day's wages.
card.after: The sisters' quarrel did not end then and there. Still, they made their own agreement: the older sister would keep the original, and the younger could come and read it.
card.presentEcho: Two people can tell different stories about the same person's memories. Before rushing to decide who is right, you can also make a place where they can open those memories and look at them together.
card.secondLook: Samira was afraid of losing her mother's papers, while Hadiya was afraid that even the names of dishes she had written would be taken from her. By lending them paper to copy onto, Zayd gave each of them time to write down her part.
card.unresolved: The sisters each gained a record of their own, but when and how they would look at the original together remained a promise they would both have to keep.
card.readerQuestion: Two sisters in the workshop are tugging back and forth on a bundle of their mother's handwritten recipes. Both say they helped create the record. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Hasan pointed to the different handwriting mixed together on the same line and asked who had written each part. As the sisters each pointed out their own handwriting, their tugging eased. Hasan put away his knife and opened the bundle.
signalMoments.connect: Hasan called to his cousin Zayd outside the door and borrowed paper and pens. When Zayd came in with the tools, Hasan put away his knife and opened the original in the middle, making a place where the two could look at it together.
signalMoments.speak: Hasan said that if he bound it as one person's book, the other would not be able to read the writing. When Samira set down the original, he asked them to open and look at it together, then requested copying tools from Zayd.

identity.region: Cairo (Mamluk Sultanate)
identity.summary: He spent his life working as a bookbinder, a craft he learned as an apprentice. He and his wife Maryam raised their daughter Nura on both their incomes. After putting his own order first and causing Maryam to miss a cloth delivery, he taught an apprentice in his later years when his hands hurt and lived near his daughter.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Hasan ibn Salim · Male
1318–1390 · Age 72
Cairo, Egypt · Mamluk Sultanate
Work · A bookbinder who made leather book covers and cases
Life · He learned to work with his hands by watching his carpenter father, then learned bookbinding from a master craftsman. He and his wife Maryam each earned money to raise their daughter Nura. After taking charge of Maryam's cloth ledger, he put his own order first, causing her to lose a customer. In old age, when his hands hurt, he taught an apprentice and lived near his daughter.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · He took time to listen to his customers' circumstances, but when his own orders piled up, he put Maryam's ledger aside.
Liked · The moment when he stamped leather and the pattern came out sharp and clear
Disliked · People folding or tearing someone else's paper without permission
Good at · Cutting covers to fit bundles of paper and folding cases

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured · His father's small ruler and an old cutting knife
Close to · Maryam, Nura, his mother Layla, and his cousin Zayd
Life he wanted · A life in which Nura could choose her own work and he could keep working as long as his hands allowed
Worry · How he would make a living on the day his hands hurt too much to make covers

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were called Hasan. You made leather book covers in Cairo in 1352. Today, I'll tell you about the day one bundle of writing came to need two covers.

Hasan was about to stamp a star pattern into a piece of leather when the door flew open. One woman entered with a bundle of papers clutched to her chest, while another held the bottom of the bundle. Neither let go, even at the threshold.

“Please make a cover for it. I'm taking it with me.” The woman who spoke first was Samira. Her younger sister Hadiya immediately cut in. “And what about me if you take it?” The papers held recipes written by their late mother. On some pages, Samira had written down the prices of goods, while on others, Hadiya had corrected the quantities of ingredients.

Samira said she was the one who had guarded the papers while their mother was sick. Hadiya said she was the one who had cooked with their mother and filled in the missing words. Hasan saw the edges of the paper crumpling little by little in their hands.

“You could make them into two books,” Hasan suggested. Samira raised an eyebrow. “Do you have two copies of the same papers?” He did not. All Hasan had were two blank pieces of leather. If he divided the original in half, both sisters would lose parts of what their mother had written on the fronts and backs.

Hasan had another worry. Two other books he had to finish before sunset sat at the edge of his workbench. If the sisters occupied his workshop, those orders would be late. Outside, a messenger from one of those customers had already knocked twice.

signalMoments.notice: Instead of telling the sisters to let go, Hasan pointed to the edge of the paper. Even on the same line, he could see different handwriting. “Who wrote this part?” While the sisters each pointed to their own handwriting, their tugging eased. Hasan put away the knife on his workbench and opened the bundle.
signalMoments.connect: Hasan went outside and called to his cousin Zayd. “Lend me some paper to write on and a pen. There's a book two people need to look at together.” When Zayd came in carrying the tools, Hasan put away his knife and opened the bundle of papers in the middle.
signalMoments.speak: Hasan stood between the two women. “If I bind this as one person's book, the other won't be able to read these words. Let's open it and look at it together first.” When Samira set down the original, Hasan asked Zayd for paper and copying tools.

episode.afterSignal:
Hasan cleared a place by the window. Zayd brought paper and copying tools. Samira opened the first page of the original. Hadiya burst out laughing as she read. Beside their mother's instruction to add “a little salt,” Hadiya had added, “Too little if my sister adds it.” Samira bit her lip, then laughed too. Before long, they were arguing again. This time, it was about the taste of the food, not the papers.

Time passed. Samira copied the quantities their mother had written onto her own paper, and Hadiya copied the parts she had corrected as well. Hasan measured each sister's paper and cut two pieces of leather. They were blank covers with no pages bound inside yet, so each sister could fill her own.

Just then, the other customer's messenger returned. “What about our book?” Hasan lowered the hand holding the leather. “It will be later than the time I promised today. I took on another task first.” The messenger left looking disappointed. Later, one customer withdrew an order, and Hasan lost part of the wages he would have earned that day.

Samira hugged the original to her chest again. When Hadiya's expression hardened, Samira said, “I'll keep the original. When you come to see it, I'll open it for you.” Hadiya did not answer until much later. “Don't just say that. Let's set a day when I can come and read it.” They agreed to meet again the following week. Even so, they argued again on their way out over which dish had tasted better.

Hasan placed the two blank covers side by side on his workbench. Maryam returned after finishing her day's cloth trading and saw the delayed books. “Why did you make two covers today?” “Because one book had two owners.” Maryam examined the covers, then said, “Then start with the overdue books tomorrow.” Hasan nodded. Tomorrow's work still remained exactly as it was.

Five years later, when Maryam's cloth business grew, Hasan took charge of the ledger. But while trying to finish his own bookbinding order first, he failed to record a cloth delivery Maryam had promised. Hasan received his own wages, and Maryam lost a customer. Maryam took back the ledger and handled the dates for her own business herself.

Nura learned her mother's cloth trade instead of working in her father's workshop. When Hasan's hands began to hurt, he taught a young apprentice how to cut materials. The record of this past life includes both the day he gave the two sisters his time and the day he put off Maryam's promise.

memories.label: His Lifelong Work
memories.detail: Wrapping bundles of handwritten papers in leather covers so they could be read for years

memories.label: What He Treasured
memories.detail: His carpenter father's small ruler and the sheath for his cutting knife that Maryam chose for him

memories.label: His Favorite Time
memories.detail: When Maryam and Nura stopped by the workshop in the evening after finishing their cloth trading

memories.label: What He Tried to Protect
memories.detail: A household where Nura would not have to take up her father's work against her will

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “I make the cover, but you choose the story to write inside.”

memories.label: Maryam's View
memories.detail: “He made time for those two sisters. But he didn't even write my cloth delivery in the ledger. The customer never came back, and after that, I kept my own ledger.”

memories.label: Nura's Memory
memories.detail: “When I said I didn't want to be a bookbinder, Father was a little disappointed, but he made a cover for my cloth ledger.”

memories.label: Zayd's View
memories.detail: “Whenever an argument broke out, he would set out paper first. Thanks to that, he used quite a lot of my paper too.”

memories.label: The Apprentice's Memory
memories.detail: “Even on days when his hands hurt, he didn't take the knife away from me. He watched beside me until I could make the cut with my own hands.”

finalMoment.place: Hasan's room in Cairo, Mamluk Sultanate
finalMoment.scene:
It is night in Cairo in 1390. I have returned to my room after eating dinner at my daughter Nura's house. Even after my wife Maryam died, I often shared evenings like this with Nura. Now I am alone in the room. Thirsty, I walk toward the water jar. I can hear the neighbors talking outside the window, and I hold an empty cup in my hand.

I take one more step, and my toes catch on the stone threshold. The cup slips from my hand, and my body pitches forward. I try to catch myself with my hands, but I am too late. The side of my head strikes the stone floor hard. A brief sound rings in my ears. When I open my eyes, the door and the water jar look tilted. I try to get up, but my arms cannot support my body.

“Help.” I open my mouth to call someone outside. Only a hoarse sound comes from my throat. I try slapping the floor with my palm. The voices outside the window continue, but I cannot tell whether anyone has heard me. Nura's house is farther down this alley. I remember the dinner we shared a little while ago. I did not say we would see each other again in the evening. Now I want to call Nura's name.

I stretch an arm toward the door. My cheek burns, and the stone beneath my hand is cold. I try to push with my elbow and move my body, but dizziness makes me stop. “Nura.” This time, the sound is even softer. I try to reach forward once more, but the door before my eyes blurs. My fingers rest against the floor and do not move.
finalMoment.afterword: Hasan died alone that night in his room in Cairo after falling and striking his head. Nura found him the following morning. She had not known that the dinner they shared the day before would be their last. Nura remembered both the day her father did not stop her from entering the cloth trade and the day her mother Maryam took the ledger back from him. The time he gave the sisters and the loss he caused Maryam both belonged to the same person's life. The record of this past life preserves in this chapter Hasan's night, which ended before Nura returned and opened the door, along with all the dinners they had shared before then.
finalMoment.artAlt: A modest room in Cairo in the Mamluk Sultanate in 1390, where 72-year-old Hasan reaches toward the door after falling beside a stone threshold at night. An empty cup lies on the floor, and no one else is in the room

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Han Yeon-ok, an earthenware potter near Jinju. After the Imjin War began, people hid grain between the kilns and the mountain paths.

When word came that the Japanese forces were drawing near, the villagers argued over which way to flee. The main road was faster, but soldiers traveled along it, while the path behind the kiln was narrow and steep.

Yeon-su said they should send the family first. Sun-deok begged them to take young Bok-i and her elderly mother along.

signalMoments.speak: “The path behind the kiln is narrow, but it leads to the northern rice-field ridge. I'll send the children and elders first.” Yeon-ok spoke loudly enough for everyone to hear.
signalMoments.explore: Yeon-ok climbed the slope behind the kiln alone first and checked the collapsed wall and watercourse.
signalMoments.protect: Yeon-ok placed Bok-i and Sun-deok's elderly mother at the front of the line and told Yeon-su to count the people from the rear.

episode.afterSignal:
The people climbed the path behind the kiln in single file. At every fork, Yeon-ok set down a shard from a broken jar.

Yeon-su resented that Sun-deok's elderly mother went ahead of his family, but he stayed at the rear and kept the line together.

Most of the villagers crossed the rice-field ridge. Yeon-ok went back for the last sacks of grain and became trapped in the fighting spreading from the fortress.

finalMoment.place: a mountain path near Jinju during the Imjin War
finalMoment.scene:
In early summer of 1593, Yeon-ok waited on a mountain path near Jinju for the last refugee cart. Her husband, Park Yun, and the neighbors sent the children over the pass first. Pointing to a side path beside the kiln where she had fired pottery, Yeon-ok guided the people into the woods.

In the distance came soldiers' shouts and the pounding of horses' hooves. Yeon-ok helped an elder over the stone wall, then ducked low. At that moment, an arrow struck her in the side. She pressed a hand to the wound, but the bleeding would not stop.

When Park Yun returned, Yeon-ok asked, “Did they make it over the pass?” Only after hearing that all the children had crossed did she lean her back against the stone wall. Her breathing grew shallow, and she closed her eyes before sunset.
finalMoment.afterword: Yeon-ok died from blood loss caused by an arrow wound on a refugee path near Jinju in 1593. Park Yun returned and recovered her body, and the neighbors who survived remembered the route Yeon-ok had shown them. The wartime background of the Imjin War is historical fact, while Yeon-ok and the specific events in the village are fictional.
finalMoment.artAlt: A mountain path in the woods near Jinju in 1593, with a stone wall and refugee cart receding into the distance, Yeon-ok pressing her side and her husband returning

card.name: Sayo
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Sayo of Kyoto. You learned to paint fans from your maternal uncle and opened a workshop with your friend Hana. After many years of painting, you handed the brush to your apprentice Miyo and spent your days welcoming customers.
card.title: A Fan for Another Daughter
card.world: Kyoto in 1675, during the Tokugawa shogunate
card.flavor: The customer did not recognize Sayo
card.opening: A customer ordered a fan for his young daughter. Sayo recognized him the moment he held out the back of his hand. The customer was her own father, who had left home long ago.
card.life: She grew up beside her mother and younger brother and learned to paint from her maternal uncle. She opened a fan workshop with Hana and worked there for many years. In old age, when her hands grew stiff, she passed the painting work on to Miyo.
card.turn: Her father, Isaburo, ordered a fan for the daughter of his second family. He did not recognize the grown Sayo, and she could have taken the deposit and finished the painting as though he were a stranger.
card.decision: Sayo returned the deposit and revealed that she was the first daughter he had abandoned. She did not promise to paint the fan, and even after hearing her father's explanation, she did not promise to reconcile with him.
card.cost: She received no payment for a fan that day. After reopening a story long buried, her hand kept stopping over her paintings for several days, but she continued the workshop work she shared with Hana.
card.after: She exchanged a few short letters with her father, but they did not live together. Sayo continued painting fans for many years while maintaining different relationships with her friend Hana, her younger brother Ryota, and her apprentice Miyo.
card.presentEcho: You do not have to forgive someone or give them an answer right away when you meet again after a long absence. You can say only what you are able to say in that moment and then leave.
card.secondLook: Isaburo said he had left to escape his debts and had been too ashamed to make contact by the time he could, but he did not ask how Omitsu and the two children had lived. Hana asked Sayo whether she wanted to stop working for the day, and even after Sayo picked up her brush, Hana did not hurry her.
card.unresolved: Sayo heard her father's explanation, but it did not erase the years he had been gone. She exchanged only a few letters with him and chose neither complete reconciliation nor a total break.
card.readerQuestion: You realize that the customer ordering a fan is the father who left home long ago. He does not recognize you and talks about a gift for his new daughter. What would you do first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Sayo. You painted fans in Kyoto in 1675. Let me tell you about the day a customer did not recognize her.

Sayo wet the tip of her brush and painted a slender mountain ridge along one side of the fan paper. At the front of the workshop, her friend Hana was neatly counting bamboo ribs. When Hana said, “A new customer,” Sayo set down her brush.

A middle-aged man came in and chose an unfolded fan. “My young daughter is turning 11. Can you paint white plum blossoms in bloom?” Sayo nodded. As he took out the deposit, she saw a small burn scar on the back of his hand. It had the same shape as the scar her father had gotten when he spilled hot paste during her childhood.

“I'll write down your name.” “It's Isaburo.” Pretending to write the name on the paper, Sayo steadied her breathing. It had been 19 years since her father left Kyoto. At 8, Sayo had watched his back from the doorway. At 27, she now stood before him. Isaburo did not recognize his daughter.

The sound of Hana setting down the bamboo ribs seemed loud. Seeing Sayo's shoulders stiffen, Hana studied the customer. Sayo picked up the fan. If she painted the white plum blossoms as though he were a stranger, she could receive the payment promised for that afternoon. She would not have to dig up the story she had buried, either.

Looking down at the blank fan paper, Isaburo said, “She's upset that I've been busy lately. This time, I'm planning to give it to her myself.” Sayo's fingertips turned cold. He had never come to her like that. Even so, she knew his young daughter was not to blame. Sayo looked back and forth between the blank paper and the deposit.

signalMoments.notice: Sayo looked again at the back of the customer's hand. The burn scar from her childhood had not disappeared. After confirming even the name Isaburo, Sayo returned the deposit. “Father, I'm Sayo.”
signalMoments.speak: Sayo opened the hand holding the deposit. “Mr. Isaburo, do you truly not recognize me? I'm Sayo.” When the man looked at her face again, Sayo pushed the money toward him.
signalMoments.release: Sayo set the deposit down in front of the customer. “I can't paint this fan. I am Sayo, from the home you abandoned.” Even after she finished speaking, she did not pick the money up again.

episode.afterSignal:
Isaburo stared at Sayo's face for a while. “The Sayo from back then has grown so...” He could not finish. Sayo barely managed to ask, “Why did you leave back then?” Hana remained in the back of the workshop but did not come between them.

Isaburo said his business had failed and he had gone to Osaka to escape his debts. He also said that by the time he could make contact again, so much time had passed that he was ashamed. Sayo did not nod. Isaburo had not even asked how their mother had sold cloth to support herself, Sayo, and her younger brother Ryota.

“Then what about this fan?” Isaburo asked cautiously. Sayo handed him the blank paper. “Give the girl a present. Another workshop can paint it. I can't do it today.” The order and the deposit went back with him. What Sayo lost was one day's payment, but her heart was shaken for far longer.

After Isaburo left, Hana handed her some water. “Do you want to stop for today?” Sayo drank for a moment, then returned to the mountain ridge she had been painting. Her brush hovered above the paper for a long time. Without hurrying her, Hana bundled the bamboo ribs. At last, Sayo added one more line for a road below the mountain.

A few days later, Isaburo sent a short letter. Sayo wrote a reply, tore it up, and then wrote only 2 lines. She told him how her mother was and where her workshop was located. She did not write that she forgave him or that he should come again. A few more letters came from Isaburo, and Sayo answered sometimes.

After that, Sayo ran the workshop with Hana for many years. Even after Hana married, she continued supplying the workshop with fan ribs. Her younger brother Ryota worked elsewhere but came to visit, and her apprentice Miyo learned the brush from Sayo. After Sayo's hands grew stiff, Miyo painted while Sayo welcomed customers. What I have told you is the story of one day in that long life: the day she met the father she had lost as a customer and told him her name.

finalMoment.place: Sayo's home in Kyoto during the Tokugawa shogunate
finalMoment.scene:
It is a late-summer morning in 1712, in my home in Kyoto. My stomach has hurt for 2 days, and I have a fever. My younger brother Ryota has come from another region and is beside me. My apprentice Miyo went out a little while ago, saying she would bring someone. Unable to bear the stuffy air in the room, I point toward the door. “I want to go out into the courtyard for just a moment.” Ryota tells me to rest for now but opens the door.

When I see the courtyard, I raise myself. The inside of my belly clenches again, but I grip the edge of the bedding and lower my feet to the floor. Ryota supports my arm. “I'll help you. Slowly.” I try to stand on both feet. The floor feels cold against my soles. It is 3 steps to the threshold, but my knees buckle on the 2nd. Ryota catches me and seats me on the edge of the veranda.

“Do you want some water?” Ryota asks. I shake my head and look through the open door. The breeze cools the sweat on my forehead. Even as Ryota supports my back, he watches the road. He is waiting for Miyo to return with someone. “Tell Hana too.” I barely finish speaking before my stomach hurts again, folding my body forward. Ryota calls my name. I reach out to grab the doorframe, but my fingertips slip.

Ryota turns my body toward him and supports me. “Sayo, look at me.” His face is close, but I cannot keep my eyes open for long. Every time I breathe in, a short sound comes from my throat. I try to listen for footsteps in the courtyard, wondering if they are Miyo's. No one comes through the door. I open my mouth to draw one more breath, but my chest does not move. Even the feeling of Ryota shaking my shoulders fades away.
finalMoment.afterword: Sayo died at her home in Kyoto in 1712, on the morning she tried to go out into the courtyard after suffering abdominal pain and fever for 2 days. The illness is unknown. Her younger brother Ryota was supporting her at the threshold, and Hana and Miyo heard the news afterward. Ryota remembered the day his sister let him go to another region without trying to hold him back. Hana remembered how Sayo would remain silent for a long time when she was upset. The 2 of them did not describe Sayo in the same words. The short letters she exchanged with her father Isaburo were not proof of complete reconciliation. The Chronicle of Past Lives closes this life by preserving both the years Sayo spent handing over paintings under her own name and the moment she tried to walk toward the open door on her final morning.
finalMoment.artAlt: A late-summer morning at the threshold of Sayo's home in Kyoto in 1712: after 2 days of abdominal pain and fever, 64-year-old Sayo collapses while trying to go out into the courtyard, and her younger brother Ryota supports her from behind

card.name: Tavi
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Tavi, who lived near Great Zimbabwe. You spent many years tending fields and harvesting crops while raising two children. When your daughter asked for grain to start her own household, you refused, though later you taught her how to choose seeds.
card.title: The Second Pot of Sorghum
card.world: Near Great Zimbabwe in the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, 1338
card.flavor: The bottom of the pot burned before the family arrived
card.opening: On the day Tavi invited the family to share sorghum porridge, she left the pot over the fire for a moment. When she returned and lifted the lid, the smell of burning rose from the bottom, and guests' voices drifted from beyond the stone wall.
card.life: She learned to tend sorghum fields and store grain, built a household with Karo, and raised Shira and Daro. After her father's death, she shared the harvest with her younger sister, Mare, and after Karo was injured, she took on more of the fieldwork. When Shira started a household of her own, Tavi refused to lend her stored grain, and her daughter's visits grew less frequent. In old age, she taught Shira how to choose seeds.
card.turn: Tavi refused her younger sister Mare's help and took charge of the meal alone. While she went to check the cover over the sorghum in the field, the first pot burned. The waiting family had already arrived, and little sorghum remained.
card.decision: Tavi did not ask her daughter to speak for her. She announced that she had burned the pot herself. With Mare's help, she used the sorghum she had been saving to cook a second pot.
card.cost: The stored sorghum dwindled, and the meal was late. Tavi had to admit her mistake in front of everyone, and Mare reminded her that she had refused help.
card.after: The two sisters continued to disagree, but they spent more days preparing harvests and meals together. A few years later, when Shira asked for grain to start her own household, Tavi refused. Her daughter earned grain by helping other households and visited less often for a while. In old age, Tavi reduced her fieldwork and taught Shira how to choose seeds, but the earlier refusal remained between them.
card.presentEcho: Sometimes work you take on alone because you want to do it well goes wrong. You can tell the people waiting yourself and choose to begin again together.
card.secondLook: Mare felt that Tavi did not trust her. Tavi took on everything, saying she also had to do the work that injured Karo could no longer do. Shira remembered both that her mother had not made her take responsibility for the burned pot and that she later refused to lend her grain.
card.unresolved: The second pot was finished, but the grain they had saved did not return. Nor did the sisters come to agree about everything.
card.readerQuestion: Your family is coming to eat, but the bottom of the sorghum porridge pot has burned. There is not much sorghum left, and your younger sister, who offered to help earlier, will arrive soon. What will you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Tavi spooned up another taste of the sorghum porridge and smelled it. When Shira frowned too, Tavi went beyond the stone wall, announced that she had burned the pot, and asked Mare to help her cook a new one.
signalMoments.speak: Before the family could see the pot, Tavi went out through the gate and said that the meal would be late because she had burned it. She told Mare she should have accepted her help that morning and asked her to work with her this time.
signalMoments.connect: Tavi first showed Mare the burned pot and said she needed help. When Mare asked how this had happened after Tavi said she would do everything alone, Tavi told the family, and Mare took out the remaining sorghum.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Tavi. In 1338, you lived near Great Zimbabwe in the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, farming the land and tending the grain. Today, I will tell you about the time a single pot made your entire family eat late.

“I'll watch the fire,” her younger sister Mare said that morning. Tavi lifted a sack of sorghum and replied, “You have work at your own home too. I'll do it today.” Mare laughed and said, “There you go again,” but the last words came out a little quieter.

It was a day when the family had agreed to gather and eat. Her daughter Shira brought water, and her son Daro stacked dry branches. Her husband Karo, who had trouble standing for long after injuring his knee, washed empty bowls in the shade. Tavi put sorghum into a round clay pot and lowered the fire. There seemed to be plenty of time before Shira's cousins arrived from beyond the stone wall.

Then Daro pointed toward the field. “Mother, the grain cover has come loose.” Afraid the sorghum drying since morning might scatter in the wind, Tavi ran to the field. She secured the cover, and on her way back, Karo waved his hand. “The pot!” Tavi ran too.

When she lifted the lid, an acrid odor rose through what should have been a sweet smell. Tavi spooned up a little from the top and tasted it. The bottom had already stuck fast, and the burned flavor had seeped all the way up. Starting over now would mean using more of the sorghum they had stored. Before long, many people would be coming in at once.

“Shall I tell them?” Shira asked. Tavi shook her head. Then Mare's voice came from beyond the stone wall. “Sister, we're here. And there are lots of hungry people!” Daro was counting the empty bowls one by one. Tavi looked in turn at the burned pot, the sack of grain, and the waiting family.

signalMoments.notice: Tavi spooned up another taste and smelled it, hoping it might still be edible. This time Shira frowned too. Tavi set down the spoon and went beyond the stone wall. “I burned the pot. Mare, will you help me cook a new one?”
signalMoments.speak: Before the family could see the pot, Tavi went out through the gate first. “The meal will be late. I burned the pot.” Mare entered with a startled expression, and Tavi added, “I should have listened to you this morning. Will you work with me this time?”
signalMoments.connect: Tavi first showed Mare the burned pot. “I need your hands.” Mare peered into the pot, then raised one corner of her mouth. “I thought you were going to do it all alone?” While Tavi explained the situation to the family, Mare took out the remaining sorghum.

episode.afterSignal:
Mare moved the burned pot aside. “How did it burn this deep?” “The cover was blowing away.” “I could have held down that cover.” Tavi could find no answer to Mare's words. When Shira brought fresh water, Mare began washing an empty pot.

Karo opened the sack of remaining grain. Tavi brought out another basketful of the sorghum she had been saving for the next month. When Daro asked, “Then do we each get two bowls today?” Mare said, “After waiting this long, you should eat three.” Laughter sounded from beyond the stone wall.

The second pot cooked slowly. Tavi watched the fire, and Mare stirred with a wooden paddle. Shira passed the time running with her young cousins along the shadow of the stone wall. When Tavi said, “We're late because of me,” Karo set down a bowl and said, “I know. But this time, you're here in front of the fire.”

The family did not eat until the sun was sinking. They could not eat the sorghum stuck to the bottom of the first pot, and their carefully saved sorghum had dwindled. As Mare received the last bowl, she said, “Next time, I'll fetch the water first.” Tavi replied, “Then I'll tie down the cover before anything else.” Once again, they both insisted that they should be the one to act first.

The sisters did not suddenly begin thinking alike after that day. A few years later, when Shira started a household in another settlement, Tavi refused her daughter's request to borrow stored grain. She worried about Karo's injured knee and the next harvest, but Shira had to earn grain to eat by helping other households. For a while, her daughter's visits grew less frequent. After losing Karo, Tavi reduced her fieldwork while choosing seeds with Shira, but that did not erase the earlier refusal.

finalMoment.place: Near Great Zimbabwe, on the road to Shira's house
finalMoment.scene:
Late one afternoon in 1361, Tavi was walking to her daughter Shira's house near Great Zimbabwe. She planned to visit her granddaughter and stay for one night. Her younger sister Mare closed the courtyard gate and followed the other two. At 66, Tavi carried only a small bundle of clothes. Walking ahead, Shira said, “Let's take the shaded road. The sun is still hot.” Tavi nodded and followed her daughter.

Above the roadside, dry branches knocked together in the wind. Shira had gone a few steps ahead when Tavi heard something large splitting above her. Before she could look up, a thick branch struck her shoulder and chest and drove her to the ground. The bundle fell from her hand. When Tavi tried to breathe in, her chest hurt. She tried to pull herself out from beneath the branch, but she could not move.

“Mother!” Shira came back and tried to lift the branch. She could not move it alone. Mare, who had been following behind, tried to push it too, then ran to call Daro and the neighbors. Shira sat close to Tavi's face. “Can you hear me? Please wait just a little.” Tavi opened her eyes and looked at Shira. Her chest felt crushed each time she tried to breathe. “It hurts,” Tavi managed to say, and Shira tried once more to lift the end of the branch.

Mare returned with a neighbor and pushed one side of the branch. It moved a little, but Tavi could not get up. She grasped the wrist Shira held out to her. Shira's hand tightened around hers. Tavi drew one breath and tried again. Her chest would not move. As Shira called her name, Tavi's hand went limp. When Daro reached the road, Mare and the neighbor were still moving the branch away.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1361, Tavi died from a chest injury caused by a broken tree branch while she was walking to her daughter Shira's house. Shira carried home the bundle of clothes her mother had brought. She remembered the days they learned to choose seeds together, but she did not forget that her mother had refused her grain when she started a new household. Mare remembered the days when her older sister refused her help and the later days when they shared the harvest. Daro, who arrived too late, heard from Shira and Mare what had happened at the end. This record of a past life preserves both the time Tavi spent beside her family and the times she turned away the requests of those closest to her in the life that ended on that road.
finalMoment.artAlt: A late afternoon in 1361, viewed upward from ground level on a road near Great Zimbabwe. Just before the accident, 66-year-old Tavi stands holding a small bundle of clothes and looks up at a large tree branch as it splits

card.name: Halil
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Halil of Beşiktaş. You spent many years repairing wooden parts and raised two children. After injuring your hand, you repaired small tools at home, and in old age you lived in a house where your children and granddaughter often came and went.
card.title: The Place He Reached Before Work
card.world: A Bosphorus steamship in Istanbul, Ottoman Empire, in 1892
card.flavor: His daughter boarded the same boat
card.opening: Halil boarded the boat to look for new repair work. It had been three years since his hand injury forced him to leave his regular job, but he still had not told his daughter. Just as the boat was about to depart, his daughter Esma came aboard.
card.life: He learned woodworking from his father and spent many years repairing wooden parts on steamships. He and Zeynep raised Esma and Murat, and after injuring his hand, he switched to repairing small tools at home. In old age, after outliving his wife, he spent his time with his children and granddaughter.
card.turn: On the day he had arranged to ask a repair shop for work, his daughter Esma boarded the same steamship. Esma asked why Halil was sitting among the passengers instead of near the workshop, holding a bundle of tools.
card.decision: Before his daughter got off at the next pier, Halil confessed that he had lost his regular job. He got off with her so he could listen to everything she had to say, missing the appointment he had promised to reach on time at the repair shop.
card.cost: He missed his first appointment to ask for a new job and had to search for another opportunity. Esma was angry that he had kept it from her for three years, and the family's trust did not return right away.
card.after: Even after missing the appointment, Halil kept looking for work and set up a small tool-repair bench in one corner of the house. Esma later made a home in another neighborhood, and even after Halil outlived his wife Zeynep, he remained in contact with his children.
card.presentEcho: Words spoken late do not solve every problem at once. Even so, some people need to hear those words before they can think together about what comes next.
card.secondLook: Esma was angrier that her father had hidden the truth from her for three years than she was about his income. Zeynep had already known about the hand injury and the loss of his job, and only after leaving the boat did Esma learn that her mother alone had known.
card.unresolved: The missed appointment could not be recovered, and his hand did not heal quickly. Esma did not immediately stay home to help her father; she continued with her own work.
card.readerQuestion: On a boat taking you to ask about a new job, you meet your daughter. She thinks you still repair boats, but you left that work long ago because of a hand injury. She will get off soon. What will you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Halil saw Esma's gaze move from his hand to the appointment note. He unfolded the paper and showed it to her, saying that he was going to ask about new work and no longer worked on boats.
signalMoments.speak: When Esma asked which boat he worked on, Halil revealed that he had stopped repairing boats after injuring his hand. When his daughter fell silent, he set down the plane on his lap and waited.
signalMoments.connect: Halil handed the appointment note to Esma and suggested that they get off together at the next pier. While his daughter read the paper, he opened his injured hand to show her.

What he disliked · Tools not being returned to their proper places

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
What he treasured · A small plane inherited from his father
Those closest to him · His wife Zeynep, his daughter Esma, and his son Murat

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Halil. You lived in Beşiktaş, Istanbul, in the Ottoman Empire in 1892. You repaired wooden parts on boats and raised two children. Today, I will tell you about the time you met your daughter on a boat you had boarded to look for new work.

Halil wrapped a plane with a worn handle in cloth and rested it on his lap. A repair shop across the water and the time he was supposed to meet its owner were written on a crumpled piece of paper. That day, the shop owner was to look at Halil's hand and decide whether to give him work.

Three years earlier, after injuring his hand, Halil had left the boat-repair job he had held for years. His wife Zeynep knew, but he had never managed to tell his daughter Esma. He worried that she might give up her own work and return home. Even as Halil helped support the household with the money he earned repairing small tools at home, whenever he met his daughter and she asked, “Are the boats running well?” he only replied, “They are.”

Just as the boat was about to leave the pier, someone tapped him on the shoulder. “Father?” It was Esma. Halil quickly folded the paper. Esma sat across from him and asked, “Aren't you repairing boats today?”

“I'm on my way to do repairs.” It was not a lie. But Esma looked at his lap. He was not wearing the leather apron he used to wear when he went to work. The tool wrapped in cloth was also different from the large tools he had used for boat repairs. Esma asked again, “Which boat?”

Esma was supposed to get off at the next pier to visit her aunt's house. Halil needed to stay aboard beyond that point to make his appointment. When his daughter stood up, he could pretend nothing was wrong, let her go, and continue to the shop. Halil rested his stiff fingers on the plane.

signalMoments.notice: Halil saw Esma's gaze move from his hand to the paper. Realizing that hiding it would only make his daughter ask more questions, he unfolded the paper. “I'm going to ask about new work. I don't work on boats anymore.”
signalMoments.speak: Halil did not give the name of a boat when Esma asked, “Which boat?” “None. I left that work after I injured my hand.” When Esma fell silent, he set down the plane on his lap and waited.
signalMoments.connect: Halil handed the paper to Esma. “You're going to your aunt's house, aren't you? Let's get off together at the next pier. There are things I haven't told you.” While Esma read the paper, he opened his injured hand to show her.

episode.afterSignal:
“Since when?” Esma asked. “Three years ago.” The boat rocked, and the paper rustled in his daughter's hand. Esma looked at the time written on it, then back at her father. “Then was it already true when I bought a new coat last winter?”

“You bought that coat with your own money.” “I know. But I still wanted to know what was happening at home.” Esma handed the paper back. Halil waited for her to tell him everything was all right, but Esma only looked out the window.

The boat reached the next pier. Esma stood. Halil looked again at the time on the paper. If he remained seated, he could still reach the shop. He wrapped up the plane, picked it up, and followed his daughter off the boat.

“Why are you getting off? You have an appointment.” “I want to tell you everything before you leave.” The two moved aside from the crowd and walked toward the end of the pier. Behind them came the sound of the boat's lines being pulled in.

Halil told her about the day he injured his hand and the small repair jobs he had taken afterward. He also told her that Zeynep already knew. Only after a long while did Esma say, “So Mother knew, and I didn't.” Halil opened his mouth to defend himself, but she raised a hand. “I don't want to hear it now. But don't hide things from me again.”

The boat departed. Halil remained on the pier and folded the appointment note. He could try to find someone to explain why he was late, but he had missed his chance to receive work from that shop that day. Esma took a few steps toward her aunt's house, then looked back. “I'll come home this evening. I need to talk to Mother too.” Halil nodded. He did not stop her to ask that they walk together.

After that, Halil set up a small repair bench in one corner of the house and repaired tools there. Esma continued with her own work, and a few years later she made a home in another neighborhood. When his granddaughter was born, Halil made her a small wooden handle. Even after he outlived Zeynep, the door of his house remained open to his children as they came and went.

finalMoment.place: Murat's room in Beşiktaş, Istanbul, Ottoman Empire
finalMoment.scene:
At dawn in late summer of 1910, Halil woke in his son Murat's room in Beşiktaş. He had come to visit the day before and stayed the night. When he sat up, struck by severe abdominal pain, the contents of his stomach surged upward. Halil barely managed to walk to the basin by the door before vomiting. Murat woke and stood behind him. “Father, when did this start?” Pressing a hand to his abdomen, Halil replied, “Just now.”

Murat helped Halil lie down on a mattress in one corner of the room and gave him a little water. Halil took one sip, but before long he had to reach for the basin again. His mouth was dry, but he could not keep the water down. Murat wiped his father's face with a damp cloth. When Halil said, “We should call a doctor,” Murat opened the door at once and asked a neighbor for help. The neighbor went out into the street to find a doctor.

As the sky brightened outside the window, Halil clutched his abdomen again and again. This time, there was nothing left to vomit. Murat sat beside him and asked, “Would you like more water?” Halil shook his head. “Just open the window a little.” Murat opened it. The sound of carts came from the street. Halil watched his son's back, then reached out over the blanket when Murat turned around. Murat took his hand.

Halil's fingertips were cold. His son said, “The doctor is coming,” but Halil felt another wave of abdominal pain. His abdomen pulled tight with every breath. He tried to ask Murat to stay beside him for just a little while. “Here...” The next words did not come. Murat leaned closer. Looking at his son's face, Halil let out one long breath. Murat called his name, but he did not breathe again.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1910, Halil died at age 75 in the room in Beşiktaş where Murat had moved. The neighbor who had gone to find a doctor returned, but it was too late. Murat remembered the final night his father spent in his room. Esma came when she heard the news. She had not forgotten the three years her father hid the loss of his job. She also remembered the day he got off the boat to listen to her, and the days afterward when he came to visit her home. The record of that past life preserves Halil's years of going back and forth between his children's homes even after he outlived Zeynep. His life ended in Murat's room.
finalMoment.artAlt: A simple room in Beşiktaş, Istanbul, Ottoman Empire, in 1910: 75-year-old Halil lies exhausted by abdominal pain and vomiting while his son Murat keeps watch beside him, holding a glass of water, as a neighbor leaves at dawn to summon a doctor

card.name: Esther
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Esther of Chicago. You learned the paper and printing trade and ran a shop with your friend Ida. After losing your younger sister, you cared for your niece Ruth, and in old age, you handed the work over to Ruth while checking manuscripts.
card.title: The Ferris Wheel That Wasn't Turning Yet
card.world: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, United States
card.flavor: The map said you could ride it
card.opening: The fair map Esther made said the Ferris wheel was open for rides. But two customers who had just returned said the wheel was not moving yet.
card.life: She learned to work with paper in her parents' bookbinding shop and opened a print shop with Ida. After her younger sister died, she cared for her niece Ruth and taught her the trade. As she grew older and her eyesight weakened, she stopped setting type and instead read and checked maps.
card.turn: Esther printed the planned illustration and wording for the Ferris wheel exactly as they were before it opened. In reality, it had not started operating yet, and customers trusted the map, walked all the way to the end of the Midway, then came back.
card.decision: Esther stopped selling the remaining maps and worked with Ruth and Ida to stamp them with a correction: “NOT OPEN FOR RIDES YET.” She refunded part of the map price to the customers who returned.
card.cost: She lost the maps she had already printed and some of the money she would have earned that day. She could not track down and correct every map already sold, so other customers might still make a wasted trip.
card.after: Later, after confirming that the Ferris wheel was operating, Esther reprinted the map. She kept exchanging letters with Ida after Ida moved to another city, and gradually handed the shop's work over to Ruth.
card.presentEcho: Even convincing words in print may not match the real landscape. When you listen to someone who has walked the route, you can redraw the map.
card.secondLook: Esther did not mean to deceive anyone; she printed the plan as fact too soon. Even so, the distance the customers walked and the money they spent did not cease to be Esther's responsibility.
card.unresolved: Some customers may not have received their money back that day. Even after a correction is stamped on the map, it cannot erase a wasted trip that has already happened.
card.readerQuestion: People trusted the fair map I made and walked a long way, but the Ferris wheel shown on it is not operating yet. What would you do with the remaining maps?

signalMoments.notice: Esther looked beneath the Ferris wheel where the boy's fingertip had stopped and saw the words “RIDE IT NOW.” The route was right, but the operating information was wrong. She circled the words in red ink and asked Ruth to bring out the remaining maps.
signalMoments.speak: Esther faced the mother and the boy and admitted that she had printed the map from the plans without confirming that the ride was operating. She said they could not sell the remaining maps as they were and stacked them on the stall counter.
signalMoments.connect: Esther asked Ruth to explain the reason for the incorrect information to customers who returned. She would correct the maps they were selling now, and she asked Ida to help decide on the new wording.
