profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Esther Morgan · Female
1855–1930 · Age 75
Chicago, Illinois, United States
Work · Producing guide maps and small printed materials
Life · She grew up in her parents' bookbinding shop and built a printing business with Ida. After losing her younger sister, she often cared for her niece Ruth and taught her the trade. When her eyesight weakened in old age, she read manuscripts and checked maps instead of setting tiny type.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · When an idea came to her, she quickly put it on paper. She could not pretend not to notice when something was wrong.
Liked · Being the first to write a new street name on a map
Disliked · Stacking sheets before the ink had dried and smudging the letters
Good at · Arranging pictures and words so strangers could easily find their way

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The wooden type case used in her parents' shop
Close to · Her friend and business partner Ida, and her niece Ruth
The life she wanted · A life in which maps made by her own hands guided someone to their destination
Worry · That if orders declined, Ida and Ruth would lose their work too

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Esther Morgan. You sold small printed maps in Chicago. Today, I'll tell you about the day when customers who had followed the routes on one of those maps returned with angry faces.

“Can you really ride a wheel this big?” A boy pressed his finger to the center of the map. Esther spread out the thick sheet of paper for him. “You'll see it when you reach the Midway. The Ferris wheel is right here.” The boy's mother paid for the map, and the two disappeared into the crowd.

It was May 1893, a few weeks after the fair opened. Esther made paper maps with her friend Ida and ran the stall with her niece Ruth. The plan Esther had consulted showed the Ferris wheel standing in the middle of the Midway. Esther drew the wheel on the map and printed “RIDE IT NOW” underneath. The iron framework of the great wheel was visible from afar, but Esther had not gone to buy a ticket herself by then.

That afternoon, the same mother and boy returned. The boy's shoes were covered in dust. His mother unfolded the map. “We went all the way here. Why didn't you write that it wasn't open for rides yet?” The boy said, “That big wheel wasn't moving. Nobody could ride it.”

At first, Esther tried to smile and ask, “Could you have gone the wrong way?” But the boy's finger traced the route on the map exactly. From the stall to the Midway, his finger stopped right in front of the Ferris wheel illustration. Ruth looked up. “Aunt Esther, are the words we printed wrong?”

Ida thought of the maps they had already sold. “If we print them again, what do we do about the ones we sold today?” Several more bundles still lay under the stall. Correcting every sheet would take time, and they had no idea where the customers who had already bought maps had gone. The mother did not hold out her hand to demand her money back. Instead, she pointed to the boy. “Just tell him properly why he had to walk all that way for nothing.”

signalMoments.notice: Esther looked beneath the wheel illustration where the boy's fingertip had stopped. “RIDE IT NOW.” The route was not wrong. Those 3 words were. Esther circled them in red ink and asked Ruth to bring out the remaining bundles of maps.
signalMoments.speak: Esther first faced the mother and the boy. “I printed it from the plans alone. I didn't check whether people could ride it today.” When Ruth looked startled, Esther said, “We can't sell the rest as they are either,” and stacked all the maps on the stall counter.
signalMoments.connect: Esther put Ruth in charge of one bundle of paper. “You explain the reason to anyone who comes back with a map we sold. I'll correct the maps we're selling now.” She asked Ida to help decide on the new wording.

episode.afterSignal:
“The wheel is right here.” Esther pointed out the illustration on the map for the boy. “But the rides haven't started yet. I wrote that without checking.” The boy looked up at his mother. “Then can we ride it later?” “When it begins operating. Not today.” Only then did the mother let out a long breath.

Ida took a wooden type case from inside the stall. Ruth folded the corners of the sheets to mark them. Esther carved the words “NOT OPEN FOR RIDES YET” into a small stamp. When Ida tested it, too much ink smeared the letters together. “If we sell it like this, people won't be able to read it either.” The 3 of them wiped off some ink with a cloth and stamped it again.

One sheet, then another. Ruth spread out each map, Esther stamped the message, and Ida set it aside to dry. Evening sales nearly stopped while they restacked the dry maps. Esther refunded part of the map price to the first customers. She said anyone who brought back a map they had already bought could have it stamped with the same notice. The boy read the red letters and asked, “This means it isn't open now, right?” Then he nodded.

Several more angry customers returned afterward. One received a refund, while another said, “Next time, go see it before you draw it.” Instead of answering, Esther took the map and stamped the notice on it. But she could not correct the maps belonging to customers who never returned.

As they packed up the stall, Ruth asked, “When the Ferris wheel opens, will we throw this stamp away?” Esther rolled the ink-stained piece of wood in her palm. “Let's put it in the case instead of throwing it away. The next time I rush, take it out and show me.” Ida laughed. “I might take it out first.” Esther laughed as she tied up the remaining maps. Laughing did not bring back the money they had lost that day.

After the Ferris wheel actually began operating, Esther printed a new map. Ida later moved to another city, and her niece Ruth opened a shop of her own. Even after Esther's eyesight weakened, she would spread out other people's maps and read them by following the routes.

finalMoment.place: Train station platform, Chicago, Illinois, United States
finalMoment.scene:
On a summer afternoon in 1930, 75-year-old Esther stood beside her niece Ruth on the platform of a Chicago train station. They were on their way to visit her friend Ida, who had moved to St. Louis long ago. Ruth pointed toward the direction from which the train would arrive. “Aunt Esther, let's sit on that bench and wait.” Esther said she was still all right and gripped the handle of her suitcase. The platform was hot, and people's footsteps were hurried.

Esther took 1 step, then stopped as the floor seemed to sway. She set down her suitcase and took Ruth's arm. “Let's sit down.” Ruth led Esther to the bench. As soon as she sat, Esther bent forward. Sweat ran down her forehead, and her breathing became shallow. When Ruth asked, “Where does it hurt?” Esther answered, “I'm dizzy.”

Ruth asked a nearby station employee for help. The employee came over and moved the people away from the front of the bench. Ruth brought water, but Esther did not have the strength to hold the cup. Esther heard the metallic sound of the approaching train and raised her head. “I suppose I won't make this one.” Ruth said, “We can take the next one. Stay here for now.” The employee asked someone else to call a doctor.

Esther leaned back against the bench. The sound of wheels drew closer, but she could no longer see where the train was stopping. Her chest barely moved as she breathed in. Ruth pushed the suitcase aside and put an arm around her aunt's shoulders. Esther took Ruth's hand once, then let it go. As Ruth called her name, Esther could not take another breath. The train doors opened, but Esther could not board.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1930, Esther died on the platform of a Chicago train station as she was preparing to leave to visit Ida. The exact medical cause was never confirmed. Ruth held her aunt's suitcase and remained beside the bench for some time after the train departed. She wrote directly to Ida to explain why Esther had not been able to come. Ida remembered the days when they had run the shop together and all the time they had spent exchanging letters after moving apart. Ruth remembered the years she had spent coming and going from her aunt's home after losing her mother, and the day she opened her own shop. The record of this past life notes the day Esther's life ended on that platform and the memories left with those 2 people.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view from a high diagonal angle beneath the roof of a Chicago train station platform in the summer of 1930. Dizzy, 75-year-old Esther stands alone, steadying herself against an empty bench, while her niece Ruth turns to look back from a few steps away. The train is still far off

card.title: Two Sacks of Rice and a Written Order
card.role: low-ranking samurai of a local warrior family
card.world: 1575 · a mountain village in Kai Province, Japan
card.flavor: A requisition order given to a low-ranking samurai during the Sengoku period
card.opening: In Kai Province in 1575, Jirobei received a written order to collect two more sacks of rice for military provisions.
card.life: As a low-ranking samurai in Kai Province, he handled village requisitions and guarded the roads. He followed orders to the letter, passing the cost on to farming families, but later kept records rather than avoiding responsibility. card.presentEcho: Even when you choose to change an order, you must record who pays the cost.
card.secondLook: Jirobei shared the burden once, but he did not make amends for his earlier requisitions.
card.unresolved: No one knows whether the copy Haru kept was delivered to Jirobei's superior.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Jirobei, a low-ranking samurai charged with guarding the roads for a local lord.

When the village fell short of its quota, his superior ordered him to collect two more sacks from the nearest farm. Genta explained that one of them was seed rice for planting the following spring.

Haru, the young retainer, suggested finding another way because the order did not name a particular farming family. Jirobei hesitated and pointed to the seal.

episode.afterSignal:
Jirobei loaded one sack of rice from his own household onto the provisions cart. Saki did not welcome her husband's belated decision, saying it had reduced their winter stores.

His superior reprimanded him for changing the order on his own, but once he saw that the required amount had been supplied, he asked no more questions.

Genta kept his seed rice, but the grain taken from him in earlier requisitions was not returned. Haru kept a separate copy of the order.

finalMoment.place: a wintry mountain road in the Kai region
finalMoment.scene:
In the winter of 1582, Jirobei was transporting grain records along a mountain road in the Kai region with three samurai. An arrow flew from below the slope, where a thin layer of snow had frozen, and pierced the hat of the man in front. Jirobei abandoned his horse and moved behind a boulder.

He tucked the bundle of documents inside his robe and told his companions to retreat along the path toward the valley. He drew his sword, but his feet slipped on the snow. An enemy spear thrust from the forest and pierced his side. Jirobei forced it back once, but could not rise again.

He lay on the snow, listening to his companions escape with the documents. In the cold wind, his breathing grew steadily shallower. He died from blood loss before the fighting ended.
finalMoment.afterword: Jirobei died in 1582 from a spear wound and severe blood loss suffered in an ambush on a mountain road. A surviving companion delivered the documents to the lord's side, but did not turn Jirobei's earlier seizure of farmers' grain into a heroic tale. The characters and events set against the wars of Sengoku-period Japan are fictional.

card.name: Hafiz
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Hafiz of Melaka. You helped with work at the harbor, then learned to play the drum and performed at celebrations in many homes. After your wife fell ill, you worked less to stay by her side, but you delayed her request to stay at your daughter's house for one season.
card.title: The Groom Asleep Beneath the Sail
card.world: The Harbor of the Melaka Sultanate in 1472
card.flavor: The drummer had to find the groom first
card.opening: It was time for the wedding procession to set out, but the groom, Faris, was nowhere to be seen. As Hafiz waited with his drum, he found the groom's red headband at the harbor.
card.life: He carried cargo at the harbor with his father, then learned to play the drum from his maternal uncle. He raised two children with Salma and performed at celebrations. When Salma fell ill, he worked less to care for her, but he waited one season before honoring her wish to go to their daughter's house. After his wife died, he spent his old age in a house where his granddaughter and neighbors came and went.
card.turn: Faris had not run away. He had unloaded a ship's cargo all night to help pay the wedding expenses, then fallen asleep in the shade of a sail. The waiting bride was angry because she thought he had abandoned her.
card.decision: Hafiz woke Faris and led him off the ship. When Faris stumbled on the narrow gangplank, Hafiz dropped his drum into the water while grabbing him, then led the procession with the crowd's clapping.
card.cost: The wet drumhead sagged, and the drum would not sound. The employer said he had not heard any drumming and paid Hafiz only part of the promised wages. Hafiz also had to repair the hide.
card.after: Faris told the bride himself why he was late, but her anger remained. Hafiz repaired his drum and continued performing at other celebrations. Years later, when his wife Salma fell ill, he worked less to stay by her side, but delayed her request to go to their daughter's house for one season.
card.presentEcho: Even when it seems as though someone has vanished, that person may be asleep from exhaustion closer than anyone realizes. Searching can sometimes cost effort and bring losses.
card.secondLook: Even though Hafiz brought Faris back, that did not erase the bride's wait. Nor did the time he later spent caring for Salma erase the fact that he delayed her wish to stay at their daughter's house.
card.unresolved: Why Faris had not mentioned the night work beforehand, and when the bride finally let go of her anger, were not resolved when the procession ended that day.
card.readerQuestion: It is time for the wedding to begin, but the groom is missing. The red cloth he tied around his head while working has been found near the harbor, and a ship is preparing to leave with the rising tide. What would you do first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Hafiz. You were a drummer at Melaka Harbor. Today, I'll tell you about the day you had to find the groom before sounding the first beat of the wedding.

Hafiz struck the drum once. Boom. The bride's relatives looked toward the end of the road. The time when the groom, Faris, was meant to arrive had passed, but not even his red headband was in sight. Faris's father asked Hafiz, “Did your drum sound too soon?” “The groom is late, not the drum.” Hafiz laughed, but no one joined him.

At Melaka Harbor in 1472, people unloading cargo mingled from early morning with those waiting for ships. Hafiz had learned to move cargo from his father and to play the hand drum from his maternal uncle. He had also watched his neighbor Faris roam the waterfront since boyhood. The previous night, Faris had gone to unload cargo from a ship, saying he wanted to earn more toward the wedding expenses. But all he had said was that he would return before morning.

The bride, Nadira, stopped adjusting her headdress. “If he wasn't coming, he could at least have said so.” Someone whispered that Faris had boarded a ship and run away. Nadira pointed at Hafiz's drum. “Why do you keep making the sound to begin when he isn't here?” Hafiz lowered the hand resting on the drum.

His 12-year-old son Idris, who had been carrying cargo, came running. “Father, I saw Faris's red cloth. It's caught on a ship's rope over there.” Faris tied that cloth around his head only when carrying cargo. The ship had just been loaded, and once the tide rose, its crew would pull in the gangplank and depart. If Hafiz simply kept waiting, he would be beating an empty drum in front of the bride.

signalMoments.notice: Hafiz examined the wet footprints beneath the red cloth. The trail led to the narrow gangplank laid out to the ship. The tips of someone's feet were visible beneath the sailcloth. Hafiz strapped the drum to his back and called Faris's name.
signalMoments.speak: Hafiz first questioned a porter beside the ship. “Was Faris aboard this ship?” “He unloaded cargo all night. He said he was going to rest for a moment and crawled beneath the sail.” Shouting, “Faris, wake up!” Hafiz stepped onto the gangplank.
signalMoments.connect: Hafiz told Idris to run to the bride's house and keep everyone there. He asked a porter who had worked through the night to confirm which ship Faris had boarded. When the porter pointed to the sailcloth, Hafiz strapped the drum to his back and headed onto the gangplank.

episode.afterSignal:
When Hafiz lifted the sailcloth, he found Faris with his head resting against a cargo sack. Faris had been snoring, but opened his eyes when Hafiz shook his shoulder. “Is it morning already?” Faris asked. Hafiz replied, “Morning is already passing, and the bride will leave too.” Faris sprang to his feet, and one of the sacks rolled away. For a moment, he hesitated between catching the sack and heading for the gangplank.

“I'll explain about the cargo. You walk.” Hafiz went first. Still half asleep, Faris stepped on the end of the gangplank. The wood rocked with the waves, and Faris's body tilted with it. Hafiz grabbed his arm with both hands. The drum strap slipped from his shoulder, and the drum splashed into the water between the ship and the dock.

Faris climbed onto the dock first. Hafiz reached into the water and retrieved the drum. When he slapped the hide with his palm, it made a soggy thud like striking wet cloth instead of its usual boom. “This was my uncle's drum.” Hafiz struck it once more. Thud. Retying his headband, Faris said, “Take the repair cost from my wages.” “Discuss the groom's wages with the bride first.”

When the two came running back, Nadira stood at the door with her arms folded. Faris wiped his unwashed hands on his clothes. “I fell asleep while unloading cargo from a ship. I wanted to earn a little more money.” Nadira watched him for a while. “You told me about the money. You didn't tell me you'd disappear all night.” Faris lowered his head. Nadira did not turn away, but neither did she offer him her hand.

Hafiz struck the wet drum again. Thud. The people in the front row laughed, and at last Hafiz laughed too. “We can't proceed with this today. But we still have our hands.” He clapped twice. Idris answered, and then a porter picked up the next beat. At first, the sounds were all out of time, but after a few steps, they came together as one. Nadira walked slowly to the rhythm. Faris followed half a step behind.

After the wedding, the relative paying Hafiz pointed to the wet drum. “I asked for drumming, not clapping.” Hafiz counted the money he received. It was less than what had been promised. The people's laughter and applause did not make up the difference. He thought about how he would have to stretch the dried hide again.

Faris came the next day to help repair the hide. When Hafiz asked whether Nadira had forgiven him, Faris answered, “She still hasn't heard everything I have to say. Yesterday, I was the one who didn't listen.” Hafiz watched only the hands pulling the cords, then chuckled. “Then go listen first today.”

Hafiz continued playing the drum at celebrations, and his children each left home. When his wife Salma fell ill, he worked less and stayed by her side. When Salma said she wanted to stay at their daughter Kamaria's house for a while, he did not help her prepare to leave, saying he feared her illness would worsen on the road. Salma did not get to go to their daughter's house until one season later. Both the time Hafiz spent by her side and the time Salma spent waiting remained.

finalMoment.place: Hafiz's Home, Melaka, Melaka Sultanate
finalMoment.scene:
On a rainy evening in 1502, 72-year-old Hafiz was moving a rolled mat propped against the wall of his home in Melaka. His daughter Kamaria and granddaughter were coming to visit the next day. When he lifted the mat, a dark snake emerged from behind it. Before Hafiz could pull his foot back, the snake bit his ankle and vanished into a crack in the wall. “Idris!” he called to his son. His ankle stung, and blood welled from two small punctures.

His son Idris came running from the next room. When Hafiz pointed to the crack where the snake had gone, Idris seated his father on the mat. After asking a neighbor to summon help, his son loosely wrapped the injured ankle in a clean cloth. Hafiz tried to move his foot, then grimaced. “Don't chase the snake.” Idris nodded. Outside the door, the rain kept falling.

As the night deepened, the ankle swelled further, and Hafiz could not hold a bowl for long. Idris supported a cup of water brought by a neighboring woman so that Hafiz could take a sip. Hafiz began asking him to repeat things he had just said. Idris asked, “Father, can you hear my voice?” Hafiz tried to answer, but only his lips moved. He reached out, asking Idris to loosen the cloth around his foot. Idris loosened the knot.

Hafiz lowered the arm Idris had been supporting and gripped the edge of the mat. There was little strength in his fingers. Idris's face blurred before his eyes, and Hafiz blinked several times. He tried to draw breath by moving his chest, but his breaths were short. Outside the door, the neighbor called out to someone returning. Hafiz tried to turn his head, then stopped. As he heard Idris calling his name, his grip on the mat went slack.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1502, Hafiz died on the same night a snake bit him at his home in Melaka. The snake's species is unknown. When the neighbor who had gone to seek help returned, Idris was still sitting beside his father. Idris remembered Hafiz telling him not to chase the snake and the hand that had clutched the mat at the end. When his daughter Kamaria arrived the next day, she also recalled how her father had made her mother Salma wait one season when Salma wanted to come to her house. She remembered, too, the days her father later came to visit his granddaughter. The record of this past life preserves both the time Hafiz spent beside his family and the time he delayed their wishes in the life that ended that night.
finalMoment.artAlt: A floor-level view inside a Melaka home on a rainy evening in 1502, at the moment 72-year-old Hafiz bends down and lifts a rolled mat propped against the wall as a dark snake emerges from beneath it near his bare ankle. His son Idris is far away in the next room, occupied with another task

card.name: Nura
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Nura of Córdoba. You carried on your parents' pottery trade and raised two children. Even after paying off your debt, you refused to lend Safiya money for repairs, and they saw less of each other. After her husband died, she spent her later years with her granddaughter.
card.title: The Two Bowls
card.world: Caliphate of Córdoba, 985
card.flavor: There was a bowl that became harder to sell the higher the price rose
card.opening: Desperate for money to repay a debt, Nura decided to sell an old bowl made by her mother. But the customer asked for two matching bowls, not one.
card.life: As a child, she learned about clay and bookkeeping from her parents, then ran the workshop while raising two children with Hasan. After paying off the debt, Safiya asked to borrow money for repairs to her house, but Nura refused because she was worried about the cost of the next batch of clay. Her daughter learned the pottery trade, while her son chose a different business.
card.turn: The missing matching bowl had not broken. Her mother's old friend Safiya had kept it. During hard times, the two women passed the empty bowls between their homes, sharing food with each other.
card.decision: Nura refused to sell the two bowls together even when the customer raised his offer. She returned the entire deposit and added one of her own coins to compensate him for waiting, then offered to make new bowls and deliver them another day.
card.cost: The customer would not wait, and the extra money Nura gave him delayed repayment of the workshop's debt even further. She and her family worked longer hours and slowly paid off the debt.
card.after: Nura and Safiya each kept one of the old matching bowls. The family paid the overdue clay bill. A few years later, when Safiya asked to borrow money for repairs to her house, Nura refused. Safiya postponed the repairs, and the two women saw less of each other.
card.presentEcho: Different family members may think of different people when they see an old object. Even after learning what it means, the problem of living expenses still has to be solved separately.
card.secondLook: Nura's debt did not vanish because she kept the bowls. She had to ask more work of her family, and the customer left. Later, she refused Safiya's request in order to protect her own money.
card.unresolved: The customer could not wait for the new bowls and left, and Nura could not gather all the money she owed the clay supplier that day. The next day, she had to promise a new date for repayment.
card.readerQuestion: On the day you decide to sell an old bowl, a customer says, “If you find its match, I'll pay you twice as much.” You do not know where the other bowl is. What would you do first?

Nura · Female

Córdoba, Caliphate of Córdoba
Work · Making earthenware and running a workshop
Life · She learned about clay and bookkeeping from her parents. She kept the workshop going while managing a household with Hasan and their two children. After paying off the debt, she refused Safiya's request to borrow money for repairs to her house, and they saw less of each other. She taught the trade to her daughter Layla, while her son Yusuf chose a different business. After Hasan died, she spent her later years with her granddaughter.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Nura. In 985, you ran a small earthenware workshop in Córdoba, in the Caliphate of Córdoba. Today, I'll tell you about the day you learned why two bowls had ended up in different homes.

In 985, Nura covered the workshop's last embers and emptied her coin pouch. Three coins fell into her palm. She had put off paying the clay supplier for five days. Hasan had loaded several bowls and gone across the river, while their daughter Layla kneaded clay that was still wet. “I promised I would pay today.” Nura muttered to herself, and Layla looked up. Nura hurriedly tied the pouch shut.

On the top shelf stood a small, round bowl said to have been made by her mother. Though it had no decoration at all, a slight thumbprint remained on the bottom. Ever since childhood, Nura had placed her finger against that mark. Her mother used to smile and say, “There was another one,” but Nura had always assumed it had broken.

A customer came in. He turned the bowl Nura had set down in the palm of his hand. “Do you have its match? I need two of the same size.” Nura was about to say no when she heard his offer. The price for two would cover the overdue clay bill and leave enough to begin the next job. “I'll look for it. Come back before sunset.” The customer left a small coin as a deposit and went out. Layla asked, “Where is the other bowl?” Nura did not know either.

As Nura touched the indentation on the bowl's bottom again, she thought of Safiya, who had often visited while her mother was alive. Safiya's house stood deep in an alley reached by a stone bridge. If Nura left the workshop, she might miss the chance to fire the bowls scheduled for that day. The customer would return at sunset, and she had to find the bowl before then.

signalMoments.notice: Nura examined the mark on the bottom. Even when her mother made bowls of the same size, she left the tip of her thumb pressed into them like that. Nura asked Layla to watch the fire, then set out through the alleys to find Safiya, who might remember the mark.
signalMoments.speak: Before setting out through the alley, Nura called the customer back. “It does have a match, but it isn't in my possession right now.” He said he would wait only until sunset. Nura decided to find Safiya and ask her directly where her mother's bowl was.
signalMoments.connect: Nura asked her daughter Layla to search the shelves again. She asked her 11-year-old son Yusuf to tell the customer to wait a little if he returned. After dividing the work between them, she went to the house of her mother's old friend Safiya.

episode.afterSignal:
As soon as Safiya opened the door, she recognized the bowl in Nura's hand. “You still have it.” When Nura asked where its match was, Safiya went into the kitchen. The bowl she took from a shelf had an identical thumbprint on its bottom. When they pressed the two bowls together, their rims fit perfectly. Nura laughed. “Mother hid it here.” Safiya shook her head. “She didn't hide it. She gave it to me.”

Even after taking the bowl, Nura could not turn away. Safiya told her the old story. When the two women were young, there were days when one house had food to spare while the other ran out, and then the situation would reverse. Nura's mother had given Safiya one bowl, saying, “Let's never return it empty.” When Safiya sent it back filled with food, Nura's mother filled it the next time. The bowl Nura remembered had always been in her own home, but its match had always been on another family's table.

“Mother never told me that,” Nura said. “Maybe she didn't want to talk about the hard days in front of you.” Safiya did not smile. Nura said she would show the customer both bowls and return Safiya's immediately. Safiya handed over the bowl, and Nura carried them both home in her arms. She could still accept the customer's money. But she could not sell Safiya's bowl without permission. If she sold only her own, she could pay part of the overdue bill at the original price, but the two bowls her mother and Safiya had exchanged would be separated again.

The customer returned as promised and examined both bowls. “Excellent. I'll pay more than I offered before.” Nura pushed Safiya's bowl aside. “This one isn't mine. And I won't sell mine today either.” The customer's expression hardened. “Then why did you make me wait until sunset?” Nura made no excuses. “I was the one who said I would look for it. I'll compensate you for your wait as well.” She returned the full deposit she had received that morning and added one of her own coins.

“I can make two new bowls the same size. I'll deliver them in a few days.” The customer took the coins. “I need them tomorrow.” He turned away empty-handed. When the door closed, Layla asked, “Then what about the clay bill?” Nura opened her coin pouch again. It held even less now. “I can't pay it all today. Tomorrow, I'll speak to the clay supplier first.” Her 11-year-old son Yusuf sighed beside her. “I'll look for more customers.” Only then did Nura say aloud, in front of both children, exactly how much they owed.

That evening, Nura returned Safiya's bowl. Safiya filled it with warm food and brought it back to Nura's house. Nura filled the bowl from her own house with different food and sent it in return. The debt passed back and forth like the bowls, but it did not disappear. The next day, Nura promised the clay supplier a new repayment date, and she, Hasan, and Layla took on more orders. Yusuf went across the road to look for customers. Not everyone liked Nura's choice, but at least they could all see the accounts she had hidden.

Nura continued to run the workshop afterward, and she and her daughter Layla paid off the overdue clay bill. A few years later, when Safiya asked to borrow money to repair her leaking roof, Nura refused. She feared losing the money she had saved for the next batch of clay. Safiya postponed the repairs, and the two women saw less of each other. Her daughter learned the pottery trade, while her son chose a different business. After her husband Hasan died, she lived with her granddaughter.

finalMoment.place: The alley outside Nura's house and inside her home, Córdoba, Caliphate of Córdoba
finalMoment.scene:
Late one afternoon in 1010, at 64, I stood outside the door of my home in a narrow alley in Córdoba. A loaded mule approached, and I stepped toward the doorway to let it pass. When one of the bundles brushed the wall, the mule twisted its body. I saw its hind leg rising and tried to pull my leg away, but I was too late.

The hoof struck my left calf. My clothes tore, and blood flowed. While the handler caught hold of the mule, I stood clutching the doorframe. “This is my house. Please call my daughter Layla.” A neighbor opened the door for me. Holding onto that person's shoulder, I walked to my room.

Layla washed the wound and wrapped it in cloth. By the next day, it was hard to put weight on my foot. On the morning of the third day, my calf grew more swollen and hot. My body shook even beneath the blankets. Layla brought my son Yusuf back again. “How many days has it been?” I asked, and Yusuf held up 3 fingers. Only then was I told that my son had come the day before as well.

That night, Layla laid a wet cloth on my forehead. Whenever the door opened, I heard footsteps in the alley. Yusuf called my name. I moved my lips to answer, but my breath came too fast. Layla held my hand. I squeezed my daughter's hand once. After that, I no longer had the strength to move my fingers. My children's voices were close, but their words became difficult to understand.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1010, Nura's wound became infected after a mule injured her leg. On the third night, as the fever and confusion worsened, the infection spread through her body, and she died in her own home. Her son Yusuf long remembered how his mother could not recall that he had visited the day before. Her daughter Layla remembered both the pottery skills her mother had taught her and the days when she had tried to keep sole control of the accounts. Nura's death did not erase the reduced visits after she refused Safiya money for roof repairs. This record of a past life preserves not only Nura's choice over a bowl in 985, but also the life that continued afterward and its end.
finalMoment.artAlt: Moments before the accident, viewed from above in a narrow Córdoba alley in 1010. 64-year-old Nura steps toward the door of her home as a loaded mule led by a handler twists its body and raises a hind leg

card.name: Karim
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Karim of Isfahan. You helped in a cloth shop before becoming a storyteller, lived close to your sister's family, and grew old teaching young people how to perform.
card.title: The Unfinished Half of the Story
card.world: Isfahan under the Safavid dynasty, 1655
card.flavor: At the most exciting moment, the apprentice interrupted
card.opening: Just as the coffeehouse fell utterly silent, the apprentice Nemat interrupted Karim's tale of a hero. “What happened to the groom?”
card.life: You grew up as the son of a cloth merchant and became a coffeehouse storyteller. You never married, kept your sister Farideh and her children close, and taught young performers. In old age, you shortened your lengthy performances and lived with your sister.
card.turn: When Nemat asked what had become of the groom Karim always skipped over, the customers also began wondering who had cared for the injured horse. Karim could have pressed on with the familiar ending of the hero's tale.
card.decision: In front of the customers, Karim entrusted the rest of the story to Nemat. Nemat said that while the hero won the castle, the groom had been unable to return home because he stayed behind to care for the injured horse.
card.cost: The customers were divided over Nemat's ending, and the coffeehouse owner cut part of Karim's pay because the performance had been interrupted midway. Karim regretted losing what felt like his final word and could not immediately tell Nemat that he had done well.
card.after: For the next performance, Karim and Nemat planned their turns separately. They did not always choose the same ending, but they told each other beforehand what stories they intended to tell.
card.presentEcho: Even in a story one person has told for years, someone else may notice a missing scene. Loss and awkwardness can remain even after choosing to make room for another person.
card.secondLook: Nemat's ending did not satisfy everyone, and the pay the owner withheld was never returned. It was true that Karim had less time to speak.
card.unresolved: Nemat said he would tell what happened next to the groom in the invented story the following day. Even afterward, Karim and Nemat often argued about which ending was better.
card.readerQuestion: Just as you are telling an exciting story in front of a crowd, your apprentice interrupts. “What about the groom who helped the hero?” Every customer turns to look at you. What would you do first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Karim. You were a storyteller who made people laugh and hold their breath in the coffeehouses of Isfahan. Today, I will tell you about the night he entrusted the ending of the story he knew best to someone else.

In 1655, there were not enough seats in the coffeehouse beside Isfahan's great square. Karim held a small wooden stick in one hand. As a boy calling customers into his father's cloth shop, he had never imagined he would stand in a place like this. Now people fell silent at a single tap of his stick. The owner, Rashid, set down a cup and whispered, “We have a big crowd tonight, so keep them hooked to the end.”

Karim began with an invented tale he had told for years. As a hero crossed a dangerous pass to reach a castle, a groom followed behind, leading an injured horse. When the hero shook off his pursuer before the castle gate, Karim whipped his shoulders around, and the customers leaned forward with their cups still raised. At the back of the coffeehouse, the apprentice Nemat mouthed the words along with him. Nemat had already memorized the story after hearing it many times.

“And so the hero presented the horse to the lord of the castle!” Just as Karim was about to bring down his stick, Nemat stood up. “What happened to the groom?” Only the clatter of dishes remained. Someone snickered. “The hero won. That's all that matters.” But another customer asked, “That's true—who cared for the horse?” Karim looked at Nemat. He could see his fingers trembling.

Karim could have ended the story as usual by saying that the hero received his reward. Rashid was also looking his way, circling one hand. He meant for Karim to wrap it up quickly. Nemat did not sit down. Karim realized that Nemat had seized upon the part he always skipped right over. The crowd's eyes moved back and forth between them.

signalMoments.notice: Karim looked again at the faces of the laughing customers. Several nodded at Nemat's question. Karim laid the stick across his knees. “Nemat, where do you think the groom went?”
signalMoments.speak: Karim told Nemat, “Tell us the ending you imagined.” When Nemat asked, “Right now?” he nodded again in front of the customers. “Right now. Because I want to hear the rest of the story that even I don't know.”
signalMoments.connect: Karim asked Rashid to make a place for Nemat to stand. The owner frowned, but one customer in the front row shifted aside. Karim placed Nemat there.

episode.afterSignal:
Karim held out the stick, and Nemat took it. But he could not utter his first words. Someone asked, “What was the groom's name?” Nemat glanced at Karim. Karim shrugged. “I never came up with one either.” Laughter broke out. Nemat caught his breath and said, “His name was Aziz.” Karim quietly repeated the unfamiliar name.

In Nemat's ending, the hero passed through the castle gate, but Aziz could not follow. Afraid that leaving the horse alone would worsen its injured leg, he stayed outside the gate and washed the wound. By the time the horse could walk again, the group bound for home had already left. Nemat stopped there. “What happened next?” asked someone in the front row. “I'll tell you tomorrow what Aziz did.”

The coffeehouse erupted in noise. Some said, “If he made it all the way to the castle, he should get a reward!” Others laughed and said, “The groom did the most work of all.” Karim took the stick back from Nemat. Normally, it would have been his turn to deliver the final line. But tonight, everyone was waiting for Nemat's next words. Karim felt the loss. He could not pretend even that feeling was noble.

After the customers left, Rashid counted out Karim's pay. It was less than they had agreed. “Your turn was interrupted in the middle. You didn't even finish.” When Karim said, “The customers are waiting for the ending,” Rashid replied, “That anticipation didn't increase today's drink sales.” Karim took the coins without another word. Nemat, standing beside the door, saw the money. “It happened because I interrupted.” Karim did not immediately say it was all right.

When they stepped outside, the shop lights around the square were going dark one by one. Nemat walked ahead. Karim called after him. “Tell me first what you're going to say tomorrow.” Nemat turned around. “Will you let me stand there again tomorrow?” “I'll speak to Rashid. But I can't quite tell you that you did well tonight. Not yet.” Nemat nodded. The two of them parted at different alleys.

The following week, Karim took the first part of the story and gave Nemat the remaining time. They traded lines in front of the customers, but outside they often argued about which ending was better. A few years later, Nemat told stories by himself in another coffeehouse. Karim stayed close to his sister's family and performed for many years. When his voice grew hoarse and long evenings became difficult, he listened for the places where young performers paused to breathe.

finalMoment.place: Farideh's home in Isfahan under the Safavid dynasty
finalMoment.scene:
One afternoon in midsummer 1678, 64-year-old Karim visited his nephew Amin in Isfahan and then returned to his sister Farideh's home. The sun was so hot on the walk home that he stopped twice in the shade of the alleys. When he entered the courtyard, his head hurt and the ground seemed to sway beneath his feet. Karim stood with one hand braced against a wall in the shade. Farideh emerged from the door opposite him and asked, “Why are you standing there?” Karim barely managed to say, “Some water.”

When Farideh brought the water, Karim took a sip. But even after she told him to sit in the shade, he remained standing and looked around the courtyard. Farideh sat Karim beneath the wall and wiped his forehead with a wet cloth. Karim asked, “Isn't Amin here yet?” He tried to say that he had just returned from Amin's home, but no words followed the name.

Farideh asked a nearby neighbor to inform Amin and find someone who could examine the illness. Karim tried to stand. “I need to go inside.” “You're home now,” Farideh replied. Karim looked at the door to his own room but frowned as if he did not recognize it. Farideh loosened his outer robe and wet the cloth again. Karim felt the cloth touch his cheek and turned his head toward it. Then he lowered his arm and closed his eyes.

Amin arrived and called, “Uncle, I'm here.” Karim briefly opened his eyes but could not look at Amin. Farideh changed the cloth on her younger brother's forehead and called his name. Karim's breaths grew short, and then for a while there was no sound. Amin spoke to him again, but there was no answer. While the sun still lingered above the courtyard wall, Karim stopped breathing.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1678, after walking the hot midday road back to Farideh's home, Karim's condition rapidly worsened, and he died before sunset that day. The precise medical cause cannot be confirmed. Farideh remembered both the times her brother listened to everything she said at home and his final moments when he could not recognize the house. Only later did Amin fully accept that his uncle had visited him on the day he died. Nemat heard the news the following day and remembered the night his teacher made room for him, as well as the later days when Karim made him revise his ending over and over. The record of this past life closes the story of Karim by preserving both the times he tried to listen to other people's stories and the times he struggled to surrender his own turn to speak.
finalMoment.artAlt: In the courtyard of a modest Isfahan home in the summer of 1678, 64-year-old Karim feels the first wave of dizziness after crossing the scorching sunlight, braces himself against a shaded wall, and presses a hand to his forehead. In the distance, his sister Farideh watches from the doorway.

card.name: Naya
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Naya of Teotihuacan. You made obsidian tools and raised a daughter, and even after your husband died, you continued working with your neighbors and lived to see your grandson.
card.title: The Bundle Behind the Wall
card.world: Teotihuacan in central Mexico around 400 CE
card.flavor: The day a friend left, one piece of luggage vanished
card.opening: On the day Ita was moving to another home, one of her bundles disappeared. As the neighbors began checking one another's rooms and the movers, Naya thought of the place behind the wall where she had hidden it.
card.life: She grew up in a place where several households shared a courtyard and learned to make obsidian tools. She married and raised a daughter, and continued working with her neighbors after her husband died. She grew old watching over her grandson after her daughter moved to another home.
card.turn: The person who took the bundle was not a strange thief. Naya had hidden it behind the wall because she did not want her longtime friend Ita to leave.
card.decision: When Naya saw that even her neighbors' rooms were under suspicion, she retrieved the bundle herself. In front of Ita and the neighbors, she admitted that she had hidden it.
card.cost: Ita had to find someone else to move the luggage that remained. The person next door had their room suspected, and Ita even refused Naya's offer to help. When the two met again several years later, they could no longer talk as they once had.
card.after: Several years later, the two met again in the same city, but they did not immediately smile as they once had. Naya went on with her daily life, working with her daughter, and Ita lived in her new home.
card.presentEcho: When her daughter moved to another home, Naya helped tie up her belongings. But that did not erase the delay to Ita's move or the suspicion cast on the neighbors.
card.secondLook: Even though Naya confessed first, Ita's moving preparations and the neighbors' suspicions had already become tangled together. Ita still had reason to distance herself.
card.unresolved: Even after they met again, it was unclear whether Ita ever came to regard Naya as the friend she had once been.
card.readerQuestion: On the day your longtime friend moves to another home, a bundle she absolutely must take is nowhere to be found. The neighbors begin looking at one another and asking, “Who took it?” What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Naya saw a neighbor examining a gray mark beneath the wall. Knowing it was stone dust from her hands that had rubbed onto the bundle, she went behind the wall first and retrieved it.
signalMoments.speak: Naya called Ita over and revealed that she had hidden the bundle. When Ita asked why, Naya replied that it was behind the wall and walked there with her.
signalMoments.connect: Naya told the neighbors to stop searching and said she had taken the luggage. When the people cleared a path, she went behind the wall in front of Ita.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Naya. Long ago, you shaped obsidian in a courtyard in Teotihuacan. Today, I'll tell you about the day you hid a departing friend's luggage and lost the trust of that friend and your neighbors.

Around 400 CE, luggage sat outside the door of Naya's neighbor, Ita. Ita had decided to live with relatives in another residential compound in the city. As children, Naya and Ita had played in the same courtyard, and they would seek each other out for help choosing pieces of obsidian. Once Ita walked out the door, hers would no longer be a face Naya saw every evening. Naya practiced saying congratulations three times, but still could not get the words out properly.

While Ita went to fetch water, Naya noticed a small bundle beside the wall. It held clothes Ita had worn and small tools. There was a little time before the people moving the luggage came into the courtyard. Naya picked up the bundle, went around a short wall, and pushed it into an empty gap. “If she's delayed just a little, maybe we'll at least have more time to talk.” Stone dust from Naya's hands left a faint gray mark on the bundle's cloth.

Ita returned and counted her luggage. “Have you seen the small bundle?” Naya pretended to sort through pieces of obsidian. Ita called over the person next door. “I left it here, but it's gone.” The neighbor said they would search their own room first, while someone else checked the people who had come to move the luggage. No one had accused anyone of stealing yet, but the way they looked at one another had changed.

Naya set down the piece of stone in her hand. If she pretended not to know for just a little longer, Ita would remain in the courtyard longer. But during that time, someone else might come under suspicion. Naya had hidden a single piece of luggage, but what had begun to twist out of shape was the bond among the neighbors.

signalMoments.notice: Naya saw a neighbor examining the gray mark beneath the wall. It was stone dust from her own hands, the same dust left on Ita's bundle. Naya went behind the wall first and retrieved the bundle.
signalMoments.speak: Naya called to Ita. “Stop searching. I hid it.” When Ita asked why she would say such a thing, Naya replied that the bundle was behind the wall and walked there with her.
signalMoments.connect: Naya told the neighbors to stop searching. “I'm the one who took the luggage.” When the people cleared a path, she went behind the wall in front of Ita.

episode.afterSignal:
The bundle emerged from behind the wall. Naya held up the gray-marked cloth in both hands. “I hid it. I thought that if you left a little later, we'd have more time together.” Ita did not take the bundle. “Then why did you just watch us search?” Naya could not answer. The person next door started to mention having searched their own room, then swallowed the words.

The people who had come to move the luggage did not wait. They loaded the other belongings first and left. With one piece of luggage still behind, Ita had to find someone else to help. When Naya said, “I'll carry it,” Ita shook her head. “Today, I'll ask someone else.” Even after hearing Naya's apology, she did not smile. Naya had never imagined that the conversation she wanted would turn out like this.

Naya also told the neighbors that she had done wrong. The person next door asked, “You wanted more time with your friend, so you let even my room come under suspicion?” Naya bowed her head. The bundle had been returned, but the person next door brought up again how their room had been suspected.

As the sun sank lower, Ita got help from another neighbor to move the remaining luggage. Naya followed her to the edge of the courtyard, but did not touch the luggage again. At the doorway, Ita turned back for a moment. “When we were children, you always took my hand when I fell. Why did you trip me today?” Naya said, “I was afraid it would be quiet after you left.” Even after hearing those words, Ita turned away and set out on the road.

The next day, the courtyard truly was quiet. Naya did not spread out her tools where Ita used to sit. A few days later, she sat there and worked. For a while, her hands were slow as they sorted the stones.

In 403, Naya lost her husband. Afterward, she made tools with her daughter. When her daughter moved to another home in 418, Naya helped tie up her belongings. After her grandson was born, she traveled between the two homes to watch the child. When she encountered Ita on the street, they exchanged greetings, but they did not talk for long as they once had.

finalMoment.place: The courtyard of Naya's shared residence in Teotihuacan, Central Mexico
finalMoment.scene:
One morning in 431, sixty-three-year-old Naya sat before a water jar in the shared courtyard in Teotihuacan. A lower molar had hurt for several days, and the area beneath her jaw had been swollen since the day before. A fever had woken her often during the night. Naya soaked a cloth in water and pressed it against her aching cheek. The pain eased a little only when the cold moisture touched it. As she reached out to wet the cloth again, the door of the home across from hers opened.

The person who came out was the neighbor next door whose room had come under suspicion long ago, the day they searched for Ita's luggage. “Does it still hurt?” the neighbor asked, and Naya nodded. “Tell my daughter… to come.” Pain shot through Naya's jaw as she spoke, and she closed her mouth. The neighbor sent word to her daughter, who lived in another compound, then returned. The two remained together in the courtyard's shade, but they did not bring up the old story of the bundle.

Naya tried to drink water. Unable to swallow even a sip, she set the bowl down. The pressure beneath her jaw grew worse, and a rasping sound came from her throat when she breathed in. The neighbor came closer and asked again where it hurt. Naya pointed first to her cheek and then to her throat. She tried to stand and go to her room, but her legs had no strength, so she remained seated beside the jar. The neighbor left the back door open.

Naya raised her head, looking toward the path her daughter would take to enter. She opened her mouth and tried to breathe, but only a little air came in. She dropped the wet cloth in her hand and braced both hands against the ground. The neighbor called her name. Naya tried to look that way, then tried once more to draw breath. Only a short sound came from her throat. Before her daughter reached the courtyard, Naya's hands went slack against the ground.
finalMoment.afterword: In 431, Naya died in a shared courtyard in Teotihuacan after several days of toothache and swelling beneath her jaw. The exact illness and what happened inside her body cannot be confirmed. The neighbor who had been beside her told her daughter what had happened that morning. That neighbor stayed with Naya while she was ill, but had not forgotten that their room had come under suspicion on the day Naya hid Ita's luggage. Naya's daughter arrived late, having left her son at another home. She remembered the day Naya had retied the cords around her moving bundles several times. Ita learned of Naya's death later and did not say that their friendship had ever returned to the way it had been. This record of a past life closes the account of this life by noting both the cost Naya imposed on others when she tried to hold someone close and the later years she spent visiting her daughter and grandson.

card.title: The Night a Torn Cloak Drew Laughter

card.flavor: When an actor froze onstage, a woman with a needle stepped in
card.opening: The performance stopped when an actor's cloak tore on a stage nail. Backstage, Martha looked from the two shirts due the next day to the needle in her hand.

card.turn: The person who came onstage to mend the cloak was not an actor but Martha. When the actor greeted her as though she were a character in the play, an unexpected scene unfolded.
card.decision: Martha set aside the shirts she had to deliver, went onstage, and sewed up the tear in the actor's cloak. The actor kept the performance going by exchanging lines with Martha.
card.cost: The performance continued, but she failed to deliver the shirts on time. Martha received no further sewing work and had to do extra laundry work for several days.
card.after: Martha shared the laundry with Ellen, making up for the reduced work over the next several days. card.presentEcho: When Martha mended the cloak, she knew only that her shirt delivery might be late. She did not know she would lose her next sewing job. Both the laughter she received onstage and the next day's laundry work remained part of Martha's life.
card.secondLook: The audience laughed at Martha's needle, but the person waiting for the shirts the next day gave the next sewing job to someone else. Ellen shared the laundry with Martha to make up for her reduced workload.
card.unresolved: There is no way to know who among those who applauded that day remembered Martha's name.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Martha. After being convicted in London and transported to Sydney, you did sewing work. Today, I'll tell you about a night in 1796 at a small theater in New South Wales, a British colony.

Backstage at a small Sydney theater in 1796, Martha sat with two shirts across her knees, sewing their sleeves. If she finished the work by the next morning, she could get more sewing. Beside her, the actor Jonah rehearsed his lines in a worn cloak. “My word is law!” Martha snorted. “Some law, when you can't even dodge a nail.” Jonah laughed and went onstage.

In the middle of the performance, a wooden board made a sharp click. The edge of Jonah's cloak had caught on a nail. As he turned, the fabric ripped in a long tear, and one side of the cloak slipped off his arm. Jonah forgot his next line. It became so quiet that even the audience's coughing could be heard.

Someone backstage whispered to Martha, “Leave it alone. You have shirts due tomorrow.” It was true. Martha had not been called to mend a cloak that night. But she could see Jonah standing there, clutching the torn fabric. If she set down the shirt in her hands, she might be late the next morning.

signalMoments.notice: Martha saw the nail snagging the cloak. If Jonah took even one more step, the fabric would tear further. Martha set the shirts down, picked up her needle, and went to the edge of the stage.
signalMoments.speak: “Don't move. It'll tear more!” Martha shouted. When Jonah turned, she set down the shirts and walked onstage with her needle in hand.
signalMoments.connect: Martha said to another actor backstage, “Please hold the cloak for me.” Once he pulled the fabric taut, Martha set down the shirts and went out with her needle.

episode.afterSignal:
Someone in the audience laughed. After all, a woman with a needle had appeared before the commander. Martha lifted Jonah's cloak with one hand. “If you raise your arm, it'll tear again.” Jonah stared blankly at her for a moment, then suddenly puffed out his chest and declared, “It seems the one holding the needle outranks me here!” Martha shot back, “The commander failed to dodge the nail.” This time, laughter spread all the way to the back of the audience.

Martha folded the torn edge over twice and stitched it quickly. One stitch, two. Jonah did not move a muscle. When another actor fed him his line, Jonah returned to the play. As Martha left the stage, she checked that the cloak was not coming apart again. The needle had pricked her palm, but the cloak held.

After the performance, Jonah came to find her. “They laughed loudest at your line.” Martha said, “I doubt anyone will laugh away my worries about tomorrow's shirts.” One shirt still needed a sleeve finished; the other, its front. A brief laugh backstage could not complete either task.

The next morning, Martha delivered the two shirts late. The woman who handed out the work had already given the next cloth to someone else. “There's nothing for you today.” Martha started to make an excuse, then closed her mouth. The applause she had received at the theater could not take the place of the shirts the woman had waited for.

Ellen divided the laundry in two and placed half in front of Martha. “We can do this together.” “It's quite a joke, asking for help with laundry after bragging that I was in a performance,” Martha said. Ellen replied, “Then give me some lines while we wash.” As they wrung out the water, the two of them laughed for a moment. For several days, Martha's hands gripped wet cloth instead of a needle.

Martha kept sewing even after her sentence ended in 1801. After living with Stephen and then separating from him, she kept her workplace going on her own. In old age, when her fingers stiffened, she passed the work with small buttons on to her younger colleague Hannah. When Martha imitated the actor Jonah's voice in front of her friends, Ellen would add, “Tell them about doing laundry with me the next day, too.” The laughter onstage did not restore the next sewing job Martha lost.

finalMoment.place: Martha's room in Sydney, New South Wales, a British colony
finalMoment.scene:
It is 1833, and I am in my room in Sydney. Fever and coughing have kept me from getting out of bed for days. As the sun sinks, Ellen pulls over a chair and sits down. Through the open door, I hear neighbors calling to one another. Ellen asks, “Shall I close the door?” “Leave it. I can hear people talking.” After finishing that sentence, I have to catch my breath.

My younger colleague Hannah stands in the doorway. “How are you today?” I try to answer with one of my usual jokes, but I cough first. As I wait for it to stop, my chest feels completely blocked. Ellen supports my back. Hannah looks at my face and says, “I'll go get someone to help,” then runs out into the yard. I raise my hand to tell her not to go, but my arm falls back onto the bed.

The door is open. In the yard, Hannah's voice calling for someone overlaps with the sound of running footsteps. I try to tell Ellen that I can hear them. When I open my mouth, only a short breath escapes. Ellen leans down to look into my face. “Martha, take one more breath.” I tense my chest, trying to draw in air. The movement stops. Voices continue beyond the door, but the next breath does not come.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1833, Martha died in her own room in Sydney with Ellen at her side. The exact cause of the fever and coughing she suffered for several days was never recorded. Hannah, who had gone out to seek help, returned and stopped before the open door. Ellen remembered that even that day, Martha had wanted to hear the voices outside. Hannah also remembered how long Martha had made her wait before sharing work with her. The chronicle of past lives records the day the life of Martha, who endured transportation and assigned labor before establishing her own business, came to an end.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view of a small room in Sydney in 1833 from a high vantage point outside an open door. In the afternoon, 65-year-old Martha sits alone on the edge of the bed, listening to voices beyond the open door

You distributed bread and beer in the Giza construction workers' village. You gave skilled stonemasons priority and reduced the porters' shares, but later made the work crews' markings public.
card.title: The Bread Mark in the Pyramid's Shadow
card.role: a bakery worker responsible for distributing bread and beer
card.world: 26th century BCE · the royal construction workers' village at Giza during the Old Kingdom
card.flavor: A ration ledger from a workers' village beside a massive stone construction project
card.opening: In 26th-century BCE Giza, Merit stamped markings on baskets of bread bound for the pyramid construction site.
card.life: She distributed bread and beer in the Giza construction workers' village. She gave skilled stonemasons priority and reduced the porters' shares, but later made the work crews' markings public. By filling the stonemasons' crew's share first, she reduced the bread allotted to the porter crew that included Kheti. The porters walked farther yet had less to eat.
card.turn: The custom of prioritizing skilled workers came into conflict with the shares owed to the porter crew that had actually worked.
card.decision: Merit recounted the people and divided the bread accordingly.
card.cost: By filling the stonemasons' crew's share first, she reduced the bread allotted to the porter crew that included Kheti. The porters walked farther yet had less to eat.
card.after: The rationing standard changed, but the earlier losses remained.
card.presentEcho: When only highly visible results are counted, the labor of transport and care disappears.
card.secondLook: Merit's new standard was fair, but it came too late.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Merit, responsible for distributing bread and beer in Giza's construction workers' village.

On a day when the stone-hauling crew returned late, the overseer ordered that the stonemasons' crew be served first. As always, Merit filled the skilled workers' baskets before the others.

The porter Kheti demanded an equal share, saying they were late only because the road had been blocked. The apprentice Nefer reported that there were more empty baskets than the ledger showed.

signalMoments.notice: Merit saw that the dirt on the empty baskets showed that the porter crew had indeed traveled the long road to the distant quarry.
signalMoments.speak: “The crews that worked today will receive rations according to the number of people, not the time they returned.” Merit said this in front of the overseer and the workers.
signalMoments.connect: Merit had Kheti and Nefer count the people in each crew and match the basket markings together.

episode.afterSignal:
She redistributed the stonemasons' extra bread to fill the porter crew's baskets. The overseer complained that this was delaying the ration distribution.

Beginning the next day, Merit recorded each crew's name and number of people together on the marking board on the oven wall.

The stonemasons received smaller extra shares, and Kheti received an equal share. But Merit could not make up for the reduced shares of the past.

finalMoment.place: Merit's home in the Giza workers' village
finalMoment.scene:
Around 2552 BCE, after the Nile's floodwaters receded, Merit lay in her home in the Giza workers' village, suffering from diarrhea and fever for the fourth day. Her husband Panesi brought her water in a small pottery cup. From outside the door, her apprentice Nefer told her that he had taken over the oven work.

Merit tried to get up and look for the ration stamp, but she had no strength in her belly. “Count the people first,” she told Nefer. Panesi told her to put the ledger aside for the day, and Merit handed the stamp to him.

As the sun sank, her hands and feet grew cold and her mouth went dry. Even when she drank water, she soon vomited it up. Panesi sat beside her and called her name, but Merit never opened her eyes again.
finalMoment.afterword: Merit died after severe dehydration from an illness believed to have been a serious intestinal infection. The exact illness is unknown. Nefer continued to count the people in each crew first, while the porter Kheti remembered that the fair standard had come too late. The Giza pyramid workers' settlement and its food supply are based on historical and archaeological context; the individual life is fictional.

card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yuran of Chang'an. You grew up at your mother's market stall, built a family, and after your husband's death, opened a teahouse with a friend, welcoming people there into old age.
card.title: The Pipa That Sounded Before the Raindrops
card.world: Chang'an, capital of the Tang dynasty, 825
card.flavor: A daughter held an instrument before her mother, who held the money meant for the roof
card.opening: On the day she was counting the money saved to repair the leaking roof, her daughter Ayin entered the teahouse carrying a pipa. Her daughter said she would leave with a musical troupe in a few days.
card.life: She learned the work at her mother's grain stall, married Guo Ping, and raised a daughter. After her husband's death, she opened a teahouse with her friend Wei Ying. Even after her daughter chose to make a living performing, she continued running the teahouse in Chang'an. In old age, she worked less and traveled as far as Luoyang to visit her daughter.
card.turn: Ayin planned to leave a few days later with other women musicians and perform in several cities. Yuran's first concern was who would help with the teahouse, but Ayin had already practiced for years and chosen her own path.
card.decision: Yuran listened to her daughter's performance to the end and gave her the money she had saved for repairing the roof to cover her expenses on the road. She personally asked the roof repairer to wait longer for his payment.
card.cost: When the first rain came after Ayin left, water leaked into one side of the house. Yuran borrowed money from her friend Wei Ying, repaired the roof the following year, and repaid the debt over several years.
card.after: Ayin left, but that did not make things easy between mother and daughter all at once. Yuran kept the teahouse open, and when her daughter later stopped in Chang'an, the first thing she asked about was the taste of the tea there.
card.presentEcho: When someone close to you chooses a different path, you may want to hold them back and let them go at the same time. The life that follows changes too.
card.secondLook: The money she gave her daughter was also the money meant to repair the roof. When the rain leaked in, Yuran had to tell the man who came to fix it that she did not have enough money. Later, she borrowed from Wei Ying and paid her back.
card.unresolved: Even on the day Ayin left, neither of them knew how often they would see each other in the future.
card.readerQuestion: Your daughter comes in carrying a pipa and says she will leave with a musical troupe in a few days. You are holding the money you saved to repair the leaking roof. What would you do first?

identity.region: Chang'an, capital of the Tang dynasty
identity.summary: She grew up at her mother's market stall, married, and raised a daughter. After her husband's death, she opened a teahouse with a friend and welcomed customers in Chang'an into old age. Later in life, she left for Luoyang to visit her daughter.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Yuran · Female
776–852 · 76 years old
Born and lived in Chang'an, capital of the Tang dynasty
Work · Helped at a grain stall and ran a small teahouse with Wei Ying
Life · She learned the work at her mother's market stall, married Guo Ping, and raised their daughter Ayin. After her husband's death, she opened a teahouse with her friend Wei Ying. Even while her daughter worked as a musician in other cities, she continued welcoming people in Chang'an. In old age, she worked less and went to Luoyang to visit her daughter.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She easily struck up conversations even with new customers, but with family, she voiced her worries first.
Liked · Talking about Chang'an with Wei Ying over cups of tea
Disliked · Her habit of going home and pouring out all the worries she could not mention in front of customers
Good at · Preparing cups and seats so customers never had to wait

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small grain measure her mother had used
Those closest to her · Her daughter Ayin, her husband Guo Ping, and her longtime friend Wei Ying
The life she wanted · To keep the teahouse open for many years and continue visiting with her faraway daughter
Worries · The leaking roof and the safety of her daughter traveling alone

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Yuran. You were someone who offered customers a cup of tea before they even asked. Let me tell you about a day when you did not know what to say first to your daughter.

825, a small teahouse in Chang'an, capital of the Tang dynasty. Yuran counted the coins again. It was the money she had promised to pay the roof repairer the next day. Rain had threatened for several days, but the morning was sunny, and customers had brought their seats out in front of the shop.

A brief note sounded from a pipa by the doorway. Her daughter Ayin had brushed its strings against the doorframe as she entered carrying the instrument. An unfamiliar woman stood behind her. Before her mother could hide the coins, Ayin said, “I'm leaving with them in three days. I'll be performing in other cities too.”

Yuran looked at Ayin's hands. They trembled far less holding a pipa than they did holding a teacup. Still, the first words out of her mouth were, “Who's going to help at the shop?” Ayin's face stiffened. “I knew that would be the first thing you'd say.” The unfamiliar woman introduced herself, explaining that she worked with other musicians, then went outside to give the mother and daughter time to talk.

“We have to fix the roof before it rains. I don't have money for you to spend on the road right now,” Yuran said. Ayin replied, “I never asked you for money. Just don't stop me from going.” Wei Ying, who was pouring tea beside them, filled only their two cups and stepped away. Yuran could not unclench the hand wrapped around the coins.

signalMoments.notice: Yuran saw that Ayin's pipa strings had been replaced with new ones. That meant she had been preparing to leave for several days. Yuran set the coins in her fist on the table and looked into her daughter's face.
signalMoments.speak: “How long will you be gone?” Yuran asked. “I don't know when I'll be back yet.” Ayin's answer was brief. Yuran stopped talking for the moment and waited to see if her daughter had more to say.
signalMoments.connect: Yuran asked Wei Ying to watch the teahouse for a while, then seated Ayin beside her. She also invited the musician waiting outside to join them for tea. She wanted to hear for herself how the decision to leave had been made.

episode.afterSignal:
Ayin said she had practiced for years and had been performing with women musicians who stopped in Chang'an. One of them had heard Ayin play and invited her to join them. Knowing her mother would worry, Ayin had put off telling her. Yuran could not remember the last time she had truly listened to her daughter perform.

“Then play for me now,” Yuran said. Ayin sat in one corner of the teahouse and rested the pipa on her lap. At first, the customers kept talking. When the tune quickened, a person lifting a teacup froze with it in hand, and the musician outside leaned against the door to listen. When the piece ended, Ayin looked at that woman's face before her mother's. That hurt Yuran a little.

“Are you going because someone else told you you're good?” Yuran asked. Ayin shook her head. “I'm going because I want to.” Yuran knew her daughter had already chosen her path. She disliked pretending that she was the one allowing her daughter to leave. “I spoke as though I had to give you permission to follow your own path,” Yuran apologized. Ayin did not smile right away. “You always do.”

Raindrops began to fall outside. Wei Ying moved the teacups farther in. Yuran pushed the roof repair money toward Ayin. “Don't miss meals on the road.” Ayin tried not to take it. “What about the house if you spend this?” Yuran said, “I'll find another way to repair it. That's my responsibility.” A moment later, Ayin accepted the coins. They still had not promised when they would see each other again.

After Ayin left, the rain found the old gaps in the roof and came through. Yuran placed a large basin beside her bed to catch the rainwater. The next day, she had to tell the man who came to repair the roof that she did not have enough money and ask him to wait. When Wei Ying heard, she offered to lend her the money. Yuran refused at first, but agreed to borrow it before winter came. Even after the roof was repaired, she spent several years repaying that debt from the teahouse's earnings.

Ayin lived far away but sometimes stopped in Chang'an. The first time she returned, Yuran asked, “What's the tea like there?” Ayin laughed and said, “Weaker than yours.” The story that followed could not be finished over a single cup.

Even in old age, Yuran continued welcoming customers with Wei Ying, gradually turning the work over to Wei Ying's nephew. Later, she was the one who set out on the road to visit Ayin in Luoyang. The story I told you today was of one day in that long life, when she truly listened to the sound of the pipa before the rain came.
