finalMoment.place: Chang'an, capital of the Tang dynasty
finalMoment.scene:
It is a late-summer morning in 852, in the courtyard of my home in Chang'an. Wei Ying lifts one side of my bedding to move me into the sunlight. My body has felt heavy for days, and I can barely cross the threshold alone. I grip the end of the blanket and try to rise, but there is no strength in my legs. “Let's just sit here.” Wei Ying supports my arm. I do not try to stand again.

Wei Ying sits in front of me and says she will send someone for Ayin. My daughter is in Luoyang. “Don't be angry if she comes late,” I say. Wei Ying glares at me. “You're still worrying about everyone else, right to the end.” I try to laugh, then pause to catch my breath. “You sit down too.” Wei Ying drapes the blanket over my knees and sits beside me.

I hear children running in the courtyard. I turn my head toward them, then grow dizzy and lean against Wei Ying's shoulder. Wei Ying calls my name. I try to answer, but the words break off and my breaths grow short. Wei Ying lays me down and shouts to a passing neighbor to go get someone. I reach for Wei Ying's hand. When our fingers touch, she grips my hand tightly.

“Yuran, I'm here,” Wei Ying says. I draw one breath, but taking the next is hard. I can hear the sounds of the courtyard, but I cannot raise my body. I tighten my grip, trying not to let go of Wei Ying's hand, but the strength drains from my fingers. As Wei Ying calls my name again, my breathing stops.
finalMoment.afterword: In 852, Yuran died in the courtyard of her own home in Chang'an, holding the hand of her longtime friend Wei Ying. No account remains of what caused her sudden difficulty breathing. Even when the neighbor who had gone to summon help returned, Wei Ying could not let go of Yuran's hand. Her daughter Ayin, who arrived late from Luoyang, remembered the day her mother had traveled far to see her. Wei Ying said Yuran was always quick to worry about others but always slow to care for her own body. The record of her past life marks the day Yuran's life ended, preserving together the years she lived far from her daughter, the friendship she spent so long repaying, and the friend who remained beside her on her final morning.
finalMoment.artAlt: A late-summer morning in 852, in the courtyard of a home in Tang-dynasty Chang'an: 76-year-old Yuran, unable to rise, lies on a low bed holding the hand of her longtime friend Wei Ying, who kneels beside her

card.name: Elias Ward
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Elias Ward of South Manitou Island. You learned carpentry at the harbor and lived with your family, then ran a small chair shop on the mainland after injuring your wrist.
card.title: One Nail in the Fog Whistle
card.world: South Manitou Island, Michigan, United States, 1885
card.flavor: On the day the fifty-two seconds of silence never came, suspicion fell on a young apprentice
card.opening: The lighthouse whistle sounded without pause in the thick fog, then suddenly fell silent. Elias, who had repaired its roof the day before, saw an empty space in his nail box.
card.life: He began as an apprentice harbor carpenter, married May, and moved to the island with their son, Sam. On the island, he repaired docks and houses, then switched to furniture repair after injuring his wrist. Because he pressed May to open a chair shop with him on the mainland, she had to leave behind her island food business and customers.
card.turn: Suspicion for damaging the fog whistle fell on Oliver, an apprentice who had passed by the storage shed. But a nail Elias had dropped near the whistle the day before could have caused the malfunction.
card.decision: Elias told the person in charge that he had lost one of his nails and suggested they inspect the inside of the whistle together before blaming Oliver.
card.cost: The nail was found, proving Oliver had not caused the malfunction, but the suspicion he had faced did not vanish at once. The person in charge told Elias not to work alone on the signal roof next time, and Oliver asked why it had taken so long for anyone to listen to him.
card.after: Afterward, he worked with someone else and counted the tools, and for a while he and Oliver did not climb onto the same roof. Later, a wrist injury led him to cut back on large roofing jobs. He opened a chair shop after moving to the mainland, but May lost the customers from her island food business.
card.presentEcho: It is hard to speak up the moment you realize you made a mistake. Even if speaking late can help someone, it cannot erase the time they spent waiting.
card.secondLook: Even after Elias revealed his mistake, Oliver remembered that Elias had not listened to him at first. When Elias returned home, May asked whether he had apologized to Oliver too.
card.unresolved: For a while, Elias and Oliver did not climb onto the same roof. Even after the whistle sounded again, the suspicion and belated explanation of that day could not be undone.
card.readerQuestion: The lighthouse fog whistle would not stop sounding in the mist, then suddenly went quiet. People suspect the apprentice Oliver, but you lost a nail on that roof yesterday. What would you do first?

Elias Ward · Male
1847–1917 · Age 70
Born in Manitowoc, Wisconsin; lived on islands in Lake Michigan and on the mainland
Work · Harbor carpenter, house and dock repairer, chair shop owner
Life · He learned woodworking at the harbor, married May, and raised their son, Sam. He lived on South Manitou Island and repaired many houses and docks. After injuring his wrist, he switched to furniture repair. In 1902, his haste to open a chair shop on the mainland forced May to leave her island food business and customers behind. They ran the shop in Traverse City, but May's lingering regret never disappeared.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Elias Ward. You were a carpenter who repaired the docks and houses around Lake Michigan. Let me tell you about a foggy day when one of his nails caught the ears of everyone on the island.

In late spring of 1885, fog hung low over South Manitou Island. Elias looked toward the lighthouse from the end of the dock. Only the upper part of the white tower was visible, and the steam whistle on the signal building's roof gave one long blast before pausing briefly. Ships used the sound and the silence to judge their position.

The day before, Elias had repaired a small roof right beside the whistle. As he replaced planks that let in rain, he set his nail box on the roof. The lid tilted when he moved the box, but he did not see any nail fall out. “Why count today when I count them every day?” he joked to his wife, May, before going home.

But that day, the whistle did not pause when it was supposed to. Once it started, the blast continued even after fifty-two seconds had passed. Inside the house, May covered her ears while kneading bread dough. Leonard, a dockworker, laughed and said, “Has the lighthouse learned its song by heart?” But he soon stopped laughing. The signal grew harsher, then cut off as if it had run out of steam. In an instant, the lake in the fog became far too quiet.

When Elias ran toward the lighthouse, the apprentice Oliver was standing in front of the signal building. That morning, Oliver had complained that he was sick of the sound and wished it would stop. When Leonard said quietly, “That boy was here,” the others looked at Oliver too. Oliver said, “I came to report a strange sound,” but no one answered right away.

Elias opened his nail box. One slot was empty where he had set aside a long nail for the roof. For the first time, the hammer in his hand felt heavy. As the person in charge asked Oliver why he had been beside the storage shed, Elias remembered the tilted box on the roof the day before.

signalMoments.notice: Elias touched the empty slot in the nail box with his finger and examined the fresh nail mark at the edge of the roof again. A nail like that could have fallen toward the whistle. He carried the box to the person in charge.
signalMoments.speak: “Wait,” Elias said in front of everyone. “I lost a nail up there yesterday.” He suggested looking inside the machine before questioning Oliver any further.
signalMoments.connect: Elias stood beside Oliver and said, “First tell me why you came here.” Oliver answered that he had come to report a strange sound. Together, they told the person in charge.

episode.afterSignal:
The person in charge waited for the steam to settle, then inspected the inside of the signal building. Elias stood by the door with his nail box. Oliver offered no further explanation. Instead, he stared down at the toes of his wet shoes. The longer they waited, the more Elias had to suppress the urge to say, “We don't know yet whether it is my nail.”

A short while later, the person in charge came out holding a long iron nail. Its bent end had the same flat head as the nails Elias had used on the roof. It had lodged inside the whistle's sound passage. “Who put this in here?” the person in charge asked, and Elias answered first. “I spilled the box up there. One was missing yesterday, and I didn't look for it.”

Leonard turned toward Oliver. “Then what about the boy?” Elias said, “I should have listened when Oliver said he came because he heard something.” Oliver looked at Elias and said, “I've been saying since yesterday that it sounded strange.” Elias could not find a reply. More vividly than dropping the nail, he saw that while he had stayed silent, no one had listened to Oliver.

The person in charge had the remaining equipment inspected and ordered another test of the blocked side. Elias could have helped, but first he had to clear away his box. He told the people waiting at the dock that Oliver had done nothing wrong. Someone said, “Then it's settled,” and Oliver walked home without a word. The suspicion he had faced could not be plucked out like a nail.

After the repairs were finished, the whistle once again gave a long blast and paused. Elias never knew whether a ship on the lake had passed safely that day or had waited. As he gathered his tools, the person in charge said, “Next time, don't work alone on the signal roof. And count everything you take up when you bring it back down.” Elias said he understood. When he returned to the shop, May asked, “Did you say that to Oliver too?” Elias shook his head.

The next day, he went to find Oliver. “I was too late to stop people from saying it was your fault.” Shaving a piece of wood, Oliver said, “I know.” Elias did not press him for forgiveness. Instead, he marked the empty slot beside his nail box again. For a while, the two did not climb onto the same roof. Elias worked with someone else and counted the tools, while Oliver continued his apprenticeship somewhere people listened to him first.

Several years later, Elias injured his wrist and stopped taking large roofing jobs. After Sam went to work on the mainland, Elias pressed May to open a chair shop with him in Traverse City. May wanted to keep running her food business on the island, but they moved in 1902. May lost her customers and closed the business. At the new shop, she kept the books but set her own working hours. Elias learned the cost of his decision too late, and he could not restore the customers May had lost. Today's story is about the earlier day when he was late to admit the truth about one nail.

finalMoment.place: Traverse City, Michigan, United States
finalMoment.scene:
On an early autumn afternoon in 1917, I walk with May along a lakeside path in Traverse City. May pulls the collar of her coat tight against the wind. “I'd like to sit in that shade for a while.” She points to a nearby tree. I say I want to look at the water a little longer first. May sits beneath the tree, and I stop a few steps ahead to watch a boat on the lake.

May calls my name. I try to turn, but the waves before my eyes suddenly seem to tilt. Strength leaves one leg, and I sink to the side of the path. I press my palm to the ground and try to rise, but my body topples to one side. “Elias?” May runs over and supports my shoulder. I try to tell her I am all right, but my tongue will not move properly. I look at May's face and only open my mouth.

May shouts to a passerby to call a doctor. The person runs up the path. I try to grasp May's sleeve. My fingertips touch it, but I have no strength to close my fingers. May places my hand between both of hers. “I'm here. Keep looking at me.” I try to nod, but my neck will not move. The wind brushes May's hair across my cheek.

May calls my name again. I draw a breath to answer. No sound comes out. May bends over and studies my face. After a while, I can no longer follow May's face with my eyes, and my hand no longer moves. My breathing stops as May holds my hand and calls my name.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1917, Elias died beside the lake in Traverse City with May at his side. The cause of the sudden paralysis on one side of his body was never confirmed. When the person who had gone to call a doctor returned, May was still holding Elias's hand. When Sam heard the news, he remembered how his father had been unable to say that he was sad when Sam left. May remembered both the days she had walked by the lake with her husband and the time she had been forced to give up her food business because of the move to the mainland. The record of his past life leaves intact the years they spent together and the costs they left each other, and records the day Elias's life ended.
finalMoment.artAlt: An angled overhead view of a lakeside path in Traverse City on an early autumn afternoon in 1917. Elias, age 70, stands looking at a boat, while several steps behind him, his wife May sits apart on a bench beneath a tree, pulling her collar tight

card.name: João Marques
card.identityLine: In that life, you were João Marques of Lisbon. You went from a boy who helped at a market stall to a tile installer, and after the earthquake, you took work meant to be shared with a friend to cover his family's rent, then taught younger workers in old age.
card.title: The Basket of Bread Beneath the Ship
card.world: Lisbon, capital of the Kingdom of Portugal, in 1740
card.flavor: The final row of the harbor scene had come from the bakery wall
card.opening: As João set a harbor scene on the wall of a shipowner's house, he saw a basket of bread in the final row. He had to remove it before the evening guests arrived.
card.life: He grew up at his mother's vegetable stall and learned to set tiles. He married Teresa, raised Maria, and worked with Luís. After the earthquake, he took a rebuilding commission he had agreed to share with Luís so he could cover his family's rent. Luís lost his wages, and the way the two men worked together changed. In old age, João taught beginners instead of working on high walls.
card.turn: The final row of the harbor scene at the shipowner's house and the final row of the market scene at the bakery had been switched. Tiago had seen the basket design inside the wrapping, but João trusted only the label tied to the outside.
card.decision: João told the shipowner that the wrong scene had been installed, then removed the tiles before they had set and, with Tiago, swapped them back for the row showing ships at the bakery.
card.cost: The corner of one tile broke, so the shipowner received his guests that evening with a blank space on the wall. A few days later, João installed a replacement painted by Luís, but the shipowner hired another installer for his next wall.
card.after: Afterward, João listened to Tiago's checks first and opened the bundles to inspect the pictures inside. Years later, an earthquake damaged his home and workplace. To cover his family's rent, João took a rebuilding commission he had agreed to share with Luís, and Luís lost his wages.
card.presentEcho: When the urge to finish quickly makes you brush aside a quiet warning, you may have to redo something much bigger later.
card.secondLook: Tiago saw the basket inside the bundle first, but João ignored what he said. Even after Soares had the blank space repaired, he did not hire João for the next job.
card.unresolved: The shipowner accepted the repaired wall but gave his next commission to someone else.
card.readerQuestion: You've nearly finished setting a ship scene on the wall of a shipowner's house in Lisbon when a basket of bread appears in the final row. Your apprentice said earlier that something about the wrapping looked strange. What would you do first before the evening guests arrive?

signalMoments.notice: João compared the edge of the basket tile with the picture inside the crate and realized that the final row from the market table had been delivered. He asked Tiago to open the other bundle too.
signalMoments.speak: João told Soares that he had installed tiles meant for another house. He said they could fix it if they removed them now, but one might break.
signalMoments.connect: João asked Tiago to tell him again what he had seen earlier. After checking the basket design inside the wrapping, they went to see the other final row at the bakery.

identity.region: Lisbon, capital of the Kingdom of Portugal
identity.summary: He grew up at a vegetable stall, set tiles, and started a family. After the earthquake, he took work he had agreed to share with a friend so he could cover his family's rent, and in old age he taught younger workers instead of climbing high walls.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
João Marques · Male
1702–1777 · Age 75
Born and lived in Lisbon, capital of the Kingdom of Portugal
Work · Tile installer, later an instructor for beginners
Life · A boy who helped at his mother's vegetable stall learned to set tiles on walls. He married Teresa, raised their daughter Maria, and worked with his friend Luís. The 1755 earthquake damaged his home and workplace. To cover his family's rent, he took a rebuilding job he had agreed to share with Luís, depriving his friend of the wages. The two men later worked together again, but they no longer shared commissions as they once had. In old age, he stopped climbing high and taught younger workers.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · He could make even a first-time customer smile, but when he was in a hurry, he did not listen to the end of what others had to say. After the earthquake, he put covering his family's rent first and even took a job he had promised to share with his friend.
Liked · Eating fruit with Teresa in the shade of an alley after finishing work
Disliked · Customers pressing tiles before the adhesive had set
Skilled at · Joining many tiles into a single picture fitted to the size of a wall

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small vegetable scale his mother used
People close to him · His wife Teresa, his daughter Maria, and his painter friend Luís
Life he wanted · To return to the family table in the evening, even after filling the walls of other people's homes
Worry · The day his aching knees would keep him from climbing high walls

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called João Marques. You were a man who set tiles on the walls of Lisbon. One day, an unexpected basket of bread appeared beneath his harbor scene. Let me tell you what happened that day.

On a clear day in 1740, the courtyard of the shipowner Soares was filled with blue ships. On every tile set into the wall, one sail joined the next, and from a distance the ships seemed to be entering Lisbon's harbor. João thought he only had to set the final row to finish. Soares was expecting guests that evening and had asked to see the wall before lunch.

His apprentice Tiago took a bundle of tiles from a wooden crate. “I think there's a basket painted on the inside.” João tapped the label tied to the outside with his fingertip. “It says it's the harbor scene. I can't stop working.” Tiago started to look again, but when he saw João applying the adhesive, he fell silent.

João set the first tile on the wall and tilted his head as he lined up the next. Something round appeared beneath the ship. Thinking it might be a wine barrel, he looked closer and saw a basket filled with bread. The leg of a table continued beside it. He stepped back. It looked as if someone had laid out lunch before the ships had even reached the harbor.

“Looks like the ships brought bread,” Tiago said, holding back a laugh. João tried to laugh too, but Soares came in, his footsteps sounding in the courtyard. “Why is there a table beneath my ship?” João looked at the tiles he had just set. He could still remove them now, but they might break. If he left them in place, the wall would be finished by evening. But it would not be the picture Soares had ordered.

signalMoments.notice: João compared the edge of the tile painted with the basket to the picture inside the crate. He realized that the final row from the market table had come here and asked Tiago to open the other bundle too.
signalMoments.speak: João told Soares, “I installed tiles meant for another house.” He added, “If I remove them now, I can fix it, but one of them may break.” Soares looked up at the wall without smiling.
signalMoments.connect: João said to Tiago, “Tell me again what you saw.” When Tiago pointed to the basket design inside the wrapping, the two went together to check the other final row at the bakery.

episode.afterSignal:
João explained everything to Soares without trying to hide it. Tiles of the same size had also been delivered to the home of Marta, the baker, and it seemed the bundles containing the final rows had been switched. Soares told him to fix it before the guests saw. “We can talk about bread at the table. It does not need to be on the wall too.” João could not tell whether it was a joke mixed with anger.

Tiago and João ran through the alley to Marta's bakery. Marta opened her crate with flour-covered hands. Inside were tiles painted with waves and the lower part of a ship. “Then a ship will sail under my table,” Marta said with a laugh. When Tiago laid out the final rows from both houses on the floor, the basket joined the space beneath the table and the waves joined the space beneath the ship exactly.

Back in the courtyard, João slipped a thin tool under the edge of the adhesive before it had dried. As he slowly lifted the tiles one by one, Soares paced by the door and Tiago caught each tile. When the final one came loose, there was a small crack. One corner broke off and struck João's apron. Tiago asked, “Did I catch it too hard?” João replied, “No. I was rushing.”

The bread-basket tiles returned to Marta's wall, and the final row of the ship scene was set on Soares's wall. But the spot meant for the broken tile remained bare white plaster. The time for the guests to arrive was drawing near. João rejected the idea of filling the gap with just any picture. He told Soares that he would have a new tile made and bring it in a few days.

That evening, Soares's guests examined the completed harbor and stopped at the gap. “Has the ship not arrived here yet?” someone asked. Soares answered, “It stopped at the bakery on the way.” The guests laughed, but Soares did not call for João. Hearing them from outside, João picked up the crate with Tiago. Tiago said, “I told you from the start.” João replied, “Yes. I should have listened to you and opened the crate.” The two ate dinner late that evening.

A few days later, João returned with a single tile Luís had repainted. This time, Tiago opened the crate first and checked that the line of the waves connected to the tile beside it. Once the gap was filled, Soares paid the price, but he hired another installer for his next wall. Marta handed the two of them some bread and invited them to come see her picture of a market table. Only after taking the bread did João say that the basket they had put on the wall last time had looked quite appetizing.

After that, João still returned to the table he shared with Teresa and Maria and continued filling walls with his friend Luís. Years later, a great earthquake struck Lisbon, damaging his home and workplace. Desperate to cover his family's rent, João took a rebuilding job he had agreed to share with Luís, and Luís lost those wages. The two men later worked together again, but they never shared commissions as they once had. What I have told you today was one afternoon in that long life, when bread appeared beneath a ship and threw an alley into an uproar.

finalMoment.place: Lisbon, Kingdom of Portugal
finalMoment.scene:
It is an evening in late summer, 1777, at a small house in a Lisbon alley. I have been lying inside with a fever for several days, but today I have come out to sit by the open doorway. My wife, Teresa, props up a low stool for me. I hear the voice of a fruit seller in the street. “They have peaches too,” Teresa says. Remembering my mother's old stall, I laugh and say, “Tell them to bring only the sweet ones.” My throat is dry after I speak.

My daughter Maria, who works at another workshop, comes out of the house holding a cup of water. She sees my hand trembling and steadies the cup for me. My throat burns when I swallow a sip. “Father, let's go inside now.” I say I want to look at the alley a little longer. Teresa places a hand on my back, and Maria opens the door wider to let in the breeze.

My body suddenly grows hot, while my fingertips turn cold. I try to sit upright on the stool, but my knees will not hold. Teresa catches my arm to keep me from falling. “Go call someone,” Teresa tells Maria. I hear Maria knocking on a neighbor's door nearby. I open my mouth, trying to draw a deep breath. My chest moves only a little.

Teresa wipes my forehead and calls my name. I move my tongue to answer, but no sound comes out. Outside the door, Maria returns and calls to someone, “Over here.” Bracing myself on Teresa's hand, I try to rise. My palm slips, and my breaths grow shorter. Looking at Teresa's face, I try to draw in air again, but none comes.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1777, João died at the doorway of his alley house in Lisbon after several days of fever and difficulty breathing. The exact name of his illness has not been passed down. Teresa held João until a neighbor arrived. Maria moved her father into the room, then closed the door. When Luís heard the news, he remembered the rebuilding job they had agreed to share, but he did not pretend that the wages he had lost that day had never been taken from him. The record of this imagined past life states that João's life—spent striving to secure a room his family could return to while leaving his friend to bear the cost—ended in that alley.
finalMoment.artAlt: An evening viewed from inside the open doorway of a Lisbon alley house in late summer, 1777. Weakened by fever, 75-year-old João sits on a low stool, his hand trembling as he holds a cup of water and lifts his head toward the alley

card.name: Malia Kealoha
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Malia Kealoha of Honolulu. You grew up in Lahaina, raised a family, and worked for many years at a newspaper print shop. There was also a time when you closed the neighborhood gathering and grew distant from a friend, and in your later years, you listened to your granddaughter read aloud.
card.title: One Line Beside the Obituary
card.world: Honolulu, capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom, 1884
card.flavor: A missing family member's voice found its way into a blank space in the newspaper
card.opening: While proofreading her neighbor Aki's obituary, Malia saw that it did not name Hana, the daughter who had cared for him for years.
card.life: She learned to mend fishing nets and read in Lahaina. She married Kanoa, raised Pua, and moved to Honolulu, where she began folding paper. After losing her husband, she learned proofreading. She used to read newspapers with her neighbors, but after the overthrow of the monarchy led to frequent arguments, she ended the gatherings at her home. In old age, failing eyesight forced her to leave her work.
card.turn: Aki's son Mika said he would not include his sister Hana in the obituary because of an old dispute over the family home. Malia could not change the words of the person who had paid for the notice however she pleased.
card.decision: Malia asked Hana directly whether she wanted to publish a memorial of her own. She asked the owner, Ben, to print one sentence Hana had written separately from the original obituary.
card.cost: Malia paid the fee for the short memorial out of her own wages. She put off buying the bookbinding thread she had planned to get for her daughter Pua until the following week, and even after the words appeared in print, Mika and Hana did not make peace right away.
card.after: Even after Pua started doing bookbinding work elsewhere, Malia continued working at the print shop. After the overthrow of the monarchy, she ended the neighborhood reading gatherings at her home because people kept arguing over the newspapers, and she and Hana grew distant for several months. The two began visiting each other again, but their hurt feelings remained. As her eyesight worsened, she reduced her work.
card.presentEcho: If you notice that someone has been left out, you can begin by asking that person what they want.
card.secondLook: To Hana, the short piece was not a declaration of reconciliation but a record of the time she had spent beside her father. Yet years later, when Malia ended the reading gatherings, Hana felt she had been pushed away. Ben also remembered that the newspaper was printed a little late because they added another piece beside the original obituary.
card.unresolved: Mika did not like the separate memorial, and the siblings' long dispute did not end that day.
card.readerQuestion: You see an obituary for a neighbor that will appear in the newspaper, but it leaves out the daughter who cared for her father every night. The son who paid for it says to leave it as it is. What would you do first before printing begins?

signalMoments.notice: Malia placed the manuscript of Aki's obituary beside the proof and confirmed that a name was missing. She realized it was not an error—the space had been left unwritten from the beginning.
signalMoments.speak: Malia followed Mika before he left the alley and asked whether he meant to publish the obituary without Hana's name. Mika brought up the dispute over their father's house and said he would not change it.
signalMoments.connect: Malia knocked on Hana's door and said she would not secretly add her name to the obituary, then asked whether Hana had anything she wanted to write herself. Hana did not answer for a while.

identity.region: Honolulu, capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom

There was also a time when she closed the neighborhood reading gathering and grew distant from her friend Hana. In old age, she read with her granddaughter.

profilePages.body:
Malia Kealoha · Female
1844~1911 · Age 67
Born in Lahaina, Hawaiian Kingdom; lived in Honolulu
Work · Folding newspaper sheets and proofreading
Life · As a child, she learned to mend fishing nets and read. She married Kanoa, raised their daughter Pua, then moved to Honolulu and worked at a print shop. After her husband's death, she continued working and read newspapers with her neighbors. When arguments at the gatherings became frequent after the overthrow of the monarchy, Malia ended them. Her friend Hana also stopped coming to the house for a while. After her eyesight worsened in old age, she listened to her granddaughter read aloud.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She observed quietly, but when a question truly needed asking, she sought out the person concerned. When conflicts dragged on, she sometimes closed her door and read alone.
Liked · Taking turns with Pua to read one newspaper page at a time in the evening
Disliked · Assuming what someone wanted without asking their name or speaking to them
Good at · Finding wrong letters in small type

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured · A fishing-net needle brought from Lahaina
Those close to her · Her husband Kanoa, her daughter Pua, her neighbor Hana, and Ben, the print-shop owner
Life she wanted · A household where time spent reading paper was both work and rest
Worries · The day her vision would blur too much to catch a letter, and the day she could not do enough to help Pua after she was left on her own

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Malia Kealoha. You were someone who examined newspaper type in Honolulu, in the Hawaiian Kingdom. One day, an obituary missing one person's name was placed before her. Let me tell you what happened then.

Late one afternoon in 1884, wind came through the print-shop window and stirred the corners of the paper. With an ink-stained fingertip, Malia followed a line on the proof. “Aki, aged seventy-one. Announced by his son Mika.” Until yesterday, a light had shone in the window of Aki's house. Today, the man who had owned that house had become a single line in the newspaper.

Malia searched for the next line. His daughter Hana's name was not there. During the years Aki was ill, Hana had heated his evening water and kept the lamp burning at night. Ben, the print-shop owner, spoke as he sorted the wooden type. “Mika brought it in himself and paid for it. We have to lock the form soon.”

Malia read the proof again. No type had been dropped. Hana had been absent from the original manuscript from the beginning. Malia could not secretly add a name to the words of the person who had paid. But if she simply let it pass, Hana would be absent from the page even on the day her father left the world. A small bell rang outside, and printing time drew near.

signalMoments.notice: Malia spread the manuscript and proof side by side near the window. Hana's name was missing from both pages. It was not an accident in which someone had dropped a letter, but a space someone had chosen not to write.
signalMoments.speak: Malia heard that Mika, who had submitted the obituary, had not yet left the alley, so she went after him. “Hana's name isn't there. Do you want it printed as it is?” He brought up the dispute over their father's house and said he would not change it.
signalMoments.connect: Malia first knocked on Hana's door. “I don't intend to slip your name in without telling you. I want to ask whether there is something you'd like to write.” Hana said nothing for a while.

episode.afterSignal:
Malia had to listen to both Mika and Hana. Mika had recently quarreled bitterly with his sister over who would keep their father's house. “It's the notice I paid for. Don't change it,” he said. Malia answered, “I'll leave your words as they are.” It was not for Malia to hear only one side of their quarrel and alter the form.

A dry lampwick lay in Hana's house. Hana said, “I don't intend to go begging them to include my name.” Malia was turning to leave when Hana asked, “Could another piece be printed beside it?” Malia said she would ask Ben whether there was a small separate space. Slipping her own name into the obituary and remembering her father in her own words were different things.

Hana sat in a chair, picked up a pencil, and set it down again. “Father was never good at saying he was sorry.” Footsteps passed outside the window. “When I came home at night, he left one lamp burning by the window. Even before he became ill.” Hana wrote this on the paper: “I remember the lamp you kept burning for me when I came home late. Your daughter, Hana.” Malia read the words back to her and asked whether she wanted them printed exactly as written, including her name. Hana nodded.

When Malia returned to the print shop, Ben had his hand on the screw of the typesetting form. “We have to close it now.” When Malia showed him the separate memorial, Ben pointed to a small blank space at the bottom of the page. “It'll fit here. But it isn't free.” Malia opened the small pouch at her waist. It held part of the wages she would take home that week. It was also the money she had promised to spend on new bookbinding thread for Pua. Malia handed the money to Ben and asked him not to touch the original obituary.

While setting the type, Ben placed the final letter of “lamp” backward. Just before the form was locked, Malia spotted the letter and corrected it. Ink spread across her hand, but she did not try to make someone else's sentence sound finer. The form was pressed, and the paper came out. At the top was the obituary Mika had submitted; below it was a separate piece Hana had written. Appearing on the same page did not mean the two siblings now shared the same feelings.

The next day, Hana folded the newspaper and placed it on her father's empty chair. Mika saw Malia and asked, “Was that really necessary?” Malia only said, “Hana wrote it herself.” Mika turned away without another word. Malia had to explain to Pua that she would buy the new thread the following week. Pua was disappointed for a moment, but she handed Malia a cloth to wipe the ink from her fingers.

Malia continued folding paper and finding incorrect letters. Pua moved to another workplace and set up a home of her own. After the monarchy was overthrown in 1893, neighbors often argued over the newspapers, so Malia ended the reading gatherings she had held at home. She regained time to read quietly, but she also went several months without seeing Hana. Even after the two friends began visiting again, they did not cover over the hurt from that time. That day's obituary was only one day in a long life.

finalMoment.place: Honolulu, U.S. Territory of Hawaii
finalMoment.scene:
One evening in 1911, my fifteen-year-old granddaughter sits beside me in our Honolulu home, reading the newspaper aloud. I am sixty-seven, and it has been a long time since I could see the letters clearly, line by line. My daughter Pua has placed a chair beside the open door and is listening. My granddaughter stops as she reads the name of a ship that has entered the harbor. “Will you read it again?” I ask, and the child traces the line with her finger.

I take the newspaper from her and try to fold it. Just then, a sharp pain suddenly strikes one side of my head. This is different from the letters that have been blurry for years. The paper falls below my knees. I reach out with my right hand to pick it up, but my arm will not move. “Pua.” My voice sounds strange and slurred as I call my daughter's name. Pua rises from her chair and grips my shoulders.

Pua looks into my eyes. “Mother, can you hear me?” I try to nod, but my body leans to one side. Pua supports me and tells my granddaughter to call a neighbor. My granddaughter puts down the newspaper and runs to the door. I want to reassure the child. I move my lips, but no words come out. The pain in my head makes it hard even to keep my eyes open.

The evening breeze comes through the open door. Outside, I hear my granddaughter calling for a neighbor. Pua lays my motionless hand on top of hers. “I'm here.” With my left hand, I grasp my daughter's sleeve. I try to see more of Pua's face, but my sight grows dark. Only the sound of my daughter calling my name again remains close.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1911, Malia lost consciousness after suddenly suffering severe head pain and paralysis in one arm at her Honolulu home. Her life ended that night while Pua stayed beside her. The exact medical cause was never determined. Pua remembered that her mother had last grasped her sleeve with her left hand. Even after bringing back a neighbor, her granddaughter could not reopen the newspaper she had left unfinished. When Hana heard the news, she remembered both the day Malia printed the memorial Hana had written herself and the time the door to the reading gathering was closed. The record of this past life preserves both the evenings when Malia shared words with her family and the months when she was distant from her friend.
finalMoment.artAlt: An evening in a Honolulu home in 1911: sixty-seven-year-old Malia sits in a chair, suddenly clutching her head and reaching her right hand toward a newspaper. Her daughter Pua and granddaughter sit apart from her in the room.

card.name: Ramana
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Ramana of Vijayanagara. You grew up working the riverside fields and repaired the capital's canals. Even while caring for his family, there were times when he put his own canal work ahead of his son Navin's ferry work, and after his wrists grew stiff, he taught younger workers the trade.
card.title: The Day Water Reached the First Field
card.world: The capital of the Vijayanagara Empire in 1442
card.flavor: While he protected the waterway in front of the house, his daughter's first seedlings were swept away
card.opening: On the morning after the rain stopped, Ramana looked from the cracked stone canal and the water leaking toward the houses to the outlet leading into his daughter Gauri's small field.
card.life: He helped work the fields in a riverside village, then learned to shape stone. He married Tara, raised Gauri and Navin, and repaired the capital's canals with Basu. He traveled back and forth to his hometown to care for his mother. During Tara's long illness, he kept working and left Navin to care for her for several days. After his wrists grew stiff, he taught others how to measure distances.
card.turn: If the stone bracing the wall shifted, water would flow toward the steps of the houses below. The outlet that could reduce the water pressure led into the vegetable patch Gauri had planted by herself for the first time.
card.decision: Ramana told Tara and Basu where he would divert the water, then opened the stone barrier at the lower outlet. Basu braced the wall while Ramana watched the flow.
card.cost: The houses stayed dry, but Gauri's seedlings were swept away. Gauri was angry that he had made the decision without even asking about her field, and Ramana could only help her replant the surviving seedlings.
card.after: Several years later, Gauri built a waterway for a new field with her father and expanded her plot. Navin learned to work on a ferry. When Tara suffered a long illness, Ramana continued his canal work and left Navin to care for her, costing Navin several days of ferry income. Ramana took on less work after Tara recovered, but that money could not be recovered.
card.presentEcho: Even when you must choose quickly, you can still look closely at who will lose what because of your decision.
card.secondLook: Tara remembered the moment the water rose toward the steps in front of the house, and Gauri long remembered the moment her father opened the outlet into her first field without permission. Years later, Navin also never forgot the days he had to stop working his boat to care for his mother.
card.unresolved: Gauri saved a few seedlings that day, but she did not forgive her father right away.
card.readerQuestion: After a night of rain, a stone canal has cracked. Water is leaking toward the steps of the houses, but if you open the lower outlet, the first field your daughter ever planted will be flooded. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Ramana stood a wooden measuring stick beneath the crack to mark the water level. In only a moment, the water rose by one finger joint. The lower outlet ended at Gauri's first field.
signalMoments.speak: Ramana asked Basu again how long the bracing stone would hold. When Basu said he could keep the wall standing if they opened the outlet now, Ramana told him that the water would flow into his daughter's field.
signalMoments.connect: Ramana told Tara, who was in the house, that they had to open the outlet. When Tara asked whether he knew they had no time to call Gauri and that these were her first seedlings, Ramana said he did and returned to the canal.

setting.polity: Sangama dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire

identity.region: Capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, Tungabhadra River basin
identity.summary: He grew up in the riverside fields and repaired the capital's canals. He raised two children with Tara. When Tara was ill, he left Navin to care for her so that he could continue his canal work, reducing his son's ferry income. After his wrists grew stiff, he taught younger workers the trade.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Ramana · Male
1404–1476 · Age 72
Born in the Tungabhadra River basin of the Vijayanagara Empire; lived near the capital
Work · Stonemason who repaired canals and reservoirs
Life · He grew up watching the waterways in his family's fields and learned to shape stone. He married Tara, raised Gauri and Navin, and repaired canals with Basu. He traveled back and forth to his hometown to care for his mother. During the year Tara was ill, he kept working and left Navin to care for her, reducing his son's ferry income. After his wrists grew stiff, he stopped lifting heavy stones and taught younger workers while measuring distances instead.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · He examined things slowly when starting a job, but when others asked for help, his body moved before he thought. At times, he also used his family's time as he saw fit.

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured possession · The wooden measuring stick he had used since his apprenticeship
People close to him · His wife Tara, daughter Gauri, son Navin, and friend Basu

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Ramana. You were a stonemason who tended small waterways in the capital of Vijayanagara, near the Tungabhadra River. Of all the canals he repaired, let me tell you about one day connected to his daughter's first field.

In 1442, when the rain that had fallen all night finally stopped, Ramana ran his palm over the wet stone. A crack the size of a fingernail had opened in a joint of the stone canal. Water escaping through it flowed toward the steps of the houses below. Basu brought a sack of earth and pressed it against the gap, but the sack slowly shifted.

“What if we brace it with one more stone?” Ramana asked. Basu shook his head. “There's too much water backed up above us. We have to open a path for it to drain downhill.” Beside the canal was a low outlet. Ramana knew where it ended: in the small field where his daughter Gauri had planted her first seedlings and carried water every morning.

Gauri had gone to the riverbank to wash the water jars. If they waited for her to return, the water might reach the steps of the houses. But if they opened the outlet, the vegetables Gauri had planted one by one would certainly be knocked down. Ramana looked back and forth between the stone barrier, the houses, and the wet ground between them.

signalMoments.notice: Ramana stood a wooden measuring stick beneath the crack to mark the water level. In only a moment, the water rose by one finger joint on the stick. The path through the lower outlet was clear, and Gauri's first field lay at its end.
signalMoments.speak: Ramana asked Basu again how long the bracing stone would hold. Pointing to the stone shifting beneath his hand, Basu said, “If we open it now, we can keep the wall standing.” Ramana said aloud that the water would flow into his daughter's field.
signalMoments.connect: Ramana ran to the house where Tara was and told her they had to open the outlet leading into the field. Tara said Gauri was at the riverbank and there was no time to call her. “You know those are her first seedlings, don't you?” Ramana said he did and returned to the canal.

episode.afterSignal:
In front of Tara and Basu, Ramana said that he would open the lower outlet. “I'll explain when Gauri comes back.” Without another answer, Tara cleared the mud from the house steps. Basu handed his friend a small hammer and pushed a new stone into the cracked wall.

At first, the stone barrier did not move. When Ramana widened the gap with the end of his stick, the rainwater forced its way through the narrow opening. Ankle-deep, the water raced along a shallow furrow. Basu's sack of earth stopped shifting. The water did not reach the steps in front of the houses.

“It's going into the field,” Tara said. Ramana had already seen it. The small earthen ridge split apart, and the seedlings Gauri had planted in neat rows fell flat. One was torn out by the roots and caught beside a stone. Ramana reached out to close the outlet again, then stopped. The water in the upper canal was still high. Closing it now might dislodge the wall they had just braced.

Gauri returned carrying an empty water jar. At the edge of the field, the jar dropped from her hand. “I planted those.” For a moment after she spoke, only raindrops struck the stones. Ramana started to say that the houses had not gotten wet, then closed his mouth. Gauri pointed at the rows submerged in mud. “Couldn't you have said even one word to me?”

“You were at the riverbank. If we'd waited, the water would have gone into those houses,” Ramana said. Gauri answered, “I can see that too.” Then she added, “But this is my field.” Tara did not step between them. Basu could not let go of the stone he was holding. Saying that it had to be done could not restore the mornings Gauri had lost.

Only after the water level in the canal dropped did Ramana gradually close the outlet. Gauri picked up a seedling caught in the mud. When Ramana found another and held it out to her, she took it but did not thank him. Without speaking, they moved the five surviving seedlings to higher ground. They could not repair the collapsed earthen ridge that day.

That evening, Ramana told Tara that next time, he would decide the course of the new field's waterway with Gauri first. Tara replied, “She won't want to listen to you today.” Gauri left the wet water jar outside the door and went into her room. The house remained dry, but only root marks were left in the field.

Several years later, Gauri and her father measured the waterway of a new field together. Navin began working on a boat at the ferry. In 1460, when Tara suffered a long illness, Ramana continued the canal work he had already accepted and asked Navin to stay by his mother's side. Navin could not take the boat out for several days and lost the money he would have earned. Tara recovered, but the work her son had missed did not return. In Ramana's long life, the day of the first field was one of the days when he used his family's time according to his own judgment.

finalMoment.place: Near the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire
finalMoment.scene:
It is a hot day in 1476, in the shaded room of a house near the capital. My stomach has hurt for three days, and I cannot rise from the mat spread on the floor. My wife, Tara, brings a small cup of water. My longtime friend Basu stands beside the open door and asks Tara whom he should go find today. I am thirsty, but when Tara tries to wipe my face, I hold out my hand for the cloth. “I can do that much myself.”

My hand trembles as I press the cloth to my forehead. When Tara raises the cup to my lips, I drink only a little. It feels as if the water I swallowed will come right back up, so I turn my head. “You need to drink more,” Tara says. “Just a moment.” My stomach twists again. Basu leaves to ask a neighbor for help, and the sound of his footsteps fades across the courtyard.

I try to push myself upright, but there is no strength in my arms. The wet cloth falls from my hand. When Tara supports my shoulders, I do not push her away this time. “Did you tell Gauri?” Even after I ask, I do not know why I am looking for my daughter now. “She'll come when she returns from the field. Navin will come back from the river too.” Tara's words are clear, but to my ears they seem to come from some distance away.

Tara raises the cup again. I open my mouth, but I cannot swallow the water. My throat is dry, and my breaths grow short. “Ramana, can you hear me?” Trying to answer, I touch Tara's wrist. The moment my fingertips reach her, she sets down the cup. Outside the door, I hear Basu calling someone. I try to keep my eyes open to look at Tara, but my eyelids keep falling.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1476, after several days of stomach pain and being unable to swallow even water, Ramana died beside Tara in their house near the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire. The exact name of his illness is unknown. Tara held her husband's hand until Basu returned with a neighbor. Navin came back after finishing his ferry work and was told that his father had already passed away. Gauri came to her parents' house the next day. The chronicle of this past life records the end of Ramana's life along with the ordinary days he spent with his family, Gauri's first field, and the ferry work Navin lost.
finalMoment.artAlt: A close, downward view on a daytime scene in a shaded room of a house near the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire in 1476. Ramana, age 72 and weakened after three days of stomach pain, presses a wet cloth to his own forehead and reaches toward a cup of water. His wife, Tara, sits apart from him

card.decision: Nafisa asked Zuhura directly where she wanted to be. When Zuhura said she would keep the beat on a hand drum at the edge, Nafisa put Salma in the center and changed the order of the circle.

card.presentEcho: When you need to change something you do together, you can first ask the other person which place they want.
card.secondLook: For Salma, the laughter that day was embarrassing, but it also became the memory of enduring her first performance to the end. Zuhura spared her leg, yet still regretted the place she lost. Mariam was left with both the memory of helping her sister for two months and the wages she never received.
card.unresolved: After the performance, Zuhura said her foot did not hurt any more than before, but told Nafisa that watching someone else dance inside the circle had left her aching inside.
card.readerQuestion: The neighborhood dance gathering is about to begin. The friend who is supposed to stand in the center of the circle is limping, and the person who could replace her still often loses the beat. What would you do first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were called Nafisa. You sold fruit in Zanzibar Town and danced with the women of your neighborhood. Let me tell you about the day the circle Nafisa led fell exactly one beat behind.

One evening in 1905, hand drums rang through a courtyard at the end of a narrow alley. Spectators sat on a stone bench beside the wall, and Nafisa retied the cloth around her waist. The group had prepared two songs. In the first, six dancers would move in a circle, and in the second, the circle would split into two lines. Salma kept rubbing her feet, saying it was her first time performing in the courtyard.

Zuhura always held the center of the circle. Whenever Nafisa missed a step, Zuhura would gesture to show her the next direction. But today, Zuhura's shoulders flinched every time she stepped on her left foot. Mariam quietly told Nafisa that Zuhura had twisted her ankle while carrying a water jar that morning. Zuhura smiled and said, “I'm fine. Just tie your cloth properly.”

The owner of the courtyard opened the door and announced that the next group would arrive soon. If they changed places now, Salma would have to move into the center. If they left things as they were, Zuhura would have to turn on her injured foot for the whole song. Nafisa looked back and forth between the hand holding the drum and Zuhura's foot.

signalMoments.notice: Nafisa saw Zuhura standing with only the toes of one foot touching the ground. She kept time with her right foot, but her left remained still behind the folds of her cloth. At the center, she would have to turn on that very foot three times.
signalMoments.speak: Nafisa went to Zuhura and asked, “Can you manage the turns in the center? If you can't, where would you like to join us?” Zuhura started to say she was fine, then looked down at her left foot.
signalMoments.connect: Nafisa called Salma over and practiced the first song's three steps with her. Salma was late on the second step, but tried again. Nafisa warned her in advance that she might switch places with Zuhura.

episode.afterSignal:
“If you take the center, you'll have to keep moving until the end,” Nafisa told Zuhura. “I don't mean you should drop out. Tell me where you want to be.” Zuhura briefly lifted her injured foot. Pointing to the small drum beside the wall, she said, “I'll sit there and keep the beat. But make sure we get to the second song.” Nafisa nodded.

Nafisa placed Salma in the center of the circle. Mariam tapped her sister's shoulder and whispered, “You fell twice on your first day, too.” “Once,” Nafisa shot back, and Mariam held up two fingers. Salma laughed, and at that very moment, Zuhura's drum sounded.

The first three steps matched. On the fourth, Salma turned too early, and on the fifth, she stopped because she thought Nafisa had stopped. The circle of six warped to one side. Laughter burst from the stone bench. Nafisa raised her palm and widened the circle a little. Still seated, Zuhura struck the drum once more, louder this time. Salma heard it and moved her feet again.

When it was time to split into two lines, the courtyard owner waved his hand. The next group was waiting in the alley. “I'm afraid you'll have to stop here.” He looked apologetic, but he could not keep the door open any longer. Nafisa did not get to begin the second song they had practiced. Even as the six dancers bowed, Salma's face burned, and Zuhura remained seated with her hand resting on the drum.

Once they were in the alley, Salma said, “I ruined the circle.” Nafisa replied, “Were you dancing alone? We all fell behind together.” But her words could not erase the audience's laughter. Zuhura adjusted her cloth and looked at Nafisa. “My foot doesn't hurt any more than before. Still, watching someone else dance inside the circle hurt.” Nafisa said, “I could see your place was empty, too.” Neither of them mentioned the next performance right away.

The next day, Nafisa sorted out the soft spots on the mangoes at her fruit stall. When Salma came and asked why she had stopped on the fifth step, Nafisa suggested they practice in the empty path between the baskets. Salma made the turn correctly on the second try. Zuhura sat across from them, resting her foot as she watched. The second song they had failed to perform still remained.

Nafisa continued selling fruit afterward. During the two months she was ill in 1913, her older sister Mariam managed the stall. Nafisa delayed paying her sister's wages because she had to cover the cost of medicine and the stall fee. During that time, Mariam lost several sewing jobs. Even when Nafisa later offered her the money, Mariam refused it and never managed her sister's stall again. When Salma chose textile work, Nafisa did not stand in her way. Even after losing her sister, she continued going to the dance group. What I have told you today is the story of one evening in that long life, when she let an injured friend choose her place and led an unsteady circle to the end.

finalMoment.place: Zanzibar Town in the Sultanate of Zanzibar under British protection
finalMoment.scene:
One night in 1942, I am alone in a small house in Zanzibar Town. I have been coughing for several days, and today I could not even go to the market. My niece Salma said she would stop by this evening, but I told her I could drink water by myself. The bowl of water I set out during the day is across the room. I am thirsty, but when I raise myself, my breath fails first.

I brace myself against the wall and take a few steps toward the bowl. When I swallow a sip, a cough bursts out and I spit the water back up. Even when I open my chest and breathe in, not enough air enters. I think I might breathe the outside air if I open the door, so I grasp the handle. As I tighten my fingers around it, I hear footsteps in the alley. “Salma?” I try to call, but only the beginning of her name comes out.

Outside the door, Salma says, “Auntie, it's me.” I try to lift the bar, but sink to my knees. My palm strikes the wooden door. Salma pushes it open and comes in, supporting my shoulders. “I'll bring you water.” I shake my head. I need breath more urgently than water. Salma leaves the door wide open and supports my back while I try to listen to the voices outside. Even my strength to cough is fading.

Salma calls my name again. I open my mouth to answer. One short breath comes in, then goes out for a long time. As I wait for the next breath, I grip Salma's arm, but my fingers loosen. Beyond the open door, the small lights in the alley blur.
finalMoment.afterword: That night, Nafisa died at the open doorway, leaning against her niece Salma's arm. The exact illness is unknown. For a long time, Salma remembered how her aunt had insisted on living alone even though she had been coughing for days. When Zuhura heard the news later, she remembered the times when Nafisa quietly folded cloth with her older sister Mariam. Nafisa sometimes helped people match their steps, and sometimes delayed her sister's wages to protect her own household. And so Nafisa's life came to an end. This record of a past life preserves both the relationships shaped by those choices and the final night when Salma opened the door.
finalMoment.artAlt: Zanzibar Town at night in 1942: 75-year-old Nafisa, short of breath and on her knees, grips the door bar while her niece Salma calls to her from beyond the opening

card.home: a small Buddhist monastery on the western Tibetan Plateau
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Tenzin Dorje, a monk who copied scriptures and taught novices at a small Buddhist monastery on the western Tibetan Plateau. He entered the monastery as a child and copied scriptures. Because he valued accuracy, he scolded a young monk for asking questions, but later taught him to leave blank spaces for passages he did not understand.
card.title: A Blank Line in the Scripture
card.role: a monk who copied scriptures and taught novices
card.world: Late 11th century · a small Buddhist monastery on the western Tibetan Plateau
card.flavor: A choice over a single line of translation at a highland monastery
card.opening: Before snow fell on the plateau, Tenzin discovered that the same line was written differently in two scriptures.
card.life: He entered the monastery as a child and copied scriptures. Because he valued accuracy, he scolded a young monk for asking questions, but later taught him to leave blank spaces for passages he did not understand. When Pema asked what a passage meant, Tenzin scolded him for not studying enough, causing him to withdraw from the public reading. For a while, Pema wrote down his questions but did not submit them.
card.turn: The pressure to finish the book clashed with his responsibility to admit what he did not know.
card.decision: Tenzin did not force himself to choose one version of the passage. Instead, he recorded the difference between the texts.
card.cost: When Pema asked what a passage meant, Tenzin scolded him for not studying enough, causing him to withdraw from the public reading. For a while, Pema wrote down his questions but did not submit them.
card.after: The answer remained unsettled, but Pema began asking questions again.
card.presentEcho: Marking what is unknown is also an accurate record passed on to the next person.
card.secondLook: Even as Tenzin taught accuracy, for a time he made those who asked questions feel intimidated.
card.unresolved: It is unknown which wording later generations adopted as the main text.
card.readerQuestion: The same line differs between two scriptures. What would you do first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Tenzin Dorje, a monk who copied scriptures at a small monastery in western Tibet.

One manuscript said, “Hold fast to the mind,” while another said, “Let go of the mind.” The young monk Pema asked which was correct.

Tenzin remembered how he had once scolded Pema for asking a question. If he chose one version and wrote it down now, the book would be complete, but the evidence would be weak.

signalMoments.notice: Tenzin noticed that a single stroke might have worn away from a character where the old paper was frayed.
signalMoments.speak: “I still do not know which character is correct. Let us write down together that we do not know.” Tenzin said this in front of Pema.
signalMoments.connect: Tenzin asked Pema and Dolma which wording they remembered seeing at other monasteries, then recorded each memory separately in the margin.

episode.afterSignal:
Tenzin left a space blank in the main text and wrote the sentences from both versions side by side in the margin.

For the first time, Pema said during a public reading, “This part is still being verified.”

A few years later, a manuscript arrived from another monastery, but it did not settle on a single answer. Tenzin stopped seeing blank spaces as failures.

memories.label: Dolma's assessment
memories.detail: “He waited too long to ask about the villagers' memories instead of relying on the words in books.”

memories.label: Favorite time
memories.detail: The empty copying room before dawn prayers

memories.label: History and fiction
memories.detail: Buddhist translation and transmission activities in 11th-century Tibet form the historical background, while the specific lives of the monastery and its people are fictional.

finalMoment.place: a small monastery on the western Tibetan Plateau
finalMoment.scene:
In the winter of 1109, after crossing a snow-covered mountain pass, Tenzin suffered from fever and coughing in the monastery's copying room. Pema, the monk he had taught since childhood, moved the brazier closer. Tenzin pointed to a blank space in the scripture he had left unfinished.

“Leave it as it is. Let someone who has verified it fill it in,” Tenzin said briefly. A harsh sound came from his chest whenever he breathed in. Pema said that Dolma, the herbalist, was coming, but the snow had delayed her on the road.

By nightfall, Tenzin no longer had the strength to sit up. Pema supported his back, but his breathing grew slower and slower. He looked once at the blank line, then closed his eyes. No next breath came.

Pema never filled in the unverified passage, and he also recorded in the margin how Tenzin had once silenced questions. The era's Buddhist translation and manuscript-copying activities form the historical background, while the people and monastery are fictional.

card.name: Mariana de la Cruz
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Mariana de la Cruz of Binondo, Manila. You grew up by the river, learned to handle cargo and ropes aboard boats, and traveled the waterways with your family. Even after your daughter made a home for herself on land, you continued working on boats, then spent your later years in a small house by the river.
card.title: The Empty Place on the Boat
card.role: The person responsible for ropes and cargo on a riverside freight boat
card.world: Manila under Spanish rule in 1832
card.flavor: Her daughter's first day at work and a promise to load the boat fell on the same morning
card.opening: On the morning of Rosa's first day learning to sew from her aunt, the promised cargo was already piled in front of Mariana's freight boat.
card.life: Born in Binondo in 1790, she grew up moving between work along the river and the market alleys. She remained close to her childhood friend Isabel for many years, married Pedro, and raised their daughter Rosa. After her father died, she took charge of the family's small transport business. In 1840, she continued using a worn rope and caused two sacks of the merchant Benito's rice to be lost. She refunded the freight charge but could not repay the value of the rice. Even after Rosa established herself on land, Mariana divided her life between the boat and home. After Pedro died before her, she taught neighborhood children the river's routes.
card.turn: Rosa could not postpone her first day learning to sew from her aunt. Counting on Rosa's labor as well, Mariana had promised the warehouse owner that two people would load the cargo.
card.decision: Instead of holding her daughter back, Mariana paid Mateo, a worker from the neighboring boat, an extra day's wage to help load the cargo. Rosa began her first job on time.
card.cost: Mateo's wage came out of that day's freight earnings. Rosa left hurt that her mother had not believed her from the start, and Mariana could not quickly get used to the empty place.
card.after: Mother and daughter lived in separate homes and occasionally met by the river. Mariana repaired ropes with her friend Isabel, and later wore the first garment Rosa made.
card.presentEcho: When someone who has worked beside you chooses a different path, even the weight of the work left behind can change. Choosing not to block that path can still leave real costs and hurt feelings.
card.secondLook: Rosa said she was not leaving because she hated the boat, but because she wanted to learn to make clothes with her own hands. Even after hearing her daughter, Mariana initially asked whether she could not stay and work on the boat.
card.unresolved: That day's freight earnings were reduced by the amount paid to Mateo. Even several days later, Rosa said she was hurt that her mother had not believed her, and it took time for mother and daughter to reach a point where they asked about each other's work.
card.readerQuestion: Your daughter is leaving today to start a new job. But you accepted a large load of cargo for the boat because you thought she would help. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Mariana counted the three bundles in front of the warehouse again. Two had to leave that day, while one could be delayed, so she calculated whether the boat could depart with only one worker if she changed the order of the cargo.
signalMoments.speak: Mariana told Rosa that although she had heard her say she was leaving today, she had assumed on her own that Rosa could delay it by a day. Rosa asked why she had not asked her again.
signalMoments.connect: Mariana went to Mateo on the neighboring boat. Mateo said his own work would be delayed and asked for an extra day's wage, and Mariana heard him out on the price.

Mariana de la Cruz · Female

Life · She grew up by the river and learned her father's boat work. She made a home with Pedro and raised their daughter Rosa. Even after losing her father, she continued working on the boat. In 1840, she kept using an old rope and dropped two sacks of the merchant Benito's rice into the river. After Pedro died before her and she left the boat, she lived among her neighbors in a house by the river.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:

Liked · The smell of the river after the rain stopped, and looking at cloth in the market
Disliked · Putting wet cargo on top of dry cargo
Good at · Estimating the required rope length from the weight of a bundle

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured item · The short wooden ruler her father used
Those closest to her · Her husband Pedro, her daughter Rosa, and her childhood friend Isabel
The life she wanted · A life in which neither work by the river nor family dinners were interrupted
Worry · That there would not be enough money to repair the boat and the family would lose its livelihood

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Mariana de la Cruz, who worked on boats by the river in Binondo. One morning in 1832, her daughter Rosa was preparing to begin a new job on land, while cargo waited on Mariana's boat. Let me tell you about that morning, when the two of them faced the day with different plans in mind.

Rosa set a small bundle down on the threshold. Mariana brushed the rope dust from her hands and smiled. “You can go to your aunt's house after we finish loading, can't you?” Rosa did not smile. “Today is my first day learning to sew.”

“You said that started next week.” “I told you last week that it was today.” Instead of answering, Mariana looked toward the river. Three bundles of cargo lay in front of the warehouse. Expecting that she and Rosa would load them together, Mariana had promised the warehouse owner they would depart before the morning was over.

Rosa picked up her bundle. “I'm not going because I hate the boat. I want to learn beside Auntie how to make things with my own hands.” Mariana said, “You can use those hands to tie up cargo here too,” then fell silent. She was the one who had been proud of those hands the first time Rosa wound a rope as a child.

signalMoments.notice: Mariana counted the three bundles in front of the warehouse again. Two had to leave that day, while the final bundle could be delayed. For a moment, she calculated whether the boat could depart with only one worker if she changed the order of the cargo.
signalMoments.speak: Mariana stood before Rosa, who was holding her bundle. “When you told me you were going today, I assumed on my own that you could delay it by a day.” Rosa asked, “So you didn't even ask me again?”
signalMoments.connect: Mariana approached Mateo at the neighboring boat. Mateo said helping load someone else's cargo would delay his own work and asked for an extra day's wage. Mariana did not return empty-handed but first heard him out on the price.

episode.afterSignal:
Mariana pressed the rope marks on her palm. If she kept Rosa there and made her work for only half a day, she would not have to pay Mateo. But then Rosa would make her aunt wait on her very first day. Mariana told the warehouse owner she would collect the last bundle in the afternoon, then called Mateo over from the neighboring boat again.

“Just help me load two bundles. I'll pay the wage you asked for.” When Mateo asked in surprise, Mariana said, “Our boat is one person short today.” Rosa, standing behind her, adjusted her grip on the cord of her bundle when she heard those words. “Am I the one who's missing?” “No. I'm the one who wrote down that your place would still be here today.”

While Mateo carried the cargo, mother and daughter could neither help each other nor turn their backs on each other. Rosa placed the wooden ruler on the edge of the boat. “It belonged to Grandfather. I thought of taking it with me, but you should use it, Mother.” Mariana did not put it back in Rosa's hand. “You'll have tools of your own. I'll keep this one.”

Rosa watched the boat glide out over the river, then walked toward the alley. She looked back about twice, but Mariana was untying the boat's ropes. Mariana waved only after the boat had entered the waterway. By then, Rosa had already reached the corner of the alley.

Mateo's wage came out of the freight earnings received that day. When Mariana returned, she personally checked the one remaining bundle, and evening came late before she finished all the work she had promised. The empty boat felt strange and made her angry, yet she also wondered what Rosa had learned on her first day.

A few days later, Rosa came to the riverside. “Auntie corrected me three times because I was holding the needle wrong.” Mariana laughed, but Rosa did not immediately join her. “I'm still hurt that you didn't believe me when I said I was going.” Mariana put down the cargo and said, “Yes. I should have listened. How was your first day?” This time, Rosa gave her a long answer.

After that, Rosa learned to sew on land and lived in a different house. Mariana traveled the river for many years, repairing the boat's ropes with Isabel. After Pedro died before her and she left the boat, she grew old listening to the sound of the water by the river. The day Rosa left was not the whole of that long life, but it was the first day the place where they had worked together changed.
