memories.label: Longtime Work
memories.detail: Tying ropes around cargo so they would not come loose when wet, and watching the order in which boats came and went

memories.label: What She Enjoyed
memories.detail: Evenings spent looking at the colors of cloth in the market with her friend Isabel and feeling the river breeze on the way home

memories.label: What She Treasured
memories.detail: The short wooden ruler her father used to measure cargo

memories.label: What She Missed
memories.detail: The sound of the water she and Pedro used to hear together on the boat before he died

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Before you tie the rope, ask where the cargo is going.”

memories.label: Rosa's View
memories.detail: “Mother stayed on the boat, and I went to land. It took a long time for us to understand each other's work, but Mother wore the first garment I made.”

memories.label: Isabel's View
memories.detail: “On the river, she moved faster than anyone. But when she chose cloth at the market, she would stand in front of a single piece for ages.”

memories.label: Mateo's View
memories.detail: “She paid me properly that day. She didn't ask me to pretend to be her daughter so she could hide the empty place, either.”

memories.label: Benito's View
memories.detail: “If the rope was old, she should have told me first. I got the freight charge back, but she never repaid me for the soaked rice. I never entrusted her with cargo again.”

finalMoment.place: Binondo, Manila, the Philippines under the rule of the Spanish Empire
finalMoment.scene:
It is night in 1857, in the bedroom of my home in Binondo. I lie there with a fever that has not broken for three days. Isabel, my friend since childhood, sits beside me and wipes my forehead with a wet cloth. I push away the blanket because I am hot, but soon I begin to shiver and pull it back. “Try a sip of water,” Isabel says, lifting a cup.

“I'll hold it.” I prop myself up on one elbow. When I reach out, I see two cups. Isabel supports my hand from beneath. The water touches my lips, but before I can swallow even one sip, I begin to cough. I turn my head to the side and have to lie down again. When the wet cloth slips from my forehead, Isabel picks it up and folds it.

“Did you tell Rosa?” I ask. My daughter, now forty-four, is at her own home across the river. “I sent someone. I'll bring her in as soon as she comes,” Isabel replies. I try to say I will wait, but my throat is dry and only my lips move. Isabel sets down the cup and calls my name. The lamplight flickers inside the room, and cold sweat beads on my feverish face.

Isabel takes my hand. I answer by squeezing with my fingertips. A moment later, I try to squeeze again, but I cannot lift my arm. My breaths grow short, and every time I look at Isabel's face, I have to breathe several times. “Mariana, can you hear me?” I want to say I can. My mouth opens, but no sound comes out. Isabel's hand is still warm. I try to draw another breath, but my body does not follow.
finalMoment.afterword: Mariana de la Cruz died at the age of sixty-seven in her Binondo home in 1857 after suffering a fever for three days. The exact illness has not been passed down. Isabel remained beside her friend through the night and did not clear away the empty cup until morning. Her daughter Rosa, who arrived too late, regretted not coming to see her mother sooner. Rosa had been a daughter who chose her own path, and she also remembered that her mother had eventually accepted that path. Mariana once spent money to protect her daughter's first day, but she never managed to repay Benito for the rice. The record of her past life preserves those different choices alongside her final night, when Isabel remained by her side.
finalMoment.artAlt: At night in Binondo, Manila, in 1857, sixty-seven-year-old Mariana, suffering from a high fever for the third day, rises from a low bed in her home and reaches for a cup of water while her longtime friend Isabel helps her, holding the cup and a wet cloth

card.name: Yusuf
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yusuf of Samarkand. You learned pottery beside your father and ran a tile workshop with Bahram. You raised two children with Layla and made patterns for buildings, and after your friend left, you grew old while dividing the work between your apprentice and your daughter.
card.title: The Unmatched Tile
card.role: Workshop craftsman who fired decorative architectural tiles
card.world: Samarkand under the Timurid dynasty in 1432
card.flavor: A tile painted with one extra petal was discovered the day before delivery
card.opening: Yusuf found a tile painted with one extra petal among the ordered star patterns.
card.life: Born in Samarkand in 1392, he grew up beside his father's pottery kiln. He opened a small tile workshop with Bahram and supported Layla and their two children. After his friend left for another city, he kept the workshop going with his apprentice, Najim. In old age, when his hands began to tremble, he put his daughter Samira in charge of business and Najim in charge of the kiln, and walked through the market with his family.
card.turn: In a box of star-patterned tiles meant for a building wall, there was one tile with an extra petal. Yusuf thought it was his apprentice's mistake, but the pattern had begun with a sample that Yusuf himself had copied.
card.decision: Yusuf did not hide the tile by slipping it into place. He showed it to the customer. The customer asked him to use that tile near the bottom but make a new one to fill the gap above.
card.cost: Firing a new tile took extra fuel, and Yusuf separately paid the wall craftsman a day's wages for the delay. He apologized to Najim for blaming him unfairly, but Najim did not smile right away.
card.after: The workshop stayed open. Najim gradually took on more of the kiln work, while Samira wrote down customers' orders and calculated prices. Yusuf exchanged news with Bahram from time to time, but they could no longer stand at the same workbench every day as they once had.
card.presentEcho: Even when traces of someone you worked with for many years remain in your heart, there are times when you must consider a promise made to someone else on its own.
card.secondLook: The extra petal was neither Najim's prank nor a secret mark. It was the result of Yusuf unknowingly copying a playful sample Bahram had left behind before departing.
card.unresolved: Instead of replacing all the tiles, the customer allowed one tile to remain. Yusuf never recovered the extra fuel and wages he spent, and Najim's hurt did not disappear with a single apology.
card.readerQuestion: One tile with a different pattern has been mixed in with the order. It has to go on the wall tomorrow. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Yusuf spread out every tile and confirmed that there was only one unusual piece. The blurred ink on the old paper matched the long petal on the new sample he had drawn.
signalMoments.speak: Yusuf placed both samples in front of Najim and said that he had copied the pattern incorrectly and had also been wrong to blame Najim. Najim did not answer right away.
signalMoments.connect: When the wall craftsman arrived, Yusuf did not hide the incorrect tile. The two of them took the tile and the samples to the customer and asked whether it should be used or fired again.

identity.region: Samarkand under the Timurid dynasty
identity.summary: He learned pottery and tilemaking in Samarkand and opened a workshop. He lived in that city into old age, sharing the work with his family and apprentice.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Yusuf · Male
1392–1464 · Age 72
Born in Samarkand under the Timurid dynasty
Work · Making decorative tiles for buildings
Life · He grew up beside his father's pottery kiln and opened a small workshop with his friend Bahram. He raised two children with Layla and made tiles for many buildings. After his friend left, he kept the workshop going with his apprentice, Najim. When his hands began to tremble with age, he divided the work between his daughter Samira and Najim and spent his time walking through the market.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · He explained patterns clearly to customers, but when a new design delighted him, he sometimes forgot his calculations for a while.
Liked · The first glimpse of blue after opening the kiln and the smell of fruit in the evening market
Disliked · Opening the kiln door too soon and letting the heat escape
Good at · Arranging many small tiles to find where the larger pattern continued

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small wooden ruler his father had used
Those closest to him · His wife Layla, his daughter Samira and son Daniyal, his friend Bahram, and his apprentice Najim
The life he wanted · To keep the workshop open for many years and eat dinner with his family
Worry · Whether he could deliver the ordered tiles on time when a firing went wrong

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Yusuf, a tile craftsman in Samarkand. It was 1432, the day before his tiles were to be set into a new wall. A pattern with no match appeared in one of the boxes, and Yusuf tried to remember where he had seen it before. Let me tell you what happened in the workshop that day.

When his apprentice Najim opened the box, the blue tiles caught the sunlight. Yusuf, who was lining up the places where the star pattern would continue, picked up one tile. “There should be six petals here.” Najim counted again. “There are seven.”

The craftsman responsible for the lower part of the building's wall was due to collect the tiles at midday. Yusuf searched the box for another tile with the same pattern, but there was none. “Did you change the sample?” The smile vanished from Najim's face. “I only copied the lines. Just as you gave them to me, Master.”

Yusuf propped the tile on the workbench and untied a bundle of old samples. At the very bottom was a playful flower drawn by Bahram, the friend who had left. One petal was unusually long. Yusuf looked at the new sample beside it and froze. He had redrawn that same long petal with his own hand.

signalMoments.notice: Yusuf spread out every tile in the box. There was only one unusual piece, and the ink stain on the old paper matched the long, outstretched petal on the new sample exactly. The line had begun with his own hand, not Najim's.
signalMoments.speak: Yusuf placed both samples in front of Najim. “I copied it wrong. I was wrong to blame you, too.” Najim did not answer right away. The trace of a petal he had erased remained at the edge of the paper.
signalMoments.connect: When the wall craftsman arrived, Yusuf did not slip the one tile in among the others and hide it. Together, they carried the tile and the samples directly to the customer. The customer also needed to know whether they would use the one tile or fire a new one and wait.

episode.afterSignal:
“How long will it take if you fire another one?” the customer asked. Yusuf replied, “We have to heat the kiln one more time. You won't be able to set it by midday.” The wall craftsman pointed to the empty wall. “I can finish up to this spot today.”

The customer placed the seven-petaled tile beside the others. “It cannot go in the center at the top. I will use it down there. But make a new tile to fill the gap.” Yusuf nodded. Explaining his friend's prank would not erase the order that had already been agreed upon.

On the way back to the workshop, Najim asked, “Why did you want to keep that one tile?” “Because Bahram drew the same flower before he left. But I said you had drawn it.” Najim did not take the tile. “While you thought I was at fault, I never even had a chance to speak.”

Yusuf kneaded the remaining clay to make the new tile. Najim sat beside him and redrew the sample without the long petal. While they prepared the fire, they spoke only about work. You could not ask someone to smile immediately just because they had heard an apology.

The next day, the new tile came out of the kiln. Yusuf separately paid the wall craftsman a day's wages for the delay. He and Najim watched the craftsman set the seven-petaled tile low on the wall. From far away it was hard to notice, but up close it was clearly different from the rest.

That evening, Layla asked, “Why are both of you so quiet today?” Najim answered first. “We've been counting petals.” When Yusuf laughed, Najim smiled a little too. Samira set dinner before them and said, “Tomorrow, don't forget to count the money as well.”

After that, Yusuf made tiles for many more buildings in the workshop. He occasionally received news from Bahram in a distant city, and he left the kiln in Najim's care more and more often. In old age, his hands trembled, so his daughter Samira kept the ledger while Najim watched the fire. That single tile was one part of a long life, not the name of every pattern he ever made.

memories.label: Work He Did for Years
memories.detail: Fitting many small tiles together to find where the wall's larger pattern would continue

memories.label: What He Enjoyed
memories.detail: Evenings spent choosing fruit with Layla at the market and comparing the colors of newly fired blue tiles

memories.label: What He Treasured
memories.detail: His father's small, worn wooden ruler

memories.label: What He Missed
memories.detail: His youth, when he and Bahram laughed as they drew different flowers at the same workbench

memories.label: Words He Left Behind
memories.detail: “Before they go on the wall, look at them one by one. After they are set, look at them together.”

memories.label: Layla's View
memories.detail: “When work went well, he was louder than anyone. Even when it didn't, he always came home for dinner in the end.”

memories.label: Samira's View
memories.detail: “Father had a good eye for color, but I was better at calculating prices. Once he admitted that, the workshop ran much more smoothly.”

memories.label: Najim's View
memories.detail: “Once, he blamed me too quickly. But the next time, he spread out the samples first.”

finalMoment.place: Samarkand under the Timurid dynasty
finalMoment.scene:
Early one morning in 1464, Layla and I are walking through the Samarkand market. As we pass Daniyal's cloth shop, the center of my chest suddenly tightens. I stop and sit on the stone steps beside a stall piled with cloth. Layla asks, “What is it?” “Just a moment.” I answer, but I cannot draw a deep breath.

Layla grips my shoulder. Pressing a hand to my chest, I try to stand, but I sink back down. The stone steps feel cold against my palm. I want to move out of the way of the people passing by, but there is no strength in my legs. “Call Daniyal.” My words come out clipped. Layla calls our son's name loudly toward the cloth shop.

Daniyal puts down the cloth he was folding and runs over. “Father, let's go home.” He takes my arm and tries to help me up, but I shake my head. The pressure in my chest grows stronger, and I cannot take a single step. Daniyal shouts for the people nearby to help. Layla supports my back and says, “I'm right here.” Instead of answering, I clutch her sleeve.

Footsteps from deeper in the market draw closer, then fade away. I open my mouth and pull for breath. A little air enters, then stops. Daniyal calls my name. I raise my head to look at his face, but my vision blurs. My grip on Layla's sleeve goes slack. I try to breathe in again, but no air comes.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1464, seventy-two-year-old Yusuf died on the stone steps of the Samarkand market. His chest suddenly hurt, and he could not breathe, but the exact cause is unknown. Layla told the people who came to help that her husband had been walking beside her only moments before. Daniyal long remembered being unable to lift his father and take him home. Samira, who arrived later, closed the workshop that day, and Najim extinguished the kiln fire and went home as well. Yusuf enjoyed the days he spent with his family, and in the workshop, he also once paid the price for hastily blaming Najim. The record of a past life does not paint everything he left behind in a single color. His life ended in the market that day.

card.name: Rosa Vega
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Rosa Vega, born in Sonora. You crossed into Columbia, where you sold bread and meals to miners and made a home with Ramón and your daughter Elena. Even after moving your business elsewhere, you continued cooking, and in old age you lived near your daughter's family.
card.title: The $3 at Dawn
card.role: A person who sold bread and meals in a mining town
card.world: A mining town in California, USA, in 1852
card.flavor: The day her brother asked for the mining license fee, flour cost the same amount
card.opening: At dawn, as Rosa counted the money she needed to buy flour, her brother Mateo asked her for the $3 mining license fee.
card.life: Born in Sonora, Mexico, in 1824, she learned to make dough and work the oven from her mother. She moved with her brother Mateo to Columbia, California, where she sold bread and hot meals. She married Ramón and raised their daughter Elena, then later worked at a restaurant in a larger city. In old age, after Ramón died, she lived near her daughter's family in Monterey.
card.turn: In July 1852, Mateo, who was not a U.S. citizen, needed a $3 monthly license to continue mining. He asked his sister Rosa for the money, but she planned to use the same amount to buy flour and firewood for the next week.
card.decision: Instead of paying Mateo's mining license fee, Rosa offered to pay him to deliver bread for her. Mateo did not want to become his sister's hired hand, so he looked for other work hauling freight.
card.cost: Rosa kept her business going the next week, but for a while she and her brother could not sit at the same table. Mateo worked with a freight wagon that day instead of going to the mine, and later returned to Sonora.
card.after: Mateo worked hauling freight before returning to Sonora. Rosa ran her business with Ramón and raised their daughter Elena. The siblings exchanged occasional letters, but they never spoke of that dawn in the same way.
card.presentEcho: Even when you want to help someone close to you, the money you need to sustain your own life is limited. A relationship can continue in a different form even after a refusal.
card.secondLook: Mateo did not ask because he was lazy. He was trying to keep mining, and Rosa's offer sounded to him like she was telling him to give up that dream.
card.unresolved: Mateo had not been able to repay the money he had borrowed the last time, either. Rosa's choice to protect her business could not protect both their feelings at once.
card.readerQuestion: Your brother says he needs $3 to work at the mine today. But that money is what you need for tomorrow's flour. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Rosa checked the remaining flour and money again. After buying firewood and flour, she had no separate $3 to give Mateo.
signalMoments.speak: Rosa asked Mateo how much he had earned at the mine. Mateo admitted that he had come back empty-handed for the past few days.
signalMoments.connect: Rosa offered to pay Mateo immediately for delivering bread the next day. Mateo asked if she wanted him to accept her pity by working at her shop.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Kind of Person She Was

Liked · The crisp end of a freshly baked loaf and the smell of earth after rain
Disliked · Guests who arrived unexpectedly for dinner without saying how many people needed to be fed
Skilled at · Judging how many people a lump of dough would feed just by looking at its size

profilePages.body:

People close to her · Her brother Mateo, her friend Luisa, her husband Ramón, and her daughter Elena

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Rosa Vega, who sold food in the mining town of Columbia. In the summer of 1852, foreign-born miners had to pay $3 a month to work in the mines. One dawn, her brother Mateo came to ask her for that money. Let me tell you what Rosa chose in front of the oven.

Rosa checked the fire before dawn. The bread was not fully baked yet, and the sack of flour for the next day was nearly empty. She had set aside some money beside the small scale. After buying firewood, nothing would remain.

Mateo removed his hat at the door. “Rosa, I have to get the license today. Lend me just $3 more.” Rosa dusted the dough from her hands. “What about the money you borrowed last time?” “I'll repay you when I find gold.” “You said that last time.”

Mateo pointed toward the mine. “I've found a spot now, too. I only need to hold out for one month.” Rosa remembered the nights when he had returned covered in dirt and fallen asleep at the table. But she also remembered the customers who bought bread every day. Without flour, she would have nothing to serve them.

signalMoments.notice: Rosa ran her fingers over the remaining flour and counted the money again. After buying firewood and flour, she could not spare $3. It might mean more than shutting down the oven for just one day.
signalMoments.speak: Rosa asked, “Tell me first how much you've earned at the mine.” Mateo admitted that he had come back empty-handed for the past few days. The numbers each of them knew were different.
signalMoments.connect: Rosa said she was looking for someone to deliver bread the next day. “I'll pay you right away for the work you do.” Mateo's face hardened. “You want me to take your pity by working at your shop?”

episode.afterSignal:
The smell of baking bread filled the room. Rosa closed the small coin purse. “I can't pay for your mining license. I need that money for flour and firewood.” Mateo stepped back from the threshold. “You think I'm going to fail again.”

“I don't know that,” Rosa said. “But I'm going to use the money I have today to make food for next week. The bread delivery job is still open.” Mateo put on his hat and replied, “I won't do that work. I'll find something else on my own.”

Rosa did not follow him. It was time to take out the bread, and even if she followed, she had no more money to give him. As she cooled the loaves on the wooden board, she looked toward the door several times. She set aside one piece, but Mateo did not come back for breakfast.

Later that day, Luisa brought the firewood. “Mateo was working with that freight wagon over there.” Rosa gripped the flour sack tightly so she would not spill it. “He didn't go to the mine?” “He says he isn't going today. He's very angry.” Rosa only said, “I see.”

A few days later, Mateo came to buy bread. When Rosa wrapped two loaves, he put one back. “I'll only pay for one.” Neither of them smiled. Rosa put the other loaf back on the plate. She did not pretend that she would not charge him just because he was her brother.

Mateo kept hauling freight and later returned to Sonora. On the day he left, Rosa handed him bread for the road. This time, Mateo accepted it. “I still haven't repaid the money.” “I know.” Rosa looked briefly at his hand holding the bread. They could not bring themselves to debate whether what had happened that dawn was right.

Later, Rosa built a family with Ramón, raised Elena, and served food at many tables. She and Mateo exchanged letters from time to time. The morning she refused to give him $3 lingered between the siblings for years, but Rosa's long life also held other work and laughter, moves, and days of growing old.

memories.label: What She Enjoyed

memories.label: Mateo's View

memories.label: Ramón's View
memories.detail: “She often got the number of customers wrong, but whenever she decided to make bread, she always lit the oven.”

memories.label: Elena's View
memories.detail: “My mother moved quickly at the shop, but when she came home, she would listen to my stories and sometimes forget that the bread was cooling.”

finalMoment.place: Monterey, California, United States of America
finalMoment.scene:
On a rainy morning in 1891, I am lying in a bed at my daughter Elena's house in Monterey. My ankle, chafed by my shoe 4 days ago, is red and swollen, and my fever has been high since yesterday. Elena changed the wet cloth all night. I said I would sit up and drink water by myself, but when I lift the cup, my hand trembles. Water spills onto the blanket.

“I'll hold it.” Elena supports the cup. One sip passes down my throat, and nausea quickly rises in my stomach. I push the cup away. I try to ask her to unwrap the cloth around my ankle, but my tongue is so dry that only her name comes out. Elena looks at the foot I point toward and says, “I'll wrap it again.” When I extend my hot foot beyond the bed, cool air touches it for a moment.

Outside the door, a neighbor asks, “Should I fetch the doctor?” Elena answers, “Yes, please hurry.” I want to tell my daughter that I am all right. But every time I catch my breath, my chest moves in short motions, and no words come out. Elena supports my shoulder and raises the pillow. I grasp her wrist. The skin against my palm is cool.

Rain patters near the window. Elena asks, “Mama, can you hear me?” I move my fingers to show that I can. My whole body feels heavier than my ankle. I try to breathe in, but only a little air enters. I try once more to hold my daughter's wrist, but my fingers loosen. Elena's voice grows faint.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1891, Rosa Vega, age 67, died at her daughter Elena's home in Monterey after her ankle swelled and she suffered a fever. It is impossible to know exactly why the fever became so severe. Elena long remembered how her mother's hand went slack before the doctor arrived. Her granddaughter was in another room and learned the news later. Mateo in Sonora was also told of his sister's death. The siblings had remained apart without resolving the debt and hurt feelings of 1852. Rosa supported her family and worked in several cities. This record of a past life recounts both the tables she sustained and the relationship that grew distant as it brings this life to its end.
finalMoment.artAlt: A rainy morning in 1891, looking into a Monterey home through a wet window. Rosa Vega, age 67, sits on the bed and spills water as she tries to hold a cup in her trembling hand, while her daughter Elena watches from a chair beside her

card.name: Manuel Ibarra
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Manuel Ibarra of Valparaíso. You hauled cargo at the port and painted backdrops for neighborhood performances in the evenings. You stayed close to your older sister Pilar and your niece Luz, and after the earthquake, you moved to Viña del Mar, where you grew old painting small signs and tending potted plants.
card.title: The Moon on the Stairs
card.role: A port cargo handler who also painted props for neighborhood performances
card.world: Valparaíso, Republic of Chile, 1900
card.flavor: The performance on the hill was about to begin, and the moon was bigger than the funicular door
card.opening: When Manuel brought over the enormous moon for that night's performance, the funicular door was narrower than the moon.
card.life: Born in Valparaíso in 1862, he learned the routes cargo traveled through the port. After learning to paint lettering, he hauled cargo by day and made props for neighborhood performances by night. He lived near his older sister Pilar and his niece Luz, and after the 1906 earthquake, he found a new place to live near Viña del Mar, where the two had moved. Once his knees began to hurt, he took on fewer heavy loads and made a living painting shop signs.
card.turn: One evening in 1900, he tried to take a moon prop he had painted to a small theater on the hill, but it would not fit through the funicular door. If he took the narrow stairs, he would not arrive by showtime.
card.decision: Manuel removed the connecting pins in the middle of the wooden frame and folded the cloth to load it onto the funicular. The wet white paint split down the middle.
card.cost: A long crack appeared in the moon's white paint, and Luz's improvised line made the audience laugh. Aurelio, who had wanted a quiet final scene, paid Manuel a little less than the agreed price for the prop.
card.after: When Luz saw the cracked moon during the performance, she cleverly changed her line, making the audience laugh. For some time afterward, Manuel and Aurelio remembered that laughter differently. Manuel continued to paint small backdrops, but from the next prop onward, he measured the width of the door first.
card.presentEcho: The same mistake can be an unexpected laugh to one person and a lost scene to another.
card.secondLook: Manuel folded the moon to arrive on time, while Aurelio lost the quiet scene he had prepared. The audience's laughter alone did not make the two men feel the same way.
card.unresolved: Aurelio never paid him the money he had withheld. Even so, the two discussed the size of the next month's prop together.
card.readerQuestion: The performance is about to begin, but the moon you made is bigger than the funicular door. If you take the stairs, you'll be late. What would you try first?

signalMoments.notice: Manuel noticed the two pins fitted into the middle of the moon's frame. If he removed them, he could fold it in half, but he was worried about the still-wet white paint.
signalMoments.speak: Manuel asked the funicular attendant whether they could load the moon at an angle. The attendant shook his head, saying that if it blocked the door, no one would be able to board.
signalMoments.connect: Manuel asked a passing cargo handler if they could carry it up the stairs together. The man said he could help, but the performance would be well underway by the time they arrived.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Manuel Ibarra, who hauled cargo at the port of Valparaíso. At night, you also put his brush to work on props for neighborhood performances. Let me tell you what happened one evening in 1900, when an enormous moon he had painted could not make it up the hill.

Manuel stretched white cloth taut over a wooden frame. He had made the frame in two halves and joined them in the middle with two pins. That had allowed him to get it out through the old warehouse door. The last coat of white paint was still wet, and even the fingers gripping the edges of the cloth were stained with it.

His friend Aurelio called from downstairs. “Get here before sunset! Luz has to say her final line beneath the moon.” Luz was Manuel's twelve-year-old niece. Today, she had her first long speech in a small performance for the neighborhood. Manuel hoisted the moon and carried it to the lower funicular station.

But one end of the moon caught on the doorframe. When Manuel turned it at an angle, the other end struck the stair railing. It was about to block even the doorway passengers used to come and go while the funicular was moving. Looking down the long flight of stairs, he could see that there was not enough time before the performance began to carry the moon up on foot.

signalMoments.notice: Manuel touched the pins in the middle of the wooden frame. If he removed both, he could fold the moon. But bending the wet white paint in half would leave a mark.
signalMoments.speak: Manuel asked the funicular attendant, “Couldn't we load it at an angle?” The attendant pointed to the threshold and said there would be no room left for passengers to pass.
signalMoments.connect: Manuel called over a passing cargo handler. “What if we carry it up the stairs together?” The man looked up the hill. “I can go with you. But your performance will be well underway by then.”

episode.afterSignal:
Manuel pressed his palm against the center of the moon. “If I leave it like this, the performance won't have a moon.” He pulled out the pins and carefully folded the two sides of the wooden frame together. The dry parts of the cloth held, but the white line he had painted last split with a crack where the cloth folded.

The folded moon fit through the door. Inside the funicular, Manuel wrapped both arms around the frame to keep the cloth from tearing any further. A passenger beside him asked, “Is that an enormous loaf of bread?” Manuel looked down at the white paint on his hands. “Tonight, it's the moon.” The passenger laughed.

When he reached the top, Aurelio was stamping his feet backstage. When Manuel unfolded the moon, a long white crack showed down the middle. “It was supposed to be a whole moon,” Aurelio said quietly. “The last scene is meant to be quiet.” Manuel picked up a brush, then set it down. If he repainted it, the paint would not dry before the performance.

The two men hung the moon as it was. When Luz came onstage, the audience fell silent. Just as she was about to say her final line, the wind shook the cloth, widening the crack in the moon. Someone in the front row snickered.

Luz looked up at the moon, then changed her line. “I think that moon hurt its knees running all the way up here.” This time, several people laughed. Manuel laughed with them, then saw Aurelio's face and closed his mouth. His friend had rehearsed to make that scene long and quiet.

After the performance, Luz pointed out the white crack in the moon to Manuel. “Uncle, people looked at me.” Aurelio handed him a little less than the money he had promised. “The laughter was good. But it wasn't the ending I was trying to make.” Manuel did not insist on more. After all, he had been the one who decided to remove the pins in front of the funicular door.

Manuel carried the empty frame down the stairs. They had decided to leave the moon in the storage room at the top. When Aurelio came to ask him to make a prop for the next month's performance, Manuel's first question was, “How wide is the door this time?” His friend smiled briefly and showed him the width with his hands.

After that, Manuel continued to haul cargo and paint small backdrops. Years later, even when an earthquake drove him from the street where he had lived, he took a scrap of stage cloth with him. He cherished the laughter from that day, but he also remembered for a long time the scene Aurelio had regretted losing.

finalMoment.place: Viña del Mar, Republic of Chile
finalMoment.scene:
On a cloudy afternoon in 1935, I am sitting in a chair in the room I rent for myself in Viña del Mar. I have had no appetite for weeks, and climbing the stairs leaves me short of breath. My older sister Pilar has brought me a bowl of soup. She sets the bowl in front of me and says, “Eat a little, at least.” I lift the spoon, then put it down. Now even the smell makes my chest feel tight.

Pilar turns to close the window a little. “I'll do it.” I rise from the chair and brace a hand on the edge of the table. There is no strength in my knees, and the room seems to tilt. Pilar turns back quickly and supports my shoulder. “Just sit down.” But even lowering myself back into the chair is difficult. I cannot release my grip on the table.

“Should I call Luz?” Pilar asks. I picture the house where my niece lives, but I have to find the breath to answer first. “Just stay a moment,” I manage to say. Pilar supports my back and lowers me into the chair. The smell of soup mingles with the wind from outside. I let out one long breath and try to inhale again. My chest barely moves.

Pilar calls my name. I try to lift my head, but only my chin moves a little. My sister's hand rests on my shoulder, and cold air enters through the open window. Even when I try to draw in more of it, only a short sound comes from my throat. The hand I had stretched toward the table falls onto my knee. My sister's voice is close, but I cannot answer her.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1935, seventy-three-year-old Manuel Ibarra died in his own room in Viña del Mar, Chile, with his older sister Pilar beside him. His strength had faded for several weeks, but the exact cause of death is unknown. Pilar remembered the weight of her brother's shoulder as she supported him when he tried to stand. His niece Luz arrived too late and sat for a while in the room her uncle had rented for himself and lived in for so long. Although Manuel lived near his sister's home, he kept a room of his own. This past-life record conveys both the final afternoon the two women remembered and the end of Manuel's life.
finalMoment.artAlt: On a cloudy afternoon in 1935, in a separately rented room in Viña del Mar, Chile, seventy-three-year-old Manuel, weakened by illness, braces himself on a table after trying to rise from a chair as his older sister Pilar supports his shoulder

card.name: Demetrios
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Demetrios of Oxyrhynchus. Born into a family of potters, you learned to write and recorded market transactions and composed letters for your neighbors. You lived alongside your wife Irene, your son Leon, and your sister Thais, and after your eyesight grew dim, you grew old writing short lists and helping children practice their letters.
card.title: The Invitation That Wasn't Sent
card.role: A scribe of letters and transaction records
card.world: Roman Egypt in 205
card.flavor: The hand writing the letter stopped at the invitation's final line
card.opening: As Demetrios was about to write the final line of the invitation, the baker Charon's voice suddenly turned hard.
card.life: Born in Oxyrhynchus in 170, he learned to write by recording the number of wares made by his family of potters. He copied market records, then began writing letters for his neighbors as well. He made a home with Irene and their son Leon and remained close to his sister Thais's family. In old age, he adjusted to his failing eyesight by writing only short lists and teaching young children their letters.
card.turn: In 205, Charon dictated a letter inviting his estranged sister Nica to a feast three days later. At the end of the invitation, he added angry words and urged Demetrios to seal it at once.
card.decision: Demetrios did not secretly change the words. Instead, he read the sentence back to Charon exactly as written. Charon tore up the papyrus and had him write the invitation again.
card.cost: The waiting messenger left for another house. The invitation arrived a day late, and Demetrios also missed the next client's record-keeping job.
card.after: Nica came to the feast, but the siblings did not reconcile at once. Demetrios regretted the wages he lost that day, and he continued writing down other people's words afterward.
card.presentEcho: Even someone who writes down another person's words can choose the right moment to let that person hear them again.
card.secondLook: Charon was angry, but he also wanted to invite Nica. Demetrios did not secretly change his words; he read them back exactly as written. What Nica actually received was the invitation Charon dictated the second time.
card.unresolved: Nica came and sat at the feast, but she and Charon did not fully talk through that day's quarrel.
card.readerQuestion: At the end of an invitation to a client's estranged sister, the client says, “I don't care if you don't come.” He urges you to write it exactly that way and seal it. What might you try?

signalMoments.notice: Demetrios saw “I would like you to come” near the beginning of the invitation and “I don't care if you don't come” at the end, side by side.
signalMoments.speak: Saying he would read the letter through before sealing it, Demetrios read aloud every word Charon had dictated, including the final sentence.
signalMoments.connect: Demetrios gestured to the messenger outside the door to wait a moment. The messenger said he had other houses to visit and could not wait long.

identity.region: Oxyrhynchus, Roman province of Egypt
identity.summary: Born into a family of potters, he learned to write and became a scribe of letters and ledgers. He lived alongside Irene, Leon, and his sister Thais, and taught children to write in his old age.

Demetrios · Male

profilePages.body:

Liked · The sound of footsteps on days when letters arrived, and the shade in the courtyard
Disliked · Being urged to seal a letter before he had heard everything

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him?
profilePages.body:

Those closest to him · His wife Irene, his son Leon, and his sister Thais
The life he wanted · A life in which he cleared the table in the evening and rested in the courtyard with his family
Worry · How much longer would he be able to write once his eyesight grew dim?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Demetrios, who wrote other people's letters in Oxyrhynchus. One afternoon in 205, his hand stopped over an invitation dictated by the baker Charon. Let me tell you about that day's letter.

On Demetrios's table lay cut sheets of papyrus and a reed pen. Outside the door stood the man who had agreed to deliver the letter. He was on his way beyond the marketplace to the home of Charon's sister Nica.

Charon set a loaf of bread he had baked that day on the table. “I'm serving food at my house three days from now. Write and tell Nica to come.” Demetrios wrote down his sister's name. Charon first said, “I would like you to come.”

But when they reached the end, Charon's voice changed. “I don't care if you don't come. Put that in too.” The day before, the siblings had quarreled bitterly over whose house should keep an old bowl. Charon still looked angry.

Demetrios wrote the words exactly as spoken. He could not remove the words of the person who had asked him to write the letter simply because he wished to. Charon pointed outside the door. “Now fold and tie it. That man has to leave soon.”

signalMoments.notice: Demetrios saw the invitation's first line, “I would like you to come,” alongside the final line, “I don't care if you don't come.” Charon had said both of them clearly.
signalMoments.speak: Demetrios said, “I will read it all the way through before sealing it.” He read aloud every word Charon had dictated, including the final sentence.
signalMoments.connect: Demetrios raised a hand to ask the messenger outside the door to wait just a moment. The man said he had other houses to visit and would leave before the sun began to set.

episode.afterSignal:
Demetrios did not fold the letter. He looked at Charon. “I would like you to come. I don't care if you don't come.” Even after hearing his own words, Charon did not answer for some time. In the alley, the messenger waited, scuffing his sandals.

“Did I say that?” Charon asked. “Those were your exact words.” Demetrios pointed to the final line. Charon did not snatch away the pen or tell him to erase the words. Instead, he turned the loaf on the table upside down, then set it back again.

The man outside called, “If not now, then tomorrow!” Demetrios could have folded the invitation. Once tied and sealed, it would have gone out on that day's journey. Charon opened his mouth, then closed it.

“Write a new one,” Charon finally said. He tore the first letter in half. “Just write that I want her to come. We'll talk about the bowl when we meet.” While Demetrios spread out a fresh sheet of papyrus, the messenger walked away toward another house.

This letter was brief. Demetrios read it again in front of Charon, then wrote Nica's name on the back. He folded the letter into a narrow strip, tied it with fiber cord, and sealed it by pressing down a small piece of clay. Charon said he would entrust it to someone else traveling that way the next morning.

By the time Charon left, the client who had wanted a ledger written had already gone home. Demetrios looked at the loaf on the empty table. When he thought of the wages he had missed, the bread was not entirely welcome. He shared it with his son Leon that evening.

Three days later, Nica came to the feast. When Charon tried to mention the bowl, Nica served some food first and set it in the place beside her. The two sat together, but they could not settle everything from their last quarrel then and there. Demetrios also stayed to eat for a while, then returned home, thinking about the list he had to write the next day.

He wrote many more letters over the years. After his eyesight grew dim and he stopped writing long texts, he sometimes taught children their letters. He did not hold up that day's invitation as an answer for the rest of his life. But whenever someone urged him to hurry and seal a letter, he first asked for time to read it aloud.

finalMoment.place: Oxyrhynchus, Roman province of Egypt
finalMoment.scene:
Late one morning in 239, I am washing the lunch dishes in the small courtyard of my house in Oxyrhynchus. My wife Irene has gone to the market, and our son Leon, who has a home of his own, is coming this evening. The moment I set down a bowl, a sudden pain strikes deep inside my abdomen. I try to straighten my back, but the pain grows deeper. The cup of water in my hand falls to the ground, and water spreads around my feet.

Bracing one hand against the wall, I take a few steps toward the front gate. “Irene.” I call her name, but there is no one in the house. A neighbor boy walking along the street sees the open door and stops. “Sir, did you fall?” “Go get my wife.” My words break off, and I clutch my abdomen. The boy runs toward the market.

I tighten my grip on the doorframe, but I cannot remain standing. My knees touch the ground, and the pain in my abdomen shoots through to my back. I try to turn and sit on the threshold, but crumple onto my side. The water spilled at my feet wets my palm. In the street, I hear someone ask the boy which house it is. “Here!” the boy calls.

“Speak slowly.” I try to say the words I used when Leon talked too fast as a child, but no sound comes out. The pain keeps me from rising. I try to draw a breath, but it breaks off short. I reach a hand outside the door. I hear running footsteps in the sunlight, and my fingers slip on the wet ground. I try to grasp the doorframe again, but my arm will not move.
finalMoment.afterword: In 239, Demetrios, aged sixty-nine, died after suffering sudden, severe abdominal pain on the threshold of his home in Oxyrhynchus. The exact cause is unknown. A neighbor boy ran to summon help, but Irene returned after her husband had died. His son Leon also came that evening and saw the dishes his father had left half-washed. Irene remembered the time they had spent sitting together in the courtyard the previous evening. The record of this past life preserves both the evenings he shared with his family and the final day that ended suddenly on the threshold.
finalMoment.artAlt: Daytime at a house in Oxyrhynchus in the Roman province of Egypt in 239: sixty-nine-year-old Demetrios, stricken by abdominal pain, has collapsed on the threshold and grips the doorframe as a neighbor boy turns to summon help

card.name: Yeonhwa
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yeonhwa of Gaegyeong. You learned to weave hemp cloth in a village and sold fabric at the capital's market. You raised your daughter Sol with your husband, Doyun, and in old age, you taught your neighbors how to weave.
card.title: Hemp Cloth Spread Before the Ox
card.role: A market merchant who wove and sold hemp cloth
card.world: 1120, Goryeo, Gaegyeong
card.flavor: When the ox charged beneath the lanterns, she spread out new cloth
card.opening: On a day when the market was crowded with people who had come to see the lanterns, an ox pulling a cart suddenly charged into the street.
card.life: Born in 1080 in a village near Gaegyeong, she prepared hemp and wove cloth. As an adult, she moved to the Gaegyeong market to sell fabric and made a home with Doyun, a woodworker, and their daughter Sol. After Doyun died, she refused to lend Sol cloth because she wanted to protect her own business, and Sol suffered a loss after buying expensive cloth. In old age, she taught her neighbors how to weave and tended a small vegetable garden.
card.turn: On the day of the 1120 Lotus Lantern Festival, an ox pulling a load was startled and bolted down a narrow market street. Ahead were people and stalls hung with lanterns.
card.decision: Yeonhwa wrapped one end of her newest bolt of hemp cloth around a post and spread it wide. When the ox veered toward the empty courtyard as if avoiding the cloth, the carter Eunseok caught the reins again.
card.cost: The ox stepped on the edge of the hemp cloth and tore it. The carter Eunseok repaid her a little at a time, but the amount fell short of the bolt's full value, and her daughter Sol worried about the cost of having less cloth to sell on the next market day.
card.after: Sol was proud that her mother had acted quickly, but she also worried about the empty space in their bundle of cloth on the next market day. Together they considered how they could use the torn fabric, and Yeonhwa never recovered the full price of the bolt.
card.presentEcho: Even when your body moves first in a split second, the next day's business still remains.
card.secondLook: Yeonhwa saw the people in the narrow street, while Sol saw the empty space in their bundle of cloth on the next market day. They worried about the same afternoon in different ways.
card.unresolved: The cart's owner repaid her a little at a time, but the total never reached the full price of a new bolt of hemp cloth.
card.readerQuestion: A startled ox is charging toward people who have come to see the lanterns. Beside you is a newly woven bolt of hemp cloth. What will you try first?

signalMoments.speak: When Yeonhwa shouted, “Clear the way! The right side is open!” people grabbed their dishes and their children's hands and backed away.
signalMoments.connect: Yeonhwa gestured for Eunseok to head toward the courtyard, signaling that she would block this side. Eunseok picked up the fallen reins and ran behind the post.

episode.beforeSignal:
In your past life, you were Yeonhwa, a seller of hemp cloth in Gaegyeong, the capital of Goryeo. One afternoon in 1120, when people had gathered to see the Lotus Lantern Festival, a bolt of cloth she treasured unexpectedly became a barricade. Let me tell you what happened that day.

Yeonhwa held the end of a newly woven bolt of hemp cloth and spread it out before a customer. Beside her, her daughter Sol neatly arranged the wooden dishes made by her husband, Doyun. The lanterns over the street would be lit at sunset, so people had begun gathering early.

A loaded cart entered at the end of the alley. Just as the carter Eunseok tried to slow the ox, someone hanging lanterns nearby dropped a wooden frame. Crack! At the sound, the ox twisted around. The reins slipped from Eunseok's hands.

The ox charged toward the crowd. Stalls displaying lanterns and dishes were packed tightly along the left side of the street. Behind a wooden post on the right was a small, empty courtyard. Yeonhwa looked down at the newest bolt of hemp cloth in her hands.

signalMoments.notice: Yeonhwa saw the empty courtyard on the right and the post in front of it. If she spread the hemp cloth wide to screen off the stalls on the left, the ox might turn toward the open courtyard.
signalMoments.speak: “Clear the way! The right side is open!” Yeonhwa shouted, and the people watching the lanterns grabbed their dishes and their children's hands and backed away.
signalMoments.connect: Yeonhwa gestured to Eunseok. “Go toward the courtyard! I'll block this side.” Eunseok picked up the reins from the ground and ran behind the post.

episode.afterSignal:
Yeonhwa wrapped one end of the hemp cloth around the post and held the other end in her hands, spreading it wide. The fabric caught the wind and flapped. When the ox lifted its head right in front of her, Yeonhwa took one step back and raised the cloth higher. The customers held their breath.

“This way!” Eunseok shouted from the empty courtyard. The ox veered right as if avoiding the swaying hemp cloth. Yeonhwa tried not to let go of the fabric, but the ox stepped on its lower edge. Riiip! The cloth tore.

Eunseok caught the reins again in the courtyard. The ox went a few more steps before stopping. Someone picked up a fallen lantern, and Sol ran to her mother. “Your hands—are they all right?” When Yeonhwa held out both hands to show her, Sol finally let out a long breath.

The hemp cloth was smeared with dirt and split by a long tear down the middle. Sol held up the torn section. “This was the cloth we were going to sell at the market tomorrow.” Yeonhwa knew. The bolt held days of work woven by hand.

Eunseok kept hold of the cart and apologized. “I'll repay you.” But the money he had with him was less than the price of a full bolt. Yeonhwa accepted as much as he could pay. The people in the street talked about how quickly she had acted, but Sol thought about the empty space in their bundle of cloth on the next market day.

When the lanterns were lit that evening, Yeonhwa and Sol walked to the end of the street for a little while. Sol said, “You were impressive, Mother. But I suppose I'll have to cut up this cloth and use it tomorrow.” Yeonhwa laughed. “We could put pieces under very small dishes.” Together they used their fingers to measure where they might cut it.

Eunseok later repaid her a little at a time, but the total fell short of the price of a new bolt of hemp cloth. Yeonhwa continued selling fabric at the market, and after her daughter moved to another market, she taught her neighbors the handwork of weaving. Sometimes she spoke proudly of the day the ox bolted, but she also remembered the weight of the cloth she had been forced to discard.

finalMoment.place: Gaegyeong, Goryeo
finalMoment.scene:
Late one night in 1149, I wake alone in my small house in Gaegyeong. My daughter Sol lives near another market. I smell something burning inside the room. The dry straw mat hanging on the wall has caught fire, and smoke is gathering at the ceiling. I reach for a bowl of water, but a cough makes me pull my hand back. I cannot see where the fire began.

“Fire!” I push open the door and step into the courtyard. I try to breathe in the cold air, but my throat stings and I cannot draw a deep breath. A neighbor from across the way runs over carrying a bucket of water. “Yeonhwa, move farther away!” I open my mouth to answer, but I cough first. My neighbor throws water toward the door and shouts to the other houses.

I walk a few steps to the large water jar in the courtyard. Gripping its rim, I sit down and straighten my back. I hear wood burning inside the room. If I stand again, I may be able to see the flames, but there is no strength in my legs. “Send for Sol.” My voice is faint. My neighbor nods and tells someone else the way to my daughter's home. I tighten my grip on the jar.

Smoke rolls into the courtyard and passes in front of my face. I cover my mouth with my sleeve and try to breathe. My chest moves only in short breaths. My neighbor sets down the bucket and comes toward me. “Rest here.” My neighbor places a hand on my shoulder, but I do not have the strength to nod. My fingers loosen from the rim of the jar. I try to draw in air again, but only a ragged sound comes from my throat.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1149, 69-year-old Yeonhwa escaped into the courtyard on the night her Gaegyeong home caught fire, but died after inhaling smoke. A neighbor was beside her, and her daughter Sol arrived after her mother had died. Where the fire began and the exact medical cause of death are unknown. Sol remembered both the evenings when she shared meals with her mother and the day in 1139 when her mother would not lend her cloth. The record of this past life preserves both Yeonhwa's warmth and her habit of protecting her own goods first, along with the night her life ended so suddenly.
finalMoment.artAlt: At night in 1149 in Gaegyeong, Goryeo, 69-year-old Yeonhwa crouches beside a water jar in the courtyard to catch her breath after escaping fire and smoke, while a neighbor throws water on the house

card.name: Zeynep
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Zeynep of Istanbul. You grew up beside your mother, who sold soap, and took charge of towels and water at a hammam. You built a family with Hasan and their daughter, Eda. After losing your husband, you refused a request from the sick Eda because you wanted to protect your wages, and in old age, you taught the work to your young niece.
card.title: The Bathhouse Where the Singing Stopped
card.role: Worker in charge of towels and water at a women's hammam
card.world: 1718, Istanbul, Ottoman Empire
card.flavor: When the wedding-bath song began, the bride asked for quiet
card.opening: Just as the singing was about to begin for a guest preparing for her wedding, the bride caught Zeynep by the sleeve.
card.life: Born in Istanbul in 1672, she helped her mother sell soap. In her teens, she began arranging towels and water jugs at a women's bathhouse called a hammam. She married Hasan, a ropemaker, and raised their daughter, Eda. After Hasan died, she kept working, afraid of losing her wages. In 1731, her adult daughter Eda had a fever and asked her to come during the day for a few days, but she did not take time off. Eda asked a neighbor to bring water and meals and paid them wages. Mother and daughter continued to visit each other, but Eda no longer brought urgent matters to her mother first. In old age, she taught the work to her niece, and when her hands began to hurt, she counted towels by the hammam door.
card.turn: In 1718, a bride who had come for her pre-wedding bath asked them to stop the singing for a while because it reminded her of her father's death. But her aunt had prepared songs and towels for the guests and was about to pay extra wages as well.
card.decision: Zeynep passed the bride's request on to her aunt exactly as it had been made and had the singing paused for a while.
card.cost: The aunt paid only part of the extra wages she had promised. Zeynep had planned to put that money toward Hasan's rope-making materials, but now they had to postpone the purchase until the next market day. The bride's grief did not vanish right away, either.
card.after: While the singing was silent, the bride and her aunt sat in the same room. Later, the aunt placed a dry towel at the bride's feet, but neither of them rushed to speak words of reconciliation.
card.presentEcho: Even when people prepare something for one another, they may want different kinds of time.
card.secondLook: The aunt had prepared a cheerful time to welcome the guests, while the bride wanted a brief silence to remember her father. The wages Zeynep was due that day mattered to her, too.
card.unresolved: The aunt never paid all the extra wages, and even Zeynep did not know what the bride and her aunt said to each other afterward.
card.readerQuestion: The wedding-bath song is about to begin, but the bride says she wants quiet. What should you say first to her aunt and the workers, who have already finished preparing everything?

signalMoments.connect: Zeynep gestured to Naziye to tell the singers to take a short break. While Naziye went over to them, Zeynep remained beside the bride.

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Zeynep, who tended the towels and water at a women's hammam in Istanbul in the Ottoman Empire. Let me tell you about a moment in 1718, on the day of a wedding bath, just as the singing prepared for the bride was about to begin.

Zeynep stacked dry towels on a shelf and straightened the handle of the last water jug. When her coworker Naziye opened the door to the resting room, the bride and her relatives entered. The bride's aunt invited each person to sit. “Today, let us make our girl smile.”

The people gathered their voices to begin the song the aunt had arranged in advance. Zeynep, too, had prepared extra towels for that day. As the first note rang through the room, the bride quietly caught the edge of Zeynep's sleeve.

“Could we have some quiet for just a moment?” the bride said softly. “It hasn't been long since my father died. Hearing this keeps making me think of him.” Her aunt was clapping toward the singers. Zeynep looked back and forth between the bride's wet hand and the dry towels her aunt had laid out.

signalMoments.notice: Zeynep saw the bride's hand gripping the towel and the aunt's face as she waited for the singing. The two of them wanted different things from the same bath.
signalMoments.speak: Zeynep spoke clearly to the aunt. “The bride says she would like some quiet for a moment. Would you please pause the singing for a little while?”
signalMoments.connect: Zeynep gestured to Naziye. “Please tell the singers to take a short break.” While Naziye went over to them, Zeynep remained beside the bride.

episode.afterSignal:
Naziye passed the message to the singers. Their voices died away one by one. The last note lingered beneath the domed ceiling and disappeared, leaving only the clear sound of dripping water. The bride loosened the towel in her clenched hand and laid it across her lap.

The aunt called Zeynep over. “I was the one who asked for the singing. I wanted the girl to turn her mind away from sorrow, at least today.” Zeynep replied, “I heard what you said. But the bride says she would like some quiet for now.” The aunt looked toward the bride, but the bride did not raise her head.

The aunt handed over only part of the extra wages she had promised. “Since the song was not finished, this is all you will receive.” Zeynep counted the reduced number of coins in her palm. She had just promised Hasan that she would help pay for rope-making materials that day. Even so, she could not speak for the bride and say that everything was fine.

Zeynep folded one more towel, placed it in front of the bride, and stepped away. Without speaking, the bride touched its edge. A little later, the aunt picked up a dry towel and placed it at the bride's feet. No apology passed between them, nor did the aunt urge her to smile now.

When Zeynep returned home and set the coins on the table, Hasan asked, “Weren't there many guests today?” “There were. The song was short.” Zeynep explained why her wages had been reduced. Hasan said they could buy the rope-making materials on the next market day, but even those words did not ease the heaviness inside her.

She remembered both the towels the aunt had prepared and the towel the bride had clutched. After that, Zeynep continued to pass busy and quiet days at the hammam as she raised Eda. The brief silence at the wedding bath was a single day within those long years, and the weight of the coins taken from her hand that day remained with her for a long time.

memories.detail: “I liked drinking tea with Mother. But when I was sick, she did not take time off work. After that, I asked the neighbors first when something was urgent.”

memories.label: Naziye's View
memories.detail: “Zeynep believed in the order of the work. Even so, when a guest wanted something, she knew how to change that order.”

finalMoment.place: Eda's house, Istanbul, Ottoman Empire
finalMoment.scene:
It is 1741 in Istanbul, at the home of my daughter Eda. Eda, who has been out during the day, returns and sets bread and warm soup on the small table. It is just my daughter and me. “How are your hands?” Eda asks. I spread my fingers to show her. “I didn't drop a cup today.” My daughter gives a short laugh and pushes the bread toward me.

I chew a piece of bread and try to swallow, but it sticks in my throat. I pound my chest. I try to swallow again, but it will not go down. When I try to draw breath, only a rough sound comes from my throat. “Mother?” Eda pushes the table aside and comes closer. When I open my mouth, Eda strikes my back hard.

I grip the edge of the table and try to stand. My knees give way. Eda supports my body and calls toward the door, “Someone, please come!” The door opens, and I hear a neighbor's footsteps. Eda strikes my back again. I can feel her palm land, but no air enters. I catch my daughter's sleeve. Eda says, “I'm here. Look at me.”

Eda's voice is close, but I cannot answer. My fingers slip from her sleeve. My daughter calls my name. I try once more to draw breath, but my throat is blocked. After that sound, I can no longer see my daughter's face.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1741, at the age of 69, Zeynep choked on bread at her daughter Eda's house and could not regain her breath. With a neighbor's help, Eda laid her mother down, then could not bring herself to clear the table for some time. She could not erase either the day her mother had failed to come when she was ill or the days when they drank tea together again. Her coworker Naziye heard the news, came to the house, and sat beside Eda for a while. Zeynep had spent many years attending to guests, and she had also once refused her daughter's request to protect her own wages. Her life ended with both of those sides of her left behind. The record of past lives writes down both women's memories together and closes this chapter.
finalMoment.artAlt: Istanbul, 1741, the dining table at her daughter Eda's house, seen through the doorway in daylight. The 69-year-old Zeynep touches her throat after choking as she swallows bread, while Eda stares at her in alarm from across the table

card.name: Luisa
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Luisa of Levuka. You grew up helping with your mother's harbor trade, then ran a small lodging house with your younger sister, Litia. You continued renting rooms even after the capital moved to Suva. While helping a guest in trouble, you made your niece Ana use her wages, and in old age, you and Ana set boundaries around money.
card.title: The Morning Two Trunks Were Switched
card.role: Owner of a small lodging house near the harbor
card.world: Levuka, British Colony of Fiji, 1882
card.flavor: Before the ship departed, the knots on two similar trunks were reversed
card.opening: On a morning when cargo for a departing ship crowded the wharf, Luisa saw that two guests' trunks had been loaded onto different piles of luggage.
card.life: Born in 1841 in Nasova near Levuka, she helped her mother sell food to people at the harbor. As an adult, she ran a small lodging house with her younger sister, Litia. She never married, but kept Litia and her niece Ana close. After the capital moved to Suva, she reduced the number of rooms. In 1898, she gave a regular guest named Tave four weeks of room and board on credit after his work dried up, without asking Ana. Ana covered the cost of the food with her own wages and postponed her plan to sell meals separately. Tave later repaid only half. In 1902, after taking charge of some of the rooms, Ana decided she would not extend credit from her share of the money without prior discussion, and Luisa accepted that. In old age, Luisa spent her time tending the mango tree behind the house.
card.turn: A hurried porter placed the similar travel trunks of two guests bound for Suva on different piles of luggage. One held tableware for a new shop, and the other held surveying tools.
card.decision: Luisa saw the different knots beneath the handles and announced that the trunks had been switched. She left Litia to welcome the new guests and ran to the wharf.
card.cost: The trunks found their rightful owners, but by the time Luisa returned, the new guests who had been waiting had gone to another lodging house. She received no payment for the empty rooms that day.
card.after: The two departing guests laughed after recovering their belongings, but Litia and Luisa lost two new guests and recorded two empty rooms in the ledger that day. Later, when the work of the capital moved to Suva, they reduced the number of rooms and kept the lodging house going.
card.presentEcho: A mistake on a busy morning can be corrected at once, but a guest you lose may never return.
card.secondLook: Luisa saw the knots, while the porter worried about the ship's departure. Litia first counted the day's wages represented by the empty rooms.
card.unresolved: They received no payment for the two rooms from the new guests who waited and then went elsewhere. While Luisa was at the wharf, Litia also had to care for the lodging house's other guests.
card.readerQuestion: You noticed that two travel trunks were switched before the ship departed. New guests are also waiting at the lodging house door. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Luisa saw that Maria's trunk, marked with a single knot, had been placed on Bell's pile of luggage. On the other pile, she could see Bell's double knot.
signalMoments.speak: Luisa shouted toward the back of the handcart that the trunk with one knot belonged to Maria and that the other trunk had two knots.
signalMoments.connect: Luisa asked Litia to welcome the new guests, then gestured to the porter at the wharf to help her find the switched trunk.

identity.region: Levuka, British Colony of Fiji
identity.summary: She grew up helping with her mother's harbor trade and opened a lodging house with her younger sister, Litia. She continued welcoming guests after the capital moved. After extending credit to a guest and making her niece Ana pay the cost, she and Ana set boundaries around money in her old age.

Luisa · Female

profilePages.body:
Personality · She quickly remembered guests' names. When a guest she knew fell on hard times, she sometimes extended credit before asking her family.
Liked · The wind that passed through the harbor and mangoes shared in the evening
Disliked · People hiding wet shoes beneath their beds
Good at · Remembering both guests' belongings and how many days they would stay

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The small wooden bowl her mother used to hold goods
People close to her · Her younger sister Litia, her niece Ana, and Tave, a harbor worker who stayed for a long time
Life she wanted · A life where she could enjoy a peaceful evening meal with her sister even on days when guests departed

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Luisa, who ran a small lodging house in Levuka, a port town in the British Colony of Fiji. In 1882, as the work of the capital was moving to Suva, two travel trunks nearly followed the wrong owners before a ship departed. Let me tell you about that morning.

Luisa tied cords around the handles of the two trunks by the door. She made one knot on the trunk belonging to Maria, who was going to Suva to open a small restaurant, and two on Bell's trunk, as Bell was going there to do surveying work. The trunks looked so similar that they might have been ordered from the same carpenter, but one rattled with dishes while the other was heavy with iron tools.

“By evening, I'll be at my new shop.” Maria smiled. Bell took out a watch, checked it, and merely nodded. At the wharf, porters hurried to carry goods onto the ship. While Luisa urged the two guests to finish their breakfast, the trunks vanished from the doorway.

Soon, two new guests stood at the lodging house door. As Luisa searched for the keys to the empty rooms, she looked toward the wharf again. Beneath Bell's pile of luggage on a porter's handcart, a cord with a single knot swung back and forth. It was Maria's trunk. On the pile of luggage for the ship across the way, she could see a double knot. If they missed their chance now, the two guests would not open each other's luggage until they were out at sea.

signalMoments.notice: Luisa remembered that although the two trunks looked exactly alike, the knots beneath their handles were different. Maria's single knot was swinging from Bell's pile of luggage.
signalMoments.speak: “Wait, that trunk belongs to Maria!” Luisa shouted toward the back of the handcart. “There's one knot beneath the handle. The other one has two!”
signalMoments.connect: Luisa handed the room keys to her younger sister, Litia. “Welcome the new guests first.” Then she gestured to the porter to help her find the other trunk.

episode.afterSignal:
Luisa gathered her skirt and ran along the coastal road. The porter stopped his handcart. “They're both brown. How do you know which is which?” “I tied the knots myself.” When Luisa held up the cord with the single knot, the porter took the trunk off the handcart.

Maria came running. “My dishes are in there. If it falls, they'll all break.” Bell went to another pile of luggage bound for the same ship, saying she would find her own trunk. The double knot was there. But because it was about to be loaded onto the ship, another porter had to lend a hand.

Once both trunks had been set down, Maria lifted the lid of hers slightly. The tin cups inside clinked against one another. Bell checked her iron ruler, then smiled for the first time. “I nearly ended up surveying a restaurant.” Maria replied, “Then I would have served tea to my guests with an iron ruler.” The porter laughed too, but hurried back toward the ship.

Luisa watched until both people had their own trunks loaded, then returned. Litia was standing alone in front of the lodging house. “The new guests?” “I had to serve breakfast to the other guests, so I asked them to wait for a moment. They went to another house in the meantime.” Litia set two unused keys on the table. They could collect that day's room fees from no one.

“Should I have stayed to watch the door?” Luisa asked. Litia shook her head. “I didn't have enough hands either. At least the people leaving will take their own luggage.” The two sisters opened the windows of the empty rooms and let in the sea breeze. Luisa could not write a number in that day's space in the ledger and left the line blank.

Even after the people who worked in the capital moved to Suva, Levuka still had its harbor and the people who remained. Luisa reduced the number of rooms and ran the lodging house for many years, eventually handing the ledger over to Ana. She laughed when telling the story of the morning she ran to recover the two departing trunks, but Litia also remembered the two rooms that had stood empty that day.
