memories.label: Her Longtime Work
memories.detail: Giving harbor people rooms and meals and keeping the lodging ledger

memories.label: Her Favorite Time
memories.detail: Sharing mangoes with her younger sister, Litia, after tidying rooms vacated by guests

memories.label: What She Treasured
memories.detail: The small wooden bowl her mother used to serve food to guests

memories.label: What Worried Her
memories.detail: Whether there would still be guests to fill the empty rooms after the capital moved

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Don't change where the keys hang. You'll always get confused when you're in a hurry.”

memories.label: Litia's View
memories.detail: “My older sister remembered people and belongings well, but I was the first to notice the two empty rooms that day.”

memories.label: Ana's View
memories.detail: “While my aunt let Tave stay, she made me pay for his food from my wages. After I took charge of the rooms, I didn't extend credit like that.”

memories.label: Tave's View
memories.detail: “When my work dried up, Luisa gave me a room. I could only repay half the credit, and I didn't learn until later that the cost had put Ana in a difficult position.”

finalMoment.place: A seaside road in Levuka, British Colony of Fiji
finalMoment.scene:
It is 1913 on a seaside road in Levuka. After the rain stops, I walk slowly with Tave, whom I have known for many years. Tave calls for me to come to the inside of the road, saying the stones near the sea are still wet. “I heard you.” I answer and take a step. The wind stirs the hair clinging to my face. Tave, who used to work at the harbor, laughs and says he now walks more slowly than I do.

The stone beneath my foot slips. I reach for Tave's arm to catch my balance, but my fingertips only brush his clothes. My body falls off the low road. Water strikes my knees, and the wave immediately behind it washes over my shoulders. I clutch a stone. Sand slips from my hand. I try to call, “Tave!” but water enters my mouth.

Tave shouts my name from the road. He crouches and reaches out, but the current keeps him from touching me. “Call someone!” I do not know whether I shout the words or only move my lips. I try to plant my feet on the bottom again. My toes catch on a stone and my body rises once, but the next wave covers my face. The taste of salt remains in my throat. There is no room to draw breath.

I hear someone else shouting in the distance. Tave seems to have caught my arm. I try to close my hand, but there is no strength in my fingers. I lose even the rough feel of the stone. The sound of water grows louder beside my ears, and then even that sound disappears.
finalMoment.afterword: Tave and the neighbors carried Luisa out of the water, but she never started breathing again. Her life of 72 years ended in Levuka in 1913. Litia, her younger sister, arrived late and asked Tave again what had happened on the road. Her niece Ana closed the lodging house for a day and also remembered the food costs she had once paid. Tave remembered both the day Luisa extended him credit and the hand he failed to grasp at the end. Luisa remembered people's belongings and gave guests rooms, but she also made someone close to her, Ana, bear a cost without asking. This record of a past life sets down this life without letting any one person's memory cover all the others.
finalMoment.artAlt: On a seaside road in Levuka after the rain in 1913, the urgent moment when Tave reaches from the stone path toward 72-year-old Luisa as a wave sweeps her away

card.name: Rafiq
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Rafiq, raised in a bird seller's household in Agra. You cared for the court pigeons before moving with your family to Shahjahanabad. While training your coworker Nadim, you kept the wages for yourself for a time, and in old age, you handed over the paid work and looked after your neighbors' birds.
card.title: The Pigeon with the Missing Leg Band
card.world: 1650, Mughal Empire, Shahjahanabad
card.flavor: He had to check the two birds posing for the painting again
card.opening: On the day the painter came to paint two birds, Rafiq noticed that one bird's ankle was bare.
card.life: Born in Agra in 1610, he grew up helping with his father's small bird-selling business. As an adult, he cared for the court pigeons, married Arifa, and raised their daughter Amina. In 1648, he moved with his family to Shahjahanabad. At home, he played an old board game with Amina. In 1664, Rafiq taught Nadim the evening feeding and cleaning duties but kept all the wages for himself. After Nadim worked late for several months without pay, he refused to work for free. Rafiq took the duties back, then handed the paid evening work over to Nadim in 1671. Rafiq believed he had been protecting his family's income, but Nadim remembered the time he had lost. Rafiq looked after his neighbors' birds and died in 1682.
card.turn: The small metal leg band on one of the two pigeons the painter was going to paint disappeared. Rafiq could tell the birds apart by their feathers, but to everyone else, the two looked too much alike.
card.decision: Before the painting began, Rafiq reported that the leg band was missing and asked his coworker and the painter to check the birds again.
card.cost: By the time they finished checking the birds, the sunlight was fading, so the painting was postponed until the next day. Rafiq was late for the evening board game he had promised to play with his daughter.
card.after: The leg band was found in the straw on the floor of the cage. The painter posed the birds again the next day and continued the painting. That evening, Amina had finished the game with her mother, Arifa, and was putting away the pieces. She and her father set up the board again the next day.
card.presentEcho: One missing marker changed the order of the day's work and the timing of the family's evening at home.
card.secondLook: Rafiq looked at the feathers, and the painter looked for the leg band. Arifa and Amina saw one empty place.
card.unresolved: They played the missed game the next day, but Amina did not revise the outcome of the game she had already finished with her mother.
card.readerQuestion: One of two nearly identical pigeons has lost its leg band. The painter is about to begin the painting. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: Rafiq saw the white pigeon's bare ankle and checked again the short gray feather at the tip of its tail. The leg band might be somewhere inside the cage.
signalMoments.speak: “Wait. This bird's leg band has come off.” Rafiq asked the painter to check again before starting the painting.
signalMoments.connect: Rafiq asked his coworker to search through the straw with him and asked the painter to perch the two birds separately for a moment.

identity.region: Mughal Empire, Shahjahanabad
identity.summary: He grew up in a bird seller's household in Agra and cared for the court pigeons. He moved with his family to Shahjahanabad. To protect his wages, he accepted several months of unpaid late work from his coworker Nadim, and in old age, he reduced his workload.

Liked · Evenings spent placing pieces on the board with Amina
Disliked · Leaving bird feed wet
Skilled at · Telling birds apart by small differences in their wing feathers and gait

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
Treasured · The worn wooden game board he had brought from Agra
People close to him · His wife Arifa, his daughter Amina, and Nadim, who worked with him in the aviary
Life he wanted · A life with time to sit and play with his family after work
Worry · Whether his family could adjust well to an unfamiliar home and new neighbors in the new capital

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Rafiq, keeper of the court pigeons in Shahjahanabad in the Mughal Empire. One day in 1650, a painter came to paint two birds. Before he could lift his brush, one pigeon's leg band went missing. Let's go to the aviary courtyard on that day.

Every morning, Rafiq opened the aviary door and washed the feed bowls. The routine had been ingrained in him since his days selling birds with his father in Agra. That day, his coworker Nadim laid down fresh straw, and Rafiq perched two similar-looking white pigeons on a low roost. One had a slightly shorter gray feather at the tip of its tail.

The painter studied the birds for a long time, then ground his ink. “Please perch the bird with the leg band over here. I want to paint the two side by side.” Rafiq reached to pick up the nearer bird, then stopped. The leg that had always worn a small metal band was bare.

Nadim craned his head forward. “Which bird was it?” “The one with the short tail feather.” Rafiq pointed. “But without the leg band, people will ask which bird is which after I paint them.” The painter was already about to draw his first line. The sunlight lingered for long only on one side of the roost.

signalMoments.notice: Rafiq saw the white pigeon's bare ankle and checked again the short gray feather at the tip of its tail. The leg band might have disappeared somewhere inside the cage.
signalMoments.speak: “Wait. The leg band it always wore has come off.” Rafiq spoke as the painter poised his brush. “Could we check the bird again before you paint it?”
signalMoments.connect: Rafiq asked Nadim to help him turn over the straw and asked the painter to perch the two birds apart for a moment.

episode.afterSignal:
“But you said you can tell them apart by their feathers,” the painter said. Rafiq showed him the short tail feather. “I can today. But the only marker left in the painting will be what my eyes saw.” The painter put down his brush and moved the two birds to separate roosts.

Nadim cleared away the straw from the aviary floor a little at a time. At first, they found only dry feed husks. The painter rolled up his blank paper and tapped his foot, saying he had to leave for his next job. Rafiq refilled the bowl with feed so the birds would not become frightened. As more hands joined the search, the two birds ruffled their wings with growing agitation.

As the sunlight crossed the wall, Nadim cried, “Here!” A small metal ring gleamed beneath the straw. Rafiq picked up the bird with the short tail feather again and checked its leg. The painter also examined each bird in turn. “Now I can paint them.” But by then, no even light remained on the roost.

The painter said he would return the next day. Nadim laughed as he closed the aviary door. “All because of one ring, we get to do this again tomorrow.” Rafiq laughed, then remembered the game board waiting at home. He had promised Amina that he would return before evening to play a game with her. He could not leave the courtyard until he had fed the birds and finished writing in the ledger.

When he arrived home, Amina had finished a game with her mother, Arifa, and was putting the pieces into a pouch. “I won the game meant for you, Father.” Amina pointed to the empty place. When Rafiq asked, “Then shall we play again now?” Arifa held out a bowl of food. “Play tomorrow. The two of us waited a long time tonight.” Rafiq took the bowl instead of the game board.

The next day, the painter posed the two birds again and continued his painting. Rafiq returned home and set up the board with Amina, but they left in its original place one of Amina's pieces from the game she had lost to Arifa the day before. Years later, even after reducing his court duties, he looked after the birds his neighbors brought to his home. Amina remembered that her father could tell bird feathers apart at a glance, yet kept asking to replay games at home that had already ended.

memories.detail: Tending to feed and water and observing the pigeons' feathers and gait

memories.detail: “Amina, let's start a new game today instead of going back to the last one.”

memories.label: Arifa's View
memories.detail: “He hated losing at home. But when we brought out the game board, he was always the first to take his place.”

memories.label: Amina's View
memories.detail: “Father could recognize a pigeon's feathers at once, but he had trouble accepting a game I'd already won.”

memories.label: Nadim's View

finalMoment.place: Backyard of his home, Shahjahanabad, Mughal Empire
finalMoment.scene:
It is late at night in Shahjahanabad in 1682. After suffering from an upset stomach for two days, I wake from sleep and go out into the backyard. On my way back from the latrine, I stop before the threshold. My legs are trembling, and I cannot take two more steps. I clutch the doorframe and call to Arifa in the bedroom. My voice is faint, so I call her once more.

When the door opens, Arifa takes my arm. “Did you come out here alone?” Instead of answering, I point into the room. Arifa crosses the threshold first and tries to pull me inside, but my knees give way. The cold ground of the backyard touches my palms. Arifa shouts to wake the sleeping Amina.

Amina comes running and sits beside me. “Father, look at me.” I turn my head toward my daughter. I have eaten almost nothing for two days. Her face keeps blurring before my eyes. I reach for Amina's wrist, but my hand falls. Arifa tells our daughter to call a neighbor.

Amina runs toward the front gate. I try to get up, but my body will not move. Arifa slips an arm beneath my shoulders and calls my name. I draw one breath, but the next does not come. I hear Arifa's voice, but I cannot answer. My eyes close as the sound of Amina's footsteps fades into the distance.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1682, 72-year-old Rafiq died in the backyard of his Shahjahanabad home after two days of illness. When Amina returned with a neighbor, Arifa was sitting beside her husband. Nadim also came when he heard of the death, but he did not turn the wages he had lost over those months into a fond memory. Rafiq took good care of birds and loved playing with his family, but he had also treated a coworker's time as if it belonged to him. The record of this past life notes that the life has ended and leaves their different memories unchanged.
finalMoment.artAlt: A rooftop view of the backyard of a Shahjahanabad home at night in 1682. 72-year-old Rafiq stands alone, clutching the doorframe of a room lit from within

card.name: Xochitl
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Xochitl of Xochimilco. You grew flowers and raised a daughter with your husband, and even after the war, you tended the fields with your relatives. After losing your husband, you lived separately near your daughter and asked her to visit almost every day, placing a burden on your daughter's farmwork.
card.title: Two Waterways to the Flower Market
card.role: A grower and seller of flowers from chinampa fields
card.world: Xochimilco under the rule of the Mexica Triple Alliance in 1518
card.flavor: At a familiar fork, her father rowed into a different canal
card.opening: When the flower-laden boat reached a fork in the canals, Xochitl saw her father rowing away from their familiar route.
card.life: Born in Xochimilco in 1490, she tended chinampa fields with her father. She made a home with her husband, raised their daughter, and carried their harvest by boat to market. Even after the war in 1521, she returned to tending the fields with relatives. After losing her husband in 1542, she lived separately near her daughter's family. She asked her daughter to visit almost every day, so her daughter paid relatives to do her own farmwork. Beginning in 1546, her daughter came only twice a week, and Xochitl prepared her own meals and tended her small field on the other days.
card.turn: On the way to market, her father took the wrong route at a fork in the canals. Even when Xochitl spoke up, her father kept rowing at first, insisting that this route could also get them there.
card.decision: Xochitl brought the boat alongside the bank and looked at both waterways with her father, then said that this time she would take the paddle at the front.
card.cost: They were late after correcting their course, and a regular customer bought flowers elsewhere. Her father was silent for a while.
card.after: They sold the remaining flowers a little at a time to people passing through the market. On the way home, her father said he would remain in charge of the flower fields, but handed his daughter the paddle for their next trip to market.
card.presentEcho: On days when long-held duties are shared, the heart may take time to catch up even after the course has been corrected.
card.secondLook: Xochitl looked at the canals, while her father looked at the paddle that had long been in his hands. Their regular customer had to buy flowers that could not wait.
card.unresolved: Some of the flowers they failed to sell that day came home with them. Her father told his daughter to stand at the front again on the next market day, but the family remembered differently who had first taken the paddle.
card.readerQuestion: A boat carrying flowers to market enters the wrong canal. The father holding the paddle says it is fine and keeps going. What would you do?

profilePages.body:

Those closest to her · Her father, husband, daughter, and the relatives who shared the work of tending the fields

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Xochitl, who grew flowers in Xochimilco under the rule of the Mexica Triple Alliance. One morning, you loaded baskets of flowers onto a boat bound for the market with your father. On a waterway they had traveled for years, the two argued for the first time over which route to take. Let me tell you about that morning.

As the sun rose beyond the edge of the low-lying fields, Xochitl sorted the flowers into baskets by kind. Her father stood at the front of the boat and dipped the paddle into the water. “I'll stand at the front today,” Xochitl said, but her father laughed. “I traveled this route before you were born.” Xochitl sat in the back to keep the baskets from tipping.

The boat passed through a narrow canal and entered a wider waterway. On the left stood two tall trees side by side. To reach the market, they needed to turn behind them. But her father rowed along the bank on the right. The waterways branched in similar directions, so at first, even Xochitl said nothing.

A neighbor's boat passed them coming from the other direction. Seeing the flower baskets, the neighbor waved. Only then did Xochitl notice the two trees receding behind their boat. “Father, this isn't the right route.” Her father did not lift the paddle from the water. “I know. We can get there this way too.” But this canal curved between fields that led away from the market.

signalMoments.notice: Xochitl saw the two trees that always appeared on the left side of the market route receding behind the boat. She realized her father had taken a different canal.
signalMoments.speak: “Father, the route to the market is behind those trees.” Xochitl spoke loudly enough for the neighbor to hear. Her father kept hold of the paddle and did not answer for some time.
signalMoments.connect: Xochitl brought the boat alongside the bank and looked at the branching waterways with her father. “This time, let me paddle at the front, and please look after the flower baskets.”

episode.afterSignal:
Her father tried to turn the boat, driving the end of the paddle deep into the mud. As the boat struck the bank, one flower basket rocked. Xochitl caught it. “Everyone saw,” her father said quietly. “Then they must have seen the two of us finding the route too,” Xochitl replied. She suggested bringing the boat alongside the nearest bank.

The two climbed onto the bank and studied the waterways again. Beyond the two trees, boats bound for the market passed in a line. Her father stared in that direction for a long time. “Lately, it's hard to see the banks at dawn.” He spoke as if making an excuse, then handed the paddle to Xochitl. She left a place for him to sit and stood at the front.

By the time they reached the market, the customer who had been waiting since morning had already selected goods from another basket. “You're late today,” the customer said. Xochitl showed her a small bundle of flowers, but the customer shook her head. Her father stepped back empty-handed. The two sold their remaining flowers a little at a time to customers passing by.

Around noon, Xochitl took out their food. Looking at the basket of flowers they had failed to sell to their regular customer, her father began, “If I hadn't taken the other route...” Then he stopped. “Next time, I'll look for the trees first,” Xochitl said. Her father did not answer at once. He plucked off a crumpled petal and set it afloat on the water.

On the boat ride home, her father retied the cords around the flower baskets. “I'm still faster in the fields.” “I know,” Xochitl answered as she paddled. “Stand at the front again when we go to the next market.” After saying this, her father set aside one bundle of wet flowers for them to take home.

That day, Xochitl returned home carrying the flowers they had failed to sell. Years later, the war reduced the number of days they could go to the market, and the family had to return to tending the fields with relatives. But Xochitl's daughter remembered that earlier morning as the day her grandfather and mother rode in the same boat yet saw different waterways. Family members told slightly different stories about who first took the paddle on the next market day.

finalMoment.place: Xochitl's home, Xochimilco, New Spain
finalMoment.scene:
It is evening in Xochimilco in 1559. I am preparing supper with my cousin in my own home, close to my daughter's house. Today is not one of the days my daughter visits. While my cousin washes the dishes, I warm the leftover food beside the hearth. “I'll do that,” my cousin says. “Sit down.” I pick up a bowl and rise.

Then my chest tightens fiercely from within. I try to set the bowl down, but the strength drains from my fingers, and it falls to the floor. My cousin turns around. “Xochitl, where does it hurt?” I try to answer, but only take a short breath. My cousin grasps my arm and lowers me to the floor. Even leaning back, my chest feels constricted.

My cousin asks a neighbor outside the open door to fetch my daughter. The neighbor's footsteps recede. I reach toward the empty bowl. My cousin brings water and moistens my lips with a little of it. Still, I cannot draw a full breath. “Your daughter will be here soon,” my cousin says.

I try to stand and greet my daughter. Even when I brace my palms against the floor, my arms cannot support me. My cousin holds my shoulders. I hear food bubbling on the hearth. I try to tell my cousin to take the bowl off the fire, but the words will not come together. I draw one breath and try to take another, but my chest does not move. My cousin's hand remains on my shoulder.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1559, sixty-nine-year-old Xochitl died in her own home in Xochimilco after her chest suddenly tightened and she struggled to breathe. The exact illness is unknown. Her daughter arrived with the neighbor and asked her cousin what her mother had been trying to do at the end. The cousin replied that the two of them had been preparing supper. As her daughter put her mother's home in order, she also remembered the days when she had paid relatives to tend her fields while she cared for her mother. The record of past lives states that Xochitl's life ended here. It preserves both the time she spent living in and protecting her own home, and the time and wages her daughter paid.
finalMoment.artAlt: An evening inside a home in Xochimilco in 1559, seen from a low viewpoint near the hearth. At the moment sixty-nine-year-old Xochitl clutches her chest and drops a bowl, her cousin turns to look from a distance

card.name: Eliška Nováková
card.home: Prague in the Kingdom of Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Eliška Nováková, who lived in Prague in the Kingdom of Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire, working as an assistant in an apothecary and alchemical workshop. She learned distillation and how to keep medicinal records at a Prague apothecary. She hid failed experiments to meet her patron's expectations, but later refused to take part in a fake demonstration of making gold.
card.title: The Red Powder That Did Not Become Gold
card.role: Assistant in an apothecary and alchemical workshop
card.world: 1609 · Prague in the Kingdom of Bohemia, Holy Roman Empire
card.flavor: A Prague workshop's promise to make gold—and its ledger
card.opening: In Prague in 1609, Eliška knew that the golden piece to be placed before the patron had already been brought from somewhere else.
card.life: She learned distillation and how to keep medicinal records at a Prague apothecary. She hid failed experiments to meet her patron's expectations, but later refused to take part in a fake demonstration of making gold. By recording failed experiments as nearly successful, she caused Tomáš to repeat work that exposed him to toxic fumes. Tomáš developed a severe cough and took time off work.
card.turn: Her desire to protect the patron's funding and her coworkers' jobs clashed with her responsibility to expose the false demonstration.
card.decision: Eliška revealed the piece and the ledger, stopping the demonstration.
card.cost: By recording failed experiments as nearly successful, she caused Tomáš to repeat work that exposed him to toxic fumes. Tomáš developed a severe cough and took time off work.
card.after: The workshop closed, and its workers had to find other ways to earn a living.
card.presentEcho: An opportunity preserved by hiding failure may come at the cost of another person's health and choices.
card.secondLook: Eliška revealed the truth, but she had remained silent until after Tomáš was harmed.
card.unresolved: No one knows whether Jakub made the same promise in another city.
card.readerQuestion: You know that the golden piece before the patron was not made today. What would you do first?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Eliška, who went back and forth between a Prague apothecary and an alchemical workshop.

Jakub promised the patron that adding red powder would turn cheap metal into gold. But Eliška's ledger showed that the same experiment had failed three times.

Just before the demonstration, Tomáš said he had seen Jakub take a golden piece from a drawer and hide it beside the crucible.

signalMoments.notice: Eliška confirmed that the cut face of the golden piece did not match today's crucible mold.

episode.afterSignal:
The patron closed his money pouch and left the workshop. Jakub angrily accused Eliška of destroying everyone's jobs.

Marta divided some of the apothecary work between Eliška and Tomáš, but their income fell.

Beside the failed experiments, Eliška recorded Tomáš's cough and the time they had worked without ventilation. They had not made gold, but the ledger no longer pretended that failure was success.

finalMoment.place: Eliška's apothecary in Prague
finalMoment.scene:
In the autumn of 1622, Eliška had been feverish for 5 days in the back room of her Prague apothecary. Marta the apothecary opened the window and changed the damp cloth. Eliška pulled the experimental ledger closer from beside her bed.

“Throw away the bottle of red powder. Don't let Tomáš touch it.” She tried to write the date, but the pen tip only scratched the paper. Marta took the ledger and read aloud the failed experiments and ventilation times in her place.

At sunset, Eliška's fever rose higher. Marta tried to give her water, but she could not swallow. Eliška heard the ledger close and let go. She stopped breathing before nightfall.
finalMoment.afterword: Eliška died in 1622 after suffering from an epidemic fever for several days. The surviving records are not enough to identify the exact disease. Marta and Tomáš carried on the apothecary and recorded successes and failures in the same ledger. Jakub blamed her to the end for taking away their jobs. The characters and events set against the background of alchemy and pharmacy in early modern Prague are fictional.

card.name: Inga Larsen
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Inga Larsen of Kristiania. You learned sewing from your mother and cut cloth in a textile workshop. You shared a room with your younger sister before they each found places of their own, and after working at several workplaces, you spent your later years near your niece.
card.title: The Blank Beside the Erased Name
card.world: 1905, Kristiania, Norway
card.flavor: A coworker asked to have her signature erased
card.opening: Just before the lunch bell rang, Inga pointed to Liv's name on the signature sheet Marta was holding. Liv had asked for the name to be erased.
card.life: Born in Kristiania in 1871, she helped her mother with sewing. She worked in a textile workshop from 1891. When she shared a room with her younger sister Astrid in 1898, she chose one close to her own workplace, making her sister's commute longer. Astrid began living separately in 1902, but the two often ate dinner together. Inga worked at several workplaces and, by 1940, lived near her niece.
card.turn: On the day when women, unable to take part in the referendum, gathered signatures to express their wishes, Liv wrote her name and then asked to have it erased. Marta, who was collecting the signatures, worried about having to collect the other names again too.
card.decision: Inga did not speak for Liv and set the signature sheet down for a moment. After giving Liv time to speak for herself, she crossed out that line and asked the others whether they would write their names again on a fresh sheet.
card.cost: Lunch ended while they collected the names again. Inga missed the deadline for her bundle of cloth, lost part of her piecework pay, and spoke less with the friend who had been collecting signatures.
card.after: The others signed the new sheet again. The line where Liv's name would have gone remained blank, and Liv did not write anything else that day. Inga returned to cutting cloth. The next day, Liv thanked Inga.
card.presentEcho: Even when voices are gathered together, each person may need room to decide whether to leave their own name.
card.secondLook: The friend collecting signatures worried that if a name disappeared, women's wishes would seem weaker. Liv thought of her brother living in Sweden, and Inga saw that the two women viewed the same sheet differently.
card.unresolved: Even Inga did not know whether Liv later signed another sheet. The awkwardness that the day's conversation left between two coworkers did not disappear overnight either.
card.readerQuestion: A coworker writes her name on a petition gathering women's wishes, then asks to have it erased. The others want to submit it quickly. What would you do?

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Inga Larsen, who worked in a textile workshop in Kristiania in 1905. That year, Norway declared that it would end its personal union with Sweden, and a referendum of male voters was approaching. Women could not vote, so they gathered names. A signature sheet was placed on the lunch table in a small workshop too. Let me tell you about that day.

During lunch, when the machines had briefly stopped, Inga picked loose threads from a bundle of cloth. Her coworker Marta placed a sheet of paper and an ink bottle on the long table. “We can put our wishes in writing too.” The workers put down their bread and lined up. Inga read aloud the sentence at the top of the sheet. These were names lending support to the decision to end the union with Sweden.

Liv took the pen in front of Inga. Her handwriting slanted slightly, but she wrote her full name. Just as Marta was about to pass the sheet to the next person, Liv held out her palm. “Wait. Take my name off.” Startled, Marta stopped her pen. “You just wrote it.” The people in line behind them wanted to finish signing before the lunch bell rang.

Liv looked at the brick building outside the window as she chose her words. “My brother lives in Sweden. What if there's a war?” Marta gripped the edge of the sheet. “I'm worried about my brother too. But this petition is our voice.” Liv nodded, but she did not pick up the pen again. Before Marta could fold the sheet, Inga pointed to Liv's name.

signalMoments.notice: Inga noticed that Liv was not looking out the window and choosing her words because she had made a mistake in her handwriting. Liv was worried about her brother living in Sweden and the possibility of fighting.
signalMoments.speak: Inga said, “It's her name, so Liv should decide. Let's listen for a moment.” She asked Marta to give Liv time to speak for herself before folding the sheet.
signalMoments.connect: Inga placed the sheet in the middle of the table so Liv and Marta faced each other. She asked the coworkers lined up behind them whether they were willing to write their names again on a fresh sheet.

episode.afterSignal:
Marta let out a long breath. “If we redo this sheet, everyone will have to line up again.” Inga said, “Then let's ask them too.” One of the workers behind them was first to say, “I'll sign again,” while another stuffed the rest of her bread into her mouth and turned back toward the table. Not everyone looked pleased.

Liv did not wait for Inga to speak for her. “I don't want to leave my name on it right now.” Marta asked, “That doesn't mean you don't care about the country, does it?” “No. But I don't want to put my name on this sheet today.” Marta drew a line through Liv's name. Worried about whether they could submit the names written below it as they were, she took out a fresh sheet.

Inga did not get to eat her bread while they collected the names again. Work began in the outer room, and the sound of cloth being cut resumed. Marta pressed a finger against the end of the new sheet. “The fewer names we have, the easier it will be for people to ignore us.” Inga could not answer her right away. Liv heard Marta's concern too.

The people wrote their names again on the fresh sheet. Inga did too. The place where Liv had stood was naturally left blank. When the line ended, the three women hurried back to work. Inga's bundle of cloth was still only half cut. The supervisor deducted from that day's piecework pay the share for the bundle she failed to finish by the evening deadline.

On the way home, Marta tucked the signature sheet inside her clothes and walked quickly. When Inga came up beside her, Marta said, “You understand why I was in a hurry, don't you?” “I do. And I know why you were angry.” Marta said nothing more. Liv walked several paces behind them, but she did not call out to Inga.

The next day, the three women measured cloth at the same table again. As Liv handed over the scissors, she said, “Thank you for yesterday,” and Inga replied, “Let's finish today's cloth first.” The awkwardness with Marta lasted a long time. Inga did not ask whether Liv signed on another day. The record of that past life does not preserve the answer either.

As the years passed, Inga moved to another workshop and taught a young worker how to read the grain of cloth. Women who once could not write their own names on a ballot later gained the right to vote. Even so, the different feelings around that lunch table in 1905 were not combined into a single line. Inga long remembered that small pause when her scissors had stopped over the cloth.

finalMoment.place: Oslo, Kingdom of Norway
finalMoment.scene:
On an autumn evening in Oslo in 1948, I set three plates on the table in my room. My niece has brought a pot of soup, and my younger sister Astrid is due a little later. When we were young, Astrid and I shared the rent and ate our meals together. Now we live in different homes. Even so, we meet like this a few times a month. I tell my niece, “Let's put Astrid's place near the door. She gets short of breath after climbing the stairs.”

Steam rises when my niece lifts the lid from the pot. I reach toward the cupboard to take out a water glass. I fail to grasp it, and it falls to the floor. The sound of it shattering is loud. My niece turns around. “Aunt, are you hurt?” “No, I...” The rest of the words will not leave my mouth. I look at my fingertips and see that my right hand is touching the cupboard door but will not move.

I try to point my niece toward the chair. My arm will barely rise, and I lean against the cupboard. My niece supports me around the waist and seats me in the chair. “Just a moment. I'll call someone downstairs.” I want to tell her Astrid will be here soon. I grip my niece's sleeve with my left hand, but I cannot say the name. My niece says, “I know. I'll stay here,” then opens the door and calls to the neighbor downstairs.

The neighbor goes out to find a doctor. My niece steps away from the broken glass on the floor and sits in front of me. Of the three plates on the table, one is still empty. I squeeze my niece's hand once, then lose my grip. My niece calls my name. I hear someone climbing the stairs. Could it be Astrid? I turn my head to check, but the door before me blurs. I do not hear the footsteps after that.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1948, Inga Larsen died beside her niece in her room in Oslo after suddenly becoming unable to finish speaking. Her younger sister Astrid arrived late that evening. Unable to clear away the empty plate, her niece wondered for a long time what her aunt had been trying to say. Astrid once walked a long way to work from a room close to Inga's workplace. Even after the two began living separately, they ate dinner together. That day, Astrid was unable to share one last meal with Inga. The record of that past life preserves both the table set with three plates and the time the two sisters spent living together and apart. Inga's life ended here.
finalMoment.artAlt: An evening in a small room in Oslo, Norway, in 1948, where 77-year-old Inga Larsen suddenly loses control of her body and her niece seats her in a chair and calls the downstairs neighbor

card.name: Josu
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Josu of Abomey. The boy who helped in the fields became a worker who repaired market awnings. When his daughter moved to another region, he refused to see her off, but later went to visit her. He grew old with his wife and longtime friend, doing small repairs.
card.title: The Shade No One Claimed
card.world: Abomey, Kingdom of Dahomey, 1760
card.flavor: Two merchants' awning came loose just before the rain
card.opening: Before the rain came, two merchants began by arguing that the awning's post belonged to each of them.
card.life: Born near Abomey in 1724, he learned from his older brother how to work with wood and rope. As a young man, he moved closer to the market, where he repaired awnings and stalls while raising a daughter with his wife. During seasons when work was scarce, he helped in the fields back home. When his daughter moved to another region in 1784, he refused to see her off, leaving his wife and daughter to share the luggage. Several years later, he visited his daughter, and in old age he made a living doing small repairs.
card.turn: As dark clouds rolled in, the knot of an awning stretched over two shops came loose. They had to secure it before the baskets of grain got wet, but the two merchants argued over who had put up the rope first.
card.decision: Josu had the two merchants hold opposite sides of the awning. Then he unwound dry rope from a new awning he was supposed to deliver that day and retied the loose knot. The grain merchant moved the first basket to the side the rain could not reach.
card.cost: The grain was saved, but reweaving the new awning delayed the delivery. The customer reduced the payment, and Josu explained to his wife why he had received fewer shell coins.
card.after: Even after the rain stopped, the merchants could not agree on who should call the awning theirs. On the next market day, each of them tied a new rope to the same post.
card.presentEcho: Even when people are fighting over an object, you can first look after whatever is directly beneath it.
card.secondLook: The grain merchant said the post was his, and the basket merchant said he had bought the rope. Neither wanted the awning to fall on his side. When Josu's customer received the promised new awning late, he reduced the payment.
card.unresolved: No account remains of anyone deciding who owned that awning. Nor did Josu ever recover the wages he lost that day.
card.readerQuestion: Just before it rains, the rope of an awning shared by two merchants comes loose. While both argue that they own the post and rope, the goods beneath it are about to get wet. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: Josu saw where the awning's knot had come loose and the dry rope on the new awning he was supposed to deliver that day. If he used the new rope, he could shelter the goods in both shops.
signalMoments.speak: Josu said, “Decide who owns it after the rain stops. For now, both of you hold the rope.” Despite their unhappy faces, the two merchants each took hold of one side.
signalMoments.connect: At Josu's words, the grain merchant and the basket merchant each held one side of the awning. While both men had their arms raised, Josu retied the rope around the post with the new cord.

setting.polity: The Kingdom of Dahomey, which paid tribute to the Oyo Empire

identity.region: Abomey, Kingdom of Dahomey, which paid tribute to the Oyo Empire
identity.summary: He grew up on a farm near Abomey and repaired awnings in the market. When his daughter moved far away, he refused to see her off, but later went to visit her. He grew old with his wife and friend, doing small repairs.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Josu · Male
1724~1795 · 71 years old
Born near Abomey · Died in Abomey
Work · Repairing wooden posts and awnings in the market
Life · He grew up in a farming household and learned about wood and rope from his older brother. He worked in the Abomey market and lived with his wife, daughter, and friend. When his daughter moved far away, he refused to see her off, but visited her several years later. When work was scarce, he helped in the fields back home, and in old age he did small repairs.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · At work, he was quick to act, but at home, even after hearing that his daughter was moving far away, he could not accept it for some time.
What he liked · The brief sound a new rope made when pulled taut
What he enjoyed · Walking with his friend and talking about funny things that had happened on the previous market day
What he did well · Reusing short pieces of wood that were nearly thrown away by cutting them to the right length

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
What he treasured · The old carving knife his older brother gave him
Those closest to him · His wife, his daughter, and the friend who shared his workplace for many years
The life he wanted · A small house with no leaks and evening meals with his family
His worry · Whether there would still be work for him when his body weakened and he could no longer lift heavy posts

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Josu, who repaired market awnings in Abomey, the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey, in 1760. The market where people displayed their goods and bargained over prices was his workplace. From Josu's long life, I will tell you about the day a single rain cloud covered two market shops at once.

Josu entered the market with a new awning strapped to his back. Though the sun was still visible, one side of the sky was quickly darkening. The grain merchant pushed his baskets farther inside, while the basket merchant next door tugged on a rope tied in his own space. Snap—the old knot came loose. One side of the awning dropped over both men's goods.

“Why are you pulling my post with your rope?” shouted the grain merchant. “I bought that rope. And I put up the post!” the basket merchant shot back. Josu caught the falling edge of the awning on his arm. A customer started to move a basket of grain, then stopped at the sound of their argument. The first thunder rumbled in the distance.

“Both of you, come here,” Josu called, but neither man moved. He examined the loose knot by the post. He could tie it if he had just one more length of rope. The new awning strapped to his back had plenty of dry rope wrapped around it. But if he unwound that rope, it would be hard to keep his promise to deliver the awning to his customer by that evening.

signalMoments.notice: Before looking at the baskets that would get wet, Josu looked at the loose knot hanging beneath the post. He also realized that the two men would have to hold opposite sides for him to fix it. He found the end of the dry rope on the new awning.
signalMoments.speak: Josu said, “Talk about who bought it after the rain stops. Right now, each of you hold one side.” Still glaring at each other, the two merchants each took a step toward the post.
signalMoments.connect: Josu placed one rope in the grain merchant's hand and held the opposite side out to the basket merchant. “This knot will only reach if both of you pull.” The two men's arms rose to the same height.

episode.afterSignal:
Raindrops made little dots in the dirt. Josu untied the knot on the new awning strapped to his back. “Doesn't that belong to another customer?” the basket merchant asked. “It does,” Josu said. He unwound one more loop of rope. The grain merchant fell silent for a moment, then moved the first basket beneath the post farther inside.

While Josu wrapped the new rope around the post, the two merchants pulled from opposite sides. When the wind pushed the awning, the grain merchant's hand slipped. The basket merchant braced his arm with an elbow. “Don't let go.” The two men did not look at each other. Josu tightened the final knot and stepped back.

Soon the rain came down hard. The grain did not get wet, and the baskets stayed dry. Only the three men's backs were soaked through. The basket merchant laughed. “We caught the rain before the awning did.” The grain merchant almost laughed too, but stopped. “It's still my post.” “You weren't the one who bought the rope.” Their argument started all over again.

Josu took the awning he was supposed to deliver home and wove in a new rope. There was no way he could avoid being late that evening. His wife took the wet cloth and hung it up, asking, “What will you tell the customer?” Josu said, “That I was late because I kept the rain off someone else's goods.” His wife asked in return, “Will that get you the full payment?” Josu could not answer.

The next day, the customer accepted the awning but paid fewer shell coins because it had arrived later than promised. Josu did not argue. When he came home and showed his wife the amount he had lost, she nodded, and together they twisted the remaining strands into rope. The loss did not simply disappear.

On the next market day, the two merchants again talked about who owned the awning. But this time, the grain merchant brought a new rope for the left side, and the basket merchant brought one for the right. Josu saw them from a distance and smiled. He could not decide the answer to the question of ownership for them, but he thought he knew whose hands to borrow when it rained.

The Record of Past Lives does not preserve the name of that awning's owner. Josu, too, was left with fewer shell coins than he had been promised. Even so, the sound he remembered was not the thunder, but the taut vibration he heard when all three of them pulled the rope together.

memories.detail: Repairing posts and awnings in the market and reusing leftover wood and rope elsewhere

memories.label: His Favorite Times

memories.label: His Wife's View
memories.detail: “He never hid a loss from me when he came home. But whenever he suffered a loss, I was the one who figured out how we would keep living.”

memories.label: His Daughter's View
memories.detail: “On the day I left, Father did not walk with me. Several years later, he came to visit me, and after that, he was always the first to ask how I was.”

memories.label: His Longtime Friend's View
memories.detail: “Even when he grew too weak to lift a post, he could still see which rope would break first.”

finalMoment.place: Abomey, Kingdom of Dahomey, which paid tribute to the Oyo Empire
finalMoment.scene:
It is night in Abomey in 1795. I have had no strength for several days and lie on a mat inside the house. My daughter, who lives far away, arrived yesterday. She says she must return home tomorrow. I heard her say it once during the day and once in the evening. My wife sits behind me and supports my body. My daughter holds a bowl of water and studies my face.

“Can't you stay just one more day?” I ask my daughter. Before she can answer, my wife speaks. “She has a home of her own to return to and care for.” My wife is not trying to drive our daughter away. She is frustrated because I keep forgetting how far our daughter must travel. I nod, but that does not erase my disappointment. My daughter says, “I'll see how things are in the morning and decide.”

My throat is dry, and I reach toward the bowl. My daughter brings it closer, and my wife raises my shoulders. I swallow a little water, then stop. I cough, and when I lie down again, my chest heaves. My daughter sets down the bowl. “Rest. We'll talk tomorrow.” I want to walk with my daughter when she leaves in the morning. Even if I can no longer walk the whole way, I want to at least go beyond the door.

“You should rest too,” I try to tell my wife, but my voice barely comes out. My wife takes my hand and says, “I'm here.” My daughter also sits in front of me, cradling the bowl in both hands. Each breath takes longer than the one before. When my daughter starts to rise, I lift my hand a little. She sits down again. I look at each of them in turn. I open my mouth to take another breath, but my chest does not move.
finalMoment.afterword: That night, Josu died at his home in Abomey with his wife and daughter watching over him. Unable to decide when to return, his daughter stayed longer. His wife made a place for her. Years before, when their daughter left, Josu had not seen her off, and his wife and daughter had shared the luggage. This time, his daughter witnessed her father's final breath. His wife also remembered the days when they had counted together the insufficient money Josu brought home. His longtime friend recalled the times they laughed together on days when they did not work. The Record of Past Lives leaves in this chapter the bowl of water his daughter set down and the next morning that never came.
finalMoment.artAlt: Inside a modest home in Abomey, Kingdom of Dahomey, in 1795, 71-year-old Josu lies on his mat at night, reaching toward his daughter's bowl of water while his wife supports his body

card.name: Lotte Neumann
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Lotte Neumann of Berlin. Born to a baker's family, you ran a small shop with your husband. After the war, you reopened it with your daughter, and for a time you kept putting off plans with Greta because you handled orders first. In old age, you cut back on bookkeeping and often met with Greta.
card.title: The Birthday Without a Cake
card.world: West Berlin During the 1948 Blockade
card.flavor: When the bakery closed, uninvited guests came in
card.opening: While her granddaughter Eva asked about the cake, Lotte put off answering. Soon, three friends Eva had invited stood at the bakery door.
card.life: Born in Berlin in 1888, she learned measuring and bookkeeping in her father's bakery. She ran a small shop with her husband and raised a daughter. After the shop was damaged in the war and she lost her husband, she reopened it with her daughter. In 1953, even though Lotte was the one who first made plans to play cards with Greta, she postponed them several times because of shop orders. Greta stopped waiting. After Lotte cut back on bookkeeping in 1956, the two played cards every week.
card.turn: On her granddaughter's seventh birthday, Lotte put off saying that she had no ingredients to make a cake. Meanwhile, her granddaughter invited the neighborhood children to the bakery.
card.decision: Lotte did not pretend ordinary bread was cake. After clearing the display counter, she lit the one candle she had saved and welcomed the paper crowns and stories the children had brought.
card.cost: Her granddaughter fell silent for a while when she heard there was no cake. Her daughter was also angry that her mother had not told them sooner, and the candle Lotte had saved for so long burned away completely that night.
card.after: After the children left, Eva smoothed out the crumpled crown and took it home. The bakery's circumstances were unchanged the next day, but Lotte told her daughter she would no longer put off difficult conversations.
card.presentEcho: Even when you cannot prepare for a happy day, you can honestly say what is missing and find time to create something together.
card.secondLook: To her granddaughter, the cake mattered more than the candle, and to her daughter, what mattered was telling the child before she was disappointed. Lotte was ashamed to face a birthday empty-handed.
card.unresolved: There is no proof that her granddaughter remembered that birthday as the best day. Nor could Lotte and her daughter immediately forget how late the explanation came.
card.readerQuestion: Your granddaughter has invited her friends to her birthday, but you have no ingredients to make a cake. The children are at the door. What would you do first?

signalMoments.notice: Lotte saw the one candle left beneath the display counter and the crumpled invitation in Eva's hand. The 3 children Eva had invited were standing at the door.
signalMoments.speak: Lotte crouched to her granddaughter's eye level and said, “I couldn't make a cake. I should have told you sooner.” Her granddaughter set down the paper crown.
signalMoments.connect: Lotte asked the children to each tell a story about Eva. Marta moved the table after clearing away the bread, and one child gave Eva a paper crown they had made.

setting.polity: The American sector of Berlin, a city divided into 4 Allied zones

identity.region: The American sector of Allied-occupied Berlin
identity.summary: She grew up in a Berlin baker's family and ran a bakery with her husband. After the war, she reopened the shop with her daughter. She postponed plans with Greta several times because of orders, but in old age, they met regularly.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Lotte Neumann · Female
1888–1962 · Age 74
Born in Berlin · Died in West Berlin
Work · Neighborhood baker, later responsible for the order ledger
Life · She learned measuring and bookkeeping in her father's bakery. She ran a small shop with her husband and raised a daughter. After the war, she reopened the shop with her daughter. She put orders first and postponed plans with her longtime neighbor Greta several times. In old age, she cut back on bookkeeping and played cards with Greta every week.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · Worried that the shop might close again, she put orders first. Even after making her friend wait, she was always the first to laugh at a joke.
Loved · The faint crackling sound of bread crust as it cooled
Enjoyed · Remembering old customers' nicknames with her daughter in the closed shop
Good at · Calculating exactly how many loaves could be baked with limited ingredients

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
Treasured · A short candle saved from the day the shop reopened
Those closest to her · Her daughter Marta, her 7-year-old granddaughter Eva, and Greta, a neighbor she had known since before the war
The life she wanted · A life in which her daughter could choose for herself whether to continue running the shop
Worry · Whether they would have to close again if supplies and fuel were cut off

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Lotte Neumann, who ran a small bakery in the American sector of Berlin in 1948. While the routes into the city were blocked, food and fuel were scarce, and the bakery carefully calculated how much it could bake with the flour that arrived. Let me tell you about the evening of your granddaughter's seventh birthday during that long season.

That afternoon, Lotte took the last loaf from the display counter. Her granddaughter Eva pressed her nose to the glass. “Grandma, where's my cake?” Instead of answering, Lotte closed the ledger. There was not enough butter or eggs, and she had no intention of taking flour meant for bread to make a cake. But she had been unable to say so all morning.

Her daughter Marta asked as she stacked empty baskets, “You still haven't told her?” Sweeping up breadcrumbs, Lotte said, “I'll tell her after we close.” Just then, the bell outside the door rang. 3 children Eva's age stood there wearing paper hats. Eva squared her shoulders. “I invited them. Today, our house is a birthday shop.”

Marta looked at Lotte. Lotte searched beside the oven and stared at the remaining flour sack. Only enough flour to draw a picture with one finger remained at the bottom of the empty sack. Would dusting it over bread make it look like a white cake? The children would know as soon as they took a bite. Beneath the display counter was one short candle she had saved from the day the shop reopened.

signalMoments.notice: As Lotte took out the candle, she saw the crumpled note in Eva's hand. “Come to the bakery. I'm turning 7.” Eva had gathered people first, not a cake.
signalMoments.speak: Lotte crouched in front of Eva. “There is no cake. I should have told you this morning.” Taking off her hat, Eva asked, “Then why did my friends come?” Lotte answered, “Because you asked them to.”
signalMoments.connect: Lotte asked the children who had come, “Do each of you have a short story to tell Eva?” Marta moved the table cleared of bread to the center, and the children straightened one another's paper hats.

episode.afterSignal:
Eva was silent for a long time. When Lotte said, “If we arrange the bread in a circle, maybe it'll look like a cake,” Marta shook her head. “Mother, what good will changing the shape do?” Lotte put the bread back in the basket. The loudest sound in the shop was Eva crumpling her paper hat.

Once they closed the door and cleared the display counter, a small table stood in the middle of the room. The first child held out a paper crown. “Mine is too big. It'll fit Eva perfectly.” The second child acted out the time Eva had read the writing on the school blackboard backward and made everyone laugh. Eva laughed briefly, then bit her lip. “But there still isn't a cake.” Lotte said, “That's right.”

Marta divided the warm tea she had saved for herself among small cups. Someone heard the sound of a plane passing outside the window and said, “Even the sky is noisy today.” Lotte took the candle from beneath the display counter. She had saved it in case it was needed on the day they reopened, when there had been no electricity. Marta said, “But you were saving that.” “Today is a day to use it too.” Lotte lit the candle.

The children took turns telling stories. One was about how Eva had refused to step aside for a neighbor's large dog even though she was afraid, and another was about how the smallest child had learned to write from Eva. The paper crown passed from head to head. When Lotte's turn came, everyone looked at her. “When I was 7, I was mixing cake batter and mistook salt for sugar.” The children laughed as if jeering. “Did you eat it?” “1 bite. My father took 2.” This time, Eva laughed for a long while too.

As the candle burned shorter, Lotte set it on the wooden breadboard. Eva clasped both hands. “Cake next year?” Lotte did not readily make a promise. “When next year comes, we'll think about it together.” Even with a sulky face, Eva blew out the candle in 1 breath. Everyone clapped, and for a moment the smell of smoke mingled with the smell of bread.

After the children left, Marta said, “If I'd known there wouldn't be a cake, I would have told Eva during the day.” Picking off the remains of the candle base, Lotte nodded. “I was ashamed, so I put it off.” Marta did not scold her further, but she did not smile either. Eva smoothed out the crown, tucked it against her chest, and went home.

The next morning, Lotte once again measured the flour and wrote in the shop ledger. The candle did not return, and the bakery's circumstances did not change. Lotte did not know how Eva would remember her birthday. She only told her daughter that the next time she had something difficult to say, she would say it before her granddaughter gathered friends outside the door.

The record of that past life does not say whether Eva missed the cake from that day or treasured the paper crown longer. To Lotte, both were true. There was no cake, and there was also an evening when people gathered for her granddaughter.

memories.detail: Matching the amount of bread baked to the order ledger and welcoming customers at the shop

memories.label: Favorite Time
memories.detail: Evenings spent listening to bread cool and remembering old customers' nicknames with her daughter

memories.label: Treasured Object

memories.label: What She Worried About
memories.detail: The fear that supplies and fuel would be cut off again, forcing the shop to close

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “Count out as much bread as we can bake, and invite only as many guests as we can count.”

memories.label: Her Daughter Marta's Assessment
memories.detail: “It was thanks to Mother that we reopened the shop. But she always waited far too long to share bad news.”

memories.label: Her Granddaughter Eva's Assessment
memories.detail: “On the day Grandma couldn't make a cake, she told me a funny story about salty bread. I remember being upset that day too.”

memories.label: A Longtime Customer's Assessment
memories.detail: “She wasn't someone who cheated people on quantities. But she hardly ever let anyone see her worries.”

memories.label: Her Neighbor Greta's Assessment
memories.detail: “Lotte was the one who suggested meeting on Thursday, but she postponed it again and again because of orders. Later, we played cards every week, but by then I was also spending time with other neighbors.”

finalMoment.place: A home in West Berlin
finalMoment.scene:
My small home in West Berlin in 1962. I have had no strength for several days and have not even been able to go to the shop. Today, my longtime neighbor Greta is supposed to come over for a game of cards. As soon as she opens the door, Greta studies my face. “We can skip it today.” “Let's play just 1 game. This time, I'm going to win.” Smiling, I pull out a chair at the dining table.

We have visited each other's homes since before the war. After I lost my husband and reopened the bakery, I kept using work at the shop as an excuse to put off sitting down with Greta. For the past few years, we have met every Thursday. Today, as Greta shuffles the cards, I count my hand. My hands are weak, and 1 card falls under the table. When Greta tries to pick it up for me, I say, “I'll do it,” and bend down. I quickly grow short of breath and lean back in the chair again.

Greta sets down the deck. “Should I call Marta?” My daughter is at the shop. I remember Eva saying she would stop by tomorrow to show me the new dance she had learned. I try to say, “I'll be better tomorrow,” but the sentence breaks off. Even when I breathe in, it does not feel like enough. Greta takes my hand and heads for the door to call a neighbor. “I'll be right back. Don't get up.” I nod.

On the table, 2 cards I have not yet played lie face down. Outside the door, I hear Greta asking a neighbor to find a doctor. When Greta returns, she sits beside me and supports my back. “I'm here.” I open my mouth to answer, but no sound comes out. I try to take 1 more breath. Greta's hand rests on my shoulder. I look at that hand, then close my eyes.
finalMoment.afterword: That day, while Greta stayed by her side, Lotte Neumann died at her home in West Berlin. A neighbor went to find a doctor, but by the time Marta and Eva arrived, Lotte had already passed away. For a long while, Greta could not clear away the 2 cards left on the table. There had been Thursdays when Greta stopped waiting for Lotte's reply, and Thursdays when the 2 of them played cards together. Marta remembered knowing that her mother had been weak for several days, yet putting off her visit until after the shop work was done. Eva was left with a dance she never got to show her. The record of that past life leaves on this page the bakery Lotte reopened with her daughter after the war and the 2 cards she never got to play.
finalMoment.artAlt: An afternoon in 1962 at a small home in West Berlin, where 74-year-old Lotte Neumann leans back in a chair beside a table holding 2 cards as her longtime neighbor Greta supports her shoulder

card.name: Yusuf
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Yusuf of Fez. The boy who carried his mother's laundry became a porter in the alleys and raised two children with his wife. When his son tried to start a different job, he kept him for one more week, causing him to miss his first opportunity. In old age, he took lighter loads and walked the alleys with his grandson.
card.title: The Alley Where the Donkey Turned Back
card.world: Fez, Sultanate of Morocco, 1870
card.flavor: With an urgent load to deliver, Harim sought out an old gate
card.opening: The house where the red cloth had to be delivered was to the right, but Harim turned left. At the third corner, he stopped before Sadiq's old gate.
card.life: Born in Fez in 1837, he carried his mother's laundry and learned from his uncle how to tie down loads. He became a porter, supported his wife and two children, and took charge of Sadiq's donkey, Harim. His daughter left for another region. In 1887, his son found a different job, but Yusuf asked him to help with that week's deliveries, causing him to miss his first opportunity. The next year, his son began working at another shop. Even in old age, when his knees hurt, Yusuf took lighter loads.
card.turn: He had to deliver a customer's bundle of red cloth before evening, but Harim kept walking toward the gate of his former owner, Sadiq. Yusuf had not asked after Sadiq for several months, either.
card.decision: Yusuf stood Harim in the shade of the gate, checked that the load was securely tied, then knocked on the door. When he heard that Sadiq had left for his daughter's home, he asked the neighbor to send him a brief greeting.
card.cost: The detour made the delivery of the red cloth late. The customer complained and said he would give the next week's load to someone else. Yusuf felt ashamed for much longer that he had not known Sadiq had moved.
card.after: Harim was not an animal who did not know the way. The next day, he walked straight through the appointed alleys, but Yusuf did not know whether the message he had sent to Sadiq ever reached him.
card.presentEcho: You might reflect on whether you keep putting off making time to check on someone who once walked familiar roads beside you.
card.secondLook: There was no way to ask Harim in words why he had stopped. To Sadiq's neighbor, the sudden visit was strange, and to the customer, what mattered first was that his cloth arrive on time.
card.unresolved: Whether Sadiq received the greeting, and whether Yusuf ever met him again, did not find an ending in that alley that day.
card.readerQuestion: You have to deliver a load before sunset, but the donkey keeps heading toward the gate where his former owner used to live. You haven't asked after that person in a long time. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: Yusuf saw that Harim was not turning down just any alley, but heading only for the gate where Sadiq had lived. Beneath the worn door handle, the small notch where Sadiq used to measure the height of a load was still there.
signalMoments.speak: Yusuf knocked on the closed door and called, “Sadiq, it's me. Just a moment.” When there was no answer, the door of the neighboring house opened.
signalMoments.connect: Yusuf asked the neighbor who came out where Sadiq had gone. The neighbor said he had moved to his daughter's home, and Yusuf did not hide that he had waited too long to ask.

setting.polity: Morocco under Sultan Muhammad IV of the Alaouite dynasty

identity.region: Fez, Morocco, under an Alaouite sultan
identity.summary: He carried loads in Fez and raised two children with his wife. When his son tried to start a different job, he kept him for one more week, causing him to miss his first opportunity. In old age, when his knees hurt, he took lighter loads.

Yusuf · Male
1837~1908 · Age 71
Born in Fez · Died in Fez
Work · Porter in the alleys of the medina
Life · He grew up carrying his mother's laundry and learned from his uncle how to tie down loads. He became a porter and raised two children with his wife. His daughter left for another region, and his son began different work after missing his first job because Yusuf kept him for one more week. In old age, he took lighter loads and walked the alleys with his grandson.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Kind of Person He Was
profilePages.body:
Personality · He hurried to keep promises made to customers, but thought his son's new job could be postponed for one week. Once his work was done, he listened patiently to other people's long stories.
What he liked · The long shafts of light that appeared in the narrow alleys early in the morning
What he enjoyed · Laughing with his wife in the evening as they imitated people they had met that day
What he did well · Tying heavy bundles evenly on both sides of a donkey

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
What he treasured · An old knotting knife his uncle gave him
Those close to him · His wife, daughter, and son; Sadiq, who taught him the roads; and the donkey Harim
The life he wanted · A home where his children could choose their own work and path
Worry · That his knees would grow worse and leave him unable to carry loads

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Yusuf, who carried loads through the alleys of Fez in 1870, when Morocco was ruled by a sultan. In the old city, where winding lanes led from one small door to another, a single donkey could move a large bundle. Of the countless routes Yusuf walked, let me tell you about the afternoon when Harim kept turning the other way.

As Yusuf tied up the bundle of red cloth, the customer said, “Come to that house before sunset. We need to spread it out today.” Yusuf balanced the loads evenly on Harim's back. There was plenty of time if they walked until the sunlight descended one level from the top of the walls. But at the first fork, Harim turned left. Their destination was to the right.

“Harim, that way.” Yusuf tugged lightly on the reins. Harim followed for a few steps, then went left again at the next corner. A child pressed against the wall to let them pass and laughed. “Mister, your donkey knows the way better than you do.” “Not today.” Yusuf frowned.

At the third corner, Harim stopped before a small wooden gate. Yusuf started to raise his hand, then stopped. Beneath the door handle was a long notch. The old porter Sadiq had made the mark with the tip of his knife while teaching young Yusuf how to measure the height of a load. After Sadiq fell ill and left Harim in his care, Yusuf had avoided this door for months, telling himself he was busy with work. The truth was, each time he passed it by, asking after Sadiq became harder.

signalMoments.notice: Yusuf realized that Harim was not searching for a new route. When he saw the closed gate and the old notch beneath its handle, he remembered mornings when Sadiq had loaded Harim here.
signalMoments.speak: Yusuf knocked on the door. “Sadiq, it's me. Just a moment.” There was no answer, and just as he was about to call again, the door of the neighboring house opened. He turned and asked the neighbor if Sadiq was there.
signalMoments.connect: Standing beside Harim, Yusuf asked the neighbor how Sadiq was. “It's been too long since I came to see him.” The neighbor pointed down the road and said it had been more than a month since Sadiq moved to his daughter's home.

episode.afterSignal:
Yusuf checked that Harim's load had not come loose, then knocked on the gate. There was no sound from inside. When he said, “Sadiq, it's me,” the low door of the neighboring house opened. A woman came out carrying a water jug. “Are you looking for Sadiq? He moved to where his daughter lives. It's been more than a month.”

“Where?” “Toward Meknes. He told a few people before he left.” The woman said no more. What hurt Yusuf more than not being one of those people was knowing that he could have been, if only he had come. Harim nudged the bottom of the gate with his nose. Still, no one came out from inside.

Yusuf asked the woman a favor. “If word reaches Sadiq's daughter, could you tell him that Yusuf came here with Harim?” The woman nodded. “It might be faster if you went yourself.” Yusuf looked at the bundle of cloth. He had to leave this house now. Without promising when he would go, he took the reins.

Harim did not resist on the way back. When they met another laden animal in a narrow alley, Yusuf was the first to step aside against the wall. By the time they reached the customer's house, the shadow had already crossed the doorway. The customer spread out the red cloth and asked, “Why are you so late?” Yusuf said, “I stopped briefly at the home of someone I knew long ago.”

Even after checking that the cloth was neither wet nor torn, the customer's expression did not soften. “I'll give next week's load to someone else. The person who was supposed to look at it today was waiting.” Yusuf did not make excuses. He could not undo the late delivery. As he turned away and loosened the donkey's straps, only pressed marks remained on Harim's back.

At home, his wife asked, “Did you truly not know Sadiq had left?” Yusuf replied, “I could have found out, but I didn't.” His wife worried more about the following week's lost work than that day's wages, but she did not tell him to go to Meknes at once, either. After they ate, Yusuf practiced tying the first knot Sadiq had taught him. His hands remembered the sequence.

The next day, Harim walked straight toward their destination at the same fork. Yusuf did not claim he had discovered why the animal had stopped the day before. But he could no longer pass without seeing the emptiness before that gate. He still did not know whether the greeting he had left with the neighbor would reach Sadiq, or whether he himself would walk the long road and meet him again.

Harim's thoughts are not recorded in the chronicle of that past life. All Yusuf knew was that, in a narrow alley, feet that had long walked beside his own stopped before a certain door, and only then did he knock on the closed gate.
