finalMoment.place: Fez, Alaouite Morocco
finalMoment.scene:
It is late morning in Fez in 1908. My son is coming to eat with us at our house today. My wife takes out one more small bowl and tells me to stay seated. I rise, saying I will bring in the cloth spread out to dry in the courtyard. My knees, which have ached for years, are a little stiff. “I'll do it,” my wife says. “I can manage this much.” I cross the threshold.

As I take a step, my knee gives way. I reach for the wall, but my fingertips do not touch it. My body falls sideways, and my head strikes the low stone threshold hard. I hear a bowl being set down and my wife calling my name at the same time. I try to lift myself, but my vision sways. My wife kneels beside me and places a folded cloth beneath my head.

“Don't move. I'll call someone.” My wife calls for a neighbor. I try to say I am all right, but my tongue will not move properly, and only a short sound comes out. The neighbor comes running and asks whether to bring water, but my wife tells him to go for help first. The two exchange hurried words. I think that when my son arrives, he will see one extra bowl laid out. Today, I meant to ask about his life before speaking of my own.

My wife rests her hand on the back of mine. “Can you hear me?” I try to move my fingers, but they do not respond well. Light enters the courtyard, and my wife's face draws close, then blurs. I try to breathe again, but my breath breaks off short. My wife calls my name once more. I cannot answer.
finalMoment.afterword: That day, Yusuf fell at his home in Fez and died beside his wife not long afterward. By the time the neighbor who had gone for help returned, it was already too late. The son who had planned to eat with them arrived after his father had collapsed. Yusuf's wife told him how his father had fallen after saying, “I can manage this much.” The son remembered missing an opportunity because he carried his father's loads during the first week he had tried to begin different work. Even so, he had a story he meant to tell his father that day. His wife, too, was left with the memory of a husband who waited too long to ask after those closest to him. Their daughter, who lived far away, came to Fez when she heard the news. The chronicle of that past life leaves in this chapter the meal the three had meant to share and the son's story that was never told.
finalMoment.artAlt: A low-angle view from inside the doorway of a home in Fez, Morocco, in 1908. Seventy-one-year-old Yusuf's knee buckles at the low stone threshold as he brings in cloth, and he reaches toward the wall while his wife sets down a bowl inside in the late-morning light

card.name: Tran Van Hoa
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Tran Van Hoa of Hue. You grew up in a riverside neighborhood, performed court music, and raised two children with your wife. In middle age, you taught younger musicians. When your daughter moved across the river, you kept putting off visiting her, while your wife went to see her even on her own.
card.title: The Rhythm of a Silent Night
card.world: Hue, capital of the Nguyen dynasty, in 1850
card.flavor: A midnight rehearsal collided with a neighbor's baby's sleep
card.opening: When Hoa struck the wooden beaters once more, the baby next door cried again.
card.life: Born in Hue in 1819, he grew up in a house near the river. He learned rhythms from a relative and became a court music percussionist as a young man. He lived with his wife and two children and taught younger musicians. In 1875, he handed the fast pieces over to younger performers. When his daughter and her family moved across the river in 1878, he could not hide his displeasure and kept putting off visiting. His wife visited their daughter even on her own. He played with his grandchildren when they came to his house, but the distance between him and his daughter never narrowed much. In 1887, after being ill for several days, he died at home with his son beside him.
card.turn: Worried about the opening beat of the next day's performance, Hoa was practicing late into the night with a fellow musician when he heard the baby next door crying and the weary voice of his neighbor.
card.decision: Hoa put down the wooden beaters and suggested to his fellow musician that they keep the rhythm using only gestures and the tips of their feet. Practicing quietly, he relearned the sequence of the opening beat.
card.cost: Unable to practice enough by listening to the sound, he was briefly late on the first movement the next day. A senior musician took Hoa aside and told him to prepare earlier next time.
card.after: The rest of the performance continued. Hoa never found out whether the neighbor's baby fell asleep that night, and his fellow musician told him that practicing in silence alone had left him uneasy.
card.presentEcho: When I am focused on my own work, I can pause and listen to what kind of noise it may sound like in a neighbor's day.
card.secondLook: For the neighbor holding the baby, sleep was urgent; for Hoa's fellow musician Binh, the next day's performance was urgent. The senior musician did not know how Hoa had practiced that night and saw only the late opening movement.
card.unresolved: No record remains of whether Hoa caught the opening beat on time at the next performance, or how the neighbor remembered that night.
card.readerQuestion: The opening beat I have to perform tomorrow still feels uncertain. But your late-night practice has woken the baby next door, and an exhausted parent has knocked on your door. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: When Hoa stopped the wooden beaters, he heard the crying ease a little. The rhythm he had thought was a small sound in his own courtyard had woken the baby next door.
signalMoments.connect: Hoa told his fellow musician Binh, “Let's put down the beaters and count it out together with our hands.” Binh asked whether they could stay in time without sound, but he sat facing Hoa.
signalMoments.speak: Hoa told the neighbor outside the door, “I didn't realize how late it was. I'll put the beaters down now.” The neighbor was too busy carrying the baby back home to offer much of a reply.

What he treasured · The worn wooden beaters inherited from a relative
Those close to him · His wife, his son, his daughter who lived across the river, and his fellow musician Binh

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Tran Van Hoa, a percussionist in Hue, the capital of the Nguyen dynasty, in 1850. Hue's court music involved many instruments and a strict order of ceremonies. From Hoa's long musical life, let me tell you about one evening when he could not make a sound.

With a performance scheduled for the next day, Hoa spread a mat in his inner courtyard. His fellow musician Binh arrived carrying two wooden beaters. “You strike first at the start, right? I'll come in after you.” Hoa nodded and sat before a small instrument. If he missed the opening beat, Binh's hands would be late too.

They played the same section together four times. On the fifth, Binh shot up a hand. “That was too fast.” Hoa said, “Again.” A breeze from the river came through the open door. After the evening meal, his wife called their two children inside. The children copied their father's rhythm by clapping, then went to bed.

When Hoa struck the beaters once more, the baby next door cried. He thought it was a coincidence and continued. Each time he struck again, the brief cry grew longer. Beyond the wall, someone paced slowly while soothing the baby. Binh said, “Let's do it just three more times.” Hoa was glad to hear it. The face of the senior musician who would sit before them tomorrow had come to mind.

signalMoments.notice: The moment Hoa stopped the beaters, he heard the baby's crying ease a little too. The rhythm he had thought was a small sound in his own courtyard was the sound of sleep being broken in the room next door.
signalMoments.connect: Hoa said, “Binh, let's put down the beaters and count it out with our hands.” Binh raised his eyebrows. “Without any sound?” Even so, he sat facing Hoa.
signalMoments.speak: Hoa went toward the open door and told his neighbor, “I didn't realize how late it was. I won't make any more noise.” Holding the baby, the exhausted neighbor only nodded.

episode.afterSignal:
There was a knock at the door next door. When Hoa went out, his neighbor stood there holding the baby. “I can bear it during the day. But today, the baby has hardly slept.” The neighbor's shoulders sagged. Hoa glanced back at the instrument inside his house. He needed more practice on the opening beat, but he might wake the baby again.

“I'm sorry. I won't make any more noise.” Hoa went back and placed the beaters on the folded cloth. Binh asked quietly, “Then what about tomorrow?” Hoa pointed to his own knee with his palm. “Start here and raise your hand. I'll move then.”

They sat facing each other. When Hoa folded and unfolded his fingers, Binh lifted his toes. The first two times, they failed to watch each other's hands and stopped. The third time, Binh's shoulders shook as he tried not to laugh. “It's like we're putting on a shadow play.” Hoa laughed silently too. But when they moved to the next part, their hands fell out of time again.

His wife brought out a small lamp from inside. “You can't see the floor. You'll trip.” She set the light at the edge of the mat, then closed the window. Hoa looked toward the neighbor's house. The baby still cried now and then, and he could not tell whether the quieter moments were thanks to him. Binh said, “If we could make the sound just once, we'd know for sure,” but he did not pick up the beaters.

At the next day's performance, Hoa looked into Binh's eyes. When the senior musician gave the signal to begin, Hoa's hand was a little late. Binh's hand also paused briefly in midair before following. The rest of the performance continued without interruption. Hoa counted the rhythm to the end, but the small gap in the opening movement lingered in his ears.

After everyone had dispersed, the senior musician called Hoa over. “You missed the opening beat. Prepare earlier next time.” Hoa answered, “Yes.” He did not mention the neighbor from the night before. That would not erase the late movement, nor would it change what the senior musician had heard.

On the way home, Binh said, “The gestures were fun, but I needed the sound.” Hoa nodded. They agreed to hold their next practice during the day. When he reached his house, the neighbor's door was closed. Still not knowing whether the baby had fallen asleep that night, Hoa rolled up the mat in his courtyard.

Instead of a perfect opening beat, the record of this past life preserves the night when Hoa laid the beaters on the cloth and two people kept rhythm with their eyes. That night's mistake remains alongside the neighbor's weary face.

finalMoment.place: His home in Hue
finalMoment.scene:
My home in Hue, 1887. I have been feverish for several days, and I lie in bed even during the day. My wife has gone across the river to our daughter's house. My son enters carrying a bowl of water and sits beside me. He has the same look he wore as a child, waiting to see if I will give him some task. I take a sip of water and hand back the bowl.

“When will your mother return?” I ask. My son says, “Before sunset.” Whenever my wife went to our daughter's house, she always said when she would be back. Several times, I said I would go with her, only to find some other task each morning. This time, too, when my wife said she was going to visit our daughter, I stayed home. My son lays a damp cloth on my forehead. “Is there anyone else you want me to call?” I shake my head, but my breaths keep growing shorter.

My son goes out to the courtyard to wet the cloth again. I hear his footsteps returning, but even turning onto my side is difficult. He tries to support my shoulders and help me sit up. “Father, look at me.” I open my eyes and search for my son's face. Even when I try to draw a deep breath, it catches in my chest. My son shouts toward the door for a neighbor. All I can think is that my wife is still across the river.

The neighbor rushes in and supports my back with my son. Someone outside says they will go and fetch my wife. My lips are too dry even to ask for water. My son holds my hand and calls my name. I try to move my fingers, but I have no strength. One short breath comes in, and the next does not follow.
finalMoment.afterword: After being ill for several days, Hoa died in 1887 at his home in Hue with his son beside him. The record of this past life does not say what illness he had. His wife returned with their daughter, and his daughter remembered all the years when her father had rarely visited her home. His son said that when his father began struggling to breathe, he and a neighbor stayed beside him. His wife was left with memories both of evenings when they laughed together and of a husband who repeatedly put off going to see their daughter. The record of this past life preserves in this chapter the years they lived on while remembering the same person differently.
finalMoment.artAlt: A modest home in Hue, Vietnam, in 1887, during the day: the adult son of 68-year-old Hoa holds the hand of his father, who lies sick in bed, while a neighbor helps beside them; his wife and daughter have not yet returned from across the river

card.name: Asta Jónsdóttir
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Asta Jónsdóttir of Reykjavík. You grew up on a farm in the southwest and learned the trade at a city photography studio. When your mother was ill, you traveled back and forth between the country home and your studio, photographing people and their workplaces. After entrusting the studio to your niece, you kept living alone in your own home and met your younger sister on days they had set together.
card.title: The Dog That Got into the Family Portrait
card.world: Reykjavík under the rule of the Danish king in 1895
card.flavor: A little tail slipped into a stiff formal portrait
card.opening: As Asta opened the lens cap, a dog's tail suddenly poked out from under the chair.
card.life: Born on a farm in southwestern Iceland in 1863, she helped prepare wool and do household chores. In her late teens, she moved to Reykjavík, learned photography, and opened a small studio. While her mother was ill, she cut back on work as she traveled between the city and the country home. She never married and remained close to her younger sister's family. In middle age, she began photographing not only studio portraits but also people at work. In 1927, she entrusted the studio to her niece. She refused her younger sister's offer to live together, but they set days to visit each other, and Asta gave her a key to the house. In 1937, she suddenly collapsed while walking along the seaside with her younger sister and died beside her.
card.turn: A family ordered a formal portrait to send far away, but the youngest child hid their dog under a chair. The moment Asta exposed the first plate, the dog dashed out, and the father reached out his arm.
card.decision: Asta developed the plate and showed the blurred photograph to the family instead of hiding it. Without charging extra, she retook the portrait using one of her own plates, but she left the child a small proof print of the first photograph, in which the dog was faintly visible.
card.cost: Asta used an extra plate and sheet of printing paper but charged for only one photograph. The father still saw the first picture, which the child loved, as a failed photograph.
card.after: The family took home the formal second photograph. The ridiculous tail in the first remained with the child, and Asta recorded the cost in her ledger.
card.presentEcho: You may be reminded that even when people see the same scene, each person may want to preserve a different face of it.
card.secondLook: The father needed a clear portrait to send to relatives, while the child wanted the moment when the dog was there with the family. For Asta, both the cost of using another plate and the studio's reputation were at stake.
card.unresolved: No one knows whether the child's proof photograph survived for long, or whether the father ever looked at it with a smile.
card.readerQuestion: Just as a family portrait was being taken, a dog hidden under the chair dashed out and blurred the faces on the first glass plate. The customer said he would pay for only one photograph. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: Asta remembered how the child had kept looking under the chair. On the developed plate, the father's blurred arm overlapped the dog's tail.
signalMoments.connect: Asta asked the child why the dog had come along. The child said, “Because he's part of our family,” and the father replied that they still needed to show their relatives clear faces.
signalMoments.speak: Holding the plate up to the light, Asta said, “The first one was blurred. I'll take it again using one of my own plates.” The father breathed a sigh of relief, while the child could not let go of the first photograph.

identity.region: Reykjavík, Iceland, under the rule of the Danish king
identity.summary: She grew up on a farm and opened a photography studio in Reykjavík. She traveled between the city and the countryside while caring for her mother. Even after entrusting the work to her niece, she continued living in her own home and met regularly with her younger sister.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who She Was
profilePages.body:
Asta Jónsdóttir · Female
1863–1937 · Age 74
Born on a farm in the southwest · Died in Reykjavík
Work · Photographer
Life · She grew up on a farm and moved to Reykjavík in her late teens to learn photography. She established a small studio and traveled between the country home and the city while her mother was ill. After handing the studio over to her niece, she lived in her own home and met her younger sister on days they had set together.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What She Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · She was quiet around strangers and joked with those close to her. Even when she needed help, she tried to manage on her own first.
What she liked · The light that lingered by the window on cloudy days
What she enjoyed · Walking with her younger sister and remembering childhood events differently
What she was good at · Waiting until a stiff expression relaxed

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her
profilePages.body:
What she treasured · The old black cloth her first teacher had given her, and the key to the home where she lived alone
People close to her · Her mother, younger sister, niece, and fellow photographers
The life she wanted · A life in which she photographed the people she wanted to photograph and remained in her own home even after she stopped working
Worries · A decline in the studio's income, and losing the right to live alone in old age

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Asta Jónsdóttir, a photographer in Reykjavík, Iceland, under the rule of the Danish king in 1895. At that time, photographs were made by exposing glass plates to light, developing them in a darkroom, and printing them on paper. Among the many people Asta photographed, let me tell you about the day a little dog slipped into one family's formal portrait.

A father, a mother, and two children entered the studio. Fastening his coat, the father said, “We're sending this to our cousins. Please make sure all our faces come out clearly.” Asta checked the light from the window and moved three chairs. The younger daughter stood by the door, repeatedly glancing down at her feet.

“Please don't move.” Asta stood behind the large wooden camera. The older child pressed their lips tightly together, while the younger one struggled to hold back a laugh. The father straightened the child's shoulders. The moment Asta opened the lens cap, a brown tail shot out from under the chair.

A little dog raced across the floor. The father cried, “Come here!” and reached out his arm. The youngest child burst out laughing, and the mother closed her eyes. Asta quickly closed the cap. There was no way yet to know what expressions the camera had captured. Holding the dog, the youngest child muttered, “He keeps barking if we leave him at home.”

signalMoments.notice: When Asta held up the developed glass plate, the father's arm faintly overlapped the dog's tail. Only then did she understand the expression on the youngest child's face as the child had checked under the chair.
signalMoments.connect: Asta asked the youngest child why the dog had been brought along. “He's part of our family too.” The father said, “Even so, our cousins need to be able to see our faces,” and led the dog toward the door.
signalMoments.speak: Asta held the blurred plate up to the light. “The first one was blurred. I'll take it again using one of my own plates.” The father was relieved, while the youngest child could not take their eyes off the spot where the dog's tail remained.

episode.afterSignal:
Asta asked the family to wait a moment. In the small darkroom, she developed the glass plate and rinsed it with water. When she held the plate up to the light, the father's face was fine, but his arm had stretched into a long blur, and a line like a dog's tail floated near the floor. The youngest child's mouth was wide open.

When Asta carefully brought out the plate and showed it to them, the father frowned. “We can't send this to our cousins. We only ordered one photograph.” The youngest child pointed at the bottom of the plate. “That's our dog.” The mother held back a laugh and placed a hand on the child's shoulder. Asta found it funny too, but a glass plate did not come free.

“I'll take it again on a new plate. I won't charge you any more.” Asta said. The father replied, “Then make it formal.” The youngest child carried the dog outside. The dog braced its paws, unwilling to leave, and the older child finally went out too to help. Worried that the picture would end up missing both children, the mother called them back. The dog stayed outside, and the children remained in their chairs.

The second time, the father's hands stayed on his knees. When the youngest child tried to press their lips closed, Asta said, “You may smile. Just don't move.” The mother's face relaxed a little too. As the cap opened and closed, the dog barked once outside. The family only glanced at one another.

A few days later, the family returned to collect the second photograph. The father checked each of the four faces and paid the price. “Our cousins will recognize us.” The youngest child asked about the first picture. Asta handed over a small proof she had printed as a test. The arm and tail were still blurred. The child looked first for the trace of the dog.

Looking at the paper, the father said, “Why keep a failed photograph?” “It's a little proof print I made. I don't intend to charge for it,” Asta replied. The father carefully wrapped the second photograph and carried it out, while the child slipped the first inside their coat. Asta never learned which of the two they hung in their home.

That evening, Asta entered two glass plates and two sheets of paper in her ledger but recorded payment for only one photograph. When her younger sister stopped by the studio and asked, “Why are you smiling today?” Asta traced the shape of a dog's tail with her hand. As she explained, she laughed again herself. But the numbers in the ledger remained unchanged.

The two photographs preserved in the record of this past life show different faces of the same family. One was fit to send far away, while the other brought to mind the patter of little paws racing across the studio floor. Asta never found out which one lasted longer.

memories.label: Her Younger Sister's View
memories.detail: “When I asked her to live with me, she said no. But she still set days for me to visit and gave me a key.”

memories.label: Her Neighbor's View
memories.detail: “Whenever I asked how she was, she always said she was fine. It was hard to know whether that meant she never needed help.”

memories.label: Her Niece's View
memories.detail: “She showed me the ledger before she showed me the camera. She said that if I wanted to do this work for a long time, I had to pay attention to both.”

memories.label: A Fellow Photographer's View
memories.detail: “She waited a long time for her subjects to relax. That meant she couldn't take as many orders in a day.”

memories.label: Her Mother's View

finalMoment.place: A seaside path in Reykjavík, Kingdom of Iceland
finalMoment.scene:
A summer afternoon in Reykjavík in 1937. I am walking along a seaside path with my younger sister. Since I entrusted the studio to my niece, we have met on days we set together. A few years ago, my sister asked me to live with her, but I stayed in my own home. That did not mean I wanted to be alone. Today, as always, she came to fetch me first and chose a path where the wind was gentler.

“When we were little, you climbed over the fence first,” my sister says. “You pushed me,” I reply. Unable to settle who is right, we laugh. I slow my steps. The center of my chest suddenly tightens, and I cannot draw a deep breath. My sister catches my arm. “Asta, do you want to sit down?” I nod, but my legs give way first.

My sister supports my shoulders and helps me sit at the side of the path. A passerby approaches and says they will call someone to help. I open my mouth to say that I am all right, but my voice breaks off after a few words. My sister holds my hand between both of hers. The sea breeze touches my face, but my breathing grows shallower. I try to squeeze my sister's hand once. I do not know whether my fingers move at all.

“Can you hear me?” My sister's face is directly before mine. I want to answer that I can. Behind us, I hear running footsteps approaching. My sister's hand is still warm, but my chest tightens once more, and then my strength drains away. I try to breathe in, but the next breath does not come.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1937, Asta suddenly collapsed on a seaside path in Reykjavík and died beside her younger sister. The exact cause of the tightness in her chest was never recorded. Her younger sister remembered both Asta's refusal to live with her and the way Asta instead set days for them to meet and entrusted her with a key to the house. Her niece recalled how, on the days the sisters had set, they always asked after each other as soon as the day's work was done. Keeping the home where she lived alone and keeping her younger sister close were both parts of Asta's life. The record of this past life leaves on this page the sisters' childhood story, on which they never agreed, and the hands they clasped on the path.
finalMoment.artAlt: A view from the water of a seaside path in Reykjavík in the summer of 1937. As 74-year-old Asta stops and clutches her chest, her younger sister, who was walking ahead, turns back

card.name: Hashim ibn Yusuf
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Hashim ibn Yusuf of Baghdad. You grew up with your parents and younger sister and learned the craft of papermaking. You married Maryam, raised a daughter, and took over the workshop. After his wrists began to ache, he taught young workers. On the day his daughter moved out on her own, he did not help her move because he refused to stop working on an order.
card.title: A Wall for Two Days
card.world: Baghdad in the Abbasid Caliphate, 1220
card.flavor: Where will the wedding guests sit while the paper dries?
card.opening: Hashim's younger sister came in carrying the wedding cloth, and Hashim saw that wet paper was stuck to the wall where she meant to hang it.
card.life: Born in Baghdad in 1190, he grew up with his parents and younger sister, Salma. He learned papermaking from his father, and from the age of 28, they took orders together. Around the age of 30, Salma's wedding overlapped with the workshop schedule. Later, he married Maryam, raised a daughter, and took over the workshop after his father's death. After his wrists began to ache, he taught young workers. When his daughter moved to a home across the river in 1246, Hashim did not stop working. Maryam and Salma carried her belongings. Hashim visited his daughter's home two years later, but she had not forgotten the day of the move. He died in Baghdad in 1251.
card.turn: Freshly made paper was stuck to the courtyard wall where Salma's wedding guests were supposed to sit, and it needed two more days to dry. With nowhere to hang the cloth, Salma felt that once again, her needs were being pushed aside for the workshop.
card.decision: Instead of peeling off the paper, Hashim borrowed an empty wall from a neighbor, moved the wedding seating, and hung the cloth himself. When the buyer came early for the paper, Hashim told him it was still wet.
card.cost: The buyer did not wait and went elsewhere. Hashim lost the price of the bundle of paper he could have sold, and Salma found it hard to believe he would stay by her side during the wedding.
card.after: Once the paper dried on time, it was sold to another buyer. Hashim sat down before the wedding food, but the old hurt between him and Salma was not entirely healed that day.
card.presentEcho: When two urgent needs compete for the same space, you can ask again who needs what kind of place.
card.secondLook: His father worried that peeling it off badly would ruin an entire bundle of paper. More than a wall for the cloth, Salma wanted Hashim to make time for her special day. The buyer needed paper to use that day.
card.unresolved: It is unknown how much Hashim and Salma trusted each other's promises afterward.
card.readerQuestion: The wall where your younger sister's wedding guests will be welcomed is covered with still-wet paper made for an order. The buyer has arrived early and is pressing you for the paper. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: Hashim paid more attention to Salma saying “again” than to the length of the wall where the cloth would hang. The edges of the wet paper were not yet ready to come away from the wall.
signalMoments.connect: When Hashim asked his neighbor Farid if he could borrow an empty wall, Farid said he could hang the cloth as long as the guests' chairs did not block his door. Salma asked whether Hashim would make time to sit at the wedding before she asked about the wall.
signalMoments.speak: Hashim told Salma he would leave the paper in place, find another wall, and hang the cloth there. He explained to the buyer who had arrived early that the wet paper could not be handed over for another two days.

identity.region: Baghdad in the Abbasid Caliphate

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who He Was
profilePages.body:
Hashim ibn Yusuf · Male
1190–1251 · Age 61
Born in Baghdad · Died in Baghdad
Work · Papermaker
Life · He grew up with his parents and younger sister, Salma, and learned papermaking from his father. As a young man, he argued with his father while helping him run the workshop. He married Maryam, raised a daughter, and took over the workshop. After his wrists began to ache, he taught young workers. When his daughter moved out on her own, he did not stop working and did not help her move. Two years later, he visited her home, but his absence that day stayed with her.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What He Was Like
profilePages.body:
Personality · He assumed his family would wait for his schedule and put off his promises. Sometimes he showed up late, but he could not give back the days he had postponed.
What he liked · The rough surface of paper freshly lifted from the water
What he enjoyed · Walking by the river with his daughter and counting the boats
What he did well · Judging with his fingertips whether paper was dry enough

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Him
profilePages.body:
What he treasured · The old reed mold his father had used
Those close to him · His father Yusuf, his younger sister Salma, his wife Maryam, and his daughter
The life he wanted · A life in which he could keep making paper for many years while still spending evenings with his family
His worry · That the pain in his wrists would leave him unable to make paper

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Hashim ibn Yusuf, a papermaker in Baghdad in the Abbasid Caliphate in 1220. At that time, people there soaked cloth fibers in water to make paper, first laying the sheets on reeds and then sticking them to smooth walls to dry for several more days. Let me tell you about the two days in Hashim's life when paper and people needed the same wall.

As Hashim pressed the corner of a wet sheet of paper onto the wall, his younger sister Salma entered the courtyard with a yellow cloth in her arms. “If we hang it here, the guests' area will look bright.” Salma pointed to the smooth wall their father had prepared. Six sheets of paper were already stuck to it.

“The wedding is in two days,” Salma said. Hashim pointed to the stack of drying paper. “I was going to peel these off tomorrow and hand them over.” Their father, Yusuf, lightly touched the edge of one sheet and shook his head. “It's still damp. If you pull it now, the edge will curl. It needs two days.” Hashim worried that the man who had agreed to buy it might come early.

Salma folded the cloth again. “Last time, too, you told me I could use the courtyard, and then all you looked at was the paper.” Before Hashim could speak, Salma added, “If there isn't a wall, we can hang it somewhere else. But this time, too, you'll work until all the food is cold before you come, won't you?” Hashim had been looking only at the paper, but now he looked at Salma.

signalMoments.notice: Hashim remembered Salma saying “this time, too.” Even if he cleared the wall, the hurt between the family members would not disappear on its own. The paper still felt cold and damp beneath his fingertips.
signalMoments.connect: Hashim asked his next-door neighbor Farid, who used the courtyard beside theirs, whether he had an empty wall. Farid said, “You can hang the cloth, but you'll have to move the guests' chairs yourself.” Salma asked, “Forget the wall. Will you sit beside me?”
signalMoments.speak: Hashim told Salma, “I won't peel off the paper. I'll find another wall and hang the cloth myself.” Even as Salma held out the cloth, she said, “Don't just go straight back to the workshop afterward.”

episode.afterSignal:
Hashim knocked on the door of Farid, the neighbor across the way. Farid showed him the empty whitewashed wall of his house. “The cloth is fine. But the guests mustn't block our door.” Hashim promised to move the chairs farther into the courtyard. As Salma handed over the cloth, she stretched out her arms as if measuring the width of the wall.

Together they carried chairs and pushed a low table. A scrap of dried cloth fell from Hashim's arm. Salma picked it up and laughed. “Are you planning to stick paper to the wedding cloth, too?” Hashim laughed as well, but they had to move the table again so it would not block Farid's door. The work took longer than expected.

Just then, the man who had said he would buy the paper entered the workshop. He looked at the six sheets on the wall and asked, “Can I take them today?” Hashim raised a hand to try peeling up the edge of a sheet, then stopped. Beside him, his father said quietly, “You can show it to him, but you can't sell it.” The corners of the paper were still wet and clung to the wall.

“They'll be ready in two days,” Hashim said. The buyer shook his head. “I need to copy a text tomorrow morning. I'll try somewhere else.” Hashim wanted to tear the paper off by force and sell it even if it ended up smaller. But behind him, he saw Salma standing with a guest's chair in her hands. He stepped aside and let the buyer pass.

After the buyer left, Hashim stared for a while at the door the man had closed. “You lost the sale,” his father said. “Yes.” Hashim went back to moving the tables. Salma said, “Don't tell me you lost money because of me.” Hashim replied, “I could have made the paper earlier yesterday. That's on me.” Even so, he still regretted the lost payment.

On the morning of the wedding, the paper slowly came away from the wall. Hashim set aside the one sheet with a slightly curled edge and tied the rest into a bundle. The guests' seating did not block Farid's door, and the cloth hung brightly on the wall. When Hashim came in late, Salma patted the empty place beside her. “Sit down. This time, before the food gets cold.”

Hashim sat, but between a few bites of food, he glanced back toward the workshop. Salma saw him and said, “The paper isn't going to run away.” He gave an awkward laugh. Across from them, their father was inspecting the bundle of dried paper. Neither man wore the expression of someone who had completely forgotten his work.

A few days later, Hashim sold the paper to another customer. He never learned where the first buyer found the paper he needed. Hashim washed the borrowed wall before returning it to Farid, and Salma folded the wedding cloth and took it to her new home in another neighborhood. The two met again at the market, but they did not speak at length about the hurt from that day.

In the record of a past life, the wall where the paper dried and the wall where the wedding cloth hung remain side by side. That day, Hashim ran back and forth trying to find a place where he could protect both. The amount he lost could be written in a ledger, but there was no column for counting the time he sat in the empty place beside Salma.

finalMoment.place: His daughter's home across the river in Baghdad, Abbasid Caliphate
finalMoment.scene:
It is late afternoon in 1251, in the courtyard of my daughter's home across the river. I am sixty-one. My daughter places two low chairs in the shade and goes inside to fetch water. “When is Maryam coming?” I ask, and my daughter replies, “She'll stop at Aunt Salma's house and come before supper.” I look around the narrow courtyard of the house where my daughter lives. I did not come on the day she moved here.

As the sun shifts, its light reaches the edge of the chair. I rise to pull the chair back a little. At that moment, a sudden, fierce pain strikes deep in my abdomen. It spreads into my back. Bracing one hand against the wall, I say, “Wait.” My daughter turns with a cup of water in her hand. I cannot take another step and sink down beneath the wall. Cold sweat beads on the back of my neck.

“Father, where does it hurt?” My daughter sets down the cup. “My stomach... my back, too.” I cannot manage a longer sentence. My daughter turns toward the door to call a neighbor for help, then quickly sits down in front of me again. I lift a hand to tell her I am all right, but my arm feels heavy. My daughter takes my hand. My palm is cold, and her hand is warm.

My daughter calls my name. I try to raise my head, but the doorway in front of me blurs. “I'm here. Can you hear me?” I can hear my daughter's voice. I open my mouth to answer, but no sound comes out. I try to draw a breath, but my chest barely moves. The strength leaves my fingers, and my daughter's voice grows distant.
finalMoment.afterword: In 1251, Hashim suffered sudden abdominal and back pain in the courtyard of his daughter's home in Baghdad and lost consciousness. He died beside his daughter before the neighbor returned. The exact illness is unknown. Maryam and Salma heard the news and arrived later. His daughter remembered both the days her father had come to visit her home and the day he had failed to come when she moved there. Maryam thought of the years she had traveled between the two homes to visit their daughter. The record of a past life says that the life of Hashim, who often put family time behind his work and sometimes came to them too late, ended there.
finalMoment.artAlt: Late afternoon in 1251, looking down from a high diagonal angle above the roof into the courtyard of a modest Baghdad home. Sixty-one-year-old Hashim braces himself against a wall as sudden abdominal pain strikes, while his adult daughter turns from the inner doorway holding a cup of water. A wide stretch of courtyard lies empty between them.

card.name: Kiya
card.identityLine: In that life, you were Kiya of the Cuzco Highlands. You learned from your older sister how to twist grass rope, and you lived with Rumi and your daughter. You and your sister cared for your sick mother, but you left more of the nighttime care to your sister. When your daughter moved into a home of her own, you had to learn new boundaries between you.
card.title: A Single Strand Before the Bridge
card.world: The Cuzco Highlands of Tawantinsuyu around 1490
card.flavor: A strand of grass for the new bridge snapped between her fingertips
card.opening: When Kiya pulled the rope, a strand of grass snapped crisply between her fingers.
card.life: Born in the Cuzco Highlands in 1451, Kiya grew up following her mother and older sister as they gathered grass and tended livestock. In her 20s, she made a home with Rumi and raised a daughter. When her mother fell ill, she cut back on work farther from home, but often left the nighttime care to her sister. In her 40s, she argued with younger workers over their methods. After her daughter moved into a home of her own, Kiya brought grass over without asking, forcing her daughter to stop her work and receive her mother. Only after her daughter asked her to give notice before visiting did Kiya begin asking which day she could come. In her later years, when her fingers grew stiff, she selected materials and taught a young relative.
card.turn: On the day they were making new rope to replace the old grass bridge over the river, long-stored grass crumbled in a section twisted by Kiya's young niece. People were already waiting to combine their rope into a larger cable.
card.decision: Kiya did not hide her niece or cover up the flaw and send the rope on. She showed the faulty section to the others. After cutting it out, she twisted it again with her niece.
card.cost: The work of gathering the ropes was delayed, so the two received their shared meal late. Kiya's niece was embarrassed in front of everyone and did not thank Kiya right away.
card.after: The retwisted rope was handed to the people making the larger cable, and later the new bridge was joined together. For a while, Kiya's niece would not sit beside her, but eventually she began checking the ends of the grass before Kiya did.
card.presentEcho: When you find a small flaw you would rather rush past in work you are doing with others, you can think about how to bring it up.
card.secondLook: Kiya's niece feared everyone would glare at them if they finished late. Kiya could not pretend not to know about the weak spot. The people waiting needed to begin their part of the work.
card.unresolved: It is not known whether Kiya's niece later inspected rope the same way Kiya did.
card.readerQuestion: A section of grass rope meant for a new bridge crumbles easily between your fingertips. People are waiting to combine it into a large cable. What would you do?

signalMoments.notice: Kiya found grass of a different color in the middle of the rope and rubbed it with her thumb. The sound strands bent, but only that section crumbled.
signalMoments.connect: Kiya asked her niece, “Where did you get this grass?” Her niece admitted that they had run short of fresh bundles, so she had taken some from a pile stored away for a long time.
signalMoments.speak: Kiya showed the weak section to the people waiting. “This part needs to be twisted again.” Her niece lowered her head, and someone complained that the work was being delayed.

setting.region: The Cuzco Highlands near the upper Apurímac River

identity.region: The Cuzco Highlands of Tawantinsuyu
identity.summary: She made grass rope in the Cuzco Highlands. She shared the care of her mother with her older sister, and it took her time to accept the wishes of her daughter, who lived in a home of her own.

profilePages.title: Page 1 · Who Was She?
profilePages.body:
Kiya · Female
1451–1514 · Age 63
Born in a village in the Cuzco Highlands · Died in a village in the same highlands
Work · Grass-rope maker
Life · She grew up following her mother and older sister as they gathered grass and tended livestock. She made a home with Rumi and raised a daughter. When her mother fell ill, Kiya cut back on daytime work, but often left the nighttime care to her sister. After her daughter moved into a home of her own, Kiya brought grass over without asking. Her daughter had to stop what she was doing to receive Kiya. In her later years, when her fingers grew stiff, she selected materials and taught a young relative how to twist rope.

profilePages.title: Page 2 · What Was She Like?
profilePages.body:
Personality · If something caught against her hands, she said so immediately. At work, she found flaws, but at home, she could not bring herself to ask first whether her help was needed.
What she liked · The dry scent of fields after the grass had been cut
What she enjoyed · Trading news with Rumi in the evening about the highland roads
What she did well · Finding places where strands differed in thickness with her fingertips

profilePages.title: Page 3 · What Mattered to Her?
profilePages.body:
What she treasured · A short grass rope that reminded her of the twisting direction her older sister first taught her
People close to her · Her older sister, Rumi, her daughter, and her young niece
The life she wanted · Sharing work with people who used the same roads and staying close to her daughter
Her worry · That her fingers would stiffen and someday keep her from twisting rope for long

episode.beforeSignal:
In a past life, you were Kiya, who lived around 1490 in the Cuzco Highlands of Tawantinsuyu, the Inca Empire. People there twisted grass into rope, then combined many ropes to span rivers with bridges. Let me tell you about a day when Kiya prepared new rope beside the old bridge near her village. These people and the commotion that day are fictional.

The sound of water rose from the river below. The old grass bridge still connected the two sides, and people had laid out new ropes beside it. Kiya and her young niece sat by bundles of dry grass, twisting small ropes. Her niece looked back at the people waiting behind them for their turn to make the large cable. “Ours is the only one that isn't ready.”

“If we rush and make it uneven, we'll be even later,” Kiya said. Her niece pouted and moved both hands faster. Kiya knew she repeated herself too often. Perhaps she had made that same face when learning from her older sister.

A little later, Kiya took the finished rope and pulled it. Snap. A short strand of grass broke between her fingers. The middle of the rope was paler and rougher than the rest. When she rubbed it again, small pieces fell away. Kiya placed them in her niece's hand. Her niece looked at her own knees instead of the river.

signalMoments.notice: Kiya ran her hands along the rope from one end and found a section of a different color. When she bent it with the same force, the sound strands flexed, but only the grass there crumbled.
signalMoments.connect: When Kiya asked, “Where did you get this grass?” her niece answered, “We ran short of fresh bundles, so I used some that had been stored in the back for a long time.” Kiya noticed how her niece watched her warily, having been unable to say in advance that they did not have enough.
signalMoments.speak: Kiya spread out the weak section of rope for the people waiting to see. “This part needs to be twisted again.” One person said, “We've been waiting, and you're only telling us now?” Her niece took a step back behind Kiya.

episode.afterSignal:
“We ran short of fresh bundles,” her niece said very softly. She had brought over grass stored in the back for a long time and mixed it into that section. Kiya blew the crumbs from her hand. “Why didn't you say we were short?” Her niece raised her head. “I thought if I said something, you'd tell me I was slow again.”

The people making the large cable came over. One of them looked at Kiya's palm and said, “If it's only that much, can't we cut it out and splice the ends?” Another shrugged, saying they had to gather the ropes before the sun rose high. Kiya pointed to the weak spot. “It breaks here. If we cut it out, we'll have to remake this whole section long enough.”

Her niece caught Kiya's sleeve. “We'll just redo it ourselves. Don't say it in front of everyone.” Kiya knew they were already watching. Without pushing her niece forward, she held the weak grass in her hand and said, “Long-stored grass got mixed into our rope. We'll make it again.” Her niece knew those words were about her, too.

Kiya cut out the crumbling part. Her niece looked at the severed rope and bit her lip. The two brought more bundles of fresh grass and soaked them in water to soften them. This time, Kiya held the first strand while her niece passed her the rest. When one end kept growing too thick, her niece was the first to stop her hands. “It's too thick here again.” Kiya nodded, loosened it a little, and twisted it again.

Behind them, someone waiting tapped a foot against the ground. A person returning from the valley on the other side crossed the old bridge and looked down at the new ropes. Kiya lowered her head so she would not have to look at him. Her niece did not suggest twisting faster. They took turns pulling the ends of the grass to make sure they did not snap.

The person who took the remade rope asked where the weak spot had been. Kiya showed him the piece they had cut out and pointed to the newly twisted section. He pulled the rope several times, then carried it away with the others. The new bridge was not finished yet. The communal meal had already begun that day.

By the time Kiya and her niece went to get food, little of the warm fare remained. Her niece sat somewhere else. When Kiya set a bundle of dry grass beside her, her niece said, “Next time, I'll inspect it first, too.” She did not sound as though she was waiting for praise. Kiya only said, “All right.”

After the bridge was joined together with new ropes, people crossed the river again. No one pointed out that small section or spoke about it. Kiya selected extra bundles so they would not run short of grass when they began the next job. For a while, her niece would not sit beside her, but when they met at Kiya's older sister's house, she would often check the ends of the grass before Kiya did.

What remains in the record of that past life is one broken strand and a meal received late. Kiya was not the person who made every rope in the bridge by herself. But before everyone joined their strength together, she did not simply pass along the one section of rope that had come into her hands.

timeline.event: Born in a village in the Cuzco Highlands of Tawantinsuyu
Followed her mother and older sister as they gathered grass and tended livestock
Learned from her older sister how to twist multiple strands evenly
Made a home with Rumi, a person from a neighboring village
Gave birth to a daughter and divided her time between household tasks and twisting rope
Cut back on distant communal work when her mother fell ill. Often left the nighttime care to her older sister
Retwisted a weak section of grass rope for a river bridge with her niece
Took part in communal work, sometimes arguing with younger workers over how to select materials
Her daughter began living nearby in a home of her own. Kiya visited without asking, forcing her daughter to stop what she was doing
Her daughter insisted that Kiya give notice before visiting. Kiya felt hurt, but afterward, she asked which day she could come
As her fingers grew stiff, she selected materials and taught a young relative instead of twisting rope for long periods
After several days of fever left her struggling even to drink water, she died beside Rumi in their highland home. Her illness is unknown

memories.label: Work She Did for Years
memories.detail: Twisting grass rope for people crossing the river, and later selecting usable grass

memories.label: People Close to Her
memories.detail: The older sister who first taught her to make grass rope, Rumi, with whom she shared news of the roads, and her daughter, who lived nearby

memories.label: Time She Enjoyed
memories.detail: Watching people come and go along the high roads with Rumi in the evening and comparing the news each had heard

memories.label: Treasured Possession
memories.detail: The short rope Kiya twisted all the way to the end for the first time while her older sister taught her

memories.label: Words She Left Behind
memories.detail: “This grass can be used tomorrow, but that grass isn't good even today.”

memories.label: Her Older Sister's View
memories.detail: “When Mother was sick, she stayed beside her during the day. But I was the one who got up more often at night.”

memories.label: Rumi's View
memories.detail: “When her mother was sick, she stayed home more, but she missed the work outside.”

memories.label: Her Daughter's View
memories.detail: “She brought grass over without asking and made me stop my work. Even after I asked her to tell me before visiting, she felt hurt for a while.”

memories.label: Her Niece's View
memories.detail: “I hated her that day. Later, I understood why she rubbed the grass with her hand before choosing it.”

finalMoment.place: The Cuzco Highlands of Tawantinsuyu
finalMoment.scene:
It is morning in 1514, inside a home in the Cuzco Highlands. I have had a fever for 3 days. Since yesterday, my throat has burned whenever I swallow water. I was supposed to sort grain with my older sister today, but I cannot leave the bedding spread on the floor. Rumi brings water and sits beside me.

“Tell my sister I can't come today.” My voice is so faint that Rumi leans closer. “I told her yesterday, too.” My sister always remembered how I had promised to work during the day but left Mother's side to her at night. Once again, I have left my sister waiting today. I try to say more, but a dry cough comes first.

Rumi holds the cup near my lips. I lift myself and take a sip, but the water runs down my chin. Rumi lowers the cup and supports my back. I try to breathe in the cold air by the window, but my breath is short. “Tell our daughter, too,” I say. Rumi says he will go get her after she finishes her morning work at her own home. I start to tell him not to make her stop her work, but instead of speaking, I grasp Rumi's arm.

Rumi calls my older sister's name toward the outside. I hear his voice, but my ears cannot reach far enough to hear an answer. I try to breathe in again. My chest moves a little, but no air enters. Rumi calls my name. The strength leaves the hand gripping his arm.
finalMoment.afterword: Kiya died at home in 1514 after several days of fever and difficulty breathing. The name of her illness was not passed down. Rumi was beside her, and her older sister and daughter arrived later. Her sister sorted alone the grain they had planned to sort on the day Kiya could not come. Her daughter did not take back her request that Kiya ask before visiting. Even so, she remembered the years when her mother had asked which day she could come. The record of this past life does not describe Kiya only as a good teacher. It preserves her life as it was, including the work she shared and the burdens she left to others.
finalMoment.artAlt: Morning inside a Cuzco Highlands home in 1514: Kiya, age 63, lies on her bedding and reaches for a cup of water while Rumi sits beside her, supporting her back. Her daughter, older sister, and the grass rope are not visible
